1. 1865: The End of the Civil War

1In early spring 1865, General Robert E. Lee knew his tired Confederate army could do no more. He had said he would rather die a thousand deaths than surrender, but he saw no other way. On April 9, he rode in a fresh uniform to meet U.S. General Ulysses S. Grant. They met at a private home in Appomattox Court House, Virginia. Grant arrived half an hour later in an old uniform spattered with mud. The two generals talked in a friendly way, then worked to end the war. For decades before the war, divisions between North and South made many people doubt the nation would survive. Slavery was a major division, and the North was a land of growing industry and small farms.

2All Northern states had outlawed slavery by 1804. The South was a cotton society, and plantation owners used enslaved labor because it was the cheapest way to grow cotton. By the mid-1800s, nearly four million Black people worked for free under threat of death. Most lived on plantations in poor housing and endured cruel treatment, and families could be separated forever. Northern abolitionists denounced slavery, which raised the question of states' rights. The Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 required people in free states to return anyone who had escaped slavery. Some Northerners helped escapees instead, and some Northern juries refused to convict them. As the nation expanded west onto lands taken from Native peoples, the South wanted a balance of new slave states so it would not lose power in Congress.

3Those tensions broke in the election of November 1860, when Abraham Lincoln of the antislavery Republican Party became president. Seven states seceded: South Carolina, Mississippi, Florida, Alabama, Georgia, Louisiana, and Texas. In February 1861 they formed the Confederate States of America. On April 12, 1861, Confederate forces bombarded Fort Sumter in Charleston after its Union commander refused to surrender. Virginia, Arkansas, North Carolina, and Tennessee then joined the Confederacy. Most Southerners rejoiced, but no one knew how horrific the war would be. For two years the Union suffered under weak generals, until Antietam on September 17, 1862, forced Lee back to Virginia. That battle let Lincoln issue the Emancipation Proclamation, though General George B. McClellan failed to pursue Lee and was replaced by Ambrose Burnside.

4The Emancipation Proclamation freed enslaved people only in Confederate areas not yet under Union control. It let them fight for the North, and nearly 200,000 Black Americans fought for the Union. It also made the war a crusade against slavery, but an amendment was still needed to end slavery. Frederick Douglass said the proclamation liberated white people and Black people, yet it was only a first step. In December 1862, the Union lost at Fredericksburg, with more than 12,500 men killed, wounded, or missing. In July 1863, General George Meade won a decisive victory at Gettysburg. About 51,000 were casualties, as many as 28,000 of them Southern, and Lee never invaded the North again. In 1864, McClellan ran as a Democrat to stop the fighting, and Lincoln believed he would lose the election.

5Lincoln won reelection and a mandate to reunite the country and end slavery. In January 1865, Congress passed the Thirteenth Amendment, which ended slavery except as punishment for crime. Grant and Sherman, both professional and effective, sought to destroy the Confederacy quickly. After burning much of Atlanta, Sherman's men marched across Georgia, tearing up rail lines, destroying bridges, and burning many homes. At Cold Harbor in mid-1864, Grant's attack caused some seven thousand Union casualties in twenty minutes. Many in the North called him Grant the Butcher, yet he trapped Lee in trenches outside Petersburg. More than four hundred women disguised themselves as men to fight, and tens of thousands worked as laundresses, cooks, and nurses. Susan Baker King Taylor, born into slavery in Georgia in 1848, taught at fourteen and served as a laundress and nurse for Black Union soldiers.

6Before dawn on April 3, Lee abandoned Petersburg with the tattered remnants of his army. His men blew up their stores of gunpowder, and Union Private Jacob Haas felt a terrible shock of the earth. Union troops then took the town amid cheers. On April 6, Grant's army inflicted about eight thousand casualties, and Lee saw surrender as the only reasonable option. On April 9, Grant let Confederate soldiers return home, keep their horses and mules, and receive twenty-five thousand food rations. Other Confederate forces soon surrendered. Jefferson Davis fled Richmond on April 2, was captured on May 10, and spent two years in prison. Lee had refused Lincoln's offer to command the Union armies because he would not fight his state of Virginia, and his Arlington estate became Arlington National Cemetery.

7Abraham Lincoln sat for a photo in February 1865, two months before his death. On April 14, 1865, John Wilkes Booth shot Lincoln in the head at Ford's Theatre in Washington, D.C. Lincoln died early the next morning in a house across the street. Booth, an actor and Southern sympathizer, was part of a plot to kill Lincoln, Vice President Andrew Johnson, and Secretary of State William Seward. Only Lincoln was assassinated, though Seward received serious knife wounds. Union troops tracked Booth and David Herold to a Virginia farm, where Booth was shot and Herold was captured. Four conspirators, including Herold, were hanged, and Lincoln was buried in Springfield after saving the Union and living to see slavery's end. Harriet Tubman, born enslaved in Maryland, escaped at twenty-seven, guided many to freedom, and led a South Carolina raid that liberated more than seven hundred people.

8By December 6, 1865, enough states had ratified the Thirteenth Amendment to make it law. Within five years, the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments gave formerly enslaved people civil rights and voting rights. In 1870, Hiram Revels of Mississippi became the first Black American elected to the U.S. Senate. After Reconstruction ended in 1877, Southern states used Black codes and Jim Crow laws to enforce segregation and weaken Black voters. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965 secured rights those amendments intended. The war also established that the United States is indivisible and that states do not have the right to secede. South Carolina seceded first on December 20, 1860, and Tennessee seceded last on June 8, 1861. Americans remain divided in many ways, yet they remain one nation, and advocates still strive for equality under the law.

9An amendment is a change or addition to a law, such as the U.S. Constitution. To be assassinated is to be killed in a planned attack, often for political reasons. Casualties are people injured, killed, or missing in war. Confederate refers to the Southern states that separated during the Civil War. The Emancipation Proclamation was Lincoln's 1863 order freeing enslaved people under Confederate authority. A fugitive is a person running from the law, and indivisible means unable to be divided. Secession means a formal withdrawal, and to secede is to withdraw in that way. The Union was the group of states that fought the Confederacy.

2. A Look at Argentina

1A picture shows a gaucho riding his horse. The topics are where the country sits, its people, its land, its history, its celebrations, its food, and a closing word. A glossary follows. A map names the neighbors Paraguay, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, and Uruguay. Buenos Aires is marked. The Pacific Ocean and the Atlantic Ocean are labeled. North America, Africa, and South America appear on the wider view. Argentina is the second-biggest country in South America. In the whole world it ranks eighth. The area is 2,736,690 square kilometers. That is 1,056,642 square miles. The Andes Mountains stand on one side. No mountain chain on Earth is longer. The Atlantic Ocean stands on the other side. Five countries touch Argentina. Brazil touches it. So do Uruguay, Paraguay, Bolivia, and Chile. Twenty-three provinces make up the country. Each province has its own government. Each has its own laws. Each has its own constitution. National law still rules. Every province must follow those laws and answer to them.

2Buenos Aires is the capital. It is also the largest city. The name means fair winds, or good winds. More than fifteen million people live there. The city claims the widest street on Earth. People call that street Avenida 9 de Julio. In English that is July 9th Avenue. The date is the day Argentina became free of Spain. The city is among the biggest ports in South America. Banking is centered there. So is food processing. So is the automobile industry. Residents are known for being friendly. Many different groups of people live in this multicultural city. Its middle class is among the largest in Latin America. A great many residents like city life and what the city offers. Traditions carried by those residents make the streets look much like a city in Europe. An obelisk stands on Avenida 9 de Julio. It was built in 1936. It marks four hundred years since Buenos Aires began. Farming has a strong place in the country's past. Pictures show farmers gathering wheat and gathering grapes. Argentina's people number more than forty-three million. More than 90 percent of them live in the four biggest cities. In Latin America, this economy ranks third. Brazil is larger. Mexico is larger. Farming is a strength. The ground holds silver and gold. It also holds oil and natural gas. Goods sent abroad include wine and beef. Lemons go out too. So do grapes, peanuts, tea, and wheat. Service jobs employ most Argentines. Work also exists in cars, cloth, energy, communications, and appliances. Film work is another path. Dozens of motion pictures are made there every year.

3Roman Catholic faith is the country's official religion. Freedom of religion is still guaranteed. People also practice Muslim, Jewish, Protestant, and Mormon faiths. Argentina can be called a melting pot, as many countries can. Peoples from all over the world came together and formed a new nation. New immigrants have always been welcome. Today, most Argentines have roots in Europe. Spanish is the official language. Because those roots are European, some people also speak Italian. Some speak German, French, or English. Visitors see European buildings in Villa General Belgrano. Córdoba is the province that holds this district. The land is shaped like a long triangle. It holds mountains, deserts, and plains. It holds glaciers, huge lakes, and seashores. Five big regions make up this varied land. The Andes form a high wall between Chile and Argentina. The Pampas are a wide stretch of flat, fertile ground. Many crops grow there. Patagonia is the largest region. Oil and gas industries are based there. The region is known for ecotourism. The Littoral region lies in the north. It has jungles and swamps. Northwest of the other regions sits a lowland called the Gran Chaco. A land map marks Iguazú Falls, the Iguazú River, and the Paraná River. It also marks Mount Aconcagua, the Pampas, and the Andes. The Pacific Ocean and the Atlantic Ocean frame the drawing. Brazil and Paraguay meet Argentina at a place called the Triple Frontier. The Iguazú River and the Paraná River form that meeting. There the Iguazú River drops over falls shaped like a horseshoe. The falls stretch 2.7 kilometers, or 1.7 miles.

4Iguazú Falls stand taller than most waterfalls in the world. They also stand wider. Millions of years ago, a volcano erupted and split the ground with a huge crack. The falls formed from that crack. Native people of the region named them in their own language. The name means big water. People count these falls among seven natural wonders worldwide. Many habitats keep the country full of birds and mammals. Toucans live here. So do Andean condors, penguins, and pumas. Tapirs, howler monkeys, and jaguars live here too. The towering Andes run the whole length of western South America. They are one of Earth's great natural features. Length is about 7,242 kilometers. That is 4,500 miles. It crosses seven countries. Its highest peak is Mount Aconcagua. That peak is 6,962 meters tall, or 22,841 feet. No peak in the Americas stands higher. Argentina's history has been long. It has also been troubled. For thousands of years, native peoples have made this place home. A Spanish invasion in the 1500s was followed by disease and by war. Many native people died. Argentina declared itself free of Spain in 1816. Spanish rule was at last driven out. Founding of the Argentine Republic came in 1853. Buenos Aires became the official capital in 1880. A Golden Age is what some people call 1880 through 1914. Railroads spread. Sheep farming grew very important. Cattle ranching did too. New roads appeared. New buildings and parks appeared too. The Great Depression arrived in 1929. The economy struggled. Military dictators rose to power. Dictatorships lasted from 1929 until 1943. Then another military leader helped throw out the government. His name was Juan Perón. A painting shows the 1816 meeting that said Spain no longer ruled the land.

5Voters chose Juan Perón as president in 1946. His popularity grew as he brought in reforms. Health services were one reform. Retirement money for most Argentines was another. He and his wife, Eva, brought these gains to the working classes. He also ignored human rights. He behaved like a dictator. A second term in office brought a drop in that popularity. In 1955 he fled to Spain. A picture shows Juan and Eva Perón. He came back in 1973. He ran for president again. He won by a decisive margin. Death came the next year. The Peróns have critics. Even so, many Argentines today remember them as good leaders. They helped the working classes. They helped modernize the country. The decades after Perón brought more takeovers by the military. They also brought economic turmoil. Since 1983, democracy has held. The economy has grown. New jobs number in the millions. The past was rocky. The future still looks promising. Modern Argentina comes alive each year in its festivals. Carnival often falls in February or in March. People dress as clowns, as animals, and as cartoon characters. Huge, colorful floats roll down the street. Musicians play. Dancers move. Onlookers enjoy the day. Festivals also honor wheat, the tango, and gauchos. San Antonio de Areco hosts a popular gaucho festival. It happens every November. Gauchos show how well they ride. The party lasts ten days. Bronco riding is part of it. Parades and dancing are part of it too. Independence has a national day on July 9. Families and friends gather to honor what happened in 1816. Traditional food and parades mark the day. In earlier times, cattle herds moved across the Pampas with gauchos. Today the Argentine spirit is what these riders represent. They are proud of their horses. A saying compares a gaucho who lacks a horse to a person who lacks feet.

6Spanish immigrants brought their own tastes to the table. French immigrants did too. So did Italian immigrants. Foods from all three cultures are popular now. Meat is easy to get. Eating beef twice in one day is not unusual. Steak and other cuts are always on hand. They are often cooked on an open pit. A barbecue is another common way. Empanadas are served almost everywhere. They are tasty pastries. The filling may be meat, vegetables, cheese, or fruit. Italian dishes are popular as well. Ravioli is one. Pasta is another. Pizza is another. Besides food, Argentines drink a tea called yerba maté. The plant is called yerba maté. Its leaves are dried, then brewed into the drink. People say it gives them energy. They say it keeps the mind alert. A dance called the tango uses complicated steps. Those steps can tell of love. They can also tell of political unrest. Every August, people travel to Argentina from around the world. They come for a tango festival. In Buenos Aires, fountains stand before the buildings of the national government. Those buildings are in Buenos Aires. European roots have shaped the country in a solid way. It has much to offer. The land is beautiful. The population has grown to include people from China. It includes people from South Korea and from other Asian nations. Argentines are committed to democracy. They feel the country will keep prospering. The country looks ahead. It sets strict rules to protect the environment. Women are urged to join the work of government. Equal rights, for every person, are part of what it stands for. Political unrest filled much of the past. Citizens still hold great hope for the future. The rest of the world shares that hope.

7A facts box lists key numbers. The population is 43,646,358. The land is 2,736,690 square kilometers, or 1,056,642 square miles. The capital city is Buenos Aires. The primary language is Spanish. The primary religion is Roman Catholic. The primary exports are beef, wine, soybean meal, cars, and corn. The currency is called the Argentine peso. The source is the Central Intelligence Agency World Factbook from 2016. The word list gives plain meanings. Middle classes are groups who are neither rich nor poor and who earn an average income. Decisive means able to choose quickly and firmly, or ending in a clear way. A dictator is a ruler who holds all power. Force is the usual tool. Multicultural means including many different groups, each with its own ideas and customs. Diverse means different from one another, or made up of different people or things. Provinces are the largest areas into which some countries are divided. Ecotourism is travel to natural places to watch wildlife and to explore, without causing damage. Reforms are acts or processes that change things in order to improve them. Turmoil is a state of disorder, confusion, or agitation. A gaucho is a cowboy of the grassy plains of South America. Volcanic describes a spot in the crust of Earth. Gases, ash, and lava pour out there. Habitats are the natural homes of plants or of animals.

3. A Railroad Across the Continent

1This book follows one great building job, a railroad from the Atlantic side of the country to the Pacific. First it explains why the land journey west was so hard. Then it asks who could pay for the line and who would do the heavy work. Next it asks which company would lay rails faster. After that it asks how a path was cut through high mountains. Then it asks where the two crews finally joined their rails. A last look sums up what the finished line changed. Hard words are explained after that. A topic list closes the book. Until the 1860s, a land journey that began in New York City and ended in San Francisco might last half a year. During those months, travelers had to bring all the food they would eat. Hunting and gathering along the way was the other choice. People went hungry. They also went thirsty. Storms and heat made the trip harsher. Sickness spread. Wild animals were a threat. Maps of the region were scarce, so a wrong turn was easy. The western paths crossed country already lived in by Indigenous peoples. Outsiders had treated those peoples badly many times. Trust had worn away. Settlers still poured toward California, thousands of them each year. Farmland there was rich. The climate was wonderful. Gold was a further lure. A belief called Manifest Destiny shaped many of these travelers. It claimed that God meant the United States to grow. Democracy was supposed to spread with that growth over all of North America. Capitalism was supposed to spread too. People already living on the land paid the price. The land itself paid a price as well. Through the 1800s, settlers hunted for a western journey that would bring less danger. Speed mattered to them just as much.

2Rail travel was the quickest option then. Eastern lines already ran in a crisscross pattern. Chicago, Illinois, was as far west as some of them went. Omaha, Nebraska, was another western end. Average speed was 25 miles an hour, which is 40 kilometers an hour. One unbroken line to the Pacific would cut the time settlers needed to reach California. People settled in the West could also return east sooner. Goods would be simpler to order. Mail would move both ways with less delay. Family members unseen for years could be visited again. Business in California was booming. A rail link would join that boom to eastern companies. It would join California to the eastern government too. The East would share in the western boom. Gains would not stop at the two coasts. Communities would grow beside the route. Men made up most of each new town. Women arrived with them. A stubborn problem remained. Who could pay for, and actually build, a line across so much rough western country? One photograph shows people posing beside a train in a crowded eastern station. A coast-to-coast railroad had been wished for over many years. Several barriers stopped it. The price was too high for one person. It was too high for one company. The machines and methods of the day also looked too weak for the job. No calculators helped the engineers. Computers did not exist for them. Airplanes were not available to survey the ground. War made planning even harder. Northern states and Southern states were already fighting the Civil War. While they fought, they could not agree on a railroad. Owners tried to hold down wages by hiring immigrant laborers. Some came from China. Others came from Ireland. Many Black workers were hired too. Pay for all of them was low. The chosen route followed the 41st parallel. The Mason-Dixon line lay farther south. In the Civil War, soldiers often tore up rail lines. They also put lines back together.

3A map dated 1862 shows the United States, with Oregon, Sacramento, Omaha, and California labeled. Northern states, territories, Southern states, and disputed areas are marked. So is the Mason-Dixon line. The wide yellow region of land that was not yet states had no rail lines. California therefore stood apart from the rest of the country. Oregon did too. Congress acted in July 1862 by passing the Pacific Railroad Act. The law required a railroad spanning the continent. A telegraph had to run with it. Both were to stretch from the Missouri River out to the Pacific Ocean. Track laying toward the east was assigned to the Central Pacific, starting at Sacramento, California. Track laying toward the west was assigned to the Union Pacific, starting at Omaha, Nebraska. Each company received enormous grants of land beside the planned line. The Cheyenne held that land. So did the Sioux. So did the Arapaho. Treaties with those tribes were broken by the U.S. government. Soldiers used violence to force people off the ground. Sale of the land then raised cash for the railroad. The same act required that government use of the rails be protected. Government use of the telegraph had to be protected as well. Thomas Durant was the Union Pacific owner. Four men owned the Central Pacific. They were Mark Hopkins and Charles Crocker. Leland Stanford was one of them. Collis Huntington was the fourth. A portrait groups Durant with those four. The heaviest labor fell largely to immigrants. Competition was built into the plan so the line would grow fast. More track meant more government money. Durant was a businessman, and he also had a medical degree. The four Central Pacific partners had made their money in the gold rush. Their crews started in January 1863, just beyond Sacramento. Accidents and natural disasters killed hundreds during the work. Many of the dead were never counted. Construction did not stop.

4Who would win the race to lay more track? The Civil War and money trouble kept the Union Pacific from starting for two years. The war was taking the iron, the gunpowder, and the workers the railroad needed. Work began soon after the war ended in 1865. By 1866, the Union Pacific looked sure to win. Irish immigrants laid track quickly across the Nebraska prairie west of Omaha. Getting ready to lay track was a careful job. First, survey crews studied the land. They drove stakes to mark the exact line. Second, graders went out. They cleared plants, filled low spots, and dug a flat, smooth bed. On the level plains, graders often had little to do. Last came the tracklayers. Most of these crews were Chinese immigrants.

5An illustration from the 1860s shows crews, many of them immigrants, building across Nebraska. Behind them a supply train already rolls on fresh rails. That train was storage. It was also a place to live. The first train to follow the new line came right after the work gangs. Steam drove its locomotive. Wood for the job rode on board. Rails, spikes, tools, and ballast rode there too. Some cars held bunks. One held a kitchen and stored food. Repair shops filled other cars. Clothing and similar goods were carried as well. The whole train worked like a town that crept forward and built the road under its own wheels. Most of its people had immigrated from Ireland, from Germany, or from the Netherlands. Veterans of the Civil War rode with them. Black people who had once been enslaved were part of the crew. Papers painted these Union Pacific men as tough and proud. All week they were said to work diligently. Sunday was free, and they gambled. Prairie miles fell behind them at a startling pace. The Rocky Mountains came into reach quickly. For Plains peoples the new rails meant their old life kept collapsing. The railroad devastated the Sioux. It devastated the Arapaho and the Cheyenne. The herds they needed were American bison. Another name for that animal is buffalo. Herds could not cross the rails on their old migrations. Officials urged settlers to slaughter bison by the thousands. Extinction nearly followed. Plains communities could not live without the herds. Disease took huge numbers of people. Hunger took more. Conflict that followed the killing took still more. A picture shows settlers shooting bison until almost none remained.

6Settlers flooded in behind the rails. Wherever a crew paused, a town appeared. Some towns vanished as soon as the work moved on. Others lasted and became major cities. Reno, in Nevada, was one. Cheyenne, in Wyoming, was another. Broken treaties had already handed Sioux, Cheyenne, and Arapaho land to the railroad companies. Those companies sold it onward to settlers. Farms started. Houses went up. Trains left litter behind them. They made noise. They dirtied the air. Engines burned wood or coal, and their sparks started prairie fires. Indigenous fighters resisted the illegal seizure of their country. Before a railroad posse could form, the fighters were gone. Supplies were taken. Livestock was taken. Some railroad workers were killed. Army protection was what the Union Pacific demanded, both for crews and for the line. General Ulysses S. Grant answered by sending many soldiers to ride beside the surveyors. General William Tecumseh Sherman gave the same order. Skirmishes with Indigenous people followed again and again. Marksmen hired by railroad officials guarded certain stretches. One picture shows the line being forced through the rugged Sierra Nevada. Far to the west, the Central Pacific crawled. Its first task was a roadbed in steep, snowy Sierra Nevada rock. The path crossed California's Donner Pass, a place with an infamous story. Pioneers stranded there in the fierce winter of 1846 starved. Locomotives of that era could not mount a sharp slope. Tight curves were impossible for them too. Jagged peaks had to be reshaped into a smooth trail with only a gentle rise.

7Workers cut solid granite back from the mountain sides. They filled gorges and ravines with rock and soil. Each load moved by wheelbarrow. The work was slow and painful. Very few people wanted to do it. Most settlers from Europe had come to California to seek gold. Some took railroad jobs. Almost every Central Pacific hire quit within a week and went looking for riches elsewhere. The company was unwilling at first. Then it tried about fifty Chinese workers. Many Chinese people hoped America would make them rich, much like other newcomers. A great number were drawn to California by the Jinshan, said jeenshahn, the Mountain of Gold. A picture shows Chinese workers loading ballast under a track. They faced racism in many places. Some bosses stole their pay. Housing was refused because of who they were. Still, they lasted longer on the jobs than the other workers.

8One picture catches loose gunpowder as it blows a piece of mountain apart. Fifteen tunnels through solid rock were required before rails could cross the Sierra Nevada. Hand drills did the boring. Sledgehammers drove them. Loose gunpowder split the stone. No other tools were used. Winter buried the peaks in forty-four separate snowstorms. Under snow that averaged 18 feet, or 5.5 meters, the men dug tunnels. They also dug rooms for sleep and for work. These were grading crews only. Track had not arrived, so no train could haul freight up to them. Ox wagons carried the loads up the slope. Hands carried what the wagons could not. Cape Horn was their most famous job, a cliff so huge they gave it that name. Stories of the work describe a method brought from China. It was old, and it was dangerous. Reed was woven into baskets that could carry two people. From the cliff top, crews lowered those baskets. Men inside drilled holes in the rock face. Black powder filled each hole. A fuse was lit. A shout warned the team above. Baskets were yanked upward at full speed. The hope was that every person would clear the blast in time. Another picture shows a tunnel being cut by Chinese workers in a wall of rock.

9Success and disaster arrived together. Hands were crushed in accidents. Feet were crushed. Whole bodies were crushed. Cold killed many by freezing. Avalanches buried whole parties alive, and some bodies stayed hidden until spring. At Strong's Canyon one slide erased an entire camp, crews and buildings together. The Central Pacific never recorded how many Chinese laborers died on the transcontinental job. One estimate puts the number near 1,200. A winter picture shows crews fighting mountain cold. The year 1867 finally brought the line out of the peaks. Utah's dry deserts waited beyond the peaks. That was the Central Pacific's next ground. A record fell on April 28, 1868. Crews laid 10 miles in a single day, equal to 16 kilometers. Charles Crocker said the men looked like an army crossing the land, with finished track appearing behind the march. Where would the rivals meet? Rocky Mountain country was far kinder to the Union Pacific than the Sierra Nevada had been to the Central Pacific. The older Oregon Trail led them along Nebraska's Platte Valley. The grade stayed gentle. South Pass, in Wyoming, carried them over the Rockies. Utah's deserts came soon after. During 1869 the two fronts drew close. The join was set at Promontory Point in Utah. The Great Salt Lake lay south of that spot. Brigham Young, who had governed the territory, was dismayed. He had wanted the rails to bend south and pass through Salt Lake City. Tourists in one picture stand by a locomotive and cars built before the 1930s, parked on a historic mountain line. The celebration day was May 10, 1869. Workers, owners, journalists, and politicians all came to Promontory Point. Racing was finished. Union Pacific rails measured 1,086 miles, or 1,748 kilometers. Central Pacific rails measured 689 miles, or 1,109 kilometers. Extra pay went to the Central Pacific because its route had crossed the Sierra Nevada.

10Chinese workers fill one picture, a reminder of how large their role was. For the ceremony, leaders of both companies were to hammer the final four spikes. Gold and silver made those four. Mines in California supplied some of the metal. Mines in Nevada and Arizona supplied the rest. Long inscriptions covered the spikes. A special hammer was required for a light ceremonial tap. Ordinary spikes went in after that show. Crews from each company dragged the final rails into line. Leland Stanford, leading the Central Pacific, lifted a sledgehammer. Thomas Durant, leading the Union Pacific, lifted one too. Each man swung and missed. Cheers came from the crowd all the same. The coast-to-coast railroad now existed. A route map uses red for the Central Pacific, which built from the west toward the east. Blue marks the Union Pacific, which built from the east toward the west. Labels include Promontory Point, Wyoming, Nebraska, Omaha, Nevada, Utah, Colorado, Sacramento, and California. Years of danger and labor had changed distance itself. New York to California was now a trip of only a few days. More lines reached Salt Lake City. Others reached Oregon Territory and the Southwest. Towns kept forming beside the rails once goods and mail moved so freely. Millions of dollars went to the Union Pacific and the Central Pacific. The money came from land sales. Along the route, that land had been taken from Indigenous peoples. Laborers got no added payment later. Families of the dead received none either. Even so, east and west were tied together by rail for the first time.

11The harder words in this book can be read this way. If someone works diligently, that person shows care, determination, and attention to small details. Discrimination is unfair treatment aimed at a person or a group over gender, race, age, religion, or some other difference. An engineer designs, builds, or repairs machines, buildings, bridges, and similar structures. An immigrant is a person who arrives to live in another country, often to settle for good. Indigenous refers to the earliest peoples of a place, or to what belongs to them. A person or event called infamous is famous because of evil, harm, or danger. A laborer earns pay by physical work. To have portrayed someone is to have described or shown that person in one particular way. Racism is unequal treatment that rests on a belief that one race outranks another. A settler makes a lasting new home in a place that was not originally home. A telegraph sends written messages as simple electric signals moving through wires. A veteran is someone who has served in the armed forces. Readers of this book will meet these topics: the Arapaho, avalanches, and a booming economy. Also the Cheyenne, China, and Chinese workers. Also the Civil War, Charles Crocker, deserts, and Donner Pass. Also Thomas Durant, gaugers, government, and graders. Also Ulysses S. Grant, Mark Hopkins, and Collis Huntington. Also locomotives, Manifest Destiny, and the Mason-Dixon line. Also the military, mountains, mail, and the prairie. Also Promontory Point, William Tecumseh Sherman, and the Sioux. Also sledgehammers, Leland Stanford, technology, and transport.

4. A Tiny Life That Feeds the Sea

1A speaker too small to see opens this book. Later pages trace who eats whom, then walk from bright water into dim water and finally into black water. The last story climbs back up. A word list finishes the book. Residents of the sea, and plenty of land animals too, treat the ocean as one huge table of food. Think of a great white shark, fierce, taking prey. Think of a blue whale, the largest animal on Earth, swallowing tons of krill. Think of seaweed in giant stands, grazed the way a salad bar is grazed underwater. A quieter fact sits under those pictures. In the end, some other sea animal eats more than 90 percent of sea animals. The voice here belongs to the little organisms that nearly always get eaten. They themselves eat nothing. No ocean species is more microscopic. The wide, complicated food web still has them at its middle.

2These phytoplankton include forms called diatoms, and a picture shows how small they are. Call the speaker phytoplankton. It is an alga, close to a plant, only far smaller. Plants grow roots. This life does not. It is not fastened to the sea floor or to any ground. Every ocean on Earth carries it in currents close to the surface, where it basks. Sunlight is not optional. Without that light it cannot live. Photosynthesis is the name of the food-making process. Chlorophyll, which is green, grabs the Sun's energy. Nutrients drawn from seawater are changed into food. Oxygen leaves as a byproduct and enters both water and air. Another picture shows that green substance inside plant cells, taking the light those cells need for the change. Billions upon billions must gather before the green can be seen, because each cell is so small. Luckily for everyone else, gatherings of that size are common. Thousands can sit in one cup of seawater. Put together, this photosynthesis gives the atmosphere well over half the oxygen Earth has.

3From space, light streaks mark a bloom where phytoplankton and zooplankton crowd together. How many of them live in a place also tells scientists whether the ocean is healthy. Algal blooms are the large green patches visible from orbit. How often those patches show up, and how far they spread, is a clue to pollution levels. Other sea creatures need those healthy numbers. Directly or indirectly, this life feeds every marine form, the largest and the smallest alike. The whole ocean's food web turns on that center. Picture a simple sandwich made with tuna. Tuna count as relatively large fish. Mackerel, a smaller fish, is what they eat. Flesh weighing 1 kilogram, or 2.2 pounds, costs the tuna about 10 kilograms of mackerel, or 22 pounds. Herring, smaller still, supplied those mackerel. The herring total was 100 kilograms, or 220 pounds. Zooplankton amounting to 1,000 kilograms, or 2,200 pounds, fed that herring. Microscopic animals make up the zooplankton. Some are krill, shrimp-like and tiny. Others are larvae, the young of jellyfish, crabs, shrimp, and further fish. Phytoplankton weighing 10,000 kilograms, or 22,000 pounds, had already fed that zooplankton. Read the links in order. Phytoplankton feed zooplankton. Zooplankton feed herring. Herring feed mackerel. Mackerel feed tuna.

4Zones of the ocean appear in a cross-section picture. A short tour can show how much life hangs on this speaker. It begins in surface water and ends in the trenches, the deepest cuts in the sea floor. Otters, one picture notes, both live and feed where sunlight still reaches. That top layer is called the euphotic zone, or the sunlit zone. From the surface it extends downward about 200 meters, a depth of 660 feet. Plants of the ocean, and phytoplankton, find the strong light ideal. Animal species mostly live here as a result. Shallow floor is often covered by seaweed, some of it green and some of it red. Giant kelp grows in thick forests and shelters many animals. Sea urchins are among them. Otters eat the urchins. At rest, an otter wraps kelp in long strands about its body. The wrap keeps sleep from turning into a drift.

5Seafood on human plates comes, nearly all of it, from the euphotic zone. Oysters, mussels, and clams occupy shallow floors. Crabs and lobsters move through seaweed beds and through coral reefs. Hunting light is good here, and food is plentiful, so most fish species stay. Swordfish are here. So are cod, mackerel, tuna, and salmon. People also eat squid and octopuses that mostly reside in this same water. A hammerhead shark in one picture is a familiar fish of the zone. Reefs of colorful coral are the places visitors like best. Plant and animal species of the ocean are concentrated there more than anywhere else. Clear tropical water with plenty of sun is where small animals called coral polyps live. Their skeletons pile up and form the reef. The community includes lobsters and crabs, plus shellfish and sharks. Lion fish are there, and angelfish, and clown fish. Brain coral and sea fans are there. Moray eels are there. Anemones look like flowers in bloom, yet they are animals. Zooplankton is caught on tentacles that sting. Huge swarms of jellyfish draw sea turtles, which are eager to eat them. Young animals shelter on the reef, then move into the open ocean when they grow up.

6Biodiversity this rich pulls in tourists and people who love the outdoors. Snorkeling and diving are favorites, above all around coral. Thousands of tons of fish also leave these surface waters. Some become food. Some become pets in aquariums of the tropics. Pollution joins that human pressure. Reefs and other parts of the zone are at risk. A polyp can be killed by dirty water. An engine can break it. A diver's step can crush it. After the coral is gone, every other reef animal suffers. Sea life here can feel the damage at once, and the damage can be devastating. The coast feels it too. During a severe storm, reefs act as shields and slow the erosion of the shoreline. That value makes care and protection urgent. Can a damaged food web be repaired? Delaware's Red Bird Reef says yes. The unlikely material is retired subway cars. Beginning in 2001, barges carried hundreds of those cars, emptied and cleaned, out of New York City. They were dropped on empty Atlantic floor off the Delaware coast. Life soon thrived on the metal. Grasses of the sea covered floors and walls. Sponges and mussels held to the sides. Fish passed in and out through the windows. Fishermen, both for sport and for sale, now treat the spot as a hot spot. Harm also falls if explorers stay gentler. Looking into a tide pool samples this zone without a destructive visit. When the tide goes out, leftover pools can hold snails and barnacles. Clams, urchins, and sea stars may be there. Mussels may be there. A hermit crab may hurry past in a shell it did not grow. An octopus may show up. You can watch all of this and stay dry. Every one of these lives leans on phytoplankton, whether the link is direct or runs through other eaters.

7Leave the euphotic zone and the water changes. Darkness increases. Cold increases. The water feels heavier. Twilight begins near 200 meters down, which is 656 feet. Another name is the disphotic zone. It reaches about 1,000 meters, or 3,280 feet. A person would be crushed by the pressure. Residents have adapted instead. Plants cannot live here, and photosynthesis cannot run. The light is too weak. Squid and octopus still keep homes in this band. Whales come down on visits from brighter water. Fish that stay all the time look unlike the fish above. Dark red or black helps them vanish into the gloom. Each species has adaptations suited to chill and dimness. One predator, the viperfish, is a frightening sight. Curved teeth, large ones, rim a mouth that gapes. Active chasing is pointless when almost nothing can be seen. The mouth waits open for a swimmer to come close enough. Hatchet fish stay small. Their bodies are thin and strangely shaped, and silvery scales cover them. Shine on those scales matches the weak light falling from higher water. Counterillumination is the name of that trick. A bigger hunter looking upward struggles to pick them out. Bodies that are nearly transparent hide other animals just as well. Giant squid, famous and seldom seen, also keep to this zone. Undersea canyons are their neighborhood. Living ones went unseen until fairly recent years. Now and then a body washed up. Now and then a sperm whale's stomach held the remains. A research ship working the Gulf of Mexico in 2009 caught one in a trailing net. The squid weighed 47 kilograms, equal to 103 pounds. Depth at the net was 457 meters, or 1,500 feet. Biology and daily habits of this mystery animal may become clearer because of that catch. One picture shows an angler fish, small and still scary. Another notes that octopuses belong to both zones, the bright one and this dimmer one.

8Phytoplankton still end up as food down here, unlikely as that sounds. Scientists use a soft name, marine snow, for the diet. What falls is dead. It is phytoplankton that have died, and zooplankton that have died. The bodies sink in a slow drift, layer after layer, like snow crossing air on the way to the bottom. Being eaten does not require living in that deep place. In the black water, tiny animals glow with their own light.

9Midnight water has no sunlight at all. Depth runs from 1,000 meters down through 5,000 meters, and farther still. In feet, that span is 3,280 to 16,404. Water here is 90 percent of the ocean. Life is almost absent. Most submarines would be crushed. Nearly anything else would be crushed too. The cold sits close to freezing. Look carefully and life still appears. Aphotic zone is the other name. Lantern fish, and many other tiny animals, wear small lights along the body. Fireflies shine by the same process. It is called bioluminescence. Bacteria can carry this light. Fish, squid, and jellyfish can carry it too. Without the Sun, the glow lets animals see. It lets them signal. Mates can be found. Food can be found. The deep-sea angler fish is a famous neighbor, and the name suits it. Females grow a stalk from the top of the head. Bacteria that glow cover the tip, bright like a bulb. Prey comes close, drawn as if the stalk were a fishing pole, and the jaws wait. Hot minerals pour from a chimney in one picture. That chimney is a black smoker. Crabs use the warmth and the nutrients. Tube worms use them. Other animals use them too. Oceanographers sometimes cut this dark region into two further zones. Trenches are one. The abyssal zone is the other. Darkness there is complete. Much of the floor lies in it: canyons, valleys, mountains, and wide plains. Faults are where trenches open. Great plates in Earth's crust collide along those cracks. Canyons and splits can reach 10,000 meters, or 32,808 feet. Cold is severe. Blackness is total. Pressure is huge. Nothing, you would think, could live there. Hot water and minerals still jet from openings in the trench floor. They rise from deep in the Earth. The warmth is enough to sustain life.

10Hot magma meets seawater, and the openings take shape. Warmth and nutrients from those openings are used by the animals much as sunlight is used up above. Chimneys is another word for the openings. Bacteria around them feed giant clams. They feed shrimp and tube worms. The year 1977 was the first time scientists found these hydrothermal vents. The place was the ocean floor beside the Galapagos Islands. A trench bottom has enormous pressure. Few submersibles, small submarines, are strong enough to bear it. One picture shows a craft built for exactly that. Back at the surface, the point is clear. Home for phytoplankton is only the top of the sea. The food web still has them in the middle, holding up every other life in the water. Size is microscopic. Impact is not. Ocean meals depend on them. Human meals depend on them. Maybe you come for reefs. Maybe you come for the dark unknown of the abyss. Maybe you come for fish and chips. Thank phytoplankton either way.

11Words in this book can be read as follows. Within the aphotic zone, the deep floor is the abyssal zone. An accumulation is a pile that builds as time goes on. An anemone is a sea animal with a plantlike form, and the tentacles often mimic petals. No sunlight enters the aphotic zone, the lowest band of the ocean. Biodiversity means how many kinds of life share Earth, or share one habitat or ecosystem. When a living body makes light by a biochemical process, that light is bioluminescence. Plant cells hold a green substance called chlorophyll. During photosynthesis it absorbs the light energy used to make food. Counterillumination hides an animal by matching a lit background with light of its own. A demise is a death, a failure, or an ending. Damage that is devastating is great and physical. Little sunlight reaches the disphotic zone, the ocean's middle band. Plants do not live there, and animals are scarce. Almost all ocean life sits in the euphotic zone, the top band. A fault is a crack in the crust of Earth, and the crust moves along it. In photosynthesis, plant cells absorb sunlight and spend that energy changing carbon dioxide and water into food. A phytoplankton is an alga of one cell, living in water. A submersible is a small craft able to work underwater, above all at great depth.

5. A Wall Through the Middle of Berlin

1A map places Berlin inside Germany. Around it sit Europe, the Atlantic Ocean, Denmark, Africa, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, Poland, Belgium, Czechia, France, Austria, Switzerland, and Italy. Seven sections shape this account. They cover a hated wall, the Cold War, the rise of the barrier, life in a split city, ways past the wall, the wall's fall, and a word list. In 1987, in front of West Berlin's Brandenburg Gate, President Ronald Reagan delivers the speech in which he demands that the wall be torn down. A wall people hated. June 12, 1987, brought a memorable address from United States President Ronald Reagan, given in West Berlin, Germany. Behind him stood the Brandenburg Gate, famous in that city. That barrier was the Berlin Wall, already infamous. Few symbols of the Cold War were more visible, or more detested. That struggle set a communist East against a democratic West. Some of Reagan's words were aimed at Mikhail Gorbachev, leader of the Soviet Union. Reagan's voice rose. He told Gorbachev to pull the wall down. Gorbachev was absent and offered no answer. The wall stayed up. Anyone there that day could imagine it standing forever. A portrait shows Mikhail Gorbachev.

2The Cold War. From 1939 to 1945, during World War II, the United States kept an uneasy tie with the Soviet Union. France and Great Britain shared the unease. They still joined forces to beat the Axis, a coalition joining Japan, Italy, and Germany. Once Germany surrendered in May 1945, the partnership began to break. The Soviet Union tightened its hold on Eastern Europe, lands its troops had occupied while chasing the German army in retreat. Those controlled nations became the Eastern Bloc. East Germany belonged to that region, and Berlin sat entirely inside Soviet territory. Once Nazi Germany was beaten, the victors split Berlin into four sectors. One victor would govern each sector: the Soviet Union, the United States, Great Britain, or France. The city's eastern sector was the Soviet share. A map of the split city shows the wall and the zones of France, the Soviet Union, Great Britain, and the United States, labeled West and East. Four nations controlled Berlin once World War II had ended. Late in the 1940s, distrust between Moscow and the nations of the West had deepened. The Soviet Union was committed to communism and wanted that ideology to spread. Democracies included the United States and Western Europe's nations, and they opposed communism strongly. During 1947, a policy called the Truman Doctrine was adopted in the United States. President Harry S. Truman gave it his name. It promised aid to any nation threatened by Soviet expansion. Because the two ideologies differed completely, hostility settled into a stalemate. People called that stalemate the Cold War. Full control of Berlin was the Soviet aim. In June 1948 the Soviets tried to get it by cutting every road into the city's western parts. An answer came from Great Britain and from the United States with the Berlin airlift. A picture shows a ragged group of Berliners among ruins while a cargo plane brings food during that airlift.

3Portraits show President John F. Kennedy and Soviet Premier Nikita Khrushchev. Food, fuel, and other necessities flew into the city around the clock. Western powers had shown they would stand for West Berlin's freedom, so in May 1949 the Soviets lifted the blockade. The airlift no longer had to continue. That first Berlin crisis was settled, yet the city stayed tense. Through the 1950s and into the 1960s, Berlin remained a headache for both East and West. Washington feared the standoff could become an armed clash, and that clash could become a full war. Soviet Premier Nikita Khrushchev, on November 10, 1958, demanded in a speech that France, Britain, and the United States quit West Berlin. Talks linking Moscow with the United States produced no progress. Berlin was a crisis nobody seemed able to defuse. The barrier rises. Another trouble pressed the Soviet Union and East Germany's government. East Germany was losing people in crowds. Many Germans in East Berlin, and in the rest of East Germany, rejected communist rule. Basic rights were missing, including the vote and freedom of speech. Wages were low, supplies were thin, and prices were high. Thousands moved to West Germany through West Berlin, which worked as an escape hatch. The border between the two Germanys was sealed tight, but Berlin itself stayed an open city. A person in the East could ride a streetcar, or hire a taxi into West Berlin, then board a plane for a West German city. Many who left were young and well educated, so the outflow threatened East Germany's economy. Some 2.5 million people, by 1961, had relocated west. East Germany's population fell by about 15 percent. Soviet leaders and East German leaders decided something had to be done. Their 1961 answer was an impenetrable wall built around West Berlin.

4Bricklayers from the East German side are shown raising the wall, a barrier meant to stop refugees from reaching West Berlin. Construction started without warning on August 13, 1961, a day later called Barbed Wire Sunday. Concrete blocks and barbed wire made the first wall. Later, concrete slabs replaced them. Those slabs rose as high as 4.5 meters, or 15 feet, with barbed wire on top, and with watchtowers and gun posts as guards. In the end there were two walls. The outer one faced West Berlin. An inner wall stood behind it. Open ground between them was about 143 meters wide, or 469 feet. People named that ground the death strip, because crossers were often shot. Through Berlin the wall ran about 45 kilometers, or 28 miles, then another 120 kilometers, or 75 miles, beyond the city, ringing it completely. Guards had orders to fire on any person who tried an escape. A picture shows cars passing the crossing called Checkpoint Charlie, headed into West Berlin. The scene is ten days after laws on crossing the border were eased. East Germany's government denied that the wall was built to stop emigration. It claimed the wall kept opponents of communism from entering and undermining the state. Walter Ulbricht, an East German leader, said they had closed every crack running through the fabric of their house and closed the holes where the German people's worst enemies might creep. With the wall up, West Berliners could enter the eastern sector only at several checkpoints. Those gates mainly served diplomats and military personnel. Fame belonged most of all to Checkpoint Charlie. Tourists had that gate as their only portal.

5Many people asked why Western allies of the United States did not stop the building. The truth was different. President Kennedy and the other Western leaders were not unhappy to see the wall rise. They had feared violence breaking out inside Berlin, or a fresh attempt to cut West Berlin off, as in the late 1940s. Nikita Khrushchev, the Soviet leader, had threatened a fresh blockade if Western forces refused to leave. When the building started, Kennedy felt relief. The wall, he said, was not a fine answer for Berlin, but it beat a war. He declared the Berlin crisis finished. A picture shows East German troops guarding the wall, with West Berlin marked on one side and East Berlin on the other. Life in a split city. Once the wall was a settled part of the landscape, people living on either side accepted it. What other choice was there? The division was inconvenient. Streets were cut. Public squares were cut. Certain districts saw the barrier run down the middle of a street or along a row of houses. West Berliners showed contempt by covering the wall's length in colorful graffiti. Daily life in West Berlin changed little. People were free to follow whatever interested them. At last they were free of the risk of a military clash. A vibrant society grew. Lights and neon blazed. Shops, restaurants, and department stores offered what a modern city offers its people. Arts thrived. Theater and music flourished, and the music embraced the youth movement of the 1960s.

6As time passed, West Berliners developed what they called a mentality like an island. In their own eyes they were an isolated bastion of freedom and of Western values, surrounded by a dark sea of communism. East Berlin was dark in a literal way. Streets were poorly lit, with no neon and no billboards. State department stores stocked only a sparse range of goods. Jobs, when they existed, were limited. Worse, secret police were everywhere. They were called the Stasi. About a hundred thousand employees worked for them, plus informers who may have reached two million, hunting people labeled enemies of the state, both inside East Berlin and across the rest of that state. Colleagues, neighbors, and friends were pushed to report on one another. Files covered citizens of East Germany numbering about five million, roughly a third of the population. Life in East Berlin, and in the rest of East Germany, grew repressive and often dangerous. Escape became a desperate wish for many. A picture shows East German police watching a photographer in West Berlin while the wall goes up. Near the Brandenburg Gate, a hole in the fence let 150 people flee west. Getting past the wall. Across the wall's lifetime, East Berliners numbering about ten thousand made attempts to reach the West. About half succeeded, and that half included some six hundred border guards. Of the other five thousand, nearly all were captured and arrested. Sentries killed approximately two hundred, or fatal accidents did. Some estimates put the dead closer to seven hundred. Methods varied. In the first days, people jumped from windows or from roofs of buildings close to the wall. Falls killed some of them. Further attempts used hot-air balloons, or sewer pipes, or cars driven at weaker stretches. Some intrepid people simply clawed at the barbed wire and tried to climb over.

7Once watchtowers and gun posts made the wall a formidable barrier, some East Berliners tunneled. They dug with painful care, across spans that reached 190 meters, or 600 feet. Many tunnels failed. Some collapsed. Some flooded. Before anyone could use them, guards posted on the border, or else the secret police, discovered the rest. About three hundred people still escaped through tunnels. Arrest for an escape attempt could mean three years in prison, and prisoners could face hard labor or torture. People who fled, and political prisoners besides them, also turned into a lucrative source of money for East Germany's government. Ransoms from West Germany, running from 1964 to 1989, covered political prisoners numbering nearly 34,000, along with 250,000 members of their families. The sums brought in German marks amounting to some 3.5 billion. That was nearly 1 billion dollars in the dollars of 1965, or close to 8 billion dollars now. Those who were ransomed could leave with nothing but their clothes. In West Germany they gained something far more precious: freedom. The wall falls. Late in the 1980s, Eastern Europe slipped from weakened Soviet control. Nation by nation, the Eastern Bloc announced freedom from domination by communists, and the Soviet Union could not stop them. The Cold War was ending at last. On November 9, 1989, a spokesman for East Germany's Communist Party announced that city residents could now pass into the western half. His intention had been an orderly change, with long paperwork. Jubilant Berliners on both sides ignored him. Thousands flocked to the wall in celebration. Many passed the checkpoints. Others climbed up with hammers and picks and knocked chunks from the barricade. People called them wall woodpeckers. Across that weekend, East Berliners numbering some two million poured into West Berlin for a joyous party. A journalist on the scene called it a street party larger than any the world had seen. One picture shows a wall woodpecker at work.

8In November 1989, thousands of Germans from east and west celebrate the Cold War's end along that barrier, on the East Berlin side of Germany. Months passed while the wall came down. Woodpeckers kept up their small demolitions. East Germany's government brought cranes and bulldozers to tear out large sections. Germany's reunification date was October 3, 1990. East Germany and West Germany were no longer separate. One nation stood again, under a democratic government. The capital moved back to Berlin. It had not sat there since 1945. Even more astonishing was the end of the Soviet Union itself. On December 8, 1991, that union was formally dissolved. A body under the name Commonwealth of Independent States replaced it, made of Russia plus several republics that had been Soviet. Truly, the Cold War was finished. Germany was unified again, yet growing pains came with integrating the sectors of east and west. Communism had been the life of two generations, who knew little of democracy or of life in the West. In time the country became whole. Today the country is a powerful European force and holds the continent's biggest economy of all. The wall that once split Germany ended by strengthening it and binding it together. Where pieces of the wall rest. The barrier was broken into many pieces. Most of the material was ground up and used in German highway building. Many chunks passed into private hands. Others were sold in Berlin souvenir shops or by sellers working online. In 2013 a large slab brought 23,500 dollars when Atlanta, Georgia, auctioned it. One piece stands inside a Rome garden belonging to the Vatican. Maybe the oddest home for a section is a men's restroom in one casino of Las Vegas. The biggest piece still intact is Berlin's East Side Gallery, 1.3 kilometers long, or 0.8 miles. Other fragments around the city remind people of a troubled past. A section is also on display inside New York City, at the United Nations.

9Words from the book A bastion is a place or a situation where certain ideas or practices survive and thrive. Demolitions are acts that destroy something completely, often with explosives. A blockade is any obstacle meant to stop passage through an area. Dissolved, a verb, means brought to an end. Communist, an adjective, concerns a belief that the government should run the economy and that individuals may not own property. Emigration is the act of leaving a country or a region to settle elsewhere. Formidable, an adjective, means impressive or powerful enough to stir respect or fear. A crisis is a dangerous, unstable time that demands attention. An ideology is the set of beliefs under an economic system, or a social or political one. Democratic, an adjective, concerns government through elections that are free and frequent, by the people themselves. Impenetrable, an adjective, means impossible to see through, or impossible to pierce. Infamous, an adjective, means famous for evil, harm, or danger. Occupied, a verb, means took or held a district using military force. People called informers secretly pass word of a crime, and a reward is often the reason. Payments called ransoms are payments demanded or made so a captive person or thing will be released. Integrating means bringing different groups or ideas together. Repressive describes rule that blocks free expression and uses force to keep people down. Intrepid, an adjective, means fearless and daring. Jubilant, an adjective, means full of great joy. Reunified, a verb, means joined again. Sectors are distinct divisions of a place. Lucrative, an adjective, means able to produce a great deal of money. Negotiations are talks aimed at a formal agreement. A stalemate is a deadlock in which neither side can win.

6. Abraham Lincoln and the Nation He Held Together

1The parts of this book follow one path. An introduction comes first. Early years come next. Law and politics follow. A divided America comes after that. The years of war come last. A word list closes the book. Lincoln grew a beard only after he had won the presidency. He had not yet moved to Washington, D.C. An 11-year-old girl was the person who suggested the beard. One picture shows the Lincoln Memorial. Washington, D.C., is the city. Millions of people visit that monument each year. In the story of American presidents, few matter more than Abraham Lincoln. He led the United States through the Civil War. The war lasted from 1861 to 1865. Northern states and Southern states fought over what the country would become. People call him the Great Emancipator. Enslaved people across the South gained freedom because of what he did. When the fighting stopped, the country stood as one nation again. It has stayed one nation ever since.

2Americans treat Abraham Lincoln as a great folk hero. Stories and legends gather around him. Pictures often show him tall. They show him lanky. They show him solemn. Memory keeps him as a common man. Regular schooling in his life was slight. A log cabin in Kentucky was his birthplace. Humble beginnings did not stop him. He became an outstanding lawyer. He became an outstanding speaker. He became an outstanding political leader. Speeches of his, eloquent ones, speak of freedom. They speak of justice. They speak of bringing all Americans together. Those words are cut into stone at the Lincoln Memorial. The memorial stands in Washington, D.C. His belief can be put in plain words. He would not accept being enslaved. He would not accept being a master either. That pair of refusals was his meaning of democracy. A picture shows a cabin built from logs. People believe those logs came from the cabin where he was born. The cabin stands at the Abraham Lincoln Birthplace National Historic Site. Hodgenville, Kentucky, is the town. Thomas Lincoln and Nancy Hanks Lincoln were his parents. February 12, 1809, was the day of his birth. The place was a small farm of log cabins near Hodgenville, Kentucky. The family later moved to Knob Creek, close by. School there included Abe. Sarah, his older sister, went as well. The schooling came only in short stretches. Those stretches fell in the winters. Nancy, their mother, pushed them to learn. Tom, their father, wanted Abe at the chores instead. Abe was seven when the family moved to Indiana. They hoped Indiana would give them a better life. A fresh cabin made of logs was Tom's work. Two years after that cabin, Nancy died. Milk sickness was the cause. Milk sickness is poisoning. The poison comes from milk or meat of cows. Those cows have eaten a certain plant. Abe mourned his mother. Sarah mourned her too. She had been hard-working. She had been loving. Soon afterward, Tom married Sarah Bush Johnston. She was a widow. She was already mother to three children. Tom had known her back in Kentucky. Love and care from her made a warm home for Abe. The same care made a warm home for Sarah. She encouraged Abe as he grew. He grew tall. He grew awkward. Hours in the woods went to his ax. He felled trees. He split logs for fences. He split logs for wagons. He split logs for farm equipment. Friends noticed a moody quiet in him. Even so, he told stories that were homey. The stories were humorous too.

3Winter school for Abe lasted only a few weeks. Each day he walked 18 miles. That distance is 29 kilometers. Most of his learning was his own work. He borrowed books from neighbors. He borrowed newspapers from neighbors. He borrowed them from travelers too. These were frontier days. People were moving west. Daniel Boone was one pioneer they followed. Johnny Appleseed was another. Other pioneers went ahead as well. Stories of those travelers widened Abe's view. Books he read did the same. The world began to look bigger than his backwoods. As a teenager he stood 6 feet 4 inches tall. That height is 2 meters. A flatboat carried him along the Mississippi River. Produce filled the boat. He floated with the current. A pole was how he steered. New Orleans, a busy port, was the end of the trip. He saw the wonders of that city. He saw its diversity. For the first time he saw Black men in holding pens. He saw Black women in those pens. He saw Black children there too. They were caged. They were chained at auction blocks. White enslavers bought them. White enslavers sold them. His feelings about ending slavery changed across his life. Hatred of the institution itself never changed. The year 1841 put him on a steamboat. The Ohio River was the route. That river was a border. Several free states met several slave states along it. A dozen enslaved people were on board. Shackles held them together. He called that sight a continual torment. The same torment returned whenever he met that river. Any line that separated enslaved Black people from free people brought the torment back. Early campaigns taught him to communicate with skill. After the river trip, his father moved the family again. The new home was in central Illinois. Decatur was the nearby town. Abe helped his father raise another log cabin. He left the homestead soon after that. He was twenty-two. New Salem was a frontier village. He worked there as a storekeeper. He worked as a surveyor. He worked as a carpenter. People also knew him as a wrestler. Inside the New Salem Debating Society, people knew his skill as an orator. The Illinois state legislature was the office he sought. The 1832 race was a loss. Two years later he won. John Todd Stuart, a lawyer and a fellow legislator, urged him to study law. Abe read law books. March 1837 was the month he passed the law exams. He joined Stuart's law practice. Springfield became his home. The Illinois legislature met in that city.

4Democratic rights for every person were the base of Lincoln's views. Wealth did not decide a person's importance. Privilege did not decide it either. Respect inside the Whig Party grew around him. Whigs wanted a strong central government. Washington, D.C., was where that government sat. Democrats were the other leading party. They believed in states' rights. In that view, a state should run its own affairs. Washington should not interfere. Lincoln was thirty when he met Mary Ann Todd. She would become his wife. She was fashionable. Her father was a wealthy banker in Kentucky. Her background and his were far apart. They fell in love anyway. Her parents objected. The couple married once those objections were overcome. November 4, 1842, was the wedding day. Robert, the couple's first son, arrived in 1843. In 1846 Lincoln won election as Illinois representative. The seat was in the U.S. Congress. The family moved to Washington, D.C. A picture shows Mary Todd Lincoln in 1846. During his time in Congress, North and South grew more polarized. Slavery was the issue pulling them apart. The North relied on paid laborers. Those laborers worked in factories. They also worked on small farms. The North wanted a strong central government. Northern states had already made slavery illegal. King Cotton ruled the Southern economy. Large plantations grew that cotton. The work was done by enslaved people. Those people had no personal rights. They had no civil rights. Most lived in very poor conditions. Treatment of them was inhumane. Southern state laws allowed slavery. Those laws protected it. Western territories were asking to become states as the country grew. One question mattered most. Would a new state be free, or would it be a slave state? The South wanted the new land for cotton. Enslaved labor was how that cotton would be grown. The North wanted independent farms. The North wanted paid labor. A picture shows a building in Atlanta, Georgia. Sales of enslaved people took place in that building.

5Lincoln was against slavery. As Illinois's representative in Washington, he still saw a legal limit. State law in the South, he believed, protected the practice there. He did fight to stop slavery from spreading into the western territories. The abolitionist movement grew during the 1840s. Its goal was to outlaw slavery. White people were among its followers. Free Black people were among them too. They called for the horrors of human bondage to stop. They demanded an end to the inhumanity of holding humans that way. Two years in Washington were enough. Lincoln went back to Springfield. For the next few years he shared a law practice. William Herndon was his partner. The practice did well. People spoke of Lincoln's honesty. They spoke of his skill in law. They spoke of his wit. They spoke of his fine oratory. February 1850 brought a family tragedy. Eddie, their boy, died of tuberculosis. He was nearly four. Both parents sank into deep depression. Signs of emotional imbalance appeared in Mary. December of that year brought another son. His name was Willie. Three years later another son arrived. His name was Thomas. Tad was his short name. Lincoln stayed very close to his sons. He was a proud father. He was a loving father. The 1850s were years of struggle between proslavery and antislavery forces. The Kansas-Nebraska Act won passage in Congress during 1854. An earlier law had forbidden slavery in those territories. The new act cancelled that ban. Residents themselves could now choose. They could choose to be a free state. They could choose to be a slave state. Popular sovereignty is the name of that idea. Letting the people decide is what it means. Stephen Douglas introduced it. Lincoln and Douglas had been political rivals for years. He was now a U.S. senator from Illinois. A map gives the picture of slavery in the country once the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854 was law. Nebraska Territory appears on it. Utah Territory appears on it. Kansas Territory appears on it. New Mexico Territory appears on it. The map marks free states and territories. It marks areas allowed to choose. It marks slave states. It marks unorganized territory.

6Lincoln decided the spread of slavery had to be opposed out loud. He also decided to seek office again. The new Republican Party was against slavery. He joined it. In 1858 that party nominated him for senator. Senator Douglas, his old enemy, was the opponent. The Lincoln-Douglas debates were held during the campaign. The whole country paid attention. A picture shows Lincoln in 1858. The picture was made two weeks before his last debate with Douglas. With great skill as a speaker, he said slavery had put the nation in crisis. A house split against itself, he said, cannot keep standing. He said this government could not last forever if half of it stayed enslaved. The other half, in that picture, would be free. Black people, he argued, held the same claim as white people. That claim was the right to life. It was the right to liberty. It was the right to the pursuit of happiness. Douglas answered from the Constitution. Equality, he said, was guaranteed only to white people. Each state, he asserted, could choose slavery or freedom for itself. A picture shows Stephen A. Douglas. Lincoln lost that election. The debates still made him popular. The Republican Party felt that popularity most. By 1860 the party wanted him for president. Rallies and parades gave him nicknames. One name was Honest Abe. Another was the homespun rail-splitter. People called him a man of the people. Equality was what he stood for. Freedom was what he stood for. The rail-splitter name came from work he had done as a young man.

7On November 6, 1860, voters made Lincoln president. The nation was the United States. The North rejoiced. The western territories rejoiced. The South was outraged. His inauguration was set for March 4, 1861. Seven states in the South cast votes to secede before inauguration day. They were leaving the United States of America. February saw a government formed by the states that supported slavery. Confederate States of America was its name. Jefferson Davis was its president. Those states prepared for war. Lincoln still hoped to avoid bloodshed. In the inauguration speech he placed the choice with the unhappy states. The momentous question of civil war, he said, was in their hands. It was not in his. A picture shows that inauguration. The date was March 4, 1861. The place was the U.S. Capitol. The Capitol was still under construction. Events then moved fast. On April 12, 1861, cannons from South Carolina fired on Fort Sumter. Northern troops gave up the fort on April 14, 1861. Both sides mobilized quickly. The Union was one side. The Confederacy was the other. They called for volunteers. They gathered arms. They gathered supplies. Lincoln's home and office were in Washington, D.C. That city belonged to the Union. Across the river he could see Virginia. Virginia belonged to the Confederacy. Superior military leadership on the Southern side won the first battle. That battle was at Bull Run. Union forces lost it. Strong commanders were hard for Lincoln to find while the war lasted. General George B. McClellan led Union armies to some successes. By 1862 those armies were stopped. Confederate General Robert E. Lee was the one who stopped them. Union forces did control New Orleans. They controlled the Mississippi River. Victories beyond that were few. The North called for action. Lincoln took on more of the military planning. Young soldiers died in enormous numbers on both sides. Others were wounded. Others were missing. The war moved into its second year. Personal loss struck Mary and Abraham Lincoln in February 1862. Fever took their son Willie. Mary never fully recovered from that grief. Abraham carried the same sadness into meetings with families. Those families were mourning their own war dead.

8A picture shows President Lincoln talking with General McClellan at Antietam. Replacement of McClellan would come soon. Bull Run's second battle went against the Union. No engagement in the war was bloodier than Antietam. Both sides suffered there. Powerful Republican senators pressed the president. They wanted abolition of slavery to become a goal of the war. Their argument was practical. The Union, they said, had to remove the issue that had caused the war. Only then could the fight succeed. Lincoln at last accepted a claim about his own power. As president, he could order abolition in the South. The Emancipation Proclamation became active on January 1, 1863. From that day forward, and for all time, it freed enslaved people in the Confederacy. The proclamation freed many enslaved people. It did not free all of them. Freedom on that first day of January 1863 covered enemy territory. Black men just freed inside Confederate areas could then join the Union fight. The North badly needed those soldiers. The war's meaning changed. It became a crusade against slavery. Border states were left out. Delaware was one. Maryland was one. Kentucky was one. Missouri was one. Those states still held enslaved people. They had never seceded from the Union. Lincoln feared a result if he freed people there. Those states might join the Confederacy. The United States would be very likely to lose the war if that happened. It would lose the South. It would lose the chance to end slavery in every state. Enslaved people who remained would wait two more years for freedom. A map shows the border states in 1863. It marks Union free states. It marks Union slave states. It marks Confederate slave states. It marks territory. Maryland, Delaware, West Virginia, Missouri, and Kentucky appear on it. No other state was created the way West Virginia was, by breaking away from a Confederate state. That Confederate state was Virginia. From 1863 to 1865, the new Union state ended slavery step by step.

9After Fort Sumter, free Black men hurried to join the Union army. At first they were turned away. They had served in earlier wars. A federal law from 1792 still blocked them.
