The law said they could not bear arms for the U.S. Army. By the middle of 1862, the Union needed more volunteers badly. That need pushed the government to lift the ban. By the war's end, Black men serving as soldiers numbered nearly two hundred thousand. A picture shows Company E of the 4th U.S. Colored Infantry. Former enslaved men made up that company. Other free Black men served in it too. Many people call Lincoln the Great Emancipator. For many Native peoples, the record he left is not a good one. He was president during a great push westward. His policies hurt Native peoples who already lived on those lands. The harm was disastrous. The Homestead Act of 1862 was one cause. Another law was the Pacific Railway Act, passed in 1862. Together they led to building the transcontinental railroad. Lost land was one result of that railroad for a great many Native peoples. It meant lost natural resources. It meant the loss of a whole way of life. Lincoln forced Native peoples onto reservations. In doing that, he carried on harsh policies of presidents before him. Those policies were discriminatory. A picture from 1864 shows Manuelito on the left. He was a Navajo chief. Notrossia and Pattia stand on the right. They were two Navajo girls. That year the Lincoln administration oversaw a removal. Navajo people were taken from their home. Some Apache people were taken too. The home region was northeastern Arizona. The march they were forced to make covered hundreds of miles. People came to call that march the Long Walk. Many died along the way. Summer of 1863 brought a Union victory at Gettysburg. Gettysburg turned the direction of the war. Lincoln dedicated a cemetery there to soldiers who had died. The speech he gave is the Gettysburg Address.

10The speech took only two minutes. People still remember its simple beauty. They remember its eloquence. He described the war as a test. He asked whether a nation built as a democracy could last. He asked the living to finish work the dead had left undone. A government of the people, he said, must not vanish from the earth. A government by the people must not vanish. A government for the people must not vanish. General Ulysses S. Grant was newly appointed. Under him, Union armies won in the West. They won in the South. Georgia saw Confederate troops go down to defeat late in 1864. They were defeated in Virginia. Lincoln began to hope the war would end. He was re-elected president. Early in 1865, Congress passed the Thirteenth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution. He cheered that passage. Slavery inside the United States was banned by that amendment. That amendment was only a first step toward equal rights for Black people. Denial stayed routine through the years of the civil rights movement in the 1960s. Jobs were denied. Voting rights were denied. Basic human respect was denied. April 9, 1865, brought the war to a close. Four years had passed since it began. Six hundred thousand lives was the cost. The Union was preserved. Slavery was abolished. Only six days later, Abraham Lincoln was dead. An assassin's bullet had killed him. John Wilkes Booth was the shooter. Booth sympathized with the Confederacy. Lincoln was at a play in Ford's Theatre. The theatre is in Washington, D.C. A funeral train carried his body back to Illinois, the state he loved. Mourners along the road saluted in silence. They were saluting a great American hero. A picture from February 1865 is among the last photographs of him.

11A timeline marks the main dates. His birth date on the timeline is February 12, 1809. Kentucky is the state listed. In 1818, his mother, Nancy, died. In 1819, his father, Thomas, married Sarah Bush Johnston. In 1834, Lincoln was elected to the Illinois state legislature. In 1837, he opened a law practice in Springfield, Illinois. In 1842, he married Mary Todd. In 1846, he was elected to the U.S. House of Representatives. In 1850, his son Edward died at age four. In 1858, the Lincoln-Douglas debates were held. Lincoln became a leader on the anti-slavery issue. In 1860, he was elected president. In 1861, the Civil War began. Confederates fired on Fort Sumter to start it. In 1862, his son William died at age twelve. The Battle of Antietam was fought that year. In 1863, Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation. The Union won at Gettysburg that year. In 1865, Confederate forces surrendered. That surrender ended the Civil War. The shot came on April 14, during the evening. He died the following day. The word list gives meanings from this book. An abolitionist worked to put slavery outside the law. Civil rights are legal rights. They are also social rights. They are also economic rights. They guarantee freedom and equality for every citizen. Eloquent speech or writing is simple, powerful, and elegant. An emancipator is a person who sets other people free. Equality means every person holds the same rights. Homespun means humble. It means a person comes from a simple rural background. To act inhumanely is to act with no dignity and no kindness. Momentous means hugely important. It means something of great consequence. An orator is a public speaker. An eloquent speaker is the kind the word points to most. To secede is to withdraw in a formal way from a group or an organization. Solemn means serious. It can also mean sad. Sovereignty means a person or a state is free to handle its own affairs.

7. Albert Einstein and the Hidden Pattern

1When Albert Einstein was five, his father Hermann showed him a magnetic compass. The needle seemed to float, and that motion woke the boy's curiosity. He wanted to know what caused it. His father turned the casing again and again in one hand. The needle hardly moved. Albert wondered why it kept aiming north. It was as if a hand no one could see were steering it. Answers were beyond a child that young. The feeling of wonder stayed with him. The feeling of mystery stayed too. Years later he wrote down the lesson of that compass. Something hidden, he said, had to sit behind the things we see. The curious child became a curious scientist. His life went into a search for that hidden something. Curiosity, kept alive, changed how people picture the universe we live in.

2The violin stayed with Einstein from boyhood into adult life. A line he liked said happiness asks for little: simple furniture, fruit, and the violin. March 14, 1879, was his birth date. Ulm, a small town in Germany, was the place. A move came the following year. Munich, a larger city, was the new home. Maja, his younger sister, was born there. She became his closest friend in childhood. The whole family shaped his life. Pauline, his mother, played the piano. She passed a love of music to him. The violin was the instrument she wanted him to learn. He disliked the strict shape of those lessons. Playing itself became something he loved. For as long as he lived, the violin stayed beside him. A way of speaking he had as a child made his parents worry. It is a habit many children show. Words he had just said aloud, he often said again to himself. The second saying was very quiet. He seemed to be checking whether the words were right. He grew out of the habit. He later became a skilled speaker in public. One picture shows him with his sister Maja. His father was an electrical engineer. Two uncles were electrical engineers too. They brought him math and science while he was still young. Algebra's basics came as a game. A medical student ate dinner with the family once a week. That student brought books. Some books were about science. Some were about math. Some were about philosophy. Einstein would pore over them for hours at a time. A geometry book held him most of all. Philosophy books helped form him too. Even as a child he could concentrate deeply. He stayed with a hard problem until every solution he could imagine had been considered.

3Math talent showed at once in school. Science talent showed at once too. So did a strong individual streak. To the boy, teachers resembled army sergeants. They drilled pupils to memorize information. They drilled lifeless facts. They did not push students to think on their own. They did not push students to hunt for new answers. Einstein wanted a creative kind of thinking that was his own. His objections in class broke the lesson's flow. One teacher finally told him to leave the school. The reason given was his attitude. The teacher said the class was losing respect for him because of Einstein's attitude. Einstein felt relief when he left. The teachers felt relief too. He was 15. Italy, where his parents were, became his next stop. A new business was the reason the family had gone to Italy. Soon after they settled, he moved once more. Switzerland was where he would finish school. At only seventeen he was accepted by a university. It was one of Europe's finest schools for science. Routine lectures were often skipped. He used the time in a laboratory. His own ideas grew there. Most of his professors saw a brilliant student. They also saw a bright future only if he would follow rules already in place. A job was hard to find after he finished school in 1900. No one doubted that he had been a bright student. His degree came from one of Europe's finest universities. Independence and curiosity had a cost. The teachers who might have helped him find work did not like him. A teaching post would have left him free to study further. He was dismayed. He was not discouraged. He did not quit. Ideas were waiting to be thought through. They were waiting to be tested. He needed time. He needed a place. Both arrived in 1902. A patent office hired him as a clerk. Bern, Switzerland, was the city. His task was unusual. Devices sent in for patent approval had to work as their inventors said they did. He was the one who checked. The job let him do what he did best. He could follow curiosity. He could question. On the first day, his boss gave him a rule. Pick up an application, the boss said, and treat the inventor's claims as wrong.

4Einstein himself held several patents. One patent covered a compass. Large amounts of iron did not throw that compass off. Metal ships took it on as standard gear. Submarines took it on as standard gear. Another patent covered a pump for refrigerators. The pump was quieter. The pump was safer. A steady paycheck and regular hours set him free. His own ideas got that free time. In spare hours he met friends. They shared his curiosity about the science of their day. Philosophy interested them too. Mathematics interested them too. Olympia Academy was the name they chose. Their eager talks often ran late into the evening. Cafes were one meeting place. Einstein's apartment was another. They talked. They socialized. Steady work and strong friendships filled those years. In that setting he began ideas that would change science for good. By 1905 he had spent three years at the patent office. Curiosity had pushed him to research. It had pushed him to study. It had pushed him to think hard about new scientific theories. He grew sure enough of the results to share them. Papers went to Annalen der Physik. That journal was the leading German science journal of the time. The first paper appeared in March 1905. Four more papers followed soon. The first paper set out his view of light. It covered what light is and how light acts. The second paper and the third paper proved tiny parts of matter. Those parts are molecules and atoms. The papers also described how those parts move. The last two papers gave new accounts of links among space, time, and moving objects. A simple diagram marks water. A water molecule holds two hydrogen atoms. It holds one oxygen atom. That fact is common knowledge now.

5What he wrote astonished scientists. They asked where such unusual ideas had come from. Anger was another response. Some people saw the work of a lifetime suddenly made smaller. Six months was all it took. He challenged more than two hundred years of accepted thought. That thought concerned what the known universe contains. It concerned how the known universe behaves. Surprise had a second cause. The writer was not a physics professor at a great university. He was a curious patent clerk. He was 26. Right after the papers appeared, his science career shot off in many directions. Attention from other scientists gave him energy. Open doors gave him energy too. He was invited to speak at science meetings. He was invited to explain the new ideas. The person who won the 1905 Nobel Prize in physics congratulated him in person. Max Planck was a famous physics professor, highly respected. Planck began teaching Einstein's ideas to his own students. Later, people called 1905 his miracle year. He once said the real wonder is that the world can be understood at all. The patent office kept him on staff through 1909. That year a full-time university post was finally offered. He was glad to accept. True to habit, he then moved from school to school for several years. He was still hunting the best place for his research. Older ideas were developed further. They were refined. The work was hard. More than once he thought the path was wrong. He could be very hard on himself. The ideas were so new, and so unfamiliar, that he sometimes feared he was losing his mind. Then 1915 brought a breakthrough. Separate earlier ideas could finally be joined into one system. General theory of relativity was the name he gave that system. Scientists around the world were excited again. In 1919, British scientists put the theory to a test. They measured where a star seemed to be during a solar eclipse. If he was right, the star would seem to stand in one place. Its real place would be another. Many people were astonished by the result. The star showed up almost exactly in the spot he had named.

6A well-known magazine later called him Person of the Century. Headlines in newspapers worldwide reported the eclipse findings. A British paper announced a revolution in science. It announced a new account of the universe. A German paper called him a new famous person in world history. It said his ideas fully overturned old pictures of nature. Fame of the highest kind arrived for him in a single night. Later voices would rank his influence first among people of the twentieth century. Success and wide acceptance did not please everyone. Many scientists had built careers on ideas he had shown to be wrong. Others refused the theories because a laboratory test would be hard. Some people simply disliked him for being a Jewish man. Prejudice toward many groups was on the rise in the country where he lived. In the next few years, friends feared more and more for his safety. A diagram, not drawn to scale, marks two spots for one star. Spot A is where the star really is. Spot B is where the star seems to be. The Sun and Earth are on the diagram. Gravity from the Sun bends a star's light. That bend makes the star seem to sit at B. It really sits at A. He would become a loud opponent of the prejudice rising in Germany. Criticism of his work from other professionals did not shake him. He knew the theories were not perfect. Each new paper brought more people to a judgment. The judgment was that his work mattered in a critical way. In 1922 he received the Nobel Prize in physics. The prize was a prestigious one.

7Fame brought more requests. People wanted interviews. They wanted photographs. They wanted speeches. They wanted writings. His feelings about the attention were mixed. The demands cut into his research. He also knew fame could open minds. It could carry his ideas to wider audiences. He used fame to point at causes he cared about. Avoiding war, whenever avoidance was possible, was a belief he held deeply. In 1914 he signed a letter against German militarism. The letter also opposed Germany's entry into World War I. Only three scientists signed it. He was one of the three. Support for Germany joining the war filled a separate letter. More than 100 scientists signed that letter. He took an active part in antiwar work. He publicly backed international groups that worked for peace. He wrote often about those antiwar beliefs. Magazines in the United States gave him credit for helping make the atomic bomb. He pushed back. Other people used his discoveries to build the bomb. He did not take part in the project. President Franklin Roosevelt did receive a letter with Einstein's signature. The letter warned how much destruction the bomb could cause. One picture shows news reporters greeting him in New York in 1921. Elsa, his wife, is with him. In the United States he saw a hard fact. Rights held by other citizens were rights Black people did not share. They did not have the same opportunities. He became a vocal activist. He spoke against prejudice. Some of his views shifted as his life went on. Pacifism did not shift. Pacifism is the belief that violence is never the answer. War is never the answer either. He advocated a world government. He set that idea above nationalism. Fame, for him, was a way to say people should not harm one another. The place they lived did not change that duty. The beliefs they held did not change it. He urged people to aim at being persons of value, not only persons of success.

8Einstein and others kept promoting peace. Even so, Germany in the 1930s moved closer to war. Until then the German government had put up with him. It had put up with his fame. It had put up with his criticism of its plans. He knew that tolerance would end. The Nazi Party was rising. His open attacks on Nazi politics made him a target. Being Jewish put a target on him as well. In 1933 he had just finished a series of yearly lectures in the United States. He sailed to Belgium. He formally gave up German citizenship. He did not go back to his home in Germany. He accepted a post at the Institute for Advanced Study. The post sat in Princeton, New Jersey. That city is in the United States. German military troops answered by seizing much of his property. Many of his papers were burned in public. They burned many of his books. They denounced him as a traitor. One picture shows him with Jawaharlal Nehru in 1949. Nehru was prime minister of India. Einstein's house was the meeting place. Princeton, New Jersey, was the town. Sailing was a pleasure for him. He often took his boat onto Lake Carnegie. That lake is in Princeton. In New Jersey the family moved into a house near his office. They soon belonged to Princeton's close community. Visitors from out of town sometimes asked where the great man lived. Townspeople answered with a question: Are you expected? That question kept strangers from bothering him at home.

9For the next 22 years he kept pushing his ideas into new areas. Some people read that effort as a sign he was losing touch. He paid little attention to that criticism. He believed a new theory was possible. His ideas and the latest theories would become one system under that theory. Dedication to the work never left him. Dedication to the ideas never left him. Breakthroughs on the scale of the miracle year did not come again. Breakthroughs on the scale of the general theory of relativity did not come again. Demand for him never stopped. He still gave speeches. He still wrote articles. He still met regularly with fellow scientists. One picture shows him going over matters with his secretary, Helen Dukas. She worked with him from 1928 on. She stayed until his death in 1955. He said few people really see through their own eyes. He said few people really feel with their own hearts. Curiosity of his kind led to many useful products. Ideas about what light is, and how light behaves, mattered here. Scientists used them to find new ways to control light. Those technologies later led to television cameras. They led to remote controls for electronics in the home. They led to flat-screen computers. Laser light was an idea no one before him had formed. That technology now serves compact discs, called CDs. It serves digital video discs, called DVDs. It serves checkout equipment in stores. His proof that atoms and molecules exist led further. A wide range of products was created or improved. Shaving cream is one. Toothpaste is one. Personal computers are one. Cell phones are one.

10His theories give scientists a framework. They use it to study objects in space. The Helix Nebula is one such object. New theories still feel his influence. New technologies still feel it. Ideas now held about how the universe began come from his work. Ideas about the nature of space come from it. Ideas about the nature of time come from it. Ideas about black holes come from it. Black holes are strange objects, and they are intriguing. His own thinking is part of that result. Discoveries he made, and equations he wrote, gave scientists a base. From that base they can grasp many sides of the universe. Only in recent years have scientists been able to test some of his most advanced theories. Only recently have they been able to confirm those theories. He said the important habit is to keep questioning, and never quit. Mystery, he said, is the most beautiful experience a person can have. Understanding a little of that mystery each day is enough. Curiosity kept him working until he died. The date was April 18, 1955. Nature's deepest mysteries were the puzzles he still chased. In that work he changed how people think. Time is one foundation he changed. Space is another. Energy is another. Matter is another. Those four are foundations of the universe.

11The word list gives meanings from this book. Advocated means supported or recommended. Nationalism means a person believes in their own nation's success and in its independence. Algebra is a branch of math. In algebra, symbols, usually letters, stand for unknown numbers. A patent is a document. It gives an inventor the right to earn money from an invention. Atoms are tiny pieces of matter. Physics studies matter with the tools of science. It studies energy the same way. A compass is a tool for finding direction. Its needle always points north. To pore over a book is to read it with great attention. Influential means having power to shape events. Prestigious means holding honor, respect, or high standing. A molecule is as small as a substance can be split and still be recognized as itself. A revolution, here, is an overthrow of older ideas or older ways of doing things. The topic list names subjects in the book. Beliefs are one. Black holes are one. His birth is one. The compass is one. Criticism is one. Being curious is one. Curiosity is one. Fame is one. Family is one. His father is one. The general theory of relativity is one. An inventor is one. A job is one. The journal is one. A laboratory is one. Laser light is one. Magnetism is one. The miracle year is one. His mother is one. Mystery is one. The Nobel Prize is one. The Olympia Academy is one. Papers are one. The patent office is one. Patents are one. Peace is one. Philosophy is one. Princeton, New Jersey, is one. Public speaking is one. Research is one. Revolution is one. School is one. Scientific theories are one. Scientists are one. His sister is one. The solar eclipse is one. His uncles are one. The United States is one. The universe is one. The violin is one. War is one. Work is one.

8. Anne Frank's Hidden Years

1The rooms where Anne's family sheltered are a museum now. Restorers have returned those rooms to the look they had in the hiding years. Visitors to the site number more than a million each year. Seven sections shape this account. They cover the move into hiding, the rise of hate and war, life under occupation, the diary as a refuge, the arrest, a terrible end, and a word list. Into hiding July 5, 1942, brought a doorbell just short of three o'clock. Anne Frank was thirteen. She thought a friend, who had promised a visit, was at the door. The caller was the postman, carrying a summons. It named Anne's older sister, Margot. Margot had to report so she could be transported to a work camp. Germany's forces had entered the Netherlands two years before. Now Amsterdam's Jewish people were being gathered. Trains would carry them to camps of that kind, and nobody knew what waited there. Edith Frank, mother of Anne and Margot, felt the letter as a blow. Stories had leaked ever since Germany overran much of Europe in the opening two years of that worldwide war, the war of 1939 to 1945. Across the lands Germany controlled, Jewish people were being gathered and sent to concentration camps. Official word about those camps was scarce. Official word about the people sent there was scarce too. Otto Frank, Anne's father, reached home a short while later that afternoon. He told his daughters the family would not be split. Otto, with Edith and their friends, had watched the danger and had laid plans that stayed secret. Anne and Margot were told to fill school bags. Into hers, Anne put a diary first. Its cover was a red-and-green checkered pattern. The diary had been a birthday gift.

2The gift had come the month before, and Anne had already filled pages with private thoughts. Family pictures show Edith Frank, baby Anne beside Edith, Otto Frank, and Margot Frank. Another shows Margot, Otto, and Anne together. Next morning the four Franks left home in heavy rain. A fake note stayed behind, hinting at an escape to Switzerland. That hint was false. Anne walked with her parents. Margot used her bicycle for several miles. Their goal was a small warehouse of the Amsterdam firm Otto had owned since before Germany's invasion. Upstairs, an apartment of small rooms swallowed the family. They would stay hidden in those rooms past the two-year mark. Danger pressed from every side, and Anne set her thoughts and feelings down on paper. Hate and war gather In World War I, from 1914 to 1918, Otto Frank served as a German officer. A soldier's medal called the Iron Cross honored that service. After the fighting, Frankfurt, Germany, became his base, and he tried several businesses. Accounts of him agree. He was kind, playful, intelligent, and hardworking. Edith came from a wealthy Jewish family. Before she met Otto she worked in the family firm. Its goods were scrap metal, and she also worked in mechanics. Their marriage was in 1925. Two daughters followed. Margot's birth year was 1926. Annelies Marie Frank, called Anne, arrived on June 12, 1929, three years after Margot. The 1920s brought Germany many hardships. War and what followed left the country broke. Desperation and anger filled many Germans. Political groups fought for power while Germany tried to become a democracy. In 1929 the Great Depression hit businesses and economies around the world, and Germany felt it with special force. A picture shows Catholic nuns feeding people in the Germany of the 1930s.

3Adolf Hitler used that turmoil. Like Otto Frank, he had earned an Iron Cross in the first world war. Antisemitism marked Hitler, and that hatred was widespread then. He blamed Jewish betrayal for his country's defeat. His book Mein Kampf, meaning My Struggle, came out in the mid-1920s. In it he set down a murderous hatred of Jewish people, and a belief that so-called Aryans stood above other races. A 1933 photograph places Adolf Hitler at the center of a group. He led the National Socialist German Workers' Party, a label usually shortened to the Nazis. Early on, many Germans laughed at that violent program. When troubles deepened, more citizens turned to Hitler as the man who would fix the country. He promised Germany would stand great again, and powerful as well. Followers' fears became pride. Their frustrations became hatred, aimed above all at Jewish people. During 1933 the Nazis seized full control of Germany's government under Hitler's totalitarian rule. Otto and Edith saw the threat at once. Law after law stripped German Jewish people of property and of rights. The couple knew the young family had to leave before matters grew worse. Otto got a chance to open a small company in Amsterdam, a large city. In 1933 and 1934 the family moved to the Netherlands. German Jewish people, counted in the thousands, fled with that same wave, and so did others whom the Nazis persecuted. When the family reached Amsterdam, Anne had not yet turned five. She was lively, outgoing, and opinionated, and she was endlessly curious about people and about the world. She was too young to grasp her parents' worry, or their sadness at leaving Germany. Her new home gave her a happy childhood. School pleased her, mostly. Friends filled her days, along with table-tennis parties, ice cream, and her family's love. A photograph shows Anne during 1939. Poland was invaded by Nazi Germany on the first day of September in that year, and that invasion set World War II alight.

4Within a year, Germany's army, together with its air force, had taken most of the west of Europe. Neutrality was what the Netherlands had declared and said it wanted no part of the war. Germany invaded regardless. On May 15, 1940, the Dutch government surrendered. The fight had lasted only five days. Nearly every Jewish person in Europe was now caught in the horror this family had hoped to escape. Under occupation For two years, Jewish people in Amsterdam lived openly under Nazi occupation. Anne's family kept days as normal as they could. Otto used contacts overseas and tried to move the family again. He looked at Great Britain, at the United States, at Cuba, at any place that might be safe. Each try was blocked or turned down. Two events in 1941 let the family hope Hitler could not keep his war going. Germany entered the Soviet Union in June. In December, war on Germany was declared by the United States, building a strong pact with Great Britain and with the Soviet side. The Franks' lives now hung on how fast Germany could be pushed back, which would free the Dutch lands and Europe beyond them. Beating the Nazis would take time, and the Franks, like Jewish families besides their own, had little of it left. Occupiers kept persecuting Amsterdam's Jewish population with further anti-Jewish decrees. By 1939, radios belonging to Jewish people were taken, and a curfew bound them. In 1940 their telephones were taken as well. In 1941 every Jewish person older than six had to display a yellow Star of David that carried the word Jew. Bicycles had to be handed in. Trams were forbidden. Cars were forbidden, even a car a person owned. Pets could not be kept. Leaving the country was forbidden. In 1942 schools shut their doors to Jewish children. Restriction piled on restriction, meant so Jewish people would be frightened, ruled, and shamed in Amsterdam and across the Dutch lands. Protest came from many Dutch people, who tried to shield Jewish friends. Arrest and prison often answered that help. The Nazis were set on wiping out Europe's Jewish people. In the Netherlands they sped the drive into the concentration camps. Once the Franks hid in July 1942, more people joined them. Hermann van Pels, Otto's business partner, arrived with his wife Auguste and their son Peter.

5Peter was sixteen. Fritz Pfeffer, a dentist, entered that shared refuge in November. Anne's diary called those rooms the Secret Annex. Careful planning had come from her father and from the other adults. The annex could be lived in, though it was cramped. It held a kitchen, a bathroom, and cold running water. About 46 square meters was the floor of the three main rooms, or 500 square feet. Each room was both a living space and a bedroom. In time a bookcase hid the single entrance. Cloth and cardboard covered the windows so no light would show at night. A portrait shows Peter van Pels. Still in place is the bookcase that concealed the Secret Annex entrance. It remains inside the Anne Frank House today. A 1935 photograph seats Otto Frank among his office staff. Moving around the circle are Miep Gies, Johannes Kleiman, Victor Kugler, and Bep Voskuijl. Years afterward those same workers fought so he and the family would survive. Helpers, Anne's word for non-Jewish friends who agreed to supply them, gave enormous aid to the Franks, the van Pels family, and Fritz Pfeffer. Food and other necessities came from those friends. The circle included people loyal to Otto Frank and to Hermann van Pels. In the circle were Jan, husband of Miep Gies, and Elisabeth Voskuijl who was called Bep, Johannes Voskuijl, Bep's father, along with Victor Kugler and Johannes Kleiman. Hiding Jewish people put the helpers at risk of prison, of deportation, and of execution. Anne wrote of them in the diary. She said they never complained, and never hinted that the hidden group was a weight on them. Each day they climbed the stairs smiling. They carried books, newspapers, flowers, and gifts.

6Holidays and birthdays brought those gifts. Conversation may have been the best gift of all. The diary as a refuge All who shared the Secret Annex understood how extreme the danger was. Capture would mean arrest at once. On weekdays, employees worked one floor below the hidden rooms, so Anne and the others had to keep perfect silence. Movement was on tiptoe. Talk was a whisper. Nobody could run water. Nobody could flush a toilet. A sound might raise suspicion and bring a betrayal. Bounty hunters were offered money for revealing Jewish people who were in hiding. In that forced quiet, Anne turned to the diary. Many entries spoke to an imaginary friend she named Kitty. Old photos of the family were pasted in. She recorded what she noticed in her family and in the people sharing the rooms, and she invented other names for them so their feelings would be protected. She also wrote what it felt like to grow into a young woman under grim conditions. Despair appeared often. So did a deep fear of being caught. The first diary filled quickly. Notebooks came next, and loose sheets of paper. A copy stands in for Anne's own diary. Writing let her manage the daily strain and shake off cares and sorrows. She dreamed of work as a journalist, or perhaps as an actress. Pictures of movie stars covered a wall in the small room she shared with Pfeffer. Once the workers left, downstairs opened to Anne and the rest, though the outdoors stayed closed. They clustered at the radio for the programs. March 1944 brought Anne the voice of a leading Dutch official on the air. He asked people in the Netherlands to write what they lived through under Nazi occupation. The pages would be a historical record, and they would be proof of crimes the Nazis committed in war. Before long Anne began revising her entries with care, as if a publisher might one day print them.

7June 1944 brought news Anne welcomed. A huge Allied invasion force had landed in France. In the east, the Soviet Union was pushing the Germans into retreat. Otto started marking the war's progress on a map pinned to the wall. A hope rose that defeat for the Nazis might come soon, and that the annex group could walk free. The arrest On August 4, 1944, secret police raided the annex. More than two years had passed since the Franks vanished into it. Even now, nobody knows for certain how the hiding place was found. A German officer leading the raid forced one helper to lead police to the hidden rooms. At gunpoint, Anne's family, and everyone with them, could only lift their hands. Police arrested Anne and her family, then searched every closet and every corner of those hidden rooms. One Nazi officer emptied Otto's briefcase, Anne's writing among the contents, because he wanted the case for the family's valuables. Diary pages lay scattered on the floor. Helper Miep Gies gathered them later and placed them inside a desk drawer. She hoped to hand them back to Anne when the war ended. A picture shows women prisoners packed into barracks at Auschwitz. Early in September 1944 a transport carried the Franks there. Auschwitz, in Poland, was the concentration camp the Nazis made most infamous. The family was split. Otto went to the men's camp. Edith, Anne, and Margot went to the women's camp. Winter cold, illness, tiny rations, and crushing labor took a terrible toll. Edith still tried to help, so Margot and Anne got that help, and she even handed them all her food. November 1 separated the girls from their mother. Margot and Anne went next to Bergen-Belsen. That camp stood in Germany and was not Auschwitz.

8A terrible end May 1945 brought the surrender of Germany, and World War II in Europe was over. Horror filled the Allied soldiers who opened the concentration camps. The mass murder Hatred in Hitler and in the Nazis fed a drive to clear Europe of groups they called inferior. Jewish people were targets. So were Romany people, gay people, and people with disabilities. Early on, the Nazi aim was to push Germany's Jewish citizens out. Many fled, at least those who could pay to leave. By 1942 the plan had turned into mass murder. Across occupied Europe, Jewish people were seized and transported into Poland and into Germany, where most concentration camps stood. Certain camps killed everyone sent to them. At others, those able to labor met a slower death, through hunger and through toil. By war's end Jewish people killed by the Nazis numbered six million, two-thirds of the Jewish population of Europe. Five million further victims came from other groups marked for erasure. A picture shows Hungarian Jewish people reaching Auschwitz around 1942. Among the camps, this one was the biggest. The dead there are thought to number about 1.1 million. Liberators saw many signs of systematic murder. Most survivors were sick, starving, and near death. Otto Frank survived and returned to Amsterdam. He already knew starvation at Auschwitz had killed his wife. He still hoped Margot and Anne lived. Heartbreaking news soon came from a person who had met the girls inside Bergen-Belsen. Typhus made them sick. February 1945 took them less than a week apart, only weeks before British forces liberated that camp. Anne was fifteen. Miep Gies placed five notebooks in Otto's hands, and loose pages of his daughter's writing that numbered more than two hundred. He began to read. The pages were more than a young girl's casual notes. They formed a memoir of her experience, and it moved him. Later he said he had not known how deep her thoughts and feelings went. A 1976 photograph shows Otto Frank.

9A book that still lives For seventy years, readers have opened Anne Frank's diary. The text now exists in more than sixty languages. One is Farsi, read in Iran. Another is Sinhalese, read in Sri Lanka. The Anne Frank Center reports worldwide sales above thirty million copies. Much of the money earned has gone to charity. The writing has been turned into an award-winning play, an award-winning film, and two television miniseries. It offers a sharp look into the mind of an intuitive teen living in a terrible time. That story warns, across every era, against hatred and against extremism. The published diary, under the name Diary of a Young Girl, reached Dutch readers two years after the fighting in Europe had stopped. In time it was known around the world. People still read it, and teachers still teach it. It honors a young girl's spirit, and it recounts daily life while terror and war pressed in. Many readers see, through Anne, the Holocaust given a personal face. She was a writer of promise. Her full life was stolen. The world also lost the full reach of her talent and of her potential. A photograph shows Anne at twelve. Words from the book Nazi, an adjective, concerns the party that ruled Germany from 1933 to 1945. An annex is a building added onto a larger one. Antisemitic, an adjective, describes hatred of Jewish people, or hostile acts toward them. Occupation, a noun, is a situation in which soldiers take control of a region or a country. Decrees are orders or decisions issued with official force. Systematic, an adjective, means done in a thorough way, or carried out by a planned method. Emigrated, a verb, means left one country in order to settle in another. Holocaust, a noun, names the Nazis' systematic killing of people in World War II, above all of Jewish people. Totalitarian, an adjective, concerns a system in which a government holds absolute power over the people. Jewish, an adjective, concerns the people of the Jews, their culture, or their religion. Typhus, a noun, is a grave illness whose signs include a dark red rash, pain in the head, and a soaring fever. A memoir is a written retelling of what a person has lived.

9. Athens Against Sparta

1Nine sections shape this account. They cover the two cities and the war's causes. Later parts cover Pericles, the plague, Alcibiades, Sicily, Sparta's fleet, the ending, Greece's ruin, and a word list. Athens, in the upper view, has always been a far larger city than Sparta, in the lower view. Reports for 2021 put 3.1 million people in Athens. Sparta's count was 18,900. The two cities Ancient Greece was shaped by the Peloponnesian War, one of its defining events. Greeks of Athens fought Greeks of Sparta, each with allies, in a civil war that ran from 431 to 404 BCE. No earlier Greek war had been fought on such a scale. The repercussions changed the path of Western history.

2Before that war, politics in Greece split into more than a thousand small city-states, and each governed itself. Geography helped build that pattern. Mountains covered the land, so messages and travel by road were hard, and neighbors shaped one another very little. Athens and Sparta led the city-states, and their ideas of government differed. A map of Greece's world during the fifth century before the common era uses a scale of 500 kilometers and 300 miles. It marks the Alps, the Danube River, Italy, the Black Sea, Asia Minor, Sparta, Athens, North Africa, Sicily, Greece, the Mediterranean Sea, Greek settlements, the Persian Empire, the Nile River, and Egypt. An oligarchy was Sparta's system. A narrow band of elite men ruled. Two kings held power simultaneously, joined by a council of twenty-eight elders. Kings and council wrote the laws and set policy. Society was strictly militaristic. Boys left home at seven to join a powerful army based on land, and they generally served until sixty. A system of serfs numbered about two hundred thousand. Their name was Helots. That system let Sparta give the whole society to war. Helots farmed the land around the city and lived on it in exchange. Spartan males could therefore spend their time fighting or training. In Athens, labor by enslaved people likewise freed the ruling classes for other work. Athenian men usually chose thought and art. They left lasting literature, architecture, drama, and philosophy.

3Ambition, wealth, and power all marked Athens. Its army was strong, and its navy was impressive. Athenians were the first people known to practice democracy. In the assembly, male citizens older than eighteen could speak and could vote. Women could not take part. Neither could non-citizens or enslaved persons, so those groups could not shape law or policy. The city paid men to attend, which gave some men of lower income a voice. Ten leading generals, the strategoi, guided the assembly as it made foreign policy and military policy. Why the war began. The two cities, Athens and Sparta, once stood as allies in the Persian Wars, when Greeks fought the Persian Empire. Persian rule then stretched from India across to Bulgaria as it is known today, and to Egypt. Two invasions hit Greece, first in 490 BCE and again during 480 BCE. On both occasions, Greek fighters won. After they turned back the second invasion, Athens founded the Delian League. Greek cities joined that alliance and banded together against further Persian aggression. The name came from Delos, the island where members met for official business. A map of the divided Greek world uses a scale of 250 kilometers and 150 miles. It shows the Aegean Sea, the Persian Empire, the Ionian Sea, Athens, Sparta, the allies of each, neutral lands, and Crete.

4Tribute from each city in the alliance kept up a fleet that Athens managed. Because Athens held both the ships and the money, the alliance turned into empire form, and the head of it was Athens. When the Peloponnesian War opened, Athens dominated nearly all of Greece. Sparta and Sparta's allies were the exception. Most of what is known comes from Thucydides, who wrote history. He had been a general for Athens, and banishment came early in the fighting after he failed to win an important battle. Exile became the time in which he wrote the war's history, using what he had seen and what eyewitnesses told him. Later historians took his meticulous book, History of the Peloponnesian War, as a model. They praised its accuracy and the author's authoritative, compelling voice. He believed the Athenian Empire's rise made Sparta nervous. He wrote that Sparta feared Athens would use power at sea for conquering Greece entirely, and to break Sparta's hold on its own allies. Tension between the cities ran deep for years. War broke out after Potidaea, a city-state in the north, rose in rebellion under Athenian rule, then joined Sparta and Corinth. Athens answered with a blockade around Potidaea. Athens, in the same period, cut trade with Megara, another ally of Sparta and a close neighbor of Athens. Farmers from Megara had worked land Athenians called sacred to Demeter, goddess of fertility and of the harvest. Sparta issued an ultimatum. End the sanctions against Megara, and lift Potidaea's blockade, or attack would come from Sparta. The Athenian Assembly rejected that demand. War began in 431 BCE.

5A map of the Long Walls shows a north wall and a south wall, the city of Athens, and the port of Piraeus. The scale marks 3 kilometers and 2 miles. Pericles and the first plan. Athens opened the war from strength at the start. During the 460s and the 450s BCE, after Persia's invasions, the city raised what people called the Long Walls. Defensive walls, two of them and both long, wrapped Athens, wrapped the seaport called Piraeus, and wrapped the land between them. Piraeus lay 8 kilometers, or 5 miles, from the center of Athens. Sparta lacked the tools to break those walls, so Athens was essentially unassailable. Farmland did not have to be guarded at great cost. Food and other needs could come by sea through Piraeus, and Athens had the wealth for that. Rich silver mines lay nearby. Years of tribute from allies had made the city an economic superpower. In 443 BCE the people chose Pericles as one of the strategoi. He was a brilliant general and an orator, and he had already led successful campaigns. His early plan for the war was radical. Citizens were told to leave houses beyond the city, and the land there. Inside the Long Walls, every citizen took shelter. He also warned against land fights with Sparta's highly trained warriors. The navy would carry the war, striking from the sea and pulling back. A bust shows Pericles. Archidamus, one of Sparta's kings, shaped the early Spartan plan. His armies burned and wrecked the country ground that ringed Athens. Each summer, warriors made a short invasion and never stayed near the city more than forty days, because they could not feed themselves longer. The raids demoralized Athenian citizens. Even so, the early war went well for Athens. The walls helped, and so did food arriving through Piraeus.

6Armor of the ancient Greek fighter. Warriors of Greece were called hoplites, and bronze armor protected them. A full set usually weighed about 32 kilograms, or 70 pounds. It included a helmet, a cuirass for the chest, greaves for the shins, and a large shield. One weapon was a spear of great length. Another was a short sword. Those were the usual weapons. Armor hid the fighter's identity, so Greeks often painted pictures on shields. Vases from Athens show hoplites whose shields carry images from lions to cups. Labels point out the helmet and the cuirass. Those vases date to the sixth century BCE. Plague, then a harder fight. Housing the whole population inside the walls, Pericles's plan, failed in a horrible way. Plague struck as an epidemic in 430 BCE. Deaths ran from seventy-five thousand up to one hundred thousand. Roughly one third of Athens died, and Pericles was among the dead. After he died, Athenian generals struck Sparta more aggressively. The push peaked during 425 BCE, in fighting that happened close to Sparta. Athens won decisively and captured 290 Spartans and their allies. Capture of a Spartan warrior had never happened before, so the haul was a heavy blow to morale, especially after many soldiers of Sparta were already dead at Athenian hands. In exchange for the prisoners, a demoralized Sparta offered peace. Athens refused. Sparta then carried the fight to Athens's allies in the north. After hard fighting there, a peace treaty was negotiated in 421 BCE. Athens freed the Spartan prisoners taken four years before. Citizens could at last leave the Long Walls.

7A short peace, and Alcibiades. Peace did not hold. Politicians in both cities urged more aggression, chasing fame and security for their states. In Athens, a young and ambitious politician named Alcibiades saw chances for himself if the war went on. He arranged a pact that tied several cities to Athens, and cities near Spartan ground, including Argos, just north of Sparta. That link separated Sparta from Corinth and from Thebes, allies to the north. Sparta's retaliation was an attack on the new allies of Athens, and the peace was over. Historians and biographers call his behavior charismatic on one side and obnoxious on the other. Accounts say he was very beautiful and quite vain. Plutarch, an ancient Greek biographer, wrote that as a boy Alcibiades refused the flute. He feared that blowing into it might leave his face looking absurd. A bust shows him. The voyage to Sicily. He kept pushing aggressive military policy. In 415 BCE he persuaded the assembly to attack Syracuse, a rich city on the island of Sicily. His argument was that Syracuse could offer ships to help Sparta. A route map uses a scale of 300 kilometers and 200 miles and marks Italy, Greece, Athens, Sicily, Sparta, Syracuse, and the Mediterranean Sea. Alcibiades led the first landing himself, with several other generals. Athens won battles but could not take Syracuse. Enemies in the assembly managed to summon him home and strip his command. Recalling him proved a costly mistake. In a surprise, he deserted to Sparta and told Sparta it should place a military advisor inside Syracuse. Using that help, Syracuse crushed Athens's fleet while it sat inside a harbor fight in 413 BCE. The defeat badly weakened Athens at sea and changed the whole war's outcome.

8Sparta takes to the sea. After the Sicilian victory, Alcibiades offered two new plans. First, Sparta and its allies began building a fleet, an ominous turn for Athens, which had held the leading power among Greek navies across many years. Following his direction, that fleet threatened Athens's shipping lanes and stirred revolt among Athenian allies. Second, Sparta planted a fortress at Decelea, a town near Athens. Attacks on the countryside became constant, and Athens lost the way to the silver mines. That loss was a major blow to its money. Citizens had to pull back inside the Long Walls again, because Spartans sat just outside. Siege turned the city into a fortress. In 412 and 411 BCE, Alcibiades helped Sparta make a treaty with Persia's King Darius II. Darius offered money for Sparta's new navy. Both powers disliked Athens and feared its military strength. The Spartan-Persian alliance was another heavy blow. Athens still fought. It rebuilt part of the navy and won several sea battles in this stretch. Despite Alcibiades, Sparta, and Persia, Athens would not accept defeat. Trouble then found Alcibiades. Athens had not surrendered, and he had started a personal quarrel with one Spartan king. He began to plan a return. Messages to the assembly promised he could bring the support of Persia's Darius. Desperate to pull Persia onto their side, the Athenians agreed. He came back and, in 410 BCE, led their fleet to a victory over Sparta.

9The war's finish That 410 BCE victory was Athens's last. Persian help for Athens never arrived. Persia kept backing the Spartan side. Growth made that navy stronger. A string of battles ended with Athens forced to surrender in 404 BCE. Victorious Spartan armies entered the city then pulled down the Long Walls linking Piraeus with Athens. Instead of the old democracy, Sparta let Athenians pick thirty men to run the city. People called them the Thirty Tyrants. Injustice and greed marked their rule, including frequent arrests made only to steal money. Democrats then revolted from Piraeus. In 403 BCE Sparta allowed democracy to return. Athenians had their beloved government again, but wealth and military power were already gone. A timeline lists the war this way. In 431 BCE war was declared and the population moved inside the Long Walls. Plague devastated Athens in 430 BCE. A brief peace came in 421 BCE. The Sicilian Expedition sailed in 415 BCE, and the war resumed. Athens won a last victory in 410 BCE. An important sea battle was lost in 405 BCE. Surrender to Sparta, and the installation of the Thirty Tyrants, came in 404 BCE. Sparta allowed democracy again in 403 BCE.

10How the war ruined ancient Greece. By the century's close, the war had ended an era. Greece lay in shambles, and the people's pride was utterly destroyed. Twenty-seven years of fighting meant Greece would never reach such heights again. Athens recovered somewhat, yet never regained its old status. Sparta kept trying to widen its influence and failed to build an empire that lasted. Lost men, ruined farmland, and weakened cities left the states susceptible to invasion from outside. In the end, that weakening opened the road to the end of freedom for every Greek city-state. King Philip of Macedon was the ambitious ruler of a small country north of Greece. He saw the power vacuum the war had made. A newly trained army let him vanquish the Greeks in 338 BCE. He forced them into an alliance and, in effect, ended their freedom. Major changes for the Western world were set moving. The war's close marked classical Greece reaching its finish, and that age gave birth to democracy and to the work of major artists, playwrights, poets, historians, and philosophers. One man dominated what followed: Alexander the Great, Philip's son. His hunger to conquer the world and build an empire clashed with Greek ideals of curiosity and of creativity. That clash set the stage for Rome's later takeover of Greece. The war brought ancient Greece, in its glory, to an end. A map shows lands of the Greeks while Alexander the Great ruled. On it, Macedonia is marked for 336 BCE, and Alexander's empire for 323 BCE. The scale is 750 kilometers and 500 miles. Waters and lands on it include the Aral Sea and the Black Sea. Also shown are Macedonia, the Caspian Sea, Asia Minor, and Athens. Rivers include the Tigris, the Indus, the Euphrates, and the Nile. Further names are Persia, the Mediterranean Sea, India, Arabia, the Indian Ocean, and Egypt.

11Words from the book. Aggression is an attack, and politics is often the motive. Dominated, a verb, means held lasting power or influence over someone or something. Authoritative, an adjective, means that displays knowledge, confidence, or power within a field. Elite, an adjective, describes those counted as the best, or those with influence, power, or wealth in the highest degree. Meticulous, an adjective, means paying careful attention to detail. Blockading, a verb, means obstructing passage through an area. Militaristic, an adjective, concerns a policy that prizes armed forces. City-states are cities acting on their own, as if each were a country. To be demoralized, a verb, means lost hope or courage, or caused that loss. An oligarchy is a country or a rule held by only a few people. Devastation is great damage. Ominous, an adjective, means threatening. An orator is someone who speaks in public, above all with eloquence. People called serfs are persons compelled to work and to dwell on ground that a person of a higher class owns. Raze, a verb, means to tear a place down completely. Simultaneously, an adverb, means at the same time. Repelled, a verb, means forced something away. Susceptible, an adjective, means vulnerable. Repercussions are effects of events, often unwelcome or unforeseen. An ultimatum is a final demand that brings consequences if it is refused. Retaliated, a verb, means struck back after being attacked. Unassailable, an adjective, means impossible to attack or to defeat. Sanctions are official steps a government or an army uses when forcing another nation to obey. A vacuum, here, is the empty gap left when a power has gone.

10. Athletes Who Opened the Way

1Name the finest American athlete from the century that just ended. Where do you start? Jim Brown comes from football. Basketball offers Michael Jordan. Tennis offers Billie Jean King. Baseball offers Babe Ruth. Those are strong answers. Each one set records. Each one changed a sport in a deep way. Any of them could be argued into the top spot. The name that was given the highest place, though, belongs to Jim Thorpe. His people were the Sac and Fox Nation. He was Native. Birth came in 1887. The place was Indian Territory, now called Prague, Oklahoma. Few athletes were as versatile. He played baseball as a professional. In his own day he was the biggest star in football. In track and field his feats became legend. A note belongs beside that story. Thorpe was born inside the United States. Even so, he was not officially a citizen. Most other Native people of that time lacked official citizenship too. Citizenship came only when the Indian Citizenship Act passed. The year of that law was 1924.

2Campus fame arrived first. The Summer Games of 1912 were still ahead. Even then, college football already knew his name. He was a known star in track and field too. Pennsylvania is where he played as an All-American halfback. Crowds loved his blinding speed. They loved his strength. A tackler in his path might be run over. A tackler might just as easily be left behind. He also punted for the team. He was the placekicker too. Baseball at the school had him as a star. Basketball did too. Golf went well for him. Tennis went well. Swimming went well. Hockey went well. Almost every sport he tried went well. At the 1912 Games he wore the colors of the United States. The events were the two hardest in track and field. One was the pentathlon, a test of five events. The other was the decathlon, a test of ten. Modern Olympic history had never included those two tests before. A picture shows him throwing the shot put. The work was packed into a few days. One day covered the pentathlon. Two more days covered the decathlon. What he did seemed past imagining. Four of the five pentathlon events went to him. He set a world record in the decathlon. Gold medals came in both tests. Sweden's king, Gustav V, summoned him forward when the awards were given. The king told Thorpe that no athlete in the world was greater. Another picture shows a long jump at those same 1912 Games. The two Olympic tests demand many skills. Together they measure all-around ability. Pentathlon events, in order, are the long jump, the javelin, and the discus. They also include a run of 200 meters and a run of 1,500 meters. Decathlon events, in order, start with a 100-meter run, the long jump, and the high jump. Shot put comes next, then a 400-meter run. Hurdles follow, at 110 meters. Discus, javelin, and the pole vault come after that. A 1,500-meter run closes the ten.

3The International Olympic Committee later took Thorpe's medals away. It also wiped his records from the books. Officials had learned about summer baseball. In 1909 and again in 1910 he played in the minor leagues. That play broke the amateur rule, at least in a technical sense. Similar summer baseball showed up in other athletes' pasts. They kept amateur status. Unlike Thorpe, they had used fake names. Thorpe told the committee he was sorry. He said the rule was news to him. The committee did not change its mind. Replacement gold medals finally reached his family in 1983. His scores, however, were not put back into the official record. After the Games, the world knew his name. President William H. Taft sent a letter of congratulations. Professional teams offered rich contracts. He said no. One added year of college football was his choice, back on the campus he already knew. The coach was Glen Warner, known as Pop. Thorpe scored twenty-five touchdowns that season. His points for the year totaled 198. He also married Iva Miller, his sweetheart from college. The year was enormous. Pro baseball came in 1913. The team was the New York Giants. A bat in his hands was a dangerous thing. Strength and speed also made the outfield his ground. Baseball skill was real, yet football was the game he liked more. Professional football was only beginning in 1915. He joined the Canton Bulldogs. Canton is in Ohio. Championships followed in 1916, in 1917, and in 1919. Summers still found him on a baseball field. The year 1920 placed him in the president's chair of the American Football Association, and he was the first to sit there. A later name for that body was the National Football League. One aim was a more popular game, especially among children. At halftime he would stand on the 50-yard line. A drop kick sent the ball over the goalposts. He then turned around and did the same trick the other way. Punts could travel as far as 75 yards. A 1925 picture shows a New York Giants game, with Thorpe handling a batted ball. Today a statue greets visitors at the Football Hall of Fame. Words under the statue list what he did in football. The statue honors a founding father of the professional game. It honors the game's first true star. It honors the athlete those hundred years placed at the very top.

4Thorpe may keep the crown as the century's finest all-around athlete. Sports fans might still offer another name. Mildred Didrikson Zaharias, called Babe, played many sports at a high level. Women's basketball was one. Track and field was one. Golf was one. Her peak years ran through the 1930s, the 1940s, and the 1950s. She competed in a serious, rough style. The age expected women to be modest and polite. Norwegian immigrants were her parents. Birth came in 1911, in Port Arthur, Texas. She was the sixth child in a family of seven. High school made her a standout. Volleyball was one sport. Baseball was one. Swimming was one. Tennis was one. Basketball mattered most, because it was the leading sport for women then. Defeat never found the team she played for in high school. Thirty points from her alone was a common night. Twenty points was then seen as a solid total for a whole team. A picture shows her shooting free throws. Track and field became the next focus. She believed in strength training. She lifted weights. Very few women did that then. July of 1932 brought a countrywide track meet, and the work showed. She entered eight events. She won five. She also won the meet by herself. Her own score was thirty points. The second-place team had twenty women, and those twenty scored twenty-two points together. The Summer Olympics came a few weeks later. She won two gold medals. She won one silver medal. World records fell in the 80-meter hurdles, in the javelin, and in the high jump. More might have been possible. Olympic rules of that time let women enter three events at most. Fame followed. She built a basketball team and toured the country. The opponents were men's teams. Attention for the women's game grew. A picture places her at the far right. Another world record fell in the hurdles. The distance was 80 meters. Her time was 11.7 seconds.

5Her largest fame was still ahead, and the sport was different. Golf was the game. She did not pick up a club until she was twenty-one. Practice was focused. Practice was determined. From 1934 on, golf was the only sport she played. A thousand balls a day was her habit. Blisters formed, and she taped over them. Her first championship arrived the following year. That year was 1935. Marriage came in 1938. George Zaharias was a professional wrestler. She had met him while playing golf. Across the next twenty years she won eighty-two tournaments. Seventeen of them came in a row. Those seasons were 1946 and 1947. In 1949 she and Patty Berg started the Ladies Professional Golf Association, the LPGA. They founded it together. Doctors found cancer in 1953, while she was at the top of her game. An operation followed. Doctors thought golf was finished for her. Only four months passed before the pro tour included her again. She needed proof, for herself and for her fans. She could still play at a professional level. A picture shows her driving toward the green. She kept playing through 1955 and 1956. Cancer took her life in 1956. She was forty-five. Family members were devastated. Millions of fans were devastated too. Two Halls of Fame hold her. Golf inducted her in 1951. Track and field inducted her in 1974, after her death. Six different times, voters chose her as Woman Athlete of the Year. Nobody else has been picked that often. A picture shows her with one of many trophies. Her fight for women athletes was fierce. Equality, in her hands, did not reach every peer. At times her comments about people of color were racist. One infamous moment stands out. She threw a pitcher of ice water. It landed on two sleeping teammates. Black women had not run on the Olympic track team of the United States before those two. Her athletic greatness is beyond doubt. Her character did not match that greatness.

6Picture major league baseball with no Frank Thomas. Picture it with no Derek Jeter and no Alex Rodriguez. Picture the Baseball Hall of Fame with no Hank Aaron. Picture it with no Willie Mays and no Roberto Clemente. Picture it without so many other brilliant Black players and Latino players. Those gaps are hard to imagine. They were possible. They did not happen, because Jackie Robinson had courage. He had determination. Major League Baseball had never included a Black player before him. His first day was April 15, 1947. A picture shows him in uniform. In that era, people of color faced discrimination in many parts of life. Sports was one of those parts. Major leagues allowed white players only. Black players who loved baseball built leagues of their own. Those leagues helped Black communities grow economically. They developed talented stars. They drew many fans. The Brooklyn Dodgers employed Branch Rickey as general manager. He knew the color bar was wrong. Talented players were being shut out because of skin color. The wrong fell on the players. It also fell on baseball. He wanted integrated teams. He knew the first person through that door would need to be special. Racism would have to be faced. The color barrier would have to break. Then he found Jackie Robinson. Hitting was a strength. Running was a strength. Fielding was a strength. He matched anyone. Fans loved the daring way he ran and stole bases. Opponents were unnerved. In 1946 alone he stole forty bases. He was a fierce competitor. A bunt could beat you. A hard hit could beat you. Character, above all, could beat you. Before that jump, the minor leagues held him for a year. His batting record was the best. He led that team to a championship. He was twenty-eight when he left the Kansas City Monarchs. The Brooklyn Dodgers were his new team.

7The rookie season was an ordeal. Players on other teams shouted insults. Pitchers threw at him on purpose. Fans booed. His family received threats. Even some teammates treated him badly. He answered with quiet dignity. He answered with determination. His temper held. His fists stayed down. Skill on the diamond did the talking. Twelve home runs came in that rookie year. Stolen bases were a category he led across the National League. He won the award given to the season's best new player. The year 1949 brought the National League batting title. It also brought the prize for the player judged most valuable. Pay in 1950 made him the top earner on the Brooklyn Dodgers. He was the leader of that team. He showed what mattered, on the field and away from it. Ability mattered. If you could play at a big-league standard, the majors were where you belonged. Other teams soon began hiring Black players. They hired Latino players too. America's best-known team sport looks different now. Players come from every race and nationality. So do coaches, managers, and owners. A note fills in his earlier life. A scholarship took him to a Los Angeles campus of the University of California. People shorten that school name to UCLA. He earned varsity letters there in baseball, in basketball, in football, and in track and field. World War II found him in the army of the United States. Black officers were scarce there, and he was among that small number. Baseball was not the only door that needed opening. Tennis needed a Black woman to open it. Althea Gibson was that player. Her parents worked as sharecroppers. South Carolina was the state, and 1927 was the year. Harlem became the family's home. She was three. Street games filled her new New York City neighborhood every day. She grew tall. She grew athletic. She dominated those games. At twelve she won a citywide paddle tennis tournament. Love of sport led her to skip school. She left school for good in seventh grade. A picture shows her working hard to build her tennis game.

8Tennis came next, and she learned it fast. Two Black physicians noticed her. One was Dr. Robert Johnson. The other was Dr. Hubert Eaton. They were searching for young Black athletes who might reach the top of tennis. They backed her growth as a player. They also made sure high school was finished. She rose to the top of the American Tennis Association. That association was all Black, and people call it the ATA. No Black woman had entered the National Indoor Championships before her. She played them in 1949. The same year brought a shut door. She was barred from the U.S. National Championships because she was Black. Those championships are now called the U.S. Open. A public outcry followed. Alice Marble led it. Marble had won the U.S. Nationals four times. The next year Gibson was invited to the U.S. Open. The year after that, a British invitation arrived. She was the first Black player asked to Wimbledon. Wimbledon, in the United Kingdom, is one of the world's biggest tennis championships. A 1956 picture shows her rushing the net at the U.S. National Championships. School continued off the court. An athletic scholarship took her to Florida A&M University. The city was Tallahassee. She played tennis for the school. She played basketball. She played golf. A degree in physical education was completed in 1953. A Grand Slam singles title had never gone to a Black player before 1956, when she won one. That win was a single major title. It was not all four of the world's top tennis tournaments in one year. Doubles brought another title that year. She and Angela Buxton won the women's doubles at Wimbledon. Singles at Wimbledon fell to her in 1957. Queen Elizabeth II handed her the trophy. New York welcomed her home with a ticker tape parade. The streets were packed with fans. The number was higher than a hundred thousand. She closed that year by taking the national tennis title held in the United States. The next year she won Wimbledon again. She won the U.S. Nationals again. Sports Illustrated put her on a cover. Time magazine did too. Female Player of the Year was the title the Associated Press gave her. The honor came two years in a row. Golf later filled her calendar. Between 1963 and 1977 she played in 171 golf events.

9Tennis alone would have secured her place among top athletes. She was not finished. Golf was the next sport. At that time it was played almost only by white people who had money. Black golfers had not held membership in the Ladies Professional Golf Association before her. She joined in 1964. People call that group the LPGA. Many golf clubs in the country still refused Black golfers. Membership was closed. The course was closed. Clubs that let her play often shut her out of the clubhouse. Bathrooms were shut too. She changed clothes in her car. Death threats arrived. Racist insults came from the crowd. She was not swayed. Some courses on the tour changed an open event into an invitational. The change was a way to keep her out. LPGA players voted to boycott those events unless everyone was welcome. The clubs backed down. Another color barrier broke. She was a fantastic athlete and a hard competitor. Two different sports gained a way in for pros who were players of color, and she was the one who opened it. She also cleared a path for later Black tennis greats. Arthur Ashe was one. Venus Williams was one. Serena Williams was one. A different legend begins with speed. James Cleveland Owens, called Jesse, was born in Alabama in 1913. He burst onto the sports scene in junior high. The city was Cleveland, Ohio. For his age group he set world records in the high jump. He set them in the long jump too. A high school track coach asked him to join the team. Family support fell partly on Jesse, so he worked after school. Showing up with the squad at the usual practice hour was impossible. Training happened at 5:00 a.m. His coach was there with him. A picture shows Jesse Owens.

10The legend kept growing. High school athletes from around the country met for a track contest. There he matched a world record. The race was the 100-yard dash. The time was 9.4 seconds. The long jump brought a new world record. The mark was 22 feet 11 3/4 inches, or 7 meters. College brought a championship meet in 1935. New world records fell in the 220-yard dash. They fell in the long jump. They fell in the 220-yard low hurdles. The 100-yard dash gave him another match of the existing world record. The time was again 9.4 seconds. No track and field athlete had ever done so much. The burst of records took about an hour. A back injury was already with him. He had fallen down a flight of stairs. Even with all those records, larger triumphs still waited. A picture shows him at the 1936 Olympic Games, several strides ahead of the field. Those Games were the Summer Olympics in Berlin, Germany. The year was 1936, just before World War II began. He was not welcome there. Adolf Hitler, the Nazi leader, ruled Germany. Hitler believed that white people who were not Jewish formed a master race. He believed that race stood above all others. Their label for Black people was the word primitive. Hitler expected the Games to prove his ideas. Owens was not intimidated by Hitler's attitude. Threats did not intimidate him either. The track in Berlin was his answer, and he gave it four times. Four gold medals were his. Olympic history had never seen that. Track and field would not match the feat for twelve years. Homecoming brought a ticker-tape parade. Admiration came with the cheers. He toured the United States. He toured the world. Young people heard a push to give a full effort. Leaders of the United States government gave him a title. He was America's Ambassador of Sports. Later life brought the Presidential Medal of Freedom. President Gerald R. Ford awarded it in 1976. A 1953 picture shows him at home, smiling widely.

11The twentieth century was an astonishing time. The professional sports world we know grew up in those years. Along the way, certain athletes stood apart from a crowd that was already full of talent. Their abilities astonished the world. Their sports changed for good. Their societies changed for the better. They helped make sure the highest level of competition would be open to everyone. Memory will keep them as American sports legends. A few words help a reader of their stories. Accomplished means to succeed at doing or achieving something. Dominated means standing above the rest through success, influence, or power inside a contest. Achievements are successes reached through effort. Integrate means to bring different ideas, or different groups of people, together. Astonishing describes something that causes surprise. Intimidated means fear, or a sense of being swamped, was pressed onto someone. Determination is the drive to keep working toward a hard goal. Omissions are things or people left out. Dignity is the quality of being worthy of respect and of honor. Revolutionized means made enormous changes. Versatile means able to serve in lots of different ways. Discriminated means given unfair treatment over race, over age, over sex, over religion, or over another kind of difference.

11. Blue Whales: Giant Mammals

1A person is about 6 feet (1.8 m) tall and weighs 175 pounds (79.4 kg). A blue whale can be 100 feet (30.5 m) long and weigh 200 tons (181.4 mt). Blue whales live in every ocean, and a large group lives in the northeastern Pacific. About 2,800 travel each year between Alaska and Costa Rica for milder water and food. Off California, biologists on a research boat scan the calm horizon. They see a spout three stories high from Balaenoptera musculus, the blue whale. Scientists study these giant mammals to learn about their behavior and migration.

2A blue whale breathes air through blowholes and has blubber plus hairlike baleen in its upper jaw. Mammals breathe air, are warm-blooded, make milk, and have hair at some stage of growth. The blue whale is the largest known animal, equal to about four brontosauruses. A typical adult weighs 200 tons (181.4 mt) and is about 100 feet (30.5 m) long. Its tongue weighs as much as an elephant, and a person could crawl through its main heart vessels. On land, gravity would collapse its body, but water buoyancy helps support it. It cruises at 5 miles per hour (8 kmph) and can reach 20 miles per hour (32 kmph). Its pectoral fins and flexible spine help it move, and watchers look for the round flukeprint its tail flukes leave.

3Its two blowholes work like human nostrils. Its lungs hold more than 1,000 gallons (3,785.4 L) of air, while adult human lungs hold about 1.3 gallons (5 L). It rises, blows air and water vapor 30 feet (9.1 m) high, and fills its lungs in under two seconds. The blowholes join the lungs by the trachea, and a whale cannot breathe through its mouth. It takes several breaths, then a flap covers the blowholes as it dives for twenty to thirty minutes. Blue whales are shallow divers and rarely go deeper than 700 feet (213.4 m). A sperm whale can dive more than four times deeper. Thick blubber insulates them, adds buoyancy, stores food energy, and helps mothers stay with newborn calves.

4Krill are the main food of a blue whale, and they often swarm near the surface. These tiny shrimplike crustaceans fit a throat that is only inches wide. Blue whales have no teeth, so they must swallow food whole. Toothed whales, such as sperm whales, are Odontoceti, while baleen whales are Mysticeti. A blue whale can have eight hundred keratin baleen plates, fringed like a mustache, that strain food. It gulps thousands of gallons of krill-filled water, then its tongue pushes the water out. The krill stay in its mouth and are swallowed whole. It makes many dives into a krill swarm, eats about forty million krill a day, and burns up to 3 million calories (3,000 kcal).

5Blue whales live in every ocean and usually travel alone or in pairs, not in pods. In winter they move toward lower latitudes to find krill.
