A popular place for Pacific blue whales is the Costa Rica Dome. There, summer currents force frigid air to the surface and support lots of plankton and krill. Throat grooves let a whale gulp up to 17,000 gallons (64,352 L) of water at a time. A female gives birth about every two or three years in warm water, after a year-long gestation. Newborns have little blubber, weigh over 5,000 pounds (2,268 kg), are about 25 feet (7.6 m) long, and swim up at once to breathe. A calf stays with its mother for at least six months, then is weaned and searches for krill alone. It may drink 100 gallons (378.5 L) of milk and gain over 200 pounds (90.7 kg) daily, and it is mature by age ten.

6Blue whales are the world's largest and loudest animals, and their calls beat a jet engine. The low sounds travel for miles, but people need special gear to hear them. Some scientists think songs act as sonar in dark water. Others think the whales sing about where they are and what they do. Leaping from the water is called breaching. A decibel (dB) measures loudness: talk is 70, a jet is 140, a rock concert is 150, and a blue whale call is 180. Only males sing, and songs differ a little from place to place. Indian Ocean whales sing four notes, and calm-sea songs can be heard 1,000 miles (1,600 km) away.

7Blue whales still fascinate researchers around the world. In the early to mid-twentieth century, hunting nearly drove them to extinction. Ships can also hit them in the open ocean. They are endangered and protected by the International Whaling Commission. Hunting bans are hard to enforce, and the population has not fully recovered. Scientists study migration and feeding to learn how these giants live and survive. They also watch environmental and human threats, hoping numbers will rebound. About ten to twenty-five thousand blue whales live today, but once there were over three hundred thousand.

12. Brothers Who Sent a Balloon Up

1A map of early balloon flights sits near Paris, in France. Labels include Gonesse, Saint Denis, Belleville, and the Tuileries Garden. Versailles and Paris are marked too. England, Germany, Italy, and Spain appear on the wider view. The Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea are named. Four dates are printed on the map. They are August 27, 1783, September 19, 1783, November 21, 1783, and December 1, 1783. A scale runs from 0 to 1 in miles and in kilometers. The topics begin with people watching a new age start. Two brothers and their big ideas come next. Then come balloons driven by smoke, a rivalry, a climb into the blue, and what lighter-than-air flight left behind. A word list ends the book. September 19, 1783, fell on an afternoon when a thrilled crowd packed the grounds. The place was the Palace of Versailles. The palace stands just outside Paris, in France. The count of people was 130,000. The event was a trial of a big balloon lifted by heated air. Two French brothers had built it. Their names were Joseph-Michel Montgolfier and Jacques-Etienne Montgolfier. King Louis XVI watched from the palace courtyard. Queen Marie Antoinette watched with him. Silk and paper formed the balloon. Gold designs lay on a blue field. The air felt tense. Nobody yet knew how dangerous flight might be. Humans were not the riders. Three animals shared the hanging wicker basket. One was a sheep. One was a rooster. One was a duck.

2The animals were part of a science test. A sheep's body was judged near enough to a human body to make a fair trial. The rooster came along for a different reason. It is a bird, yet it cannot fly very far up. The duck, which does fly high, was there to reveal any other danger in the trip. A pit fire supplied smoky heated air, and that air went into the balloon. Release came a little past 1:00 in the afternoon. Watchers stared as it climbed. The height was about 460 meters, or 1,500 feet. Eight minutes after that, it came down to Earth. The landing was 3.2 kilometers away, which is 2 miles. The animals were not hurt. A dream as old as people, flight, had begun at last. The path was open for humans to rise into the clouds. Much of the credit belonged to the Montgolfiers. Those two brothers were among sixteen children. Their parents were Pierre Montgolfier and Anne Montgolfier. Home was Annonay, a town in the south of France. Pierre made paper and did well at it. Writing paper for King Louis XVI's court came officially from his factories. That contract kept the family financially safe. Joseph and Etienne took charge of the family firm in the 1770s. Spare hours were plentiful for other interests. Flight began to fascinate Joseph when he was in his early forties. From the 1600s onward, scientists had hunted for a craft lighter than air. Buoyancy would be what held it up. Nobody had yet learned how to build that craft. The ancient Greek mathematician Archimedes was the first to understand buoyancy. Density is the weight of an object for a set amount of space. Buoyancy compares that density with the density of a fluid the object sits in. A fluid here may be a liquid. It may also be a gas. If the object is less dense than the fluid, an upward force acts on it.

3Joseph had a theory. A gas lighter than air, held inside a light shell, might push upward hard enough to matter. He read about hydrogen. People then called it inflammable air, because it can explode. Scientists had known of this gas for quite a while. Early chemists sometimes made a gas that could burn. They did not know what the gas was. In 1766 an English chemist, Henry Cavendish, showed that the gas was an element. Inflammable air was the label he chose. A French chemist, Antoine Lavoisier, gave it a new name in 1783. The name was hydrogen. Joseph packed small paper balls with hydrogen and let them go. The tests disappointed him. The balls rose only a few meters, then sank. Hydrogen atoms are tiny enough to slip through paper. They then spread out into the air around them. Elements are the chemical pieces that build the universe. Atoms make up every element. An atom is the smallest bit that still acts like that substance. Oxygen is an element. Hydrogen is an element too. One atom of oxygen can join two atoms of hydrogen. Together they make one molecule of water. Joseph searched for a different way to build what he called an ascending machine. One day he watched shirts dry over a smoky fire. The cloth puffed upward. Like most people, he had watched smoke leave chimneys. Smoke, he decided, was the answer. A picture shows Joseph-Michel Montgolfier. Early in 1783 the brothers burned many materials that can catch fire. They wanted the ones that made the most smoke. Damp straw mixed with chopped wool won that test. The smell was awful. The smoke still lifted any light container. A picture shows Jacques-Etienne Montgolfier. The brothers decided the smoke held some unknown part that could lift things. They named that wonderful stuff Montgolfier gas. No such stuff existed. Hot air itself did the lifting. Heat makes the molecules in air move faster. The air then spreads out and grows less dense. Inside a balloon's envelope, that lighter air carries the balloon up.

4The brothers still did not grasp the real science of hot-air balloons. They kept trusting Montgolfier gas. They kept making smoke that smelled foul. Their test balloons worked, so they had no cause to doubt the idea. They tried several materials for the envelope. Silk was one. Paper was another. Linen was another. The balloons also grew larger as the work went on. Each one climbed higher than the last. Crowds started to notice. On June 4, 1783, the town square in Annonay was full. The test used a large balloon of cloth with a paper lining. Nobody rode in it. Amazed watchers saw it climb some 2,000 meters, or 6,560 feet. The flight lasted ten minutes. It came down about 2 kilometers away, which is 1.2 miles. Tests like this one set off a balloon craze across France. The excited French first called the craft ascending machines. Later they said aerostats. The word balloon came only after the Montgolfiers had made history. It was taken from the French word ballon. In French it names a big play ball. The brothers wanted the French Academy of Sciences to recognize the work in an official way. A seal of approval from that famous body helped inventors a great deal. It raised their prestige. It won admiration. They hoped it would also win the king's support. The ruler, in turn, would enjoy public praise for backing a striking step in technology. The academy refused to approve them yet. It chose to wait, in case a better balloon appeared. Jacques Charles, a physicist, was the chief competitor. He wanted to build a balloon that used hydrogen. The Montgolfiers had dropped hydrogen long before. Hot air was their choice. Charles still saw strong promise in hydrogen. In July 1783 he started building. Public gifts paid for the work. Two brothers helped him. They were Nicolas-Louis Robert and Anne-Jean Robert. Both were professional engineers. The three made a small test balloon of silk. A rubber coating kept the hydrogen from leaking out.

5Meanwhile the Montgolfiers won a large victory. Reports of their tests reached King Louis. He asked them to come to Paris. He wanted a dazzling balloon that would show his glory to every part of France. As favorites of the king, the brothers now got money from the government. Charles had to settle for kind words from the Academy of Sciences. Public money, at least, was already his. Both teams raced to be first to send people up in a balloon. The contest stayed fairly friendly. As summer faded, each side was nearly ready to show its balloon. Hydrogen is the lightest element. It weighs only one-fourteenth as much as air. At first it looks like the ideal gas for a balloon. It is dangerous, though. It catches fire. It explodes with ease. Helium is a clearly better gas for this use. It is the second-lightest element. It does not burn. It does not explode. Lighter-than-air flight with helium is fully safe. Helium stayed unknown until the 1880s. Balloon makers in the 1700s could not get it. August 27, 1783, brought a big crowd to a lawn inside Paris. The Eiffel Tower stands on that ground today. People had come to see the Charles balloon leave the ground. A famous American was in the crowd. Benjamin Franklin was serving as ambassador from the United States to France. The balloon was fairly small. Its width was about 4 meters, or 13 feet. Red stripes took turns with white stripes. The white ones had gone yellow. A rubber mix rubbed on the silk had stained them. Charles and the Robert brothers made the hydrogen on the spot. They poured sulfuric acid onto half a ton of scrap iron. The brothers Montgolfier and Jacques Charles shared one question. Could people build a device lighter than air that would let humans fly? They followed a set of steps called the scientific method. First, ask a question. Next, study what is already known. Then build a hypothesis. Test that hypothesis by watching or by experimenting. Study the data and decide what it shows. Last, tell others what you found.

6Late in the afternoon, the balloon with no pilot was set free from its ropes. It climbed fast. It flew toward the northeast for under an hour. The landing was about 15 kilometers away, or 9 miles, in the village of Gonesse. Frightened villagers saw a strange monster from the sky. They attacked it with pitchforks. Paris then waited for the Montgolfiers. On September 19 they sent up the test balloon and its animal riders at Versailles. The animals came down safe. A trial with humans could finally happen. The king feared a failure in the air. He suggested prisoners already sentenced to death as the first human riders. Others talked him out of that plan. A science teacher volunteered instead. His name was Jean-Francois Pilatre de Rozier. A soldier volunteered with him. That soldier was the Marquis d'Arlandes. Their famous flight was on November 21. This time the start was on the edge of Paris. The balloon was grander than the one before. It stood 23 meters high, or 75 feet. Gold designs covered it. One design was Louis's monogram, two capital L letters wound together. Another was a ring of fleurs-de-lis. Those are lilies drawn in a formal style. They stood for French royalty. Airships of our time include blimps. A blimp keeps its shape only by the pressure of the gas inside. Dirigibles are different. They have a frame on the inside. A picture shows a modern blimp. De Rozier stood on one side of a platform at the balloon's base. The marquis stood on the other side. The craft, called an aerostatic globe, lifted off. The landing came after twenty-five minutes. The distance was about 8 kilometers, or 5 miles. It settled between two windmills outside the city. People hailed both men as heroes. Benjamin Franklin watched that flight. Another watcher asked what use the balloon had. Franklin's reported reply compared the question to asking the good of a baby just born. December 1 came only ten days after the Montgolfier success. Jacques Charles rose with a partner on that hydrogen balloon. The partner was Nicolas-Louis Robert. No people had gone up in a hydrogen balloon before them. They left from the Tuileries Garden in Paris. The flight lasted more than two hours. A town about 36 kilometers off, or 22 miles, was where they came down. In later years the Montgolfiers sent up several more balloons. The French Academy of Sciences honored the brothers. King Louis raised their father, Pierre, into the nobility.

7Love of ballooning soon moved across Europe. The dangers showed themselves before long. In June 1785, de Rozier tried to cross the English Channel by balloon. His copilot was Pierre Romain. Both were killed. Pioneers still kept improving balloon designs. The work went on well past the early excitement that faded late in the 1700s. In the 1800s, craft lighter than air gained rudders. They also gained propellers run by motors. By the 1930s, giant airships carried passengers back and forth over the Atlantic Ocean. That golden age of airships stopped short in 1937. Fire broke out on a German airship called the Hindenburg. It crashed as it tried to land in New Jersey. Airships today are used mostly for advertising. You can often see them over open stadiums at big sports events. Balloons filled with gas are used mostly to collect weather facts. Hot-air balloons are used mostly for fun. Many places hold a festival each year. The sky fills with hundreds of bright balloons that ride on heated air. The scene can make balloon fever look as if it never stopped. The word list gives plain meanings. Immersed means dipped or set into a fluid, or into anything that surrounds a thing completely. Airships are aircraft with no wings. They can be steered and powered, and gas inside the body makes them lighter than air. Inflammable means able to catch fire easily and burn fast. Buoyancy is the ability, or the tendency, to float. Intrigued means very curious or deeply interested. Chemists study the elements of chemistry. They also study how chemicals affect each other. A molecule is the tiniest piece of a substance able to stand alone. One atom or several atoms form each molecule. Combustible means catching fire or burning with ease. A physicist is a scientist who studies what energy and matter are like. An envelope is the outside bag on an airship. A balloon that uses heated air is one example. The bag holds gas or heated air. Prestige is a high level of respect. An experiment is a scientific test or trial.

13. Changed Genes on the Plate

1Tucson, Arizona, is where demonstrators protest foods made as GMOs. The Monsanto company is part of what they protest. Sale of a new tomato inside the United States was approved in 1994. Approval came from the FDA, the Food and Drug Administration. Flavr Savr was the tomato's name. Its seeds had been altered by researchers in a laboratory. Ordinary tomatoes soften after they ripen. This new kind stayed firm for a long time. Pickers could leave it on the vine longer. Markets still received it in good shape. Labels stated clearly that the seeds were genetically modified. Sales were strong at the start. Safety worries flipped public opinion within two years. The tomatoes left the market. Argument about genetically modified organisms, GMOs, had started. Doctor Virginia Ursin, shown in the main photo, worked on those first genetically modified tomatoes. A smaller photo shows the fruit.

2Farming began, and people started breeding plants so food crops would exist that the wild does not offer. Corn as we know it never grew wild. A wild grass called teosinte was the starting point. Farmers saved seed only from plants that had the qualities they wanted, then planted that seed again. Fields today are still improved by that same method. Newer methods, built over the past few decades, let scientists introduce foods that had never existed. Look, taste, and behavior can change without waiting through generations of plants. A new gene, placed in a seed in the laboratory, can give a new trait. Another kind of plant can supply the gene. A wholly different organism can supply it too. USDA, the agriculture department of the United States, describes most corn the country now grows. A soil bacterium called Bt supplied genes that were added. Insects that ingest Bt are killed by it. Insects that feed on the new corn can be killed by the corn as well. Genetic engineering is the making of a brand-new organism. Genes of existing organisms that are not related are combined. The new varieties are called genetically modified organisms, or GMOs. Everyday shopping in the United States already includes some of them. Where are these foods, and what are they? The USDA puts genetic modification at about 40 percent of every crop the country grows. Alfalfa is among the crops changed most often. Cotton is too. Canola is on the list as well. Corn is on it. Sugar beets are on it. Soy is on it. Zucchini is on it. The corn crop is about 90 percent GMO. Cotton matches that share. Soybeans match it too. Modified foods show up in surprising places. Corn is more than a cob roasted for a treat. It is more than a snack popped for the movies. The kernels go further.

3Corn meal is one product made from those kernels. Corn syrup is another. Cereal then uses those products as ingredients. Cookies use them. Pet foods use them. Countless other foods use them too. An estimate says GMOs show up in 60 to 80 percent of processed foods sold across the country. A GMO food of some kind has already been eaten by most Americans, often without their knowledge. A full reading of a label can still hide which ingredients were changed in a lab. Change is what some people seek. They want the U.S. government to force a label on every product that includes a GMO ingredient. Most products must already carry a label. The label lists ingredients. It lists nutrition facts. Shoppers, these people argue, deserve to learn whether they are eating a GMO. Every food in the picture above is made with corn. Benefits and risks both attach to these foods. By the middle of the 1990s, these products were part of what people in the country ate. Speakers for the technology listed many gains for farming worldwide. Families and the environment, other people fear, may face risks from the modified foods. Most GMO crops on the market were changed by added genes. The genes help the crop resist pests that eat it. They also help it resist chemicals that kill weeds. Fewer pesticides on the fields are possible, some experts say. An herbicide can cover a whole field. Unwanted weeds die. GMO crops built to survive those chemicals do not. Time and labor drop when farmers spray whole fields of GMO crops with herbicides.

4Fewer chemicals, some scientists say, can make farming less harmful to the environment. Food can be safer for people to eat. Yields can rise, and profit can rise with them. Other researchers see a different total. Chemical weed killers, they say, have been used in greater amounts since GMO planting began. Insects and weeds may grow stronger. They adapt to insecticides built into the crops. They adapt to heavier herbicide use. Stronger chemicals may eventually be needed against these new superbugs and superweeds. Humans and the environment could face new safety risks from that cycle. Supporters answer that unknown risks are smaller than a larger hope. Genetically engineered crops might solve world hunger. Earth's human population is growing, and bigger yields will be needed to feed it. Researcher David Weisser says a limit on GMOs hurts only the people who are starving. Opponents answer with a different danger. The same few GMO varieties, planted by more and more farmers, leave the food supply easier to hurt. A warning comes from experts at Princeton University. Disease can move faster through plants when fewer varieties are grown. Picture one GMO corn seed used by everyone. A disease that destroys that corn would destroy a whole key source of food. Scientists at Cornell University record how fast genetically modified plants grow. Petri dish lids are where those rates get written down. Seeds for GMO crops are developed in laboratories. Growing them in real life is part of the experiment. Effects on the surrounding environment, and on the plants and animals living there, show up only then. Wind can move pollen from a GMO field. A neighboring field of wildflowers can receive it. Fertilization of some of those wildflowers is possible.

5Wild plants might then show traits that engineers built into the crop. More studies are needed. Ladybugs, bees, and butterflies help farmers, and the effects of GMOs on them are not settled. Some shoppers fear a second effect. A crop whose job is to destroy insect pests might destroy helpful insects too. Proof of that fear has not been shown. Pollination of crops, and of other plants, is work the monarch shares with many helpful insects. Monarch numbers have fallen by almost 90 percent across the past twenty years. Scientists do not agree about Bt. Do Bt toxins hurt monarch young after they hatch and start eating GMO plants? That is the unsettled question. One group of experts blames heavy spraying. Weed killer on crops that resist herbicides is wiping out other plants monarchs need in order to live. Another group says the reason is different. Open land the monarchs can call home is scarcer than in the past. GMOs might not be the cause. Who gains from GMO crops is its own question. Small-scale farmers have seen mixed results from a wide shift toward an industry built on GMO crops. Drift can carry pollen off a GMO farm and onto a next-door farm that did not use those seeds. A farmer may end up raising a crop that was never planted on purpose. Organic farms that do not buy GMO seeds can be hurt by that. Ownership of the seeds stays with the company that developed them. Farmers do not own them. Holding seed back to plant the following year breaks the law. Milkweed is the main food of monarch butterflies. Herbicides sprayed on neighboring GMO fields are cutting the amount of milkweed down. Health is the next debate. Supporters of growing these foods say serious human health problems can be eased by them. Poorer regions of the world could receive more food. Some GMO crops have been built to fight disease. Rice is one example.

6Vitamin A is what scientists are trying to make that rice produce. The rice itself has been changed. In some places, diets lack vitamin A, and blindness is widespread. The new rice might help. Other people say more study of long-term health must come before humans eat genetically modified food. Crops made to kill insects worry them. So do crops sprayed heavily with herbicides. Diseases such as cancer are the fear. New food allergies are another fear. GMO foods can carry proteins people have never eaten. Common food allergens include soy. Eggs belong on that list. Milk and peanuts belong on it too. Across twenty years, studies have asked how risky these foods are for health. Whether the answers are good enough is still debated. Proponents point to one review of nearly eighteen hundred published papers. Those papers, the review concluded, did not show harm to human health from GMOs. Oregon, despite protests, passed a law in 2013. The law stops any ban on GMO crops inside the state. Almost three hundred people signed a statement in that same year. Scientists were among them. Other experts were among them. Their claim was that science has not shown GMO safety. Opponents point to several hundred studies of their own. Harm to human health and to the environment is what they say those studies show. Charts in some studies track rises in depression, in weight gain, and in Alzheimer's disease after GMO foods reached the market. Agreement on the conclusion fails because agreement on the evidence fails. Each side asks whether the other side's research is fair and accurate. Safety studies are not reliable, opponents say, because the companies that profit from the crops are the ones that run them. Industry advocates call the studies favored by anti-GMO activists flawed. They also call those studies biased. Patents on most genetically engineered seeds belong to private companies. Some independent researchers report trouble.

7Unbiased studies of those seeds are hard for them to do. Any new technology hides its full good effects and its full bad effects until study has lasted a long time. Nations do not answer the label fight in one shared way. This country answers differently from many nations abroad. More than sixty countries have taken one of two paths. Some ban GMOs until later study can prove them safe. Others require a label on foods that contain GMOs. The United States allows GMO foods on the market unless harm can be proved. Special labels are not required by the government. Opinion polls still show a wish held by most shoppers here. They want labels when ingredients were genetically modified. In the United Kingdom, an item that contains GMO foods must carry a label. In the United States, some foods that are not GMO carry labels of their own. Clear labels, many people believe, would let them choose whether to eat GMO foods. New laws are being sought in the states where some of those people live. Most of the efforts so far have failed. No state had required GMO labels earlier than Vermont. In 2014 that state demanded labels on GMO foods sold inside its borders. Some businesses across the country have made a pledge. Specialty grocery stores are among them. Any GMO food they sell will be labeled. An environmental meeting in Paris ran for two days. The year was 2012. France's prime minister, Jean-Marc Ayrault, is shown standing. He voted to keep a temporary ban on growing GMO foods in his country.

8Laptops in a lab record temperature and light. Scientists want to learn how those variables change the way plants grow. Companies that develop genetically modified foods, grow them, and sell them say a label rule would hurt their business in an unfair way. Facts about GMOs will not reach the public through labels, their spokespeople argue. Fear is already widespread. Any label that says GMO, some of them say, will stop people from buying. Mandatory labels, many insiders fear, will push every GMO product into one lump. More fear would follow. New GMO products that might help people later would be hindered. Labeling every product, they add, would be expensive. It would be complicated. Only about two decades have passed since people began eating food grown from genetically engineered seeds. Hundreds of published reports have looked at benefits and at risks. Many people still believe the question of safety is unsettled. Seed saving is one reply to a related loss. More than three hundred unique kinds of corn were sold as seed to farmers a hundred years ago. Commercial corn today mostly comes from hybrid seed, and from only a few varieties. Historic and traditional foods have disappeared in many cases. Historic varieties of fruit in the United States, and of vegetables, have lost 90 percent of their number. Seed banks have been started around the world. They save seed from traditional crops, also called heirloom crops. A wide set of crops can be kept. Growers' know-how can be saved along with the seed. The hope is more food choices for generations still to come.

9Words from this book have set meanings. Agriculture means farming as a science or as daily work, including the raising of livestock. Something altered has been made different. To assess a thing is to judge it or measure it. A beneficial effect is useful, favorable, or simply good. A biased view gives unfair weight to one opinion, one group, or one cluster of beliefs. Consumers buy goods or services, or they rent them, and then they use what they got. Genetically refers to heredity and to how living things vary. Herbicides are agents, biological or chemical, whose job is to kill plants that are not wanted. Hinder means to slow a process, hold it up, block it, or bring it to a stop. Ingest means to take food in, or to take in some other substance. A mandatory rule is one a person is required to follow. Pesticides are substances, chemical or biological, that kill animals or plants seen as harmful. Processed food or material has been treated so it lasts longer or works better. Proponents speak in favor of an idea. Another word for them is advocates. A vulnerable thing can be hurt with ease.

14. Chichén Itzá

1A map shows Maya land in Mexico, Belize, Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador. It marks Uxmal, Palenque, Tikal, Cancún, and Cozumel, near the Gulf of Mexico and the Pacific Ocean. In the Yucatán jungle stand the ruins of Chichén Itzá. The Maya built this city of huge stone buildings and paved roads. Its name means “at the mouth of the well of Itzá.” The Itzá lived in the north, and the wells were useful and sacred. A dozen statues or more held offerings for the gods. People lived there from about 450 to 1450, then most left, but the city was never fully empty.

2A temple carving shows a jaguar, ruler of the underworld, eating a human heart. Many buildings were restored, and carvings made with stone tools teach scientists about early Maya life. The great stepped pyramid stands in the center, with the Temple of Kukulcán on top. Kukulcán is a winged serpent, the creator and the god of rain, wind, storms, and life. Priests offered gifts to the gods in this temple and in others. At the Great Ball Court, two teams played Pitz with elbows, hips, and knees. They hit a rubber ball made from forest latex, and one likely aim was a stone ring. The game was for fun and retold creation, while other buildings lined up with solstices, eclipses, and the moon.

3The city includes the Sacred Cenote, a fresh water cenote, and the Great Ball Court. It also holds the Venus Platform, the stepped pyramid, the Temple of the Warriors, and the Ossuary. El Caracol, the Snail, and Casa de las Monjas, the Nunnery, stand there too. Scholars think the Maya chose this spot because of two cenotes. A cenote is a place where water rises from under the ground. One gave fresh water, and the Sacred Cenote was a path toward the rain god Chac. Gifts in the water were meant to bring rain for crops. Scientists found tools, pottery, gold, incense, and bones that show human sacrifice.

4A wall painting from the Temple of the Warriors shows a waterside village and warriors in canoes. Chichén Itzá was one of many large Maya cities. Over four thousand years, their lands spread across Mexico, Belize, Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador. These groups shared related languages, similar gods, writing, and calendars. In early times, cities such as Palenque and Tikal rose in the south. By about 1000, war, drought, or crowded cities may have moved the center north. The south lost people, while Chichén Itzá became the most powerful city. Some farmers still grow corn, beans, and squash together, then burn plants or rest the soil.

5Casa de las Monjas, the Nunnery, is built in the Puuc style. Groups from the Yucatán, the southern lowlands, and the Gulf of Mexico conquered the city. A group from Central Mexico may not have been Maya at all. This mix made many building styles. From the 500s to the 900s, Puuc buildings had strong lines, plain below and carved above. Uxmal, west of the city, shared that style. In the 900s, new rulers may have been Toltec people or the Itzá. Later carvings of winged snakes and jaguars match Toltec art 930 miles west, and Chacmool statues hold gifts on their stomachs.

6Each column around the Temple of the Warriors is carved with a Toltec warrior. The columns were painted long ago, and some paint remains. The Maya did not keep every old building, but they did not always tear them down. They often built a larger structure over an older one and left it inside. This may have kept holy power, marked passing time, or saved labor. Workers built the stepped pyramid and the Temple of the Warriors on earlier buildings. Each raised road had boulders, then finer stone, gravel, and powdered limestone. Seventy to eighty roads linked the buildings and cenotes, and the road to the Sacred Cenote still remains.

7The Haab is a 365-day sun calendar, with eighteen months of 20 days and one month of 5. The Tzolk’in has 260 days, which may be nine cycles of the Moon. The Calendar Round pairs these days, and the same pair returns after 52 years. These calendars show skill in astronomy, and the Maya also invented zero. Some Maya communities still use the calendars today. The pyramid has four stairways of 91 steps, plus the top, one step for each day of the year. Each stairway may stand for a season and help people know when to plant. El Caracol, Spanish for “the snail,” is a high round tower aimed at Venus.

8More than six million Maya people live in Central America and southern Mexico. They speak more than thirty languages, but words for house, sun, time, mother, and corn sound almost the same. Family, community, corn, and the sky still matter in their lives. They join the modern world while keeping old languages, traditions, and ties to land and sky. A Maya woman and children walk through a traditional market in Guatemala. Chichén Itzá is a top site in Mexico, and more than one million people visit each year. Tourism money helped the government restore it and still helps local Maya towns. The pyramid steps wore down, and since a visitor died in a fall in 2006, climbing is forbidden.

9At one time, about fifty thousand people lived in or near Chichén Itzá. Scientists still learn from the treasures they left behind. Digging has revealed much, but there is still a great deal to learn. Only five years ago, archaeologists found jade beads and knives in the Holtun cenote. They also found animal bones and ancient human remains not far from the pyramid. They found signs that the pyramid lines up with the Sun’s path over that cenote. The land and the descendants of the Maya may have more to tell. People are still listening.

15. China's Northern Dragon Wall

1One stretch of the wall stands near the border with North Korea. A World Heritage Site title went to the Great Wall of China in 1987. The naming body was UNESCO, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization. Picture a wall longer than the gap between the North Pole and the South Pole. Line up every piece of this wall in one straight path. The path would reach about that far. The work is an amazing act of engineering. It is an amazing act of design as well. Few building jobs in history have been so ambitious. It is also one of the most famous landmarks people have made on Earth. It stands as proof of the long, rich story of China. Voters placed it on a list called New Seven Wonders of the World. For visitors to China, it is the largest attraction. It is also the most popular one.

2Builders raised the Great Wall along the northern edge of China. The work lasted many centuries. The aim was protection from invaders. Another aim was to shield Chinese culture from ideas coming in from outside. The wall did not always stop those invaders. Even so, a person who meant China harm, or meant its civilization harm, still had to get past a huge barrier. The route of the wall stays near the south side of Inner Mongolia. Inner Mongolia is a region of China that governs itself. When the wall was built, peoples who were not Chinese usually controlled that region. The map also shows Mongolia, Inner Mongolia, Beijing, and the Yellow Sea. Jiayuguan marks the western end. A map key notes important stretches and the Inner Mongolia border. A scale bar shows 150 km (93 mi.). Mountain passes far to the west are where the wall starts its path across China. Planners followed feng shui (FUNG SHWAY). That old Chinese art and science sets rules for space. The rules say how things should sit in relation to energy moving over the land. In feng shui, the land itself is a living dragon. Chinese builders shaped the wall so it would move with the land in a harmonious way. People often call the Great Wall a sleeping dragon. Gansu (GAHN-soo) Province holds the tail, and that end is the western one. Liaoning (lee-OW-ning) Province holds the head. That province sits in the east. Moving from the western tail toward the eastern head, the body crosses deserts. It crosses steppes. It crosses rugged mountains. It crosses lakes and rivers. It crosses fertile lowlands. It crosses beaches. The wall is not one unbroken line. Many separate pieces were built across the centuries. A truer name might be the Great Walls of China.

3Badaling is one piece visitors know well. It stands north of Beijing, the capital, by about 70 kilometers (43 mi.). Nine sections lie parallel to one another. From Beijing (bay-ZHING), several main sections can be reached by going no farther than 121 kilometers (75 mi.). In 2007, a vote placed this wall on the list called the New Seven Wonders of the World. Preservation is strongest at Badaling (BAH-dah-ling). Crews have restored it in a deep way. Its path bends through steep mountains to the northwest of Beijing. The path covers about 12 kilometers (7.5 mi.). Watchtowers there number forty-three. Huanghuacheng (hwong-HWAH-chung) sits still farther toward the east, up in the mountains. That piece is about 10.8 kilometers (6.7 mi.) long. The land around it holds lakes. In summer, yellow flowers cover the ground, and the section is named for those flowers. Two large Chinese characters are cut into an enormous rock that sits under the wall. The characters mean firm and strong. High mountains on the east side of Huanghuacheng carry an especially scenic portion. The stretch after that is Mutianyu (MOO-tyen-yoo), and it extends 2.25 kilometers (1.4 mi.). Parapets appear again and again along it. Watchtowers number twenty-two. Three of them guard a platform at a gateway. Simatai (SU-mah-tie) is northeast of Beijing. Roughly 5 kilometers (3 mi.) is the length there. Major restoration has taken place there as well. Visitors remember how steep it is. Thirty-four watchtowers rise along it. Mandarin Duck Lake splits them, with about half on each side. A short distance south of Simatai is Juyongguan (JOO-yoonggwahn). It occupies a valley that mountains encircle. Soldiers used it as a stronghold. Fierce battles happened there many times. One feature is a platform made of white marble. Sacred statues and writings fill an arched doorway in that platform. High peaks are the route of the Mutianyu section. Some of that section is granite.

4Officials celebrated after a 2009 survey at the Badaling Great Wall. The wall, they found, stretched farther than earlier belief. The government of China has carried out many surveys of this kind. Inside China, people call the wall Wan Li Chang Cheng. Those words point to a long wall measured as ten thousand li. One li is a Chinese unit. It equals about half a kilometer, which is one-third of a mile. Ten thousand of those units come to about 5,000 kilometers (3,100 mi.). China's State Administration of Cultural Heritage, as late as 2009, reported that the real length was not much past that older figure. A five-year survey finished in 2012. Workers combined GPS with 3-D modeling. They also used pictures from satellites, maps made from the air, and drones. The new total was larger. Count every section, and the length is about 21,196 kilometers (13,171 mi.). Long ago, small nomadic tribes of hunter-gatherers lived on land that is China today. Season by season, they moved. Wild animals and plants gave them food, clothing, and other necessities. Near 4000 bc, tribes on more fertile ground started growing crops. They started domesticating animals too. Villages of small size appeared. Farming groups ringed those villages with walls. Raids by northern nomads were what the walls were meant to discourage. By 500 bc, many independent states made up China. A king ruled each state. War set state against state. States in the north also fought enemies beyond them. Some kings hoped to unite every state and rule the whole set. The years from 475 to 221 bc are the Warring States Period. Fighting then was intense. Builders added many more walls so each state could protect itself. Qin (CHIN) was the most powerful state by 221 bc. It seized control over the whole of China. Zheng (ZHUNG), a ruthless fighter, became emperor. His title was First Sovereign Emperor of China. His power was extreme. Historians record a confident line of his. The dynasty, he said, would endure for ten thousand generations.

5Thousands of warriors shaped from clay were made on Zheng's order. Horses of clay were made too. At his death, they were buried beside him. He also ordered a border wall so enemies could not easily harm China. The planned length was almost 4,828 kilometers (3,000 mi.). Conditions for the workers were extremely harsh. Rumor says the construction killed four hundred thousand people. The year of Zheng's death was 210 bc. Afterward, the Great Wall was left to decay. Emperor Wu Di lived from 151 to 87 bc. He was sixth among the Han emperors. He ordered a fresh western section. Its length was 483 kilometers (300 mi.). He also had a string of separate watchtowers placed beyond the wall. From ad 386 until 1279, one ruler after another repaired pieces of the wall. Some of them lengthened it. Up to the early twentieth century, Chinese history was a run of dynasties. In each dynasty, rule passed down inside one family. Keeping invaders out was the wall's main purpose. The Mongols still invaded in the middle of the 1200s. Their leader was Genghis Khan. They created the Yuan (yoo-WAHN) dynasty. During their control of China, they let the wall go unmaintained. Hongwu drove those Mongols out in 1368. He became the new ruler. The Ming dynasty was his creation. Rebuilding the wall was his answer to the Mongol threat. The task was massive, because disrepair was extreme. For roughly the next 275 years, Ming emperors kept rebuilding and expansion at the top of their plans. Most new lengths were placed a little to the south of the older line. After the Ming years, crews have mostly repaired and renovated. A hidden mortar ingredient turned up in recent research. That ingredient is sticky rice. Experiments found the ideal mix. The rice should be 3 percent of the blend with lime. The result is stronger than mortar made in modern times. Today's reconstruction follows that old, tested recipe.

6The Great Wall rose in stages that covered thousands of years. The builders included soldiers. They included convicts. They included prisoners of war. They included peasants. Others joined as well. Force sent some of these people to the work. The conditions they faced were brutal. Early pieces used hang-tu, a rammed-earth method. Packed earth was pounded down inside a frame. Wood or bamboo formed that frame. Some desert spots had no soil. There, packed sand and shrubs from the desert were used instead. Three steps explain hang-tu. Workers first stood up a frame of wood and packed it with earth, or with sand plus shrubs. They next kept building until the height matched their plan. They last took the frame off. Hang-tu first showed up more than two thousand years ago. Those early walls stood apart around villages. They did not form a single long barrier. Growth in China brought change in its walls. A dynasty sited new work by looking at where enemies stood at the time. From 770 to 476 bc, the Zhou (JOH) dynasty used hang-tu walls to surround small states. The Warring States Period came next, from 475 to 221 bc. Walls then shielded large states that battled one another. The Qin dynasty, from 221 to 206 bc, produced large sections that ran without a break. Wall built in that era passed 5,000 kilometers (3,100 mi.). Many people call that Qin wall the original Great Wall. Towers used wood and brick that the sun had baked. Inside, a ladder climbed to a top platform. A parapet with crenellations ringed that platform. Crossbow archers were stationed in the towers. Spacing put any enemy between two towers inside shooting range. Hang-tu walls joined the towers. Four horses could travel abreast on the top. Outposts on the wall's north side housed several hundred soldiers each. A sighting of the enemy brought a signal to the other towers.

7A section measuring 483 kilometers (300 mi.) was added under the Han dynasty. That dynasty ran from 206 bc to ad 220. The Sui dynasty, from 581 to 618, carried out extensive rebuilding. The Song dynasty, from 960 to 1279, added still more building. The Ming dynasty, from 1368 to 1620, took on major repairs and major rebuilding. Some hang-tu stretches were clad in brick or in stone by order of Ming emperors. The crews included architects, stonecutters, and bricklayers. Wooden molds shaped large bricks. Kilns baked them. Mortar then filled the spaces once the bricks sat in position. Where extra fortification was required, stone was chosen, because stone outlasts brick. A drawing of a Ming wall shows the parts from top to bottom. Crenellations and a parapet crown it. A paved surface lies under them. Brick or stone forms the wall. Earth and stones pack the inside. A base of stone supports everything. At Simatai, the section is 5.4 kilometers (3.3 mi.) long. Beacon towers there number thirty-five. More than ten million visitors enter China each year with this wall as their goal. Watchtowers along the sections reach an amazing 25,000. Outposts reach 15,000. All sections together measure about 21,196 kilometers (13,170 mi.). No other chain of structures has ever been built. Width at the widest place is about 9 meters (30 ft.). About 8 meters (26 ft.) is the height of the tallest place. Sea level is the lowest point. The highest point rises more than 500 meters (1,600 ft.).

8Over many years, heads of state on the Badaling guest list have numbered more than 370. Famous people of other kinds have come as well. Sightseers reach China from around the globe because they want to see this wall. Separate sections offer different days out. Millions make the trip every year. Nearly all of them share one piece of advice. Build your fitness before the visit. Sections seen most often lie close to Beijing and are simple to reach. Badaling leads that group. It was restored and opened to the public before any other section. The year was 1955. People have described it as the grandest stretch. Renovation upon renovation also makes the walk there the safest. The Great Wall Museum is on that site. Its nine exhibition halls cover history. They cover construction. They cover art. They cover culture. Crowds are thinner on sections other than Badaling. Slopes on many of those sections are much steeper. Anyone fortunate enough to explore should expect long walks. Climbs will fill the day. Cameras will come out often. A guide can teach the wall's past and the way it was built. Cable cars run at some sections. Hikers can leave one section and walk to another. Overnight camping is possible. Mutianyu offers a toboggan run. Simatai offers paragliding. The Great Wall Marathon serves people who want an extreme sport. Few marathons anywhere are more challenging. The first race was in 1999. Runners number 2,500. Their home countries number more than 60. One runner called the event beautiful. He called it the harshest race of his life.

9Jinshanling (JEENshahn-ling) lies a little more than two hours north from Beijing. The section runs about 10 kilometers (6 mi.). Some rumors claim the Great Wall shows up from space. The claim is false. The wall can still amaze a visitor. Its length is nearly half of a full loop around Earth's equator. A fresh section came to light in 2011. The place was Mongolia's Gobi Desert. William Lindesay, a British explorer, led the expedition. What turned up was a length of 100 kilometers (62 mi.). Blocks of volcanic rock form one part. Mud and shrubs form the other. Carbon dating let scientists place the find. The link is the Western Xia (SHEE-yuh), a dynasty whose years were 1038 to 1227. Before the find, historians had not credited that dynasty with wall building. Work began over two thousand years ago, and this landmark still draws wonder. Further study, and further sections, will open new views of China's colorful past. These words belong with the story. Brutal describes something extremely hard to endure. A test called carbon dating measures age by reading certain carbon left in a very old object that once was alive. A nomadic life means shifting from place to place and keeping no permanent home. Restoration means returning a thing to the condition it had at the start. Domesticating is the raising of an animal or a plant until living with people is easy, or until people gain from it. Spatial refers to space and to the way objects fit inside that space. To traverse is to move across an area or through it. Heritage is a custom, a way of living, or a trait passed along by older generations.

16. College Basketball's Wild March

1A picture shows City College of New York with the men's trophy for NCAA Division I in 1950. Topics run from the wildest time of year, to now or never, to how the event works. Then come brackets, women's wins, surprise winners, a closing word, and a word list. April 4, 1983, is the day of the game. The whole country is watching a national championship game. North Carolina State, the Wolfpack, faces the Houston Cougars. Houston is heavily favored. The Wolfpack are underdogs. This is the biggest game they have ever played. Seconds remain. The score is tied at 52 to 52. Wolfpack guard Dereck Whittenburg has the ball. Time is almost gone. He has to throw the ball toward the net and hope. The shot comes up short. Teammate Lorenzo Charles appears and catches the ball in the air. He dunks it as the clock hits zero. Fans have just watched a huge upset, and one of the most thrilling, in college basketball's past. Chaos and celebration explode together. A picture shows Lorenzo Charles. That moment is the heart of March Madness. The mix is excitement, high stakes, and unpredictability. Sixty-eight teams play. One loss ends a team's run. Anything can happen.

2College sports in the United States are run by the NCAA. The long name is the National Collegiate Athletic Association. University sports fall under it too. It organizes them, coordinates them, and regulates them. March 17, 1939, opened a historic run for the men's basketball tournament at Division I. Only eight teams were invited then. Decade by decade the championship grew into a huge phenomenon. It sweeps the country every March. Canada has a single NCAA member. That school is Simon Fraser University. It is in Burnaby, British Columbia. From 1939 on, people have called this event March Madness, though that is not its formal name. Some of history's finest basketball legends reached the world through this event. Many players sharpen their skills in college. The road into the National Basketball Association, the NBA, runs through this tournament. The NBA is the league for professional men. Shaquille O'Neal first made his mark here. So did Earvin Johnson, known as Magic. Larry Bird, Michael Jordan, and Stephen Curry did too. Many others did the same. A picture from March 20, 2016, shows a Xavier guard. He reacts after Wisconsin beats his team on a shot at the last second. Most of those NBA legends did play in this tournament. They still belong to a tiny elite. Scarcely 1 percent of the men who play Division I get an NBA draft call in a given year. For almost every player, college is the last stop in a basketball career. Glory has to come now, or it will not come. They play with passion. It is common to see a player drop to the floor at the final horn and break into tears. Joy is sometimes the cause. Disappointment is sometimes the cause. Love of the game is always the cause.

3The road to a championship is long. It is also demanding. In 2016, 351 schools fielded a men's Division I basketball team. Regions split those teams into 32 conferences. The conferences are not all the same size. Every team wants a place in the tournament. Only 68 get in. Each conference holds its own tournament. The 32 conference winners earn a spot at once. A selection committee picks the other 36. Athletic directors sit on that committee. Conference commissioners sit on it too. Ten people serve. They weigh many factors. Statistics are one tool. Talks with coaches are another. They also talk with one another. Then they vote. The vote comes a few days before play starts. People call that day Selection Sunday. A picture shows the pep band and the mascot of the University of North Florida. They celebrate on Selection Sunday in 2015, after learning their team is in. A 2016 sheet maps the men's Division I championship. It shows a South bracket and the later rounds. Rounds on the sheet include a first round and a second round. Regionals come next, then national semifinals, the Final Four, and the championship. Four regions each send a winner toward the Final Four. The regions are South, East, West, and Midwest. Names printed on the sheet include Kansas, Oregon, and Austin Peay. Colorado, Connecticut, and Maryland are there. So are Oklahoma and Villanova. South Dakota State, California, and Hawaii appear. Arizona, Wichita State, and Miami of Florida appear too. Buffalo, Iowa, and Temple are listed. UNC Asheville, North Carolina, and Syracuse are listed as well. In 2016 the South's winner was Villanova. Villanova was also the champion of the whole nation. North Carolina is named in the championship part of the sheet.

4The name March Madness fits. Every March, the country is overtaken by pure frenzy. It is among the most popular sports events in the United States. Even people who do not follow sports join in. The fun of a bracket is a big reason. A bracket is a grid of every team in the tournament. People mark who they think will win each game and advance. The grid also shows the route a team must travel to reach the title game. Millions fill out a grid each year. Some picks rest on statistics. Some people play it safe and choose the teams ranked highest. Others love cheering for underdogs. Nearly everyone says they hold the winning strategy. Nearly everyone is trying to beat someone else. The someone may be family or friends. It may be coworkers. It may be strangers online. One famous fan is former president Barack Obama. All eight years of his presidency included a televised grid. A picture from 2010 shows Duke's head coach. He hands Obama a copy of the men's bracket. That year's title went to Duke. The team is called the Blue Devils. They visited him at the White House. His picks did not go well, though. In 2009 he did correctly choose the champion. That team was the Tar Heels of the University of North Carolina. While he was in office, he never picked another champion. Emilia, a girl of eleven, wrote to him in 2015. Her grid had beaten his, and she teased him about it. She said he was a fine president, yet not the sharpest person at picking a bracket. He wrote back. He sent a photo he had signed. It showed him beside the grid he had filled in. The note said that next time he would ask her before he chose.

5Across her career, Patricia Summitt collected 1,098 wins. No one in NCAA basketball history has more. Her coaching years with Tennessee ran from 1974 to 2012. The team was the Lady Volunteers. They reached the tournament every time. Early on, money was the problem, not a bid. When she began, a sale of donuts paid for the uniforms. In 1982 the NCAA opened a women's tournament under the March Madness name. It started with 32 teams. The field has doubled since then. Public interest keeps growing. The Huskies of Connecticut have been the most dominant side in the women's event. They have eleven national titles. The Volunteers of Tennessee rank second, with eight. Some people say Breanna Stewart, a Husky, may be the finest player in the history of women's college basketball. From 2013 through 2016 her team took the title four years straight. The award title is Most Outstanding Player. She received it in every one of the four seasons. A picture shows Breanna Stewart. The stories people love most are Cinderella stories. A Cinderella team is an underdog given poor odds. Because a single loss ends the run, any team can fight its way to a shocking upset. The 1985 title game looked hopeless for the Wildcats of Villanova. They faced the Hoyas of Georgetown. Georgetown was the defending champion. It had won in 1984. It also held the top rank that year. Villanova sat in eighth place. Many people said only a miracle could save them. No miracle was required. What they needed was the finest performance their lives would ever hold. In basketball, a field goal is any basket except a free throw. It is worth two points or three, based on how far the shooter stands from the basket. Field goal percentage counts successful field goals against all the ones a team tries. A higher share is better.

6A picture shows a Villanova Wildcat full of joy. The team had just beaten Georgetown for the 1985 national title. The Wildcats stunned Georgetown. Final Four history had never seen a higher share of field goals made. The share was over 78 percent. They made 22 shots out of 28. That shooting won Villanova its first men's national title. The score was 66 to 64. The Jayhawks of Kansas had a stunning run in 1988. Star player Danny Manning led them. People nicknamed the group Danny and the Miracles. Nobody thought they would win. Nobody thought they would come close. The season had included eleven losses. No later national champion has lost that many games. Kansas took another March Madness title in 2008, with Danny Manning helping. This time he was an assistant coach. In the 2016 opening round, the Blue Raiders of Middle Tennessee looked outmatched. They faced the Spartans of Michigan State. The Spartans were ranked second. Many people thought they should have been ranked first. Fifteenth was the rank given to the Blue Raiders. Most fans treated the game as a light warm-up for Michigan State. What followed is often called the biggest one-game upset this tournament has seen. The Blue Raiders beat Michigan State and knocked that team out. The score was 90 to 81. Middle Tennessee did not win the whole tournament. It did ruin a great many brackets in the first round. A picture shows a Blue Raider shooting against a Spartan in that 2016 opener.

7Two pictures close the story. On the left, Duke celebrates a win over Wisconsin in the 2015 men's title game. On the right, Maryland beats Louisville in 2014 and moves on to the women's Final Four. Every March, millions watch Cinderella teams and rising stars. They watch astonishing plays. They watch shots that win the game as the buzzer sounds. Dreams either come true or vanish for good. That feeling is passion. That event is March Madness. Good luck filling out your grid. Everyone hunts for a perfect bracket. A prize went on offer in 2014. Billionaire Warren Buffett put it up with a loan company called Quicken Loans. The prize was $1 billion for a bracket with every game right. Nobody managed it. Getting every game right is wildly unlikely. The chance is as rare as 1 in 5 billion. It may be as rare as 1 in 135 billion. As far as anyone knows, a perfect bracket has never been chosen. The word list gives plain meanings. A bracket is the grid used to match foes inside a tournament. A single-elimination tournament is a set of games in which one loss stops the loser from going on. Chaos is confusion, or a lack of order. Dominant means more important, more effective, or more powerful than others. Statistics are numbers that are collected, organized, and studied. Drafted means chosen from a group to play for a professional team. A strategy is a plan made with care. It aims at a problem or at a goal. Legends are well-known people. A special skill or a special feat is why people know them. Underdogs are the sides expected to lose. Regulates means controlling how something behaves so it works properly or follows rules. Unpredictability means you cannot tell what will happen before it happens. Upsets are results in sports, or in other contests, that nobody expected.

17. Colosseum

1The map shows Rome in Italy, by the Tyrrhenian Sea, the Adriatic Sea, and the Mediterranean Sea. Europe, Asia, and Africa appear on the map too. The Colosseum is one of the most popular tourist sites in Rome. It stands in the heart of the city as an important ruin of ancient Rome. It is an amphitheater, a round or oval building with seats in curved rows around an open space. The audience surrounds the stage, so it is easier to see the action. This example of Roman architecture was the world’s largest amphitheater when it was built. It still shows the power and lasting impact of the Roman Empire.

2Today Rome is a sprawling city known as the Eternal City. Visitors from around the world come for its museums, historic monuments, and food. The Colosseum stands among many ruins in the busy modern city. Long ago Rome was the center of the Roman Empire, and its laws and buildings still shape other countries. Concrete, perfected by the Romans and used in the Colosseum, is still used for strong, long-lasting structures. Completed in 80 CE, this famous landmark is impressive even as a ruin and recalls Rome’s wealth, power, and fierce, grisly battles. The Roman Empire began under Emperor Caesar Augustus in 27 BCE and ended in 476 CE. At its peak it covered much of Europe, the Middle East, and parts of North Africa, and held fifty to sixty million people, about one-fifth of the world.

3Its first name was the Flavian Amphitheater, honoring the Flavian emperors who ruled from 69 to 96 CE. Emperor Vespasian began the work, and a marble bust shows his slight smile and reported wit. He tore down the palace of Nero, a cruel and unpopular emperor, to wipe out memories of him. After Vespasian died of natural causes, his son Titus finished the Colosseum. Military conquests paid for a building meant to entertain citizens and show Rome’s power. More than 292,000 cartloads of travertine from local quarries went into the outer wall alone. Much of the hard labor was done by Jewish people enslaved after the first Jewish-Roman war. They walked inside a circular wheel so its shaft and pulley could lift stones on a bar.

4An aerial view shows the Colosseum’s massive size, about that of a modern sports stadium. It is 189 meters, or 620 feet, long and 156 meters, or 512 feet, wide. It could seat over fifty thousand spectators, more than other amphitheaters then. Wooden planks on the floor were covered with sand from Egypt. It had four floors, with eighty arches on each of the first three and rectangular windows on the fourth. The arches held the stones above them, and first-floor arches were entrances and exits. Professional sailors used ropes on spokes, fixed to beams in wall holes, to open or close the canvas velarium for shade from the Sun. Stairs and most seats were travertine built in workshops off-site, while ringside marble seats were reserved for the most important Romans.

5Below the floor was the hypogeum, a network of rooms, cells, and tunnels. Its name means underground in Latin. People and animals waited there until lifts raised them to the arena floor. Clever machines could open a cage door and a trapdoor at the same time. Statues of famous Romans filled the outer walls. Gladiators and animals came out from cages under the arena. Free women and enslaved men and women watched from the very top.

6Violence was part of Roman culture, and myth says Romulus killed his twin Remus after an argument about where to build Rome. Art of myths, fights, and conquests reminded people of Roman might and the emperor, and a mosaic shows two gladiators fighting. Games began at dawn with trumpets, a chariot procession, and a gladiator salute, and they lasted until dark. In the morning, people, often women, fought comic duels with wooden weapons. Roman slavery was not based on skin color or origin, and most enslaved people were wartime captives sold by generals such as Julius Caesar. Animals from the empire, such as lions, tigers, elephants, hippos, and bears, were paraded, fought, or hunted. Afternoon gladiators were seen as rough men outside society, from criminals and enslaved people to freemen and retired soldiers seeking fame. A winner might get money or freedom, while a loser stood for the glory of war and a noble death.

7Gladiators trained at a school called a ludus. Equites fought on horseback with spears, Bestiarii fought animals with spears and knives, Samnites carried shields and spears, and Retiarii used nets and tridents. Each fight was different, sneak attacks from behind were banned, and about 90 percent of gladiators survived. A gladiator did not have to die if the fight was entertaining. They used tridents, nets, helmets, swords, and shields of different shapes. Emperors took part in hunts of lions, elephants, bears, tigers, deer, goats, dogs, leopards, crocodiles, boars, hippos, and rabbits. Most of those animals were trained to fight, but some were trained to do tricks. Referees called summi rudii oversaw the fights, and a wounded gladiator could ask for mercy as the crowd gave a thumbs up or thumbs down.

8Between four and six million tourists visit the Colosseum each year. Income decided where people sat, and seating was split into four sections. The emperor, senators, and special priestesses had the closest marble seats. Nobles sat second, free Roman men sat third, and women and enslaved people, lower in status, used wooden top benches or standing room. Actors and gravediggers were strictly banned from the Colosseum. Games ended after four centuries, and by 600 CE neglect, lightning, and earthquakes had severely damaged the building. Christian leaders called the games immoral, and money and military crises ended spending on repairs as interest faded. The Colosseum was abandoned and used as a quarry, and its stones form the steps of St. Peter’s Basilica in Rome.

9Natural disasters and vandalism have destroyed nearly two-thirds of the Colosseum. Since the early 1990s, projects have brought major renovations. A cleaning of the outer walls was finished in June 2016. Workers restored the facade and removed dirt, soot, and grime from car fumes. On weekdays, only cabs and buses may travel around the Colosseum. On weekends, only people on bicycles or on foot may pass. It is one of the most famous monuments to survive from the ancient world and a top place to visit in Italy. In 2007 it was chosen as one of the New Seven Wonders of the World, and nothing is a greater symbol of Rome’s power and history.

18. Copying the Designs of Nature

1A peacock spreads his feathers when he hopes to attract a mate. Those feathers are not truly as full of color as they look. Pigment is not what makes the bright hues. Structures in the feather bend light the way a prism does. Swarming locusts raise a different puzzle. How do they avoid crashing into one another? Tiny brains give them a reaction time much quicker than a human brain. Motion is sensed and answered at speeds that leave people behind. Living creatures fill nature, and each one has specialized adaptations for survival in the wild. For centuries, people have marveled at the unusual qualities of plants and of animals. A science called biomimicry now studies a practical hope. Lessons from nature might solve human problems. Lives might improve in ways that are sustainable.

2Life is what bio means. To copy is what mimic means. Biomimicry is those two words joined. Biomimetics is a second name for the work. People learn the adaptations of other organisms and then imitate them. Biologists take part. Other scientists take part. Designers and engineers take part. Organisms are watched inside their ecosystems. Human situations that might gain from a similar plan are considered next. Other creatures are not there to be exploited. The point is to understand principles behind natural behavior and features, then to use those principles. A cousin of this work is called reverse engineering. One way to fix a problem is to study it and invent an answer from nothing. Another way is to find a similar problem already solved and ask whether that answer can travel. Biomimicry follows the second way. A design that already succeeds, or a behavior that already succeeds, is fitted to a new job. Light bends in a peacock feather, and some e-reader screens copy that bending. Images of many colors can be made with little energy. A close photo shows a peacock feather. The science can feel young. Its beginnings reach back across centuries. Leonardo da Vinci lived in the Renaissance. He was a scientist and an inventor. Nature was his teacher. How birds manage to fly was one question he pursued. Flying machines came out of that study. Tools came out of it. Weapons came out of it. More designs came out of it. A drawing he made shows one flying machine. Janine Benyus stands among the first experts of the modern field. Peers work with her. Two questions stay in front of them. How would nature handle this problem? Which problems are worth the work? Animals meet difficulties in the wild. People can watch those answers and turn them toward human difficulties that look similar. One aim of hers is to teach more people about the field. Her work has received several awards. A photograph shows Janine Benyus.

3Velcro appears under a microscope next to a burr. In 1941 a Swiss engineer, Georges de Mestral, hiked an autumn meadow with his dog. Burrs, which are prickly seeds, stuck in the fur. A microscope showed dozens of tiny hooks on each seed. Hair was gripped. Thread was gripped. Those hooks help with seed dispersal. Animals that pass by, and people who pass by, sow the next crop without planning to. After that, de Mestral built a cloth version of the same hook-and-loop idea. The name of his version is Velcro. Two pieces of cloth can hold objects together for a time. Tools are not needed. Hundreds of uses have appeared in homes. Hundreds have appeared in businesses. Space missions have used it too. A second invention sits in the road. Bumps that shine in street pavement can save a driver when the night is dark. They are seen in many countries. Percy Shaw created them in 1933. Fog covered the road on a night drive. Eyes of a cat shone back inside his headlight beams. Copy that shine, he thought, and drivers would be safer whenever the view is short. He had to learn the cause of the glow first. Night is when cats are active. They are nocturnal. A reflective surface sits behind the retina. Eyeshine is the name of the effect. It helps the cat see without daylight. Shaw shaped a small sphere. Its surface was like the surface inside a cat's eye. The creature supplied the product's name. Years have changed the Cat's Eye road marker. Bright glow remains. A safe path through darkness is still marked. One picture shows light returning from a cat's eyes. Another shows a Cat's Eye standing in Yorkshire, in the United Kingdom.

4Some eyes cut reflection instead of raising it. A moth's eyes can take in light wavelengths coming from any direction. Survival depends on that adaptation. Eyes that swallow light, rather than bounce it, do not draw predators. Researchers who wanted antiglare computer screens noticed the same trick. Microsized lenses cover a moth's eye. Dome-shaped patterns on those lenses help the eye absorb light instead of reflecting it. A microscopic view shows that surface. Similar tiny patterns were stamped onto coatings for screens. Reflection fell. Glare fell. Computer work became less likely to cause eyestrain. Paint and roof tiles that clean themselves are another case. People more often call the lotus plant a water lily. Some parts of the world revere it for a pure, clean look. Ponds and rivers where it grows are full of mud and grime. The leaves stay relatively clean anyway. What seems smooth is not smooth. Microscopic bumps cover the surface. A water drop has only a few points to rest on. A small tilt, or a small motion, sends the drop rolling. Dirt and grime leave with it. Paints and roof tiles were made with bumpy surfaces that copy a lotus leaf. Rain then washes the outside of a house that uses them. A photo shows water beading on a lotus leaf.

5A photo presents a kingfisher. Tokyo is where a Shinkansen train is arriving at a station. Japan runs this train, and it ranks among the fastest on Earth. Top speed is 320 kilometers per hour, which is 199 mph. Loudness once put it among the world's noisiest trains as well. A tunnel crossing built waves of air pressure. The waves exited at the speed sound travels. Residents nearby heard a thunderous blast, a sonic boom. Startled people were also frightened. The fix came from watching a kingfisher. This small bird dives. Head and beak are shaped so the bird can leave one fluid and enter another. Little resistance shows up. Little speed is lost. Train designers gave the nose a form based on that beak. Noise dropped. Tunnel speed rose. A modeled swimsuit is worn by a swimmer in another photo. The suit was meant to act like shark skin. Scales of a shark are pictured. A great white shark is pictured. Ocean life for sharks began before dinosaurs existed. Water travel shaped their bodies. Smooth, quick gliding comes from tiny scales that are grooved. Racers in the pool wanted more speed. Suits that copied shark skin were the trial. The help looked real. At the Sydney Olympics in 2000, 80 percent of athletes in the copied suits received medals.

6Vents along the sides of the Eastgate Centre, and vents at its top, let hot air out. A termite mound releases heat in a related way. An adult human can stand shorter than some of these mounds. Rising hot air is the basis of the cooling. A complicated set of tunnels and vents does the work. The paths start deep underground and reach the mound's crown. Heat leaves at the crown. Air that is cooler rises from underneath. The inside temperature stays steady and pleasant. Zimbabwe's city of Harare holds the Eastgate Centre. Builders kept the termite lesson in view. Materials that resist heat are used. Special vents sit at the top. Air conditioning is not required for cooling that big building. A normal building of equal size would use far more energy. This one uses only 10 percent as much. California's Moss Landing power plant was an early site for turning carbon dioxide into cement. Corals suggested the process. Seawater meets carbon dioxide from the air, and the mix becomes calcium carbonate. Spectacular reefs of great size are built by corals from that mineral. People can turn the same gas into a building material. Industry throws carbon dioxide away as waste. Coastal plants that once would have poured huge amounts into the sky now bubble the gas through seawater. Cement gains one of its ingredients that way. Smoke is not where the gas ends. Carbonate locks it in for good. Cleaner air is one result. A raw material in common use is the other.

7Knockoffs of nature are not the whole of biomimicry. Many gains come from fitting natural answers to human problems. One gain is plain. Long ages of trial stand behind nature's strategies. They succeed in real life. Survival of the organisms that depend on them would fail otherwise. Elegance is another surprise, and it often comes with simplicity. See how a burr is built, and the build is not terribly complex. A lotus leaf is the same. Effectiveness is still high. Plants live and flourish because of those parts. The greatest gain may be a light touch on the environment. Other species leave a smaller mark than humans do. Our ecological footprint is sizeable. Waste appears when goods are made. Waste appears again when goods are thrown out. Chemicals hurt people. Trash hurts people. Other inhabitants of the planet are hurt too. Bottles of plastic and other trash cover a beach in one photo. Taking resources out of Earth until they are gone is an old pattern. So is contaminating ecosystems in order to meet our needs. A wiser picture sees the environment as one system and asks about our part in it. Waste in nature becomes a supply for some other organism. Food can come from a dead tree. Shelter can come from it. Hundreds of living things can take energy from that tree. An ecosystem's pieces cooperate without exhausting resources or harming them. Sustainable is the word for that cooperation. Building such environments took many thousands of years. A role belongs to each living thing and to each adaptation. Biomimicry offers a look at how those environments continue. It also offers a look at how the organisms share the work. Moss and mushrooms on a fallen tree appear in a photo.

8What we learn can change how we live. It can change how we make the things we use. Challenges can be met in more sustainable ways. Nature can be the cue. People can be careful about which resources they use. They can think about what happens when they are finished with those resources. Artificial leaves are one look ahead. Solar panels are often seen as an ecological way to make energy. The usual way of making the panels is not very ecological. Silica for solar cells must be mined and processed. The work costs a lot. It uses a lot of energy. Safe disposal of that waste is difficult. Silica is what traditional solar cells are made from. Solar Ivy acts like artificial leaves. Sunlight becomes energy, as it does in a tree. Photosynthesis may hold a better path. Green plants turn light into food energy that way. A new kind of solar cell is under experiment. Organic dyes in it copy the way green chlorophyll in plants takes in sunlight. Cost may be lower. The method may be sounder for the environment. Power from the Sun could be captured and used with less harm.

9An ice fish from the Antarctic is pictured. Icy weather is hard on vehicles and on machines. Chemical antifreeze is the usual way to stop parts from freezing. It works. Living tissue, though, finds it highly toxic. Careful handling is required. A second kind of antifreeze is not toxic. Life in the Antarctic depends on it, and so does life on the cold floor of the ocean. Extreme cold is no barrier for some fish. A natural protein in the bloodstream stops ice crystals from forming. Similar proteins are a hope of researchers. Organs saved for human transplant might be preserved by them. An inset photo, taken through a microscope, shows silk being made for a web.
