That fact became clear as they traveled. The journey lasted more than two years. The group came home with journals. They came home with drawings. Hundreds of plant samples came home with them. Animal samples came home too. The trip laid groundwork for taking land in the West. Indigenous peoples already lived there. The impact on them was severe. A picture shows Lewis and Clark's group moving through the Louisiana Territory. During those same years, an old ally was at war. France fought Great Britain in a raging struggle over who would dominate Europe. Neutrality for the United States was Jefferson's aim while he was president. He wanted the country out of that war. The presidency passed to James Madison. The year was 1808. He hoped for the same neutrality. Neutrality did not hold. British ships began seizing U.S. ships. French ships did too. They searched the ships. The aim was to stop supplies from reaching their enemies. Britain also seized sailors who had been born British and were now American. Those sailors were forced to serve Britain. Citizens of the United States had won independence from Great Britain. Tyranny from that country had returned. Madison sent a warning in 1812, during his presidency. Britain must stop searching U.S. ships. Britain must stop seizing them. Otherwise there would be war. The reply did not satisfy him. He declared war on June 18, 1812. The United States had no navy fit to fight Great Britain at sea. An invasion aimed at conquering British-controlled Canada failed. Facing that powerful nation again was beyond what the army could do. War then continued for two years plus half a year. Both countries' agreement is the heart of the Treaty of Ghent. The day was December 24, in the year 1814. They agreed to end the war. A picture shows a sea fight on August 19, 1812. Victory in the picture goes to a U.S. ship named Constitution. The beaten ship is the British Guerriere.

10One more battle still followed, even though peace was official. On January 8, 1815, Americans won a decisive fight. It was the Battle of New Orleans. General Andrew Jackson led them. He did not know a peace treaty had already been signed. British dead in that battle came to almost three hundred. The loss ranks among the worst defeats Britain suffered. Fewer than twenty men died on the U.S. side. The win sent a clear message. The western part of the country was truly under the United States, not under Great Britain. A winning feeling spread among citizens. They believed the War of 1812 had gone their way. The honest result is different. Victory belonged to neither country. Perhaps the most important result was a feeling. Because the win came late, the United States of America finally felt like one nation. A timeline gathers the larger story. From 1754 to 1763 came the French and Indian War, also called the Seven Years' War. From 1764 to 1765 came the Sugar Act, the Quartering Act, and the Stamp Act. The year 1767 brought the Townshend Acts. The year 1770 brought the Boston Massacre. The year 1774 brought the Coercive Acts, also called the Intolerable Acts, and the First Continental Congress. The year 1775 started the Revolutionary War and brought the Second Continental Congress. July 4, 1776, was the day the Declaration of Independence was signed. The year 1781 ended the Revolutionary War, and all thirteen states approved the Articles of Confederation. The year 1786 brought Shays' Rebellion. The year 1787 brought the Constitutional Convention. The year 1791 saw every state ratify the Constitution, and it saw the Bill of Rights ratified. The year 1812 opened another war with Britain. The year 1814 brought the Treaty of Ghent, which ended the War of 1812.

11These words belong with the story of the new government. Amend means to make a change that improves something. Authority is the power to govern, to give orders, or to decide, and it can also mean the people who hold that power. Checks and balances divide power. Each branch of government holds some. No one branch is supposed to dominate. A compromise is a decision in an argument where each side gives something up in order to agree. A constitution is the basic set of laws that tells how a state or a nation is run. When people or groups discuss a question they do not agree on, that talk is a debate. The executive branch is the one that leads. It also carries out the laws. Incurred means brought upon oneself, especially a negative or unwanted result. The judicial branch tests laws against the constitution. Lawmaking belongs to the legislative branch. Prosperity can mean success. It can mean wealth. It can mean good fortune. Official approval is what ratified means. Fighting authority, or fighting power, is what a rebellion means. A representative is chosen to stand in for others. Speaking can be the job. Voting can be the job. Acting for a group can be the job. Citizens elect the leaders in a republic. They elect the representatives too. Revenue is money received from selling something, from taxing it, or from investments, goods, or services. Sovereign means independent and able to govern itself. Harsh acts by someone in power count as tyranny. Cruel acts by a powerful group count too.

30. From Shells to Invisible Cash

1A bill can be worth far more than the sheet it is printed on. This book follows trade before coins. It follows objects that stood for value. It follows metal coins and paper bills. It follows the reason money has worth. It follows the work of keeping bills genuine. It follows checks and cards, which are money you cannot hold. A word list and a word finder close the book. Plain paper has little worth. One paper bill can equal many thousands of dollars. One check can equal millions. The printed bill is worth far more than its paper. Where did money start? What gives money its value? Why do people want it? Makers and users agree, and that agreement is what makes money valuable. The government that sends the money out agrees. The mint that stamps coins agrees. The mint that prints bills agrees. Banks that store the money agree. Buyers and sellers agree that money they accept has worth. At first, people traded objects that were valuable in themselves. Later they traded objects that only stood for those valuables. New tools then made money no one can see. That unseen money lets people exchange goods around the world. It also lets them exchange services. The two sides do not need to meet in one place.

2Thousands of years ago, a trade was the way to get a missing item. A trade was also the way to get an item people could not make. Families near the sea held fish. They held salt. They held shells. Families near the mountains held fruits. They held wood. They held furs. The sea families and the mountain families exchanged those goods. People still trade goods with one another now. Hand your lunch apple to a classmate and take that classmate's candy bar. That exchange is bartering. Bartering has several problems. Wants differ from person to person. Needs differ too. You may want another person's goods. That person may not want yours. The reverse can be true as well. Many goods weigh a lot. Many are difficult to carry. Many spoil or wear out quickly. It is hard to say how many of one item match a set number of another item. Raw materials raise a value question. Finished goods raise a different value question. Barter let people obtain products they could not produce alone. Currency later let people trade those objects and leave the goods behind. Barter's problems are the reason people invented currency. A currency object stood for a set value. One group might set a cow at twenty shells. That group might set a large fish at two shells. Goods could be exchanged for currency. Currency could be exchanged for goods. Every person in the exchange had to accept the currency's value. Each culture chose its own currency to stand for its goods. The chosen objects were nearly always easy to carry. They were also rare. People could not simply pick them up from the ground. Rarity raised the value people assigned. The work of finding the object raised that value too.

3Ancient currency included stones that were bright. It included stones that were full of color. It included shells with stripes. It included shells with spots. It included leaves from particular trees. It included feathers from particular birds. Lumps of silver served as currency. Lumps of gold served as currency. Salt served as currency. Honey served as currency. Bread, spices, and gems served as currency. In ancient Rome, bags of salt were a soldier's pay. People from Africa to Asia traded speckled shells that were rare. Only scattered islands in the Indian Ocean held those shells. Workers in ancient Egypt were paid in honey. They were paid in bread as well. Some Native Americans traded with wampum. Wampum is beads made from clam shells. Treaty-making used wampum too. Eagle feathers were currency for other Native American nations. Bundles of tea leaves were the Chinese currency. Tobacco leaves were the currency of European colonists in North America. A hard question remained. How much was one particular object worth? A much larger shell might seem to deserve more value. Stripes on a shell might have meant one thing. Dots might have meant another. You might meet someone who gave your shells no value at all. Trade worked only when each side wanted the other side's goods. Trade also required agreement on value. Old coins carried a stamped image of the king. Precious-metal coins were one answer to the trouble with ordinary objects. Precious metals are rare. Many cultures treat them as valuable. Shaping them is easier than shaping shells or feathers. Weighing them is easier too. Metals weigh more than shells. They weigh more than feathers. They last longer. Travel damages them less. Weather damages them less. The first coins were produced 2,600 years ago. The place was Sardis, in Lydia. Lydia now lies inside Turkey. A lion's head appeared on some of those coins. The name for them was trites. Coins moved quickly from Lydia into neighboring Persia. Persia is the country now called Iran. Coins moved into Greece as well. The earliest coins used a natural mix of gold and silver. Workers struck some of them. Workers cast others. The mix is called electrum.

4Electrum coins looked rough. They looked crude. The sides had no patterns. Sizes were not standard. Weights were not standard. Later coins used pure metal. Copper was one of those metals. Bronze, silver, and gold were the others. Those later coins had standard weights. One side carried the ruler's seal. The seal was proof of the coin's quality. Some people shaved metal from coin edges. They saved the shavings until they could make extra coins. Ridges cut into the outer edge were meant to stop that. A shaved coin was easier to spot because of the ridges. Words appeared on Greek coins. An owl appeared on them. Athena, a goddess, was shown in portrait on those coins. Early coins in Europe often showed a god's head on one side. A god's symbol sometimes took that place. The maker's seal sat on the other side. Later European coins put rulers' heads on one side. Detailed symbols of the empire filled the other side. The pictures showed when a coin was made. They showed where it was made. They showed who made it. Modern coins still show presidents. They show kings. They show queens. Some even show which mint struck them. Chinese workers melted copper and poured it into molds. That method is called casting. A square hole was cast in the center of each Chinese coin. A ribbon could hold thousands of them. A stick could hold them too. The Chinese name for these coins was cash. Pictures were not used. Words on the cash coin stated its worth. That stated worth is the denomination. Bronze was also used for Chinese coins. Silver was used. Gold was used. Coin-making belonged only to the government. The center hole made a string of coins easy to carry. A stick of coins was easy to carry too.

5Paper money came long after paper itself. Paper was invented 1,900 years ago. The inventor was Ts'ai Lun, a man in China. Money did not use that paper until 700 years had passed. Copper for coins ran out in the Chinese government. Printing paper money was the switch that followed. Wooden blocks made the earliest paper money. Carved designs filled those blocks. Carved denominations filled them too. Ink covered the blocks. The blocks were pressed onto paper rectangles of one set size. Workers used red ink. They used black ink. Banks that issued the bills put seals on parts of them. Officials who issued the currency added their names. They added their seals. Coins could still be used. Paper money was lighter, and it soon became the favorite. Flying cash was the Chinese name. A breeze could blow the bills away, and that is why the name fit. A European invention changed currency's form. It also spread the use of currency. In the middle of the 1400s, Johannes Gutenberg invented a press with movable type. Metal type blocks did the printing. Images reached the paper faster than they had on the old wooden-block presses. The images were also clearer. Machine printing of paper money became possible because of Gutenberg's press. Hand printing was no longer required. Early paper money in China looked like those block-printed bills.

6Coin making is harder than it looks. A government first decides that new coins will be made. Then a series of steps begins. A designer draws both sides of the coin. The drawing sits on a large sheet of paper. Sculptors build a large model. The model has depth as well as height and width. An engraving machine reads that model and cuts a die. A die is the stamp that marks a coin. The die goes to mints. A mint is a factory that turns out coins. Mints slice blank disks from a rolled sheet of the correct metal. Those disks are called blanks. The metal sheet can stretch as far as five football fields. Heat is applied to the blanks. Then they cool. Then they are washed. Then they are dried. An upsetting mill is the machine that raises the coin's edge. A coin press pushes the die's pattern into the coin. Inspectors look for mistakes. A coin with an error is melted. The metal is used again. Armored trucks carry the finished coins to banks. Banks once stored gold bars. The bars stood for the total of everyone's money. A gold coin has value as metal. A silver coin has value as metal. A copper coin has value as metal. A paper bill, by itself, has very little value. People mainly agree that metal outranks paper and ink. Four cents, in U.S. money, is all it takes to print one bill. The paper is part of that cost. The ink is part of it. The printer's pay is part of it. One paper rectangle may be worth one hundred dollars. Another may be worth a single dollar. The government is the one that says which is which. The year 1900 brought the Gold Standard Act from the U.S. Congress. Each dollar out in public use had to be matched. The match was one dollar's worth of gold held by the government.

7The gold was kept in a bank. That store of gold tied every dollar bill to the number printed on it. The printed number is the face value. The nation kept its gold in set storage sites. One site was the bullion depository at Fort Knox, in Kentucky. Another was the depository at West Point, in New York. Bullion means metal in bars. In those years a bank would give gold that matched your dollars. By 1971, most countries had left the gold standard. Daily life simply needed too many bills. The bills stand for more wealth than the world's gold can cover. They stand for more goods than that gold can cover. They stand for more valuables too. Britain made the gold standard official history in 1931. Forty years after Britain, the United States did the same. Governments now count the goods inside a country. They count the resources. They release enough currency to stand for that total. One country's money can gain value against another country's currency. It can lose value too. The swing depends on how much the country produces. It depends on how well its businesses do. The name for this setup is a floating currency system. Fiat money is the name for these currencies. Paper, unlike metal, has no value inside the material itself. Paper currency serves only as a means of exchange. Many people say currency should come only from governments. A government is the body that tracks the real goods behind the currency. It also tracks the real resources. Some people still try to make money themselves. The false money they make is called counterfeit. Counterfeit has no worth. Goods do not stand behind it. Resources do not stand behind it. No government made it. A bank will refuse counterfeit. A store will refuse it. A restaurant will refuse it. Other companies will refuse it. False bills in daily use also pull down the value of real currency. With fakes nearby, a person cannot be sure a bill is genuine. Here is a test. Take a dollar bill. Take plain paper. Take construction paper. Take cloth. Take tissue. Trim each piece to the bill's size. Trim each piece to the bill's shape. Shut your eyes. Use only touch to pick out the real bill. People who handle heaps of cash can feel the difference. Cashiers can. Bank tellers can. Could your fingers do it?

8Crossing from one country to another is now easy. Changing money at every border can still be a bother. Most nations of Europe joined into one group. That group is the European Union. Many members made their money match, so one euro has the same worth in each of those nations. Every member country mints its own euros. The back of a euro shows a picture. The picture stands for the country that minted the coin. Copying money is hard on purpose. Most countries use special methods that copiers struggle to match. From 1879 onward, one firm has made the paper for every U.S. bill. The firm is Crane & Co. Its town is Dalton, Massachusetts. A secret formula goes into that paper. About one quarter of a U.S. dollar is linen. About three quarters is cotton. Red silk threads are scattered through the sheet. Blue silk threads are scattered through it too. Engraving and Printing is the bureau that locks the exact mix away. Coca-Cola guards the recipe of its famous soda in a similar way. Under the portrait, a special thread glows under ultraviolet light. People also call that light black light. Genuine ink sits slightly above the paper. A fingertip can feel it. The raised method is called intaglio. Say it in-TAL-ee-o. Special pens are used in banks. Some stores use them too. On real cotton and linen, the pen's ink shifts from black to yellow. On a fake printed on cellulose, the ink stays black. Cellulose is paper that comes from wood. The largest currency on Earth belongs to the Yap Islanders. Their home is an island on the equator, close to Indonesia. Their coins are giant stones. A full-grown Asian elephant is a fair match for the weight of those stones. Each stone has a hole. A stick through the hole lets the islanders roll the coin. Bill pictures are drawn so that copying is difficult. The printed words are planned the same way. The portrait is big and full of detail. It does not sit in the exact center. Very thin dashed lines build the face. Bill patterns are tiny. They are complex. Seeing them is hard. Copying them is harder. A serial number sits on every bill. It records the time of printing. It records the place of printing. Several ink colors appear on many bills. Magnetic ink appears on many bills. Dichroic ink appears on many bills. Tilt a dichroic mark and the color changes. The paper formula is special. The government keeps the ink formulas secret in the same spirit. Holograms appear on some bills. Watermarks appear on some bills. A light behind the bill is what reveals the extra image.

9Checks and cards are money you do not see as cash. Bank accounts are common among adults. A bank records the sum in each account. A check is an official note for a stated sum. When the check is written, the bank subtracts that sum from the account. One slip of paper can stand for a very large sum. Debit cards link to many checking accounts. A debit card can pull cash from the account. The machine for that cash is an automatic teller machine, or ATM. The same card can pay a shop. It can pay a restaurant. A credit card looks similar to a debit card. It also looks similar to the way a checking account pays. The difference is borrowing. The money does not come out of savings. It comes as a loan from the bank. A credit card can buy something that costs more than the savings on hand. Paying the loan back is not the whole bill. An extra charge is added. The extra charge is interest. A slow repayment lets interest pile up. The pile can grow large. Borrowing on a credit card again and again can turn costly. An ATM can hand out account cash at any hour. Tough plastic is the material of a debit card. Tough plastic is the material of a credit card. One side carries the person's name. It carries a number that belongs only to that card. The bank that opened the account has its name there too. A magnetic strip crosses the top of the back. Coded details about the account sit in that strip. Newer cards add a microchip. The chip uses radio frequency identification. The short name is RFID. The chip is set inside the card. More personal account detail fits on the chip than on the strip. A reader machine takes the swipe. It then reaches the bank by an electronic message. The message asks whether the account holds enough money. It can also ask whether enough credit remains. If the answer is yes, money leaves the person's account. It arrives in the account of the store. It may arrive in the account of the restaurant. It may arrive in the account of the company. One plastic card is easier to carry than a stack of bills. The owner's name is on the card. The owner's details are on the card. Stealing that money is harder than stealing bills.

10Danger sits inside credit cards. Borrowers forget that the money must be paid back. Careless use leaves some people deep in debt to the banks. The banks then take back the purchased things. That taking-back is called repossession. A negative mark then goes onto the person's credit history. New borrowing may stay closed for a long time. A plastic card is harder to see than a handful of bills. The card can still purchase the same goods. Unseen money lets us trade with people in far countries. Catalogs help that trade. The Internet helps it too. A credit card can buy from a person in another country. It can buy from a company there. The payment changes by itself into money the seller can use. An online card purchase can move money across an ocean at once. Three thousand years ago, the trade was a swap of goods. It was also a swap of services. Bills are a tool of trade today. Coins are a tool of trade today. Unseen money is a tool of trade today. What form might money take after another three thousand years? A stock market is a place where people buy stock. It is a place where they sell stock. Stock means shares of companies. The company's value pushes the stock price up. It pushes the stock price down. Until a sale happens, the money inside the stock is not real.

11Accumulate means to build up over time. It means to collect more and more. Barter means to swap goods or services. No money is used in that swap. Bullion means bars of gold, silver, or another metal. Those bars are not coins yet. Circulation means money is in use. People pass it from person to person. Counterfeit means a copy made to look real. It is often a copy of money. Currency means money people accept. It stands for goods and resources. Denomination means the face value of one kind of money. Dichroic means a surface shows new colors. Light can bounce off it or pass through it. Encoded means put in a special code. Fiat money is paper money. You cannot trade it for coins. Its worth is the worth a government sets.

31. From the Tee to a Tiny Cup

1This book starts with a famous short shot. It then separates hobby players from pros, looks at the game worldwide, traces its birth, explains play, names great players, notes strange obstacles, and lists words to know. People have called Larry Mize's winning hit at the 1987 Masters the finest chip the sport has seen. It is the last day of that Masters. The club is Augusta National. The place is Augusta, in Georgia. Larry Mize is still fairly new to this stage. A hard task sits in front of him. Tall grass stands between his ball and the green. The ball must finish on the putting green. He takes a few practice swings to settle himself. Then he plays a clean chip. The ball travels in a curve above the tall grass. It bounces several times. It rolls onto the green. It drops straight into the hole he wants. Mize wins. The crowd erupts. A first look makes the sport seem simple. The whole task looks like dropping a ball into a cup. The truth is far from simple. Skill takes patience. It takes balance. It takes focus. It takes a great deal of practice.

2More than sixty million hobby players enjoy the sport around the world. An estimate for 2013 put American players at 23 million. They practiced on private courses. They practiced on public courses. Some courses cost a lot. Many public courses stay affordable. Beginners can join junior programs. They can join college programs. Those programs let young people learn, practice, or compete. Only a small group of pros plays tournaments full time. Their pay comes from prize money. It also comes from endorsements. The best men play the PGA Tour, which is based in the United States. PGA means Professional Golfers' Association. They also play the European Tour. They play the Japan Golf Tour. They play several other tours. The best women play the LPGA Tour, also based in the United States. LPGA means Ladies Professional Golf Association. The Champions Tour is for men older than fifty. The Legends Tour is for women pros older than forty-five. Men's golf has several top events called majors. Women's golf has majors too. A tour win brings prestige. A major win brings prestige. Both also bring money. Most pros make a living by teaching. Others run courses or clubs. A list ranks countries by how many courses they have. The United States has 17,672. The United Kingdom has 2,752. Japan has 2,442. Canada has 2,300. Australia has 1,500. Germany has 684. France has 559. China has 500. Sweden has 480. South Africa has 450. A map shows the Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian oceans beside those countries. Players live in more than 130 countries. The sport is especially loved in the United States. It is especially loved in Great Britain and in Japan. No other country comes close to the United States in the number of courses. A different comparison sets courses against population. On that comparison, Scotland ranks first. New Zealand is next. Australia follows. Ireland follows Australia. Many places also offer indoor digital simulators. Golfers use them to improve.

3Scotland in the 1400s is where the modern form started. It likely reached England early in the 1600s. Soon after, it reached Australia. It reached India. It reached other British colonies. By the late 1800s it was popular in many parts of the world. Some historians think the earliest balls were wooden. Early in the 1600s, leather balls stuffed with feathers replaced them. People called those balls featheries. Featheries cost a lot. They damaged easily. Players chose clubs with wooden heads so the balls would suffer less damage. The high price kept most people from playing. In 1848, makers created a rubbery ball called the gutty. They used tree sap that had been dried and molded with heat. Lower prices brought more players. The tougher ball let players start using clubs with iron heads. Balls with a rubber core, wrapped in rubber thread, first showed up in 1898. Players liked them because they traveled farther. Dimples on the surface became standard in the 1940s. Those dimples help a ball climb higher. They help it travel farther. A hole diagram names the fringe, which is longer grass around the green. It names the hole, marked by a flagstick. It names the putting green, also called the green. It names a water hazard and the fairway. A bunker is a shallow dip in the ground. Sand usually fills it. A lip or other barrier usually makes the shot harder. The rough holds trees, shrubs, and long grass. The teeing ground is where the hole begins.

4The game demands calculation. It demands concentration. Players strike a small, hard ball. They use different sticks, called clubs. The aim is to send the ball a long way through the air. Then it must travel a shorter way along the ground. It must finish in a small hole. The winner uses the fewest strokes, which means the fewest hits. Play happens on a course. That course is a large piece of land. Mowing and trimming mark the parts of each hole. The word hole has two meanings. One meaning is the small cup the ball must enter. The other meaning is each section of the course. A course has nine sections or eighteen. Each section starts on a teeing ground. A tee is a little peg, and players often stand the ball on it. The fairway is the long band of grass between the tee and the hole. Players putt on the short grass that circles the hole. People shorten that name to the green. From tee to hole, the distance runs from 100 to 600 yards. That span is 91 to 549 meters. Several strokes are usually required. Wooden tees pushed into the soil hold the ball steady. One pictured hole is nearly ringed by water and by rough. A large bunker sits there too. Other holes may have fewer of these obstacles. Hazards are obstacles that players try to miss. Escaping a hazard can cost extra strokes. Extra strokes hurt a score. Bunkers are one main kind of hazard. Water is the other main kind. Every hole also has a rough. That outer zone often has longer grass. It often has shrubs and trees. Less tidy grass makes a clean strike harder. Shrubs and trees can block a shot. A usual game is eighteen holes. Courses often build eighteen holes, each with its own layout. On a nine-hole course, players sometimes go around twice.

5Each hole receives a rating called par. Par depends on how far the hole sits from the tee. For that hole, par names how many strokes a strong round should take. Most holes are par three, par four, or par five. A great player sometimes needs even fewer strokes. Add the pars of all eighteen holes and you get par for the course. A typical course sets that total at seventy-two. At the end, players who went out together compare full-course totals. A group is usually two, three, or four people. The lowest total wins. A player may also go out alone. Solo play is for practicing the details of the swing. It is also for beating par, or for beating an earlier score on that same course. A swing has three parts. They are the backswing, the downswing, and the upswing. A good swing asks for careful attention to many details. Scoring compares strokes with par. A bogey means the hole took one extra stroke. Two extra strokes make a double bogey. A birdie means the hole took one stroke fewer than par. An eagle means two strokes fewer than par. One perfect shot from the teeing ground all the way into the hole is a hole in one. That shot is a reason to celebrate. Eighteen holes can take three hours. They can take as long as five. Hobby players often ride in carts. Pros must walk the whole course from hole to hole. Helpers called caddies carry the clubs. Clubs come in four main kinds. Irons are for shorter shots. Woods, also called fairway metals, send the ball a long way. Wedges make a short, high shot. They also lift the ball from sand. Once the ball reaches the green, a putter is the club that rolls it. Irons, woods, and wedges each include many clubs. Different head shapes change how high the ball flies.

6Players wear loose clothes so they can move. A glove helps the grip. Shoes have spikes. Manners on the course matter. A good shot takes deep concentration, and players respect that. They avoid loud talk. They avoid noise. They step back when someone is about to swing. If a ball in the air is heading toward another person or group, the hitter shouts Fore. That shout is a warning to look out. Another courtesy is replacing divots. A divot is a chunk of grass a club knocks loose. Polite players leave the course ready for the next group. Jack Nicklaus carries the nickname Golden Bear. Most people rank him as the greatest player the sport has known. His pro years ran from 1961 to 2005. He won more than one hundred events. Six of his wins were at the Masters, a record. His majors totaled eighteen. Patty Berg turned professional in 1940. Twenty-nine amateur titles were already hers before she turned pro. As a pro she won sixty tournaments. She won fifteen majors. She helped found the LPGA. She was its first president. Her work opened a path for women in pro golf. Eldrick Tont Woods is known as Tiger. Many people rank him among the best players active now. His gift was already clear at age eight. He turned professional in 1996. He was twenty. The next year he won the Masters. No younger man had taken that title. On the PGA Tour, his career win total is higher than that of any other player still active.

7Baboons interrupted the 2008 Women's World Cup in South Africa. Players expect bunkers. They expect ponds. Sometimes a hazard is a surprise. South Africa's Nedbank Challenge in 2014 had a baboon racing along a fairway. Kangaroos in a herd bounced across the course at the women's Australian Open of 2013. The strangest setting of all was the Moon. Astronaut Alan Shepard reached the Moon in 1971. While he was there, he hit a few golf balls. Very few players will ever play on the Moon. Very few will share a course with baboons. This old sport is open to anyone who has a club and a ball. Practice teaches young players a lesson millions already know. At least one astronaut knows it too. The game can feel far beyond ordinary life. Words to know. Amateurs are people who play for fun or as a hobby, not as a job. Durability means strength, or the power to last. Endorsements are paid words of approval for a product or a service. Etiquette names how people in a group are expected to act politely. Focus means attention gathered on one thing. Mechanics means the small details of how something works. Prestige means a high level of respect. Professional means the player is paid, and the play is not only for fun. Propelling means pushing a person or a thing forward. Simulators are machines that copy the look or the conditions of something, usually for practice. A tournament is a series of contests that names a final champion. Unique means one of a kind.

32. Games for Athletes Who Adapt

1Akiko Adachi, from Japan, makes a throw in goalball. The match is for women. The Games are the Paralympics of 2016. The city is Rio de Janeiro, in Brazil. The parts of this book come in this order. A remarkable swimmer comes first. Then come athletes who adapt. Then comes how these Games began. Then come the Games as they are now. Then come the events. Then come the many ways events are adjusted. Then come athletes from many countries. Then comes excellence in sport. A word list comes last. A Remarkable Swimmer He Junquan is a swimmer who races at the highest level. Say his name HU jin-CHEN. China is the country he has represented. He has entered several Paralympic meets. Four Summer Games produced nine gold medals for him. Silver medals numbered six. Bronze medals numbered six as well. Several world records fell along the way. The record is even more striking because he has no arms. Beijing, in 2008, hosted one of those Games. In the final of the 50-meter backstroke he looked ready for another gold. He neared the last wall ahead of the field. The crowd screamed and pushed him on. A reporter who was there wrote a line about the noise. Anyone there who could stand was up on their feet. A side note belongs here. A drowning child was once pulled to safety by this swimmer. The child had fallen into a river. He used his legs to hold the boy up and to push him to safety. A photo shows China’s He Junquan leaving the starting block. The race is 200 meters. The year is 2008. The city is Beijing.

2Two Games That Are Not the Same The names Special Olympics and Paralympics sound alike. The events are very different. Only athletes with intellectual disabilities may enter the Special Olympics. Six is old enough to enter. The Paralympics focus on athletic contest at an elite level. The Special Olympics focus on sport as a way for every participant to reach further, no matter the skill. A 2016 photo shows people entering a Special Olympics contest in Washington State. A race ends when a swimmer touches the last wall with some part of the body. Just before that wall, He Junquan slowed a little. The only part he could use for the touch was his head. That slight slowdown let Daniel Dias of Brazil tap the wall first. Dias reached with an outstretched arm. He Junquan dropped to second. Silence hit the crowd. Dias had the race. Junquan had their hearts. At the medal ceremony after the race, a silver medal went around his neck. He took a bouquet of flowers in his teeth. He bowed, which showed respect. The moment showed an amazing athlete. It also showed a good sport. That spirit is what these Games are about. Athletes Who Adapt An adaptive athlete competes with one or more disabilities. The disability may be physical. It may be intellectual. Arms or legs are missing for some of these athletes. Others use a wheelchair to get around. Some have limited vision. Some are fully blind. Many disabilities are not obvious, yet they affect life in important ways. A person may be born with a disability. An injury or an illness may change a life later. Adaptive sports let these athletes stay active. They let them enjoy contest. They let them use the body in astonishing ways. Desire plus hard training has let adaptive athletes excel in a chosen sport. Some go on to the highest level of all. How the Paralympics Began From 1960 onward, athletes who adapt have had a contest of their own. People call it the Parallel Olympics. Those Games are also called the Paralympics. Ancient Greece is where the Olympic idea began. Four years separated each set of athletic contests. A date often given is 776 BCE. An earlier start is possible. By the fifth century CE, those ancient games had stopped. Official revival came in 1896.

3The first Paralympics came about fifty years after that revival. They grew out of a program in England. Recovery was the aim, for British veterans hurt in World War II. That war ran from 1939 to 1945. The veterans had spinal injuries from combat. British neurologist Sir Ludwig Guttmann thought the program up. Say his name LOOD-wig GOOT-muhn. His aim was to make the contest into a prestigious event, in the way the Olympic Games are prestigious. Rome’s Games in 1960 were the first to be official. The city was Rome, in Italy. About four hundred athletes came. They represented twenty-three nations. They contested eight events. Archery was one. Fencing, swimming, and basketball were others. The first Winter Games came in 1976. Sweden was the host. Nordic skiing was included, for athletes with amputations and for athletes with visual impairments. Both the summer edition and the winter edition have followed a four-year rhythm ever since. From 2001 on, hosting the Olympics, in summer or in winter, carries an official duty. The matching Paralympics must be hosted too. A note about Dr. Guttmann belongs here. He was Jewish, and Germany was his first home. While he still lived there, sixty other Jewish people were saved by him from death that was otherwise sure. German officers were told the patients could not leave, because they were too ill. England became his home prior to the start of that war. The Games Today Physical disabilities do not bar an athlete from today’s Games. They are open to visual disabilities and to intellectual disabilities. Ten categories are used. Inside each category, athletes are classed by how their ability compares in the sport they choose. Organizers group people whose disabilities affect performance to a similar degree. Those athletes then race or play one another. One race can include a swimmer whose spinal cord was injured, beside athletes who have cerebral palsy. Athletes with limb differences can share it too. Men may run the 100 meters as many as fifteen separate times. Fifteen classes of athletes are the reason. Wheelchair basketball, like other team sports, assigns points to each player based on disability. A lower score means a more severe limitation. A higher score means a lesser one. A team may put on the field only a set maximum of points at one time. The rule keeps the match fair against the other team. The system is not perfect. Mistakes happen. The International Paralympic Committee keeps reviewing the classes. It keeps refining them, so the contest stays as fair as possible.

4Sitting volleyball is the sport in this photo. A player sets the ball. The match is at the 2012 Games in London, England. Events at the Games Many events are adapted forms of Olympic sports. Athletics, meaning track and field, is one. Cycling, rowing, and swimming are others. Alpine skiing and snowboarding are others. Some sports exist only at these Games. Football played with five on a side is one. Goalball is one. Sitting volleyball is one. Para ice hockey is one. Here are some events that belong only to these Games. Sitting volleyball began in the Netherlands in 1956. It was an activity for soldiers who had been hurt. It mixes volleyball with sitzball. Sitzball is a German game. Players stay seated, and there is no net. Whenever a player hits the ball, some part of the body must stay seated on the floor. The net for men is 1.15 meters high. That is 45 inches. The net for women is 1.05 meters high. That is 41 inches. Athletes may compete if they have a spinal cord injury. Amputations qualify. So do cerebral palsy, brain injury, and stroke. Para ice hockey is fast, and fans love it at the Winter Games. Athletes with physical disabilities in the lower body play it on ice. Sticks send a rubber puck into the other team’s goal. Sweden is where the sport was invented, in the 1960s. Players do not wear ice skates. Each sits on a sledge. One blade, or two, sits under the sledge so it can glide. Two sticks move each player around the rink. One end of a stick has a hooked blade, for handling the puck and for shooting. Metal forms a pick on the opposite end. The pick digs into the ice so the player can maneuver. Football with five players on a side, also called soccer, is exciting. Everyone except the goalkeepers has a visual impairment. Outfield players wear blackout masks. The masks make sure nobody can see, whatever the degree of visual disability. The ball has a device that makes noise. Players dribble and pass by following that sound. Walls surround the pitch, which is the field. A full-size football pitch would be larger than this one. Tackles, fouls, and penalty kicks are part of the game, as in football. There is no offside rule. A sighted guide for each team stands on the sideline and shouts instructions.

5Many Kinds of Adjustment Visual disabilities are met with many kinds of changes in these events. Goalball was created for these Paralympians. No other sport in the Games is reserved in this way. Limited eyesight is required. Three players make a team. They stand inside fixed boundaries. The aim is a large ball made of rubber. It must land in the goal of the other side. Bells inside the ball jingle, which tells players where it is. Every competitor wears a blackout mask. Vision is fully blocked. Runners and field athletes who cannot see, or who see only in part, also get sound as a guide. Spoken information gives cues. Clapping gives cues. Electronic signals give cues. When those sounds are in use, the crowd must stay completely silent. A guide runner uses the lane beside the athlete. A tether, fastened loosely at the wrists, usually links the two. The tether itself gives cues. The guide may also speak. Summer events include archery, athletics, badminton, and boccia. They include canoe, cycling, and equestrian. They include football with five on a side, and goalball. They include wheelchair fencing, wheelchair rugby, and wheelchair tennis. They include judo, powerlifting, rowing, and shooting. They include sitting volleyball, swimming, and table tennis. They include taekwondo, triathlon, and wheelchair basketball. Winter events include Alpine skiing and biathlon. They include cross-country skiing and Para ice hockey. They include snowboard and wheelchair curling. In cycling, an athlete with a visual impairment uses a bicycle with two seats. A pilot sits in front and steers. The athlete pedals. Swimming uses helpers called tappers. One stands at each end of the pool. Each holds a long pole. The pole taps a swimmer who is nearing the wall. Every swimmer must wear goggles that have been blackened. That rule stops a partly sighted swimmer from gaining an edge. A photo shows a tapper warning a swimmer who cannot see well. The finish wall is near.

6Medal winners in the shot put celebrate. Sajad Mohammadian represents Iran. Aled Davies represents Great Britain. Tyrone Pillay represents South Africa. Rio de Janeiro, in Brazil, hosted those Games in 2016. Athletes from Many Countries One lasting challenge is diversity. The Games want athletes from countries all over the world to be represented. Countries with high-income economies show up more than their share. They can spend more money and more resources on equipment and on training. The problem is not only here. It is true of the Olympic Games. It is true of many other international sports contests. Prejudice against athletes with disabilities is still a barrier in many countries. Support for adaptive athletes, and for this competition, is still growing steadily. Five accomplished athletes, from different countries, show what that support can mean. Chantal Petitclerc of Canada won gold in an 800-meter race. The year was 2008. The city was Beijing. Say her name SHAWN-tel PE-tee-klair. She lost the use of both legs at age thirteen. She was at a friend’s farm when a heavy door from the barn dropped onto her. After the accident she could not join gym class. Swimming replaced gym class, on the orders of the physical education teacher at her high school. The swims were four days each week, during the lunch hour. At eighteen she entered her first wheelchair race and finished last. That result did not stop her. Love for the sport had already taken hold. Barcelona in 1992 brought her two bronzes. The sport was wheelchair racing. She kept competing at later Games. She ended her career after Beijing in 2008. Fourteen of her medals were gold. Twenty-one medals was the full count. Five world-record times in wheelchair racing were set along the way. After sport, she became a senator. The province was Quebec, in Canada.

7Ntando Mahlangu comes from South Africa. The first name is said n-TAHN-doh. The family name is said mah-LAHN-goo. His nickname is Blades. He was born with fibular hemimelia. Below the knee, the legs did not develop. The condition was the cause. Childhood was spent in a wheelchair. He could not walk. At ten he chose amputation at the knee. He had learned that the surgery would let him wear prosthetics. Walking became possible. Running became possible too. Before that year ended, his first blades for running arrived. Jumping Kids, a charity in South Africa, was the source. Catching him has been difficult from then on. His first Summer Games were in 2016. The city was Rio de Janeiro, in Brazil. Silver came in the 200 meters, in a men’s race. People treat him as a rising star among Paralympic runners. He was only fourteen at that first Games. A photo shows Terezinha Guilhermina crossing the finish. Her guide is overjoyed beside her. The medal is gold. The year is 2012. The city is London, in England. Terezinha Guilhermina is from Brazil. Her first name is said te-re-ZEE-nyah. Her family name is said geel-air-MEE-nah. Like several siblings, she was born with retinitis pigmentosa. Full blindness came from that rare genetic disease. Running started when she was twenty-two. A sister lent the shoes. Her Paralympic entries began in 2004, and she entered four Summer Games. She won four gold medals. She won four silver medals. She won three bronze medals. Colorful blindfolds during her races are part of what she is known for.

8Momoka Muraoka is from Japan. Her first name is said MOH-moh-kah. Her family name is said moo-rah-OH-kah. Doctors named the illness when she was four. It is called transverse myelitis. Inflammation of the spinal cord is what it causes. She needed a wheelchair to get around. Sit-skiing began at age nine. At fourteen she started working toward the Paralympic Alpine ski team. Her first Winter Games were in 2014. The city was Sochi, in Russia. She entered three events. She fell in one. She did not medal in the others. Pyeongchang, South Korea, in 2018, went better. She won one gold medal. She won two silver medals. She won two bronze medals. A photo shows her in a sitting super-G. The year is 2014. The place is Sochi. Devendra Jhajharia was born in India. His first name is said de-VEN-drah. His family name is said JAH-jah-ree-ah. At eight, he was climbing a tree. A live electric cable was in contact with one branch. His hand met that branch. The shock nearly killed him. His left arm was burned severely. Doctors could not save the left hand. After the accident, former playmates shunned him. They taunted him. They ridiculed him. Facing those children felt impossible. The house became the place he shut himself inside. His mother would not let him stay indoors. A sport was what she insisted he try. He made a javelin at home and threw it on his own. A district title came at age fourteen. Nobody had formally trained him. The homemade javelin was what he threw. His first Paralympic gold in the javelin came in 2004. The city was Athens, in Greece. A second gold came in 2016. Rio was the host, in Brazil. India had never had a Paralympian with two golds before him. Both of those golds came with world records.

9A goal is scored by Joshua Sweeney. He competes for the United States. The goalkeeper is Vladimir Kamantcev of Russia. The year is 2014. The Games are the Winter Paralympics in Sochi. Excellence in Sport The Paralympics began in a humble way in 1948. Scope and spectacle now put them beside the Olympics as a rival. The human spirit, at its strongest, is on view in a way that inspires. The Olympic Games do this too. These Games are showcasing top athletes who reach excellence in the sports they chose. These athletes are strong examples of competitors who worked hard to reach greatness. That same spirit will show at the Games for years ahead. Words to Know showcasing (v.): displaying what is strongest in a person or in a thing. representation (n.): including different kinds of people so that every group is present. prosthetics (n.): body parts that are made, not born. prestigious (adj.): treated with respect and held in high regard. rehabilitate (v.): to bring someone back to health, or back to ordinary activity. overrepresented (adj.): appearing more often in a group than that group's share of the whole population would lead you to expect. medal (n.): a prize given for a win, above all in a sports contest. maneuver (v.): to move about, or to guide how something moves. impaired (adj.): damaged, weakened, or disabled. electrocution (n.): injury or death caused by electric shock. amputations (n.): losses of limbs from surgery, from injury, or from disease. adapted (adj.): changed so it fits a new situation, or a specific one.

33. Genes Behind the Work We Do

1A question waits for many young people. What work will you want when you are grown? A doctor is one answer some imagine. A detective is another. Farm animals, zoo animals, or a home full of dogs are other dreams. One science sits inside all of those jobs. That science is genetics. Look around a family and similarities may show. Hair may match. Fingers may run long. Noses may stay small. Traits like those can travel down from grandparents and from parents. A generation or two may be skipped. If someone says your eyes were inherited from your mother, the meaning is simple. She passed that trait to you. Genetics studies how every living thing passes traits on. The passing happens through genes. A gene is a unit of heredity. It sets traits in living things. An early estimate put the human gene count near two million. Research that started in the 1990s changed the figure. The Human Genome Project did that research. The revised count is about twenty-four thousand. A chimpanzee has a little fewer. Humans do not have as many genes as scientists first believed. The rest of that comparison comes next.

2Shared inherited traits are why relatives look alike. Alleles are the different versions a gene can take. Two alleles are common. Brown eyes may come from one allele. Blue eyes may come from the other. Three or more alleles show up in other genes. Blood type uses the alleles A, B, and O. The material of a gene is deoxyribonucleic acid, called DNA. The long word is said dee-AHK-see-rye-bow-noo-KLAY-ik. DNA is a code. The body uses it to build what it needs. Enzymes for digesting food are one product. Pigment for eye color is another. The shapes DNA forms are called chromosomes. Forty-six chromosomes sit in each human cell. Twenty-three come from the mother. Twenty-three come from the father. You are the person those two sets make together. A detective's work and the raising of dogs may seem far from this science. They are not. Farming belongs with it. So do animal breeding, cures for disease, and the blocking of illnesses that might come. Solving crimes belongs with it too. More jobs join the list. Genetics is a young science. Even so, people were using genetic tricks to improve crops and animals by 5000 BC. Simple versions of those tricks are still in use. Selective breeding is one of them. Scientists pick plants that show traits they want. Fast growth is one example. Fruit that looks good is another. Those plants are bred with others that share the traits, or that bring different traits also wanted. Good traits then reach the next crop. Faster growth can be the result. Better fruit can be the result. Other liked traits can be the result too. Most food people eat has been genetically modified. Breeding did some of that work. Technology did the rest.

3Supermarket tomatoes come in many types. Selective breeding of tomato plants produced them. Scientists try to propagate several traits. Crops that grow faster are one goal. Crops that yield more are another. Better color and better taste matter. So do durability and the power to resist disease. Wheat is another everyday crop shaped by genetic methods. Soybeans are too. Corn is too. One wild tomato gave rise to dozens of varieties. More control is what scientists hope for later. Food plants could carry higher protein. They could carry lower oil. They could grow faster than older versions. Animals are part of the same work. Chickens can be bred to lay more eggs. Pigs and cattle can be bred so the meat has more fat, or less, matching what people want. Cows can be bred to grow faster and to give more milk. Chocolate milk is still out of reach. Someone is probably trying. Faster crops, better taste, extra milk, and meat with little fat sound like clear gains. Not everyone agrees. Genetic diversity, some say, is damaged when crops and animals are altered. Breeding for only a chosen set of traits can lose other useful traits forever. A single virus could then wipe out a whole species, because diversity is too thin to resist it. A stranger question follows. What would a cross of two wholly different animals produce, a dog and an elephant for instance? Would the result be an elephant that barks, or a dog with a trunk? Breeding across species is complex. It can sound ridiculous. Experiments in that kind of cross are underway now. Worry follows for some people. The new creatures might harm the environment. They might harm people. Piglets from selective breeding grow up faster than wild cousins do.

4Every pairing is not possible. Most genetic crosses stay inside one genus. Success between two species requires chromosomes that match up. Animal young from a cross are usually sterile. Genetic problems in the hybrids are the reason. Plant hybrids are different. They can be fertile. Crops that resist disease more strongly may come from them. Flowers of rare beauty may come from them. This argument will likely stay loud in years ahead. Supporters want food productivity to rise. Opponents fear effects nobody can yet see. The environment is one worry. Human health is another. A side note explains GMOs, genetically modified organisms. Individual genes are snipped from one organism and implanted in another. Extra nutrients are one result. Vitamin B added to rice is an example. Built-in pesticides are another result. Preservatives built into a crop are another. Worries remain. Further studies must finish before the European Union will allow GMOs. A ban is in place until then. Many people in the U.S. want labels that point out foods containing GMOs. Animal breeders borrow methods from plant scientists. Selective breeding is one. Hybridization is another. Crossbreeding is the other name for hybridization. Different varieties are bred, or even different species, so the best traits of both can meet. A female horse and a male donkey can produce a mule. Toughness comes from the donkey side. Agility comes from the horse side. Mules make strong work animals. They cannot reproduce. The picture shows a donkey, a horse, and the mule that those two yield.

5Show dogs are the only goal for many breeders. Other breeds were shaped for a job. Hunting is one job. Herding is one. Guarding is one. Spaniels were among the earliest hunting dogs. Springer spaniels are a familiar kind. Cocker spaniels are another. Spain is where they were first bred. Water birds such as ducks were the prey. Land birds such as pheasants were the prey too. Breeders decide which traits a dog should have. Parents are then chosen so those traits reach the pups. Large spaniels exist. Small ones exist. The larger dogs today are called setters. The Irish setter is one. The name setter comes from what they do. They set, which means they crouch, when they find wild game. Irish setters appear in a photo. Herding is something border collies do extremely well. Herding itself was bred into some dogs because people wanted it. Cattle and other livestock are protected and rounded up by herding dogs. Border collies are popular for that work. Australian shepherds are popular for it too. The breeding was so successful that herding continues even without training. Owners often say the dogs try to herd cars. They try to herd people as well. Hundreds of years went into the border collie. Cattle and sheep along the border of England and Scotland were the original herd. Several herding breeds, the border collie among them, were mixed to develop the Australian shepherd. Settlers from England brought those dogs along when they moved to Australia. Wide use of these dogs continues on the open fields there. Cattle are raised there. Other livestock are raised there too.

6Guard work shaped other dogs. The Doberman pinscher is one common guard dog. The German shepherd is another. Louis Dobermann, a watchman in Germany, first bred Dobermans in the late 1890s. A ferocious reputation followed. Newer breeders have worked hard to make the breed calmer and friendlier. The year 1899 is when breeding of German shepherds began. Old herding dogs and farm dogs are their ancestors. Training can send them into many jobs. Herding is one. Police work is one. Leading people who are blind is one. Hybrids are common too. A hybrid here is a cross of two or more breeds. Mutts is the everyday name. Some people think a hybrid is the finest pet. Favored traits from each parent can meet in one animal. A caption credits mutts with favored traits drawn from many breeds. Programs that breed animals in captivity have helped pandas. Zoos do more than teach and entertain. Research on animals happens in many of them. Genetics is one research area some zoos pursue. The aim is survival of species far into the future. Endangered species get important help from this science. Threatened species do too.

7Captive breeding is one tool zoo scientists use. Animals living in captivity, zoos included, are bred so genetic diversity inside a species stays broad. Some young born in captivity go back to wild groups. New genes arrive with them. Survival chances rise. Release works only if the animals can live on their own and can reproduce. Many endangered and threatened species are part of this work. The red wolf is one. The gorilla is one. The panda is one. The cheetah is one. The rhinoceros is one. A photo shows a cheetah. A second kind serves species near extinction. Those animals cannot live in the wild. Reproduction happens where the animals are protected. Importance does not make captive breeding a full replacement. Wild living and wild breeding still matter more. Zoo staff also teach the public a protection lesson. The home places of endangered species need care. The home places of threatened species need care too. Rhinoceroses and tigers, if left unprotected, may survive only as words in books for people not yet born. A side note names the wolves. Only two wolf species are known anywhere. The red wolf is one. The gray wolf is the other. The southeastern United States is where the endangered red wolf lives. Cold lands in the arctic, and subarctic lands across the globe, are where the gray wolf lives. The gray wolf was once common. Its return inside the United States happened only a short time ago.

8A magnifying glass is no longer the whole toolkit. Police use genetics and DNA when they solve crimes. Detectives use them. Lawyers use them. Every gene holds DNA. That code sets an organism's genetic traits. DNA differs from one organism to the next, as fingerprints do. A lab agent is shown working on DNA evidence. Fingerprints of criminals go into a database. A print at a crime scene can be matched to a known criminal. DNA fingerprinting is the name for using DNA the same way. A fingerprint does not have to be found. Gloves and wiped surfaces are common, because many criminals know about prints. Skin in a small piece is enough for a DNA fingerprint. A single hair is enough. A drop of fluid is enough. Blood can serve. Saliva can serve. Leaving no skin, no hair, and no fluid is almost impossible. Microscopic traces of DNA fall wherever a person goes. Skin cells under a victim's fingernails can be read for their DNA. A sample from a suspect can be compared. A match brings investigators closer to an answer. Thomas McGowan is shown in the center, with his lawyers. Jail had held him for twenty-three years. The imprisonment was false. DNA evidence showed he could not have done the crime he was accused of.

9DNA databases are growing inside law enforcement, beside the old fingerprint files. Convicted criminals have their DNA fingerprints stored. Other evidence from crime scenes is stored too. People jailed for crimes they did not commit have been freed by DNA. The first use of DNA fingerprinting was in 1985. Many crimes have been solved with it since then. Contamination could hurt the accuracy of a test. Misuse is another fear. Both worries are real for some people. Use will continue while the method identifies criminals and closes cases. Health work uses genetics too. Medical scientists and healthcare scientists diagnose disease with it. They treat disease with it. They try to prevent disease with it. New medicines come from it. Genes that cause particular diseases are being found. Medicines and vaccines can then be aimed at those genes, to cure or to prevent. Genetics counselors help parents, and people who may become parents, judge the odds. DNA sequencers let scientists compare how different DNA samples are related. Parents can learn whether certain diseases would be inherited by their children. The odds concern genetic disorders passed from parent to child. A choice about having children can rest on that news. So can a plan for caring for a child who has a genetic disorder. Cystic fibrosis is one disorder that may be passed on. Huntington's disease is another. Breast cancer is another. A side note marks the year 2000. Scientists finished the Human Genome Project. It is a full map of where every human gene sits. About twenty-four thousand human genes stand in a set order on our chromosomes. Ten years of powerful computers were needed to count them and locate them. Missing genes cause many diseases. Genes in the wrong place cause many diseases too.

10Jobs in genetics are many. The field is exciting. It is a fairly new branch of science. Fresh developments arrive almost every day. Fresh chances arrive with them. Plant breeding is one path. Animal breeding is one. Medicine is one. Criminology is one. Other fields link to genetics as well. Careers connected to this science are abundant. A library can offer more to read. The Internet can too. Cloning's first healthy mammal was a sheep. Cloning means making an exact genetic copy of one living thing. February 1997 was the birth month of the first cloned sheep. Her name was Dolly. More paths are open for a curious reader. Library shelves hold books on genetics, and a librarian can point to them. News in local papers and national papers covers the field. Magazines, television, and radio cover it too. Genetics is still new, and it is still controversial. Stories to watch include crimes closed with DNA. They include cloning experiments. They include medicines newly built with genetics. They include argument over foods and animals that were genetically modified.

11A few words close the book. Alleles are the alternate forms a gene can take. Captive breeding means breeding animals that live in captivity so they can later be released to the wild. Characteristics are features that help identify a thing or a group. Chromosomes are rod-shaped structures inside cells, and they carry genes. DNA is the code that stores a living thing's genetic information. The letters stand for deoxyribonucleic acid. Enzymes are proteins in plants and in animals. They set off certain natural chemical reactions. Genes are the basic units of heredity. Traits ride on them into the following generation. Genetics studies that passage of traits across generations. Related species that share features are grouped as a genus. Hybridization breeds two different species so traits of both can combine. Inherited describes what was received from parents or from earlier ancestors. To propagate is to make something again and again, or to reproduce it. Selective breeding mates chosen plants or animals so the traits in their young can be improved or controlled. Sterile describes a living thing that cannot produce offspring. A trait is a feature or a quality. Animals have them. Plants have them. Things and groups have them too.

34. George the Third of Britain

1A map shows England, Ireland, and Scotland. The topics run from a determined leader to childhood, then the Seven Years' War. A family of his own comes next. Angry colonists and the American Revolution follow. Illness and further revolution come after that. The close covers his decline and a fresh look at the king. A word list ends the book. In 1785, King George III of England faced John Adams. Adams was the American ambassador standing there. He had crossed to England to deliver a message. The United States and England had lately been enemies in war. Adams hoped to calm that anger. Britain felt the sting of humiliation. Its American colonies had been lost in 1783. Adams spoke in a humble way. He held out friendship from the United States. Words such as honor and affection carried his good wishes. The king's stiff manner eased. A smile came. He answered that the friendly overture was welcome, and that he took it with pleasure. Adams bowed. Then he left. Alone, the king hoped his royal duty had been met. He had fought to keep the empire whole. The American colonies were lost anyway. He made up his mind that no such loss would happen again. A picture from 1785 shows John Adams on the left. He was the first ambassador the United States sent to England. He reaches an offering toward George III, who stands on the right.

2June 4, 1738, was the birth day of a boy named George. His mother was Princess Augusta of Wales. This child would one day rule the strongest empire on Earth. The royal house he entered was led by his grandfather. That grandfather was King George II. George's father was Frederick, Prince of Wales. Frederick was the king's oldest son. A portrait shows George as a boy. Hatred ran both ways between the king and Frederick. The household lived with heavy tension. Frederick once gathered people to fight his father in politics. King George II answered by banishing that son from court. Growing up in that strain, young George was an emotional child. Learning came slowly to him. Reading was still beyond him at age eleven. Fine tutors were hired for him and for his brothers and sisters. His father badly wanted a great king in this son. He hoped this son would outdo George II as a ruler. At twelve, George became the heir. Frederick had been next for the crown. A lung ailment killed him. The boy who would be king leaned hard on Lord Bute. Bute was teacher and advisor. George trusted him and looked up to him. Bute taught him to notice the harsh political fights around him. Those fights would be his when he wore the crown. John Stuart was a Scottish nobleman. He was the third Earl of Bute. People called him Lord Bute. He became a chief advisor to King George III. Most of the fights were between two powers. The monarch was one side. He kept a private ministry of advisors. The other was Parliament, the body that made Britain's laws. A British monarch today is mostly a figurehead. The work is largely ceremony. In George's lifetime the monarch still held real power. By the middle of the 1700s, Britain mattered greatly in world affairs. It ruled colonies in India. It also ruled colonies in North America. Those lands supplied raw materials. They were also fresh markets for goods made in Britain. The nation was rich. It was willing to fight other countries when its interests needed protection.

3One of those wars was still going when King George II died without warning. The year was 1760. The crown of Great Britain passed to George III. Ireland's crown passed to him as well. He was twenty-two. Britain had been in the Seven Years' War since 1756. The war had two theaters. One was fighting in Europe against France and against other states. The other was fighting France in North America. Land was what the battles were about. In North America, people called the same war the French and Indian War. The prize there was the Ohio River Valley. French claims on that ground stopped Britain's colonies from spreading. If Britain held the valley, it would be the main colonial power on that continent. A picture puts George Washington on a horse. Command in that North American fight made his reputation. In that war he fought for the British side. A 1763 map shows British land in North America. Purple marks Britain's land at the start of that war. Red marks land gained once the war ended. Each win over the French, in Europe or in North America, delighted George III. He could take little of the credit. The credit went to William Pitt. Pitt had been war minister for King George II. He drew up the battle plan that worked. The public adored him. Lord Bute disliked him strongly. Pitt belonged to the powerful Whig party.

4The Whigs wanted elected members of Parliament to hold more power. They wanted the rest of the British government stronger too. They wanted the king's power cut back. Bute was a firm believer in monarchy. He told George III to block the Whigs whenever he could. William Pitt was the man to oppose most of all. Bute and Pitt clashed hard over ending the war. Fighting cost a great deal. Pitt did not want a finish. He wanted the war to grow. The king chose Bute's side. Pitt left his post in 1761. Ordinary Britons were furious to lose the Pitt they loved. Their anger landed on Lord Bute. At one public gathering, the removed Pitt drew cheers. Bute was attacked. George III refused to drop his loyalty to Bute. He named Bute prime minister. That job led the king's ministry. From that seat, Bute worked out a formal treaty. The Seven Years' War ended in 1763. Britain gained world power it had never held before. The talks wore Bute down. He resigned at once. King George III had to stand alone. A note beside Pitt's picture says he deserved most of the credit for beating France. Lord Bute still stood against him. He pressed George III to stand against Pitt as well. The closest political guide was gone. A life partner had arrived instead. George read through a list of princesses who could marry. His choice was a young German princess, Sophia Charlotte. The wedding was in 1761. They hardly knew one another. They still got along very well. Over a marriage of fifty-seven years, she bore fifteen children. George liked to think of himself as a plain man. Great power did not change that view. People soon nicknamed him Farmer George. Farming interested him. He often walked the farms that lay across royal land. Sophia Charlotte reached England, met the king, and wed him on the following day. His private life was settling into shape. The slow study of his boyhood gave way to a strong work ethic. People who watched him saw a determined man. They also saw a tenacious one. He kept studying how government worked. Politics got the same careful study.

5Acts approved by King George's government helped start a revolution. American colonists took those acts as insults. First came a proclamation in 1763. It closed some North American land to settlers from the colonies. War debt was drowning Britain. A string of colonial taxes followed. The Sugar Act put a tax on molasses brought in from abroad. The Stamp Act made colonists stick a paid stamp on every printed item. The Townshend Acts came in 1767. They taxed paint, glass, and tea. George III sent British troops into colonial cities. The troops were there to make people pay. Colonists burned with anger. They answered with boycotts of British goods. Protests turned violent. Tax collectors feared they might be killed. John Wilkes was one of the king's sharpest foes in politics. He sat in Parliament. He spoke out against the government. A 1763 article attacked the king's ministry. It called for that ministry to be thrown out. Wilkes never stopped demanding liberty for people in Britain. America's Founding Fathers came to see him as a hero. Colonists were angry for another reason. Parliament did not include them. Their cry was, No taxation without representation. The sour bond with the king turned on a late night. The date was December 16, 1773. Colonists dressed as Native Americans. They boarded two British ships tied up in Boston Harbor. The ships were loaded with crates of tea. In a bold protest, the colonists split the crates open. They poured the tea into the harbor. News of that Boston Tea Party reached the king. Anger and resolve filled him. He swore the American rebels would be punished. He said the choice was made. The colonies would have to win, or they would have to give in. To force that surrender, he shut Boston Harbor. He put martial law on Massachusetts. The British military was in charge there. War could not be avoided. The Boston Tea Party stirred colonists who felt British taxes were crushing them.

6In 1776, American Founding Fathers wrote the Declaration of Independence. The paper set out how the colonies would be free of British rule. The American Revolution's first shots came in 1775. The places were Lexington and Concord, in Massachusetts. British troops met a local militia. A militia was a band of armed men outside the national army. Home in Britain, the king needed extra troops if he hoped to win. He hired about thirty thousand German mercenaries. They were well trained. People called them Hessians. With those Hessians, Britain won important early fights. Colonial troops under General George Washington were pushed back. The retreat carried them into New York and into New Jersey. On Christmas night in 1776, Washington struck the Hessians by surprise. British forces were badly shaken. Wins then swung from one side to the other. In 1777 the British took Philadelphia, the colonial capital. At Saratoga, in New York, they suffered a clear defeat. France wanted payback for losing the French and Indian War. Early in 1778, France joined the colonists. Britain kept fighting. In the southern colonies, British attempts to win came to nothing. British General Charles Cornwallis gave up to George Washington. The place was Yorktown, Virginia. The day was October 19, 1781. When George III heard of the surrender, he would not believe it. He wanted the fight to go on. His ministers knew the war had ended. Parliament knew it too. Lord North was prime minister and a friend of the king. He could not back a plan to keep fighting. People tried to blame the king for losing the colonies. He answered that he was not guilty of the harms that had taken place. A New York picture shows colonists tearing down a statue of this king. They did it when they declared they were free of Britain.

7The thirteen colonies were gone. By the late 1780s, a new fear rose. People worried the king was losing his mind. He was often anxious. His behavior turned strange. He struck out with his body. He shouted at people. He said things that made no sense. His body showed worse signs. His eyes bulged. They looked yellowish. His urine turned purple. Doctors were baffled. They could only use the treatments common in that age. They bled him. They blistered his back. They made him drink castor oil. A harsher step came next. He was kept apart from others. If he spoke when he should not, he was punished hard. The rough discipline seemed to help, little by little. He recovered in 1789. At times the illness made him burst out in violence. He had to be held down. A political cartoon is called The Rival Gardeners. It shows George III and Napoleon each tending a garden. The gardens stand for lands they each had to watch. Ireland brought him another revolution. Most people there were Catholic. Britain was Protestant. It passed laws that cut the rights of Irish Catholics. General Cornwallis halted the Irish Rebellion of 1798. In 1800 the parliaments of the two nations joined. The joined country took a longer name. It was called the United Kingdom. Great Britain and Ireland were both part of that name. France, his old enemy, was at war with Britain again. A revolution in France in 1789 threw out the king. By 1799 a young general led France. His name was Napoleon Bonaparte. He was hungry to conquer Europe. Great Britain was on that list. George III started readying his country for one more war. The Napoleonic Wars went on until 1815. That was the year Great Britain finally beat Napoleon.
