8The year 1809 found King George III at age seventy-one. He was in his fiftieth year as king. Old age brought him more popularity than he had known before. The next year brought a terrible private loss. Princess Amelia was his youngest daughter. She died. Tuberculosis was the cause. She was only twenty-seven. Her death seemed to start a slide in his health. Mind and body both failed. He was nearly blind. He was very thin. The mental illness that had hurt him decades earlier came back. Violent swings of mood grew more common. A note says George IV was king for ten years. Those years ran from 1820 to 1830. The year 1811 brought a change for his son. Regent was the new role for his son George. The son was Prince of Wales. A regent is a temporary ruler. Parliament made that change by an act. January 1820 was the month the king died. His son then became King George IV. Tens of thousands came to the royal funeral. Memory paints King George as strong and also hard to sum up. Some historians see the king who lost key colonies in America. They also see the king who beat Napoleon. Other historians look mostly at his mental health. Many have started to rethink those views. A large number now think the mental signs may have come from a rare illness of the body. As a ruler, he always set his country first. He led it to wins in the Seven Years' War. He led it to wins in the Napoleonic Wars. He also fought to hold Britain's American colonies. His home life has been studied more carefully. The record shows a hard worker. It shows a loyal husband. It shows a loving father. His reign lasted sixty years. No monarch before him had ruled so long.

9A timeline lists the life of George III. June 4, 1738, was his birth. The year 1751 was the death of Frederick, Prince of Wales, his father. The year 1756 was the start of the Seven Years' War. The year 1760 was the death of his grandfather, King George II, and the year George became king. The year 1763 was the end of the Seven Years' War. Fighting in the American Revolution opened with shots in 1775. The year 1781 was the British surrender to American colonists at Yorktown. In 1788 George III began to show signs. The illness of his mind looked serious. A year later he took up his duties again and seemed cured. The year 1798 was when Britain stopped the Irish Rebellion. The year 1809 was his celebration of fifty years on the throne. The year 1815 was the British defeat of Napoleon. The year 1820 was his funeral, and thousands attended. The word list gives plain meanings. An ambassador is an official who goes to a place, or lives there, and speaks for a country or its people. Mercenaries are soldiers who will fight for any army that pays them. A ministry is a branch of government led by a minister. The word can also mean the building where that work is done. Banishing means forcing someone to leave. Boycotts are refusals to buy something, or to join in, so that a point is made or a change is forced. An overture is an act or an offering meant to open the way to something larger, such as a friendship. An ethic is a moral rule that steers how a person acts. Parliament writes the laws for the United Kingdom. Expansion is growth in size, amount, volume, or scope. A proclamation is an official announcement made in public. A figurehead is a leader in name only, with no real power. Tenacious means stubbornly set on a goal, or persistent.

35. Goliath Beetles: Giant Insects

1Male Goliath beetles have Y-shaped horns used for fighting. There are about a million known insect species, and nearly half are beetles. Goliath beetles belong to this common group, but they are not common insects. They are swift and solitary, and they are hard to find and study. They are more than two thousand times as large as their ladybug cousins. Young larvae are even bigger and weigh nearly twice as much as adults. A larva can be 5 inches long and weigh 3.5 ounces. An adult is 4.33 inches long and weighs 1.7 ounces, smaller than a hand about 7.44 inches long.

2Beetles come in many shapes and sizes, but Goliath beetles are the heavyweight champs. Fossils from three hundred million years ago show giant centipedes and dragonflies with hawk-sized wings. Less oxygen and simple body systems keep Goliath beetles smaller than prehistoric insects. A Hercules beetle can reach 7 inches, including 4 inches of horn. A rhinoceros beetle is 6 inches long, mostly because of its huge horns. A Goliath is about 4 inches long, yet it weighs a hefty 1.7 ounces. No two beetles share the same markings, so early naturalists named over two dozen kinds by mistake. There are really six types, including cacicus, goliatus, regius, orientalis, atlas, and albosignatus.

3Early British naturalists called them zebra beetles because of bold black-and-white stripes. Those markings may hide a beetle against leafy plants. All beetles have two pairs of wings. The dark hind wings look leathery, but they are thin and strong enough to lift the body. Hard front wings, called elytra, cover the folded flying wings like armor. Goliath mouths are made for chewing, and the beetles drink tree sap. They are too heavy for flowers, so they climb with sharp claws to eat sap and rotting fruit. Like other insects, they have a head, thorax, abdomen, jointed legs, and an outside skeleton.

4X-rays showed that holes in a London museum beetle were gunshot wounds. A scientist said the beetle was shot while flying upside down. There are more than one hundred beetle families, and Goliaths belong to the scarab family. That family also includes rhinoceros beetles and dung beetles. Goliaths fly so well that early collectors shot them out of the sky. Dr. Brett Ratcliffe says they are very hard to watch in nature. Their wing covers stay in place while the flying wings unfold, which may help them take off fast. Their fan-like antennae open to find food, smells, and mates, and only scarabs do this.

5Goliath beetles live in tropical African rainforests and savannas. A dry season lasts several months, but the beetles are seen mainly in the wet season. Rain helps trees make fruit and sap, and leaves give the beetles cover. Experts think monkeys and large birds might eat them, but no one knows for sure. These speedy flyers hide in the treetops. They may gather where food is plentiful, yet they are not social insects. Dr. Ratcliffe says they like to spend time alone unless they seek a mate. Males use Y-shaped horns to push other males from feeding sites that may attract females.

6Wet and dry seasons shape the Goliath life cycle, and the months change by place. Goliaths change from egg to larva to pupa to adult. Adults spend most of their lives mating. A female uses her wedge-shaped head to dig a burrow, lays over one hundred eggs, and dies soon after. Eggs hatch in about two weeks, and the eyeless, wingless grubs eat and grow underground. They likely eat rotting plants in the wild, and in captivity they also eat smaller insects. In about four months they can grow 5 inches long, nearly like a dollar bill, and weigh 3.5 ounces. Inside thin soil cells, wings and legs form, and moisture later wakes the sleeping adult.

7The speedy Goliath is an elusive giant that is hard to spot and harder to catch. Bold stripes and huge size make it a favorite with insect fans. Some people even keep Goliath beetles as pets. Scientists have learned much by studying these captive insects. A Goliath can be almost as large as a human hand. It is as big as a songbird and striped like a zebra. It is also as agile as an aerial acrobat. These beetles fly quickly, and they are one amazing insect!

36. Goliath Bird-Eating Spiders: Giant Arachnids

1Goliath spider babies look like small adults. Early explorers named them after seeing one eat a hummingbird. These fierce hunters are among the largest spiders in the world. Their fangs are 0.75 inches, or 2 centimeters, long. The fangs give off strong venom that stops prey from moving. They harm mice, small mammals, and insects more than people. A Goliath can be 12 inches, or 30.48 centimeters, across and weigh 6 ounces, or 0.17 kilograms. A human hand is about 7.44 inches long and 3.3 inches wide.

2Golden color on some Goliaths gives them the scientific name blondi. About nine hundred kinds of tarantulas have been identified. They live in rainforests, deserts, grasslands, and mountains. Their homes include the United States, Central America, Africa, Asia, Europe, and Australia. Goliath bird-eating spiders are the largest tarantulas in the world. They have eight eyes, eight legs, and two main body parts. Legs join the cephalothorax, which holds the brain, eyes, fangs, mouth, and stomach. The abdomen holds silk glands, and sensory hairs cover the body.

3Goliath tarantulas are mainly covered in coffee-colored hairs. Some parts are light tan or reddish, and other parts are darker brown. Long legs are mostly dark brown, but hairs are lighter at each knee. They weigh more than any other spider, up to 6 ounces, or 170 grams. Stretched legs span almost 1 foot, nearly the size of a dinner plate. Eight eyes see light levels, but not fine details, so hairs sense vibrations. Hairy mygalomorphs have jaws that move up and down, and pedipalps pull prey to the fangs. Each leg has six joints, a bite hurts like a wasp sting but is not deadly, and some South Americans hunt them.

4Goliath spiders live in Guyana, Suriname, Venezuela, French Guiana, and Brazil. They stay in hot, steamy, swampy parts of South American rainforests. Rainforests cover about 6 to 7 percent of Earth but hold more than half of its species. By day they rest in underground burrows or in holes under rocks. They live alone unless guarding young or seeking a mate, and at night they stay near home. They hunt crickets, frogs, beetles, bats, mice, and sometimes a small bird. They do not spin webs, but silk lines the burrow and makes a mat at the entrance. Hairs feel vibrations on the mat, then fangs nearly an inch long inject venom that paralyzes the prey.

5The mouth is a short straw that can only suck, so food must be liquid. The spider sprays digestive juices from openings near the fangs to dissolve prey. A large tarantula can turn a mouse into hair and bones in about thirty-six hours. These aggressive spiders may rear up, hiss by rubbing leg hairs, or shoot stiff barbed hairs. Those hairs can sting eyes, skin, and throat, as some scientists have found. Hawks, owls, skunks, and snakes may eat them, but the spider wasp is a deadlier hunter. A female wasp stings a spider so it cannot move, digs a hole, and lays an egg on its abdomen. The larva crawls inside and feeds, saving the organs until the end.

6A Goliath molts much like a Honduran tarantula pushing off old skin. It leaves the old exoskeleton behind as a new hard covering forms underneath. While molting, the spider is weakest and easiest for predators to catch. Adults molt once or twice a year, but young spiders molt more often. A leg can break off in an attack and grow back at the next molt. The new leg may be weaker, and claws, sense organs, and spinnerets can grow back too. Some females live over twenty-five years in captivity, but males live under ten. She lays about fifty eggs in a silk sac, and the blue-black young change color as they grow.

7Goliaths have been around for millions of years, and they have not changed much. Their size fascinates local people, scientists, and spider fans. We are still learning how they regrow limbs and how venom affects prey nerves. Like all living things, they have an important role where they live. They help keep rodents, insects, and other species in check. They also provide food for a number of predators. Learning about them shows how rainforest species are linked and why their home should be protected. If you are in their territory, watch from a distance, because they are huge, hairy, and interesting.

37. Great Mosque of Djenné

1People near the Great Mosque of Djenné pass it on the way to markets and rivers. Djenné is one of the oldest towns in sub-Saharan Africa. This small town in Mali, West Africa, has about thirteen thousand people. This unique mosque is one of the greatest buildings in sub-Saharan Africa. Mosques are places where Muslims worship, and they follow Islam. Islam has more than one billion followers and five pillars. The pillars are a statement of faith, prayer, fasting, charity, and a trip to Mecca. Mecca is the birthplace of Islam. The Great Mosque is the world's largest mud building. Travelers visit it to study and worship.

2Djenné is hard to reach by usual travel. It lies on a floodplain between the Niger and Bani Rivers. People can get there only by ferryboat. In the thirteenth century, Djenné stood on the trade route from the coast to Timbuktu. Timbuktu lies 483 kilometers to the north. Traders passed through Djenné, and the town grew. From the thirteenth to the sixteenth centuries, the market was the main income. Merchants traded salt, cloth, copper, and silver for gold, kola nuts, and leather. The route spread Islam, which came to Mali in the ninth century and grew under King Mansa Musa in the 1300s.

3A drawing from 1896 shows the second Great Mosque of Djenné. The first mosque began in the thirteenth century under King Koi Konboro. He built it on his palace site with local materials and a traditional design. Later rulers added towers and walls, but rain ruined the mud by the 1800s. In a holy war, tribal leader Seku Amadu of the Tukulor Empire took Djenné. Islamic law did not allow him to tear the old mosque down. He left it unused, and the building fell apart. From 1834 to 1836, he built a low, huge, plainer mosque with minarets on a nearby site. In 1893, French forces took the city and replaced the ruined mosque with a school.

4Workers must fix the walls every year, or rain will wear the mosque down. The mosque we see today was finished in 1907 on the first mosque's site. New research says Djenné's masons' guild, not the French, built it. They used forced labor from nearby villages. Workers mixed tons of sand, mud, rice husks, and water to form bricks. This was the last full rebuild. Wind, rain, and heat still crack the walls. Yearly repairs reshape it, so it may look different from the first mosque. It is plain, unlike carved and tiled mosques in Egypt, India, and Turkey. Its sun-baked walls rise 16 meters. They turn warm in bright sun. Palm sticks called toron stick out from the walls.

5The qibla prayer wall faces east toward Mecca and looks over the market. Three boxlike minarets rise from the wall. Each has a sculpted ostrich egg on top. The egg is a sign of purity and fertility. The tallest minaret is 16 meters high. Five times a day, a man from the mosque calls Muslims to prayer from the minarets. People climb spiral stairs to the towers. Visitors use one of six stair sets to enter. The prayer hall can hold three thousand people. The building covers 5,625 square meters. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1988. The smooth walls are 41 to 61 centimeters thick. They have eighteen projections. The mosque sits on a platform 3 meters high.

6Half of the mosque is covered by a roof on ninety wooden pillars. Roof vents have ceramic caps that come off so hot air can escape. The other half is an open court for public prayer. An arched walk goes around that court. A man spreads mud on the outer wall to care for the building. Bricks, mortar, and plaster are made from mud mixed with butter and clay. Sun-baked bricks called ferey can be 61 centimeters thick at the base. The mud bonds the bricks and gives the walls a smooth, sculpted coat. By day the walls stay cool as they store the Sun's heat. At night that heat warms the inside.

7West Africa has sharp changes in heat and damp air. Toron sticks poke out at even spaces and help stop the walls from cracking. These sticks also serve as scaffolding for the yearly repairs. The building sits on a platform 3 meters high to avoid floods from the Bani River. Ceramic gutters on the roof carry rain away from the walls. Workers climb the outside on the toron when they make repairs. At the Plastering of the Great Mosque, thousands race to cover walls hurt by heat and rain. Children carry baskets of mud, and the whole town helps preserve this central mosque.

8Before the festival, people collect fine clay from the Niger and Bani Rivers. Women bring water to special pits. Young boys mix the plaster there. A race decides who first carries the plaster to the mosque walls. Men press the mud onto cracking walls. Music and food are part of the day. Musicians encourage the workers. Elders sit in a place of honor and give advice. Children sing and play. Only Muslims may enter the mosque. Others may only look from outside. Constant plastering weakened it. A 2006 fear of collapse paused the festival. The festival returned in 2012.

9Foreign investors have offered to rebuild the walls in concrete and to tile the sand floor. Those changes would improve the structure. But they would remove a tradition that unites the people of Djenné. In 1988, the United Nations made Djenné a World Heritage Site. This protection helps preserve the city’s history. The Great Mosque is blocked from big modern changes. For now, the people will keep their heritage and their yearly festival. Exterior lighting is one of the only modern additions to the mosque.

38. Great Zimbabwe

1All of Great Zimbabwe's walls were built without mortar, including the Hill Complex. Bird sculptures, even a damaged one, show that birds were important symbols. Tall stone ruins in southern Zimbabwe are all that remain of the city called Great Zimbabwe. The mighty walls have interested Western scholars since Europeans began studying them in the late 1800s. The site shows life in a thriving African civilization from the eleventh to the fifteenth centuries. Many parts of this history remain a mystery. No one knows why the prosperous city was abandoned.

2Zimbabwe is a landlocked country just north of South Africa and west of Mozambique. Zambia and Botswana are inland neighbors in southern Africa. The ruins lie in the southeast, near Lake Mutirikwi and the town of Masvingo. The name may come from a Shona phrase that means "stone houses." Shona is one of Zimbabwe's three main languages. In 1980, Zimbabwe gained independence from Britain and took the ancient city's name. About 728.4 hectares hold the Hill Complex, the Great Enclosure, and the Valley Ruins. Stone and daga buildings of clay and gravel stand there, with many daga homes in the valley between them.

3The Hill Complex was probably the religious hub, and the kings lived there. The Valley Ruins were likely home to the people of the city. Experts think the wealthy lived inside the Great Enclosure. Some walls are 11 meters, or 36 feet, high, like a three-story building. Some are 6 meters, or 20 feet, thick, and they curve without a break. In places the walls are quite smooth and decorative. The oldest part sits on a steep northern hillside with a stunning view. Six posts topped with birds suggest rituals, and chiefs may have lived at this center.

4The Great Enclosure is the largest ancient African structure south of the Sahara Desert. This oval stone ring is 250 meters around, up to 11 meters tall, and used about one million stones. An inner wall runs for about 55 meters and leads to a completely solid conical tower. The tower's purpose is a mystery, but the enclosure may have been a royal palace. It was built in the 1300s, with daga houses and smaller walls for family compounds. Portuguese explorers told of the stone walls in the 1500s. Later Europeans doubted that local African builders could do such fine work. Eight soapstone birds on columns inspired the symbol on Zimbabwe's flag and coins.

5Builders stacked stones into high curving walls. Some Europeans thought Phoenicians from the eastern Mediterranean had built the city. They pointed to wood they believed came from the north. Amateurs ignored African pottery, spearheads, and tools, and they damaged parts of the site. In 1905, Randall-MacIver used artifacts and daga buildings to show that Africans built it. Later archaeologists agreed, and some tools match Shona items from the 1800s. Most scholars think the Shona, here since prehistoric times, built the city. Work began about one thousand years ago, lasted over three hundred years, and sometimes took in huge boulders.

6Stonemasons cut bricklike stones from the granite boulders common around the site. They heated big stones with fire, then poured cold water on the red-hot rock. The sudden change made the stones split along straight lines. Workers stacked them with no mortar, a rare method that many call Africa's finest example. Hill Complex walls used both boulders and cut stones. Moss grows on walls inside the Great Enclosure. Each wall is thicker at the base, so it tapers and the tall stacks do not topple. The walls hold no weight and may have meant defense, elite privacy, or royal authority.

7The Shona have lived in this area since the Iron Age, beginning in the third century. The land suited farming and livestock, and people mined gold, iron, copper, and tin. They used these resources for trade and crafting. After about 1000, the society of farmers and herders formed states with central power. That was when they were likely building Great Zimbabwe. By the fourteenth century, it was a trading city at the heart of a powerful empire. With the valley, it likely held over ten thousand people, perhaps twenty thousand. Elites lived in stone homes, peasants used daga houses, and gold traveled routes to the Indian Ocean.

8Archaeologists found West African metal ornaments, Middle Eastern glass, and Chinese porcelain. These prove extensive trade, and local works of art show the city's own traditions. Stone altars suggest a religious center like the one-god faith of the Shona today. Scholars do not know why the wealthy city was largely empty by the mid-1400s. Maybe grazing and farming depleted the soil, so people could not grow enough food. Or they moved to seek better trade as other areas rose in power. People still worship and visit, but tourists, climate, and invasive plants damage the ruins. Laws since 1893 and UNESCO's 1986 listing still leave an urgent need for funds and careful study.

9Stars illuminate the beautiful ruins of Great Zimbabwe at night. This site of historical significance reveals life and global trade in medieval southern Africa. The ruins give captivating glimpses of a thriving empire. Still, they keep many secrets. What was the purpose of the conical tower inside the Great Enclosure? Why was the great city deserted after centuries of prosperity? With proper care and study, perhaps the walls will reveal the answers.

39. Gridiron: Downs, Scores, and Fans

1This book opens with a famous catch. It then looks at a favorite American sport, play in other countries, how a game works, how the sport began, famous players, fans, and words to know. Dwight Clark made a catch that seemed beyond human reach. He played for the San Francisco 49ers. Many call it one of the greatest moments the sport has ever had. The day was January 10, 1982. The Dallas Cowboys faced the San Francisco 49ers. The match was the championship game of the National Football Conference. The short name is NFC. The winner would reach the Super Bowl, the sport's top game. The 49ers trailed 27 to 21. Fifty-eight seconds remained. Quarterback Joe Montana threw the ball high. Montana aimed at the rear of that scoring area. Dwight Clark jumped far above the defenders. He caught the ball. The 49ers won that game. They also won the Super Bowl that same year. Over the next eight years they added three more championships. Last-second thrills like this one fill stadiums with thousands of people. They also hold millions of viewers to their televisions in football season. The game is spectacular. Its competitors are fierce. Its fans are devoted.

2Inside the United States, this sport sits at the top. It has held that place for about thirty years. Pro games draw huge interest. College games do too. The National Football League runs the pro game. The short name is NFL. A typical game draws around seventy thousand people. The playoff weeks lead to the Super Bowl. That championship is among the biggest sports events on Earth. College play is governed by the NCAA. Those letters stand for National Collegiate Athletic Association. In the United States, college football ranks third in popularity. The NFL is ahead of it. Major League Baseball is ahead of it too. Most women who play do so as amateurs or as semipros. Fewer young people are taking up the sport. For children younger than fourteen, many adults judge the contact too hard. A photo shows the Denver Broncos against the St. Louis Rams. The crowd at Mile High Stadium has no empty seats. A map marks IFAF nations across six land areas. The long name is International Federation of American Football. Those areas are North America, Europe, Asia, Africa, South America, and Australia. The map also shows the Atlantic Ocean, the Indian Ocean, the Pacific Ocean, and the equator. The short name of that federation is IFAF. Many countries play the American game. It is not yet as global as some other sports. Interest is still growing. Membership in IFAF tops seventy nations. Those nations sit on six continents. Canada has had its own form of the game since the late 1800s. Canadian play is similar. The field size differs. The number of players differs. Some rules differ. Most people picture an outdoor field. Indoor play is possible too. The 1980s brought an indoor version named arena football. Its rules fit a smaller field. The result is a faster game.

3A field diagram gives the main measures. College posts and pro posts measure 18.5 feet from side to side. That width is 5.6 meters. The goalpost is 10 feet tall. That height is 3 meters. A score can come from a kick that clears the bar while staying inside the uprights. Depth of the scoring area is 10 yards. That depth is 9.1 meters. A touchdown requires the ball to be carried into that area. A pass that is caught there also counts. One marked distance on the diagram is 160 feet, or 48.8 meters. Another is 360 feet, or 109.7 meters. Hash marks appear at each yard. Markers appear every 5 yards. The 50-yard line marks the middle. It sits 50 yards from either end zone. That distance is 45.7 meters. An arrow on the 10-yard line points toward the nearer end zone. Markers also show an end line, and they show a goal line. The sideline borders the field. People nickname the sport the gridiron. Yard lines plus hash marks make a grid, and that grid earned the nickname. In a game, two teams try to move the ball toward the other end zone. They try to get it in, which scores a touchdown. One method is to run with the ball. The second method is a throw toward a teammate nearer the scoring area. A completed pass means the teammate catches it. After the catch, a further advance is allowed. An interception means an opponent catches the throw. The catching team then owns the ball. An incomplete pass stops play. Nobody caught it, and it fell to the ground. Attackers form a line that is also called a platoon. That group's job is to score. A defensive platoon tries to stop the other team from scoring. A 2014 photo shows a New Mexico running back diving for the end zone. The opponent is Arizona State.

4Early balls were probably oval rugby balls. An inflated pig bladder sat inside a casing of pig hide. Those balls were hard to throw. Later the bladder was dropped. The shape was made smoother. Today's balls are cowhide. Some people still call them pigskins. At any moment, each club has just one platoon on the grass. Which platoon depends on who controls the ball. Each platoon has eleven players. Six points is the value of a touchdown. The offense usually scores it by running the ball into the other end zone. A pass into that end zone can score it too. A touchdown is not limited to the offense. One way is to recover a fumble. A fumble is a ball an opponent loses control of. Another way is to intercept and reach the other end zone. After a touchdown, a kick through the goalposts adds one point. A run or a pass into the end zone adds two points. A field goal is worth three points. It is a kick between the goalposts. If tacklers down the ball carrier inside the carrier's own scoring area, the play is a safety. The defense then receives two points. A 2014 photo shows Team Germany, which has the ball. Their stance faces Team Sweden along the scrimmage line. The game is in Austria. Play starts with a kickoff to the offense. That team advances in stages. Each stage must be at least 10 yards. That distance is 9.1 meters. The offense has four chances, called downs. Those chances must produce the needed 10 yards, or a score past the goal line. If it gains at least 10 yards inside the four downs, it keeps the ball. It earns a new first down. It may then try for another 10 yards. Every play starts at the line of scrimmage. That line is imaginary. It crosses the field. Its place comes from where the last play ended. Penalty yards, if any were given, also move it. Teams use many specialized plays. A play is a plan for moving the ball. If the offense cannot gain 10 yards in four downs, it gives the ball up.

5Defense uses two main plans to stop a score. Bringing down the runner is a defender's aim. They also try to force fumbles and interceptions so they can take the ball. A tackle is complete when one knee touches the ground. It is also complete when both knees touch. That contact ends the play. Running out of bounds ends the play too. In pro games, true playing time is sixty minutes. College games use the same sixty minutes. That clock divides into four quarters, and those quarters make two halves. High school games are shorter. They last forty-eight minutes. A tie at the end of sixty minutes adds overtime. That extra period is fifteen minutes. A full game usually lasts about three hours. The extra time comes from stoppages. A player may go out of bounds. A penalty may be called. A pass may fall incomplete. Players wear a helmet and a chin strap. They wear shoulder pads, a jersey, and gloves. They wear hip pads, pants, and thigh pads. They wear socks, knee pads, and shoes called cleats. Pads under the uniform help prevent injury. A diagram places both platoons at the line of scrimmage. On defense the marks are S for safety, CB for cornerback, and LB for linebacker. DT means defensive tackle. DE means defensive end. On offense, C means center and G means guard. T means tackle. TE means tight end. WR means wide receiver. QB means quarterback. RB means running back. Jobs on the field are specialized. The quarterback leads the offense. In the huddle, that player calls the play. From his spot, the center shoves the ball back through his own legs. The ball goes to the quarterback. That move is the snap. It is also called hiking the ball. The quarterback may then run. The quarterback may pass. The quarterback may hand the ball off. The same diagram shows where attackers and defenders stand. A referee watches the rules. Six other officials watch with the referee.

6Birth of the sport came late in the nineteenth century. Several universities in North America played it. It grew out of two English games. One was soccer, also called association football. The other was rugby, short for rugby football. Rugby is somewhat like soccer. Rugby uses the hands as well as the feet. Two universities in New Jersey played a game like soccer. Princeton was one of them, under the older name College of New Jersey. The other was Rutgers. Other universities in the Northeast began to play that game too. Harvard University preferred a style closer to rugby. Yale University picked up that style, and other schools followed. Walter Camp studied at Yale from 1876 to 1881. People call him the Father of American Football. He was Yale's captain. Inside the Intercollegiate Football Association, he held an important place. He pushed for rule changes. Those changes turned the old game into the American game played now. At first, the same players handled both attack and defense. Separate units for attack and defense arrived in the 1940s. Separate units later became the usual way. A picture shows Walter Camp. Jerry Rice is the best wide receiver the sport has known. He played twenty seasons, starting in 1985. He won three Super Bowls with the San Francisco 49ers. Nearly forty NFL records stand under his name. Joe Montana may be the most gifted quarterback the sport has had. His NFL career began in 1979 with the 49ers. Jerry Rice joined that team in 1985. Together they made the 49ers a dominant NFL force for several years. Four Super Bowl titles for the 49ers came with Montana leading. He retired after the 1994 season. He left with many playoff records. Walter Payton was a running back for the Chicago Bears. He played thirteen seasons, beginning in 1975. All-star selection for the Pro Bowl came his way nine times. He helped his team win the Super Bowl in 1986. For a time he held the NFL record for career touchdowns. He held the record for rushing yards. He held records in many other categories too.

7Students can play in several ways. Towns and schools often run youth leagues. Those leagues use tackle football. Touch football is another form. Flag football is another form. Those two forms are less rough than tackle. Many lovers of the sport would rather watch. Fans show their love in many ways. Some wrap up warm and sit through temperatures below freezing. Others wear wild clothes. Others paint their faces in team colors. Some wear gear that matches a team theme. Fans of the Dallas Cowboys may wear a cowboy hat. Fans of the Arizona Cardinals may wear a yellow beak and a feathery red crest. A fan can find great fun in this beloved American sport. A player can find great fun too. There is plenty of excitement for everyone. A photo shows fans proving their loyalty to a favorite team. Words to know. Advocated means supported or recommended. Amateur means not professional, and done as a hobby. Dominates means keeps strong power over something or someone. The end zone is the area past the goal line and before the end line. Blockers up front clear a path, and that help lets the runner score. A platoon is a group of teammates who share one job, such as attack or defense. Possession means control or ownership. Specialized means built to do one particular task. Spectators are people who watch and do not take part. Strategies are thought-out plans for a problem or a goal. Ultimate means the best or the greatest, or the thing that comes at the end. Vying means competing.

40. Helping Wild Animals Heal

1This book walks through wildlife rescue in order. An introduction opens it. Wildlife rehabilitators come next. Rescue comes after that. Rehabilitation follows. Release follows rehabilitation. Disaster rescue has its own part. A closing, a word list, and a topic list finish the book. A header names the Tucson Wildlife Center. A wild animal in trouble is a reason to tell an adult immediately. If no trusted adult is near, a phone book can help. Look under the words Wildlife Rescue. Look under the words Animal Rescue too. A baby bird may hop on the ground with no parent in sight. You might wonder what to do if that bird seems orphaned. You might find a rabbit that cannot seem to hop. You might see a raccoon that wobbles and sways as it walks. Many people are unsure which actions help. They are also unsure which actions harm. People with special training know the right response. The raccoon is one animal they know should be left alone. A raccoon that walks that way is probably sick. They know whether the rabbit can be helped. They know whether that rabbit can go back to the wild. They can judge a baby bird and decide what care, if any, it needs. They can also teach other people how to help. One picture shows Topsy. Topsy is a female great horned owl. She is three months old. A windstorm blew her from the nest. Rescuers took her in after the fall. Neck injuries are healing. Back injuries are healing too.

2Wildlife rehabilitators are the people who give aid when wildlife is sick, hurt, or orphaned. Rehabbers is the short name. Rehabilitate means to bring an animal back to good health. Rehabbers rescue wild animals. They care for those animals while healing goes on. When recovery allows it, they release the animals into the wild. Their training covers many fields. Some are nutritionists. A nutritionist knows what each species should eat. A nutritionist also knows how much food is right. Others are behaviorists. A behaviorist has studied how wild animals act. That study helps the person understand one animal. It also helps the person predict what that animal will do. Some rehabbers are animal-housing specialists. They know which cage, pen, or other enclosure fits each species. An injured animal may need one special kind of shelter so it can heal safely. One picture shows caretakers treating a sea turtle. The injury is in the turtle's right flipper. Rehabber Lisa treats a young javelina named Tripod. A car hit Tripod. One back leg was lost in that crash. Common causes of injury include being hit by vehicles. Hitting other objects is another cause. Poisoning is another. Illegal hunting is another. Litter and pollution are another. Animal attacks are another. Many rehabbers can treat illness in wild animals. They can treat injuries too, in the way veterinarians do. Not every rehabber is a veterinarian. Not every veterinarian knows wild-animal care. Most rehabbers focus on capture and transport. Safe handling of wildlife is a skill they have. That skill protects the animal. It also protects the rehabber. More people now live where wild animals live. Rehabbers are needed more often because of that. Farming takes land. Houses take land. Businesses take land. Natural habitats are destroyed. Natural foods are destroyed. Animals then face a higher chance of being orphaned. They face a higher chance of injury. They face a higher chance of death. People and human activity cause most wildlife injuries.

3Some rehabbers are generalists. They work with many mammals. They work with many birds. They work with many reptiles. Other rehabbers are specialists. A specialist may focus only on owls. Another may focus only on bats. Another may focus only on ocean animals. Urban wildlife is a common patient. Those animals live in cities or towns. Squirrels are one example. Raccoons are another. Foxes are another. Some brave rehabbers work with dangerous animals. Bears are among them. Mountain lions are among them. Bobcats are among them. Most rehabbers treat animals that are indigenous. Indigenous means the animal already belongs to the rehabber's home region. Special permits allow that work. Special licenses allow it too. Exotic animals are different. They are not native. They migrated to the region, or people brought them. A rehabber needs extra training for those animals. Extra licenses are required. Extra permits are required. One picture shows a Florida state wildlife worker. The worker is examining a panther kitten. Many centers focus on particular species. They still talk with colleagues who know other species. A different kind of animal may arrive and need help. People often ask how someone becomes a rehabber. Many begin as volunteers. They learn inside the homes of trained rehabbers. They learn in those rehabbers' backyards. Volunteers are not paid. Most rehabbers are not paid either. Rehabbers often buy food with their own money. They buy medicine with their own money. They buy shelters with their own money. Donations sometimes help. The gifts come from people. They come from businesses. They come from other organizations that care about wildlife. Helpers act because they care about animals. They want the animals to get healthy. Good care of wild animals also supports healthy habitats. It can prevent illness in people. It can prevent injury to people. One picture shows a volunteer holding a baby red-tailed hawk. A rehabber removes a bandage from the hawk's leg. The leg broke when the hawk fell from its nest.

4Two rules come first if you meet an animal that may need rescue. Do not touch the animal. Call an adult right away. The adult can phone a wildlife rehabber. That rehabber is trained for rescue. Watching, while you stay in a safe spot, is a way you can help. Note where the animal hides. Rescuers can then find it when they arrive. Small holes in a cardboard box let you cover a small animal that is hurt. A laundry basket can do the same job. The cover shields the animal from predators until help comes. One picture shows a rescuer giving water to a koala. He had saved that koala from a wildfire. Some behaviors mean you should stay away. They can mean the animal is sick and dangerous. A bat on the ground is one warning. A wild animal that seems tame is another. Extra drool is another. Foam around the mouth is another. An animal that cannot move is another. Extreme anger in the animal's look is another warning. A nocturnal animal is normally active at night. Daytime activity in that animal is a warning. The warning is strongest for a raccoon. It is strong for a skunk. It is strong for an opossum. It is strong for a fox. It is strong for a bat. Hurt, frightened animals can be injured further if they are held the wrong way. They can die from that handling. The wrong enclosure can injure them. It can kill them. Wild birds may break bones while trying to escape a wire cage. They may damage feathers in that struggle. Parents may abandon a baby if they smell a human on it. This risk is greater for mammals than for birds. Mammals have a sharper sense of smell. Injured wild animals are often scared because they are in pain. They may bite to defend themselves. They may kick. They may scratch. They may peck. They may stab. Help from people is something these animals do not recognize. Diseases in wild animals can pass to humans. They can pass to pets. Among wild animals, bats rank higher as carriers of rabies. Coyotes are more likely. Raccoons are more likely. Foxes are more likely. Skunks are more likely. Rabies is a deadly disease. Every warm-blooded animal can catch it. Humans can catch it. Possible exposure means treatment must start without delay.

5People sometimes take baby animals from home when no danger exists. The result can be tragic. A hopping baby bird may not be an orphan. It may be a fledgling. A fledgling is a young bird learning to fly. Before they can fly, fledglings practice by hopping along the ground. Parents usually watch them. People may not be able to see those parents. Baby rabbits are sometimes taken by mistake. Baby seals are sometimes taken by mistake. Baby deer are sometimes taken by mistake. None of those babies may be in trouble. It is normal for them to rest quietly. A beach can be the resting place. Grass can be the resting place. The mother may be eating nearby. Judgment belongs only to people who have learned how these animals normally live. They can tell whether human help is needed. If help is not needed, removal from the mother hurts the baby's chance to survive. A baby that is not wounded does not need rescue. Some people think taking a wild animal home is a kindness. Love of wildlife is not the same as skill to care for it. Wild animals need far more training than dogs and cats need. Taking a wild animal home is also against the law. Think of yourself hurt in an accident. You would not want a random person to take you home and treat you. You would want a trained helper, such as a doctor. A nurse would also fit that need. You would want a clean place. You would want the right equipment. You would want the right medicine. Wild animals deserve that same high level of care. One picture shows veterinarians examining a red panda. They are using medical equipment. Spring is the busiest season for wildlife rescue. Wild animals give birth in spring. Babies are weaker then. They often cannot survive alone. A car that hits the mother can leave the baby an orphan. A hunter can kill the parents. A predator can kill the parents.

6A checkup is the first step at a rehabilitation center. First aid is part of that step. New arrivals are quarantined. Each one stays in its own cage. The goal is to stop a possible infection from reaching the other animals. Rehabbers write detailed notes on every animal. The notes show whether the animal is improving. They show when medicine is due. They show when feeding is due. Problems at these centers vary widely. Broken bones must be treated by veterinarians first. Diseases must be treated by veterinarians first. After that treatment, the animal can rest at the center and get well. Igor is a black vulture. He had been fed birdseed. Meat was the food he needed for good health. His bones grew fragile. They broke during his rescue. Healing may happen in one place. Recovery may happen in another. A small dark cage may be the first room for a hawk whose wing is broken. The dark cage lets it stay calm while healing begins. Once the bone has healed, an outdoor flight cage may be next. There the hawk can exercise. There it can learn to fly again. Young injured animals often need extra care while they heal. As they grow stronger, an adult animal may share their space. The young animal can learn from that adult. Hunting for food in the right way is one lesson adults give. One picture shows birds that have been rehabilitated. They practice flight inside a flight cage. Release waits until they have healed enough. Infant animals must stay warm. An incubator can provide that warmth. Hot-water bottles in the cage can do it. Heating pads can do it. Lightbulbs in the cage can do it.

7Most wild animals fear people. Life away from home adds stress. A wild animal can die if stress rises too high. Workers limit contact with people for that reason. They keep noise low. They cover cages with towels. Other techniques are used as well. They also avoid staring. In the wild, a stare means an animal is being hunted. One picture shows a puppet standing in as a mother. The young condor then does not imprint on the humans who feed it. Early in life, a baby animal imprints on its mother. Daily watching of its mother teaches a baby duck what kind of bird it is. Rehabbers work hard so baby birds do not imprint on people. If they do, they grow up believing they are human. Humans, not their own kind, become the company they seek. Raptors are birds of prey. A raptor that imprinted on people can be dangerous once it is outdoors. Other birds can become dangerous in the same way. A hiker may draw that bird's wish for attention. The hiker may not know the bird is used to people. The meeting can hurt the hiker. It can hurt the bird. Because of that risk, these birds often cannot return to the wild. Meat-eaters at a center need meat if they are to heal. They need meat if they are to grow strong. Rehabbers collect roadkill for that food. Roadkill is the name for animals that cars or trucks have just hit beside a road. Freezers hold mouse-cicles. A mouse-cicle is a frozen mouse used as food. Some centers raise their own animal food to save money. Quail are raised that way. Mice are raised that way. Rats are raised that way. Rabbits are raised that way. One picture shows a volunteer feeding a mouse by hand. The patient is an adult red-tailed hawk. The hawk is almost completely blind. Each animal must get its natural foods, or something close to them. Some foods make wild animals sick. Some foods hinder normal growth. For many baby animals, milk from cows does extreme harm. It can even kill them. Natural foods prepare a rescued animal to live in the wild later. Orphans that grew up at a center need those foods most. A taste for human food can be a problem after release. Failure to learn hunting can be a problem. Failure to learn how to forage can be a problem. The animal might starve.

8Release begins with a choice of place. Rehabbers start that search long before the animal is ready. Natural history of the species is essential knowledge. A possible habitat is judged against what that animal needs. The qualities of the place are judged too. The chosen area must offer plenty of food. It must offer water. It must offer shelter. It must be safe from contact with humans. The animal itself must be healthy enough to go. Running, climbing, swimming, or flying has to come easily. It must be able to see. It must be able to hear. It must be able to locate food. It must be able to avoid predators. It must be able to be social with its own kind. A wildlife biologist is often asked to help with the release. An ornithologist is often asked too. Their help keeps the process smooth. One picture shows a Tasmanian devil. It will be examined before release. The first release step moves the animal outdoors. Animals of the same species share that outdoor space. The space may be a pen. It may be a cage. Outdoors, the animal adjusts to weather. It also adjusts to seeing humans less often. Slow release is common for young animals. Orphans are the clearest case. A pen is set in a safe wild place. The door stays open so the animal can come back. Food continues until it is clear the animal can feed itself. Fast release is common for animals that were rescued as adults. Life in nature is already familiar to those adult animals. A release site is where those adults are carried. The best site is near the place they were found. Then they are let go. One picture shows a group of onlookers. A rehabber opens a carrier door. A bald eagle flies free.

9Return to the wild is impossible for about half the animals in these centers. They are too sick, or the injuries are too severe. Many have lost limbs. Many have lost beaks. Many have lost wings. Many have lost eyesight. A bird whose injured wing heals badly could not fly in the wild. A bird with only one eye could not hunt there. Sometimes it is clear the animal will never survive outdoors. Sometimes it will not survive at the center either. Rehabbers then face a hard choice. Pain can make euthanasia the kindest choice. Euthanasia means a quick killing without pain. It can end the suffering. One picture shows an adult female great horned owl. A wing injury keeps her from flying quietly. The noise warns the prey she hunts. Release is impossible for her. Human activity is not the only source of wildlife injury. Natural disasters injure animals too. Wildfires are one kind. Tsunamis are another. Hurricanes are another. Terri Crisp gives much of her time to animals hurt by natural disasters. In 1986 a wildfire raged in California and trapped a Shetland pony. She coaxed the pony into a car and rescued it. Alaska in 1989 was where she worked during the oil spill known as Exxon Valdez. Sea otters were among the animals she tried to save. Loons were among them too. In 1992 she worked after Hurricane Andrew. Hundreds of hurt animals were part of that rescue. She founded Noah's Wish. The group trains volunteers. Those volunteers rescue animals put at risk by natural disasters. One picture shows Terri Crisp holding an animal she rescued. Her rescues have followed earthquakes. They have followed fires. They have followed floods. They have followed hurricanes. They have followed oil spills. They have followed tornadoes. They have followed other disasters.

10Before the Asian tsunami of 2004 reached land, many wild animals ran inland. That knowledge was remarkable. Pets did not fare so well. Farm animals came through the disaster poorly. Some people in the struck areas depended on working farm animals. Many of those animals were killed. Many were injured. Many were left in devastated places with no food. The Humane Society International joined other organizations. Volunteers joined them. Together they helped the animals. They also helped the people who cared for those animals. The aim was to get lives back on track. One picture shows a man in high water after the tsunami. The month was December 2004. He carries his daughter. He carries their dog. They are moving toward safety. A role remains for animals whose return to the wild will never happen. Rehabbers use them as ambassadors. The animals help teach respect for wildlife. Children learn about wild animals that live nearby. Adults learn that too. They learn to respect habitats. Respect lets wild animals keep finding food. It lets them keep finding shelter. Rehabbers do important work. They care for injured wild animals. They return many of those animals to the wild. You can help by respecting wildlife. Seeing an animal in distress is a reason to phone a rehabber. One phone call may give that animal a chance. The chance is to grow up. The chance is to live free and healthy. One picture shows a bird of prey used as an ambassador. Children learn from it about animals that live near them.

11These meanings belong to words in the book. An ambassador represents a country, a species, or a cause. Coaxing means winning agreement by gentle persuasion. Colleagues are people who do similar work. Devastated means destroyed by violent force. Exotic means the animal comes from another place, and that place is often distant. A fledgling is young, and flight is the skill it is still learning. To forage is to search for food or to gather it. An incubator is a warm enclosure for a baby animal. Indigenous means native to one particular place. An ornithologist is a scientist whose study is birds. Quarantined means kept apart so disease will not spread. Veterinarians are doctors for animals other than humans. They treat illness. They treat injury. The topic list names subjects in this book, without page numbers. Animal housing is one topic. Natural history is one. Babies are one. Animals that cannot be released are one. A behaviorist is one. A nutritionist is one. Capture and transport are one. An ornithologist is one. Care is one. Orphans are one. Causes of injury are one. Predators are one. Contact with humans is one. Rabies is one. Terri Crisp is one. Rehabbers are one. Dangerous animals are one. Release is one. Disease is one. Recovery is one. Exotic animals are one. Respecting wildlife is one. The Exxon Valdez oil spill is one. Rules for children are one. Fast release is one. Slow release is one. A flight cage is one. Spring is one. Food is one. Substitute parents are one. The Humane Society International is one. Training is one. Hurricane Andrew is one. A tsunami is one. Imprinting is one. Urban wildlife is one. Indigenous animals are one. Veterinarians are one. Licenses and permits are one. Volunteers are one. Money is one. A wildlife biologist is one.

41. Holding Back the Colorado

1This book begins with a wild river. It then shows the dry region around the site. It explains a dam unlike any other. It follows the work of preparing the ground. It follows the building itself. It describes a visit. A final look treats the dam as an engineering marvel. Word meanings come last. A watershed map places Nevada, Utah, and Colorado around the Colorado River. Lake Mead is marked. So are California, New Mexico, and Arizona. The Pacific Ocean and the Gulf of California frame the wider picture. Through the southwestern United States, the Colorado bends and keeps moving. Desert country would be parched and lifeless without the water it carries. Farmers have used the banks for centuries. Irrigation from this river kept their fields alive. Spring snowmelt was the hard part. The river swelled and often drowned farmland. Later it fell away until only a trickle remained, and crops died. That unreliable supply turned some early settlers away. It pushed others to seek control of the flow. Hoover Dam came out of those efforts. Americans treat it as an iconic landmark. Visitors still feel awe. More than seventy-five years have passed since the concrete was set.

2Las Vegas, Nevada, lies about 30 miles to the northwest. That distance is 48 kilometers. The dam itself sits on the line between Arizona and Nevada. Black Canyon is where it spans the Colorado. The surrounding country belongs to the Mojave Desert. Say that name moh-HAH-vee. Heat and dryness rule there. Plants are so scarce that large stretches resemble a moonscape. North of the wall, Lake Mead breaks that dryness. The lake is the reservoir held by the dam. It did not exist until construction made it. People made this lake. Inside the United States, no lake of that kind is larger. Shoreline runs for 550 miles, which equals 885 kilometers. Plants and animals of fourteen hundred species live in and around it. One view pairs the lake with the river. Another shows people out boating, skiing, and fishing. Measurements help explain the size. Thickness at the crest is 45 feet, or 13.7 meters. Each of four intake towers stands 395 feet tall, or 120.4 meters. Water for the power plant is controlled by those towers. Height from foundation rock up to the crest is 726.4 feet, or 221.4 meters. The top width, measured across Black Canyon, is 1,244 feet, or 379 meters. Weight passes 6,600,000 tons. In metric tons that is 5,987,419. Down at the base, thickness reaches 660 feet, or 201 meters.

3No taller dam existed anywhere when this one was new. Engineers treated the job as a remarkable feat. Two older ideas share the design. One is the gravity dam, which fights the push of stored water by sheer weight. The other is the arch dam. Its curve faces upstream. Water mostly meets the steep canyon walls, and those walls squeeze the arch. The squeeze makes the structure stronger and shoves it into the ground. A sketch labels the downstream side, the gravity portion, the arch, and the upstream side. People class Hoover Dam as an arch-gravity dam. Electricity is made in its power plant from the river's energy. Seventeen turbine generators sit inside. The current serves roughly 1.3 million people. Interest in controlling the Colorado rose as the twentieth century opened. In earlier years the river emptied into the Gulf of California. A canal changed that. The year was 1901, and the builder was a private company. The canal's name was the Alamo Canal. It turned water aside so California's Imperial Valley could be irrigated. Crops then flourished on land that had been dry. Livestock flourished with them. Floods in 1905 were severe enough to wreck the gates that controlled the canal. Imperial Valley was left devastated. People living there wanted a bigger canal, one the government would keep up, so irrigation could return. Arthur Powell Davis argued that a dam would spread the benefit to more people. His post was chief engineer. He later became the first person to direct the Reclamation Service. The office belonged to a federal department, the one called Interior. A later name for the service was the Bureau of Reclamation. Dams in the western states are the work most often linked to this agency. Canals in those states are linked to it as well. Davis gave Congress a report on the Colorado in 1918. A decade passed. Then the Boulder Canyon Project Act went through Congress. Hoover Dam was approved in that law. So was the All-American Canal, meant to bring Imperial Valley its water. An appropriation bill followed in 1930. President Hoover's signature on that bill let building begin.

4Black Canyon, pictured before any work, was the real construction site. The Boulder Dam name still stuck until 1947. Renaming that year honored Herbert Hoover. He had been the thirty-first president. Choosing ground was step one. Planners wanted a place that could store the most water safely, with the least effort and the least cost. Two canyons led the list. One was Boulder Canyon. The other was Black Canyon. A gap of 20 miles, or 32 kilometers, separated them on the border of Arizona and Nevada. Surveyors from the Bureau of Reclamation checked both. Mapmakers went with them. Granite in the walls made Boulder Canyon the first pick. Faults, which are cracks, later showed up in that granite. Black Canyon replaced it. Andesite breccia formed the bedrock there and formed the walls. That kind of rock had no cracks. Housing was poor at the start. Tents held some workers and their families. Baths happened in the river. The start date was March 11, 1931. Around them the Great Depression had brought staggering hardship to the economy of the United States. Work drew 21,000 unemployed men into southern Nevada from across the country. A large share came in the summer of 1930. Actual building was still far off. Blame for the Depression fell widely on President Hoover. His answer was jobs. He wanted the largest number of workers he could hire. He told crews to survey and begin other early tasks even though lodging was missing. Drinking water was missing. A hospital was missing. Camps ran without electricity. They ran without running water. Rough as it was, the men needed wages badly.

5Six Companies won the contract. Behind that name stood six construction firms. Dams, bridges, tunnels, and roads were work they already knew well. Charge of engineering fell to Frank Crowe. Innovative methods had marked the many western dams he had built. Moving the Colorado off the site was phase one. Blasting opened four tunnels. The Arizona bank got two of them. The Nevada bank got two. Above the future dam, a cofferdam formed a watertight barrier and steered the current into those tunnels. A matching cofferdam closed the lower end. A barrier of rock stood there too. Water downstream could not creep back, so the site stayed dry. Labels on a diversion map point out the Arizona tunnels, the Nevada tunnels, both cofferdams, and the rock barrier. Heat was extreme, and the tunnel crews worked all seven days of every week. May 1931 opened this enormous task. Rocks fell on the crews daily. Blasts shook the canyon. Diesel trucks poured out fumes. Pace had to stay fast. Until the tunnels existed, no one could start the dam wall. Overhead, high scalers knocked loose stone off the walls. They also cut the grooves that would grip each side of the future dam. Jackhammers were their tools. Dynamite was another. Wooden swings held them 800 feet over the river, a drop of 244 meters. Temperatures climbed as high as 120 degrees Fahrenheit, or 49 degrees Celsius. Dozens died when rocks or tools fell. Deaths tied to the building totaled ninety-six.

6More than the wall was rising. For roughly five thousand workers and the families with them, the U.S. government built Boulder City. Houses were part of it. A hospital was part of it. So were plumbing and systems for sewage. Night recovery got easier once the town was ready. Injuries could be treated. Heat exhaustion could be treated. A photograph presents Boulder City as suburban housing the government put up for these crews. Supply trains needed tracks, and those tracks were laid. A road joined the town to the dam site. Power had to come from far away. A line 222 miles long, equal to 357 kilometers, ran from San Bernardino in California and ended at Black Canyon. January 29, 1932, was the day crews broke out at the upriver mouth of Nevada's first diversion tunnel. Three more openings followed not long after. Concrete then lined every tunnel. November 1932 was when they could take the river. Cofferdams came next, one upriver of the future wall and one downriver. Diversion of the water, once those barriers stood, beat the schedule by nearly a year. Pumps emptied the site after the river had been shifted. Solid bedrock had to carry the dam. Silt and stones buried that rock under 135 feet, or 41 meters. Thousands of years of Colorado flow had laid the cover down. June 6, 1933, marked the end of that enormous dig. Building the dam could finally start. Concrete in all the structures totals 4,360,000 cubic yards. The metric figure is 3,333,459 cubic meters. Picture a highway 16 feet wide, or 4.9 meters, running from San Francisco until it reached New York City. This concrete could pave that road. Rock, earth, and sand dug from the project passed 5,500,000 cubic yards, or 4,205,052 cubic meters. A road made from that spoil would be even larger. One picture shows crews excavating where the foundation would sit.

7Columns of stacked blocks form the dam. It was never poured as one single mass. Wet concrete rode down in huge buckets. Each bucket emptied into its own wooden form, a mold waiting below. Puddlers smoothed what had been poured. Air bubbles had to go, or the hardened concrete would be weaker. Heat was the next danger. A chemical reaction inside the pour could crack it. Steel pipes were laid in the forms first, a maze 582 miles long, or 937 kilometers. Each pipe measured 1 inch across, which is 2.54 centimeters. Cold water kept moving through them. Grout replaced that water after cooling. A finished form was taken apart once its concrete had set. Workers stood the same form up again on the new top and poured another lift. That is how each column grew. Spaces left between columns received grout too. Spillways were added after the columns stood and the grout was in. Floodwater from the Colorado would have somewhere to go. It would drop through the spillways and never reach the crest. A crest overflow would wreck the power plant. Two of the old diversion tunnels, converted for the new job, would carry spillway water away. Last came the power plant and the four intake towers that would meter water toward it. Plugs closed the two inner diversion tunnels along roughly a third of each tunnel. Penstocks, which are steel pipes, went inside. Flow from each intake tower to the power plant is what those penstocks govern. Falling water carries energy. A hydroelectric plant turns that energy into electricity by way of turbine generators.

8Spread of cities was one result of Hoover Dam. Natural habitats changed as well. Look at the desert tortoise in the Mohave Desert. Before 1950, about two hundred of them might live in one square mile. That area equals 2.5 square kilometers. A square mile now holds only five or six. Groups are trying to guard what habitat the tortoise has left. A picture shows the animal. Completion arrived on February 1, 1935. Tunnels that had carried the Colorado around the site were plugged. Behind the wall, the river climbed. It spilled over the cofferdam. Lake Mead was the result. The full project had used about 21,000 men. A typical day saw 3,500 of them. The peak day saw 5,218. Spending reached about $165 million. Today's economy would put that at $3 billion or more. Dedication day was September 30, 1935. President Roosevelt spoke while the structure was still known as Boulder Dam. In his words it stood as the world's greatest dam. He ranked the work as an engineering win of the highest kind. American resourcefulness, American skill, and American determination were the qualities he named. Tourists inside the visitor center get a view straight down, like a bird over the wall. Guides lead tours that show details the public does not usually see, both in the dam and in the power plant. Visits have been welcome since 1937, and millions come every year. Displays explain how nature shaped this region over time. They tell the dam's own history. They tell how the Bureau of Reclamation worked to settle the West and to support irrigation. Highway 93 lets drivers cross the crest. An overlook gives broad views. Dam tours and power-plant tours are both offered. Those tours draw close to one million people a year. All year, Lake Mead is a place for fishing. Boating and picnics fill the calendar too. Plants and animals of the area can be watched and photographed.

9Taller dams exist now. By 2014, the count of higher dams was twenty-six. Fame still keeps Hoover Dam near the front of the list. Remote country was among the hardest problems, though not the only one. Roads, electric power, and houses had to appear before the main work was possible. Size alone counted as a technical achievement. Dam design everywhere learned from it. So did dam construction. Labor by the original builders still benefits millions. Water reached California because of the dam. It reached Arizona and southern Nevada. Power did too. The Southwest could flourish after that change. Building the landmark, and living with its impact, remains an unforgettable piece of United States history. Sunset light on the dam, seen from the Mike O'Callaghan-Pat Tillman Memorial Bridge, fills one last picture. A short list explains difficult words. Money set aside in a formal way for one use is an appropriation. Solid rock under the soil is bedrock. When substances turn into different substances, that process is a chemical reaction. Divert means to send something onto a new path. Digging out or uncovering material is excavating. A new and original idea can be called innovative. Something parched is extremely dry and short of moisture. Recovering or restoring a thing is reclamation. A reservoir stores a large body of water for drinking or for farms. Finding a way past problems is resourcefulness. Spillways give water a path around an obstacle, and a dam is one such obstacle. A turbine has a fan-like shape and takes energy from moving water, from wind, or from steam.

42. Homes in Dry Lands

1Friends who are Bedouin embrace in the Sahara. The place is Morocco. Four scenes sit together. Egypt's Sahara holds an oasis, and palm trees stand near it. Flowers grow in sand dunes in Australia. Water runs in the Sonoran Desert. Bolivia holds the largest salt flat on Earth. A dictionary usually calls a desert a dry land. The wording may add that the place is inhospitable and that life there is scarce or absent. Some desert regions match that wording. Other desert landscapes are full of life. Trees can grow there, and shrubs, and cacti, on the sides of mountains where many kinds of creatures thrive. A different desert can look like a sea of sand without end, dunes rolling like waves. Streams and rivers cross some desert regions. Those waters may go dry at certain times of year, or stay dry for a long stretch.

2Shared traits do exist. A desert is arid. Precipitation in a year is usually under 25.4 centimeters, which is 10 inches. Soil tends to be dry. Plants are fewer than in other places. Great cold is possible in some deserts. Sun and heat are what most of them have. Close to one-fifth of the land on Earth is desert. Hot deserts stand on five of the seven continents. Europe is an exception. Antarctica is the other. Size varies too. A desert can be small. A desert can be huge. A trip around the world can show more of these lands, and more of the first peoples of these lands. Their history there runs for thousands of years. In India's Thar Desert, children run as a group. Mali's Sahara is where a woman of the Tuareg people cooks a meal outside her home. Survival in the desert works as survival works anywhere. People adapt to what surrounds them. Food must be found. Water must be found. Shelter must be found. Any hard place on Earth asks the same. Basic needs have to be met, or life fails. For the people who live there, though, a desert is more than a struggle to last. It is home. It is a way of living. Libya is where a man of the Tuareg people rides a camel among a crowd.

3Desert People of the Sonoran. Heat and dryness mark the Sonoran Desert. It covers 310,800 square kilometers, or 120,000 square miles, from the southwestern United States into northern Mexico. Rain can stay away for months. A summer day can hit 49 degrees Celsius, or 120 degrees Fahrenheit. Winter nights can fall below freezing. Set beside other deserts, this one is relatively lush. It is relatively bountiful. Nearness to the ocean is why more rain falls here than in any other desert. Summer monsoons often soak the whole of it. Shade trees grow. So do large cacti, among them the saguaro, pronounced suh-WAR-oh. Summer flowers grow as well. The Tohono O'odham, pronounced toe-HOE-noh OH-eh-dom, are Indigenous people of this desert. They are one of three main groups inside the wider O'odham people. Their name means desert people. A map of the region marks California, New Mexico, and Arizona. It marks the Pacific Ocean and Mexico, within North America. Native plants in the Sonoran Desert number more than 2,500. No other desert in the world has more. Across thousands of years, water came from the desert, and so did food and a place to shelter. During the last few hundred years, newcomers from Europe arrived. Newcomers from the United States arrived too. They moved onto that land. Bit by bit they took ground where O'odham life had already lasted for thousands of years. Four tribes now divide the ground that holds many of the O'odham. One tribe is the nation called Tohono O'odham. The O'odham language is also spoken by people of the Gila River community. It is spoken at Ak-Chin. It is spoken at Salt River, a community also called Pima Maricopa. Each of those is an Indian community. Differences in the language show up from tribe to tribe. Sells, Arizona, is the largest community. The nation called Tohono O'odham has its capital there. Life today is on reservations and also off them, in towns and in cities. Francine Jose displays baskets. Relatives made them long ago.

4Floodwater was their irrigation. Diverting water was one method. Planting sites were chosen with care. Dryland farming became a mastery. Corn grew. Squash grew. Beans grew. Modern life drew more O'odham people as time passed. Further ground was lost to others. The government of the United States pressed them to take up the ways of that country. Traditions were still defended across the years. Many O'odham fold pieces of those traditions into lives of the twenty-first century. Farming is one piece. Cooking old recipes is another. Making baskets is another. Saguaro fruit, and the harvest of it, matters deeply to the culture of the Tohono O'odham. Spring brings beautiful flowers. They open on the cactus. Large red fruit follows, ripe in the middle of June. The fruit is taken from the tops of these giant cacti. Height can reach 22 meters and more, which is 75 feet. Tools made for the job are used. Wine is made from the fruit. That wine has an important place in the New Year celebration, held early in July. Around 1907 an O'odham woman gathers the fruit, in the upper photo. The lower photo shows the same traditional tools still in use. A map of the Sahara marks Morocco and Tunisia. It marks Western Sahara, Algeria, and Libya. Egypt is there, with Mauritania, Mali, and Sudan. Niger and Chad are there. The Atlantic Ocean borders Africa. Yearly rain in certain stretches of this desert stays under 25 millimeters, which is 1 inch. The Bedouin and the Sahara. Northern Africa holds the Sahara, from rocky ground to dunes of sand, across 8.6 million square kilometers, or 3.3 million square miles. Heat is extreme. Dryness is extreme. A storm there is most likely to be sand, or dust. So little rain falls that few plants flourish, and few animals do. Bedouin people, pronounced BED-oo-in, live across the Sahara in North Africa. The Middle East is home to them as well. Their name comes from Badw, an Arabic word for the people of the desert. Children of the Bedouin get ready to race camels.

5Homes in this Bedouin village are built from dry vegetation. The village is in Egypt's Sahara. The upper photo shows them. Rugs and pillows, bright with color, fill a Bedouin tent in Oman. The lower photo shows the inside. Nomadic life was the old pattern for the Bedouin of the Sahara. Rainy winters were for roaming. Dry summer months sent them back, with herds of camels, of sheep, or of goats, to land that had been cultivated. Water came from oasis to oasis, or from wells they dug. Home was a low black tent called a bayt, woven from goat hair or from the wool of sheep. Sun, wind, and blowing sand were kept out. Air could still move, which mattered in the intense heat. Bayts are still home for some Bedouin. A camp can be taken apart quickly, packed, and set up somewhere else. More than a hundred years have seen other countries take over land the Bedouin had long used. Nomadic life is gone for many. What remains is seminomadic. Others have settled. Towns and cities hold their houses. Apartments hold them too. Ancestors' ways are still followed by some. Even a nomadic family can now buy supplies at a market or from another seller. Herding animals is no longer the only usual work. Many other jobs are held. Inside a home in Oman, a mother who is Bedouin smiles. Her son is with her. Near Petra, in Jordan, a Bedouin village is called Umm Sayhoun.

6A map places the Gobi in Asia, between Mongolia and China, with the Indian Ocean marked nearby. Mountains blocked the rainy weather that would have let plants flourish, and the Gobi formed as a rain shadow desert. Nomads of Mongolia and the Gobi. Southern Mongolia reaches into northern China across 1.3 million square kilometers, or 500,000 square miles. Rock covers most of that Asian desert. People there are very few. Mongolia's first people have a language in which Gobi means large and dry. A place with no water is another meaning. Horses, sheep, goats, and cattle were the old herds of the Mongolian nomads who call this cold, windy desert home. Two-humped camels, the Bactrian kind, were herded too. A woman of Mongolia moves her animals through the Gobi. Outside the family ger, a boy from that same land is running. A ger is a yurt: a round tent that can be carried, built on a wooden frame and covered in felt. Harsh heat, cold, and wind are what the felt holds off. People are sheltered well. Animals can still suffer in that weather. Recent decades have seen families leave nomadic life by the thousands upon thousands. Several causes drove the move from desert to city. Winters of unusual harshness, and summers of unusual dryness, cost thousands of families their animals. Some lost every animal they had. Shifts in government hit herders as well, and earning a living grew hard. Since 1989, Mongolian nomads moving to the capital of Mongolia, looking for food and for work, have numbered more than half a million. Most brought the ger along. Districts of these tents grew up inside the city.

7A Way to Live. Thousands of years have passed with people calling deserts home. Challenges differ from one desert to the next. Solutions have always been found by the first peoples of each desert, so the place would serve them. In earlier times, homes, food, and water came almost only from what the local land offered. Much is different now. Modern lives are what many desert dwellers lead. Traditional lives, the lives of ancestors, still continue for some. Traditions of the desert community are still celebrated by many. Demand and reward sit together in desert life. Deep respect for the environment has always marked the peoples who make a desert home. Ample gifts are honored and used. Great power is acknowledged, and so is beauty. The United Arab Emirates has a crowded road. A man leads a camel along it. Ample describes a supply that meets the need, or passes it. Arid describes a place that is very dry. Bountiful means giving in a generous way. Cultivated describes land prepared for farming or for gardening. Dismantle means to take something apart. Dwellers are the people who live in one set place. Other animals that live there count too. Incorporate means to join something in, or to include it as a piece of a larger whole. Indigenous describes a people's tie to being the earliest to inhabit a place.
