Irrigation is the practice of bringing water to land or to crops so growth is helped. Monsoons are storms of a season. They bring heavy rain. Teeming means filled with. Tribes are groups. The people in one group share culture. They also share land.

43. How Animal Parks Changed

1The design of modern zoos can help people learn about animals and their natural habitats. When you visit a zoo, do you wonder how humans began to keep other animals? Some animals are kept in small cages, while others have more space to roam. Some zoos are larger and more modern than others. Do animals at different zoos appear to receive different care? Zoos have changed over the centuries, and they continue to change today. Zoos vary in size and in the money they have for expansions and upgrades. We will look at how zoos began and how their purpose has changed.

2Most of the great civilizations kept wild animals on display. Long ago, only kings and other rulers could afford this privilege. Keeping animals became a symbol of wealth and power. Animals were given as extravagant gifts, similar to gold and gemstones. Rulers kept exotic animals for their own enjoyment, so cages were made for viewing more than comfort. Explorers brought animals they had never seen home with spices, jewels, and silk. Alexander the Great, who lived from 356 to 323 BC, kept bears, monkeys, and elephants. He left his collection to King Ptolemy I of Egypt.

3Aristotle spent time watching the animals out of curiosity. He wrote History of Animals and described several hundred vertebrate species. In ancient Rome, deadly fights between captive animals or people were seen as sport. Leaders set wild animals such as lions and bears against each other and against gladiators. Countless animals died in shows that activists today would call cruelty. Many animals were caught in the wild, while others were bred in captivity. During the Middle Ages, most people paid little attention to nature. By the 1200s, rulers again exchanged animals as gifts.

4Frederick II was king of Germany from 1212 to 1220 and Holy Roman Emperor from 1220 to 1250. He kept cheetahs trained for hunting. He traveled with lions, elephants, camels, and other creatures to Germany for his wedding. The animals were decorated with ornaments, gems, and expensive cloth. Animals on display were still objects of curiosity in small cages with metal bars. They had no way to hide or to keep their natural behaviors. In the 1700s, the power of kings and queens declined, and common people gained decision-making roles. The sole right to keep and study wild animals came to an end.

5During the French Revolution of the 1790s, a royal collection moved to the Jardin des Plantes in Paris. This Garden of Plants became the first known public zoo. Circuses and traveling shows with exotic animals were popular in the future United States. Displays of North American animals, minerals, fossils, and plants attracted crowds. In the 1700s, London citizens could visit the collection at the Tower of London. They could pay a small sum or donate a cat or dog as food for the bears or big cats. In 1816, the Royal Menagerie still had small cages and viewing spaces. The early 1800s brought larger cities and natural areas saved as parkland.

6With more open space, more zoological parks and gardens were created. People could see a variety of animals and plants. London's Regent's Park Zoo was established in 1828 to study captive animals and help their wild relatives. It became the example for zoos in Europe and the United States. Zoos gave people a respite from dirty cities and close glimpses of wild animals. But zoos did not guarantee adequate care by today's standards. Little was known about nutritional and environmental needs, so health often suffered. Social animals that lived in family groups were caged alone and felt stress.

7Bare concrete cages could be hosed down easily. Most animals had no objects to climb except sleeping shelves for big cats. Zoo animals had nothing to interrupt boredom or provide stimulation. Early zoos rarely displayed information about origin or natural habits. Most visitors learned only the animals' names and feeding times. Over time, it became harder to obtain animals from the wild. Foreign governments treated wildlife as valuable resources that should be purchased. Some sought-after animals had been trapped and hunted nearly to extinction.

8These changes pushed zoos to care better for animals that were not easily replaced. Zoos shifted from pure entertainment to health needs and captive breeding. Research showed animals bred more if they were healthy and if their space felt like home. The new tiger compound at the San Francisco Zoo gives more room to roam, run, and climb in safety. The 1960s brought changes in values, including greater importance for the natural world. In the 1970s, organizations pressed zoo managers to improve care. Some believed all zoos should be closed and captive animals freed. The Association of Zoos and Aquariums stressed education and science, and zoos began to cooperate.

9Because zoos cooperated, animals received better care in more natural homes and bred with greater success. Captive breeding of giant pandas is always challenging, but San Diego Zoo has maintained success. The scimitar-horned oryx, an antelope from northern Africa, now exists only in zoos and is extinct in the wild. As people multiply, they destroy habitats for food, building materials, and farmland. Some species survive only in zoos, so breeding and reintroduction are their best hope. The AZA now places education, conservation, and study above entertainment. Zoos must keep pace with changes in attitudes, technology, and the environment. Species Survival Plans focus many zoos on endangered species and on genetic diversity.

10Genetics studies how traits pass from one generation to the next. Genetic material in each cell is like a blueprint for body structures and behaviors. Inherited differences, such as faster hawks, create genetic diversity. Diversity helps a species adapt and makes it less vulnerable to extinction. The black-footed ferret plan started with seven founders from the Great Plains. The red wolf plan had fourteen founders after this rare dog nearly vanished. Releases began in the late 1980s at North Carolina's Alligator River refuge, and by June 2007 more than 200 lived in 39 centers. Animals stay at many zoos, are moved for mating, and are tracked to protect diversity.

11More than one hundred SSPs exist, and the National Zoo works with Brazil on golden lion tamarins. Conservation is the main zoo focus, yet many visitors still come to be entertained. A giraffe-feeding platform at Reid Park Zoo in Tucson sends most profits to conservation. Enrichment includes hidden food, ice for polar bears, and frozen treats such as ratsicles and fishsicles. Training can help lions touch a target so staff can give care with less stress. Staff salaries can be about 60 percent of costs, and a new exhibit may cost millions of dollars. Feeding about 500 animals can total 168,000 dollars a year. Today's zoos are far from old royal collections, and their animals remind us to protect wild habitats.

44. How Hip-Hop Grew

1Cheryl James stands in the center of a photo. Sandra Denton stands on the right. Together they are known as Salt-N-Pepa. On the left is their DJ, Deidra Roper, known as DJ Spinderella. The parts of this book come in this order. The opening looks at the 1970s, in the city of New York. After that, the book tells how hip-hop started. Then come the four pillars. The DJ is one pillar. Breaking is one pillar. Graffiti art is one pillar. The MC is one pillar. Then come women in hip-hop. Then comes controversy. Then comes a golden age. Then comes Across an Ocean. Then comes The Music Does Not Stop. A word list comes last. The City in the 1970s During those years, the city’s economy was coming apart. Manufacturing in the city was in decline. Unemployment rose because of that decline. Poverty followed. Homelessness followed. Crime rose. Roads, buildings, and other public works were crumbling. Even so, officials cut money for schools. They cut money for community services. They cut money for job programs people needed in order to face these problems. A photo shows boys standing before painted graffiti. New York is the city in the picture. The decade is the 1970s. Racism over many decades had built economic walls. People of color hit those walls. Black people hit them in particular. Most could not afford to leave the city. Many white residents did leave. Neighborhoods that were already poorly served got worse. Those neighborhoods were home to many people of color. Still more businesses shut their doors. Jobs disappeared. Clubs disappeared. Movie theaters disappeared. With those losses, youth here needed fresh ways to have fun and to express themselves. What they invented was not limited to a fresh musical style. They started a whole cultural movement.

2How Hip-Hop Was Born Cindy Campbell was a teenager with a plan. The afternoon was hot. The season was summer. The year was 1973. Clive, her older brother, was the person she asked to spin records. The event was a party before school started again. DJ means disc jockey. Home for the party was the South Bronx. That neighborhood sits inside New York City. Most people there were Black or Puerto Rican. Jamaica was the country the Campbell family left. Their new home was the United States. Five years had passed since that move. Local parties were part of Clive’s childhood back in Jamaica. The person at the decks spoke while the songs played. The music played on sound systems that could be carried. His nickname was Hercules. On stage he used the name DJ Kool Herc. Fancy equipment was out of reach. He chose records from his own collection. Two turntables were hooked to an amplifier made for a guitar. The same record played on both turntables. He moved between them so the percussion breaks would last longer. Those breaks were the best part for dancing. A photo shows DJ Kool Herc performing in England. The party was a huge success. Fame across the whole Bronx arrived before another day had passed. He did not know what the coming decades would bring. He later said the people in the room had no sense that history was happening. Nobody knew a cultural revolution was starting. The title people later gave him was Father of Hip-Hop. Griots and the Path to Rap During those performances he drew on a Jamaican practice called toasting. In toasting, a voice talks. Sometimes the voice chants. A rhythm runs underneath. The 1950s are when this practice caught on. An older West African tradition stands behind it. That tradition belongs to griots. Say the word GREE-ohz. A griot is a storyteller. A griot is a poet. A griot is a singer. A griot is a historian. Many people who love hip-hop treat rappers as griots of the present day. A rapper, like a griot, tells the community’s story. Struggles are recorded. Triumphs are recorded. The telling entertains, and it also informs. In that way, history and culture of the community are shaped and kept. A griot from Mauritania is shown performing in New York City.

3Four Main Parts This culture is larger than its music. It is not only music. At the start, the community had no clubs for shows. It had no stages for dance. It had no galleries for art. Artists carried their creativity into the streets instead. The street was the stage. The city was the audience. Four pillars, or key elements, hold the culture up. One pillar is the DJ. Another is breaking. Another is graffiti art. The last is the MC. The DJ A DJ’s job is to keep music going without a gap. One turntable is ending a song. The second turntable brings the next song in. The change from song to song feels smooth. Few sounds mark hip-hop as clearly as scratching. Pioneering DJs in New York City developed it. Grand Wizzard Theodore was one of them. The scratch comes from a hand moving a vinyl record back and forth. The record is playing on the turntable while the hand moves it. Grandmaster Flash appears in a 2002 photo, working the decks at an event. What those early DJs noticed was a favorite part of each song. They loved the break beat. That is the stretch of a song when every sound drops out except the drums. DJ Kool Herc repeated that stretch. So did other early DJs, including Grandmaster Flash. Both turntables carried one identical record. With these methods, DJs built new music out of older music. The idea reached far beyond hip-hop. It shaped music makers for years afterward. The influence was profound. Breaking Break dancing is a name some people use. Dancers who started this in the street wanted a different word. Breaking was the word they kept. The names they chose included b-boys. They also chose b-girls. Breakers was another name. The year 1984 is the date of a photo. B-boys are shown competing.

4While a break beat played, breakers showed skills they made up in the moment. Six kinds of movement were typical. Top-rock is fast, skilled work with the feet. The breaker is standing. Down-rock is footwork too. The floor holds both hands and feet. Acrobatics are what power moves demand. They demand speed, agility, and strength. A freeze is a sudden stop of every motion. The breaker holds a pose. The pose is often unusual or difficult. Balance on one hand is one example. Balance on the head is another. Popping is a flowing motion of arms and of legs. Locking snaps a limb into a held spot. The angles are often sharp. Dance battles were common. Two breakers took turns, or two crews did. Each side showed its best moves. People stood in a circle and judged creativity and skill. The style was easy to recognize, and that fame spread. Fans of hip-hop all over the world took the dance up and loved it. Graffiti as Art Graffiti is writing, or it is drawings, painted on property that belongs to the public. It existed long before hip-hop rose. In the early 1970s it became an important part of hip-hop culture. A canvas was not the surface. Artists painted buildings. They painted subway cars, trains, and bridges. Part of the thrill was simple. Thousands of people would see the work every day. Marking public property is against the law. Outlaw artist was an identity many of them claimed. Beyond this culture, vandalism was the label people used. Inside the culture, it was art. In time, artists were asked to show work in major galleries around the world. Museums have kept famous pieces from hip-hop’s graffiti years. Art books have kept them too. Lady Pink is shown working on a painting. The painting honors women who took part in hip-hop. Several of the first artists are named here, along with several of the best known. Sandra Fabara is one. The name Lady Pink is hers. Next on the list is Fred Brathwaite. Fab 5 Freddy is the name he uses. Another artist on the list is Jean-Michel Basquiat. Donald Joseph White is one. He is known as Dondi.

5The MC Early on, the word for a rapper was MC. The letters expand into the phrase master of ceremonies. Beside the DJ, the MC worked as a partner of sorts. The DJ mixed dance music so the party would continue. The MC took the microphone. Call-and-response was used to lift the crowd and pull people in. Soon the talk turned into rhymes that locked to the music. Rappers are judged on content. They are judged on flow. They are judged on delivery. Content can cover many subjects. Clever lines about self-confidence are one kind. Comment on society and on politics is another. Good flow means the lyrics stay on the beat. Good delivery means a voice people can tell apart from others. Words are spoken clearly. Breathing does not break the flow. Knowledge, a Fifth Pillar Many fans count knowledge as a fifth pillar. KRS-One, and other legendary MCs, say the other four elements are bound together by knowledge. Greatness requires knowledge of one’s own history and identity. It requires knowledge of the community’s history. It also requires knowledge of hip-hop’s history, its values, and its ideas. That knowledge lets artists grow and find fresh ways to express themselves. Social change can then be pushed forward by the art. Women Who Shaped Hip-Hop Women have helped shape this culture from the start. Sharon Green was one of the earliest. She is MC Sha Rock. She is considered the first woman to rap. Breaking, as a b-girl, was how she started. The neighborhood was the South Bronx. Her age was fourteen. MC skills developed quickly after that. A record deal in 1979 made her the first woman rapper to get one. Funky 4 + 1, her group, shared that deal. National television came two years after that. No hip-hop group had performed there before them. Sylvia Robinson is sometimes called the Queen of Rap. She is sometimes called the Mother of Hip-Hop. She ranks among the most influential music producers ever. In 1979 she founded Sugar Hill Records. No hip-hop label had come before it. Early records that many people still know passed through her production. “Rapper’s Delight” was one of them. The Sugarhill Gang performed it. It was the first hip-hop hit across the nation. At the time, hip-hop was mostly unknown outside New York City. Listeners elsewhere in the country met hip-hop through this record.

6Men dominate the hip-hop industry. Men dominate the music industry in general. Women in hip-hop have faced sexism from the start. Later popular styles, made by male artists, often used lyrics that showed no respect for women. Those lyrics became a staple. Several rappers changed the music and pushed it forward. MC Lyte was one. Queen Latifah was one. Salt-N-Pepa was one. Lady B was one. Lauryn Hill was one. They used hip-hop to strengthen themselves and to strengthen other women. Rap became a platform. They talked about treatment of women inside hip-hop. They talked about treatment of women in the wider culture. Roxanne's Revenge Lolita Shante Gooden was fourteen and already among the strongest rappers of her time. Most people know her as Roxanne Shante. The year 1984 brought a release from her. The song’s title was “Roxanne’s Revenge.” The subject was the sexism women go through. Success for the song was huge. Finals of a freestyle MC contest came the following year. She was the clear winner of the last rap battle. A low mark from one judge kept the win from her. The reason came out years afterward, when that judge explained it. He was a well-known MC himself. He believed a young girl winning would make people take hip-hop less seriously as art. She lost the battle. She still went on to make two rap albums. Younger women in hip-hop later had her as a mentor. Rapped in Controversy Hip-hop started as music for parties. Even the earliest artists still spoke about serious social problems and political ones. They were honest about racism they had lived through. They were honest about poverty, violence, and injustice. Grandmaster Flash, together with the Furious Five, was among the first. Their song “The Message” came out in 1982. It was a blistering picture of urban poverty. Street misery in New York City was part of that picture. Public Enemy, in the later 1980s, turned music into a voice for Black pride. Racism faced by Black people in this country was in the songs too. Lana Michelle Moorer is the name MC Lyte was given. She broke barriers in the industry. Her music took up racism. It took up sexism. Drug use, and the harm it did in her community, was in the music. She is shown on stage in 1993. The city is New York.

7Few hip-hop groups of that era carried more influence than Public Enemy. The years were the late 1980s and the early 1990s. Argument followed the group as well. In the 1990s a style called gangsta rap began to dominate hip-hop. Lyrics in that style often struck some listeners as offensive. As the style grew more popular, the music industry pushed it ahead of other styles. Many Black artists could not get a record deal unless their music fit this genre. With that rise, many people outside the culture started to treat all rap as offensive. Poetry is how many other listeners have understood rap. Older poetry and rap share a great deal. Both use rhythm with skill. Both use rhyme. Both tell stories. Maya Angelou, among the most celebrated poets, saw the link too. Famous rap artists worked with her. She was a source of inspiration for them. A photo shows her speaking a poem aloud. President Bill Clinton is being sworn in. Roots in Spoken Poetry Poetry spoken aloud during the 1960s made rap’s later rise possible. The Last Poets were one performing group. New York City was their home. The Watts Prophets came from California. They spoke poems over a bongo beat, or over jazz. The poems carried weighty messages. Black pride was one. Racism, poverty, and justice were others. People often treat these poets as the step that came before. Hip-hop of recent times followed their work.

8A Golden Age Hip-hop music spread across the country in the mid-1980s and the early 1990s. The culture changed because of that spread. New artists brought new musical influences. Diversity grew. Styles innovated. Local radio stations wanted new hip-hop. Club DJs wanted it too. Mainstream popularity and success shot upward. Record companies began spending large sums to produce new albums. Different cities grew different styles. New York City produced hardcore rap. It also produced boom-bap. Los Angeles, California, produced G-Funk. It also produced gangsta rap. Run DMC was among newer artists who mixed hip-hop with music of other kinds. De La Soul used pieces of jazz and of blues. A Tribe Called Quest did that too. The result was called jazz rap. Salt-N-Pepa built a brighter, upbeat style. People called it pop rap, or hip pop. Sampling was one defining habit of this era. A sample is a piece of one song reused inside a different song. Artists pulled samples from many genres. Jazz was one. Blues, soul, and rock were others. Movie sound was sampled by some artists as well. Across an Ocean Almost 9,000 miles lie between the Bronx and New Zealand. That distance is about 14,484 kilometers. Hip-hop made that crossing early in the 1980s. The Maori were ready to listen. New Zealand’s Indigenous Polynesian people go by that name. Black communities in the South Bronx had faced a similar squeeze at the start of the 1970s. Disadvantage was the setting for large numbers of Maori. Money was harder to come by. Crime was higher. Health care and education were hard to reach. They felt mainstream culture in New Zealand did not show them. Hip-hop spoke strongly to that feeling. Maori bands took it up as their own music. Upper Hutt Posse was one band. Third3ye was another. The Music Does Not Stop As rap grew more popular around the world, the culture became a global phenomenon. It took root in France. It took root in Mexico. It took root in New Zealand and in South Africa. Break dancing seized imaginations when films arrived. Wild Style came out in 1982. Breakin’ came out in 1984. The dance became popular in the United Kingdom. Japan took up the dance. Germany did too. So did Russia. So did South Korea. Today, striking graffiti can be seen on city streets in many places. Brazil is one. Morocco is one. China is one.

9Graffiti covers a building in Brazil. That image sits at the top. Hungary is the site of a dance contest. The dancer is a b-girl, and she is from Japan. That contest is the left-hand picture. England is where one member of a Muslim duo performs. The music is hip-hop. That image sits at the right. Hip-hop became a sensation across the globe. Few resources were on hand. That shortage produced musical inventions that rank among the century’s most creative. New forms of artistic expression came out of it too. Hip-hop still shapes many parts of popular culture around the world. The mark has lasted. Words to Know sensation (n.): a person or a thing that stirs great excitement. transition (n.): a passing into a new stage, a new place, or a new condition. portable (adj.): easy to carry or to move. pioneering (adj.): bringing in ideas or methods that are new. profoundly (adv.): in a strong or intense way. innovation (n.): the act of bringing in something new, or of inventing it. genre (n.): a category of literature or art marked by a shared style or form. economic (adj.): related to buying and selling of goods and services. distinctive (adj.): having a quality or characteristic that is different and notable. culture (n.): a particular society with its own ideas and customs. ceremonies (n.): formal events that take place on special occasions. phenomenon (n.): an event or an occurrence that is remarkable.

45. How the Colonies Broke with the Crown

1A map of North America in 1750 shows who claimed which land. New France covers a wide northern stretch. British Canada sits nearby. British colonies line the Atlantic coast. Louisiana is marked. So is a disputed zone. Florida appears. New Spain appears. The Atlantic Ocean and the Pacific Ocean frame the continent. More than 200 years ago, colonists began a war against an empire. They came out of that war as the winners. Their homes were in the land now called the United States. The empire they fought was Great Britain. Britain was already old, rich, and strong. It wanted a larger empire. It wanted firm control of land in the place Europeans then named the New World. That name covered the Americas. North America was part of it. Central America was part of it. South America was part of it. Britain was not alone in that desire. Other countries in Europe wanted American land too.

2Europeans saw raw materials in the New World. They also saw room for populations that were growing at home. Indigenous peoples were already there. They had lived on that land for thousands of years. Spain began colonizing in the 1400s. Spanish colonizers enslaved Indigenous people. They also killed Indigenous people whose families had lived there across thousands of years. Deaths by the 1700s stood in the millions. Violent fighting caused many of those deaths. Disease brought by Europeans caused many more. In eastern North America, Great Britain seized Indigenous land by force. On that land Britain set up thirteen colonies. People who crossed the Atlantic to live in those colonies were called colonists. The ocean distance let them form their own ideas. It also let them form their own habits. Each colony held a charter from the British king. Each colony also had a legislature. Property owners in the colony elected that legislature. A strong independent spirit grew from this life. That spirit later fed the Revolutionary War. The break is striking because the two sides had once been partners. France and Great Britain spent the 1700s fighting several wars. North American land was the prize. Colonists stood with Britain in those fights. Their shared foe was France. The 1750s brought the same hunger for land. France wanted it. England wanted it too. For hundreds of years the two kingdoms had competed in Europe for power and territory. The same rivalry crossed the ocean. French explorers had traveled a long route. The route started at Newfoundland. It followed the St. Lawrence River downstream. The Great Lakes were on it. The valley of the Ohio River was on it too. Trading posts along that route were the work of French fur trappers. England claimed those same regions. England urged colonists to settle them. Indigenous nations nearby usually had a warmer tie with the French. Relations with the British were harder. Years of trade explain that bond. British settlers kept pushing west and leaving the East Coast behind. They claimed ground where Indigenous people had lived for centuries. They claimed hunting ground too. Indigenous people wanted those ancestral lands back. A painting shows the Battle of Fort Duquesne. The name is said as doo-KAYN. The year of that battle is 1754.

3Many Indigenous nations joined France. They hoped to protect trade. They hoped to protect their lands. They hoped to protect their independence. Other nations joined Great Britain. They were promised some land in return. The Cherokee were among them. The Catawba were among them. So were nations of the Iroquois Confederacy. France had partners too. The Delaware sided with France. The Shawnee sided with France. The Ottawa sided with France. Forts rose across the valley of the Ohio River. Both European powers built them. Each fort was meant to guard a claim. Early in 1754 the French raised Fort Duquesne. The name is said doo-KAYN. Today the city of Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, stands on that spot. Britain had started a fort in a place that could control the whole valley. French forces drove the British workers off. The French then finished the fort themselves. A map of the fort labels the Ohio River. It labels the Allegheny River. It labels the Monongahela River. Britain sent a young surveyor to tell the French to go. His name was George Washington. Eight other men went with him. The French would not leave. Washington, his men, and Seneca allies then struck a party of French scouts. Ten of the scouts were killed. Twenty-one others were captured. Washington's group next built Fort Necessity. It stood about 60 miles from Fort Duquesne. That distance is 96.5 kilometers. In the summer of 1754 the French took Fort Necessity. Washington and his men gave up. After the surrender, they got away. Washington later served as a volunteer aide. He worked beside Britain's General Edward Braddock. Braddock meant to push the French out of the Ohio River Valley. Fort Duquesne was the place to start. French soldiers hid in the woods. Indigenous allies hid with them. They waited beside the marching British columns. Then they sprang an ambush. General Braddock was killed. More than half his men were killed too. The British who lived panicked. They ran. Many people call this clash the opening true battle in a conflict named the French and Indian War. A wider struggle contained it. People know that wider struggle as the Seven Years' War. Colonists remembered the surprise style of fighting. In the American Revolution they later used the same guerrilla warfare against British soldiers.

4A later map shows land claims once the war had ended. British Canada remains in the north. The Atlantic Ocean and the Pacific Ocean still frame the land. Thirteen colonies sit along the east. Some inland ground is marked British but reserved for Indigenous peoples. New Spain and Florida appear as well. In 1756 Great Britain officially declared war on France. Formal fighting started that year. Battles had already been fought in the two years before. Those earlier battles took place in North America. They also took place in Europe. Britain sent more soldiers to the colonies. France sent more soldiers too. Early on, France looked likely to win. Indigenous allies helped the French. The French also understood frontier fighting better than the British or the colonists. The balance changed by 1758. Britain's force on the continent had grown to almost 42,000. Those troops hit key points. Fort Niagara was one. Lake Champlain was one. Quebec was one. France lost its link to the Ohio River Valley. It lost its link to the Mississippi River. It lost the port at New Orleans. France had claimed all of that land. Supplies from those places had kept the French alive in North America. The winner of the war was Great Britain. A peace called the Treaty of Paris was signed in 1763. East of the Mississippi, French claims across North America were wiped away. British colonists could now move into land France had controlled. Florida stood at one end of the newly open land. Canada stood at the other. For Indigenous nations the change was a disaster. Colonists took still more of their land. For a short time after the French defeat, colonists were glad to belong to Great Britain. Many of them had fought next to British troops. They had shared an enemy. Once France was beaten, that feeling changed. British protection no longer seemed necessary to many colonists. They no longer wanted British oversight either. Several British moves after the war made them angry. King George III and Parliament raised colonial taxes. The goal was to shrink the huge debt the war had created. Britain also posted soldiers in the colonies to guard the bigger empire. Colonists were told to house those soldiers. They were told to feed them. Britain tried to slow American settlement farther west. Leaders hoped that limit would mend ties with Indigenous nations.

5A year had passed since the peace signed in Paris. The new year was 1764. Parliament passed the Sugar Act. An older law was being widened. People called that older law the Sugar and Molasses Act. It dated from 1733. Colonists who bought Spanish molasses now paid a tax. French molasses was taxed too. Spanish sugar was taxed. French sugar was taxed. Coffee gained a tax. Some textiles gained a tax. The law also tightened rules on lumber leaving the colonies. Iron exports were regulated further. Markets where colonists could sell their goods were limited. Cheap sugar from Spain and from France became too costly. Colonists had to buy British sugar instead. The money helped the British government pay war debts. The colonial economy was thrown off by the change. In 1765 Parliament passed the Quartering Act. The Seven Years' War had ended. About 10,000 British troops were still in America. The act told colonists to lodge those troops in private homes. The soldiers lived with families. They did not have to pay rent. No duty required them to help around the house. Every colony refused except Pennsylvania. What New York would not give was billeting. Billeting means food and a place to stay. Parliament answered by suspending New York's governor. It also suspended the colony's legislature. The punishment was meant to force obedience. The tax that truly enraged people was the Stamp Act. Parliament passed it that same year. It was Britain's first serious try to press authority over the North American colonies. Printed paper now required a stamp. The stamp was British, and colonists had to pay for it. Books were taxed. Newspapers were taxed. Calendars were taxed. Playing cards were taxed. Other paper goods were taxed. Hidden in the details was an income tax. It was the first tax aimed only at the American colonies. Colonists did not want an outside power taking their money. British leaders felt they had carried the colonies for too long. In Britain's view, colonists owed support to the government. That government had been their protector. That government had also fought France beside them. The loudest colonial complaint was about voice. The government that taxed them gave them no say. People cried out that tax without representation was wrong. They wanted Parliament to hold a voice that belonged to them. Other English subjects had that kind of voice. King George disliked being told what to do by colonists. He believed the American colonies should pay to support his empire.

6The king considered how to strike back at the rebellious colonists. At the same time, the colonists began to act together against the taxes. Over the years they had built ways to govern themselves. Virginia's elected assembly was the House of Burgesses. It made laws for that colony. It was founded in 1619. No earlier elected assembly existed in a North American colony. Other colonies treated it as a model. Among the British colonies, the Virginia Assembly was the earliest body voters had elected. In 1765 its members debated whether the Stamp Act was fair. Patrick Henry was a young lawyer. He stood and made a claim. Only people of Virginia, he said, could place a tax on Virginians. The assembly accepted his stand. Some people still called him a traitor. They said he was arguing against the Crown. Women in the 1700s were mostly shut out of politics. They still served the patriotic cause. A group called the Daughters of Liberty organized boycotts. Members joined the boycotts themselves. Many women bought the goods a household needed. Some ran small shops. Because of that, refusing British goods hit British merchants hard. Women also formed sewing circles to aid the revolutionary cause. Newspapers printed Henry's position. Soon protest against the Stamp Act spread through all 13 colonies. Samuel Adams added his voice. He was a tax collector. He was also a politician from Massachusetts. Adams, Henry, and others who stood with them gained a name. People called them Patriots. They stood with their colonies and against the king. Support for King George earned a different name. Those colonists were called Loyalists. Their loyalty was to the Crown. Some Patriots formed the Sons of Liberty. The Daughters of Liberty were already organizing. Both groups urged people not to trade with Britain. They urged people not to buy British goods. Some colonists even attacked British stamp agents. Parliament had more acts still to pass. More attacks were still to come.

7In October 1765, representatives from nine colonies traveled to New York. Thirteen colonies existed, so four stayed away. People call that meeting the Stamp Act Congress. Its request to Parliament was a repeal of the Stamp Act. Repeal means to cancel it. King George said yes to canceling it. The year of that yes was 1766. The calm did not last. In 1767 the Townshend Acts became law. They taxed glass. They taxed paint. They taxed lead. They taxed paper. They taxed tea. The money was supposed to pay for running the colonies. Anger rose again, just as it had against earlier taxes. Colonists boycotted British goods. To boycott is to refuse to buy. In 1770 Britain withdrew every Townshend tax except one. British merchants were losing income. Tea was the one tax that remained. Strain between Patriots and Great Britain kept growing. British soldiers spread through the colonies to make people pay. Each new tax added resentment. One night in Boston, resentment turned into violence. The French and Indian War was over. In the years that followed, many British soldiers lived in Boston. Open trouble stayed rare for a time. Colonists hated having soldiers in their houses. Years passed with both groups sharing the same streets. The date was March 5, 1770. That night a rowdy Boston crowd picked a fight. The fight was with some British soldiers. The soldiers fired into the crowd. Five colonists died. Those colonists had been armed only with snowballs. They also had sticks. They also had stones. Samuel Adams, a Patriot, saw a chance. He wanted more colonists to favor independence. Paul Revere was his friend. Adams asked him to make a picture. Revere was a silversmith. Revere engraved the scene. He printed it. He sold it as a poster. Adams named the fight the Boston Massacre. The printed image showed soldiers firing. The crowd in the picture looked peaceful and finely dressed. Newspapers printed the image too. The picture did not tell the night truthfully. It still did what Adams wanted. Many colonists became enraged. The picture people remember is that engraving of British force used on colonists who looked peaceful.

8Many people believe Crispus Attucks was the first to die in that Boston crowd. He lived in the city. He worked as a whaler on ships in Boston Harbor. Freedom from Great Britain was a belief he held strongly. Speakers at his memorial praised his bravery again and again. A picture records his face. Tea was all that remained of the Townshend taxes. The tea tax itself was not new. In 1773 the Tea Act was revised. Colonists were required to buy tea from only one seller. That seller was Great Britain's East India Company. The company was failing with money. Colonists still had no seats in Parliament. They were angry that some taxes had never been canceled. In December 1773 a frustrated group acted. They climbed onto a British ship. They dumped tea into Boston Harbor. The load was 342 chests. Their clothing copied the dress of the Mohawk Nation. The disguise was meant to keep blame off them. Britain was not fooled. Britain was not amused. Leaders decided the time for goodwill had ended. People later called the night the Boston Tea Party. Summer of 1774 brought the reply. King George and Parliament passed the Coercive Acts. Colonists renamed them the Intolerable Acts. The laws were written to punish rebels. Punishment would last at least until Britain was paid back for the tea. One law shut Boston Harbor to every ship. Many workers in Boston lost their jobs. Families feared they would starve. Colonists elsewhere felt sorry for Boston. They were furious at Great Britain. Colonial assemblies spoke up for the city. British governors in those colonies often did not want that support declared. Britain named General Thomas Gage governor of Massachusetts. He was sent to Boston to take the city in hand. He brought 4,000 troops. Colonists had to house that army. They had to feed it. The Intolerable Acts pulled the colonies together against Britain. The Stamp Act had done something similar before. In September 1774, delegates from twelve colonies met in Philadelphia. The meeting was the First Continental Congress. Every colony sent people except one. The missing colony was Georgia. A picture shows Patrick Henry speaking. The listeners look fully absorbed.

9The delegates demanded a repeal of the Intolerable Acts. They also demanded a colonial voice in every tax law. Parliament refused both demands. Mutiny was the word Parliament used for the colonies. The delegates declared more boycotts. Those boycotts covered all British goods. They knew their choices might bring war with Great Britain. They agreed to gather again in 1775. Meanwhile they told colonists in Massachusetts to store weapons. Massachusetts looked like the right place to start. The Continental Congress began training fighters. People called them militiamen. People also called them minutemen. Colonists were getting ready to fight for independence. Many of them no longer believed the old country. Many no longer trusted it. Patriot soldiers earned the nickname minutemen for their speed. They could seize their weapons and be outside within a minute. Most of them did not even have uniforms. In Boston, General Gage grew alarmed. Reports said colonists were storing weapons at Concord. Concord lies about 20 miles west of Boston. That is 32 kilometers. The date was April 18, 1775. That night he sent out 700 British soldiers. The mission was secret. They were to seize the weapons. Gage also hoped to arrest two rebel leaders. One was Samuel Adams. The other was John Hancock. Both were in Lexington, a town near Concord. A picture shows General Thomas Gage. The plan leaked through a Patriot doctor. His name was Samuel Prescott. He warned the militia that British troops were on the way. Before the soldiers reached Concord, they met a waiting group. Lexington's village green held seventy waiting militiamen. The British tried to walk past them. Then a shot rang out. Nobody had ordered it. Nobody knows which side fired it. That shot began the Revolutionary War. A later poem by Ralph Waldo Emerson gave the moment a famous name. The poem is called Concord Hymn. In the fight that followed, eight militiamen died. Ten more were wounded. British losses were heavy. The soldiers still marched on toward Concord.

10Boston still tells a famous tale about Paul Revere. The tale says he warned the fighters at Lexington and at Concord that British troops were approaching. The tale is taller than the truth. Something else is true. What Revere did do was send someone to observe the soldiers. The spy was to hang lanterns in a church tower. The number of lanterns would show the route. One lantern meant the soldiers were coming by land. Two lanterns meant they would cross the Charles River. That night Revere saw two lanterns. He left Boston on horseback. William Dawes rode with him. They headed toward Concord to spread the warning. Samuel Prescott joined them on the road. British officers stopped Revere. They stopped Dawes too. Prescott got away. He was the rider who actually reached the militiamen with the warning. A picture shows the famous midnight ride that stories still give to Revere. In Concord the British wrecked some supplies. Most of the weapons were already gone. Americans had hidden them before the troops arrived. Hancock escaped arrest. Adams escaped too. Massachusetts militia reached Concord with nearly 500 men. At the North Bridge they attacked British soldiers who were worn out. The next day the British began marching back to Boston. The attack continued along that road. Militiamen hid behind trees. They hid behind stone walls. From there they fired into the British lines. That same style had shown up before. French fighters used it in the war that also involved Indigenous nations. So did those Indigenous fighters. Trained British professionals felt humiliated. They had lost to colonists who were quickly trained and poorly matched in equipment. The dead numbered 273 on the British side. The dead numbered 93 among the militiamen. The Revolutionary War was underway. A picture shows Patriot troops facing British soldiers. Lexington, Massachusetts, is the town in the scene. The ground under them is the village green.

11These words help a reader follow the story. Allies are people or groups that join others for a shared cause. A colonist is a person living in a colony. The word also fits a person who helps found one. Delegates are chosen or elected people who speak and act for others. Economy means how money circulates. It moves through industry. It moves through trade. It moves through finance. The setting may be a country or a smaller region. Export means sending materials or products away so they can be sold somewhere else. To found something is to create it or set it up, as with a group or an organization. Guerrilla warfare is irregular fighting, often a surprise attack, by small independent bands of soldiers. Imposed means forced on people by power or by authority. A legislature is an elected group. Its work is writing laws and changing laws. Levied means collected by a government, as a tax is collected. Migrated means moved on purpose from one region to another to live or to work. Mutiny is a refusal to obey a government or another authority, a rebellion. Parliament is the lawmaking body of the United Kingdom. Two houses form it. One is the House of Commons. The second house is the House of Lords. Basic substances used to make other things are called raw materials. Regulated means controlled in amount, rate, speed, or behavior so that something worked properly or followed rules. Reimbursed means paid back for money already spent. Stationed means assigned to a place. Stockpile means to keep a large supply for a later need.

46. How the Piano Took Shape

1Steinway is a major maker of high-quality pianos in New York and in Germany. The piano is perhaps the world’s best-known instrument, and its sound is easy to recognize in any music. It did not always sound this way, because its early relatives sounded very different. The first widely used keyboard was the clavichord, used in Europe in the 1400s. No one knows who invented it. It was a long wooden box with wire strings of different lengths inside. A soundboard under the strings vibrated and helped project the tones. It could be 122 to 213 centimeters long, and people set it on a table to play it in fifteenth-century homes.

2Bartolomeo Cristofori made keyboards in the early 1700s and wanted players to control the volume. He changed the harpsichord so strings were hit by a leather hammer, not plucked by a quill. When you press a key, the hammer shoots up and strikes the string from below. When you release the key, a damper falls on the string, stops it vibrating, and ends the note. Players could play loud or soft notes, so he named it the pianoforte, Italian for soft and loud. In time the name became piano, and a 1720 Cristofori grand is the oldest one left in the world. Other makers added to his design, including the German Silbermann. Bach, who had written many harpsichord pieces, did not think much of it, so an upset Silbermann destroyed it with an ax!

3It took a while for European musicians to accept the piano, but Bach grew to like it. Haydn and Mozart wrote many piano pieces, and by the late 1700s Europeans wanted more piano music. In big music halls, felt hammers replaced leather ones and made a rich, warm tone. Keyboards grew from fifty-four to eighty-eight keys, longer wing-shaped grands held more strings, and metal soundboards gave a purer sound. Good players were said to tickle the ivories, because wooden keys were covered in ivory from elephant tusks. Countless elephants died, but today it is illegal to use ivory, and keys are covered in plastic. In 1955, Louis Pratt was a master ivory cutter, and his company made keys from African elephant tusks. At first all pianos were grands, but in the nineteenth century popular demand led to smaller, less expensive home pianos in Europe and North America.

4In the nineteenth century, women were encouraged to play the piano. The idea was not to make them performers, but wives. Women with musical ability were seen as refined and charming. Playing also let women give lessons and earn their own money. Such chances to earn money were limited then. An old postcard shows a woman and a child playing a duet. As more pianos were sold, people played different kinds of piano music. African Americans sang and played gospel, then tried new styles that led to ragtime, a jazzy music just for piano.

5Many world-class pianists became known for different types, or genres, of music. Scott Joplin was the son of a railway worker and the King of Ragtime. His Maple Leaf Rag, published in 1899, is the most widely known ragtime hit. Sergei Rachmaninoff was an early twentieth-century Russian composer and an accomplished pianist. He wrote and performed many beautiful classical piano pieces. Billy Joel, the Piano Man, made his name starting in the 1970s by writing and performing rock tunes that featured the piano.

6Recorded music in the early twentieth century made piano sales drop, since people could listen at home without owning or playing one. Makers built self-playing pianos to draw buyers. Foot pedals pumped a device that held paper rolls, and punched holes made the notes play. Anyone could play the piano with no lessons needed! This player piano from the late 1800s is driven by an electric motor. Digital self-playing pianos came in the 1980s, and a button started a chosen electronic file while the keys moved. These pianos could also be played normally, with eighty-eight weighted keys that felt like a regular piano. A digital piano sounds and feels like a piano but is lighter and cheaper, and many families own one today.

7By contrast, the keys of digital keyboards are not weighted. The most popular size has only sixty-one keys. These keyboards are light, sturdy, and easy to move. Some traveling bands use them. An Australian band includes a digital keyboard player. Many keyboards can sound like other instruments, such as a trumpet or a flute. Some make effects like a chirping bird at the touch of a key, and Cristofori would be amazed at these new sounds. Whether it is a digital keyboard or a concert grand, the piano remains one of the most popular instruments around.

47. Hunger Close to Home

1State cards called Electronic Benefit Transfer cards look like credit cards. They took the place of food stamps. School's final day has arrived. A long summer break thrills almost everyone. A boy named Aaron is the exception. He sinks in his chair. His head rests on the desk. His stomach growls. School lunch was his only meal today. He knows the cupboards at home hold nothing. His mother holds two jobs. Even so, food money is gone by the month's end. He lets out a sigh. A long summer stretches ahead of him. Aaron is not alone. Millions of children in America are hungry each day. You might be one of those children. United States Department of Agriculture is the long name behind the USDA. That agency counted households in 2019. It found 35.2 million Americans in homes it called food-insecure. People in those homes could not always get enough food for everyone who lived there. Children made up 10.7 million of that count. About one child in seven in the United States was food insecure.

2Hunger causes pain. It also causes stress. A health agency called the CDC studied children who eat too little. Its long name is the Centers for Disease Control. Prevention is part of that name too. Those children have more health troubles than children who eat enough. They also miss more school. Once they are in class, focusing is harder. Learning is harder too. Tiredness from hunger keeps them from enough exercise. The harm lasts. Young bodies grow quickly. Young brains develop quickly too. Too little food can slow the body. It can slow the mind as well. The United States raises food in huge amounts. It sends millions of pounds of food to other countries. The government runs programs for people who cannot pay for meals. Hunger in the United States is still an epidemic. The question is why. Trouble can strike any family. A factory shuts, and a parent loses work. A guardian falls ill and cannot work. One parent, raising children alone, has to remain at home. The reason may be an aging relative. The reason may be a sick child. Lost pay, or pay that was never enough, forces hard choices. Sometimes the choice is bills or meals. Millions of Americans hold full-time jobs and are still food insecure. Since the 1950s, housing has cost more. Medical care has cost more. Food has cost more. Those rises have outstripped the wages of most people. The lowest legal pay was fixed in 2009 by the federal government. It was $7.25 for each hour. A full-time year at that rate is $15,080. Many jobs at that pay hire people only part of the time. The aim is to skip benefits. Health insurance is one benefit they skip. Taxes and insurance can squeeze people who earn more than that too. USDA numbers say women are more than 60 percent of the adults who get food help. The National Women's Law Center reports another gap. Low-paying jobs are where women land more than twice as often as men. Even in matching work, a woman is still likely to be paid less than a man. In 2019 the Institute for Women's Policy Research measured full-time pay. Women earned 81.5 cents for each dollar a man earned. The U.S. Census counts single parents who care for children. Women are more than 80 percent of that group. They are twice as likely as single fathers to live in poverty. A mother in poverty often means her children live in poverty too.

3Help with food from the federal government started as help for farmers. The time was the Great Depression. From 1933, the USDA bought crops farmers could not sell. Those surplus crops went to people who needed them. In 1939 the government printed real stamps. People used the stamps to buy surplus food. By 1964, buyers could choose any kind of food. Surplus food was no longer the only choice. A new name arrived for the Food Stamp Program in 2008. It became the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP. The new name showed a fresh focus on nutrition. A picture from the Great Depression shows the government handing out extra food. The goal was to feed hungry Americans. A chart asks who gets SNAP. The chart's source is a research group. Its name joins the Center on Budget with Policy Priorities. People who are elderly, along with people who have disabilities, are 23 percent. Children are 44 percent. Other adults are 33 percent. In 2018, nearly two-thirds of SNAP users were children, elderly people, or people with disabilities. Income is what the federal government checks before it grants food stamps. In 2020, a two-person family earning $17,240 in a year sat at the poverty level. That is the government's name for that line. A single parent at the minimum wage, working full time, earns $15,080 a year. That parent and that child both live in poverty. SNAP served Americans in 2019. The number was above thirty-five million. A month of food-stamp help averages under $5 for each day.

4A second federal program has a long name. WIC stands for a long federal title. It begins with Special Supplemental Nutrition Program. The program serves women. It also serves infants and children. People call it WIC. It helps women who are pregnant. It helps children younger than five. The foods are chosen for nutrition. Milk is one. Baby formula is another. Baby food is another. The National School Lunch Program, or NSLP, reaches more than thirty million children. It serves free lunches at public schools. It also serves lunches at a lower price. A family may take part regardless of income. First Lady Michelle Obama pressed for a new law. Congress approved a 2010 law. Its name begins Healthy, Hunger-Free. The ending is Kids Act. Funding for NSLP went up. New rules for nutrition were set. That was the first such reset in thirty years. A picture shows children eating a free lunch at a school in Oregon. Some schools with low incomes get federal money for breakfast. The same money covers lunch. Every student at those schools can eat free. The government offers a safety net to many hungry Americans. The money set aside for federal food programs still changes from year to year. Politics shifted, and the program was cut hard in 1980 and 1981. Some of that money was put back by 1990. In some years Congress removes billions from SNAP. In some years it adds money for school lunches. People argue about the size of the federal food budget. They argue about who should be fed. They argue about the test for who qualifies. One example is the poverty measure still in use. It was first built in the 1960s. The formula does count inflation. It does not count other costs that keep rising. It does not count the way family budgets have shifted. Childcare has climbed faster than food. Housing, transportation, and education have climbed faster too. More families now strain to pay what they owe. Qualifying is not the same as receiving help. Plenty of people never learn that they qualify. Plenty do not know the steps to apply for SNAP.

5Shame stops others from asking. An application often means leaving work for part of a day. It also means finding a ride to a government office. Missing work is a cost that hungry people cannot pay. A chart titled A Spike in SNAP counts participants in the millions. The Great Recession hit the United States at the close of 2007. It lasted several years. The 1930s Great Depression was the last time the economy had dropped this far. Jobs vanished for millions. In time, millions of those jobless Americans used SNAP to help buy food. Month by month, more people met the rules. More of the people who met the rules joined. By 2012, SNAP reached more than 46 million people. That was a rise of 76 percent from the start of the Great Recession. The U.S. Department of Agriculture is the source of those figures. High-poverty places are often food deserts. A food desert is a place large grocery stores do not serve. Some are city centers where shops have shut. Others are country places with few people. A trip of ten miles for groceries is more than many can pay. Fifteen miles is too far as well. They buy simple food at small shops nearby. Prices there are usually higher. Quality meat is often missing. Fresh produce is often missing too. Minority communities suffer in a special way. Many of them cannot reach the big chain supermarkets. When federal money cannot cover every hungry American, local programs step in. Food banks exist in every state. They gather food from growers. They gather it from restaurants and from grocery stores. Charities then give it out. Food pantries are one kind of charity. Soup kitchens are another. Both serve the public. Cans and other foods that do not spoil quickly are common. Fresh produce is hard to store, so banks often skip it. Community gardens can close part of the nutrition gap for people with less money. Neighbors plant the food. They tend it. They pick it for home use or to share. The United States and Canada together have more than eighteen thousand of these gardens. Many of them grow vegetables for a nearby food bank.

6A picture shows a mother and her children in Colorado. They plant tomatoes in a garden at a middle school. The harvest is meant for a local food bank. Feeding America is the biggest nonprofit that helps families in America. Food banks in its network number more than two hundred. It has sixty thousand food pantries. About twelve million kids get meals from them each year. Charities still supply less than 6 percent of food help in the United States. Costs go up. Pay stays flat. Federal food programs get cut. These groups then find they cannot cover the need. Food runs out. Families are turned away. A nonprofit called AmpleHarvest links gardens that have extra produce with food charities. The link covers more than 7,500 charities. Washington, D.C., is home to the Central Kitchen, where volunteers cook. That kitchen turns out 4,500 meals each day. The meals go to shelters for people without homes. They go to soup kitchens. They go to other programs too. Kids themselves can act, beyond stamps and banks. Students in Concord, New Hampshire, held a hunger banquet for parents. The price of a seat was canned food for the pantry. In Bellingham, Massachusetts, a class of sixth graders filmed a video about hunger. The video won an award. It was meant to build awareness in town. Other students have raised cash for food banks. Bake sales were one way. Selling art was another path. So were washing cars, walk-a-thons, and read-a-thons. More kinds of fundraising have been used as well.

7Sam Adamo played his cello at a local farmers' market. He gathered $700 for the food bank near him in Rhode Island. Carson Pazdan loved to cook. He made a cookbook written for kids and by kids. Sales brought in more than $20,000. The money went to the Northern Illinois Food Bank. Macy Stewart was nine. She handed out empty bags at school. She asked classmates to fill the bags for St. Mary's Food Bank. The bags held 844 pounds of food. That weight is 383 kilograms. St. Mary's Food Bank stands in Surprise, Arizona. It was the first food bank in the world. The year it opened was 1967. William Winslow was seven when he saw a problem. Wake County, in North Carolina, had children who would lack food over spring break. A Mexican restaurant in town was the partner he requested. Customers who brought food got free cheese dip. The food was for BackPack Buddies. That program sends weekend meals home with students who need them. Next he asked a local grocery store for a spot outside the door. He wanted to tell shoppers about the program. One weekend produced 1,400 pounds of food. That is 635 kilograms. Cash gifts added $305. The gift meant extra food went home over spring break. William is in fourth grade now. He still runs a fundraiser every year. In 2016 he signed up 171 volunteers and organized them. They collected gifts at ten grocery stores. The gifts became eleven thousand meals for children in the region. In 2017 he hoped to spread the work across North Carolina. He swims. He is a Cub Scout. He says he is only a regular kid who gets involved. Any child can help, he says, if that child decides to try. In 2016 he gathered 8,100 pounds for BackPack Buddies. That weight is 3,674 kilograms.

8A map called Map the Meal Gap shows how common food insecurity is. One band is 4 to 14 percent. The next is 15 to 19 percent. Then comes 20 to 24 percent. Then 25 to 29 percent. The highest band is 30 percent or more. The map lets you compare hunger inside your own state. You can then set your state and your region beside other places. Ask where the share of food insecurity is highest. Ask where it is lowest. A household garden can send extra produce to a nearby pantry. You can also plant one more patch just to give away. Kids can give part of an allowance. They can ask others to give too. Children in Loudoun County, Virginia, made a simple plan. Each lunch they bought included a dime for the food bank. A school can run a drive to buy goods that food banks need. A nearby business can join the school in collecting funds. Learn what the nearby bank and the charities are short of. Learn which season brings the greatest need. Tell friends what you learn. Tell family and neighbors. Hunger in one's own town is something most people know little about. A letter to the local newspaper can teach them. You can study hunger where you live and read that report aloud in class. Letters can go to your representatives in Congress. Letters can go to state government and to local government. Ask them to back programs that keep every child fed. A letter-writing drive at school can tell officials what you think. The resources exist to keep children like Aaron from going hungry again. What is still needed is the will to do it. A phone line is there if you need food, or if somebody close to you does. Call 1-866-3-HUNGRY. Spanish speakers can call 1-877-8-HAMBRE. The National Hunger Hotline links callers to places that give emergency food. It also links them to government help and to other social services.

9The word list gives plain meanings. Access is a way to get near something, to enter it, or to be able to use it. Awareness is knowing that something is real. Benefits are money or services a government or a company gives someone. A campaign is a set of planned actions aimed at one goal. A census is an official count of the people in an area. An epidemic is something harmful or unwelcome that shows up suddenly in a community and spreads fast. Federal means the central government. That government shares power with states or with regions. Food assistance is help from federal programs for people who need food. Food banks are groups or centers that gather food and pass it to people who need it. A food stamp is a coupon, or another paper, that the government gives so people can buy food. Minimum wage is the smallest hourly pay the law allows. Nonprofit means the work is not done in order to make a profit. Outstripped means one thing passed another by being bigger, quicker, or stronger. Poverty is the condition of being poor. Surplus means more than needed, or what is left over.

48. Hybrid Animals

1The ancient Greeks imagined centaurs, minotaurs, griffons, and manticores. Those mixed creatures may not exist, but animal hybrids do. Hybrids combine traits of different species and are more common than most people realize. A hybrid has parents of two different species. A horse mother and a donkey father make a mule. A donkey mother and a horse father make a hinny. Parents that are too different may have no live young, or weak young. Closer parent species are more likely to have healthy hybrid offspring.

2A hybrid's name can depend on which species is the mother. The mother often shapes the hybrid's traits. Mules are generally larger and hardier than hinnies. Like many hybrids, mules and hinnies are sterile. They cannot make sperm or eggs. A mule gets thirty-two horse chromosomes from one parent and thirty-one donkey chromosomes from the other. A mule has sixty-three unmatched chromosomes and no pairs. Body cells can copy them, but meiosis needs each chromosome to meet its match.

3Horse and donkey chromosomes do not look alike, so they cannot form pairs. Some cells get too many chromosomes, and others get too few. These cells rarely survive. People breed hybrids to combine the best traits of both parents. Mules are hardier, more sure-footed, and easier to care for than horses. Zebroids gain zebra disease resistance and a gentler domestic nature. Beefalo stay hardy and lean, and they can breed if bison is three-eighths or less. Hercules the liger weighed nearly 1,200 pounds, and the reverse cross is a tigon.

4Hercules, the world's biggest cat, is a liger, and so is his brother Aries. Ligers do not occur naturally because lions and tigers live in different habitats. Accredited zoos avoid this mixing, but some breeders and preserves sell it. Other big-cat mixes include leopons, jaguleps, and lijaguleps. Their males are usually sterile, but their females can often bear young. Camels and llamas rarely mate, even when given the chance. Zedonks, zorses, and zonies mix zebra traits with donkey, horse, or pony parents. A Savannah cat is dog-like and long-legged, and a cama is strong but calmer than a camel.

5Medicine can fertilize eggs in a test tube instead of inside an animal. That is how the first cama, a camel-llama hybrid, was born. Scientists hope it will join camel strength with a llama's calmer nature. Hybrids can also appear when related species live and meet in the same place. Scientists often call a species a group that can interbreed and make viable young. A Great Dane and a Chihuahua are both Canis lupus familiaris. Two fruit flies may look alike but be different species. Most hybrids are not separate species because they cannot reproduce.

6In 2009, a narwhal-beluga hybrid was spotted off the coast of Greenland. Scientists do not know if it can make reproductive cells. These hybrids are extremely rare, so a mate of its own kind is unlikely. A male hybrid lacks the narwhal's spiral tusk, which matters when a female chooses a mate. Ring species make the species line even trickier. Picture preschoolers in a circle playing telephone. Each neighbor is similar, but the message changes around the circle. Adjacent ring species can interbreed until the ends of the ring overlap.

7Seven Ensatina salamanders in California came from the same Oregon ancestors. They spread south, adapted, and formed a ring around the San Joaquin Valley. Neighbors are similar enough to interbreed. In southern California, Ensatina eschscholtzii and Ensatina klauberi do not interbreed. There the ring is broken. Where ranges overlap slowly, hybrids appear but rarely change the parent groups. If separated species meet suddenly, hybrids may compete for food, land, or mates. They may also change the genes of one or both original species.

8The Arctic is warming two to four times faster than the rest of the world. Animals are shifting north as ice melts and temperatures rise. Grizzly bears and polar bears now meet and interbreed. A grolar bear spotted in 2006 had thick white fur, brown legs and paws, and a wide grizzly-like head. Later finds include a second-generation hybrid, so some can reproduce. Polar bears risk extinction, and every mixed birth can dilute Arctic genes. Zoo grolar bears may hunt seals but swim less strongly than polar bears. No one yet knows how well wild grolar bears survive.

9If grizzlies greatly outnumber polar bears, hybridization can overwhelm the rarer bear. A half hybrid bred to a grizzly can leave one-quarter polar bear genes. Another cross can leave only one-eighth. Polar bears could disappear unless they breed with polar bears often enough. Scientists list thirty-four likely arctic mammal hybrids, and many may be fertile. In Ontario, smaller southern flying squirrels are moving into northern flying squirrel range. In one northern group, 4 percent are now hybrids, and they can reproduce. Scientists also ask how to join spider silk with large amounts of mammal milk.

10Spider silk is stronger and more flexible than steel or Kevlar. It is hypoallergenic and fights microbes, so it could help in medicine. One ounce needs fourteen thousand spiders, and spiders eat their neighbors. Scientists inserted golden orb weaver silk proteins into goat DNA. The goats make those proteins in their milk, and labs extract them. Armstrong and Sweet Pea are twin spider kids made this way. Because the genes were added in embryos in the lab, these goats are transgenic, not hybrids. Hybrids may harm biodiversity or speed adaptation, and only time will tell.

11A hybrid is offspring from two different parent types, breeds, or species. A species is a similar group of living things that can reproduce. Sterile means not able to produce offspring. Chromosomes carry genes, and DNA is the code of genetic information. Meiosis makes reproductive cells with one copy from each chromosome pair. Interbreeding mates different species, and transgenic means genes were transferred between them. Biodiversity is the variety of life, and expediting means speeding a process up. To fertilize is to join male and female cells, and an embryo is early unborn young.

49. Japan's Path to Anime

1Japanese animator Hayao Miyazaki does many other jobs. He directs. He produces. He writes scripts. He writes books. He draws manga. A 2014 picture shows him speaking to the press at Studio Ghibli. He helped found that studio. Topics run from an introduction to art for everyone, then from curious sketches to comics. Later topics are cartoons that begin to move, the grief and lessons of war, anime now, and a word list. A picture pairs cave paintings at Lascaux, in France, with clay tablets from Mesopotamia. Both tell stories from long ago. Pictures existed long before written words. Many ancient cultures told stories with images. Some images were prehistoric paintings on cave walls. Some were fine figures cut into clay. The style showed how those artists saw themselves. It also showed how they saw the world they lived in. As language grew, people more often recorded ideas with written symbols. Words did that job too. Art stayed important to storytelling anyway. Today, images are not only paintings and drawings. They also move, in movies, in animated cartoons, and in video games. One widespread style of moving art comes from Japan. Japan is an island nation in Asia. People call the style anime. It is hugely popular all over the world.

2The story of this art goes back over two centuries. Earlier than the nineteenth century, large scrolls held most traditional art from Japan. The methods were exact. They took a long time. One method used a single long brushstroke for each image. Another method cut a reversed picture into a woodblock. Artists then spread a thick coat of ink and pressed the block onto a surface. That press made a print. The slow, difficult work made art costly. Only rich people in Japan could buy scroll art and enjoy it. Color prints needed a separate block for every color. Some finished pictures used twenty blocks. In 1814 a new art appeared. People called it manga. The sketches were drawn freehand on paper. Katsushika Hokusai was the artist who taught with these sketches. He urged students to draw pictures of their own. The students sketched and shared the work. Funny pictures caught on with the public. Because they were quick and easy to make, more people could afford them. Traditional scrolls had been out of reach for most. Manga was open to all Japanese people, not only affluent buyers of art. Japanese manga found its own strength in the late 1800s. Until the middle of that century, Japan stayed secluded. Contact with other nations was small. An 1853 naval trip from the United States changed that. Japan was pushed to unlock its ports. Trade with other countries was the demand. By 1858, trading ships regularly crossed the Pacific. They carried goods to six Japanese ports and back out again. British merchants rode those ships to the insular island nation. American merchants did too. Newspapers and magazines from home came with them. The word manga joins two Japanese words. Man means curious. Ga means sketches. Together they match the English word cartoon. Katsushika Hokusai was the first to use the term. He used it for the funny drawings in his own sketchbooks.

3Artists of Japanese manga were intrigued by what they saw in those papers. Political cartoons were one style. Comics were another. They began to use Western forms in their own work. Sequenced panels that tell a story were one of those forms. Soon, manga faces showed some of the strong feelings seen in Western drawings. By the start of the twentieth century, manga showed up often in Japanese newspapers. Political cartoons in that style made fun of the news of the day. Comic strips gave children and adults simple, funny stories. More and more readers loved these lively pictures. Strips in the papers look much like the Western strips they echo. The new century also brought a new entertainment: motion pictures. Studios in the United States started making movies. Other Western nations did too. Crowds flocked to theaters. The medium spread to more countries. Japan was one of them. The earliest movies were short. They were black and white. They were silent. Recorded talk was missing because the machines of the time could not match sound to the picture with accuracy. Musicians in the theater played as the film ran. Words on the screen explained the action. They also explained what the characters said. With no way to record voices, actors needed other tools for feeling. The acting was silent and still very dramatic. Faces and gestures were exaggerated. A picture from the 1917 silent film Patria shows actors. They use overly dramatic gestures in place of spoken lines, so viewers can read the feeling. Cartoonists everywhere were fascinated by movies. In the United States, illustrators found a way to make still sketches move. Walt Disney was one. Max Fleischer was another. Popular comic characters came alive on the big screen. Like live-action films, those cartoons had no sound. Music played while they ran.

4Characters in the cartoons told the story with movement. Gestures and expressions did the same work. People called the films shorts. A short ran for less than ten minutes. Children loved them. Adults loved them too. Theaters showed them before a full-length feature. In Japan, manga artists started making animated shorts of their own. Seitaro Kitayama was one of them. Bold manga faces suited the big action and the big expressions that silent stories needed. The Japanese name for these cartoons was animeshon. It came from the English word animation. In time the name shrank to anime. Better machines brought color to Western cartoons. Recorded talk arrived too. In the 1930s, cartoonists in America were pushed toward figures that looked more real. They were also pushed to make the motion more real. A process called rotoscoping helped. A movie projector threw a live actor's image onto a clear drawing board. The artist traced the outline onto a plastic sheet called a cel. A small action, such as sitting down, needed many cels. The result was impressive. Disney's first full-length animated film used this look. Snow White is the start of the title. The Seven Dwarfs completes it. It also used a new method called multiplane animation. The goal was a realistic background and realistic action. Different background pictures were painted on glass panels. The panels were stacked. During filming, the layers slid back and forth. That motion added depth and a sense of movement. Japanese anime later added sound. It did not copy Western tricks for a realistic look or for realistic motion. Animators kept treating the work as real art. The camera style matched other long Japanese films. A shot would hold still for a long time, then jump to a close-up for drama. Body movement was not casual. It was deliberate and carefully planned. Each small motion mattered to the plot. Artists also kept drawing in the black-and-white style that marked the work as truly Japanese. Walter Lantz Productions used rotoscoping to give characters motion that looked more natural. The artist traces the drawn figure over film of live actors.
