5Anime has a look of its own. Backgrounds carry a great deal of detail. Characters are often full of energy. Expressions and gestures are exaggerated. Action is shown from angles that Western cartoons rarely use. Some of those angles are extreme. Eyes matter most of all. Large eyes mark a character as childlike and trustworthy. Smaller eyes, pulled into a squint, mark sneakiness. Tiny eyes mark evil. Shape and size do not stay fixed. Embarrassment shows as a blush across the nose. Scratching behind the head makes that embarrassment look stronger. Anger can show as blue lines across the face. It can show as narrowed eyes, as bulging veins, or as drops of sweat. Hair has its own style too. It is often brightly colored. It is styled in striking ways. It changes shape to show movement and feeling. Pictures label faces as embarrassed, happy, sad, and angry. Cost is one reason the look stayed put. Backgrounds are essential. Methods such as multiplane animation, with layers that shift, cost a lot. World War II began in 1939, and that start was a second reason. Japan's leaders wanted citizens on their side. To build pride in the nation, they banned films from other countries. Cartoons from those countries were banned too. They also ordered art that praised certain Japanese values. That art was supposed to attack Japan's enemies. Some animators refused the censorship and left Japan. Others kept releasing work in secret. Capture meant punishment. Posters of the time urged people in Japan to back their government against those enemies. The war's end was terrible for Japan. Nearly two million people in Japan were dead by the 1945 surrender. Atomic bombs destroyed Hiroshima. They destroyed Nagasaki too. The ruin changed the people deeply. It changed their art. Light fun gave way to heavier themes. Artists in manga and in anime began to argue for peace. They argued for justice and for freedom.

6Television, a technology of the 1950s, often carried those messages. Home viewing was now possible, and the audience grew because of it. One of the most popular shows came from a manga comic called Mighty Atom. Osamu Tezuka drew it. Mighty Atom was the hero. He was a boy built as a robot. Rockets took the place of feet. His endurance was beyond a human's. The program sent him across the world. His task was to rescue it from danger. The program became one of the best-loved television shows in Japan. American viewers made it a hit in the early 1960s. They knew it by another title. The title was Astro Boy. The first Astro Boy series ran for two years. Reruns of those episodes played into the early 1970s. Other cartoon shows followed. People called them mecha. The heroes were teens and giant robots. Monsters were the threat they fought. During the 1970s, Japan loved a mecha show called Mazinger Z. Its hero was a super robot. A special metal found on Japan's Mount Fuji was what the robot was made from. Astro Boy first reached viewers on New Year's Day in 1963. Anime today, like manga, has grown more specialized. Characters and plots aim at particular audiences. Shonen is Japanese for young boy. Its plots stress action and comedy. Dragon Ball Z is one example. It first played in Japan in 1989. Television stations around the world still show it. That run lasted from 1989 to 2003. Shojo is Japanese for young girl. Early stories centered on feelings and on relationships. Later stories added more active heroines. Those heroines take part in romance and in adventure. A 1990s series called Sailor Moon is a classic shojo example. The artist is Naoko Takeuchi. It follows a girl in middle school. A magical brooch gives her power. She becomes a guardian of Earth and defends it from evil forces. The character shows up in at least three films. She also shows up in thirty-nine video games.

7Through the 1980s and the 1990s, studios in Japan made anime films that became hits in many countries. Hayao Miyazaki released Nausicaä in 1984. The rest of the title is the Valley of the Wind. It did very well. A young princess is at the center. Her task is to rescue her planet. In 2001, the anime Spirited Away reached movie theaters. A young girl is the focus. She steps into a world filled with spirits. Hayao Miyazaki directed it. People praised the artistry highly. In time the film won an Academy Award. The prize was for the best animated feature. Money earned since the 2001 opening is above $396 million. Anime also lives in the newest media of this century. Dozens of video games now grow out of manga comics. Others grow out of anime shows and films. Fans love the way a game lets them take part. Favorite characters step into those games. Astro Boy is one. Naruto, Digimon, and Pokémon are others. Dragon Ball Z is another. They carry out their missions when a player presses a button. Screen pictures act out bold adventures, in the spirit of figures made long ago. The lively characters of anime, though, push the art of modern storytelling much further. The word list gives plain meanings. Affluent means rich, with plenty of money and plenty of things. Insular means cut off from other people or cultures, or showing a sheltered view. Affordable means a price that is reasonable, not too high. Intrigued means very curious or interested. Animated means made from drawings in a series so they seem to move. Manga means Japanese comic books and picture novels. Plied means traveled the same route again and again. Anime is a Japanese style of animation used in film and on television. Synchronize means lining things up so their timing agrees. It can also mean making events happen as one. Censored means checked so that content seen as threatening or offensive can be removed. Traditional means tied to a custom that has lasted a long time. Flocked means a crowd came together, or a crowd moved as one.

50. Jonas Salk and the Polio Vaccine

1Posters warned the public to avoid districts where polio had hit. As summer opened in 1953, families across the United States prepared for terror once more. Nearly fifty-seven thousand people had fallen ill with poliomyelitis the summer before. People also call that sickness polio. Twenty thousand were left unable to walk well, or unable to walk at all. Children made up most of that group. Deaths added another three thousand. Usually the poliovirus brought symptoms similar to a cold. The path ran from mouth to digestive system. Real harm began if the virus reached the bloodstream. Nerves for arm muscles and leg muscles were injured. Breathing could fail when chest muscles were paralyzed. Pools were shunned. Packed public places were shunned too. Homes were quarantined by police. Hospitals received the sick children. Months might pass before a child left. Years might pass. A single hope was left. The country heard from Doctor Jonas Salk that a vaccine against polio would soon exist.

2Salk's birthplace was New York, and the year was 1914. Only two years of life were behind him when polio's first epidemic reached the United States. Jewish parents from Russia raised him. Success was demanded of all three boys in the house. School came easily to Salk. Townsend Harris Hall took him at twelve. Gifted students were the ones that high school served. City College of New York had him by sixteen. Helping humanity was his aim. Congress was the office he hoped to seek, so law was the study he chose first. His first chemistry class turned him toward medical research. Fighting disease became the goal. World War II was just beginning for the United States when his schooling ended. Medical research mattered to the military. Influenza, or the flu, and other illnesses of the breathing system had killed over forty thousand American soldiers in World War I. Troop protection was the aim. Influenza shots started in the U.S. Army in 1943. A diagram explains antibodies. Each virus carries a site where binding can happen. Antibodies grab the viruses. Infection of the body is blocked by that grab. After the grab, a virus cannot let go and seize a healthy cell. Labels on the diagram mark the virus and the antibody. At the University of Michigan, Doctor Thomas Francis held a grant for a flu vaccine. Salk was hired into that lab. He understood the body's reply to a virus. Special proteins called antibodies are produced for the fight. A blood test of his design revealed how many antibodies were present. Symptom-watching was no longer required. A count of antibodies showed whether a vaccine was working. Formalin, a chemical, killed the flu virus while the outer appearance stayed unchanged. Recognition by the body still happened, and antibodies still formed. Success followed. Killed-virus flu vaccine from the Michigan team spared thousands of lives. The flu itself could not come from that shot. At thirty-two, Salk accepted leadership of a lab of his own. Pittsburgh's university made him head of its Virus Research Laboratory.

3A name change came in 1979. National Foundation for Infantile Paralysis, called the NFIP, took the new name March of Dimes. America's thirty-second president was Franklin D. Roosevelt. Youth and polio had left him paralyzed. Help for others with polio was the reason he created the NFIP in 1938. Running it was a job he gave Basil O'Connor, once his partner in law. Vaccine research gained NFIP money in 1946. Counting the types of poliovirus was the opening task. Three types were already known. Dozens of types, as with the cold virus, would mean one vaccine could not shield people from all of them. Nature gives polio only to humans, which makes lab work hard. A brain injection can infect a monkey. Old typing was slow. A monkey first received the unknown strain. Illness and recovery let antibodies develop. A known type, such as type 1, was given after recovery. No new illness meant the unknown strain was type 1. Illness meant the whole test began again with type 2, then with type 3. Waiting through illness, recovery, and illness again ate up months. Speed and accuracy were what Salk expected from a different plan. A light dose of the unknown strain would infect the monkey. Sickness might never show. Antibodies would still form in the blood. A known type 1 virus came next. A flood of antibodies would mean the unknown strain was type 1. Growth of the virus would mean type 2, type 3, or a type still unnamed. Glass plates called petri dishes are where scientists grow samples of virus. Microscopes can hold those plates.

4Salk's idea drew scorn from most scientists at that year's NFIP meeting. A loud and famous polio researcher, Doctor Albert Sabin, was one of them. Funding went to the traditional typing method. Salk's method was passed over. He still believed the new way was more efficient. Extra hours in the lab let him run both methods. Success, speed, and a much smaller need for monkeys all favored the new process. Another discovery caught his notice. Three researchers made the find. John Enders was one. Fred Robbins was another. Tom Weller was the third. They grew poliovirus inside tissue cultures. A culture of that kind is living material grown outside a body. Antibody tests in those cultures succeeded for Salk's group. Three types, and only three, were confirmed. One year was enough. Three years had been the old expectation. A sidebar on polio today reports seven countries with the disease as of 2015. Recent years have seen the numbers climb. War is one reason. Refusal to vaccinate is another. Containment once limited polio to three countries. Officials say the United States has eradicated it. Vaccination goes on anyway. Someone could carry the disease in from abroad and start an outbreak. Worldwide eradication is true of smallpox, which is a different case. Conflict returned to the research in 1950. Should vaccine virus be alive or dead? Long-lasting protection, said most scientists and the outspoken Sabin, required live virus. A weak form is developed and placed in the shot. Antibodies follow the injection, and immunity follows the antibodies. Disease usually does not follow. Equal protection, Salk argued, could come from killed virus, the sort already used for flu. Safety was higher too. Polio could never start from a virus that was already dead. Both approaches received NFIP money this time. Fifty researchers joined Salk. Ease was not part of the job. Careful killing of the poliovirus was required. The flu work had shown them a chemical that worked, so they used it again. Temperatures were varied. Strengths were varied. Again and again the liquid was strained and mixed. The size is shocking. Line up a million viruses and they fit in a single inch. One survivor among them could still set off the deadly disease.

5Children were the next question, once monkeys had responded to the vaccine. The 1930s offered a devastating warning. Polio appeared in children who had been vaccinated in those early tries. Survivors were the subjects in 1952. They could not walk, or walking was hard. A second case was impossible, because the disease had already come. Antibodies rose in their blood, so the vaccine was doing its work. Children who had never caught polio were vaccinated next. Protective antibodies formed. Ill effects did not. The following NFIP meeting was where Salk planned to report. Secrecy around the lab was tight. News of a coming announcement still reached reporters. A cover photo of Salk ran with an article in Time magazine. Phone calls began. Visits began. Progress slowed under the interruptions. Help came from a talk with O'Connor. Radio would carry Salk's explanation. A vaccine was close, but much labor remained. Concentration on making the vaccine required quiet. Hero status arrived overnight anyway. Saving the children was the role the public gave him. Hundreds of vaccine vials passed under his review in the Pittsburgh lab. Fury spread among Sabin and the other researchers. Many contributors had been credited in the radio remarks. Credit-hogging was still what the critics heard. Journals and official conferences, they insisted, are where real scientists speak. Radio is not.

6Sabin's workplace was the University of Cincinnati, and his staff worked beside him. Salk ignored the distractions and went back to the bench. Another thirty-five thousand people caught polio in 1953. Wife, three sons, lab workers, and Salk himself received the vaccine once he trusted it. A giant field trial before the next summer was what O'Connor and the NFIP demanded. The plan meant shots for hundreds of thousands of children. Perfection of the vaccine, Salk felt, needed more time. Delay also felt wrong. Polio was likely for thousands of children if the team held back. States, schools, and parents received O'Connor's call for volunteers. Doctors were organized by the thousand. Nurses were too. Health-care workers were too. Data analysis went to Doctor Francis, the boss Salk had once had. Output from Salk's lab was too small. Pharmaceutical makers joined the effort. Keeping the virus structure while killing it was so exact that two manufacturers, out of five, were ready in time. History had not seen an effort of this size. Dollars needed for the trial came to 7.5 million. Today's price for the same event would pass 66 million. Polio season was only a few months off. Participation reached almost two million children. A button reading Polio Pioneer went to each one. Vaccine reached some. A placebo reached some. A control group was the label for the rest, who were simply tracked. Collection and study of the results then filled months for Francis. National hero and national villain were both possible endings for Salk. Elementary children in 1954 are shown with a nurse, getting ready for their polio shots. Listening on April 12, 1955, were millions of people. Radio carried the moment for some. Closed-circuit television carried it for others.

7A full auditorium faced Francis. Speakers were turned on inside department stores. Court trials were suspended so judges could hear. After explaining the trial, Francis gave the figures. Type 1 was blocked sixty-eight percent of the time. Type 2 was blocked every time. Type 3 was blocked ninety-two percent of the time. The vaccine, he said, works. Safe was his word for it. Effective was his word. Potent was his word. Newsrooms heard the result at a run. Bells rang in churches. Streets filled with cheers. A score below perfect displeased Salk. His speech, given quietly, claimed full effectiveness should have been the result. An ingredient never tested had been added by a manufacturer. Time later showed that claim was true. Thanks went to researchers across many years. Thanks went to volunteers and to donors of money. Pittsburgh colleagues were mentioned as a group. No single name from that team was spoken. Anger in the science community deepened. An imperfect score had been laid on someone else. Colleagues had not been named. Forgiveness never came from some of them. Interviews still mobbed him. Gifts and money arrived. All of it was passed to the NFIP. Perfecting the vaccine pulled him back to the lab. Positive trial news and the approach of summer led the NFIP to hand out free vaccine. All five manufacturers supplied it. Weeks later, trouble showed. Polio struck some children who had been vaccinated. A live-virus vaccine was still Sabin's project. He spoke the fear many shared. Stop making it and stop handing it out, he said, until safety could be repeated every time. Daily signs at shot stations reported how many people had serious effects. Panic was not Salk's response. Proper preparation, he knew, left the vaccine safe. One manufacturer was the source investigators found. Virus-killing instructions had been ignored there. That supply was withdrawn. Shots for everyone else continued.

8Fewer than one thousand polio cases remained by 1962. Production cost was high, even though Salk's vaccine worked. Approval for Sabin's live-virus vaccine came in the United States that year. Price was lower than for killed virus. A sugar cube replaced a course of injections. Popularity followed. Inside the United States, polio that started on its own was last recorded in 1979. The live-virus vaccine was the source traced for most cases that lingered. Mutation inside the intestines can let that live virus cause illness. Only a small share of treated people are hit. Exclusive use of killed virus was the United States decision in 2000. First to develop a polio vaccine was Salk. Elimination of the disease inside the country finally came from his version. A boy in 1967 is shown taking Sabin's vaccine from a sugar cube. Fresh aims followed. Humanity's good was the purpose of the Salk Institute, founded in 1960, a home for scientists. Cancer research continued there under Salk himself. So did work on HIV and AIDS. Five books came from his pen. Death in 1995 ended the work. Leading-edge research still happens at the institute. Nobel Prize winners have been among its people. No Nobel Prize ever reached Salk. Sabin said that Salk had discovered nothing. The National Academy of Sciences is a prestigious body. Membership there never came for him. Every other major polio researcher was elected. Decades of polio findings were pulled together by Salk. New ideas were applied. The first polio vaccine was the product. Thousands of children escaped the deadly disease. Gratitude came from the country, from the president, from Congress, and from the wider world. Time magazine built a list of one hundred figures who mattered most across the twentieth century. His name was on it. A U.S. stamp carried his image. His son described the greatest gift. Research in medicine, that gift said, ought to face the problems of humankind. It ought to make a difference. The goal was met.

9A short list of words closes the story. Something contagious can pass along by contact with people or with other living things. Something devastating brings heavy harm to body or to feelings. An epidemic is disease moving fast inside a community. A field trial checks a new product, or a new process, in the place it is meant to be used, and asks whether it is effective. A grant formally gives land or money, from government or from another institution, for one stated aim, research included. Immunity means a person or animal can resist illness. To be paralyzed is to have movement taken from one or more body parts. Pharmaceutical points to medicines and the drugs inside them. A placebo looks like treatment but has no real effect, and tests often give it to a comparison group. Polio is an acute virus illness striking skeletal muscle and also the spinal cord. Someone prestigious is honored and stands high in respect. A quarantined person or place is isolated so sickness will not travel. Someone recruited has been brought in to take part. A strain is viral organisms of one species, grouped together. A vaccine uses microbes that are weak or dead, and it trains the body to battle stronger microbes of the matching kind.

51. Lewis and Clark, Part Two: West to the Sea

1This book names several Indigenous nations. One is the Chinook. One is the Nimíipuu, also known as Nez Perce. Sahaptin is another name for that same people. Sahaptin is said suh-HAP-tin. One is the Niitsitapi, also known as Blackfoot. One is the Apsáalooke, also known as Crow. Canada and the United States both appear on the map. Order of the parts An opening comes first. The push toward the Rockies comes next. The mountain crossing comes next. The downstream run on the big river comes next. The road back comes next. The expedition’s effects come next. A closing follows. A word list is last. Opening France was paid 15 million dollars by the United States. The year of that payment was 1803. Today that payment would be about 310 million dollars. The purchase was a promise from France. France would stay out of the way. The United States intended to take Native lands that lay past its western edge. The deal is called the Louisiana Purchase. An army expedition left on May 14, 1804. Later, people would call it the expedition of Lewis and Clark. Exploring as far as the Pacific was the aim. The route also prepared the ground for conquest by the United States and for settlers. November found them 1,500 miles from the start. In kilometers, the distance is 2,414. Winter quarters were chosen beside a town belonging to the Numakiki. That name is said noo-MAH-kee-kee. The leaders were Meriwether Lewis and William Clark. A trapper from France joined them at that camp. His name was Toussaint Charbonneau. His name is said too-SAN shar-buh-NOH. He was to help them talk with Native peoples. The lands ahead would be new. English was not the everyday language there. French was not either. Travel resumed on April 7, 1805. Sacagawea came with Charbonneau. Her name is said sah-kah-gah-WEE-ah. She was Shoshone. Charbonneau held her in slavery. Jean-Baptiste, their baby son, came as well.

2The Push Toward the Rockies Another name for the travelers is the Corps of Discovery. Fort Mandan is where they departed. The Missouri was the river they followed upstream. The Great Plains lay across their path. Numakiki land was part of that path. So was land of the Hiraacá, said hee-RAH-tsah. So was land of the Oceti Sakowin. The first half of that name is said oh-CHEH-tee. The second half is said shah-KOH-wee. So was land of the Tsitsistas, said tsit-SIS-tahs. Bison fill the journals Lewis and Clark kept. One herd might hold ten thousand animals. Numakiki country and Hiraacá country fell behind them. Ahead was land the Oceti Sakowin shared with the Blackfoot Confederacy. The Rocky Mountains appeared soon after. Nothing then inside the United States stood so tall. Lewis put a hard fact in his journal. The days ahead would be far more difficult. Boats on the river struggled, and then boats could not go on. A canoe turned over in the water. Every canoe had to be hauled over dry ground. The barrier was the Missouri’s Great Falls. A month and a half, or nearly that, went into the haul. The Continental Divide came next. On one side of that divide, rivers flow toward the Atlantic. On the other side, they flow toward the Pacific. Historians think the two leaders grasped a truth there. No water route in the north linked those two oceans. The passage people had hunted for, the Northwest Passage, was only a myth. Blackfoot Confederacy Outsiders often say Blackfoot. They also say Blackfeet. The people call themselves Niitsitapi, said neet-SEE-tah-pee. The homeland was huge. Montana’s Yellowstone River marked one edge. Alberta’s North Saskatchewan River marked another. Canada is the country Alberta belongs to. Eastward, the Great Sand Hills were a boundary. Westward, the boundary was the Continental Divide in the Rocky Mountains. Niitsitapi people still live on those old homelands. They also live beyond them. Many separate groups make up the nation, and each governs itself. Their languages are near kin. In earlier times the groups joined as Siksikaitsiitapi. The opening of that name is said seeg-see-GAY. The rest is said tsee-tah-pee. The joined name outsiders use is the Blackfoot Confederacy. A photo shows members of the Blackfeet Nation holding the nation’s flag.

3The Mountain Crossing Height stopped the expedition cold. The Rockies were the reason. Two horses were all they had brought. The full corps needed many more, and so did the gear. The Continental Divide still had to be crossed. Finding the Shoshone, and speaking with them, was work Sacagawea did for the corps. Newe is the name those people use for themselves. It is said NOO-uh. Their chief, Cameahwait, walked out to greet the travelers. His name is said kuh-MAY-uh-wayt. Joy struck Sacagawea when she knew him as kin. A brother is what historians think he was. A cousin is the other possibility. Newe uses one word for both. Cameahwait’s people sold horses to Lewis and Clark. The mountain trip could start again. A stay with the Salish Nation came before the next attempt. Eleven days were spent in the high crossing. Many nearly died of thirst. Many nearly died of hunger. Cold that froze them nearly finished the rest. The far slope let them out in terrible shape. Nimíipuu people, said nee-MEE-poo, were the ones who found them. Those hosts gave shelter. They gave food. They nursed the travelers back to health. Historians of the Nimíipuu say the hosts taught canoe travel through that country. They also taught the visitors how to search the land for wild food. New canoes were made for the guests. Horses for a later mountain return were promised and set aside. Two weeks of rest and new supplies followed. Goodbyes were said. The river then carried the corps onward, with the ocean as the aim.

4Downstream on the Great River The Clearwater was the first river under the canoes. It joined a bigger river, the Snake. The Snake carried them into the Columbia. Native peoples across this region mostly call the Columbia by another name. That name is the Great River. The corps now crossed Nimíipuu land. Meetings with Native peoples stayed rare until the ocean itself. At the Pacific, trade with the Chinook Nation was heavy. The Clatsop took part in that trade. Winter needed a fort. Fort Clatsop was the name they chose. Hardship outdid the winter before. The camp beside the ocean lasted three months. Rain failed to fall on only twelve of those days. Sickness from infection spread among the men. Sickness from poor food spread too. They were miserable enough to leave before winter finished, and to turn toward home. A photo shows Chinook people with their flag. A courthouse in Tacoma, Washington, is behind them. Salmon and the Peoples Who Knew Them Colonization had not yet arrived when salmon-filled rivers supported a rich mix of cultures in the Pacific Northwest. Smaller communities were the usual form. Family ties and trade bound those communities closely. Upper parts of the Clearwater, and of the Snake, were Nimíipuu country. People there shifted among camps as the seasons changed. Fish were one reason for the moves. Hunting was another. Gathering was another. Trade was another. The Yakama are one modern tribe from this history. The Walla Walla are another. The Umatilla are another. Along the Columbia, Chinook reliance on salmon was heavier still than among nations farther upstream. Many peoples who did not farm had to move. The Chinook could remain in the same towns through every season. Today these nations work to guard salmon and to bring their numbers back. The fish and the people have always belonged to one shared life.

5Going Back Nimíipuu advice said not to cross while the Rocky Mountain pass was frozen. Lewis and Clark tried anyway. They had to turn back. A full month with the Nimíipuu followed, until winter was truly gone. Eastbound travel, after the mountains, was much quicker than the westbound trip. St. Louis was only three months away. Old steps were mostly walked again. Native communities that had sheltered them outbound were visited once more. On Apsáalooke land, and on Niitsitapi land, Clark cut his name into a big rock. Apsáalooke is said ahp-SAH-loh-gah. Niitsitapi is said neet-SEE-tah-pee. Pompeys Pillar is the name he gave the spot. Young Jean-Baptiste’s nickname, Pompey, was the source of that name. September 23, 1806, was the day St. Louis saw them again. The whole trip had lasted two years, four months, and ten days. The carved name is still visible. Pompeys Pillar is now a national monument. Montana is the state. Effects That Followed Rewards came from the U.S. government when the trip ended. Lewis got 1,600 acres. Clark got the same. Each other white man who finished received 320 acres. Native peoples had been pushed off every acre of that reward land. No pay went to Sacagawea. No reward went to her. York got nothing either. He was a Black man held in slavery, and he traveled with the group. His later life is uncertain. Clark’s account says York asked for freedom over many decades and was refused. Clark claimed a freeing happened at some point before 1832. Historians doubt that claim. Some think it was invented to cover an escape. The escape, they say, happened while the expedition was still underway. A visitor among the Apsáalooke in 1832 reported a Black man living with them. The same report came again in 1834. The man said the Lewis and Clark journey had included him. Age and looks fit York. Lewis lived only six more years. A gunshot killed him at a Tennessee tavern where he was staying. That same year took Sacagawea. Her age was twenty-five. Illness is the likely cause. Her children went to Clark to be raised. Charbonneau was the one who sent them. Jean Baptiste was one child. Lizette, a baby girl, was the other.

6Politics filled Clark’s later life. Thomas Jefferson, then president, gave him a post. The title was Superintendent of Indian Affairs. Government plans toward Native peoples were his to direct. Six presidents kept him in that post. The plans he carried out were meant to take Indigenous land. They were also meant to push Native peoples off their traditional cultures. Whole nations were relocated by force under his watch. The conditions were brutal. Deaths reached into the thousands. Pressure produced many treaties with Native nations. Clark was the negotiator for a large share of them. Communities that resisted U.S. restrictions faced violent steps he ordered. After the expedition, invasions of Native land by the United States grew enormously. Army support backed those invasions. Force moved Native peoples onto small tracts called reservations. Leaving was forbidden. Starvation struck many people there. Outbreaks of deadly disease struck them too. Violence was used to strip away traditional religions. Languages were attacked. Foods were attacked. So was every other piece of culture. What the expedition wanted, and what came after it, shaped U.S. policy toward Indigenous peoples. Those effects are still felt. Cultures have been protected anyway. Lands have been protected anyway. Make Them Change, or Make Them Leave William Clark spent years as Superintendent of Indian Affairs. In that time he put both main U.S. approaches into practice. Assimilation was the first. It means Native peoples were forced to drop their own culture. One example ran through the nineteenth century and into the twentieth. Children were taken from Native families by force. Boarding schools were where they were sent. A child who spoke a home language was punished. A child who kept up cultural practice was punished. Removal by force was the second approach. The Trail of Tears is a notorious case. Guns compelled a march out of the Southeast. Oklahoma was the far end of that march. The Cherokee were among those forced to go. The Chickasaw were among them. The Choctaw, the Creek, and the Seminole were among them too. At the boarding schools, leaders made children abandon traditional clothes. Hair worn in traditional ways was banned as well.

7Closing Heroes is what Washington, D.C., called Lewis and Clark once they returned. Memory still casts them as brave explorers for many people. Science they gathered had been unknown to settlers from Europe. Westward growth of the United States drew on their travels. Pictures often dress them as frontiersmen. Empty land is what some people imagine they crossed. Independent nations already lived on that land and governed it. Without help from Native peoples, success was unlikely. What followed was tragic. Violent conflict with the U.S. government was opened by the journey. The people who had made the journey possible were the ones who paid. Expansion of the country came at a great cost to them. They had flourished on those lands since a time older than memory. Words to Know brutal (adj.): cruel, violent, and without pity. myth (n.): a traditional tale that accounts for events, for nature, or for customs, often with supernatural beings. capsized (v.): flipped in the water until the underside, or a side, pointed upward. emerged (v.): came into view from inside something, or came out. navigate (v.): to guide travel along a chosen path to a destination. exchange (v.): giving one thing while receiving another. overseeing (v.): keeping watch so that a task is carried out as it should be. extensively (adv.): across a wide span, and with a lot of detail. policies (n.): the course a government, a business, or a group plans to follow. forage (v.): searching out food or supplies, and collecting them. relocations (n.): times when people or things are moved elsewhere. immemorial (adj.): so old that no one remembers the beginning, and no record marks it.

52. Locked Up at Home: Japanese Americans in the Second World War

1Honolulu, Hawaii, woke on Sunday, December 7, 1941, under broken cloud. Daniel Inouye was seventeen. Church was his plan for the morning. A radio in the house played music. A broadcaster cut across the songs. Pearl Harbor, he said, was being attacked. He yelled that the warning was real. He yelled it a second time, so no one would call it a drill. Daniel stepped into the front yard with his father. Bursts of antiaircraft fire puffed in the distance. They rose from the direction of the naval base of the United States. Three fighters then roared over the yard at rooftop height. Daniel saw the paint clearly. Years later he recalled a pearl-gray body. A red dot marked each wing. Those marks told him the planes were Japanese. He understood the moment. He felt that the life he knew was over. Japan's navy had struck without warning. The aircraft had left carriers far out at sea. Pearl Harbor held the Pacific Fleet of the United States. Fire took the harbor. In a 1941 scene, the line of ships called Battleship Row burns under the attack.

2That day, four battleships went down. Further ships sank with them. Destroyed aircraft numbered 188. Deaths among Americans passed 2,400. On the following day, war was declared. Japan was the nation named, and the United States had entered World War II in an official way. Daniel's father was an arrival from Japan. He had come at age three. Daniel's own birth was in Hawaii. Citizenship was his by law. Even so, father and son both felt an instant fear. They feared what a fight with Japan would mean for people like them. The fear had to wait. Smoke and flame still climbed over the harbor. Daniel had medical training and worked as a volunteer. He bicycled toward the ruins. Five days passed while he aided the wounded. Loyalty did not protect him. Suspicion now covered him. It covered every person of Japanese ancestry on the soil of the United States. Panic after the harbor By the time bombs fell on Pearl Harbor, near the close of 1941, the wider war was already fierce. Japan's armies had entered China in 1937. They stood ready to take the rest of Asia. Germany, under the Nazis, had struck Poland in September 1939. From that point, German forces overran nearly the whole of Europe. Italy joined Germany and Japan. People called the three-nation pact the Axis. Their armies looked too strong to stop. The United States had kept clear of the fighting. President Franklin Roosevelt, like many Americans, expected that distance to end. He thought the country would be pulled in sooner or later. Even before the harbor attack, a major buildup of forces was underway. In autumn 1941, Roosevelt called for an inquiry. It examined Japanese Americans. It examined immigrants from Japan. The places were the West Coast and Hawaii. Would they stay loyal to the country they had joined? Or would old ties to Japan turn them into enemies? The inquiry's answer was calm. Ethnic Japanese residents gave Americans nothing to fear. A long bias against Asian people still sat in many minds. Towns held deep prejudice. Hostility toward Japanese neighbors ran deep. Employers often paid those neighbors less than they paid Caucasian workers. California held the great majority of ethnic Japanese people. Farmers from that community were succeeding more each year. Many Caucasian owners of land treated them as rivals they did not welcome. Then the harbor attack landed. Shock mixed with rage. Wild stories spread at once. The stories said Japanese troops might soon land in California.

3Fear and war fever whirled into hysteria. A family link to Japan was enough to draw suspicion. Roosevelt signed Executive Order 9066 on February 19, 1942. People knew it as the exclusion order. Military commanders of the United States gained power to remove anyone they judged a possible enemy. The power applied inside military exclusion zones. Bases and other sensitive sites sat in those zones. Plans followed to clear every person of Japanese ancestry from West Coast districts. The destination was imprisonment in incarceration camps. Voices in print After the harbor attack, newspaper writers stirred fear of Japanese people and old prejudice. Columnist Henry McLemore, in January 1942, wanted every Japanese person on the West Coast removed at once. He wanted them sent far inland, and not to a pleasant region. He stated his hatred of Japanese people. He said the hatred covered every one of them. On February 2, 1942, W. H. Anderson wrote for a Los Angeles paper. He compared a Japanese American to a viper, saying the hatching place does not change the snake. A child of Japanese parents, he claimed, grows up Japanese and not American. Author Kiyo Sato later described her family being pushed from home. No helper existed, she wrote, not even a church. After the president put his name to an order meant to push them out, she felt that any cruelty was allowed. She asked how he could treat citizens of his own country that way. Banishment by one's own country, she said, is the loneliest feeling there is. Forced removal People of Japanese ancestry formed only a small share of the United States population in 1941. Mainland residents of Japanese ancestry numbered about 127,000. The West Coast was home to 112,000 of them. First-generation immigrants from Japan were called Issei, pronounced EE-say. Law barred them from citizenship. The bar extended anti-Chinese rules written in the late 1800s. Their children, born in the United States, were Nisei, pronounced NEE-say. Birth here made the Nisei citizens. Evacuation orders still reached every ethnic Japanese person. Removal covered anyone at least one-sixteenth Japanese. A single Japanese great-great-grandparent was enough. Within a week of the harbor attack, war was also declared against Nazi Germany. Fascist Italy was named in that same step.

4German Americans and Italian Americans were detained in the thousands, but only for parts of the war. Only those of Japanese descent faced a wholesale lockup based on ethnicity. Notices went up across the western states in April. Families with Japanese roots had seven days for settling affairs. When those days ended, they reported to assembly centers and waited for trains to incarceration camps. They could carry only what their arms could hold. Losing home and business so suddenly struck Japanese Americans as a terrible blow. Farmers searched for friends who might tend the land in their absence. Houses and goods had to be sold in a few days. Opportunists used the neighbors' predicament. The prices they paid for houses were very low. Losses for many Japanese Americans included everything they owned. In San Francisco, a merchant preparing for incarceration nailed a sale sign to his store. Ten camps appear on a map of remote ground. California held Tule Lake and Manzanar. Wyoming held Heart Mountain. Idaho held Minidoka. Utah held Topaz. Colorado held Granada. Arizona held Poston and Gila River. Arkansas held Rohwer and Jerome. A shaded exclusion area covers the coast. Protest from other Americans was rare. Court challenges by Japanese Americans met deaf ears. Robert Kashiwagi's family was forced from a Sacramento home. Decades later, in a documentary, he said he had trusted the Bill of Rights to shield him. That trust lasted until he was ordered onto the evacuation train. War fever could not be beaten back. Anti-Japanese feeling could not be beaten back either. About 110,000 Japanese Americans went to fifteen assembly centers. West Coast states used fairgrounds, racetracks, and stockyards for those centers. Families lived there in rough temporary quarters.

5Horse stables and other makeshift rooms housed them before the next shipment. Ten incarceration camps were the destinations. American citizens made up two-thirds of the group. The other third were immigrants from Japan who lived in the United States legally. Hawaii's story ran a different course. The islands then held 158,000 ethnic Japanese people. They were nearly 40 percent of Hawaii's population. Much of the labor in farming, transport, and other trades came from them. An estimate said ethnic Japanese workers were 90 percent of Hawaii's carpenters. After the December 7 strike, rebuilding the harbor depended on that skill. Officials in the United States proposed locking up Hawaii's Japanese population for security. Business leaders on the islands fought the idea hard. They said plantations and other firms could not spare that workforce. The argument won. Hawaii's incarcerated number stayed below 1,800. Martial law still covered Hawaii. A strict curfew came with it. The army censored every letter and every publication. It watched communications by ethnic Japanese people closely. Life inside the wire West Coast arrivals began reaching the incarceration camps in May 1942. They left trains or buses and met soldiers of the United States. Guns and bayonets were in the soldiers' hands, as if the newcomers were troops taken in battle. Seven was the age of Joyce Nakamura Okazaki. Her family was forced to Manzanar. That camp stood in California. She later described barbed wire all around her. Eight towers held armed sentries. Most camps sat in dry, remote country. Utah, Colorado, and further western states held them. Summer heat was fierce. Winter cold was fierce. Dust hung in the air most days. Drafts cut through the barracks. A 1942 picture shows a soldier on guard at Manzanar, shortly before that California camp was complete.

6Builders had rushed the barracks and done poor work with cheap materials. Beds were cots. On cold nights a woodstove gave little warmth. Families often shared barely furnished rooms with strangers. Mess halls served the meals. Toilets offered no privacy. School-age children among the incarcerees numbered more than thirty thousand. Almost no plan existed for their schooling. Rooms were overcrowded because few teachers would work at the camps. Books were scarce. Textbooks were scarce. Desks were scarce. Doctors were rare. Clinics stayed short of staff as a habit. Some of the nurses, doctors, and dentists were Japanese Americans. Their pay sat at a poverty level. In that harsh setting, incarcerees tried to hold on to dignity and to stay active. Committees organized camp life. Sports filled empty hours, and baseball led the list. Japanese American teams from several camps rode out to nearby towns and played local squads. A later rule let some college-age incarcerees leave. Their studies were at Midwest colleges and at colleges farther east, but only where Japanese Americans were accepted. A camp refrain was shikata ga nai, pronounced shee-KAH-tah gah NYE. In a loose Japanese sense, it says that a thing cannot be helped. People told one another to keep calm and to avoid a rash act they would regret. Resentment toward the government of the United States still had no exit. Racism aimed at them and their families felt humiliating. Mistreatment in the camps felt humiliating. Above all, they felt their country had betrayed them, and that other Americans had too. Fred Korematsu took his case to court Fred Korematsu, a Japanese American, was arrested in 1942, tried, and convicted for refusing the evacuation orders. He chose to fight the verdict. He hoped to show that locking people up for ethnicity violated the Constitution. In 1944 the case climbed to the Supreme Court of the United States. Nine justices kept the conviction, by 6 votes to 3. They said wartime peril outweighed a person's rights. In 1983 a federal judge wiped the conviction away. His name was cleared by that ruling. During the hearing he asked officials to admit the wrong. He wanted safeguards so no citizen would face the same fate, whatever that citizen's race, creed, or color. President Bill Clinton, in 1998, handed him the Presidential Medal of Freedom.

7Service and a fight for honor In 1943 the War Department of the United States needed more soldiers. So did the Office of Naval Intelligence. Recruiters visited the incarceration camps. Questionnaires asked how Americanized the incarcerees were. They asked if camp Nisei of fighting age would serve in uniform. Most of those men said yes. They set one condition. Their families must be freed, and citizen rights must be restored. The military refused to consider that bargain. Even so, 6 percent of camp Nisei still volunteered. They hoped a uniform would change public opinion by proving American loyalty. The Nisei fighters stood out, and then did more. Japanese Americans made up most of the 442nd Regimental Combat Team. The unit went to Europe and faced German and Italian troops. Go for Broke was the motto they carried. Courage on the field matched it. Purple Hearts for combat wounds went to nearly ten thousand of them. More than six hundred died. Medals of Honor, kept for the highest valor, went to twenty-one. Daniel Inouye was one of those twenty-one. The youth who had watched Pearl Harbor burn later fought for his country. A grenade blast cost him his right arm. Hawaii later sent him to the Senate, and he stayed for a long service. When fighting stopped, few units in United States history carried more decorations than the 442nd. President Harry S. Truman spoke to them afterward. He said they had beaten the enemy overseas and prejudice at home. A 1946 picture shows President Harry Truman greeting World War II veteran Wilson Makabe with a handshake.

8Late in 1944, Germany and Japan were headed for defeat. Officials began to plan the closing of the incarceration camps. For more than two years, Japanese Americans had lived as prisoners of their own government. Then the gates opened. Survivor Aya Nakamura called the exit a great day. Passing the gates felt wonderful, she said, because she finally knew she was headed home. A look backward On January 2, 1945, the exclusion order was canceled, and the lockup of Japanese Americans officially ended. Allied victory was near, so officials no longer saw a need for the camps. The Pacific fighting ended the next August, when Japan surrendered. Each camp survivor received 25 dollars and a train ticket. The hard question was the destination. Many had no house waiting. Thousands had lost businesses and property during the incarceration. Some returnees had to drive out people who had moved into the old homes with no right to be there. A few neighbors welcomed Japanese American friends. Many towns answered with distrust and discrimination. Money paid to mend a wrong, or to compensate for it, is a financial reparation. During 1948, senators approved a claims law for the evacuation of Japanese Americans. Payments to incarcerees eventually totaled 38 million dollars. One major newspaper reckoned that sum as less than ten cents for each dollar lost when people were pulled from businesses, homes, and careers. Four decades later, the 1988 Civil Liberties Act received President Ronald Reagan's signature. Each camp survivor was paid 20,000 dollars. Deep emotional scars remained, and so did psychological ones. Many parents pushed their children to shine at school and at work, hoping that success would block another victimization. For decades, most other Americans forgot this unjust chapter. During the 1970s the silence cracked, because survivors in greater numbers described their years inside. Congress formed a commission in 1981. It found no proof that any Japanese American, or any Japanese immigrant, had committed anti-American espionage or sabotage in the war. Fifty years had passed since the harbor was struck. The year was 1991. President George H. W. Bush offered another formal apology. A nation, he said, cannot really know itself unless it looks straight at past glory and past disgrace. Locking up Americans whose ancestry was Japanese, he said, had been a great injustice. He promised it would not be done again.

9Japanese Americans have kept reminding fellow citizens of that promise. Since the war, some voices in the United States have urged rounding up other groups and repeating the same wrong. Camp survivors have been among the loudest people saying no group should ever be treated this way. George Takei worked as an actor and as an activist. He was five when Arkansas became the place of his family's incarceration. He called the mass lockup a choice soaked in racism, in war hysteria, and in a failure of political leaders. Mistakes of that past, he said, must not return. To hold that line, civic leaders have to resist fearmongering, and they have to know the history so it never cycles back. Three images show him: as a child of the Rohwer camp in Arkansas, as the officer Sulu on television and in movies, and as a speaker on political issues across later years. Words from the book Hysteria, a noun, is a blast of negative feeling so strong that behavior flies out of control. Ancestral, an adjective, points to relatives who lived long before. Barracks, a noun, is a plain building, or a group of them, put up to house many people. Incarceration camps are sites where people are kept by force without a trial. Injustice, a noun, is unfair treatment of one person or of a group. Detained, a verb, means held in custody. Evacuation, a noun, is the moving of people because safety is at risk. Martial law, a noun, is a special rule set laid on a community and enforced by soldiers in war or in an emergency. Exclusion, a noun, is the act of barring people from a place or from a privilege. Opportunists are people who grab an advantage from events as they arise. First-generation, an adjective, describes people who settle in a country new to them. Prejudice, a noun, is an opinion shaped in advance, and it is usually hostile.

53. Machines Steered by Radio

1One picture shows a father and a son enjoying a car they steer from a distance. The same scene is the doorway into this book. Pages ahead cover a new speed record, the start of radio control, and the basic parts. They also cover cars, races, and flight, then the years still to come. A word list ends the book. Jet engines power some of these small aircraft, including the one in a second picture. Niels Herbrich lives in Germany. Before he flies, he works through a preflight checklist. The airplane is red. Its wings sweep backward. Nothing about it is an ordinary full-size jet. A car trunk can hold the whole craft. Even so, it is nearly as fast as a full-size airliner. Herbrich pilots it without ever leaving the ground. The engine is turbine-powered, and it hums as it comes alive. Moments later the sound is an ear-splitting whine. A burst of flame shows. Grass streams under the jet as it skids and then climbs. Whoosh. A handheld radio remote is the pilot's only link. With it he makes the jet roll. He also makes it bank along the course.

2Peak speed for this RC jet is 440 miles an hour, or 708 kilometers an hour. A new mark now stands in Guinness World Records, and Herbrich is the one who set it. Helicopters, trucks, cars, boats, and planes under radio control have been toys for children and for adults across many decades. Few of them match Herbrich's jet for speed. Fun is another story. They match it there. The idea of the first radio-controlled machine came from Nikola Tesla. Birth came during a lightning storm. The date was July 10, 1856. The town is now called Smiljan, in Croatia, and it is pronounced SMEEL-yawn. Invention became his work. Experiments with electricity later stirred other people to create radios. Radar and robots grew from that same spark. While he was still young, he imagined a boat guided by radio waves. Those waves are airborne ripples, invisible, of electromagnetic radiation. Wireless tools, including machinery under radio control, rest in part on his Tesla coil. By 1898 the work had carried him to New York City. The event was the first Electrical Exhibition at Madison Square Garden. Attendees saw a boat that answered radio commands. Shock and delight mixed in the crowd. Radio itself was still unknown to most of them. A picture from that year shows the world's first boat of this kind, and the stir around it. Signals left a transmitter Tesla had made at home. They reached a craft 4 feet long, which is 1.2 meters. Show builders had filled a big tank with water just for this display. The boat floated there. Graceful turns followed his silent commands. Lights even blinked to solve math problems shouted by the audience. Stun turned into argument. Mind control was one accusation. Magic was another. Someone guessed a trained monkey hid in the hull. Levers were the real machinery. Gears, springs, and motors worked with them. A coherer, which is a switch woken by radio, ran the set. Front pages carried the story. Teleautomaton was Tesla's own word for it. A toy was not his goal. He hoped for a navy contract. Torpedoes, he thought, could be steered through the water by this device. The U.S. Navy never bought it.

3Wartime brought limited use. World War I ran from 1914 to 1918. World War II ran from 1939 to 1945. Wide use waited for 1957, when the Space Age began. Through the early twentieth century, the gear suited big machines. Motors needed bulky equipment and bulky batteries. Murray Hill, New Jersey, is where Bell Labs worked. In 1947 that lab invented the transistor. Vacuum tubes gave way to something smaller, safer, and more reliable. Transistors use metals and semiconductors to amplify electric currents. They do not use filaments in a vacuum. Everyday life then opened up. Military work and industrial work were no longer the only homes for remote control. Electric motors shrank once engineers applied transistors. Toys gained transistors too. A hobby was born. RC can be read as remote-controlled. R/C is the same shortening, and radio-controlled is the other meaning. A wire still joins some vehicles to a controller. Radio frequencies carry the link for most modern ones, with no wire at all. Hundreds of vehicle types now exist, from robots to boats to drones in the air. Workings differ. Three shared parts do not. The remote, called a transmitter, sends radio signals on one specific frequency. Those signals include steering. They include throttle. A receiver inside the vehicle keeps listening. Decoded signals become electric current for servos, the mechanical motors that steer and drive. Batteries feed both ends of the link. What is radio? It is electromagnetic energy, kin to the energy we see as light. Invisible waves carry it through the air, and most walls do not stop them. Wave size and frequency, the count of waves each second, decide the form. One radio wave may outstretch a football field. Another may be near the length of a bicycle. Each second can hold from 1 million waves up to 100 million. Light belongs to this energy family. So do microwaves and X-rays. Those three have shorter wavelengths and higher frequencies.

4Stores first offered RC cars during the middle of the 1960s. Power is higher now, and the cars are smaller. Some burn gasoline. Some use electricity. Some burn glow fuel, a high-performance mix that people nickname nitro. Fumes are not a battery problem, and noise stays low. Recharging or swapping is frequent, so an afternoon means packing several batteries. Nitro models and gasoline models beat battery models on speed and on how long they run. Fuel bottles have to come along. Mess and higher upkeep costs come with them. An ordinary toy shop can sell a basic car. Price stays low, and care is simple. Hobby-grade cars are what serious drivers choose, and the price can reach several hundred dollars. Kits let builders start with every part in one box. Bodies can be painted. Parts can be swapped. Accessories include metal gears of a higher grade, shocks that work better, and body pieces that replace worn ones or improve them. Larger motors and larger engines are common changes. An RTR car, short for ready-to-run, arrives already assembled for drivers who prefer that. Three cars on nitro race a track in one picture. Shape and size vary whether the car came from a kit or came already built. Touring cars copy famous road cars. A Porsche 911 is one example. A Chevy Camaro is another. A Ford Mustang is another. Track surface can decide the choice: carpet, concrete, or asphalt. Off-road models win fans because tires are often large and shock absorbers are heavy-duty. Uncut grass does not stop them. Empty lots do not stop them. Dirt fields do not stop them. A few resemble monster trucks of an older style. Others resemble pickup trucks with a sporty look, or buggies that are vintage. Specialty units sometimes sell for a short time only. Collectors then treat them as editions.

5Some owners live to race. A park or an empty lot is enough for a friendly contest. Organized events use tracks built like real speedways. One contest is called the East Coast ProCup Challenge. Another is the Serpent Cup. Sorting follows size and class. It also follows kit-built or not, and it follows the engine. Power may come from electricity, from nitro, or from gasoline. Sports cars form one racing class. Touring cars form another. Off-road vehicles form another, split into four-wheel drive and two-wheel drive. On August 10, 2013, buggies built for dirt flew off jumps and caught big air. The scene was a national competition for RC cars in Kingsville Township, Ohio. Straight-line races usually need a drag strip or an airfield, any long paved open space. Oval tracks that close on themselves are another choice. So are rough courses full of hills and obstacles. Truck pulls and tractor pulls rank among the most exciting dirt events. Wheeled sleds behind RC trucks weigh 35 pounds at the light end and 100 pounds at the heavy end. That span is 16 to 45 kilograms. An average bulldog is a fair comparison. A German shepherd is another. Flight hooked Bob Motta in Danbury, Connecticut, during the 1960s. He remembers that bite of interest clearly. His first radio plane copied the F4 Corsair. The real Corsair served the U.S. Navy in World War II. The Marine Corps flew it then too, and again in the Korean War. Lately he favors models from World War I. His Nieuport 28 copies a French fighter with two wings. Advances in the planes amaze him. Miniaturization of the electronics, he says, is when things really took off. Stunts fill a 2009 competition picture. Hobbyists take to the sky in planes, in blimps, in helicopters, and in newer drones. Beginners usually start on trainers, sometimes nicknamed foamies. The design is simple so flying stays easier. Foam keeps the weight down. A crash is less likely to ruin the model. Several flight modes often give a new pilot a path that grows harder step by step.

6Sport planes are the usual next step once a trainer is mastered. Complicated aerobatic maneuvers are within their reach. Planes made for precision aerobatic flying forgive less. Sport planes forgive more. A special wing on many of them helps a new pilot hold the plane upside down. Motta has been told, by people who fly the 747 jumbo jet, that a model can be harder than a real airplane. His own view is that the pilot stays on the ground and must spend every sense, since a climb always ends in a return. Computer networks now link some RC cars. A tablet or a smartphone, plus a wireless connection, does the steering. Radio waves carry those networks as well, so the link is natural. A few machines do more than drive. The Rover Revolution is one. It resembles a four-wheeled robot. Cameras number two. A microphone and a speaker ride along. Video, talk, and listening all stay available while it rolls. Warbirds are popular copies of fighters from the two world wars. A picture shows a German triplane of the first of those wars. Kits exist, and so do ready-to-fly models, marked RTF. On the flight line they always draw attention. Owners may build a plane, paint it, and customize it. Motta once spent hundreds of hours on a single assembly. After a crash he keeps every piece that is still sound. Those pieces become spares.

7China in 2013 is the setting of one picture. A boy guides an RC mini helicopter along an obstacle course in a competition. Almost-Ready-to-Fly planes, marked ARTF, can be bought now. Motta compares the old two hundred hours of building with about twenty hours today. The result, he says, can still look good and earn respect. Fewer pieces mean less assembly time. Weight can be higher, and a repair can be tougher. A helicopter that carries one rotor on the top of its fuselage can outdo a plane in difficulty. Careless first flights go badly. If the new pilot has not studied, more than half crash inside the opening minute. Indoor practice is kinder with mini helicopters, yet skill still takes repetition. Lessons from the small craft transfer to bigger helicopters. Camera-carrying quadrocopters joined training missions of international search and rescue groups beginning in 2013. Quadcopter is the other name. Four blades spin, most often at the corners, and flight can aim any direction. An autogyro sits between plane and helicopter in looks. Forward motion comes from a propeller, mounted either at the nose or at the tail. Unpowered blades above then spin and hold the craft up. Autorotation is the name of that effect. Runways are unnecessary for every one of these copters, both for leaving the ground and for returning.

8One picture catches a delivery quadcopter in flight, a package held underneath while the test goes on. Hobby use is only part of the story. The same basic technology flies drones whose pilots sit miles off. Science uses them. Industry uses them. The military uses them. A neighborhood may already have seen one overhead. Farmers can send a camera drone to locate insects that harm crops, rather than inspect each field on foot. Hospitals have moved human organs by drone so a transplant can happen in another place. Package delivery by drone has begun at some companies. February 2014 sent drones to watch a volcano as it erupted in Indonesia. Major games and major shows now draw television crews who fly drones. Footage is amazing, and the performance is not disrupted. Regulations from the Federal Aviation Administration, the FAA, cover operators who fly for pay and operators who fly for fun. Public safety is the goal. A century back, this would have seemed like magic. Ordinary days now include it. The play is still a blast.

9Hard words from this book can be read this way. Aerobatic refers to aircraft moves in the air that are challenging or thrilling. Counterparts are people or things that line up with one another in job or in function. A drone is an aircraft or a ship with no crew aboard, run from somewhere else. Electromagnetic radiation is energy carried as electromagnetic waves. Expel means to push a thing out from the place that held it. A filament is a thread, or a threadlike piece, that conducts electricity. Light bulbs contain examples. The fuselage is an aircraft's main body. Industrial points to the making of goods, especially where machines, automation, and technology do the work. Miniaturization is the designing or the making of a smaller version. A phenomenon is something you can observe happening, or a person or thing admired because an unusual ability makes it impressive. Precision means being exact or accurate. A replica is a reproduction or a copy. A semiconductor can move some heat or some electricity, yet less than a true conductor moves, and electronics use these materials often. A throttle is the valve that sets how much fuel an engine receives. A transistor is a small electronic part that manages the flow of electricity in a device. A transmitter is the device that sends electromagnetic signals outward. Radio signals and television signals are examples. Turbine-powered describes a machine driven by a turbine, a fan-shaped device that takes motion from water, wind, or steam. Vintage describes something old that still has good quality, a classic.

54. Machu Picchu

1Machu Picchu stands in the Andes Mountains of Peru, in South America. A map of the area also shows Brazil, Bolivia, Chile, the Urubamba River, and the Pacific Ocean. The city is 2,350 meters, or 7,710 feet, above sea level. Dense fog often surrounds it, so people call it the City in the Clouds. The peak is high enough that clouds often come to visit. In the Inca language, machu means old, and picchu means peak. Most of the modern world did not know this city for over four hundred years. In 1911 it was found again and seen as a priceless treasure of the Inca Empire.

2Hiram Bingham was an American explorer. He studied old charts and texts. He believed a hidden Inca capital lay in the Andes. Spanish invaders had never found that city. He went to Peru to search. A local farmer told him of a city left long ago. Bingham climbed a steep path full of plants. Through vines and trees he saw stone walls, terraces, and sacred temples. He made the site known. Other visitors may have come decades earlier. They did not talk much about it. No written Inca language has been found, so experts make careful guesses. Some think a small group in the Andes began by 1400 to take over others. They would trip them with bolas.

3A statue of Pachacuti stands on the road up to Machu Picchu. From 1438 to 1471 were prosperous years, as his army defeated many kingdoms and reached present-day Ecuador. Machu Picchu was most likely built for him, but no one knows why. Bingham first called it the birthplace of Inca society, then a last refuge from Spanish conquistadors. That refuge was in the jungle, many kilometers away. Archaeologists were still digging at part of the site in 2016. A failed theory said it was a temple for chosen women of the Sun god Inti. In 2000, a Yale expert found only half the skeletons were women, and some were infants and children, so they were not priestesses.

4Many other ideas called the city a prison, a trade hub, a women's retreat, a king's crowning place, or a crop station. Today many experts think it was a royal estate for emperors and nobles. The Inca began building in the fifteenth century on a spot chosen for defense. From the peak they could see people in the valley, but people below could not see the city. Steep mountains would have made the city hard to attack. A rain-fed spring feeds the hill, and a stone base still marks where the water comes out. A canal carried river water to fountains that still flow, but it may not have watered the terraces. Bingham thought a nearby granite quarry meant shorter stone hauls, but most stones there are fairly small.

5The Inca may have split rocks with wet wooden wedges that froze and pushed the stone apart. Ice takes more space than water, but this does not explain the smooth straight granite blocks. How they shaped those huge stones remains a mystery, even with today's tools. The stones fit so tightly that no mortar was used, and a knife will not fit between them. The walls are still strong after centuries on the mountaintop. An urban part held homes for workers, the king, and officials, and a farm part grew crops. The Temple of the Sun may have been a solar observatory, and some think only priests could enter. On the summer and winter solstices, light from an east window shines on a large center rock.

6A plan of the city shows the royal palace, the main temple, the Temple of the Sun, homes, open space, and farms. Experts think rich and powerful Inca built it in the 1450s as a place to relax and host guests. About 150 homes, all about the same size, housed about 750 people. The royal palace of Pachacuti may have been the grandest. The western Acropolis holds the Temple of the Three Windows, with the largest known windows in Inca building. The Intihuatana Stone nearby is a sundial carved as one piece and standing 1.8 meters, or 6 feet, tall. At midday on the equinoxes that start spring and autumn, the Sun is over the pillar, so it casts no shadow. A rough Quechua meaning of Intihuatana is to tie up the Sun, and dozens of south terraces support one another on the steep slope.

7About 200 centimeters, or 79 inches, of rain fell each year. Water seeped to a layer of rocks and gravel, then flowed by aqueducts into the forest below. This kept the terraces and other structures from collapsing, and they still stand today. People lived in the city only until the early or mid-1500s. Huayna Capac ruled from 1493 to 1527 over more than twelve million people who spoke at least twenty languages. After he died, his sons Huascar and Atahualpa fought a civil war that began in 1529. Atahualpa won in 1532, but a few years later Pizarro arrived with 180 soldiers and 37 horses. The Inca had never seen guns or horses in battle, thousands died, and Pizarro ordered Atahualpa killed despite over 22 metric tons of gold and silver.

8A painting shows how the first meeting between Pizarro and the Inca ruler might have begun. Atahualpa's death led to the empire's downfall, and people lived at Machu Picchu for only a few decades more. No evidence shows that conquistadors attacked or even reached the mountaintop city. Civil war and smallpox, brought to Mexico by Europeans in the 1520s, weakened the empire and cut the population by 95 percent. Food may have stopped, and the remote site was too hard to keep without support. Trees and vines hid the city for centuries, and only locals who farmed in the area knew it. Peru is proud of Machu Picchu, named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983 to help teach Inca culture. Bingham took thousands of artifacts to Yale, and in 2007 most were returned after almost a century of requests.

9Since 2011, the government of Peru has limited daily visitors to 2,500. Security cameras, timed visits, and certified guides add more protection. These rules help preserve the ancient ruins. Historians still study Machu Picchu and hope to find new facts about the Inca. We have learned a great deal about their history and customs. Many mysteries about this amazing culture and place remain. Three train lines take people to the site. Some adventurous tourists take a hard hike of three to four days to get there.

55. Napoleon and the Empire That Broke

1A map shows French power at its greatest reach in 1812. Marks distinguish the French Empire, allies of France, enemies of France, and countries France controlled. Seven sections shape this account. They cover one fateful choice, the young officer, the seizure of power, rule from the desk, wars across Europe, the collapse, the legacy, and a word list. In 1812 Napoleon orders French troops over the Neman River and into Russia. One choice that changed everything Early in 1812, Napoleon Bonaparte weighed his next move. He ruled France and most of mainland Europe. Doubt was scarce, and he had little cause for it. He expected huge success from whatever he tried. Since 1799, army after army had fallen to him, and he had become ruler of a French empire that grew greatly under his command. In 1812 his eyes turned east, toward Russia, a nation both vast and sprawling. Russia defied him by keeping up trade with Great Britain, his greatest enemy and the one he had failed to conquer. An alliance between Russia and Britain was forming, and it threatened his power. He decided the time had come to invade. It would be the most disastrous choice of an infamous career.

2The young officer Birth came in 1769, on Corsica, a Mediterranean island lately ceded to France by treaty. The other party was the Italian Republic of Genoa. He was the fourth of eleven children in a family of the minor Italian nobility. Grade school on Corsica led to two military schools in France. Other students teased him for lower social rank and for weak French. Intelligence and a gift for mathematics were on his side. In 1785 he finished as a second lieutenant of artillery, completing in one year a course that usually took two. A picture shows the young Napoleon mocked by classmates inside a military school set in the north-central part of France. The French Revolution began during 1789. Napoleon had nearly reached twenty. Across ten years it ended France's monarchy, which had held power for a very long time. He embraced the Revolution's early Enlightenment ideals, including freedom from government oppression and a brotherhood of all male citizens. Early in 1793, revolutionaries executed King Louis XVI in public. That killing opened a bloody stretch called the Reign of Terror. Queen Marie Antoinette died in it, along with many nobles, officials of the government, and revolutionaries who had led. The terror left France without strong leadership at the top. An opening appeared for the ambitious Napoleon, who began to picture himself ruling a huge empire. A 1793 picture shows Louis XVI, king of France, led to execution before a revolutionary crowd.

3Early in the Revolution, Napoleon was only a captain, serving Corsica in the regular army. The year 1793 sent him to aid forces of the Revolution, facing the British, at Toulon, a city in southern France. Other nations in Europe, Britain among them, wanted the Revolution stopped and the monarchy restored, because they saw a threat to their own kings. Napoleon drove the British out and took Toulon back. The success made him a brigadier general at twenty-four. In 1795, royalist forces that wanted the monarchy returned tried to seize power in Paris. Napoleon was called to stop them. For crushing that revolt, the Directory named him to command what was called the Army of the Interior. The Directory was the committee in charge of France across the years 1795 to 1799. In 1796 he married Joséphine de Beauharnais, pronounced BOH-ar-nay. She was a widow, and two children were hers. The husband before Napoleon, a general, had been executed in the Reign of Terror. France was learning his name as a leader who could get hard jobs done. Success fed his ambition. Taking power Victories continued, built on a battle method that worked again and again. He held a large reserve while he studied the enemy line for its weakest point. At the decisive moment the reserve went in and broke that weak link. In 1796 the Directory gave him the French forces in Italy and told him the job of pushing Italian armies, and Austrian armies, off the peninsula. A series of battles did it. He claimed Italy for France and came home a hero. A picture shows him leading troops in the Piedmont, a region of northern Italy. That Italian fight opened a pair of wars, and it came first, as France tried to grow an empire by spreading revolution. European nations joined to stop France and to hold their monarchies together. Historians call them the French Revolutionary Wars, running from 1792 until 1802.

4During 1798 a small army under Napoleon entered Egypt. The aims were to guard French trade routes and to cut Britain's commerce linking it to the Middle East. Several land battles in that campaign went his way. At sea he lost. A British fleet beat a French one off Egypt's coast. People call that fight the Battle of the Nile. It set aside any scheme for invading England. A portrait shows Admiral Horatio Nelson. On Europe's mainland Napoleon won battles. At sea, hope died against Britain's own seagoing master, Admiral Horatio Nelson. Nelson commanded at the Nile, and again at a still larger naval fight in 1805. That October, his tactics crushed a fleet of France and Spain, Spain then being France's ally. The place was Trafalgar, off Spain's southwest coast. The battle opened a century of British supremacy on the sea. In 1799 Napoleon used his military skill to stage a coup and overthrow the Directory. He made himself first consul of the republic and took a dictator's powers. He was then leading the Revolution's second war, against an alliance headed by Austria and Britain. A peace treaty followed in 1801, but peace rarely lasted long in the Napoleonic years. A picture shows him in crown and robes at the 1804 coronation in Paris. In May 1804 he took the title Emperor of the French. December 2 brought a ceremony inside Paris, at Notre-Dame Cathedral. He set that imperial crown onto his head by himself. The country of France had just rid itself of kings. An emperor now ruled.

5Rule from the desk Inside France he launched sweeping reforms. He built a central government that was strong and orderly, created a national bank, and reorganized the police. Relations with the Catholic Church were repaired, and Catholicism returned as the national religion. His most noted domestic policy may be the French Civil Code, later called the Napoleonic Code. It standardized the law. Before it, each town and each province kept its own customs. The code took rights from women and gave authority to fathers and to husbands. Family wealth sat in their control, and so did property and children. Male citizens gained rights that were equal, plus liberty in religion. Colonial enslavement, earlier abolished in France, was brought back. People of every social standing felt the code's effects. Women and children lost ground. Men gained freedom. A picture suggests that wide effect. He also reformed the economy, the law courts, and higher education. Tax collection had relied on elected collectors.
