Statistics are numbers that are gathered, arranged, and studied. A strike is a negative call. It comes when a batter swings and misses, lets a good pitch go, or hits a foul that is not caught. Plays are judged by an official called an umpire. Vying means competing.

61. One Hour Inside a Great Art Museum

1Thousands of famous works fill this museum. One of them is a painting by Vincent van Gogh. The picture's title is Self-Portrait with a Straw Hat. The painter shows his own face. More than six million people walk through the doors each year. A huge staircase rises in front of me. Those stairs climb to the main entrance. The building is the Metropolitan Museum of Art. New York City is the city around it. Ms. Kessler, my English teacher, gave us a job. We must join a guided tour. Afterward we write an essay. The essay compares three artworks. It must show how they are alike. It must also show how they are different. At first the assignment sounds useless. I wonder if art is nothing but paintings hung on a wall. I climb slowly. Still, I reach the top and step inside. The entrance room is called the Great Hall. People of every age stand around me. Their backgrounds are not all alike. Many different languages fill the air. Some adults draw their own versions of the art. Some children draw too.

2A young woman stands in the middle of a group, and I join them. She introduces herself as Jada. Art history is her subject at a college close by. The museum also employs her as a docent, a person who leads visitors. She shares background before we walk. Opening day was in 1870. The building covers the length of four city blocks. Inside are more than two million objects. The oldest come from ancient times. The newest come from the present. Our route will cross the whole museum. It will take one hour. Jada calls it a highlights tour. We will study only a few pieces. Millions of others remain in storage and on the walls. Her talk keeps going, and my interest grows with it. Jada strikes me as someone easy to like. Now I truly want to know why she cares so deeply about art. Pretty pictures may not be the whole story. A scene of the Great Hall shows the first room visitors enter. Signs there explain the collection. They also explain the exhibitions. Another scene shows Egyptian galleries. Mummies are on view. So are other objects taken from tombs. Those Egyptian rooms are where our walk begins. Enormous glass cases line the way. Mummies fill them. Other amazing artifacts fill them too. I wish we could linger. The schedule will not allow it. This place is huge. Falling behind the group is not an option. Then we reach a vast room. The ceiling is high. A real temple of stone stands on a raised base. Shallow water in a pool rings that base. Light pours in through a giant window wall. Jada gives the temple a name. It is the Temple of Dendur.

3Jada tells us about the Aswan Dam on the Nile River. In 1933 the height of that dam was raised. Massive floods followed. During part of every year the water covered this temple. Other historic sites went under as well. Destruction was a real threat. A rebuild of the dam came in the 1960s. After that, the danger to the sites was permanent. Fifty countries joined a rescue. The United States took part. Together they shifted twenty-two historic temples to safer ground. Egypt then handed this saved temple over as a gift. The receiver was the United States. The gift was a way to say thank you. Jada describes how this gallery copies the temple's original setting. The pool plays the role of the Nile. The windows play the role of outdoor sunlight. Construction happened around 15 BCE. Egypt then belonged to the Roman Empire. A chieftain from Nubia dedicated the building. One dedication was to Isis, a goddess of Egypt. Another was to his sons, Pihor and Pedesi. The Nile had drowned both sons. Picture writing covers the front face of the temple. Jada asks us to notice it. Princes appear in those pictures. The pharaoh appears too. They bring offerings to gods and to goddesses. The picture writing, called hieroglyphs, takes two forms. Outside, carvers cut the images down into the wall. That cut-in style is sunken relief. Inside, the images stand out from the wall. That raised style is raised relief. Electric lights are what we depend on now. Long ago, light came only from the sun. Candles gave light too. So did oil lamps. In a dark inner room, pictures that stick out were easier to see. A person could feel them as well. English names are scratched on the stone. Visitors did that carving from the seventeenth century through the nineteenth century. Spray paint did not exist yet.

4A dim hallway is our next path. Jada leads, and the hall opens into the American art wing. We step into a huge room. Stained glass, three stories tall, lights the space. A handsome staircase takes us up toward American paintings. Furniture galleries wait up there too. The number of objects stuns me. Even these stairs have a past, Jada says. Their first home was a Chicago building called the Stock Exchange. That structure was among the earliest skyscrapers in America. Builders finished it in 1894. My hand follows the banister as I go up. Copper forms a detailed geometric pattern there. I stop and look down into the wide gallery. Colored glass sparkles along the walls. The next room holds a painting I recognize at once. It is enormous. The title is Washington Crossing the Delaware. The painter was Emanuel Leutze. The year was 1851. George Washington appears with his troops. They are out in harsh weather. Their boat is on the Delaware River, and the river is icy. The date in the scene is Christmas night. The year of that night is 1776. American history class is where I first met this image. Washington's men struck a British loyalist camp without warning. Jada warns us that the scene does not tell the past cleanly. Several details are historically wrong. The clearest mistake is the flag. The American flag is painted in, yet the country had not adopted it by the time of that fight. She adds a second problem. The boat was not big enough for Washington to stand. Standing would have flipped it. Leutze still made those choices. He wanted a stronger feeling from anyone who looked. Jada asks us to look with careful doubt. She names that habit a critical eye. Question the content. Learn the history behind it. In this canvas, Washington is meant to represent ideas. America, in those ideas, is powerful. It is unique. It is righteous. Other paintings in this same museum reply to Leutze's scene. Jada tells us to look for them. Some were made by Black painters. Some were made by Indigenous painters. Their aim was a picture of America with more complexity. The canvas size is 12.4 by 21.5 feet. That equals 3.78 by 6.47 meters.

5Down we go again. Rooms along the way hold furniture. Lamps fill some of them. Other objects help each room rebuild one specific time. The walk feels endless. At last a long hall opens. Knights in full armor sit on horses that are armored too. They seem about to charge straight at us. A glass case is Jada's next stop. The case holds French armor for a whole body. The date is about 1600. Steel is the main material. Gilded decoration makes it beautiful. Preservation looks almost perfect. Silk the color of yellow still lines the helmet. Straps of red leather barely look worn. Fancy as it is, this suit saw real battle. Jada is clear about that. A saddle was made to match. So was a headpiece for the horse. Walking around in it is hard to picture. Fighting in it is harder still. The weight shows, and the number confirms it. Altogether the suit comes to 77 pounds. That is 34.9 kilograms. On battlefields, kings wore suits like this. Other noblemen did too. Tournaments were another place for such armor. A side room comes next. More armor waits there, but these are helmets. They come from Japan. Samurai warriors once wore them. Those warriors were a military elite. From the twelfth century to the nineteenth, they gained power in Japan. The power was political. It was social. It was economic. Outside Japan, few arms-and-armor collections are this large. The helmets in front of us do not match one another. Materials change from one to the next. Size changes. Shape changes. One of them holds my attention. A bright red flame decorates it. A tiny figurine grips a sword. The century is the sixteenth. Makers shaped it to echo hats that older men wore in that era. The figurine stands for a Buddhist guardian. Wisdom is what that guardian protects. Once I know a hidden history, an object such as this helmet makes more sense. I understand its purpose better.

6More than 17,000 works sit in the Greek and Roman rooms. A statue at one side shows an Amazon warrior who has been wounded. It dates to the first century CE or the second. Our path is a long hallway. White marble statues gleam along both sides. Jada explains that Romans made almost every statue here. Almost every one copies a Greek sculpture. The Greek versions were several hundred years older. Metal, not marble, was the Greek material. Bronze formed the bodies. Copper picked out small parts. Silver did too. Lips were among those parts. Eyelashes were too. Later people melted many of the metal works. They needed weapons. They needed coins. Surviving metal sculpture is therefore rare. The white we see today is also misleading. Jada says ancient marble was not left bare. Statues received bright paint. Temples did too. A small room is our next stop. Its name is cubiculum. Painters covered its walls, and those walls traveled here. Their first home was the Italian village of Boscoreale. The name is said boh-skoh-re-AH-le. Brilliant color fills the paintings. The scenes show a sanctuary in the open air. Jada tells us about August 24 in the year 79 CE. A famous volcano, Mount Vesuvius, erupted. Deadly ash fell in enormous amounts. Villages all around were hit. People were busy with everyday life. Nothing had warned them. Ash buried them in layers. Deaths were many. Damage was huge. The same ash saved things as well. It sealed cities the way a time capsule would. Architecture survived inside that seal. Artwork survived too, including the walls of this room. The paintings themselves are older than the eruption. They go back to 70 BCE. More than a hundred years separate the art from the disaster. The method on these walls is fresco. Painters spread water-based color directly on the plaster. Up on the roof, the Roof Garden offers one of the museum's strangest exhibit spaces. Every spring, work by an artist of our own time goes on view. The backdrop is stunning. The famous skyline rises behind it. Green trees of Central Park do too. One installation on view is by Hector Zamora. He is an artist from Mexico.

7A gallery sign explains art from Oceania. Those are islands in the Pacific Ocean. Melanesia is one group. Micronesia is another. Polynesia is a third. We leave the small painted room behind. The next rooms focus on Africa. Oceania has rooms too. So do the Americas. Nothing looks the same. Lighting has changed. Sound has changed. The design of the exhibits has changed. Wooden boats of giant size hang overhead. We pass beneath them. Masks line the route. They are elaborate. Shapes vary. Colors vary. Materials vary. No two are the same. Jada pauses. She asks what we ourselves count as ordinary beauty. A specific purpose stood behind many objects in this museum. Being pleasant to look at was not the chief aim. Beauty is still there, but each object has its own kind. Learn the maker's intention, she adds, and the link can grow stronger. The link is to the object. It is also to the maker. One African gallery stops me. A male figure stands there. The figure looks impressive. Height is only about 3.5 feet. That is 1.1 meters. Jada identifies a power figure from Africa. Nails cover the wood. He looks as if he is in command. His open mouth could belong to a leader shouting urgent orders. The eyes seem full of wisdom. They seem perceptive too. Makers from the Kongo peoples created him. His role was to hold particular forces of power. His role was also to display authority. A round cavity sits in a prominent place on the stomach. Ritual medicine once filled it. A beard was there at the start. Organic matter formed it. Palm extract was one ingredient. Fibers were another. The organic parts decayed. Nails that once fixed the beard did not. Old age is what the beard represented, Jada says. Wisdom is the other meaning. People turned to this sculpture for legal agreements. They turned to it to stop conflicts. They turned to it for healing the sick. Another name for these Central African figures is minkisi. Special sculptors did not work alone. Ritual leaders worked with them.

8A new nail went into the body whenever people sealed an important agreement. That nail was the record. I stop and sort through the day. Cultures I had never studied are now in front of me. Time periods I had never pictured are here too. Skip this visit, and I would have missed them. Another thought follows. Only a few hours back, any other plan would have sounded better. Jewelry in this gallery includes an ear ornament from Peru. Turquoise is one material. Gold is another. Further materials are mixed in. Visitors in a nearby scene study paintings of very large size. The room belongs to modern and contemporary art. That is our next stop with Jada. Dates on these works run from 1900 to now. Paintings of every size fill the rooms. I struggle to name what they depict. Upstairs, one big canvas stops us. My first thought is a child in a rage, flinging paint. Jada names the artist. He is Jackson Pollock, from America. He helped found a movement. The movement is abstract expressionism.

9Autumn Rhythm is the title on the canvas, with Number 30 beside it. Pollock finished it in 1950. Jada says he and other artists in that movement refused familiar subjects. Familiar techniques were refused too. Feeling, and a personal bond with the work, mattered more. They painted without a fixed plan. Gesture was a focus. Color was a focus. An image a viewer could recognize was not. Pollock did not stay with a brush. His choice was action painting. Paint was poured. It was splattered. It was thrown. Canvases rested on the floor. A standard easel was not part of the process. Tradition lost its hold on these artists. The later direction of art changed because of them. Our next stop is a painting of vivid red. Arrows run across it. Circles do too. Shapes like stick figures appear as well. A head similar to a mask sits at the top and seems to stare. The maker is Jean-Michel Basquiat. One parent was Haitian. The other was Puerto Rican. Brooklyn is where he grew up. Brooklyn is my home too. His first art was graffiti. The years were the 1970s. They continued into the 1980s. Graffiti is exactly what this canvas brings to mind. Detail is everywhere. Color is everywhere. Lines cross and recross. Some spots look sprayed. New York itself comes to mind. The city is exciting. It is busy. Possibility seems to fill it. We finish at a cloth work titled Street Story Quilt. Colorful fabric carries another view of New York life. Apartment blocks in the quilt match the kind of building I live in. Figures tell part of the tale. Written text tells the rest. The main character is a boy. His age sits below mine. The difference is only a few years. Harlem is his neighborhood. Faith Ringgold is the artist, Jada tells us. Art is only part of her work. She campaigns for the rights of women. She campaigns for civil rights as well. Museum doors were often closed fifty years ago. A Black artist could be shut out. A woman could be shut out. A Black woman, and Ringgold is one, could face both exclusions. She became known for speaking out against that unfairness.

10Splashed paint would not have counted as art in my old view. Graffiti would not have counted. A quilt would not have counted. Jada's account of where artists find ideas has shifted that view. I also hold on to something else she said. A lovely landscape is not, by itself, the test of good art. A person painted to look real is not the test either. Context helps us judge why a work matters. Inspiration helps. The mark a work leaves on a culture helps too. From those clues we decide what we ourselves think. I still have thinking to do. Even so, her meaning is starting to land. One visitor strolls by two abstract canvases. Barnett Newman painted the one on the left. Mark Rothko painted the one on the right. Both hang among modern and contemporary works. Outside, the front steps draw crowds. Visitors like to gather there. My legs are tired by the time the walk winds down. Hundreds of European paintings pass beside us. I only glimpse some famous ones. Van Gogh is among them. Monet is among them. The giant staircase takes us down. The Great Hall is the end of the tour. So much has passed in front of me that I feel overwhelmed. The learning feels just as large. Awe is the right word for the Met. One hour felt like a trip around the world. It also felt like a trip backward through time. I have to confess a mistake. I had not understood why art is important. The city meets me at the exit. Sights rush in. Sounds rush in. Smells rush in. I sit down for a rest. The seat is the great steps outside the entrance. Ideas for the essay are still fresh, so I want them on paper. Choosing will be the hard part. Which pieces can I compare when every piece seemed wonderful? I am certain of a return visit. The next one will last longer. The next one will be for me, not only for class.

11A few words help with a visit like this. Abstract expressionism is a way of painting that shows emotion through shapes and patterns instead of only through people or objects. Artifacts are things humans made or used in the distant past. Conventional describes what is common, what is traditional, or what most people accept. Cultures are the customs and ideas of particular groups of people. A docent guides visitors, most often in a museum or a similar cultural site. A facade is the front face of a building. Galleries are rooms or whole buildings where the public comes to see art. Highlights are the parts of an event that stay most memorable, important, or exciting. Illuminated means lit. Intentions are plans, goals, or the purposes behind an action. Intricate describes something very detailed, complicated, or complex. Organic describes what comes from a living thing. Replicate means to reproduce something or to imitate it exactly. A sanctuary is a place of safety, and it can also mean the protection that place gives. Statuesque describes someone tall, beautiful, and dignified.

62. Peach Baskets and the Orange Ball

1Only a few tight seconds remain on the clock. The score is level. A player bounces the ball toward the far end and hunts for a gap. The pass comes suddenly. A teammate is waiting near the other team's hoop. That teammate leaps and slams the ball through the hoop. The buzzer sounds at the same moment. Time is gone. A standing crowd, fully charged, roars. This game is finished. A photo from 2013 shows another tight finish. The Philadelphia 76ers react to the game-winning point. The other side was the Brooklyn Nets. The 76ers won 121 to 120. The win came in overtime. The same sport is played in many places. In Burkina Faso, in West Africa, wheelchair players wait under the hoop for a rebound. The setting may be a pro arena. It may be a game with neighborhood friends. Either way, the sport is thrilling. It asks players to be lightning fast in the mind. It asks them to be lightning fast in the body. Every arena shares one joyful aim. Send an orange ball through a hoop.

2The sport began in 1891. The inventor was Dr. James Naismith, born in Canada. He taught physical education at Springfield College. That college is in Massachusetts. He wanted restless students busy indoors. Rainy days were a problem. Cold winter days were a problem. He wrote the rules himself. Peach baskets were fastened by him onto the rail of a balcony. One basket stood at each end of the gymnasium. Those baskets still had bottoms, unlike hoops now. A ball that dropped in had to be lifted out by hand. Later the bottoms came off. Metal hoops took the place of the baskets. Early play had no dribbling. Players moved the ball with a bounce pass. The first college game came in 1892. Inside the United States the sport caught on fast. Schools took to it in particular. A ball was enough to start. A basket was enough. A court was enough. Naismith was born in Canada. He studied physical education in Montreal. Teaching then carried him out of Montreal and into the United States. Many Native peoples name their style rez ball. Rez is short for reservation. College play among Black schools held its opening conference in 1916. From then on, the sport was more than a game for Black communities. It was woven deep into Black culture. The sport matters to Native peoples as well. From 1870 until 1978, U.S. officials removed many Native children from home. The children lived at schools. They played this sport there. Over time it became part of Native culture. Native players usually use a style that is unusually fast. The sport's popularity widened after World War II ended. Wounded servicemen came home. Wheelchair play grew popular with them. The ball was not always orange. Before the 1950s the color was brown.

3Lots of people play today. Men play. Women play. Boys play. Girls play. Almost every nation has players. The American National Basketball Association began in 1949. The short name is NBA. That league was central to the huge growth of pro play. It is the biggest pro basketball organization. It is also the most famous. It has thirty teams. College play fields more than three hundred teams across the nation. The largest college body is the NCAA. Those letters stand for National Collegiate Athletic Association. Nearly every high school has a team. Women were already active in 1892. That was only one year after Naismith invented the game. Lisa Leslie is a WNBA superstar. Diana Taurasi is a WNBA superstar. Maya Moore is a WNBA superstar. The letters WNBA stand for Women's National Basketball Association. Women's play has gained a much bigger group of fans. A 2015 college photo shows Jackie Young on the left. She shoots over Caylie Young. France's women's team stands with silver medals. The medals are from the 2012 Olympics. Fan numbers keep rising around the world. Player numbers keep rising too. The rise covers women and men. It covers amateur play and pro play. FIBA counts at least 450 million players worldwide. FIBA is French. The first words are Fédération Internationale. Then comes de Basketball. Leagues exist all over the world. A global championship is the FIBA Basketball World Cup. It is held every four years. The Olympic Games have featured the sport since 1936. There it is a highly competitive event. China has loved the sport for about one hundred years. India has loved it for about that long. Australia has too. The Philippines has loved it especially. The Philippine Arena is the largest basketball building in the world. It can hold fifty-five thousand fans. The next-largest buildings are in the United States. Serbia has one of them. Canada has one of them.

4A game is split into four quarters. In the NBA each quarter lasts twelve minutes. Each team puts five players on the floor. The court is a rectangle. A hoop hangs on a backboard at each end. The hoop is 10 feet above the floor. That height is 3 meters. The aim is the higher score. Points come from shots through the other team's hoop. A made shot is usually worth two points. Beyond the arc that marks three points, a made basket counts as three. Foul shots can add points too. After a foul, the referee may award the fouled player some free throws. A foul happens when another player breaks the rules. The break can be an accident. It can be on purpose. Unfair body contact is a foul as well. The referee blows a whistle. Hand signals show which foul occurred. The award may be one free throw. It may be two. It may be three. The number depends on the kind of foul. Each of those shots is worth one point. The shooter stands behind the free-throw line. The defending team may not interfere. Free throws often decide a win or a loss. Players keep shifting into spots where they can shoot. They also shift into spots for a pass to a teammate who has a good look. The other side tries to block shots. It tries to steal the ball. The ball may move only by a dribble. It may also move by a pass. As play runs up and down the court, a team flips to defense or to offense. The flip depends on who has the ball. Zone defense is one common plan. In a zone, each player guards a section of the court. Person-to-person defense is the other common plan. In that plan, each player guards one opponent. Attacking plans vary. Often a player without the ball dashes or changes direction. That move is called a cut. The cut is made so the player can catch a pass and shoot. A court diagram labels the midcourt line. It labels the baseline, the sideline, and the three-point line. It labels the free-throw line, the center circle, the top of the key, and the basket. It labels the key. The spots are center, small forward, shooting guard, point guard, and power forward. The short marks are SG, PF, PG, C, and SF. The other team is marked as the opposing side.

5A missed shot can bounce off the hoop. It can bounce off the backboard. Players from both teams jump for that rebound. A strong rebounder helps the team keep the ball. Coaches assign roles, which are the positions. Ball handling is usually sharpest in the point guard. That player sets up the attack. The point guard controls the ball. The job is to get it to the right teammate at the right moment. The shooting guard takes many long shots on offense. On defense, that guard faces the other team's best player on the perimeter. The small forward uses speed. On offense the small forward scores close to the basket. On defense the small forward steals. The power forward attacks with the back toward the basket. On defense the power forward plays under the basket. That player may instead guard the other power forward. The center uses height to score. The center uses height to protect the basket. Manute Bol shares the NBA height record with Gheorghe Muresan. Each stood 7 feet 7 inches. That height is 231 centimeters. History's shortest NBA player was Muggsy Bogues. He stood 5 feet 3 inches. That height is 160 centimeters. The court has had many outstanding players. Their personalities were vivid. Their feats broke records. George Mikan stood 6 feet 10 inches. That height is 208 centimeters. The 1950s made him an early example of a big man. He changed what the sport was. Before him, people thought the game belonged to small, quick players. Wilt Chamberlain played in the 1960s and the 1970s. He stood 7 feet 1 inch. That height is 216 centimeters. He held the top marks for scoring. He held the top marks for rebounding. He held the top marks for durability. Many rank him among the finest players in NBA history.

6Kareem Abdul-Jabbar kept changing games for his teams. His high school team won seventy-one games in a row. It was little surprise that he became the NBA's all-time leader in points. People call Lisa Leslie a mother of the WNBA. Her skills were phenomenal. She ruled the court through the 1990s. She ruled it through the 2000s. Four Olympic golds came with the American squad. Voters named her WNBA MVP three times. MVP means Most Valuable Player. She won two WNBA championships. Earvin Johnson is known as Magic. He became famous with the Los Angeles Lakers. He became famous with the Olympic Dream Team. Fans were amazed by his command of every part of the game. His passes were surprising. They were skillful. They looked almost like magic. Michael Jordan is often called the greatest player the sport has had. He holds an impressive stack of records. People nicknamed him Air Jordan. They nicknamed him His Airness. The names came from his leaps and his famous slam dunks. Three Ohio state titles came while LeBron James was still in high school. Right after graduation, the Cleveland Cavaliers picked him. No younger NBA player had ever been named Rookie of the Year. He also became the youngest to reach ten thousand career points. Maya Moore starred in high school. She starred in college. Her college team won ninety games in a row. That streak broke records. Soon after joining the WNBA, she ranked among the top scorers. Wide praise placed her among the sport's finest women athletes. Four championships came with her help. Two Olympic gold medals were hers.

7The sport has traveled far from a simple start. News coverage keeps fans interested all year. Courts sit in neighborhood parks. They sit at schools. They even sit in some driveways around the world. A person who wants to learn can do so with ease. Schools offer ways to practice. Community clubs offer ways to practice. They offer ways to join a team. Nobody knows where the next great stars will appear. The Cage is a famous court. It stands on West 4th Street in New York City. Words to know. Acclaim means strong, eager praise. Competitive describes a rivalry among people, teams, or businesses. Defense is the effort to stop the other team from scoring. It also names the players who do that work. Dribbles means moving a ball ahead with repeated bounces. In this sport the bounces come from the hands. The same word can cover taps in soccer or field hockey, by feet or by a stick. Durability means a person or thing can stay strong for a long while. Interference means blocking something from going forward or from being finished. Leagues are groups of teams that play one another. Offense is the effort to score on the other team. It also names the players who try to score. Opposing describes a clash or a contest with someone or something. Phenomenal means amazing or impressive. A rebound is the bounce back off a hard surface. Strategies are thought-out plans aimed at a problem or a goal.

63. Petra

1Hundreds of artifacts are on display in Petra Museum, but many others were lost to thieves. People can see Petra in two days, but locals say five days are best. Visitors should walk a lot, wear strong shoes, and bring sunblock, sunglasses, a hat, and a camera. Water is needed because the desert can get very hot in summer. Wind, water, and salt from the Red Sea can damage the stone when salt forms crystals in tiny holes. Tourists also wear down surfaces by touching, sitting, and walking on them. In 1985, the Rose City became a UNESCO World Heritage Site, which helps protect and conserve it. Historians say a church mosaic of a spotted giraffe was made by someone who had never seen one, so it looks like a camel.

2British author T. E. Lawrence wrote that you cannot know Petra's beauty until you see it. In the early 1800s, Swiss explorer Johann Ludwig Burckhardt heard of a hidden city in the Middle East. It lay in a remote Jordan valley of red, gray, and black sandstone, known to Bedouin nomads. During conflicts he dressed as an Arab, crossed a narrow canyon in 1812, and was the first European since the Crusades to see Petra. The Crusades dated from 1095 to 1291, and over four hundred thousand people visited Petra in 2015. Petra became a New Seven Wonder of the World in 2007 and was on Smithsonian magazine's 2008 list of twenty-eight places to see before you die. At the Visitor Centre they buy tickets and enter the Siq on foot, by horse cart, horse, donkey, or camel. No motors are allowed. Explorers start at the Treasury. The design mixes Mesopotamia, Greece, Rome, India, and Egypt.

3Little Petra is a smaller site 8 kilometers, or 5 miles, north of Petra. Like Petra, people can enter it only by a narrow canyon. Nabataeans carved the buildings directly into the sandstone rocks. Many historians believe ancient traders stayed in Little Petra when they visited the larger city to the south. A second idea is that carvers set strong rods in the rock to hold a wooden board they stood on. After each level, they would have moved the rods and the board lower. Scientists still seek clues, and stairways, water channels, and other features were carved into the cliffs and canyons. Tools included picks, chisels, mallets, and hammers, and toothed claw chisels may explain coarse diagonal lines in the stone.

4Petra is in southwestern Jordan, in a valley between the Dead Sea and the Gulf of Aqaba. The Gulf of Aqaba is a northern extension of the Red Sea. The ancient city is about 185 kilometers, or 115 miles, southwest of Amman, Jordan’s capital. It stood on important trade routes between the Middle East, Asia, and Africa. Petra is in one of Earth’s driest deserts, surrounded by red sandstone cliffs and gorges. The Siq, pronounced SEEK, is 1.2 kilometers, or 0.75 miles, long and up to 80 meters, or 262 feet, high. The Siq leads in from the east, and the region’s map also names Israel, Syria, Iraq, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and Ma’an. The nearest year-round water is Ain Musa, or Moses’s Spring, about 8 kilometers, or 5 miles, away, and a dry riverbed nearby can flash flood.

5The city of Petra gets its name from the Greek word for rock. Its nickname, the Rose City, comes from the color of the rock. Petra spans 264 square kilometers, or 102 square miles. The city center along the Colonnaded Street measures about 6 square kilometers, or 2.3 square miles. Most of the stone city is carved from sandstone cliffs, but some building work was also done. There are hundreds of tombs, many with sacred writings, and civic buildings from its time as a trade center. Temples, monuments, altars, and houses are there too, and many structures are over 30 meters, or 100 feet, tall. Unfinished work suggests they cut one level at a time, stood on the step, then cut lower for freestanding stone.

6Petra's structures are two main types, freestanding buildings and rock-cut monuments. Rock-cut monuments were carved into the cliffs, and they were harder to make and more impressive. The towering Monastery is 45 meters, or 148 feet, tall, and these works are large, beautiful, and richly designed. Freestanding buildings rose from the bottom up, but rock-cut monuments were carved from the top down. Unfinished monuments, carved only at the top, confirm this top-down way. There were few trees, so wooden scaffolding was not used. Sandstone was the main building stone. A Siq flood dam, channels, pipes, aqueducts, cisterns, reservoirs, and tunnels served at least twenty thousand people. In 1993 Jordan's Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities made Petra a park that includes ancient trade roads around the city.

7The Treasury, called al-Khazneh in Arabic, is Petra’s most famous monument and the first sight out of the Siq. The Street of Facades leads into the city center and is lined with tall tombs and some smaller tombs. The Theatre was cut from solid rock and has suffered great damage. The Royal Tombs, some of them very decorated, are where kings were buried. The Colonnaded Street runs through the center of the city. Petra Museum was founded in 1994 and holds more than six hundred artifacts from many eras of Petra’s history. The Monastery, called al-Deir, is among Petra’s largest monuments. Floor mosaics in the church show many animals and figures of the seasons, ocean, Earth, and wisdom.

8In 330 ce, Roman emperor Constantine I, a Christian, moved the capital from Rome to Byzantium to spread Christianity. Byzantium later became Constantinople, which is now Istanbul. Petra’s people slowly adopted Christianity, and the change showed in their city. Petra Church was built around 450 and remodeled between 500 and 550, when large mosaics were put in. During that time, some tombs were turned into churches. A huge earthquake in 363 ce damaged the water system and nearly half the city, and it likely helped cause Petra’s decline. Another large earthquake struck in 551. Arabs took over the region in the early 600s, and by the end of that century the last residents had left.

9While Petra was thriving, the Roman Empire was expanding east into the Middle East. In 106 ce, the Romans peacefully took control of Petra. Evidence suggests that life there went on much as before. Still, Roman rule changed the city’s design and added new roads lined with columns. The Romans ruled Petra for three hundred years, then moved their trade focus north and used more water routes. Those changes made Petra less important as a trade center. Columns on the Colonnaded Street show Roman style, though floods have hurt it, and a normal walk west takes about twenty minutes. Most visitors take longer to see the Treasury, Street of Facades, Theatre, Royal Tombs, museum, and Monastery.

10People have lived in the Petra area since at least 7000 BCE. The Nabataeans, called nab-uh-TEE-uns, were nomadic Arabian herders of camels, goats, and sheep who founded the rock city. Their power grew in the first millennium BCE as they took over trade routes linking the Middle East, Asia, and Africa. They traded incense from Arabia, spices from India, and silks from China. For hundreds of years these tent nomads gave water and shelter and charged foreigners tolls. No one knows why they left nomadic life, but Petra became a center of people, goods, money, and culture. Their capital Raqmu, founded around 300 BCE, flourished in the first century BCE, and the empire reached parts of Jordan, Syria, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and Israel. Not much is known about them apart from Sun worship. A winter solstice light falls on the Monastery podium. Sunlight reaches 80 percent of the main structures.

64. Prehistoric Giants (Other Than Dinosaurs)

1Georges Cuvier showed how scientists picture an extinct animal such as Megatherium. William Buckland found a tiny mammal jaw bone with a dinosaur toe bone. He and Cuvier decided mammals lived in more ancient times than people had known. Many giants were not dinosaurs. Giant shellfish, insects, centipedes, fish, amphibians, birds, reptiles, and mammals lived long ago. A giant ape lived too, almost like King Kong! Paleontologists use shells, footprints, and fossils, and DNA can show links to living animals. More than 99 percent of all animal species that ever lived are now extinct.

2Scientists divide Earth's history into eras and periods. The breaks are often marked by animal change, climate change, or mass extinctions. The first known animal appeared about 600 million years ago. Cameroceras lived in North America, Meganeura in Europe, and Arthropleura in North America and Europe. Leedsichthys lived in France and Chile, while Koolasuchus and Liopleurodon lived in Europe. Elasmosaurus lived in North America, Russia, and Japan, and Cymbospondylus lived in North America and Europe. Ornithocheirus lived in South America, Europe, Africa, and Australia. Other giants lived in the Americas, Mongolia, Siberia, China, and Southeast Asia.

3In the Paleozoic, giant invertebrates flew and lived in the oceans. From 470 million to 440 million years ago, all animals lived in the ocean. Cameroceras had eight tentacles and a cone shell that might grow 36 feet long. It shot water through a tube, then grabbed trilobites and tore them with its beak. People once thought shells of its small relatives were unicorn horns. Meganeura lived 311 million to 282 million years ago in swampy forests. Its wingspan was 2.5 feet, so it was the largest insect ever known. Extra oxygen made the air heavy and helped giant animals grow.

4Arthropleura was the largest land arthropod ever. It looked like a centipede with 60 legs and could grow longer than 8 feet. It lived in swampy forests from 340 million to 280 million years ago. Its body had 30 hard plates, with a pair of legs under each plate. Heavy oxygen in the air helped it grow so large. Leedsichthys was the largest fish ever and could grow almost 55 feet long. It lived from 165 million to 155 million years ago and filtered small animals with more than 40,000 thin teeth. It may have died out when seas became lower and food grew scarce.

5Koolasuchus was a slimy giant salamander about 17 feet long. It lived in swampy forests from 137 million to 112 million years ago. Its wide, flat head held more than 100 long teeth for catching prey. Eyes on top of its head let it watch prey while buried in muddy water. Climate change shrank its swamp habitat, and giant amphibians died out. Cymbospondylus was a fishlike ichthyosaur about 33 feet long. It breathed air, gave birth to live young, and lived 240 million to 210 million years ago. Its long, pointed snout held rows of small teeth for fish and shellfish.

6Liopleurodon had a mouth about three times larger than that of Tyrannosaurus rex. Its strong jaws could kill any animal in the sea. Openings at the top of its mouth let it tell where a smell came from. It lived from 160 million to 155 million years ago and could grow 49 feet long. Pliosaurs had short necks and strong jaws, while true plesiosaurs had long necks and small heads. Elasmosaurus also grew about 49 feet long, mostly in its neck and tail. Most of its length was neck and tail, with 76 vertebrae, while a human neck has 7. Its long neck let it sneak under a school of fish, and it had four diamond-shaped flippers.

7Ornithocheirus lived near coasts and lakes from 140 million to 70 million years ago. It may have been the largest pterosaur, with a wingspan up to 40 feet. Its body was about 11.5 feet long, but it probably weighed only about as much as you. It dipped its long beak and swallowed a fish whole. Colonies of these flyers built nests on cliff tops. Gastornis was a flightless terror bird about 7 feet tall. It lived in forests and swamps from 56 million to 41 million years ago. It may have weighed more than 1 ton, and scientists are not sure if it ate meat or plants.

8Phorusrhacos was a terror bird up to 10 feet tall with a short, sharp claw on each wing. It hunted in plains and woodlands from 27 million to 2.5 million years ago. It may have run 43 miles per hour after young saber-toothed cats and small horses. It may be related to seriema birds, which slam prey on the ground until it is dead. After giant reptiles died out, giant mammals began to fill the world. Some scientists think better mammal hunters later left terror birds with no food. Indricotherium was a rhino relative at least 15 feet tall and weighed 16 tons. From 30 million to 25 million years ago, it ate high leaves and stored fat and water for dry seasons.

9Gigantopithecus was a real giant ape that lived from about 8 million to 100,000 years ago. Some males stood 10 feet tall and weighed more than 1,000 pounds. Females were about half that size. It ate bamboo, fruit, seeds, and other plants in Asian rainforests. Homo erectus lived nearby and may have used so much bamboo that the ape died out. A woolly mammoth looked like a huge, hairy elephant with long, curved tusks. It stood almost 12 feet tall and used its tusks to clear snow while searching for plants. Early humans hunted mammoths and painted them, and mammoths died out when the ice age ended.

10Megatherium was a giant ground sloth of the last ice age. It lived from about 2 million to 8,000 years ago and was almost 20 feet long. It is related to the much smaller tree sloths of South America today. Fossil footprints show it could stand and walk upright, using its tail for balance. Hard, bony plates under its long fur helped protect it, as an armadillo's plates do. Blue whales, great white sharks, giant squids, and grizzly bears are giant animals today. Elephants, giraffes, ostriches, condors, and anacondas are large animals too. Many are threatened, so people should protect their habitats.

11This book names many prehistoric giants found as fossils. Invertebrates include Cameroceras, Meganeura, and Arthropleura. Fish and amphibians include Leedsichthys and Koolasuchus. Reptiles include Cymbospondylus, Liopleurodon, Elasmosaurus, and Ornithocheirus. Birds include Gastornis and Phorusrhacos. Mammals include Indricotherium, Gigantopithecus, Mammuthus, and Megatherium. Paleontologists study these fossils from many eras and periods.

65. Puffins

1A horned puffin tries to land on a rock in the Alaska Maritime National Wildlife Refuge. Puffins look funny and colorful, so people call them clowns of the sea. They have plump bodies, black and white feathers, and bright beaks. They stand upright and walk with a firm step. Their playful ways make these strong little birds hard to resist. If you see a puffin, you are not likely to forget it.

2Puffins spend most of their lives on the open ocean. They belong to the auk family, and all four species dive well. They use their wings like flippers and their feet to steer. They can dive 100 feet or 30 meters, stay under about half a minute, and search for fish. They fly well too and flap their wings up to 400 times a minute. From mid-spring through summer they nest on islands and cliffs in the North Atlantic and North Pacific. A large Atlantic colony is in the Labrador Sea near Canada, and at sea puffins ride waves in rafts. The Atlantic puffin is Fratercula arctica, Latin for little brother of the north.

3Atlantic puffins are the smallest and look the most plain, even in breeding feathers. Adults are 10 to 12.5 inches, or 25 to 32 centimeters, tall. They live on both sides of the North Atlantic, and 60 percent breed along Iceland. The beak tip is bright orange, with a blue-gray part and a yellow line. Orange legs and a white face, chest, and belly stand out against a black back and upper wings. Horned puffins average 15 inches, or 38 centimeters, and live in the North Pacific. They live mainly south of the Arctic Circle and have a white face and underside. Black lashes sit over each eye, a black line runs back on the head, and the beak base is yellow.

4Tufted puffins have the largest range of the puffin species. They live on both sides of the North Pacific, from Alaska south to Japan and central California. Adults average 15 inches, or 38 centimeters, and have a black chest and belly. In winter they are black with large red-orange beaks. In summer they grow a white face mask, an olive-yellow beak part, golden plumes, orange feet, and eye rings. Rhinoceros auklets live on the Pacific coast of North America and on the coast of Asia near Japan. Adults average 13.8 to 15 inches, or 35 to 38 centimeters, and the breeding bill has a short horn. They are mainly brown, with two white head stripes, and some call them cousins, not true puffins.

5Puffins usually return from the sea in late March or early April. They often live in colonies of several thousand and keep the same mate and nest each year. Each pair makes a burrow about 3 to 6 feet, or 1 to 2 meters, deep, and the female lays one egg. Tufted puffins, European Atlantic puffins, and rhinoceros auklets dig burrows in soft soil. Horned puffins and North American Atlantic puffins often nest in rock cracks on coastal cliffs. Parents take turns on the egg, and both feed the chick until it can fly in one to two months. A new chick is a puffling, and it leaves on its own when it is ready. They like sand eels, herring, and hake, and they can carry fifteen or more fish at a time.

6Humans have hunted puffins for meat, eggs, and feathers for centuries, and some still do. People take more food fish than can be replaced, and climate change warms seas and cuts cold-water fish. Some fish are too big for chicks or less nutritious, so food for puffins is limited. Nets, pollution, disturbed nests, and predators such as gulls, eagles, rats, and foxes also harm them. People work to help puffins, and healthy oceans help these birds thrive. Dr. Stephen Kress grew interested in nature in fourth grade when suburbs wiped out habitats near his home. In the early 1970s he visited Eastern Egg Rock off Maine, where Atlantic puffins had lived one hundred years earlier. He founded Project Puffin, sponsored by the National Audubon Society, and the island had 148 pairs by 2014.

7An Atlantic puffin stands outside its den on a coastal cliff in Iceland. Puffins stay out at sea for much of the year. They come to land only in the breeding season. You will mainly find them on remote cliffs and islands. Choose a place that allows wildlife viewing, and do not disturb nesting birds. A long hike may give only a far look at one or two puffins. A boat tour can bring you closer, and guides know good places and puffin habits. Bring binoculars and a camera, because these small clowns will amuse and fascinate you.

66. Ready for Rising Seas?

1Giant chunks of ice break from the Perito Moreno Glacier in Argentina. They fall into Lake Argentino. Amsterdam has 105 kilometers of canals. The city is accustomed to water. Scientists predict seas there will rise about one meter in the next century. People love the sea, so many great cities stand on coasts. In the next hundred years many coasts may see a 0.6 meter rise. For some places that rise means disaster. What can be done about the encroaching sea?

2Oceans have been rising for more than one hundred years. The rate has increased in recent decades. Scientists track tides and read satellite data. Tide stations show local change. Satellites measure the average height of the whole ocean. Two main factors cause the rise. Warm water expands and takes up more space. Melting land ice is now the main cause.

3Thermal expansion led sea level rise for more than a century. In recent years ice loss has caused twice as much rise. Since 2003 melt from Greenland and Antarctica has caused nearly 80 percent of the rise. If Greenland's ice all melted, seas would rise about 6.7 meters. If Antarctica's ice all melted, seas would rise 61 meters. Neither event will happen overnight. Greenland's ice sheet is nearly the size of Mexico. Antarctica's sheet is larger than the United States and Mexico combined.

4China is the world's leading carbon polluter. If emissions stay high, 145 million people there face coastal flood risk. Shanghai's maps show two futures based on fossil fuel use. Over 70 years the grounding line of Pine Island Glacier retreated about 48 kilometers. The grounding line is the point where the glacier starts to float. In 2015 an iceberg of 583 square kilometers broke off that glacier. In July 2017 an ice sheet ten times larger than that iceberg snapped off West Antarctica.

5Since the Industrial Revolution of 1760 to 1840, people have burned huge amounts of coal and oil. They have also cut down vast tropical forests. These acts raised carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. The gases trapped heat like a blanket around Earth. Warm water then thinned the West Antarctic Ice Sheet. Most glaciers there melted and retreated. If all emissions stopped tomorrow, seas would still rise 0.36 to 0.79 meters by 2100. Oceans and ice would keep adjusting to gases already in the air.

6Not every place has a rising sea. In Juneau, Alaska, land has risen as much as 3 meters in two hundred years. It may rise another 0.9 meters by 2100 as glacier ice melts away. From 1880 to 2010 global seas rose about 20 centimeters on average. The highest future scenario is a rise of about 200 centimeters. Rising seas will erode shores and put some places underwater for good. Eight of the world's ten largest cities sit near a coast. Roads, bridges, subways, homes, and sewage plants will be at risk.

7Cape Hatteras Lighthouse is the tallest lighthouse in the United States. When finished in 1870, it was the world's tallest brick building. It stood 457 meters from the ocean. Seas on the Outer Banks rose two to three times the global average. By 1970 the lighthouse was only 37 meters from the water. In 1999 the National Park Service moved it 488 meters inland. It moved on hydraulic jacks and steel beams at 1.5 meters a minute. The move took twenty-three days and left the lighthouse without a crack.

8New Orleans lies near the Gulf of Mexico, between the Mississippi River and Lake Pontchartrain. The city sits about 0.6 meters below sea level and has always faced storms. In 2005 Hurricane Katrina's surge broke levees and flooded 80 percent of the city. The levees were rebuilt and raised, with gravel and gates. Experts warn these barriers can only do so much as seas rise. The city may create artificial wetlands, but they need space and time. Many houses stand on stilts, and floatable homes could rise 3.7 meters on poles. The city is also building better plans to get people to safety fast.

9From 1970 to 2003, Kushiro had the world's highest rate of sea level rise. The water rose more than 0.8 centimeters per year. That rate means more than 0.9 meters in one hundred years. The same rise could erase more than 90 percent of Japan's sandy beaches. Thirty million people within 9.7 kilometers of the sea would be at risk. Tokyo has more than thirty-seven million people and is building huge levees. Along the Arakawa River, officials pay people to relocate for up to four years. New levees slope gently so floodwater flows away instead of breaking them.

10Fiji is a small island nation east of Australia in the South Pacific Ocean. Coastal cities there could see more than 0.6 meters of rise this century. That rise will be hard on tourism, which the economy depends on. Too many people near the sea have exposed the coast to erosion. Clearing mangrove forests has hurt catchments that collect and drain water. Suva is strengthening laws to protect mangrove forests and coral reefs. Officials also want new mangroves and artificial reefs along the coast. Some small coasts may be evacuated, though retreat can be costly and hard.

11Venice was built on 117 islands in a lagoon beside the Adriatic Sea. Its buildings sit on submerged wood with waterproof rock on top. Extreme tides called acqua alta flood the city more often as seas rise. They combine a very high tide, low air pressure, and a scirocco wind. That wind pushes water up the Adriatic Sea into the lagoon. The city is putting seventy-eight mobile gates on concrete foundations. When a high tide looms, the gates can rise and seal off the lagoon. They should protect Venice from tides almost 3 meters high for a century.

12Most studies look at global warming impacts by the year 2100. Yet sea level rise will last twice as long as human history. The best defense is to cut gases that warm the air, especially carbon dioxide. This is hard because people use more energy as the population grows. Failed laws make emission cuts even harder to achieve. If we burn only another 5 percent of fossil fuel, warming could stay under 2 degrees Celsius. Experts say more than that is dangerous for humans and most living things. People inland must help avert this crisis, because a lot is at stake.

67. Rights Set Down Beside the Highest Law

1Lorena, the mother of Mary Beth Tinker, appears with her and with Paul, the younger brother. Mary Beth is reacting to court news from 1969. A black armband had gotten her suspended at junior high. The pages after this one take up the country's highest law. They tell how a written list of rights was joined to that law. They spell out what the list guards. Later changes come after that, along with people who still had to struggle. A last look and a word list close the book. During 1965, five students in Iowa's city of Des Moines wore black armbands inside school. Punishment came from the school district. The bands were a protest, and the protest stayed peaceful. The target was the Vietnam War, fought from 1955 until 1975. Leaders of the district ordered the bands taken off. The students would not obey. Suspension from school followed. Three of them, together with their parents, sued the district. America's highest court, the United States Supreme Court, heard that lawsuit in 1969.

2Judges on the U.S. Supreme Court said the armbands could stay. No disturbance had come from the students. Other students' rights had not been blocked. An amendment inside the U.S. Constitution was the basis of the ruling. Judges treated the black bands as speech. Protection for that speech sits in the First Amendment. That amendment is one piece of the Bill of Rights. The Bill of Rights names the opening ten amendments. Citizen liberties are what those amendments guard. A large building for the United States Supreme Court stands in Washington, D.C. The Bill of Rights belongs inside the U.S. Constitution. When the United States formed, that Constitution became its earliest law and its highest one. Government work takes its framework from it. Any further law has to follow the principles written there. Earlier, the land was not yet one country. Great Britain had planted thirteen colonies on ground seized by force, ground Native peoples had held. Rule came from the British Parliament and from King George III. Colonists in America had nobody speaking for them in Parliament. A widespread feeling grew that their rights were ignored. Revolution began among the colonists in 1775. Independence from Great Britain was declared in 1776, one year later, and the United States was established. Britain refused to accept those steps. Fighting lasted seven further years and stopped at last in 1783. Visitors in the city of Washington, D.C., can see the original U.S. Constitution.

3Men who helped set up the United States of America are known as the Founders. Their communities treated them as respected leaders. Wealth was common among them. So was a strong education. Law or politics was the background of most. While the war with Great Britain went on, these men built a confederation of states. Power at the center of that confederation was weak. A congress was created to watch over ordinary government business. The congress had a president. Kingly power was something the Founders refused to hand their leaders. Most powers went to the states instead. Once the war was over, the system looked unsuccessful. Change was the decision. Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, was the meeting place in 1787. A constitution was the writing job. Rules and guidelines for a fresh system of government were the aim. Debate over the Constitution happened at Independence Hall in that same Pennsylvania city. More strength for the central government was wanted. People call that central government the federal government. The Founders still refused to allow enough strength to strip citizens of rights and freedoms. Their goal was a democracy. In that form of government, citizens hold power. Choosing leaders is their right, and elections are the method. Native nations supplied ideas the Founders borrowed. The strongest inspiration was the Haudenosaunee Confederacy. Several Native nations belonged to it. Together they ran a government that covered many states. Each nation also kept a government of its own. September 1787 was the finish of the new constitution. By the middle of 1788, approval had come from every state except two. The Constitution was now the law of the land. Election made George Washington the earliest president. Opening words of the U.S. Constitution are We the People. Protection still did not cover every person in the original document. Enslaved people were left out of the rights it outlined. Native peoples were left out. Most women of that time were left out too. Later amendments, and later laws, widened those rights to reach these groups.

4Creation of the Constitution left women out. Many women still helped build the new nation. Essays by women took up politics. Other essays took up gender equality. Still others took up abolition. Political issues were discussed in gatherings the women hosted. Some women sat in on sessions of Congress. Political rallies included them. Abigail Adams stands among the most influential of these women. She was married to the Founder John Adams and served as his close advisor. One letter to her husband carried a famous request. Her request was that he remember the ladies while the new constitution was being written. North Carolina voted against the Constitution. Rhode Island did too. Approval was refused. Joining the new government was refused too, until rights were set down in a bill. Federalists, some of the Founders, warned that such a list could be dangerous. A written set of rights, they said, might teach people a false lesson. Anything missing from the list might look unprotected. James Madison, a leading Founder, shared that view. Thomas Jefferson, another important Founder, took the opposite side. A bill of rights, he said, was necessary. Jefferson and other Antifederalists wanted certain rights guaranteed. No government should be able to remove them. Both Madison and Jefferson came from Virginia. That state's constitution already held a Declaration of Rights. Bills of rights appeared in several state constitutions. Jefferson wanted citizen rights written out inside the U.S. Constitution. Agreement from Madison came at last. He began building a bill of rights. One model was the Declaration of Rights from Virginia. Another, dated 1215, was the Magna Carta. The English Bill of Rights, dated 1689, was a third model. A picture places James Madison above Thomas Jefferson. Both helped make the Bill of Rights. Madison read bills of rights from other states. Delegates offered suggestions, and he listened. His proposal to Congress was twenty amendments. Congress reduced the count to twelve. States received those amendments in 1789. North Carolina was now willing to ratify. Rhode Island was willing too. By the close of 1791, ten of the twelve had yes votes from three out of every four states, the share the rules demanded. Those ten became the Bill of Rights.

5Limiting a government's powers with a bill of rights did not begin in the United States. England's version passed in 1689. More than 100 years separated that law from the American one. Written documents that guard civil and political rights now exist in most democracies around the world. A written constitution with a bill of rights exists in Canada. New Zealand has one. South Africa has one. Germany has one, and so do India and Japan. Forty-seven nations in Europe and nearby have taken up a pact named European Convention on Human Rights. Five important rights of a person sit in the First Amendment. Speech is one of them. Sharing ideas in public cannot be answered with jail. Criticism of the government does not remove that shield. Citizens may also petition. They may ask for changes to laws they reject. Peaceful gatherings for protest are allowed as well. During the civil rights movement, large peaceful protests were among the strongest tools. In 2017, members of the Lakota nation protested in North Dakota. An oil pipeline was being built through lands they hold sacred. The press is another First Amendment protection. News may be shared by journalists. Opinions may be shared too. During the 1700s, the public got information only from newspapers and other printed materials. Radio now falls under press freedom as well. Television does too. So does the Internet. Religion is a further First Amendment right. One official religion is the pattern in many countries. It is not the pattern here. Special preference for one faith over another is blocked. Americans may follow any religion. They may follow none.

6Owning weapons is a citizen right under the Second Amendment. Using weapons is part of that right too. Some readers think the amendment was aimed only at militia groups. The National Guard is an example of such a group. Other readers think every U.S. citizen received the right to own weapons and to use them. British soldiers, before the Revolutionary War, could take over private homes. The Third Amendment stops officials from making citizens shelter soldiers in their homes. Under the Fourth Amendment, a search needs a solid reason. An arrest also needs a solid reason to think a crime was committed. A judge must be asked for a warrant. Without it, police cannot search someone's property. They cannot take that property either. People accused of crimes are covered by four amendments: the Fifth, then the Sixth, then the Seventh, and also the Eighth. The Fifth says nobody can be pushed into a criminal trial without good reason. The reason must support a belief that guilt is possible. A criminal offense means a crime against the public or against a state. Court must prove the charge before any punishment. The Sixth requires a trial as soon as possible. The trial has to be public. A jury must be present. A lawyer is a defendant's right. Knowing the accuser is a right as well. The Seventh deals with a civil case. A jury trial is a right in that setting too. The Eighth rejects punishments that are cruel and unusual. Fines that climb too high are rejected too. In the era of that amendment, burning with red-hot irons was a punishment some criminals faced. Others were locked in wooden stocks where the public could see them. Those punishments are forbidden now. A painting made in 1805 shows a crowd in Great Britain. People shout insults at men standing in wooden stocks. The stocks were the punishment for their crimes.

7Rights that the earlier amendments never named are covered by the last two parts of the Bill of Rights. The Ninth says that listing some rights does not cancel others. Citizens may hold further rights. The Tenth says government holds only powers the Constitution gives it. Any power left unlisted is held by the states, or else by the citizens. Dates that matter for the U.S. Constitution include these. Fighting in the American Revolutionary War starts in 1775. The Declaration of Independence wins approval from the Continental Congress in 1776. That war ends in 1781. Writing of the U.S. Constitution happens in 1787. Approval comes in 1788. The Bill of Rights, meaning those opening ten amendments, is added in 1791. Slavery is abolished by the 13th Amendment in 1865. The 14th Amendment, in 1868, grants citizenship rights to everyone born in the United States. Naturalized people are included. The 15th Amendment, in 1870, gives every male citizen the vote. Color does not block it. Race does not block it. Women gain the vote through the 19th Amendment in 1920. The voting age drops to 18 under the 26th Amendment in 1971. More amendments arrived after 1791, the year those ten amendments were attached. A new amendment is hard to pass. Only Congress may propose one. A Constitutional Convention may propose one too, if two-thirds of all state governments call for it. After a proposal, three-fourths of all state governments must vote yes. Ratified is the word for an amendment that becomes law. Twenty-seven amendments stand in the Constitution today. After the Bill of Rights, two of the most important are the Thirteenth and the Fourteenth. They passed once the Civil War was over. That war ran from 1861 to 1865. Slavery inside the United States was made illegal by the Thirteenth Amendment. The picture is an illustration of a celebration. People who had lived in slavery mark the passage of that change.

8Citizenship in the U.S. reached formerly enslaved people through the Fourteenth Amendment. Children born to immigrant parents received it too. Equal protection of the laws was promised to every U.S. citizen. Race was not allowed to change that promise. Racial segregation of public schools in the U.S. ended largely because of this amendment. During the 1940s, Oliver Brown tried to place his daughter in a school close to home. He was a Black man in Topeka, Kansas. White students were the ones that nearby school served. The school said no. A school for Black students was the only option, and it sat farther from her home. Brown carried the dispute into court. By 1954 the dispute had reached the Supreme Court. Nine judges, the full bench, said public-school segregation by race broke the Fourteenth Amendment. Schools serving white children and schools serving Black children were not equal. Historians treat the ruling as one of the Court's most important. Suffragists march because they want women to gain the vote. Inside a democracy, voting ranks among a citizen's most important rights. Before the Constitution, land ownership was required. White men made up most of the owners. All white men received the vote in 1856. Most Black men still lacked a legal vote until the Fifteenth Amendment in 1870. Women received the vote from the Nineteenth Amendment. Their organizing and their fight lasted more than seventy years. Passage came in 1920.

9Americans are now supposed to have their rights guaranteed by the Bill of Rights and by later amendments. Fights for those rights still happen often. Alondra Jones, in 2000, was an honor student living in California. Her high school sat in a low-income area. Black students and Latino students made up most of the enrollment. Textbooks were too few. Computers were absent. Upkeep of the buildings was poor. Rats infested them. Another high school showed her a sharp contrast. Books were there. Computers were there. Buildings were clean and safe. She understood that her own school got far less money than other schools in the state. A 2006 photo shows Alondra Jones speaking at an ACLU conference. Almost one hundred other students joined her lawsuit. A group known as the American Civil Liberties Union did the filing. That nonprofit legal group defends rights held by American citizens. Judges in the case said California had failed to give students equal protection. The Fourteenth Amendment demands that protection. A good education, the court said, was every student's right. Socioeconomic status could not erase it. Samantha Elauf was seventeen in 2008 when she asked a clothing store in Oklahoma for a job. A hijab was the reason for refusal. Many Muslim women wear that head covering. Store leaders said it broke the dress code for employees. A federal body, the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, took the store to court on her behalf. The lawsuit climbed to the Supreme Court. A 2015 ruling favored Samantha. Judges said the store had discriminated against her on account of her religion. She stands with her mother before the Supreme Court building. Across history, different groups have kept struggling for rights. Peaceful protest has been one of their methods.

10Rights held by single persons have a United States story that opens with the Constitution. Perfection was not part of that document. When it was written, protection left out most people in the country. Later generations fought to gain what the Constitution promised citizens. They fought to keep those rights as well. Alondra Jones belongs in that line of people. Samantha Elauf does too. More than two hundred years have passed since people penned the Bill of Rights. Scores of later amendments, plus many laws, have widened the shield so every citizen is covered. Advocates still push for equality. They still push for protection under the law. Call a change, or an added piece, an amendment when it alters a document or a law. Someone who is excluded has been kept outside a group. The Bill of Rights names the opening ten amendments of the United States Constitution, and those amendments guarantee chosen rights. Federalists backed ratification of that Constitution. The same label also names the Federalist Party. A confederation joins states, provinces, or groups under one organization, while central authority stays limited. A petition is a formal request in writing, or a formal appeal, sent to authority. Official approval is what ratify means. Written rules and principles that United States laws rest on are the Constitution. Speaking or acting for another person, or for a group, is representation. Finding fault, or judging with disapproval, is criticizing. A warrant is an order in writing that allows an arrest or a search. Equality is the condition in which the same rights belong to everyone.

68. Shackleton's Ship in the Ice

1Beside the stuck ship, the crew of Endurance pose together for a photograph. Six sections shape this account. They cover the trap, the lost south, waiting on the ice, the run to Elephant Island, the deadliest water, the safe return, and a word list. Ice closed on Endurance before anyone in the crew could step onto the Antarctic mainland. Caught The ship was trapped. January 1915 found Endurance inside the Antarctic Circle, locked in pack ice. The crew felt sure the ice would break, as it had for earlier ships, and let them sail. They trusted Sir Ernest Shackleton, a veteran explorer of the Antarctic, to lead them out. Ice kept closing. The strong wooden hull stayed fast. Weeks became months. Shackleton and the men waited in hope the ice would set them free. That release never arrived. A daunting task remained. They sat in the most isolated region on Earth. Home did not know their fate or their position. Satellites did not exist, and neither did radios that could reach far. No call for help was possible. Survival meant saving themselves.

2Lost in the far south Sir Ernest Shackleton conceived the Imperial Trans-Antarctic Expedition. He and a team would land on the Antarctic coast, travel by dogsled, and try a crossing of the continent that no party had completed. Their mission sat in Britain's long custom of exploration, a custom that had mapped and recorded much of the globe. Antarctica was still among the least known places. Harsh conditions demanded huge supplies, careful plans, and real courage. Shackleton had that courage, and the Antarctic was not new to him. Two earlier expeditions there had made his name. He led in a way that was tough and fair. He never ordered a job he was unwilling to do with his own hands, and the men respected him for it. Bold years at the poles By the late eighteen hundreds, explorers from the West had walked nearly every land on Earth. Polar regions still hid mysteries that drew daring travelers. Teams that included Ernest Shackleton tried for the South Pole twice, in 1902 and again in 1909. Both times they were turned back. In 1911 the Norwegian Roald Amundsen and his team were first to stand at the globe's southernmost point. Only weeks later, Britain's Robert Falcon Scott reached that same point. On the way back, Scott died on the return, and so did the four men with him, from hunger and from cold. A photograph shows the Trans-Antarctic crew aboard Endurance. Shackleton picked that ship himself, impressed by a stout hull built to meet heavy ice and push through it. The crew he gathered was hardy and experienced. Captain Frank Worsley would prove a superb navigator under the worst conditions. Frank Wild, a close friend, was second-in-command. The rest were skilled and resourceful, qualities Antarctica's surprises required. Endurance left Great Britain in August 1914. On December 5, 1914, four months later, it cleared the final harbor. That harbor was South Georgia Island, lying in southern seas of the Atlantic. Pack ice, which ringed much of the continent, met the ship only two days out. Engines and a strong prow drove it forward through the floes.

3January 18, 1915, brought ice that shut the ship in completely. About 160 kilometers, or 100 miles, still lay between them and the planned landing. The continent might as well have been the Moon. From that spot, no march could reach it. Odd storm patterns kept the ice locked even in the season when it should have split. Mile after mile of extra ice piled up between the men and any escape. By February they knew the only course was to wait for a change. The twenty-eight men aboard stayed comfortable and in good spirits. The ship was strong, and the hull was thick. They worked, read, played records on a phonograph, and staged talent shows in the warm interior. Food and other stores would last many months. Hope rested on November, the usual month for the ice to break. A picture shows the crew playing soccer on the ice, with the trapped Endurance looming behind them. Another shows Frank Wild looking over the wreck of Endurance. November never came for the ship. Pressure ice closed in during September. That ice is made of huge blocks driven by wind, by currents, and by storms. It squeezed the ship as a nutcracker squeezes a shell. Aboard, the men despaired as the ship slowly tipped. The hull bent, then cracked, then split. Sounds from the wood reminded them of a dying animal's moans and wails. Late October brought the moment they could not avoid. Shackleton ordered the ship abandoned. Useful supplies were salvaged. Each man could take one set of clothes, plus a parka. He might also take boots in two pairs, and mittens in two pairs, against cold that dropped below zero and could kill.

4Three lifeboats were moved from the ship onto ice that seemed safer. Those boats were the only hope of getting home, but the trip would require further provisions. A heavy duty sat on Shackleton, who felt a heavy duty to save the men. He meant to walk them across the ice to an emergency cache kept for shipwrecked sailors. November 1 was the start. They did not get far. Ice ridges two stories high crisscrossed the ground. The march was exhausting, then dangerous, then impossible. After only 3 kilometers, or 2 miles, Shackleton called it off. Camp went up on the largest, steadiest ice floe they could reach. The wreck's skeleton was still visible in the distance. November 21 let them see Endurance vanish under the ice. More supplies were fetched from the first camp. Another march, ordered in late December, again gained little ground. A new large floe became the campsite. They named it Patience Camp. The floating pack would have to carry them to water where the boats could launch. From there they would sail for any land they could find. A picture shows the camp on the floe after supplies left the doomed ship. Waiting on the ice Patience Camp was harsh and offered no mercy. Extreme cold and frequent storms mixed with gear and clothing that stayed soggy. Most men slept packed into five tents. Baths were impossible, and so were clean clothes. They knew how to bear hardship all the same. Cards passed the time, and so did the few books they shared. A sailor who had made a simple banjo led songs. Talk returned again and again to food. Far from any town, they still rarely went hungry. Two meals a day were the rule, nearly always a high-calorie stew they called hoosh. Crushed biscuits and water went into it, along with pemmican, a mix of dried meat and fat, and sometimes fresh seal or blubber.

5Hunting parties added sea lions and penguins to the stores with good luck. Seal blubber also burned well as cooking fuel. Under them, the ice drifted wherever the ocean currents shoved it. Captain Worsley took the position often with a sextant, a tool that reads the Sun or the stars and turns that reading into a location. Patience Camp crept toward the pack's edge, where a launch might be possible. In March 1916 the men felt the ice rise and fall underfoot. Worsley's figures said they had drifted more than 3,200 kilometers, or 2,000 miles, since the trap closed on Endurance. Ice grew fragile. Boats were readied for a sudden launch. On April 9 the opening they had waited for appeared, and the boats went in. Some men rowed. Others at the bow shoved ice blocks aside. They pushed for open water, then turned the boats toward Elephant Island. Nobody lived there, and help was far, but solid land raised the chance of living. Toward Elephant Island. Muscle, mind, and will were all Shackleton's men had against the nightmare of Antarctic seas in storm. The boats had no engines.
