Oars, arranged as two sets, and sails of small size were the only propulsion. On nights both long and dark, each of the three crews fought to keep one another in sight among monstrous waves. What followed mixed agony with tenacity. Hurricane-force wind, slashing sleet, and rain battered the boats. Freezing water poured across the gunwales. Ice arrived with frost and coated every surface and every person. Seasickness and frostbite hit the crews. After a turn at the oars, men huddled for warmth. Sleep was nearly impossible.

6Worsley's navigation in those conditions seemed miraculous. On day seven, Elephant Island's high peaks rose dead ahead. The crew, barely asleep across those seven days, finally camped on a narrow rocky beach. April 16, 1916, was a first return to land after 497 days that Endurance's men stood on land. It was still nowhere they wanted to stay. No ship had a reason to pass close enough to see them. Someone had to go for help. A little more than a week later, Shackleton, Worsley, and four others left once more, using the James Caird from among the lifeboats. Frank Wild stayed in charge of the twenty-two who remained. Every hope rode on that dash. Nobody dared picture failure. Portraits show Ernest Shackleton, Frank Wild, and Frank Worsley. The deadliest water The James Caird was altered for the trip. Sides were raised, and a canvas deck was stretched overhead against wild water. Supplies went into the bottom, and so did hundreds of pounds of rocks, weight that would hold the craft level when the weather grew rough. South Georgia Island was the aim, the same island they had left close to eighteen months before. Reaching it meant 1,287 kilometers, or 800 miles, of the world's most treacherous sea. A picture shows Shackleton, Worsley, and four others launching the James Caird toward that island.

7The boat was 6.7 meters long, or 22 feet, and its crew of six fought for every mile. Waves were huge. Weather struck from every side. Usually only the person on the rudder, Shackleton or Worsley, kept a head above the deck in order to watch the sea. Down below, the rest huddled below, soaked by waves that washed in without pause. Teams traded turns on the sails and on a hand pump that kept the boat from flooding. Off-duty men tried to snatch sleep near the prow. More than once, sleet and freezing rain sheeted the boat in ice and added dangerous weight. Men crawled onto the deck at the risk of their lives and chipped the ice away. The boat kept plowing, day and night. One night Shackleton held the rudder and glanced back. A white line hung in the dark above him. He first thought the clouds had broken. Then the line climbed, and terror hit him. What rose was a rogue wave, gigantic, showing only its crest at first. Shackleton shouted for the men to hold on. The wave struck like a giant's fist and flung the boat ahead. In a moment the hull was half full of water. They bailed with anything their hands could find. Those desperate efforts saved them. Seventeen brutal days ended when South Georgia Island appeared at last. That view was a sight they welcomed. Worsley had worked another piece of navigational magic, finding a speck of land in an endless ocean. The six men, past exhaustion, stumbled ashore. The shore they had reached was the island's western coast. The whaling station lay on the other side. Sailing around was judged too dangerous, so someone would have to walk 35 kilometers, or 22 miles. Saying it was easier than doing it. Glacier-capped peaks split the island, and nobody had climbed them. After days of rest, three men started up: Shackleton, Worsley, and Tom Crean. Slopes led them in among the glaciers. Walls made of rock blocked the way and forced them to turn back. Ice fields were so steep that steps had to be chopped. They slogged upward to the ridge that divides the island. Just over that ridge, Shackleton saw a new danger closing in. They stood high on a slope. Night began to fall. Around them the temperature was dropping fast.

8A lower elevation was the only way to avoid freezing, and they needed it quickly. Debate was brief. The three sat on the snow, linked arms and legs, and shoved off. They slid down on their backs. In less than two minutes, they dropped more than 305 meters, or 1,000 feet. Laughter burst out as they stopped. Then they stood and walked on. The next afternoon, May 20, 1916, three filthy, bearded men in torn clothes walked into South Georgia's whaling station and were taken to the manager. The hike had run thirty-six hours without a break. A picture shows the twenty-two on Elephant Island waving at rescuers. Their marooning there lasted over four months. All safe. Back on Elephant Island, the twenty-two stayed careful in their hope. The soonest rescue they expected was late May 1916, and only if Shackleton had succeeded. May passed, then June, then July. As August's days ticked away, they feared the worst. Each day they still climbed to a lookout and scanned the sea, then slouched down disappointed. On August 30, sharp eyes caught smoke standing like a pillar where the sky met the sea. A signal fire was lit in a hurry. Yelcho, sailing under Chile's flag, came steaming into sight. A small boat dropped over the side. In its prow the men soon knew a familiar shape. Shackleton called out, asking how they were. Some wept in relief. Three earlier tries to reach them had failed, turned back by dangerous ice or by mechanical trouble. He had refused to quit. This time he had returned to Elephant Island.

9The party that had left for Antarctica, upward of two years earlier, numbered twenty-eight men. All twenty-eight were going home. The odds had included a wrecked ship, months below zero on treacherous ice, and deadly seas crossed in small boats. Every man who left on Endurance lived. The story remains one of the greatest survivals ever lived or told. A map traces the path from the trap to the rescue, bending past South Georgia and the Antarctic Circle. The dated steps are these. Endurance sticks fast on January 18, 1915. In October and November 1915 the ship is crushed and sinks. Patience Camp is founded in December 1915. Lifeboats leave for Elephant Island on April 9, 1916. Arrival there is April 16, 1916. The James Caird leaves for South Georgia Island on April 24, 1916. From May 10 to May 20, 1916, the party reaches that island and crosses it for help. The Yelcho lifts the stranded crew on August 30, 1916. The map also marks Elephant Island, the Weddell Sea, and Antarctica, with scales of 0, 200, and 400 miles, and of 0, 400, and 800 kilometers. Words from the book. A cache is a place where supplies or valuables are stored or hidden. An expedition is a journey made for a set purpose, or the people who make it. Isolated, an adjective, means far apart from people and apart from objects. To liberate, a verb, means to set free. Pack ice is a broad sheet of sea ice made when smaller pieces crush together and freeze. Propulsion is the act or the force of pushing forward. Provisions are supplies, especially those carried on a journey. A prow is the bow, the forward tip of a vessel. To have salvaged, a verb, means saved property from harm or ruin. Tenacity is stubborn persistence. Treacherous, an adjective, means dangerous. Uninhabited, an adjective, means no people live there.

69. Ships Across the Panama Isthmus

1On the canal's eastern side, ships move through the Gatun locks. What became a modern marvel started as a dream that seemed beyond reach. August 15, 1914, turned the dream into a fact. Narrow locks let the cargo ship Ancon pass. High mountains rose around the route. West was the direction, through a canal that had opened only just then. Triumph was the feeling for a great many people that day. Journeys that once filled months could finish in mere days. Cleverness of human planners was one cause. Technology from America was another. Labor from thousands of workers was another. Length of the canal was fifty miles. The world had not witnessed an engineering job of this scale. Earth was gouged from the isthmus for ten years. Obstacles without number had to be pushed back. The new water path would serve trade. It would serve military ships. It would serve pleasure traffic on the sea. Two oceans, the Atlantic and the Pacific, would be joined.

2A map of the shortcut shows the prize. New York and San Francisco lie on far sides of the United States. The drawing also marks the Atlantic Ocean, the Caribbean Sea, the canal itself, the equator, South America, and the Pacific Ocean. Using the canal, the trip is 5,300 miles, or 8,370 km. Going around South America, the trip is 13,000 miles, or 20,900 km. World trade grew because the canal opened. Power in the world grew for the United States as well. A century and more has passed, and thousands of ships still make the crossing. Some are yachts. Some are aircraft carriers. One great ocean is tied to the other. The wish to join those oceans is older than the twentieth century. Spanish explorers of early times were first to imagine the waterway. Skill to build it was not theirs in the 1700s. Separate plans were drawn in the early 1800s by Britain and by France. Neither government carried a plan forward. Public imagination locked onto a cross-isthmus canal in 1848. That was the year gold showed up in a California streambed at Sutter's Mill. Fortune hunters left the East and hurried west. Rail lines did not yet cross the continent. Stagecoach routes did not either. The nation was young. West of the Mississippi, much of the land was still wild. Mountains, plains, and deserts made the land journey long and full of danger. The sea looked somewhat safer, so many travelers chose it. Even so, sailing from New York all the way to San Francisco took far longer than the walk across land. Prospectors who sailed had two choices ahead of them.

3Panama could be the first stop. Travelers would cross the isthmus on land, then board another ship for California. Or one ship could make the whole voyage and pass Cape Horn, the south tip of South America. Wind and rough water made that longer route more dangerous. About seven days were needed to get across the isthmus. The week was neither comfortable nor pleasant. Canoes dug from logs carried people on the Chagres River. Mules carried them next, along an old trail the Spanish had used. A railroad, Americans of the mid-1800s decided, would make the crossing easier. Building started in 1850. Regular trains were running by 1855. The line measured 47 miles, or 75.6 km, and it tied the Atlantic shore of the isthmus to the Pacific shore. Travel grew faster and easier. A canal still seemed, to many, the better crossing. Success had already come to Ferdinand de Lesseps, a Frenchman, on Egypt's Suez Canal. That canal ran 102 miles, or 164 km. Someone with his record looked right for a shorter cut across Panama. Labels on a map include the Caribbean Sea and Panama City. They include the canal and the Gulf of Panama. They include Costa Rica and Colombia. They include the Pacific Ocean. The country is a curved ribbon. It ties Central America to South America. Nowhere else is the land between the two oceans so narrow. Rain comes often. The air is hot and humid. Jungles are thick. Plants and animals are many. A French company formed in 1879 to dig the canal. De Lesseps, experienced, was placed in charge. Ten years, he believed, would be enough. Suez had taken twice that long. France first needed Colombia's treaty. Colombia owned the isthmus at the time.

4Workers in great numbers, plus heavy machines, were moved to the isthmus by de Lesseps and by his assistant, Philippe Bunau-Varilla. Digging began. Management came easily to de Lesseps because he was enthusiastic. Engineering did not. Egypt's flat sand was nothing like Panama's mountain jungle, and he missed that gap. Progress stayed slow. Only small pieces of jungle were cut at a time. Rain fell in steady sheets. Heat stifled the crews. Week followed week. Mudslides took many lives. Accidents took more. Mosquitoes spread tropical disease and took still more. Little had been gained after seven years. Bankruptcy ended the French effort. The man who had beaten the desert left Panama without honor. Investment had passed 287 million dollars, a sum above 7 billion dollars in today's money. A muddy ruin was nearly all that remained. Lives lost numbered over twenty thousand. Ten more years passed with the work stopped. Other countries had seen the French pain and did not want the task. Death and disease made the region look like a miserable swamp to many nations. Opportunity was what the United States saw. Dates mark the American chapter. November 18, 1903, brought a treaty between the United States and the new Republic of Panama, so building could start. June 28, 1904, brought the first workers from America. November 12, 1904, brought the first steam shovel. November 21, 1904, brought the first written case of yellow fever in the workforce. July 26, 1905, brought John Stevens to lead the job. August 15, 1914, brought the official opening. January 1, 2000, brought control to Panama. A wider role for America in the world was beginning as the century began. Office came to President Theodore Roosevelt in 1901. He saw a Central American canal as America's road forward. Businesses in the east could reach fresh markets in Asia. Commerce would gain a highway. Naval fighting would gain a strategic tool.

5In 1906, President Theodore Roosevelt of the United States sat in a large steam shovel to test the machine. The wish to build was firm. Fresh barriers rose, and Colombia was the largest. Nicaragua, farther north, had been the first American site. Bunau-Varilla, who had served with de Lesseps, argued against that site. Leaders agreed to restart on the ground the French had chosen. Colombia still held Panama. A treaty with Colombia was signed, then rejected by that country's congress as unfair. Roosevelt would not take the no. He gave help to Panamanian revolutionaries. Their target was the government that had turned him down. A coup on November 3, 1903, let rebels seize the region. The fight was over by sunset. Formal recognition of independence from Colombia came from the United States three days afterward. Workers by the thousand poured into the new country. New machines for digging came with them. The cut they were sent to make ran almost 50 miles, or 80.5 km. It began at Colón. It ended at Panama City, beside the Pacific. Malaria and yellow fever struck the Americans as they had struck the French. Treatment for those illnesses, or for other mosquito-carried illnesses, had reached more than 85 percent of the workers by 1906. Bodies suffered. Minds suffered. An army doctor, William Gorgas, was asked by Roosevelt for a plan. Eggs of mosquitoes are laid in water. Panamanian teams walked the streets and emptied barrels that held standing water. Homes were sprayed with insecticides by fumigators. Bed netting was required so sleeping workers would not be bitten.

6Results followed Gorgas's plan. Yellow fever cases stood at only twenty-seven by August 1906. By November, new cases that people contracted had fallen to a single patient. Gorgas would not see another yellow fever victim. Malaria fought harder. Gains still came. Early 1910 found the malaria death rate under 1 percent. Roosevelt's order was to make the dirt fly. An experienced engineer, John Wallace, led the start of building in 1904. The order was hard to follow. Mud, thick and sticky, was what the steam shovels lifted, not dry soil. Fresh mud slid into a trench almost as soon as a load left it. Most of the American workforce had quit Panama by June 1905. The labor felt endless. A 1913 picture shows many large machines, powered by steam, cutting the central mountains. Danger of failure hung over the job. Wallace quit. John Stevens took his place. The new engineer pushed hard. Seventeen thousand workers were worried and low in spirit. They wanted direction. Stevens studied the mess before he acted. Hauling spoil away at once mattered more than the size of any shovel, so he halted the digging. Roads went in. Sections of the old Panama Railway were repaired and renewed. He also tended to the people. Churches rose. Hospitals rose. Mess halls and schools rose. Spirit improved. Families of skilled workers from the United States got houses without paying rent. Weekends brought dances and band concerts. The building plan itself changed. Sea level had been the old target for the cut. Mountains stood in that path, and cutting through them would have added years.

7Another barrier was the Chagres River, running high beside the mountains. Locks in a series were Stevens's answer. Each one would stretch past the length of three football fields. Ships would climb the mountains by those locks. A dam on the Chagres would form a huge lake. Water would move from the locks into the lake and back out again. Think of the locks as stairs. A ship would climb, cross the lake on top, and descend. Crews dug from both ends of a lock and aimed to meet. Each chamber was 70 feet deep, or 21.3 m, and 110 feet wide, or 33.5 m. Building the giant locks filled four years. Stevens then left without warning in 1907, despite the success. Roosevelt's next choice came from the Army Corps of Engineers. The officer was Major George Washington Goethals. Supervision of the build passed to him. Systems, repairs, and the start of excavation had been much of Stevens's contribution. The three lock sets could rise under Goethals. Gatun Dam was begun across the strong Chagres. Behind it would sit Gatun Lake, then the biggest lake people had ever made. Finish came in 1914, and the locks behaved as designed. A major route for ships was the result. Crossing the country grew harder because the canal cut Panama in two. For years, barges and ferries did that crossing. Swing bridges, narrow ones, later stood at Miraflores and at Gatun. They could open for land traffic only when no ship was in the way. A bridge that never had to close to cars was the real answer. In 1962 a four-lane span called Bridge of the Americas was finished at the Pacific entrance. Another bridge followed in 2004, placed 9 miles, or 14.5 km, to the north. Easing crowded traffic was the aim, on the road called the Pan-American Highway. At the Pacific mouth of the canal, the Bridge of the Americas stretches across the water.

8Seen from the north, and not drawn to true size, a side picture explains the locks. A lock gate is labeled. Sea level is labeled. A lock is labeled. The height of Gatun Lake is labeled. Numbered steps tell the story. An open lock receives the ship. Closed gates and rising water lift the ship to the next lock's height. Further locks continue the lift until Gatun Lake's height is reached. The far locks reverse every step after the ship has crossed the lake. Caribbean waters and Pacific waters bound the drawing. Miraflores Lake is marked. Gatun Lake is marked. So are the Gatun locks, the Miraflores locks, and the Pedro Miguel locks. Watertight walls form each lock, with great steel doors at both ends. Engineers raise the water. They also lower it. The front door opens for a ship that needs to pass. The ship enters. The door shuts. Valves then let water in from the lock that sits higher than the ship. Rising water lifts the ship. Three locks are enough to reach the inland lake. Draining, not filling, is the return trip. The ship sinks to the height of the lock ahead. American control lasted until the close of 1999. Panama received the canal under a treaty. Wear was plain by the early years of the twenty-first century. Yearly traffic passed fourteen thousand ships. Yearly cargo passed three hundred million tons. Larger ships and fewer jams required a rebuild. Voters in Panama said yes in 2006. Two added sets of locks were approved, plus two new lanes of navigation tying them to the old channels. Completion came in 2016. Forty thousand workers had spent ten years and 5.4 billion dollars. Ships of modern size can enter. Daily cargo is, in effect, twice what it was. Extra width lets tugboats steer the ships. Mule locomotives are no longer required. The long story of the canal gains one more feat of engineering.

9A last page sets the meanings of useful words. Accommodate means to hold someone or something, or to create the space to do so. A canal is a dug water path across land, made so boats can travel. Commerce is trade, the buying of goods and the selling of them. In this book, contracted means an illness was caught. A coup is a small group's sudden seizure of leadership, often in a government or a business. Engineering uses science and math to design things and to build them. Ingenuity is skillful cleverness in the face of a challenge. An isthmus is a thin land bridge between bigger masses of land. Locks are stretches of river or canal with gates, where the water is lifted or dropped so boats can continue. Mosquitoes spread malaria, a dangerous disease of the tropics. Marine describes whatever belongs to the sea. Morale is the confidence or the eagerness a person or a group feels while chasing a goal. Naval describes whatever belongs to a navy. Someone who perished has died, often suddenly, by violence, or without warning. Refurbishing is repair or change that makes a thing better. To scale something is to climb it when it is high or steep, or to arrive at its top. Something stalled has quit moving ahead, or has quit working all at once. Transcontinental describes a thing that reaches across a whole continent.

70. Should the Zoo Grow?

1The Sunday paper costs $1.50. A Note from Terry Shaw. He edits the Springfield Daily Star. Last week many of you read the news. One of the richest people in our town gave a large sum to the local zoo. Growth is now possible. The zoo can become one of America's leading centers for wildlife conservation. The gift also set off a heated debate here. Letters arrived from many citizens. Some want the zoo to grow. Others say zoos are cruel. They call them outdated institutions that ought to shut. People in the middle like parts of zoo life and still see problems, even at the best zoos. To push that talk further, we print a small set of readers' letters. The letters hold many of the arguments on each side. Facts sit beside opinions. Together they may help our city choose. They may also help us judge what should happen next for the animals living at our zoo.

2More room to swim and to play might come to this penguin if its zoo grew. For: Reasons to Keep Zoos. A duty toward the other living beings. Wildlife biologist Suzanne McCoy sent this letter. I give the growth of the Springfield Zoo my strong support. In recent decades, awareness has risen. People see more clearly the dangers facing the environment of Earth. The natural world is being changed in ways that put many animal species at risk. Kinds of animals that stayed in balance on this planet for millions of years now face extinction. The damage is ours to repair. We can clean the environment. We can move toward greener ways of living. We can spend every effort on species whose lives our actions threaten. Working as a pair, the Los Angeles Zoo and the San Diego Zoo pulled the California condor back from extinction.

3Habitats are being wrecked on purpose, and many species are pushed past the point where they can survive. Wild land is taken for resources. It is taken for farming. What remains breaks into smaller pieces that no longer connect. Animals are cut off from others of their own kind. Finding a mate grows harder. I want our Springfield Zoo inside the work of breeding animals that are endangered. Absent zoos, those animals could vanish completely, and the time could be short. People who work in zoos labor very hard so these species can survive. In some cases an animal born in a zoo can be sent back to the wild. Many zoos partner with people and with groups in the animals' home regions. Together they set up wildlife refuges. Local farmers are taught methods that harm the environment less. Other programs help wild animals stay in their native habitats, so a move to a refuge is not required. Children and grandchildren will inherit a world from us. What kind should it be? Variety and beauty in nature are incredible. If our descendants are to know them, wild animals must be preserved, and that takes work. A larger Springfield Zoo lets our community speak more actively for conservation. It also lets our zoo join the saving of many species that might otherwise die out. Pandas of the giant kind are only a single case. Thousands of species face the chance of dying out.

4Rare looks at how many species behave in nature can come from educational exhibits. Zoos provide priceless education. Retired teacher Roy Chen sent this letter. Education is a central job of zoos. Millions of people get to see wildlife with their own eyes and to value it. They leave knowing more about how varied life on Earth is. They also leave with a feeling that they are stewards, people responsible for the environment. In 2007 a study's results were printed. The study had run for three years. The group behind it is the AZA. Those letters stand for an association that serves both zoos and aquariums. The title was Why Zoos and Aquariums Matter. A real shift in visitors' views on conservation follows a visit to a zoo or an aquarium that the AZA has accredited. Meeting wildlife up close in these places moved more than half of the people surveyed. They wanted a larger part in conservation work. More than half also said the visit tied them more closely to nature. Research says young people need hours in nature if they are to build values about the environment. For someone who lives in a city, a zoo or an aquarium may be the best opening onto life beyond concrete and steel. Books can hand children facts about animals. So can online resources. Nothing replaces meeting the natural world directly. Each year, zoo visits in North America outnumber the crowds at every professional sporting event combined. Learning shows young people a chain. Change one element, and an ecosystem feels it everywhere. Change one ecosystem, and the whole planet feels it. Trouble has come to our planet. Every citizen needs a personal sense of duty toward the well-being of all forms of life. Zoos do important work in growing that sense of duty toward the natural world.

5Against: Reasons to Reject Zoos. Zoos teach the wrong lesson. Animal-rights activist Jose Gonzales sent this letter. Local talk about growing the zoo has left me more and more upset. No person has a right to seize a wild animal. No person has a right to shut one in a cage. Freedom belongs to wild animals as fully as it belongs to humans. A message goes out from zoos. Keeping wild animals so we can be entertained is treated as fine. Some people then decide an exotic animal can be a pet. They lack the training. They lack the facilities. Proper care is beyond them. How some zoo animals are kept is a grave problem. Zoos that are private businesses feel pressure to earn a profit. Cutting corners is one result. Proper care is skipped. A case makes the point. In 2007 a Siberian tiger got out. The place was an enclosure belonging to the San Francisco Zoo. Visitors had likely teased it. It climbed a wall. One person was killed. Two others were hurt. Then the tiger was shot. The wall it climbed sat four feet under the height that standards recommend. When the emergency came, the response from some of the staff was slow. Both a tiger and a visitor died. The zoo had not followed the guidelines of its industry. Those guidelines exist to keep animals safe and to keep visitors safe. Tatiana was that Siberian tiger. She was killed in 2007 after leaving the enclosure. The zoo was in San Francisco.

6Wanting to help is not enough. Keepers can care, and animals can still suffer when freedom is gone. A study that ran a long time looked at bears and at big cats. Captivity hits these animals among the hardest. In the wild their roaming covers huge distances. A small space brings them great stress. Unnatural actions appear once they are kept in zoos. They pace. They sway. They roll their heads. They walk tight circles. People who are mentally ill have shown repetitive movements of a similar kind. Behavioral trouble in some zoo animals is so serious that drugs are given on a regular schedule, only to keep them calm. Some zoos aim at entertaining people. The full range of what the animals need is not the aim. Life can be shorter for some wild animals kept captive. Health trouble can last a long time. Elephants in captivity show the pattern. Arthritis appears. Diseases of the feet appear. Psychological problems appear. A zoo worker checks an elephant's foot, looking for signs of disease. A study from Britain measured enclosures. Safari parks and zoos in the U.K. were measured. Set against the least range those animals need where they are free, the average enclosure is smaller by a factor of one hundred. A further study looked at zoos across the world. For polar bears, room in a zoo is tinier by a factor of one million than the room they have where they roam free. Herd animals are used to big groups where they are free. In zoos they are often housed alone, or with only one companion of their species. Exercise enough to keep the body healthy is often missing. Wings of birds are clipped so flight is impossible. Animals that live in water get far less water than they need.

7Education is what zoos claim to offer. Most visitors still give each exhibit only a few minutes. They tend to treat the animals as a show. The National Zoo employs a curator who watched how visitors behaved. More than seven hundred visitors were watched. The conclusion was blunt. Officials, the curator said, should quit fooling themselves. An animal behind a wall of glass does not carry the huge teaching value they imagine. Proper learning about an animal has only one path. The animal must be seen in its natural habitat. If this dolphin could speak to these children, what would it say about a life in captivity? Taken by beings from another world. Concerned citizen Tamyra Green sent this letter. Picture an ordinary day. A spaceship lands nearby. Aliens step out, aggressive, armed with weapons far beyond ours. They tranquilize you. A tiny crate of metal receives you. The trip ends on their home planet. Town, neighborhood, parents, and friends are gone for good. The journey is long, and moving about is forbidden. You ask to stretch your legs. The request is ignored. Not a word of your language is understood. Even if it were, your needs would not matter. Your wishes would not matter. What matters to them is a human to add to a collection.

8The spaceship sets down on their planet. Your place is a small cage with bars. Inside sit a bed, a chair, and two books. On the back wall hangs a painting. It is large. Its subject is a television. Visitors to their zoo are supposed to picture you in the setting you came from. That is what your captors want. Food arrives once a day: meat loaf and carrots. How would that life feel? Animals we seize and force into zoos face nothing different. Rhinos are intelligent. Boredom can take hold of them quickly once they are captive. The Editor Again. You have now read a set of readers' views, some for zoos and some against. What is your own view? Zoos are complex. They are controversial. A settlement of the argument is unlikely any time soon. One case can be made that every zoo has to be judged on its own. A small roadside zoo, owned privately, differs a great deal from a large zoo in a city. The city zoo may have enclosures that look like nature, programs that breed animals in captivity, and biologists with deep expertise. Further thought may show that zoos cannot be stamped simply good or simply bad. We invite a list from you. Write the goals you believe every zoo ought to keep at the center. Today's problems might teach zoo professionals. They might learn from mistakes. They might improve the zoos we have, or they might build better kinds of zoos later. Which issues matter most for zoos to face?

9Some studies find a much shorter life for elephants that are captive than for elephants that are wild. Accredited means approved because a set of standards has been met. Conservation means protecting natural resources and keeping them from being lost. Controversial means stirring a great deal of disagreement. A curator is the person who runs an exhibit. An ecosystem takes living things and the habitat around them and treats that whole as one community. Exotic means unusual, and usually from a place far away. Extinct means wiped out completely. Outdated means behind the times, no longer matching how things are now. Psychological means having to do with the mind and with emotion. Stewards are guardians, people who take care of something. Tranquilize means to give a person or another animal a drug that brings calm. Wildlife refuges are lands set apart so wild animals can be protected and preserved.

71. Spaceships from Private Builders

1A spaceplane called Dream Chaser was drawn up to carry fresh supplies to the International Space Station. The contents are separate parts, not one long line. A Time Closes comes first. A Time Opens comes next. Another Race Into Space follows. A Ticket Aboard is one part. Delivering the Goods is one part. Carrying People is one part. Stations Owned by Companies is one part. Closing Words ends the list. July 10, 2011: the shuttle Atlantis lines up to join the station called the ISS. This flight is the last of the shuttle program. A Time Closes. Darkness still held the early morning of July 21, 2011, when the space shuttle Atlantis came down in Florida, at the center named for Kennedy. Twelve days in space were behind it. Shuttle missions had been flying since 1981, and this landing was number 135. No NASA shuttle would make the trip to space again.

2Reusable spacecraft began with the space shuttle. Five names filled thirty years at the center of the United States space program. Columbia was one. Challenger was one. Discovery, Atlantis, and Endeavour were the others. People rode them. Scientific experiments rode them, up into orbit around Earth. Satellites were launched, brought back, and repaired. The International Space Station, the ISS, is the largest thing ever built in space, and the shuttles helped put it together. Once Atlantis was on the ground, museum displays were all that remained for these craft. Huge crowds came to watch the launches. They were a spectacle. May 7, 1992: three NASA astronauts, outside the shuttle Endeavour on a spacewalk, seize a satellite that is not working. Age was one reason the shuttles retired by 2011. Cost was another. Each launch was expensive, and upkeep was difficult. Some feats belonged to the shuttle alone, such as taking a satellite out of orbit and bringing it safely home. Experience showed a different truth about simpler jobs. Launching a satellite cost too much to continue. So did hauling crews and cargo up to the station. NASA could not keep paying.

3Sadness followed the end of the shuttle program, yet the times were shifting. Hauling people and cargo back and forth, Earth to space, was a business NASA was leaving. The long name of that agency is National Aeronautics and Space Administration. Science in space, and exploration, had been the original mission. NASA was turning back to that. New plans would send robotic rovers outward. People would go too. Mars was among the exciting destinations. For the first time, everyday kinds of missions were handed to companies that work for profit. After the shuttles, exploration is where NASA will put more of its effort. A drawing shows the rover Curiosity being set down gently on Mars. A Sky Crane does the lowering. Yuri Gagarin, pictured at the lower right, went where no person had gone. He traveled into space first. April 12, 1961, he circled Earth in a Vostok rocket, shown at the left. A Gemini-Titan rocket appears at the upper right. It helped America prepare. The goal was a trip by astronauts that would reach the Moon. A Time Opens. Companies that sell their work had a great deal to learn. A spaceship is hard to build. Fuels are dangerous. Speeds are high. Temperatures are extreme. The vehicle must stay safe through all of that. It must also stay on course, and the systems for that have to be invented.

4The Space Age opened in the late 1950s. Only two superpowers could then pay for vehicles that reached space, and only they had the resources and the technology. One was the United States of America. The other was the Soviet Union. More nations entered later. So did some companies. The 1960s saw private firms build communications satellites of their own. Government rockets still had to lift them. By the 1980s, private firms were building rockets of their own to place satellites in orbit. Change was obvious by the mid-1990s. Companies that were smaller and newer were coming in. Experience was thin. Enthusiasm made up for it. Computers, and other technical advances, brought space within reach of many entrepreneurs. Firms competed for a share of the business. Four sorts of missions are now on company drawing boards. Tourists would ride out to where space begins, then return. Supplies and equipment would reach crews already in orbit. Crews would be ferried to space stations and home again. New stations would be put up by the companies themselves. History was made in 2004 by SpaceShipOne. No earlier spacecraft had put a human aboard, reached space, and been paid for by private money rather than by a government. Another Race Into Space. A nonprofit foundation devoted to education announced a contest in 1996, meant to hurry private spaceships along. The prize was the Ansari X-Prize. Ten million dollars waited for a private firm. That firm had to build a spaceship and fly it. One person, at minimum, had to be aboard, with seats left for two further people. Space was the destination. Height had to reach at least 62.1 miles, or 100 km. The ship had to come home, then do the whole trip again inside two weeks. Twenty-seven teams joined, from seven countries. Eight years passed before anyone claimed the ten million dollars. An American firm, Scaled Composites, won. Its vehicle was SpaceShipOne. The year 2004 saw that small spaceplane fly the first privately funded human trip to space, and the second.

5Winning took two vehicles working as a pair. SpaceShipOne did not roll down a runway like an airplane. It did not blast off atop a rocket. A special airplane, White Knight, carried it high. Release came at 50,000 feet, or 15.2 km, from beneath the carrier's belly. Seconds later the spaceplane's rocket engines roared. Speed passed 3,000 miles per hour, or 4,828 kmph, close to fourfold the pace at which sound travels. The climb went beyond 62.1 miles, or 100 km, just past the edge of space. A drawing shows the rocket engine lighting seconds after White Knight, the mothership, lets go. A Ticket Aboard. SpaceShipOne led the way for a new fleet that will take tourists into space. Virgin Galactic has joined with the makers of SpaceShipOne so people anywhere in the world can buy a trip. Tickets are already for sale at 200,000 dollars a passenger. That sum is large. It is still below a hundredth of the sums private citizens had been paying for a trip into space. Tourism in space began in 2001. The payer was Dennis Tito, an American. The sum was 20 million dollars, paid to a firm called Space Adventures. A Russian Soyuz rocket took him to the International Space Station. Eight days passed aboard the ISS before the return to Earth. After him, other private citizens paid from 20 million dollars to 35 million dollars for trips of the same kind. Richard Garriott, a famous designer of computer games, was one. Anousheh Ansari, an Iranian-American businesswoman, was another. The prize carries her family's name. A picture shows her on the ISS in 2006.

6Early space tourists, year by year, were these. Dennis Tito, American, 2001, 20 million dollars, 8 days. Mark Shuttleworth, South African, 2002, 20 million dollars, 11 days. Gregory Olsen, American, 2005, 20 million dollars, 11 days. Anousheh Ansari, Iranian and American, 2006, 20 million dollars, 12 days. Charles Simonyi, Hungarian and American, 2007, 25 million dollars, 15 days. Richard Garriott, American and British, 2008, 30 million dollars, 12 days. Charles Simonyi again, Hungarian and American, 2009, 35 million dollars, 14 days. Guy Laliberte, Canadian, 2009, 35 million dollars, 11 days. Every one of those early tourists rode a Soyuz rocket to the ISS. Virgin Galactic's spaceplane for paying tourists is SpaceShipTwo. White Knight Two is its mothership. The design resembles SpaceShipOne, but the craft is larger: two pilots, and as many as six passengers. The trip reaches where space begins, then turns around. A full loop around Earth is not the plan. About six minutes of weightlessness will come once space is reached, and then the ride home. Many windows fill the passenger area, for views of Earth and of space. Return begins when the pilot tilts the wings, and the tilt slows the vehicle. In that pose SpaceShipTwo behaves like a giant shuttlecock from badminton, and the fall toward Earth is much slower. Heat stays lower on the way back in, so the heavy shield other spaceships need is unnecessary. Leaving from White Knight Two means less fuel to reach space. Lower cost follows from that saving. Descent to 13.2 miles, or 21.24 km, is the moment the pilot sets the wings back to normal. A glide then aims at the big runway of Spaceport America, in New Mexico. About two hours is the expected length of the whole flight. October 2014 brought a death. A test flight in California ended with SpaceShipTwo in a crash. One of the pilots did not survive. New technology rarely advances without sacrifice. George Whitesides, chief executive of Virgin Galactic, said that space is hard. Work toward safe flight for paying customers is what the company plans to continue. Wings stand in their tilted pose on a model of that spaceplane.

7The year 2001: shuttle Discovery lifts freight toward the station. The load rides in the bay built for a payload. Delivering the Goods is this part of the book. Long stays in space depend on regular shipments. Gear and supplies must keep leaving Earth. The Ansari X-Prize contest ended in 2004. Soon after, NASA said it would offer prizes. A private firm could win by finding a clever method, and a cheap one, for shifting freight upward to the station. Money would follow, and so would technical help, so the winning designs could be built. Still more private companies started work on new vehicles. Spaceships were no longer a task only for NASA and other governments. Possibilities were visible to many people. SpaceX has worked hard on a vehicle for regular deliveries to the ISS that do not cost too much. Dragon is the craft. It flies with no crew, and it can be used again. A Falcon 9 rocket carries the Dragon capsule up. SpaceX is the firm that designed that rocket and also built it. Near the ISS, Dragon waits. A bump into the station would be an accident to avoid. When the crew is ready, the station's robotic arm grabs the craft and pulls it in to dock. A drawing shows a SpaceX Dragon capsule on its way to the ISS.

8NASA set 2012 as the year those supply runs would begin. Cargo also comes home, and that return matters just as much. Leaving the station, Dragon hits the water. The ocean is the Pacific. The nearby coast is California's. SpaceX pulls the capsule from the water and uses it again. Falcon 9 is made of two sections. Both are meant to fly again. On the pad at the Kennedy Space Center sits a Falcon 9. A Dragon capsule is mounted above it. The place is Cape Canaveral, Florida. A drawing shows the shuttle Atlantis joined to Russia's Mir station in 1995. Carrying People. A space station is a craft parked in a long-lasting orbit around Earth. Modern ones are often built from many smaller pieces. Each piece can be sent up from Earth on its own. Once the station is finished, crews come aboard to work and to live. Other spaceships can dock. Long missions and what they do to people are studied there. Experiments in low gravity are studied there too. Near-weightlessness is the daily condition, so many tests can be run that Earth itself would not allow.

9No larger space station has ever been built than the International Space Station. Many nations helped. The price ran to billions, counted in dollars. Size is almost exactly that of a football field. On a clear night the naked eye can pick it out from Earth. A crew first came aboard on November 2, 2000. Emptiness has not returned since. Visitors number over two hundred, drawn from fifteen nations. Safe trips for people, from Earth out to a station like this one and back, are an important job. Large solar panels supply the station's power. Wire in the power system runs more than 8 miles, or 12.9 km. SpaceDev is the builder of Dream Chaser. The craft is meant to carry seven people out to the station and home again. The year 2010 brought a NASA request. Commercial companies were asked to design craft that move people to space stations and home. Seven astronauts had to fit. The ship had to be able to stay docked as long as 210 days, then fly back to Earth and land safely.

10Boeing showed its Crew Space Transportation craft, the CST-100, in 2013. Astronauts will ride it to the ISS. Early designs were judged by NASA, and money went to four companies so their plans could grow. Sierra Nevada offered a space glider, the Dream Chaser. It looks like NASA's shuttle, only smaller. A rocket would carry it up. The return would be a glide. SpaceX built a version of Dragon with room for a crew, for trips to stations and back. Two further firms, Boeing and Blue Origin, also drew capsules. A rocket would lift them. The end of the mission would be a splash into the ocean. Stations Owned by Companies. A few minutes of weightlessness is what a flight like SpaceShipTwo can give a tourist. A stay of weeks, or even months, is a different wish. At least one firm is trying to make space hotels real. The firm is Bigelow Aerospace. Its idea is a balloon habitat. Folded, the habitat fits in a rocket's cargo area. In orbit, it expands. Six people are the goal, in a volume about as large as the ISS. Mylar, a strong fabric, is the skin. A station made of fabric sounds strange. Bigelow engineers say the fabric will actually do better than metal. NASA thinks the habitats are safe as well. A purchase is under study at the agency, so the station could be made larger. Readiness is not here yet. Two empty test models went up in 2006 and in 2007. If the plan holds, inflatable habitats will later be launched and joined into the first space station that a private firm owns.

11Models, built life-sized, show the inflatable habitats of Bigelow Aerospace. Closing Words. One era of space ended with the shuttle's last flight. An exciting age of commercial flight began at the same moment. Firms owned by private hands, in country after country, are pushing designs off the drawing board and into real hardware. Tasks that once belonged only to government space agencies will soon be done by private spaceships. New choices will appear for sending cargo up, for sending people up, and for remaining in orbit a long time. Is the commercial space age one you are ready for? Aeronautics is the science of flight, and also the practice of it. A capsule is the part of a spacecraft that can come away, holding people and their instruments. Commercial describes what has to do with buying and with selling. Docking is the joining of two vehicles while they are in space. Entrepreneurs are people who start businesses of their own and run them. A forerunner is one that comes first, with others following. Inflatable describes what can be filled with a gas, air among them. A mission is a set purpose for an action, a special task. An orbit is the path one object in space takes as it circles a larger object. Re-entry is coming back down into the air that wraps Earth, after being beyond it. A device is called robotic when a program tells it which tasks to do. A spacecraft is a vehicle for travel in space.

72. Speed on the Ice

1People play hockey in lands that stay hot and in lands that stay cold. A world map of the game marks Europe, North America, Asia, Africa, South America, and Australia. The Atlantic Ocean, the Pacific Ocean, and the Indian Ocean separate those lands. The equator runs across the warm middle of the map. One famous moment in the sport came on May 10, 1970. That date was the fourth game of the Stanley Cup Finals. Those finals are the top series in men's hockey. The Boston Bruins met the St. Louis Blues. Boston had already taken the opening three games. The score sat at 3-3 when period three ended. Overtime was only forty seconds old. Boston center Derek Sanderson sent the puck onward. It reached defenseman Bobby Orr. Orr was feared for a hard slap shot. His shot beat the St. Louis goalie and crossed the goal line. The goal earned the Bruins the Stanley Cup. Boston had gone twenty-nine years without that trophy. A picture freezes Orr with both arms up. A Blues player hooks Orr's skate in the same instant. The trip throws Orr into the air. Plays decided in a final second fill a rink with electric energy. The sport is also built on speed. Players bring deep passion onto the ice. Energy, speed, and passion have made hockey a sport known on every continent. Fans in many countries stay devoted to it.

2Organized hockey is played in more than seventy countries. In 2013 the International Ice Hockey Federation surveyed the sport and found it growing. The survey counted 1.64 million players worldwide. Canada leads with more than seven hundred thousand players. The United States comes next with more than five hundred thousand. The Czech Republic is another strong hockey country. Finland is one too. Sweden belongs on that list. Russia does too. Germany, Switzerland, Japan, and France do as well. Men first played hockey at the Olympic Winter Games in 1924. Women's hockey joined those Games in 1998. Most games are played indoors. An indoor rink can keep the ice frozen in every season. In cold places, players also skate outside on frozen ponds and lakes. Some outdoor games use buildings made for other sports. Many towns keep a pond or an outdoor rink where people of every age can practice. The best players in the world compete in the National Hockey League. The league opened in 1917. Its first five clubs all came from Canada. The first United States team was the Boston Bruins, started in 1924. The league now has thirty teams. Seven of those teams are based in Canada. Twenty-three are based in the United States. Each season ends with a championship series. The winner receives the Stanley Cup. Many people say that Cup is the toughest prize any pro sport asks a team to win. The reason is a long and exhausting post-season. Canada has had a women's league, the Canadian Women's Hockey League, since 2007. A United States league, the National Women's Hockey League, formed in 2015 and helps the women's game grow. Youth programs and college programs give young players a place to compete. Hockey stands sixth if you list the pro team sports of North America. It is especially loved where the weather is cold. As pro teams moved south, warmer regions gained fans too.

3Hockey is a fast team sport played on ice. The ball of the game is a hard rubber puck. The puck is 3 inches, or 7.6 centimeters, across. It is 1 inch, or 2.5 centimeters, thick. Players carry long, thin sticks built for this sport. With those sticks they control the puck, pass it, and shoot it. Controlling the puck with the stick is called stickhandling. A goal is scored when the puck enters the other team's net. When time runs out, the side that has scored more goals is the winner. Players must skate forward with great skill. They must also skate backward. They must turn and stop in an instant. They must pass, shoot, and block shots while moving very fast. A picture shows a Chicago center racing through Boston defenders. Skaters can reach 20 miles per hour, or 32 kilometers per hour. The playing surface is a marked hockey rink.

4Each team fights to hold the puck so it can score. Offense is whichever side is controlling the puck. Defense is the side that does not have the puck. A pair of blue lines cuts the ice into three zones. The middle zone is called the neutral zone. Each team's defending zone sits on one side of that middle. An attacker may not enter the other defending zone early. The puck must cross the blue line first. A team usually keeps six players on the ice. Each of the six has a different job. Five of them roam the whole rink. Those five try to score. They also try to stop the other team from scoring. If the other team has the puck, they try to take it. The five are a center, a left wing, a right wing, a left defenseman, and a right defenseman. The center leads the attack. That player usually leads rushes through the center lane. Wings do most of their work along the edges of the ice. The defensemen mainly work to keep goals from being scored. Every skater must switch quickly between attack and defense. The switch depends on which team holds the puck. The goaltender, also called the goalie, guards the net. The goalie is the main player who must stop scores. No other player is allowed to stop the puck with a hand. Using another body part to stop it is also limited to the goalie. The goalie mostly stays in the crease. The crease is a half-circle painted in front of the net. A shot can travel faster than 100 miles per hour, or 161 kilometers per hour. Stopping a shot that fast is a hard job. Goalies wear special pads on their legs. They also wear two different gloves. The stick hand wears the blocker. The catching glove is used to grab the flying puck. A goalie stick has a wider blade. The wide blade gives extra help in blocking shots.

5A professional game has three periods. Each period lasts twenty minutes. Youth games use shorter periods. A tie after period three brings a five-minute overtime. The first team to score in overtime wins. Every period opens with a face-off. That face-off takes place in the circle at center ice. Each team puts one player in the circle. The referee stands there too. The referee drops the puck. The two players battle to control it. Face-offs also follow a goal. They follow a penalty. They follow any stop in play. Eight other dots on the rink can host those later face-offs. Winning the drop is a point of pride. They use many methods to win the drop. Referees punish both small offenses and large ones. Small offenses include elbowing and kneeing. They also include stopping a player with a stick or with part of the body. Large offenses include jabbing someone with a stick. Deliberate fighting is a large offense. So is a cruel hit that drives a player into the boards face-first. A penalized player must leave the ice. That player sits in the penalty box. The sit lasts two minutes or five minutes. The length depends on how serious the rule break is. Until that player returns, the team plays with fewer skaters. The game often turns physical. Players wear gear so they are less likely to get hurt. The gear includes shoulder pads and elbow pads. A helmet covers the head. A mask shields the face. A guard protects the mouth. It includes padded pants or shorts, gloves, and shin pads. It includes the stick and the puck. Skates have steel blades. The boots are stiff. They shield the feet. They also brace the ankles.

6Hockey grew out of old field games that used both a ball and a stick. Versions of those field games existed in ancient Egypt. Ancient Greece had them too. Ancient Persia did as well. Ice-skating grew popular in Europe in the seventeenth century. People in several countries then played games on ice. Early hockey was a casual game. It had no set rules. Players used a ball. A ball was hard to control on ice. It also put players and watchers in danger. Eastern Canada wrote the earliest hockey rules. People called that set the Halifax Rules. They were made in eastern Canada. James Creighton came from Nova Scotia, an eastern province of Canada. He carried those rules to Montreal, in Quebec. In that city he shaped a new set called the Montreal Rules. Official play began with a game on March 3, 1875. The site was a covered skating rink. The city was Montreal. That game introduced a wooden disk, the puck, in place of a ball. Hockey became an instant favorite in Montreal. In the decades after, it spread across Canada. It also moved south into the United States. Frank Zamboni later built a machine that pours water over rough ice. The water freezes into a smooth sheet. Rinks in the National Hockey League have used that machine since 1954. Wayne Gretzky is widely called the best player ever. He played as a professional for twenty years, beginning in 1979. He led the Edmonton Oilers to the Stanley Cup four times. He also set astonishing records for goals and for assists. Fans nicknamed him The Great One. Bobby Orr was a Boston Bruins player. His time there ran from 1966 through 1975. In the 1969-1970 season he scored in overtime. That goal brought Boston a Stanley Cup, its first in twenty-nine years. Across those years he collected many awards. Some named him most valuable player. Others named him the top scorer. His fame helped hockey take hold in the United States. Hayley Wickenheiser joined Canada's National Women's Team in 1994. She was fifteen years old. With her on the roster, Canada took seven medals at the world championship for women. She has also earned five Olympic medals. Her career has strongly shaped the growth of women's hockey.

7Hockey is hard to play. A committed young player can still become skilled by learning the rules and by practicing. Players need to skate well. Even strong skaters must expect serious bruises. Millions of people of every age stay hooked on the game anyway. Jeremy Rupke coaches hockey. He also keeps a website that helps players build skills. He has loved the sport since he could walk. A picture shows him with a team he coaches. In his view, the game is fast and full of action. It demands quick thinking. It demands communication. It demands a high level of skill. Everyone on the ice works as one team toward one shared aim. He says the sport is a fine way to have fun. It is a way to test yourself. It is a way to make many new friends. He also describes a special feeling when play begins. The rest of life seems to pause. Once the puck is on the ice, worries fade. Only the player and the game remain. Some useful words belong with this sport. Astounding means so surprising that it causes wonder. Collegiate describes something linked to college or to college students. Facilities are buildings or spaces stocked with gear that makes a task easier. Flanked means set along one side or both sides. A hazard is a possible danger. Influence is the power to affect people or things. An infraction is an act that breaks a rule. Neutral means not tied to either side in a contest. Passion is very strong enthusiasm for an activity. Proficient means skilled at a task. A referee is the official who makes sure a game follows the rules. Vicious means purposely cruel or violent.

73. Stephen Hawking and the Shape of the Universe

1Eight sections shape this account. They cover a wonder that never faded, childhood, university years, doctoral work and the start of everything, new finds and honors, hard years and new tools, a lasting gift, and a word list. Stephen Hawking watches the first preview of his television show, Stephen Hawking's Universe. A wonder that never faded Stars held Stephen Hawking from the time he was a boy. As a child he liked to watch the stars at night, and his family stood next to him. His mother once said that his sense of wonder never weakened. Personal obstacles of a staggering size stood in his path. Wonder still pushed him into a career known around the world. He became a physicist working from theory, and among the most famous scientists who ever lived. For more than fifty years he produced discoveries that broke new ground, on the nature of space, of time, and of the universe. His life ended on March 14, 2018. Gone was a mind both brilliant and deeply curious.

2Childhood Stephen William Hawking's birth date was January 8, 1942, and the place was Oxford, England. Both parents had graduated from Oxford's great university, among the world's most prestigious universities. Medicine was his father's field. He researched tropical diseases. Philosophy, politics, and economics filled his mother's studies. Among the children, Stephen was the eldest of four children, with two sisters and one brother. His birth fell during World War II, while Nazi Germany bombed England heavily. Economic recovery in England took many years, and money in the Hawking house was tight. The family prized education and prized intellectual inquiry. Books filled every conceivable space. Talk around the family was vigorous and ranged widely, including topics that were controversial. Stephen once said outsiders might have found the family eccentric. He was glad to grow up where minds were kept busy. He went to Saint Albans School, which stands close to London. His marks were only average, yet classmates saw a strong intellect and nicknamed him Einstein. Albert Einstein, a scientist born in Germany, lived from 1879 to 1955. The Nobel Prize in Physics came to him in 1921. People count him a genius. Few physicists have influenced modern science more. Electric trains fascinated Stephen in childhood. As a teen, hobbies showed a keen scientific mind. He built model boats and model airplanes. Complex games for a board were among his inventions. With friends, he also assembled a computer at home. Those friends also talked for long stretches, on subjects running from physics to philosophy.

3At the University of Oxford, Hawking was younger than most of the other students, and he felt cut off from them. Years at university A scholarship carried Stephen into the University of Oxford in 1960, when he was seventeen. Mathematics was the major he wanted. Oxford offered no degree in mathematics, which sent him into physics, especially cosmology, the science of how the universe began and how it developed. Chemistry was part of his work too. Coursework did not challenge him much, and he did not give his studies real devotion. He later described a fashion at Oxford then: students tried to do as little as they could. His own schoolwork took about an hour a day, a fact that later brought him no pride. Even so, honors marked his graduation in 1962. In that last Oxford year, physical problems appeared now and then. He tripped. Objects fell from his hands. His speech slurred. A doctor did not examine the symptoms until the next year. Tests brought a grave diagnosis: amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, pronounced ay-my-uh-TROH-fik LA-tuh-ruhl skluh-ROH-sis. People usually call it ALS, and they also call it Lou Gehrig's disease. Hawking met Jane Wilde at Oxford, and marriage came later. Doctors said Stephen had only a few years left. Devastation followed that news. His age then was twenty-one. A few things kept despair from taking him completely. He saw a patient in the hospital die. That sight reminded him how some suffering was worse than his own. A dream showed him that goals remained, including a doctorate. He was also in love with the student Jane Wilde. He married her afterward. The diagnosis pushed his life toward scientific work and research. That focus, with his bond to Jane, gave him purpose and a will to keep living.

4What the illness does ALS, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, is a group of diseases. They strike nerve cells that control muscles a person moves on purpose, including muscles used when a person walks, talks, chews, or breathes. Weakness or stiffness appears. In time, movement, speech, eating, and breathing can all fail. Muscles waste away. No cure exists. No treatment stops the progress or turns it back. Symptoms can still be managed. Research hunts the causes and hunts new treatments. Diagnosis for most patients comes after age fifty, and breathing trouble kills them within a few years. About one in ten lives ten years or longer. Hawking was a rare case. ALS was with him across a stretch past fifty years. Physicians are not sure why. One possibility is slower progress because the illness was found while he was young. A doctorate, and the start of everything In 1962, aged twenty, Hawking entered a doctoral course in cosmology. The place was the University of Cambridge, and he studied the universe more deeply. This time he applied himself, and he found that he liked the work. Much of his study asked how the universe began and how it grew. The work is largely theoretical, built on mathematical principles, because the universe is far too vast for the observation and testing common in other sciences. His questions circled the central problem of cosmology then: did the universe have a beginning? People have asked that at least since the thirteenth century. Opinion splits. Some say the universe repeats expansion and contraction without end. Others say an enormous explosion began it. In the twentieth century, study of that origin grew more rigorous. A 1929 observation suggested the universe was expanding, and that finding pointed toward a theory of a big bang, and that account most scientists accept today.

5For years, scientists set the big bang aside. A single moment of creation seemed to imply a religious agent, or a supernatural one. Hawking asked whether a big bang could happen on its own, with no such agent. In graduate school he followed the work of physicist Roger Penrose, who studied a star collapsing under gravity belonging to the star itself. Penrose's assertion was that the star would crush itself into a tiny point of infinite density. He called that point a singularity, and he placed it at a black hole's middle. Science treats the big bang as an account of how the universe probably began. On this theory, everything started as one hot, dense point in space. An explosion set about 13.7 billion years before the present drove a rapid expansion that still continues. Mathematical models and formulas support the theory, and so do observations of radiation that may come from that explosion. A diagram shows the universe growing. A black hole is a region where gravity is so strong that nothing pulled in can leave, not even light. The pull is intense because matter sits squeezed inside a very small volume. Physics has an inverse square law: gravitational pull strengthens as an object's surface sits closer to its center. Black holes cannot be seen. Effects on nearby objects reveal them, and scientists watch those effects with satellites and with telescopes. Hawking grew curious about a link that ties black holes to the big bang. His effort went on unceasingly as he applied Penrose's singularity to the universe as a whole. Simply put, he treated the expanding universe like a film and ran the reel in reverse within his thoughts. One artist pictures gas being drawn into a black hole.

6Run backward, the universe shrank and shrank until only a tiny point remained. Hawking realized the universe itself must have begun as a singularity. Those findings let him finish a doctoral thesis in 1966, and the thesis lifted his standing in cosmology a great deal. While the doctorate was underway, he applied for a research fellowship at the University of Cambridge, and he received it. The money let him marry Jane, his girlfriend. The wedding was in July 1965. Jane soon saw that she shared Stephen with another love, which was physics. In 1979 Cambridge University gave him one of its most renowned teaching posts. New finds and honors Research on black holes continued, and other important discoveries followed. His place in cosmology grew as he opened new ground again and again. Physicists then generally agreed that nothing could leave a black hole. Hawking studied particles at a black hole's edge, where fierce gravity pulled them inward. His math said something else. Some particles got away instead of being swallowed. At first he thought the math was wrong, so he checked further. After several months he decided the first result was right. Some particles really could escape, and a black hole gave off particles in a way like a hot object losing heat. In 1974 he announced the idea later called Hawking radiation. Physics was stunned at first. In time, scientists accepted the result as accurate. That discovery, and another about black holes exploding, brought many major awards.

7In 1974, the California Institute of Technology gave him a visiting professor's post, and the family shifted their home to Los Angeles. Home life grew chaotic. His health was failing. Robert and Lucy, both still small, needed care, and both burdens fell hard on Jane. Then a devastating change hit his ability to work. His hands failed, so he could no longer write calculations. He had to rely on visualization, picturing the universe in order to understand it. Hawking and his family returned to England in 1975. Research went on, and papers about his discoveries were published. In 1979 he was named Cambridge's Lucasian Professor of Mathematics, a post of real distinction that Sir Isaac Newton had occupied in an earlier century. Hawking kept it through thirty years. That year brought a third child, Tim. A picture shows him with daughter Lucy, son Robert, and wife Jane. Hard years and new tools Failing health made him face, every day, the chance of dying at any moment. In 1982 he set a new goal: a popular book on how the universe began, clear to millions of readers and not only to scholarly scientists. By 1984 the first chapter was done, a book contract was in hand, and the rest of the writing was underway. Health kept sinking. On a 1985 trip to Switzerland, a chest infection became pneumonia. He was hospitalized and placed on a ventilator, a machine that helps a person breathe. Jane arranged a flight back to Cambridge. Doctors there saw no choice but a tracheotomy, surgery to help him keep breathing. The operation cut an opening in the trachea, the windpipe, and that opening blocked his speech. A tracheal cannula is the breathing tube such surgery inserts.

8Even before the operation, his speech had grown more and more unintelligible. After it, he could not communicate at all. The time was extremely bleak. He could not voice his thoughts, scientific ones included, and he might have to drop both the book and the career. For a while, communication had one path only. Someone pointed at letters on a display, and he moved his eyebrows to choose. Round-the-clock care was also required, which strained home life terribly. Months later, word of his predicament reached a computer programmer in California. That programmer had built a way for people who live with ALS to communicate. He got one at once. Letters or words could be chosen on a computer tablet fixed to his wheelchair, and a voice synthesizer spoke the choices. In 1985 his fingers still worked, and a handheld clicker made the selections. When that ability went, a cheek muscle moved a sensor. The same system let him read email, use the Internet, and write, practice, and give speeches. Speech restored his eagerness for the book, and he worked hard to finish it. The appearance of his book, A Brief History of Time, in 1988 put it on the best-seller list at once, and copies sold out. It stayed on that list across a stretch longer than four years. Sales to date pass ten million copies, in forty languages. The book brought heavy attention from the media. He welcomed it, because it meant people wanted to learn how the universe works. Other books for general readers followed, including several children's books written with his daughter Lucy. Scientific publications of his own numbered more than one hundred. He traveled and spoke widely. Awards, prizes, and medals arrived, among them twelve honorary degrees. Readers felt moved to think about the universe. Fame strained the marriage. A separation from Jane came in 1990. Divorce followed in 1995. A wife who followed was Elaine Mason, and those years together numbered eleven.

9A short record of his life runs this way. Birth came January 8, 1942, with Oxford, England, as the place. Undergraduate study at the University of Oxford began in 1960. A doctoral program at the University of Cambridge began in 1962. ALS was diagnosed in 1963. A Cambridge research fellowship arrived in 1965, the year he married Jane Wilde. The doctorate was earned in 1966. Hawking radiation was announced in 1974, the year he entered the Royal Society of London. Appointment as Lucasian Professor of Mathematics at Cambridge came in 1979. In 1982 he was made a Commander of the Most Excellent Order of the British Empire, the honor called CBE. Speech was lost in 1985, and a voice synthesizer took its place. A Brief History of Time appeared in 1988. His first children's book, George's Secret Key to the Universe, written with daughter Lucy, appeared in 2007. The Presidential Medal of Freedom came from United States President Barack Obama in 2009. The Paralympic Games featured him in 2012. The movie The Theory of Everything, a celebration of his life, appeared in 2014. Death came in 2018. London's 2012 Paralympic Games placed him before a huge crowd at the opening. Television appearances were numerous. A space-travel series used him as a guest in one episode. Comedy programs showed him several times as a cartoon. The 2014 film The Theory of Everything earned high acclaim. His speech nodded to a scientific habit of gathering knowledge by direct observation, and he told the crowd that curiosity toward the universe should continue.

10In his last years he served Cambridge's university by directing its research for a department joining applied mathematics with theoretical physics. He also founded the Centre for Theoretical Cosmology. Students learned from him, and he kept exploring what the universe is. Travel beyond Earth Aggression and self-destruction in humanity worried him deeply. He thought people might wipe out their own species, and perhaps the planet. His belief was that humans would one day need to settle other worlds. In 2007 he felt weightlessness aboard a zero-gravity aircraft. A picture shows him floating on that flight. A gift that lasts Hawking asked large questions about what the universe is, and he opened new regions of scientific thought. Many of his ideas have lasted. Others have not. He still took on questions that have no easy answer, and he modeled inquiry that was both rigorous and fearless. That example fueled a wealth of research, as other scientists tested his ideas and asked questions of their own. His years run from 1942 to 2018. The science was remarkable. So was the unbridled zest for life that inspired people. Brilliance and a curiosity that would not stop sat in his mind. Severe limits from illness did not remove his drive to locate a purpose for life, and a meaning in it. Birth fell three centuries after the death of Galileo, the Italian astronomer. Death fell on Albert Einstein's birthday. It fits that those dates tie Hawking to two scientists who also changed how people think about the universe.

11Words from the book Acclaim, a noun, is strong or enthusiastic praise. Asserted, a verb, means stated something with force or confidence. Compressed, a verb, means squeezed tightly together. Conceivable, an adjective, means able to be imagined. Controversial, an adjective, describes a subject that stirs wide disagreement. Cosmology, a noun, is the study of how the universe began and what it is. Devastating, an adjective, means causing great harm to body or to feeling. A diagnosis is the naming of an illness or an injury. Eccentric, an adjective, means strange, or behaving unlike what people expect. A fellowship is money given to a graduate student who teaches or does research. Infinitely, an adverb, means without any limit. Inquiry, a noun, is the act of seeking information or of asking. A predicament is a fix that is hard, unpleasant, or confusing. Prestigious, an adjective, means highly honored or respected. Radiation, a noun, is energy sent out as waves or as particles. Rigorous, an adjective, means very strict or demanding, and also careful and exact. Staggering, an adjective, means shocking in its scale. A synthesizer is an electronic device that makes and shapes sound, often for music. A theoretical physicist explains and predicts nature by using mathematics and abstract ideas. Unbridled, an adjective, means free of restraint. Unceasingly, an adverb, means without a stop. Unintelligible, an adjective, means impossible to understand. Vigorously, an adverb, means with energy and force. Visualization, a noun, is the forming of a mental picture.

74. Taj Mahal

1Agra, in India, is the home of the Taj Mahal, near the Yamuna River. The Taj Mahal is known for its perfect symmetry. It is the most magnificent creation of the Mughal dynasty. The Mughals ruled northern India in the 1600s. They competed to build the most beautiful mansions and memorials. Their name gave us the word mogul, for a very rich and powerful person. They are famous for jewel-covered art and grand buildings. Shah Jahan, the fifth Mughal emperor, built their most famous tomb, the Taj Mahal.

2Most people picture the mausoleum with its immense white dome. The Taj Mahal is really a 16-hectare, or 42-acre, paradise home for Shah Jahan’s favorite wife, Mumtaz Mahal. Buildings, walls, gates, and gardens are symmetrical, like the Islamic idea of a perfect heaven. Flowers and fruit trees once grew there, but grass fills the grounds now. Four water channels divide the garden into four equal parts that meet at a central pool. They symbolize the four heavenly rivers in the Koran, the Islamic holy book. The Great Gate has octagonal towers with white domes, and its arch frames the onion-shaped dome. Visitors pass this red sandstone and marble gate, marked with words from the Koran, toward the couple’s tomb.

3From the gardens, visitors see the mausoleum reflected in the central water channel. It stands on a raised marble platform, with four minarets like guards at the corners. Each minaret is more than 40 meters, or 130 feet, tall. Translucent white marble covers the tomb and minarets and can seem to glow as the light changes. White is the Islamic color of mourning and shows the faith of the person buried there. A red sandstone mosque and assembly hall stand on either side. The tomb has four long walls and four short walls, because Muslims link eight with paradise. Mumtaz Mahal’s sarcophagus is centered, Shah Jahan’s is the only off-center part, and a marble screen surrounds both.

4The upper sarcophagi are cenotaphs, or false tombs for visitors, and the real graves lie in a room below. Taj comes from the Persian word for crown. Some experts say the rich mausoleum honors Mumtaz like a jewel-covered crown. Vines, flowers, butterflies, and gems such as jade, turquoise, and lapis lazuli cover the inside. A thin sheet of pearls was made to cover her sarcophagus on holy days. Few Mughal monuments were built for a woman, and his other two wives lie in unmarked buildings near the Great Gate. Shah Jahan met Arjumand Banu when he was fifteen and she was fourteen, and they married in 1612.
