Mumtaz Mahal means Chosen One of the Palace, but painting noblewomen was forbidden, so no true portrait survives.

5Shah Jahan showed skill in battle early, at the peak of Mughal rule. For eighteen years Mumtaz traveled with him, even when he went to war. In 1631 she died in his battle camp while giving birth to their fourteenth child. She was only thirty-eight years old. Heartbroken, he gave up jewelry, fine clothes, and music, and he delayed his sons’ weddings for two years. Each Wednesday, and for a month each year, he banned celebrations and made his court wear white. He chose riverside land in his capital, Agra, where Mughal royalty had garden mansions. A slow bend in the Yamuna protected the bank, mirrored the marble, and fed the garden channels.

6Most mausoleums stood in the center of a garden, but Mumtaz’s tomb stands at one end. Across the Yamuna to the east is the Moonlight Garden, once found in ruins. Archaeologists think visitors viewed the mausoleum from there by moonlight. Restored in the 1990s, it was one of Shah Jahan’s favorite spots for viewing her memorial. Construction began in 1632, about a year after her death, and it was the dynasty’s largest project. More than twenty thousand workers, more than a thousand elephants, and craftsmen from many lands took part. The tomb is about 70 meters tall, its dome is 44 meters tall, and the dome may weigh 11,000 metric tons. The work took 22 years and about 32 million rupees, and the minarets slant so they would fall outward.

7Gems and marble of different colors came from China, Tibet, Afghanistan, and other countries. Teams of twenty to thirty oxen hauled the white marble hundreds of miles on carts. Workers built a dirt ramp 4 kilometers, or 2.5 miles, long and used scaffolds, ropes, and pulleys. The Taj is open from sunrise to sunset except Friday, when local Muslims may pray at the mosque. Moonlight visits are offered on the full moon and the nights just before and after, except during Ramadan. Three sons fought to rule, and Aurangzeb held Shah Jahan in Agra Fort until Shah Jahan died in 1666. From a room in the fort, he could see the Taj Mahal only from far away. Looters later took gems, lamps, and carpets, and a British viceroy in Agra began repairs in the late 1800s.

8Iron foundries and factories in Agra sent out pollution, and acid rain harmed the white marble. A yellow fungus called marble cancer began to discolor and eat the soft stone. Behind the tomb, the Yamuna carries sewage and garbage, and scientists think the gas may stain the marble. Moisture from thousands of visitors’ breath also helped damaging algae grow. In 1982 India created the Taj Trapezium, and a 2-kilometer emission-free zone followed in 1984. In 1996 the Indian Supreme Court ordered nearby industries to use natural gas or move outside the zone. In 2001 the Taj Mahal Conservation Collaborative began cleaning stains with detergents and clay packs. The tomb has survived earthquakes, lightning, wars, and floods, and hard work still protects it.

9Early in the morning and later in the day, visitors see unforgettable changes of light on the Taj Mahal. Shah Jahan wanted a memorial so magnificent that the whole world would admire it for all time. Thousands of people visit each day, and millions come each year from around the world. The United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization named it a World Heritage Site. An international vote made it one of the New Seven Wonders of the World. Centuries after it was built, the Taj Mahal remains one of the most beautiful memorials ever created.

75. The Air War That Saved Britain

1Indian pilots reach London in 1940. They are ready to fly for the Royal Air Force. This account has six parts. One part is a choice not to give up. One part is the buildup in the air. One part is the sky battle. One part is the long bombing of cities. One part is Britain's proudest time. The last part is a word list. On the beaches at Dunkirk, French soldiers wait. British soldiers wait with them. They have no clear idea of what comes next. The part about not giving up starts here. In June 1940 the fighting on Europe's main land was nearly finished. Adolf Hitler led Nazi Germany. Only nine months had passed since that nation opened World War II. The opening blow was the attack on Poland on September 1, 1939. Germany had grown into a very strong power on the Axis side. Allied powers stood against it. Both Britain and France belonged to that Allied side. They said they were at war two days after Poland was attacked. In the months after that, Denmark fell, then Norway, then the Netherlands. May 1940 brought the German blow to Belgium and to France. Close to 400,000 troops from Britain crossed to the main land to help. Germany's forces were too strong, and they were also too quick. Belgium was in German hands after a little more than two weeks. The French army and the British army were falling back at full speed.

2By May 27, hundreds of thousands of British and French soldiers were trapped at Dunkirk, a port in France. Capture or being wiped out looked almost sure. Then an amazing rescue began. For the next week, navy ships, fishing boats, and boats of ordinary people crossed the English Channel. That Channel is the Atlantic stretch between the British Isles and the main land of Europe. By June 4, about 338,000 troops had been set down in safer Britain. Only the Channel now seemed to block a German landing. Prime minister Winston Churchill spoke to the nation. He wanted people ready for a fight that looked sure to come. He called for strength and confidence. He told them to guard the country at any cost. He said never to give up. Pictures show the boats at work. The air war called the Battle of Britain was about to open. A picture shows the Women's Auxiliary Australian Air Force at work on a plane. Next comes getting ready to fly. In 1938, many Britons feared war with Nazi Germany. Hitler had made his forces bigger and looked ready to use them. British leaders got ready for the worst, and their own forces grew. After war was declared, every fit man had to sign up. Young men and young women joined the army, the navy, and the air arm. They signed on in Britain and in empire lands, among them Australia, Canada, India, and Kenya. Britain watched the Luftwaffe, Germany's air arm. Leaders prepared for a war fought mainly from the sky. The Royal Air Force, the RAF, built new fighters and sent them up. Air bases grew. Cities were ringed with guns that could fire at planes.

3Ordinary people would fill key jobs across a wide range. War factories hired hands to build planes, tanks, ships, and guns. Children joined drives to gather scrap metal and paper. Families were urged to plant gardens and to save food. Food sharing by set amounts began. Posters were printed and hung to lift mood and to ready people for danger. Above all, the public was told to stay calm and carry on. Air Raid Precautions, or ARP, started in 1937 to plan the answer to air attacks. Firefighters and rescue crews were trained for the wreck bombing would leave. From 1939, ARP wardens made people follow blackout rules. Street lights went dark. Windows needed black curtains, so bomb crews overhead could not see targets. A picture shows an ARP warden near London setting the blackout hour. Some families built Anderson shelters in the back yard. Part of each sat under the ground, with iron sheets on top. Six people could fit inside. In 1939 the Home Guard took shape. Many helpers were past the usual age to join up. They promised to fight if German troops landed. Plans moved children, older people, and hospital patients out of big cities. Some went to the British country side. Others went to far empire lands, among them Canada and Australia. The first wave began on September 1, 1939, the first day of the war. Children left their families. Most stayed with complete strangers. In time some 3.5 million people, mostly children, went by train or ship to safer ground. A picture shows children in London waiting to be sent away.

4A June 1940 map of Europe marks who held the land. Ireland sits apart from the fighting. Separate marks show Axis control, lands that stayed neutral, and Allied control. The map names England, the Netherlands, the English Channel, Germany, Belgium, and Luxembourg. It also names the Atlantic Ocean, Austria, Switzerland, France, Italy, Portugal, and Spain. Once France fell in June 1940, Britain had no ally left on the main land of Europe. Held land sat just across the Channel. At the narrowest, that water was only 30 kilometers, or 18 miles. Some people in the government thought giving up was the only wise path. Churchill was not one of them. He was a strong leader, new in the job of prime minister. He had studied how Hitler worked. He believed the leader meant to take Britain. A low hard voice and bright speeches let him win over his ministers. He argued that defending the home land was the only choice. An April 1940 picture shows him speaking to sailors in London. Another shows British troops on the English coast, ready for a German landing. When Britain made plain it would keep fighting, Nazi planners wrote a plan to land. They code named it Operation Sea Lion. German soldiers, counted in the tens of thousands, would cross on troop ships from the newly held coasts of France and Belgium. Soldiers trained to jump from planes would drop in. No day was fixed. Both sides thought the landing had to come before winter. After that, the stormy Atlantic was as deadly as a weapon. Germany's first job, before any landing, was to destroy the Royal Air Force. While those planes remained a threat, a crossing could kill very many on the ships and many men trying to reach shore. July 1940 brought the first German war planes over Britain.

5A British Spitfire fighter is shown chasing a German bomber, the Heinkel He 111, in the Battle of Britain. The sky battle starts here. German raids opened early in July. The Luftwaffe tested what the RAF could do and learned all it could. Those first blows fell mostly on the Channel. Supply ships were sunk, and port cities were bombed. From August the attacks grew much heavier. Bombers and German fighters crossed in wave after wave and struck targets in Britain. RAF pilots flew straight at those groups. They tried to knock the attackers from the sky or push them off their path. Britain held two gains the Germans never fully grasped. Radar came first. The name means finding direction and range by radio. The new gear sent radio signals that found incoming planes. It warned the RAF that an attack was near. Pilots then rushed up and tried to cut the raiders off. Because of radar, defenses could gather where they were needed. Towers for the system stood along the shore. German crews tried to wreck them and had only limited success. Women gave key help through the Women's Auxiliary Air Force, the WAAF. Women served at radar stations. As plotters in command rooms, they steered RAF fighters toward Luftwaffe groups. They also ran big guard balloons. Those huge balloons hung over cities and pushed enemy planes higher, which made the bombing less exact. Service in the WAAF passed 180,000 women by 1943. A picture shows WAAF plotters at their boards while aircraft fill the sky.

6A member of the Women's Royal Naval Service works the Colossus computer. That computer let Britain read Germany's coded army notes. Britain's second gain was a great secret of the war. By the middle of 1940, Polish and British experts had broken the secret codes in German messages. British chiefs could read hidden notes on plans and on how fights would be run. In the sky battle, those notes often warned of a raid before Luftwaffe planes left the ground. Through August the raids wore the RAF down. Flyers and ground crews were tired. Many flew several tasks a day. Each task was a fight that could kill them. Planes, air fields, and other sites were smashed faster than crews could mend them. On August 24, 1940, several German planes bombed parts of London where ordinary people lived. Until then raids had aimed only at army sites and factories. People today think that hit was an accident. Churchill ordered a strike on Berlin at once. The next night more than seventy British bombers flew deep into enemy land. Their bombs did small damage, but British spirits rose. German leaders were stunned and angry. Their air chief had promised no enemy bomb would ever land on Berlin. Early in September the method changed. Raids hit factories and neighborhoods in London and other large cities. The sky battle became a fight against the people. Britons called it the Blitz. A picture shows Hermann Goering, the air chief, speaking with an official of that air arm.

7Planes of the fight come next. Britain's Supermarine Spitfire was a fighter. Its speed could reach 594 kilometers an hour, or 370 miles an hour. Its climb could reach 11,000 meters, or 37,000 feet. It was easy to handle and very fast. Eight machine guns rode on it, and each gun could fire 350 rounds. Germany's Messerschmitt Bf 109 was a fighter the Luftwaffe had already proved in battle. It was faster than the Spitfire and matched it in turns. These planes guarded the German bomber fleets. The Messerschmitt Bf 110 used two engines and two crew. It was slow, and RAF fighter groups tore those planes apart. Britain's Hawker Hurricane was a fighter that could also drop bombs. It could meet German fighters and could bomb German ships. Top speed was 541 kilometers an hour, or 335 miles an hour. The Heinkel He 111 was a German mid size bomber. It did the most harm in the sky battle and again in the Blitz. Five crew flew it. Its bomb load passed 2,268 kilograms, or 5,000 pounds. The Avro Lancaster was a heavy bomber and one of the war's best night bombers. Some were changed so they could carry a bomb of 6,250 kilograms, or 14,000 pounds. Cities under bombs come next. Britain's press made the name famous. The German word Blitzkrieg means a war like lightning, and that word supplied the name. German leaders wanted to scare Britain's people, drain their will to fight, and smash war factories. In a furious speech, Hitler promised to lay Britain's cities to waste. September 7, 1940, opened the Blitz. More than three hundred German bombers hit major cities across Great Britain, with six hundred fighters alongside. Bombs burst in neighborhoods and in streets. That day's raids killed 430 people who were not soldiers and badly hurt about 1,600 more. In later days, weeks, and months, bomber waves kept dropping blast bombs and fire bombs. German fighters tried to hold the RAF off. A picture shows London still smoking after that first mass raid, dated September 7, 1940.

8German Heinkel He 111 bombers, flying as a group, are shown over the English Channel. September 15 brought raids of special force. London suffered two huge Luftwaffe attacks. They started just past midnight and lasted until the next dusk. German aircraft in the attack numbered nearly 1,900. The attack lasted nearly 24 hours. Crews were surprised again by how many Spitfires and Hurricanes rushed at them. They had been told Britain's fighter command would soon have no aircraft left. Once more the RAF stopped Germany from winning a clear result. Each year, people remember the date as Battle of Britain Day. When raids were spotted, air raid sirens roared and told city people to take cover. Some went under bridges. Some used church basements or storehouse basements. Others used shelters built at home. Few of those places were safe from a direct hit, or from a blast that landed close. A picture shows a bus in a hole left by a bomb. That bomb wrecked part of a London station on the underground railway. The raids forced Britain to face an ugly truth. Wealth or being poor could decide who lived. People with money could flee to country houses. Officials with means could hide in rooms under the ground. An average family got little thought. Neighborhoods of working people were especially open to harm, and German bombers hit them often. Many families watched homes burn or blow apart. Deep shelters under the ground were needed, but the government was slow. Officials feared that crowds in underground train stations would upset the stations' work. They also feared some people would hide below and refuse their jobs, to avoid being outside while bombs fell. Tickets were bought all the same, and people slept on the platforms.

9Bombs kept falling, and the public grew angrier that leaders did so little for safety. Some staged protests to force attention onto the danger. At last those leaders admitted they must do more for the people who could be hurt most easily. Shelters in London's underground stations were approved and set up. A bunker system went up that could shield some 64,000 people. People living in London at the time were thought to number 8.6 million. A picture shows Londoners waiting out a raid down in a train station. Bombing cities brought results Germany had not planned. Most British people drew together and defied Germany. They stood with Churchill. War bonds became one way they paid for the fight. The Home Guard gained more helpers, and so did other groups. Neighbors took in family and friends whose houses were gone. Instead of breaking the will to fight, the raids often built a warm bond and a harder will. Ideas of giving up faded. The switch also gave the Royal Air Force a break it badly needed. Attacks on air fields, hangars, and plane factories had nearly cracked the force. Skilled pilots were few and worn out. Without meaning to, the German high command let the RAF recover and regroup. British bombers flew tasks of their own to keep Germany off balance. They hit factories. They hit bases and ports where a landing was being prepared. Landing craft and other ships were destroyed. Rail lines that fed those gathering places were blown up.

10In the middle of September, welcome news came from Britain's spy service. Hitler had chosen to put the landing off. Winter was close. Atlantic storms would soon rise. The RAF was still just as hard to beat. Bombing of cities, though, was nowhere near finished. As September closed, more Luftwaffe attacks shifted to night. Darkness made German planes very hard for the RAF and for other defenses to find. Factory cities took the worst of it along with London. Regular targets included Manchester, Glasgow, Belfast, Birmingham, and Bristol. Port cities suffered too. The Luftwaffe hoped to cut off help that came in ship groups from Canada and from the United States. On May 10, 1941, after eight months of bombing, those huge raids flew for the last time. June brought a surprise German drive into Russia and into the wider Soviet Union. With that, the Blitz ended. Across both the sky battle and the bombing of cities, Britain was battered and burned. Deaths of ordinary people reached some 40,000. Homes destroyed or badly damaged passed a million. Hitler's grand plan had been blocked, and the country lived to fight on. The proudest time comes next. Britain had stood up under everything Nazi Germany could drop. Its forces could now gather again, rebuild, and arm again. By early 1942 a strong tie bound Britain to the Soviet Union and to the United States. That second partner had joined the fighting in December 1941. Bombers and fighters from the United States joined the RAF against targets Germany held on the main land. By lasting through the Luftwaffe's huge set of raids, Britain kept a base that Allied air work could not spare. British and American air power together pounded Germany's forces, its factories, and its cities. In June 1944, several years afterward, Britain was the ground from which the Allies landed in France while Germany still held it. A 1944 picture shows American troops training for that landing.

11Ruin stood all around, yet people in Britain tried to keep ordinary life going. On June 18, 1940, still before the Battle of Britain opened, Prime Minister Winston Churchill gave a speech. He urged people to meet their duty to the country. Future generations, he said, should look back and call the time Britain's finest hour. For many British people, the country's conduct in World War II, and its courage, still stand for that finest hour. Words from the book come last. Propaganda means stories or claims that are false or stretched, spread to sway people or to push one view. Allies are people or groups that join others for a shared cause. Blitzkrieg means a sudden, strong military blow meant to win quickly. Radar is a device that finds or tracks objects by sending radio waves and catching them after they bounce back. Camaraderie is the warm feeling shared by companions who pass their days side by side. Civilian concerns people outside the army and the police. Rationing is the controlled sharing of goods and services when supplies run short. Luftwaffe is the name of Germany's air force. Royal Air Force is Britain's air force, shortened to RAF. Paratroopers are soldiers trained to leap from planes and fight behind enemy lines. Vulnerable describes someone who can be hurt with ease. Prime minister is the government leader in most countries that use a parliament.

76. The Amazing Brain

1Your brain weighs only 2 percent of your body. It uses more than 20 percent of your energy. About 86 billion neurons carry signals for thoughts, memories, and feelings. They help you ride a bike and remember your teacher's name. Neurons form more than 125 trillion connections called synapses. There are more synapses than stars in 1,500 Milky Way galaxies! This wiring is the control center for your whole body. Signals travel to different parts of the brain and body.

2The brain stem, cerebellum, cerebrum, corpus callosum, and two hemispheres are main brain parts. Neurons link these parts and also reach your muscles and senses. The brain stem controls breathing, digestion, heartbeat, and other survival processes. It also controls your fight, flight, or freeze response. The cerebellum coordinates balance and adds targeting instructions to movement. With its help, you can touch your nose in one smooth motion. It stores procedural memory, so practice can make movements automatic. Exercise strengthens the brain, and muscle memory may slow diseases like Alzheimer's.

3The cerebrum is almost 75 percent of the brain's volume and almost 85 percent of its weight. Thought, speech, learning, emotions, and sense signals are handled there. A stream of signals can become a purple bus or a crowing rooster. Without the corpus callosum, you could see the bus but not say what it was. Computers remember more precisely, but brains adapt better to change. The left hemisphere controls the right side of the body, and the right controls the left. The right brain usually handles creativity and vision, while the left handles speech, writing, and math. The corpus callosum links the hemispheres, and each one has four lobes.

4In 1848, an explosion sent a three-foot iron rod through railroad foreman Phineas Gage's head. The rod passed through his left eye and frontal lobe. He survived, but the hole did not affect his memory or his ability to think. He became rude, thoughtless, and stubborn. Friends said he was no longer Gage. Losing part of the frontal lobe changed his emotions and attention. That lobe also handles problem solving and speaking, while other lobes handle movement, hearing, memory, and vision. Doctors did not keep his brain, but 1914 war injuries helped them start brain maps. Injury studies found essential regions, yet mapping structure is not the same as mapping function.

5An EEG can show normal activity in a four-year-old and light sleep in another person. In the 1920s, Hans Berger built a machine to measure electrical activity in the brain. An electroencephalogram uses electrodes on the head to see signals as you walk, talk, or read. The brain wave rhythm it measures is called a Berger's wave. Everything you do begins with tiny electrical signals in your brain. Without implanted electrodes, an EEG detects only signals near the surface. In the 1990s, fMRI began mapping active regions by measuring blood flow. It is noninvasive and indirect, because active neurons need more oxygen.

6Two medical professionals can review an fMRI of the brain. More blood flow deep in the brain usually means more active neurons. An fMRI shows regions used when you sing, laugh, or startle in more detail than an EEG. fMRI stands for functional magnetic resonance imaging. Decoded signals might control a robot or help people with disabilities communicate. Electrodes detect the signal, and the decoded information can run a mechanical device. In 2013 at the University of Washington, one person's signal moved another person's finger over the Internet. Weeks earlier, a Harvard team used a brain signal to move a rat's tail.

7Your brain works best with proper care, so use it. Violin practice can make the brain area for the left hand larger. Hard new puzzles build connections, but easy games you already know may not. Try sudoku if you like words, or try drawing if you like numbers. Blueberries and walnuts have nutrients that help the brain work smoothly. Eight weeks of meditation at a Harvard study changed regions for learning, memory, and emotions. Dr. Arthur Kramer says children who exercise often have better memory, attention, and test scores. Dancing builds new connections and can calm stress, which may reduce pain and tension.

8At Northwestern University, Dr. Ken Paller points to evidence that the brain replays memories in sleep. That replay may help skills and information stick in memory. Too little sleep decreases your ability to learn and think. Experts recommend between seven and nine hours every night. Dr. Ann Mckee says protection is the most important key to brain health. Cerebrospinal fluid and a hard skull guard the brain against some injuries. A fall from two or three feet, a hard hit, or a violent shake can cause a concussion. Most mild ones heal with rest, but swelling can cut off oxygen in minutes, so wear a helmet.

9Autonomic actions happen without your choice. The brain stem sits at the top of the spinal cord and controls basic functions. The cerebellum is at the lower back of the brain and helps balance and smooth movement. The cerebrum is the largest part in many mammals and controls thinking, feeling, and communicating. Hemispheres are halves, and lobes are rounded sections such as those in the brain. Neurons carry information, and a network is a connected group that communicates. Electrodes let electricity flow, and a noninvasive test does not cut into the body. To decipher something is to work out a hard meaning, and onset means the start.

77. The Ancient Stone Ring on Salisbury Plain

1A monument from before writing comes first, then a Stone Age site and a landscape crowded with monuments. A project lasting 1,500 years follows, with questions about purpose, the site in our time, a story still unfolding, and a word list. Among prehistoric places, Stonehenge ranks with the most visited in the world. Long ago, people in the south of England spent enormous effort. They stood a ring of huge stones upright. The name of that monument today is Stonehenge. Centuries later, many of the great megaliths lie fallen. Fascination remains. It remains even though the original purpose was forgotten. Roughly nine hundred years ago, Geoffrey of Monmouth, a historian in England, tried to explain the mystery. His tale was fanciful and concerned Merlin, wizard of the legends about King Arthur. Merlin, he wrote, told another king to build a memorial meant to last forever. Stonehenge was the outcome. Magic from Merlin, Monmouth claimed, helped the building, and he set the date about sixteen hundred years ago.

2Investigators have studied Stonehenge for hundreds of years. Archaeologists are among them, along with historians and scientists. They want explanations from science, not from the supernatural. Digging at the site has searched for clues. History, builders, and purpose are the targets. What has been learned matches any legend for wonder. Kings, wizards, and magic fill those legends. An age of about two thousand years was once the scholarly guess. Shock followed when research pushed the start much earlier. Work had begun three thousand years before that guess. The time was the Neolithic period, from 10,000 to 2500 bc. People in Britain still lacked metalworking. The wheel had not been invented. Archaeologists are tracing where the bluestones began. Those stones are a rare kind used at the monument. A locator map sets the site inside the United Kingdom. Waters shown are the Atlantic Ocean and the North Sea. Scotland is marked, with the cities Edinburgh and Glasgow. Northern Ireland is marked, with Belfast. Ireland is marked, with Dublin. England is marked, with London. Wales appears as well. Wider labels reach Europe, then Asia, then Africa. Earth and huge rocks are the building materials. The Washington Monument towers more. Egypt's great pyramids are more enormous. Majesty here comes mostly from how old and how mysterious the place is. Visitors cross a grassy plain in England's south. Standing stones, massive ones, slowly enter view. Circles sit inside other circles. A ditch forms the outer ring. Raised soil, an embankment, is surrounded by that ditch. Diameter is about 110 meters, which is 360 feet. The famous stone ring stands at the center. Many of its stones are gone.

3More than one kind of stone appears at Stonehenge. Sandstone slabs that stand and form the outer ring are known as sarsen stones. About 36,000 kilograms, or 79,366 pounds, is the weight of the largest. Lintels of stone lie across the tops. Once, those lintels linked every standing stone. Inside the sarsen circle lie smaller boulders, the bluestones. Their rock is dolerite, a coarse kind of basalt. About 2,994 kilograms, or 6,600 pounds, is the weight of the largest bluestone. Another set of standing stones sits inside the sarsen ring, arranged like a horseshoe. Together they make trilithons. Each trilithon is a square arch: two upright stones and one lintel across them. Width is about 6.7 meters, or 22 feet. Height is 9 meters, or 29.5 feet. An artist has drawn the monument as it may have looked when finished. Labels point to a trilithon, a lintel, the bluestones, and a sarsen stone. Seventeen sarsen stones still trace the Sarsen Circle. Thirty, archaeologists believe, stood there once. Average weight of the large blocks is 22,680 kilograms, or 50,000 pounds, heavier than a school bus. Height is more than 5 meters, or 16.4 feet. Stones that stand alone also belong to the monument. The Heel Stone is one. The Slaughter Stone is another. Both lie outside the Sarsen Circle. During the thousands of years since, people may have hauled some stones off. Others likely sank. Rituals of importance were probably held here. Crowning a ruler may have been one. Celebrating a harvest may have been another. Honoring dead ancestors may have been a third. Some experts think entry was limited to high priests or to other religious leaders. Ordinary people stayed outside the sacred stone circle.

4Rolling hills and grasslands make up Salisbury Plain, and Stonehenge stands there. Life on that plain seems to reach back past ten thousand years. Woodland covered it in the Neolithic period, and animals were plentiful. Hunter-gatherers found a place of plenty. Ancient pits dug up by archaeologists hold flint tools, flint weapons, and animal bones. The abundance of food, experts speculate, may have made the area feel sacred to those Neolithic people. Around 7500 bc a slow change began to shake the culture. Hunting and gathering gave way, little by little, to farming. Food could be produced more reliably. Larger groups could be fed. Big social projects became possible. Enough food meant less time spent farming and hunting. More time remained for monuments such as Stonehenge. Sheep graze the lush grass of the plain beside the stones. Evidence from archaeology puts the start of building near 3000 bc. Work continued across generations, past a span of one thousand years. Moving the giant stones, and setting them, is viewed as one of early humanity's great engineering feats. Distant quarries, archaeologists believe, supplied the sarsen stones. Distance was about 32 to 48 kilometers, or 20 to 30 miles. Wheels and wagons did not exist yet. How, then, were the stones hauled? Far-fetched answers have included giants, magic, and even aliens from space. Realistic options are what archaeologists have chased. Experiments have tested Stone Age methods for moving sarsen-sized stones. Replica stones of similar weight were loaded onto wooden sledges. Those sled-like platforms slid on wooden rails slicked with animal fat. Dozens of volunteers pulled. The trials showed the trip to the site was possible. That method is now a leading theory.

5Bluestones were a harder puzzle for many years. Nowhere near Stonehenge is a source for them. Research eventually reached Wales. A quarry there lies northward by more than 241 kilometers, or 150 miles. Some unknown reason made the builders believe those heavy stones were worth a staggering journey. Rafts may have carried them, some experts speculate, floating along the ocean coast until the stones were nearer the site. Volunteers in London, during May 2016, tested whether people could pull a heavy stone block like the ones at Stonehenge. No machinery was used. Standing the stones up was a separate engineering problem. One possible method began with a pit under every long stone, right at its foot. Wooden wedges could be pushed, bit by bit, under the top end, lifting it slowly. Once the upper end had risen far enough, the lower end fell down into that pit. Ropes then pulled the stone upright. Other researchers picture a different lift. Wooden platforms were built beneath the stones. Setting lintels onto the trilithons may have demanded the most planning and the most skill. Ramps of dirt and wood, high enough to meet each pair of uprights at the crown, are one possibility. A sledge could carry the lintel. Teams with ropes would ease the lintel upward along that ramp until it sat where it belonged.

6Innovative engineering came from these master builders. Their languages are nearly impossible to recover. So are the religions they followed. Writing was not used. Little of their art survives. Archaeology is the only source of modern understanding. Skeletons of people found near the site, and animal bones, have been tested. The tests offer striking clues about origins. Some builders seem to have come from Wales. Others came from lands nearby. A quarry in Pembrokeshire, Wales, is under excavation. The bluestones may have started there. Newer finds say a few people migrated from still farther off, from mainland Europe. The size of Stonehenge suggests separate groups joined forces. Knowledge, skill, and muscle were shared. A skeleton was found in 2002 near the town of Amesbury, about 3.2 kilometers, or 2 miles, from the stones. Death came about 4,300 years ago, while building was still underway. Importance is clear from the grave. Gold jewelry was inside, along with arrowheads and stone wrist guards. Archers of that time commonly wore such guards. Chemicals in the teeth were tested. Growth happened in mainland Europe, near the lands that are Germany and Switzerland today. The reason for the move is still unknown. Distance was more than 1,126 kilometers, or 700 miles. Death came far from home. Burial was with honor. Many objects surround this Amesbury Archer's skeleton. A knife is there, along with pots, rings, and earrings.

7Mystery surrounds the purpose, yet the design holds clues. A practical use, such as shelter or a market, does not seem to have existed. Experts are therefore convinced the place was an open-air temple. Visits were for spiritual reasons. Religious uses, researchers believe, shifted across the long history. Ceremonial uses shifted too. A burial ground was likely the beginning. As many as 240 burials have been unearthed nearby. No Neolithic burial ground in England is larger. Cremation was common. Weapons and jewelry went into some graves. A skeleton of a Neolithic man found at the site is displayed with a reconstructed face. The visitor center near Stonehenge holds them. Astronomy supplies another popular theory. Some giant stones line up with the sun's motion. Summer and winter solstices make this especially clear. About June 21 each year is the summer solstice, the longest day. At dawn, sunlight reaches straight to the monument's center. About December 22 is the winter solstice, the shortest day. At sunset, sunlight passes straight through the gap in the biggest sarsen pair. The layout works, in a sense, like a giant clock for the seasons. Farmers needed that information to plan planting. A further theory has appeared in recent years. Some experts think the project was huge because it was meant to unite people nearby. Tribes from far away, the evidence suggests, traveled to Stonehenge, and many stayed for good. Trade may have drawn them. Shared protection may have drawn them. Plenty of food in the region may have drawn them too.

8Sunrise on June 21, 2014, sends light through the stones. That date is the year's longest day. Europe's prehistoric landmarks include this one among the most famous. What the public sees now is not the view from 1900. By then, most giant stones had tilted or fallen. During the last century, heritage groups put parts back, guided by archaeological evidence. Cranes lifted some stones in 1958. Concrete anchored some of the uprights. Restorers believed the public would then see the original look more clearly. Watchers in 1958 saw England's largest crane set a lintel across two upright stones. Study of the monument and the land around it continues. The newest technology maps what lies underfoot. Magnetometers detect magnetic fields. Laser scanners measure possible archaeological sites with precision. Radar that penetrates the ground can scan down to 9 meters, or 29.5 feet. Tourists can use the visitor center and handle its exhibits. Houses of the Neolithic have been rebuilt with authentic materials and methods, including thatch on the roofs, based on finds nearby. Volunteers show old rope weaving, pottery making, and the grinding of grain. Yearly visits top nine hundred thousand. Two children try to drag a sarsen stone. Other visitors step into reconstructed huts of the kind the builders might have lived in.

9An ancient time and place left this amazing landmark. Visitors are struck by how cleverly the designers aimed the monument at the sun. Massive stones let people picture hundreds of workers moving them to the site together. Teamwork and muscle, visitors may realize, were required to raise the stones and to link them. For centuries the circle was a central sacred site for people of the surrounding lands. UNESCO, the United Nations body for education, science, and culture, gave it the title World Heritage Site. Special recognition and protection were the judgment. Imaginations around the world are stirred by it today. England has other stone circles. A larger one stands at Avebury, 40 kilometers, or 25 miles, to the north. A lintel is a piece of stone or of wood. It lies over an opening. A window is one such opening. A door is another. Scientists who study remains of ancient cultures are archaeologists. Ceremonial describes what relates to a formal event, or what is used for one on a special occasion. Large stones that prehistoric people built with, or set up as monuments, are megaliths. An embankment is dirt piled as a wall or as a mound. It may hold up a road. It may keep water back. Neolithic names the Stone Age's latest stretch. Polished stone tools and weapons mark that stretch. A way of life, a tradition, or a trait passed from one generation to the next is heritage. Quarries are dig sites for stone. Marble comes from them too. So does slate. Cleverness or skill used on a problem or a challenge is ingenuity. Returned to an earlier condition is what restored means. A solstice is one of two moments in a year. At those moments the Sun stands farthest from the equator. Creating something new and original is what innovative means.

78. The Boy King and a Death Unsolved

1A British archaeologist named Howard Carter found the tomb of King Tut. A photo shows him studying the golden sarcophagus while the dig was underway. This book follows the find, Tut's homeland, his family, the boy who ruled, the end of a ruling line, the tomb, the suspects, the body, the question of a solution, and words to know. The date of the find was November 4, 1922. The place was Egypt's Valley of the Kings. Egyptian workers helped him. The tomb belonged to Tutankhamun. Say that name toot-an-KAH-muhn. Most people say King Tut. His reign in ancient Egypt sits more than 3,300 years in the past. He became pharaoh at age nine. Say pharaoh FAIR-oh. His rule lasted under ten years. Death came suddenly when he was about nineteen. Ever since the burial was found, people have asked how the young king died. They have asked why. Archaeologists work a bit like detectives. Pronounce that job title in two beats: AR-kee, then OLL-oh-jist. They study evidence. They ask questions. Answers are often hard to reach. The work feels like a jigsaw that is missing many pieces. They study the tomb. They study the body. They study the person's belongings. They also study writing on papyrus. They study words cut into stone. Some of those texts lasted through the centuries. The questions include where Tut lived. They include what his health was like. They include who his family and friends were. They include whether he had enemies. Those answers may unlock the largest question. Why did this king die so young?

2Ruling families called dynasties governed ancient Egypt for about three thousand years. There were thirty of those families. Historians sort them into periods. The list runs from the Early Dynastic Period to the Old Kingdom. Then comes the First Intermediate Period. Then the Middle Kingdom. Then the Second Intermediate Period. Then the New Kingdom. Then the Third Intermediate Period. The Late Period closes the list. A kingdom was a time of strong central government. An intermediate period was a time of weaker central government. Tutankhamun belonged to the 18th Dynasty. That family was the first to rule in the New Kingdom. The New Kingdom began around 1550 BCE. Tut's birth came almost two hundred years after that beginning. In that Egypt, religion filled daily life. People worshipped hundreds of deities. A fuller picture of Tut's life, and maybe of his death, needs that religious history. One image shows how Tut may have looked, with his funeral mask behind him. At the opening of the New Kingdom, two gods stood above the rest. One was Ra. Say it RAH. The other was Amun. Say it AH-muhn. People believed Ra lived inside the Sun. Art often showed him as a falcon. It also showed him as a man with a falcon's head. A sun disk sat on his headdress. His main center of worship was Heliopolis. Heliopolis lies near today's Cairo. Art usually showed Amun as a man. His headdress was tall and carried two plumes. His main center of worship was Thebes. Thebes lies near today's Luxor. In the 18th Dynasty, Sun worship took a new form for some Egyptians. They took an old sun symbol, the Aten. Say it AH-tuhn. They treated the Aten as a new god who created the world. Art showed a large golden disk. Rays of light reached from the disk toward Earth. The rays often stopped close to royal faces. Each ray ended in a hand. The hand held an ankh. The ankh stood for life. A map shows ancient Egypt.

3As the Aten grew more important to nobles, other gods received less worship. For most people the Aten was simply one more god among many. Some household shrines included him. He was no threat to older beliefs until a young man became pharaoh. That man was Amenhotep IV. Say it ah-muhn-HO-tep. His rule began in 1352 BCE. Egyptian art gives him a long face. It gives him thin calves. It gives him a belly that sticks out. Many theories try to explain why his pictures differ from the usual Egyptian style. Various diseases are among those theories. Some experts think artists gave the Aten female features. They say the god had traits shared by men and by women. Amenhotep grew up inside the newer Aten faith. He saw the Aten as a god for every person in the world. The god was not for Egyptians alone. Aside from Cleopatra, no Egyptian queen is as famous as Nefertiti. Say it neh-fer-TEE-tee. Pharaoh Akhenaten favored her above his other wives. Once the prince's mother died, Nefertiti likely raised young Prince Tutankhaten as a stepmother. That prince later became Tutankhamun. Death came for Nefertiti while she was still in her early thirties. The pharaoh believed the Aten made the world at the start of time. He believed the Aten ruled it alone. He believed the bright rays kept giving the world life. Some experts give Amenhotep IV the title of first monotheist in the world. Others say that label does not fit. He admitted other gods existed. He simply chose to worship only the Aten. He expected Egyptians to worship him. He believed he stood equal to the god. The people did not accept that. At home they kept the old gods. Public worship was aimed at Amenhotep IV. Early in his fifth year he took a drastic step. He began a religious revolution. That means a sudden, total change in Egypt's official religion. He announced that public worship could honor only the Aten. He took a new name, Akhenaten. Say it ahk-eh-NAH-tuhn. The name means He Who Serves Aten.

4Akhenaten shut temples where people worshipped Egypt's other gods. He tried to destroy those temples. Public holidays tied to gods other than the Aten were banned. Religious festivals tied to those gods were banned too. His harsh acts upset a huge population used to many gods. The priests who served those gods were angered. People in several Egyptian regions tried to halt the wrecking of nearby temples. The pharaoh's army was able to control them. He also ordered a new capital. The chosen ground had never held a building. The site was north of Thebes. He called it Akhetaten. Say it ahk-eh-TAH-tuhn. The name means Horizon of Aten. Priests of Amun and followers of Amun called the move a heresy. It went against the religion most Egyptians accepted. Today the area is called Amarna. The upheaval is called the Amarna Revolution. A temple carving at Amarna shows Akhenaten and Nefertiti. Nefertiti may have been Tut's stepmother. Three of their children appear with them. King Tut was born in that new capital. The year was about 1345 BCE. His name was Tutankhaten. The name means the Living Image of Aten. Genetic tests in 2010 let researchers name the mummies of his parents. They identified mummies of his grandparents too. The tests used DNA taken from bones. Tut's father matched the mummy who may be Akhenaten. They built a family tree of five generations. The tests show Tut's mother as a full sister of Tut's father. The samples could not identify her any further. Royal families in Egypt often married close relatives. Other cultures of that time did the same. The marriages kept land inside the family. They kept the power that came with the land. Akhenaten died in 1336 BCE. He had ruled for seventeen years. The next events puzzle people as much as Tut's other mysteries do. At best, the old evidence does not go far. Scholars have offered several theories about who took the throne next. In the last century they found signs of two rulers with very short reigns after Akhenaten. One was Smenkhkara. Say it smen-kah-RAH. Akhenaten may have been his brother. Tutankhaten may have been his brother. The other short ruler may have been Nefertiti. The proof is still too thin for anyone to be certain. The throne stood empty again within three or four years of Akhenaten's death. Tutankhaten became pharaoh at age nine.

5Before his reign, and during it, Tut lived as a wealthy person. He wore jewelry of gold and of silver. He wore linen clothes. He used perfumed oils. He used makeup. Archaeologists found all of these kinds of things in his tomb. Court custom would have sent the pharaoh hunting beside his royal companions. The hunt often used a bow. It often used a moving chariot. Two chariots were placed in the tomb. Nearly fifty bows were placed there. Board games were placed there for the afterlife. The games included senet. They included hounds and jackals. During his reign he married his half-sister Ankhesenpaaten. Say it AHNK-eh-suhn-PAH-ah-tuhn. Nefertiti and Akhenaten's third daughter was this queen. She Lives Through Aten is the meaning of her name. At least two girls were born to Tut. Both daughters died. Several servants worked in his court. His personal attendant was Tutu. Years of service to the family were already behind Tutu, as with many house workers. The service went back to Tut's grandfather. That grandfather was King Amenhotep III. Other servants, some younger than the king, helped with even the smallest tasks. One servant was a cupbearer. The cupbearer's job was to keep drinking cups full. The young king's cup came first. Military decisions mostly fell to other people, since the pharaoh was only a boy. They did most of the political work. Two men mattered most. Ay was one of them, and he was old. His title was Commander of Chariotry. He had been a chief administrative adviser since Akhenaten's reign. Horemheb, the second man, was a general in the army. Say it HOR-ehm-heb. His titles included Great General of the Army. Both men had served Akhenaten. People think both strongly disliked Akhenaten's religious changes. They hoped the young king would restore the old gods. They hoped he would restore the old ways of worship. Horemheb appears in a wall painting as King Tut's general and adviser.

6Ruins remain from Akhenaten's city of Akhetaten. The city was built around 1348 BCE. Tut felt the pressure of Horemheb and of Ay. They persuaded him to end worship of the Aten. Above all they wanted Amun restored as chief god. The boy king followed their lead. Tutankhaten was set aside. The new name was Tutankhamun. The new name means the Living Image of Amun. The queen took a new name too. She became Ankhesenamun. Say it AHNK-eh-suhn-AH-muhn. By swapping Aten for Amun in their names, king and queen sent a message. Priests of the older faith could read those names as a sign that royalty was dropping Aten worship. Historians are sure Ay and Horemheb drove the changes of Tut's reign. Tut was very young. Historians believe he did what he was told. As part of the return to older ways, the court moved back to Thebes. Akhetaten, once thriving, was left to decay under the Egyptian sun. In 1327 BCE, King Tutankhamun died. He was about nineteen. Ancient texts never officially recorded how he died. That silence created a mystery. Workers mummified the young pharaoh. His grave was a tomb set inside the Valley of the Kings. Near Thebes, that valley served as a large cemetery for royalty. Other New Kingdom kings were buried in the same way. Tut had no surviving children. The throne was open to another person in the royal court. Ay had long experience there. That experience made him the new pharaoh. He married Tut's widow. Ankhesenamun never appears in the historical record after that. Ay ruled only four years. He died in 1323 BCE. Horemheb then became pharaoh. A pharaoh, like a person today, had more than one name. There was a name from birth. Other names came when the person became pharaoh. Those names often sat inside an oval. The oval is a cartouche. Say it car-TOOSH. Ancient Egyptians believed names held great power. They thought a name written on an object could harm that person if the object was broken. They thought it could even kill the person.

7After sixteen years on the throne, Horemheb ordered a destruction. Everything linked to the Aten religion was to be destroyed. Everything linked to Akhenaten was to be destroyed. He wanted a break from earlier leaders. He wanted to show devotion to Amun. He even counted his own reign as if it began when Amenhotep III's reign ended. He acted as if Amenhotep IV had never ruled. He acted as if Tut had never ruled. He acted as if Ay had never ruled. His men demolished the Aten's abandoned temples at Amarna and in other parts of Egypt. They smashed statues of Akhenaten and of his family. Statues of King Tut were smashed. Statues of Ay were smashed. They gouged names and faces out of wall art. Later, workers took away the stone blocks that carried that art. A digger there always hopes to meet a ruler's tomb that is still sealed. Twenty-seven years passed under Horemheb's rule. He died in 1295 BCE. His death ended the 18th Dynasty. Ramses II came afterward, a major ruler in the 19th Dynasty. Ramses II's grandfather had served in the army with Horemheb. Ramses II kept taking building stone from the site. That plunder finished the destruction of Amarna. Broken pieces of Akhenaten's once-splendid capital vanished under drifting sand. People forgot the city. In the 1800s, many archaeologists from Britain and from Europe went to Egypt. They wanted to read Egyptian writing called hieroglyphics. Say it hy-ur-uh-GLIF-iks. The writing covered many walls and monuments. It revealed a great deal about how pharaohs lived. Scholars had long been stuck on that ancient writing. In 1798 Napoleon brought an army to occupy Egypt. A soldier in that army found an object more lasting than the occupation itself. It was a flat black rock. Three languages were carved on its surface. Two were forms of ancient Egyptian. The third was Greek. Translation of the remaining languages took the following twenty-five years. They used the Greek text as a key. They used knowledge of Coptic, an Egyptian language, as a key. Progress jumped when a single scholar noticed a key difference. Ancient Egyptian was not simple picture writing. Its symbols stood for sounds, not for whole words. The Rosetta Stone, that same rock, still ranks among archaeology's greatest finds.

8Archaeologists learned that a pharaoh's tomb held whatever a person might need after death. They dug up many tombs in hope of money from those sacred objects. They were always disappointed. Robbers had already emptied those tombs many years earlier. Early in the 1900s, scholars still believed one royal tomb there had never been located. It was the tomb of Tutankhamun. They believed every other known pharaoh there had already been found. A determined British archaeologist, Howard Carter, hunted for Tut. More than five years brought no success. His patron agreed in 1922 to pay for a final season of digging. The patron was the fifth Earl of Carnarvon. Time was running out. Then his luck changed. Later that year he found the tomb. Almost nothing in it had been disturbed. The riches included thrones. They included jewelry, weapons, and statues. They even included food for the afterlife. Tutankhamun's mummy wore a large gold mask. It lay inside three coffins, one nested in the next. Those coffins sat in a sarcophagus of quartzite. Four shrines of wood covered with gilt were nested around the sarcophagus. They filled the room. The innermost coffin was pure gold. It weighed about 242 pounds. That weight is 110 kilograms. Carter's find caused a sensation. No pharaoh in history became better known than Tut. Carter could open the tomb only with permission from Egypt's government. In the late 1800s that government wrote rules for foreign archaeologists. One rule said that an intact tomb must keep every artifact in Egypt. Carter argued with the government. His claim was that the burial had already been opened. He claimed he could take half the treasure back to England. In the end, every artifact stayed in Egypt. The golden funeral mask stayed. The jewelry stayed. The statues stayed. Today Egypt's government works with researchers from other countries. It allows objects from the tomb to travel on tour. Egyptians have the last word on that treasure.

9Dying young was not rare in ancient times. In ancient Egypt the average life lasted about thirty years. Many people did not even reach that age. Even so, some historians had reasons to suspect foul play. They saw a teenage king already weak from disease. They saw genetic disabilities. Motives belonged to several figures around the throne and the ruling household. Ay and Horemheb guided many of Tut's decisions. Both became pharaohs after he died. Tut had no natural heir. If they wanted power, they had to move before any child of Tut survived. They also had to move before adulthood let him shove both advisers away. Ay showed a hunger for power by marrying Tut's widow. Horemheb may have drawn suspicion from some people of that time. A statue in his tomb carries an inscription. That carved text declares his innocence in any wrongful killing. The words might instead concern Ay's death. Horemheb's turn came after only a brief rule by Ay. If Tut was murdered, those two men were the likeliest suspects. Other people also fell under suspicion. Some researchers named two servants as possible killers. One was the cupbearer, who could reach the king's drink without limit. The other was Tutu, who could reach the king himself without limit. Few people were allowed into the king's bedroom. Those two were among them. Either man could have killed the pharaoh. A heavy object might have struck the king's head. A push might have sent him down stairs. Poison might have gone into his food or his drink. A wall painting of Ay was found in Tut's tomb.

10For years, people guessed that a blow to the head killed Tut. Pictures from X-ray work on the mummy supported that guess. One study came in 1968. Another came in 1978. Both came from the School of Dentistry at the University of Michigan. The pictures showed damage at the back of the skull. Experts called that damage strong proof. They said a heavy object had hit the back of his head. In 2005, researchers in Cairo decided to test that idea. An Egyptian archaeologist, Dr. Zahi Hawass, led the group. An advanced form of X-ray was the tool they used on the mummy. The method is CT scanning, also called CAT scanning. A CT scanner takes many X-rays. Each X-ray comes from a different angle. A computer turns that information into images. Those images are much more detailed than pictures from an ordinary X-ray machine. Hawass announced a clear result. A blow to the head was definitely not the cause of death. In his view the harm to the skull came after death, which is what postmortem means. That word means it happened after death. Tut was already dead. The damage probably came during mummification. A photo shows Dr. Zahi Hawass beside Tut. The mummy is about to go into the CT machine. The scans also showed several physical problems the young king lived with. He had a cleft palate. He had a club foot. Walking was extremely painful. He needed a cane. Walking sticks in the tomb, canes among them, numbered more than 130, and they were decorated. The scans showed something else that might explain the death. Shortly before he died, he suffered a broken leg. The leg had not healed properly. Hawass said an infection may have grown from that injury. Death may have come a few days later. A different group of experts finds no trace of infection. Between 2007 and 2010, the remains got another look from Hawass and fellow researchers. This time they used genetic tests. Two important conditions appeared that they had not seen before. One was repeated attacks of severe malaria. Malaria was common in Egypt. By itself the disease probably would not have killed him. Great weakness may have followed that illness. The other finding was bone necrosis. That is a breakdown of bone. It was in the bones of his left foot. The condition may have left him open to other infections. Those other infections have not yet been found.

11Does the mystery end there? Did the young king die from physical problems piled together? Did an accident play a part? Did a disease play a part? Did an infection from the broken leg play a part? Could the cause simply have been natural? Some members of the Hawass team, once the scans were read, suggested a different story. The leg may have broken while Tut was being embalmed. Other scholars still feel sure of a different cause. They think Howard Carter's team broke the leg. The break would have come years ago, when the team lifted the body from its coffin. Poison is still possible. A failed attack might also explain the broken leg. If any of those ideas is right, definite proof may never appear. More evidence keeps arriving. More pieces of the jigsaw keep turning up. Theories about how the young king lived become easier to test. Theories about how he died become easier to test. Different experts may still read the same clues in different ways. What is your reading? A photo shows Carter's team taking objects out of the tomb. Words to know. An archaeologist is a scientist who studies what ancient cultures left behind. Deities, in religions with one god, are the supreme beings and creators. In religions with many gods, deities are those gods or goddesses. Deterioration means becoming worse as time passes. Dynasties are lines of rulers from one family in a country. Embalmed means a dead body was treated so it would not decay. A headdress is fancy wear for the head, and ceremonies are a common time to use one. Hieroglyphics is a writing system of pictures or symbols. Those marks can stand for words, syllables, or sounds. Ancient Egyptians used it instead of an alphabet. An inscription is words cut into stone or metal. Belief in a single god is what makes a person a monotheist. Papyrus is a paper made from stalks of a grasslike plant. Ancient cultures used it. A pharaoh is a ruler of ancient Egypt. Postmortem means happening after death. Protruding means sticking out. Remnants are small parts left after the rest is gone. In ancient times, a sarcophagus was a coffin or a tomb cut from stone. It is often carved and richly decorated. Terminated means reached an end, or caused something to end. Unrestricted means having no limits. Vast means great in size, in number, or in amount.

79. The Branch Led by the President

1President Johnson signs the 1964 Civil Rights Act. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. stands just behind him and watches. The parts of this book come in this order. An opening scene comes first. Next is how the Constitution sets up the president’s branch. Then comes the way Americans pick a president. Then come the offices inside that branch. Then comes the work a president does. Then come famous actions by that branch. Then comes the system that limits each branch. A closing comes after that. A word list comes last. Opening Lyndon B. Johnson faced the television cameras. He began, “My fellow Americans.” He told the country he would now make the Civil Rights Act law. The year of that act was 1964. Johnson said people of every race must be treated the same. Classrooms were included. Hotels were included. Restaurants were included. The voting booth was included. Before this law, Black Americans were barred from the schools white Americans used. They were barred from the same restaurants. Voting was often blocked for Black Americans. The country is still working so that every person can vote. Johnson ended his speech and signed. Each letter got a new pen. Each period got a new pen. Each dash got a new pen. He used more than seventy-five pens before he finished. The pens became gifts for supporters standing in the room. King was one of the people who received a pen.

2That signing was a major day in the history of the country. A president’s ordinary day is still packed. Members of Congress may come in for a meeting. A speech may go out on television. A school or a hospital may get a visit. A bill may be signed into law. Leaders from other countries may be hosted. The president leads the U.S. government. No two days match. This is the executive branch doing its work. The Executive Branch Inside the Constitution American leaders adopted the Constitution in 1788. It set out laws and principles for governing a young country. The system has changed as it grew, but it is still in force. The document is a plan for the government. Three parts, called branches, divide the government. The president leads the executive branch. That branch runs most government work and most departments. The legislative branch is the House of Representatives together with the Senate. It speaks for citizens and writes laws. The judicial branch runs the justice system through courts. At times the branches work together and meet in the middle. At other times they stand against each other. Article II of the Constitution states what the executive branch may do. Its job is to carry out laws that Congress has written. To do that, it names the people who head federal agencies. The cabinet is part of that group. Writers of the Constitution argued about this branch. Who would be trusted to put laws into action? England’s king had just been defied in a rebellion. Some writers feared a single head of state with too much power. A return to rule by one king was what they feared. George Washington served first in the office. His service began in April 1789. It ended in March 1797. He also signed the Constitution, as one of 39 men.

3Once the Revolutionary War ended, leaders tried a different system. They tested a government in which nobody was assigned to enforce the laws. That government collapsed after eight years. The people who framed the Constitution decided the country needed a powerful office to lead the government. One person would lead it. That person is the president. They gave this office wide powers. At times this leader may decide without the others, when the nation needs that speed. This office is nothing like a throne. Voters choose who holds the office. Congress watches many of the president’s acts. Federal courts watch them too. Three basic tests are written into the Constitution. The president must be at least 35 years old. The president must be a citizen by birth. The president must have lived in the country for 14 years or longer. John F. Kennedy was 43 when he entered office. To this day he is the youngest person elected president. Americans pick a president through a set of steps. Pure democracy is not the system used here. That system would give every citizen an equal say in each decision. It is a representative democracy instead. People elect officials, and those officials decide in the public’s name. A presidential election shows how this works. When citizens mark a choice for president, that vote is not the last word. Article II says electors from each state make the choice. Those electors form the Electoral College. The word college makes people think of a campus. No classes meet there. It is a group of voters whose job is to select the president. Victory in the nationwide vote of the people usually brings the presidency as well. That pattern does break. Population sets how many electoral votes each state receives. A small state gets more electors per person than a large state does. Small states then have a voice. States with more people cannot simply run the election. Many voters still dislike this college. They dislike it because one person’s vote does not count the same as another’s.

4In 2016, Hillary Clinton was the nominee on the left of a photo. Donald Trump was the nominee on the right. Nearly three million more people marked a ballot for Clinton. Trump still took the election, because he collected more electoral votes. A close nationwide count can let electoral votes decide the winner. The winner can be someone with fewer votes across the whole country. Winning the electoral votes that matter in certain states is enough. By 2020, five presidents had lost the popular vote and still won the electoral vote. Offices in the Executive Branch Many agencies and officials report to the president. They help carry out the laws. A vice president is part of the branch. Voters elect the vice president on the same ticket as the president. Several duties belong to the vice president. One is casting a vote that breaks a tie in the Senate. Another is stepping in if the president cannot keep serving. Sometimes a president dies. Sometimes a president must leave for another reason. The order of who comes next is fixed. The vice president is first. The Speaker who leads the House is second. Next is the Senate officer known as president pro tempore. After that come the heads of departments. The secretary of state is the first of those heads. More than once in U.S. history, a vice president has moved into the top office. Death of the person in office is one reason. Resignation is another. After John F. Kennedy was assassinated, Lyndon B. Johnson took his place. That happened in 1963. Richard Nixon later stepped down, and Gerald Ford replaced him. That happened in 1974. Laws from Congress are carried out through a wide net of federal agencies and departments. The Central Intelligence Agency is one agency. The Environmental Protection Agency is another. The Treasury Department is one department. The Education Department is another. The president appoints many of the people who lead these offices. Those leaders form the cabinet. Agencies have multiplied since those first years. Only four people sat in the cabinet Washington assembled. The cabinet now has more than a dozen.

5The president’s work is set out in the Constitution. Article II gives the president wide powers. One example is command of the armed forces. American forces can be sent anywhere in the world. The purpose may be to keep peace. The purpose may be to protect interests of the United States. The president may also pardon people guilty of federal crimes. State crimes are outside that power. Diplomacy means handling the nation’s ties with other countries. That work belongs to the president and to this branch. The president names ambassadors. The Senate must confirm them. Those ambassadors represent the country in other lands. In 2018, Elizabeth Richards spoke with Lebanon’s army chief of staff. Her post was ambassador in Lebanon. Peanuts brought in from other countries face a tax near 164 percent. The point is to help peanut farmers in this country. The president can make trade agreements with other countries. American companies are the ones these deals are meant to aid. Tariffs are another tool this office can set. A tariff is a special tax on goods the country imports. A huge number of officials are appointed by the president. Supreme Court justices are among them. Cabinet members are among them. Heads of agencies are among them. The Senate must approve many of these choices. This office also fills a great many jobs. While one Congress serves its two years, this office names people for almost 70,000 jobs. Federal judges are in that group. U.S. attorneys are in that group. Ambassadors and others are in it too. The Senate usually approves most names quickly. That is not always true. Nominees for the Supreme Court nearly always face a hard review before the Senate says yes.

6The president has a large part in how laws come to be. This branch does not write the laws. It can accept a law Congress has made, or it can refuse it. Both houses must pass a bill by a majority vote. The bill then goes to the president. A signature turns the bill into law. The president can say no to the bill with a veto. A vetoed bill does not become law on its own. It becomes law only if Congress votes it through again. Two-thirds of the members in each house must vote yes. That second vote overrides the veto. The refusals by presidents now add up to more than 2,500 bills. In March 1985, Ronald Reagan vetoed a bill. The bill would have sent aid to farmers. These famous actions are another power of this branch. The president can also issue executive actions. They tell federal offices what this leader wants done. They direct what the government does. Some of these choices change daily life for citizens in a deep way. During the Civil War, Abraham Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation. The year was 1863. It said that enslaved people in the rebel states of the South shall be forever free. In 1935, Franklin D. Roosevelt ordered a new agency into being. It was the Works Progress Administration, the WPA. It hired thousands of Americans. The jobs came when the Great Depression was at its worst. That depression filled the 1930s. WPA workers built roads. They planted trees. They even painted murals. In 1939, men from the Civilian Conservation Corps planted seedlings. The hillside in Oregon had been cut clear of trees. Like the WPA, the CCC was his project for putting people to work.

7An executive order in 1942 forced a Japanese American family from home. They were among 117,000 people sent to live in prison camps. Some executive orders have done harm. One infamous case followed a surprise attack. Japan struck Pearl Harbor, in Hawai'i. Because of that strike, this country entered the Second World War. That war ran from 1939 to 1945. After the attack, Roosevelt signed an order. It let officials order citizens of Japanese ancestry to leave the places they lived. They were placed in detention camps. Inside the camps, officials treated them as if they opposed their own country. People call Franklin Delano Roosevelt FDR. He was president number thirty-two. He was the first president elected four times. He is still the only one. His years in office ran from 1933 to 1945. In that time he guided the country for nearly the whole of that war. He died in 1945, just before the war ended. After his death, an amendment to the Constitution capped the presidency at two terms. The Constitution makes each branch a check on the others. The three branches are executive, legislative, and judicial. No one branch is supposed to take too much power. The veto is one check on the lawmaking branch. Congress checks the president in return. It can accept or reject people named to the Supreme Court. It can accept or reject cabinet appointees. Treaties also need the Senate’s approval. A treaty is a peace agreement between nations. A formal declaration of war belongs to Congress alone. Overriding a veto is difficult, so Congress has another path. It can revise the bill. Parts the president dislikes can be cut or changed. If the new version passes, the president may sign it the next time.

8Richard Nixon speaks a farewell to his staff. The day is the one after he resigned in 1974. Congress can also remove a president through impeachment. The House is where the charges are written down. The House votes on whether to send the case to the Senate. The Senate then holds a trial. A guilty finding removes the president from office. The House has voted to impeach a president four times. Andrew Johnson’s term was 1865 to 1869. Bill Clinton’s term was 1993 to 2001. Donald Trump faced impeachment two times between 2017 and 2021. The Senate cleared all three men. Steps toward impeachment also began against Richard Nixon. His term was 1969 to 1974. The formal vote never came, because he left office first. The executive branch checks the judicial branch as well. The judicial branch checks the other two. It decides whether Congress’s laws follow the Constitution. It decides whether the president’s orders follow the Constitution. Courts halted immigration orders that Barack Obama had issued. In 2014 he tried to use such an action in two ways. Some immigrants without papers would get work permits. Deportation would be blocked for them. The Supreme Court stopped those actions. A photo shows Obama in 2014. The people who framed the Constitution first gave more power to the lawmaking branch than to the executive. Since then, executive power has grown. One old check has slipped into the background. The last time Congress declared war was 1942. Every military action since then has been led by the executive branch without that declaration. The Vietnam War is one example. The Iraq Wars are another.

9A painting from 1856 shows George Washington speaking. The scene is the Constitutional Convention of 1787. Closing So far, the government the framers set up in 1788 has bent without breaking. It has recovered from strain. What this branch is allowed to do tends to shift as years pass. The way people read the Constitution shifts too. Even so, this branch has been able to carry out the nation’s laws. The lawmaking branch still limits the president. The courts still limit the president. The three branches stay in balance. What ties the three together is the Constitution. What a president is able to do will probably keep shifting. New challenges in the years ahead will shape that change. Words to Know pardon (v.): to forgive a mistake or a wrong act. cabinet (n.): the circle of people who advise a president, or who advise another country’s leader. resilient (adj.): able to get past trouble, or to recover quickly. dominate (v.): to control something, or to overpower it. trade agreements (n.): deals between countries about how goods and services will be exchanged. executive (adj.): describing the part of government that heads the country and puts its laws into effect. veto (n.): a refusal to approve a bill, so the bill does not become law. federal (adj.): belonging to the national government that splits power with the states or with regions. acquitted (v.): cleared by an official finding that no crime or wrong was proved. impeachment (n.): a formal charge of wrongdoing brought against someone. ambassadors (n.): officials who travel to a place, or live there, to represent their country or its people. overriding (v.): taking over from something else, canceling it, or putting something in its place.

80. The Case of the Disappearing Honeybees

1A healthy honeybee colony moves into a new hive. Think of your favorite fruit. Imagine a world where that fruit is very rare or gone. Many nuts, vegetables, and flowers could be gone too. Honeybees do more than make honey. They pollinate plant blossoms, and one in three bites of food comes from their work. In 2007, honeybee numbers began to fall fast, and the reason puzzled scientists. The problem slowed, but the first cause is still a mystery, and researchers still work to save the bees.

2Honeybees live in colonies where each bee does a special task, and they must work together. A lone honeybee outside may not survive more than twenty-four hours. They collect pollen and nectar, and one healthy hive can visit more than 100,000 flowers a day. Pollen moves from anthers to pistils, and pollination leads to seeds. In October 2006, a Florida beekeeper found four hundred hives nearly empty after three healthy weeks. Only food, baby bees, and a few queens remained, and twenty million bees had vanished. No dead bees lay on the ground, and full frames were later empty. The same losses appeared in the United States, Europe, China, and other regions.

3In the winter of 2006 to 2007, about 750,000 of 2.4 million U.S. bee colonies vanished. Beekeepers lost 38 percent on average, and two billion bees vanished in California almond groves in 2008. Scientists named this colony collapse disorder, or CCD. Most bees vanish in weeks, few dead bees are found, and only the young and the queen stay. Tests of wax, pollen, and bees showed many diseases and weak immune systems. Fungal bacteria made eating hard, and acute bee paralysis virus showed up in many CCD hives.
