These germs seemed to be results of CCD, not the cause. A mite called Varroa destructor sucks bee blood and leaves open wounds.

4Nosema apis is another parasite. It makes spores that infect bee intestines and eat the bee from the inside. These parasites were known before, so something else seemed to trigger CCD. Years ago, small family farms grew many crops. Today many huge farms grow just one crop, such as wheat, corn, or soybeans. One bloom season leaves bees with no pollen or nectar after the flowers fade. In the United States, farmers try to spray when plants are not blooming, yet pesticides still showed up in CCD hives. More than a billion pounds of chemicals are used on crops each year.

5Neonics are systemic pesticides that spread from treated seeds through the whole plant. They last a long time, kill pests, and some scientists link them to a fast rise in CCD. They may weaken immune systems or harm how bees learn, remember, and navigate. Timing matches CCD, but research now points to a mix of causes, not one cause. In 1958, Mao Zedong’s Great Sparrow Campaign killed hundreds of millions of sparrows in China. Locusts ate the crops, up to 45 million people starved, and heavy pesticide use later left some areas without bees. Farm workers now use cotton swabs to pollinate fruit trees, bloom by bloom. Bees have lived 150 million years, but for 10,000 years people have changed how and where bees work.

6Ancient Egyptians floated beehives on rafts down the Nile to follow the bloom. Today, trucks move hives all over the United States. Bees pollinate about 15 billion dollars of food there each year. Around Valentine’s Day, bees work 600,000 acres, or 242,811 hectares, of blooming California almond trees. Almond trees need honeybees, and managed colonies fell fast as the call for pollinators grew. After the bloom, bees are shipped again, and sugar water instead of nectar is like junk food. Millions die from the stress of these trips. Crops that need bees most include almond, apple, broccoli, blueberry, cherry, cucumber, watermelon, tangerine, lemon, cotton, peanut, and grape.

7By one estimate, two-thirds of all U.S. bees meet on these huge farms. Travel spreads parasites and disease, and antibiotics in sugar water can weaken bees and kill helpful bacteria. Over time, bacteria may resist those drugs. CCD seems to be a mix of biological, chemical, and physical stresses, with no single full cure yet. Prevention has improved, and CCD rates have dropped, but not enough. The Africanized honeybee is a hybrid of European and African honeybees. Some escaped a Brazilian lab in 1957, reached the United States in 1990, and are more defensive but healthier. They do make honey and pollinate, and some beekeepers welcome them as an answer to CCD.

8Honeybees need many kinds of plants, and native wildflowers give a longer foraging season. People can plant native blooms in yards so bees meet fewer pesticides. Rooftop and backyard pollinator gardens are popular in rural and urban places. Bees visit parks and gardens, make honey, and pollinate native fruit trees and plants. Colony collapse is falling, but many native bees are endangered and may die out. Neat lawns, fewer native plants, and more crop honeybees make food and shelter hard for wild bees. Farmers can set aside land for native plants that feed bees all year, not just a few weeks. Bees help many species, including humans, so protecting them helps us too.

9Apiaries are hive places, pollinate means moving pollen to fertilize a flower, and fertilization joins male and female cells. A pathogen causes disease, parasites feed on others, and pesticides kill harmful animals or plants. Systemic means affecting a whole body, and a disorder is an unhealthy condition. Demise is an end or death, onset is a start, and compromised means damaged. To forage is to search for food, and migratory means moving between regions at set times. Contagion is a spreading illness, and susceptible means easily harmed. Sanctuaries are safe places, and bustling means rushed and noisy. Gruesome means causing shock or disgust.

81. The Creator's Fast Field Game

1This book asks why the sport dazzles, where it began, who can play, how the rules work, who the heroes are, and how an old game faces the future. A word list closes it. A photo shows a Cornell player carrying the ball against Syracuse. This thrilling game grew from a field contest that ranks among the oldest on Earth. Europeans who reached North America took the game from First Nations people. Those Native players had used various forms for centuries. It is the fastest game played on a field. It is also one of the hardest and most exciting to play. Watching it is exciting too. It shares a great deal with soccer. It shares a great deal with hockey and with basketball. Through most of the 1900s, athletes who played it were fairly few. They lived in only a few regions. Popularity is now booming. The sport is moving into the mainstream, above all as a youth sport.

2Experts think the game grew among the Algonquin tribes. Their home was the valley of the St. Lawrence River. That valley is in today's Canada and in today's New York. In time the game traveled far west. It traveled far south. Tribes used different names. The Algonquin name is baggataway. The old form was very unlike today's game. A field could stretch for miles. A side rarely had fewer than one hundred players. Sometimes a side had as many as one thousand. Most tribes still used a curved stick. The stick was 3 to 4 feet long. That length is 0.9 to 1.2 meters. A net on the stick passed the ball, carried it, and shot it. The ball was stuffed deerskin. Early contests were huge. They could last as long as three days. A sketch by the artist H.W. Hall shows First Nations players and other players. A large crowd in Canada is watching. First Nations people treated the game as a sacred rite. They believed the gods watched over it. Many tribes called it the Creator's game. They used it to toughen young men. They used it to strengthen them. They used it to settle large tribal disputes. They used it to strengthen tribal fellowship. A demonstration by a local tribe took place in 1834. The crowd was mostly white and Canadian. The place was a racecourse in Montreal, in Quebec. The game took hold in that region. Soon Canada had many clubs for white players. It had many clubs for First Nations players too. George Beers, a dentist in Montreal, set the rules on paper in 1860. Because today's rules rest on his, people call him the father of modern lacrosse. His rules set the size of the stick. They set the size of the ball and of the goal. They set how many players would take the field. They set the size of the field.

3The 1870s were the years when the sport surged inside the United States. Clubs appeared in New York City. They appeared in Baltimore, Boston, and Philadelphia. They appeared in Newport, Rhode Island. Boys in private schools played. Elite colleges in the Northeast played. Rosabelle Sinclair had been on the first international team from Scotland. She brought the women's game to Bryn Mawr School in Baltimore. Play was limited to the teams of these schools. People therefore treated it as a gentleman's sport. The joy of playing was the reason they took the field. They did not play for paying crowds. They did not play for advertisers. Gifted athletes who could have enlarged the sport chose not to join. They moved toward sports that offered fame and fortune. Another stall came from a lack of gear, including the sticks, called crosses. Before the 1970s, stick-making belonged to certain Mohawk artisans in Ontario, Canada. American demand was low, so factories had little cause to turn out sticks in bulk. They already mass-produced baseball gloves and basketballs. Cheaper sticks of light metal reached the market in the 1970s. From then on, American interest climbed sharply. Today men play all over the world. Women, boys, and girls play too. Some teams use an indoor form called box lacrosse. They play it in hockey rinks that have no ice. Outdoor tournaments often use football stadiums. Levels of play vary widely. The Federation of International Lacrosse is the group. Its nations come from around the globe. It holds a men's world championship every four years. It holds a women's world championship on the same cycle. North America has two leagues at the professional level. Major League Lacrosse is the outdoor league. It has eight teams. The National Lacrosse League is the indoor box league. It has nine teams. College teams for men and for women play hard in the United States and in Canada. Northeastern colleges have long treated the sport as huge and competitive. Interest is spreading fast. College programs now treat it as a major sport. The Summer Olympics included it twice, in 1904 and in 1908. A 1908 photo shows the Canadian winners.

4In the United States the fastest growth is at the youth level. High schools are growing fast too. As young people across the country take up the game, college play will surely grow. Pro play will grow as well. Outside North America, small devoted groups have long existed in Australia. They have long existed in England. Some of history's best players came out of northern England. Manchester, a large city, is the heart of that area. Over the last thirty years the sport has grown across Europe. It has grown across East Asia. It has grown across the globe. Someday it may be the next huge international sport. The game shares many traits with soccer, hockey, and basketball. It is still its own sport. The most distinctive tool is the crosse, the stick every player uses. Players cradle, catch, pass, and shoot with it. Cradling is a back-and-forth motion of the stick head. That motion keeps the ball in the pocket while the player runs. Hands on the ball are allowed for the goalie alone. In that limit, the rule matches soccer. Men wear more protective gear than women. The women's game allows less body contact, so their gear is lighter. Gear can include the crosse, an eye mask, a helmet, and a mouth guard. It can include shoulder pads, gloves, rib pads, and arm protectors. It can include cleats. Goalkeepers often add a throat guard and extra chest padding.

5Length of the stick's shaft runs from 2 feet to 5 feet. That length is 0.6 to 1.5 meters. A triangular head sits at the top. A net is fitted to the head. The goalkeeper's head is larger. The goal is 6 feet high. It is also 6 feet across. That height is 1.8 meters. The ball is rubber. Its circumference is about 8 inches, or 20 centimeters. A men's field is 110 yards long. That length is 101 meters. The field is 60 yards wide. That width is 55 meters. A midfield line crosses the field. An X marks the center. Every period opens with two rivals facing off on that mark. A whistle blows. Each player tries to win the ball. A men's team has ten players. Three attackers stay on the other team's half. Three defenders stay on their own half. Three midfielders cover the whole field. A goalkeeper guards the net. Women's fields carry fewer lines. Women's teams put twelve players on the field, not ten. The aim is the higher number of goals. A goal comes from hurling the ball into the other net. It can also come from bouncing the ball in. Whoever wins the face-off then sprints toward the opposite goal. That player may shoot. That player may pass to an attacker who is well placed to score. Defenders try to protect their goal. They try to take the ball. They may poke the carrier with their sticks. They may slap the carrier's stick so the ball pops free. The sport does not allow a tie. Sudden-death overtime settles a tied match. Playing time is one hour. Men split that hour into four quarters of fifteen minutes. Women split it into two halves. Women's play also zones the field differently. Body contact is much more limited in the women's game. Every form of the sport shares speed. The running is breathtaking. The maneuvering is breathtaking. The teamwork is complex and breathtaking. Shots at the goal can pass 100 miles per hour. That speed is 161 kilometers per hour.

6Oren R. Lyons is a legendary goalkeeper. The Onondaga Reservation was his childhood home. His most important work later happened away from the field. He played at Syracuse University. In 1957 that school named him an All-American. After sport, he became a spiritual leader. His title is Faithkeeper of the Onondaga. The Onondaga are one of six nations in the Iroquois Confederacy. Indigenous communities worldwide have gained from his humanitarian work. Jim Brown is remembered as one of football's all-time greats. In 1971, football's professional hall of fame added his name. His first love, though, was lacrosse. Many call him the greatest American player the sport has had. Manhasset, on Long Island in New York, was his hometown. That area has a long lacrosse culture. He excelled at Syracuse University. For him, no other game let his athletic gifts out so fully. Syracuse was also Gary Gait's school, just as it was for Jim Brown and for Oren R. Lyons. Gary and his twin, Paul, broke nearly every college record there was to break. The twins changed the sport through speed. They changed it through trick handling of the ball. Gary later succeeded in the National Lacrosse League. He succeeded in Major League Lacrosse too. He remains Syracuse's all-time leader in goals. He now coaches the women's team there. Jen Adams leads the women of Loyola University, which is in Maryland. Earlier, the young player left Australia for America and shattered many marks in the women's game. She is famous for speed. She is famous for agility. She is famous for team play and for sportsmanship. Her 445 points for Maryland's Terrapins set a record. In 2009 she played for Australia at the Women's Lacrosse World Cup.

7Oregon High School Lacrosse Association is the group behind the high-school match in the photo. Popularity today is higher than at any earlier time. Across hundreds of years, the older form belonged to First Nations people, and later the name lacrosse stuck. For many tribes it was a deep spiritual tradition. It was a political tradition too. People on every continent play it today. It is growing fast. More and more people are taking it up. Speed draws young athletes. So do the unusual challenges. So does the way teammates must play together. Youth clubs are appearing across North America. No one knows where the next Jen Adams will appear. No one knows when the next Jim Brown will appear. Words to know. Inducted means formally admitted to a group. Adapted means changed to fit a new situation. Agility means being able to move quickly and easily. Mainstream means the leading ideas, habits, or trends of a group. Cradle means to hold or support something gently. Maneuvering means moving around, or guiding how something moves. Gravitated means moved toward something, or became interested in it. A rite is a ceremony for a religious or other solemn event. Humanitarian describes work that helps people, especially by easing pain and suffering. Spiritual concerns a divine being, the soul, or the spirit. Zoning means setting an area apart because its features or its rules are special. Indigenous means native to a particular place.

82. The Farmer Who Swore the First Presidential Oath

1A painting shows Washington with his family at Mount Vernon. George Washington took the oath as the first president on April 30, 1789, in New York City. He looked out at the cheering crowd. Years earlier, he could not imagine this day when he took his first military job. He stood straight at Federal Hall as Robert Livingston came near with a Bible. Livingston was the chancellor of New York. Washington put his hand on the Bible and swore to do the job of president. He swore to protect the Constitution, and he became the first president.

2George Washington was born on February 22, 1732, in Westmoreland County, Virginia. At age three his family moved to Mount Vernon. When he was eleven his father died, and his half brother Lawrence helped raise him. In 1752, after Lawrence died, George took the estate at age twenty. He saw himself as a farmer. In 1753 he asked French settlers to leave the Ohio Valley, but they refused. On May 28, 1754, he led a surprise attack at Fort Duquesne.

3The attack killed the French commander and twelve soldiers, and Washington took the rest prisoner. He was made a colonel as the French and Indian War, part of the Seven Years' War, began. In July the French took Fort Necessity, a weak fort in the open, and Washington had to surrender and retreat. He felt let down because Virginia gave him little help, his army was small and hungry, and royal officers doubted him. Still, people called him a brave commander, and in 1758 he helped General John Forbes take Fort Duquesne. He retired as an honorary brigadier general, went home, and in early 1759 married widow Martha Dandridge Custis. She brought thousands of acres and more enslaved people, whose labor helped make the family rich. After George died in 1799, Martha freed his 123 enslaved people. She did not free them after she died. Her 153 enslaved people were split among grandchildren in 1802, and families were torn apart.

4From Mount Vernon, Washington watched Britain tax the colonists on sugar and tea in the 1760s. Britain used harsh steps and even closed Boston Harbor, and the colonists stood together against this. In September 1774 he joined the First Continental Congress in Philadelphia, a secret meeting of nearly two months. He was not ready for full independence, but he backed military action and took charge of Virginia's volunteer armies. In May 1775 the Second Continental Congress made him commander of the Continental Army, and he refused any pay. He began on July 3, 1775, added ammunition, won early fights, and the next March drove the British from Boston to New York City. Thomas Jefferson led the writing of the Declaration of Independence, approved on July 4, 1776. Washington then faced General William Howe, and battles followed at Long Island, White Plains, Trenton, Princeton, Brandywine, Germantown, and Monmouth.

5The British navy controlled the waters around New York City. In the summer of 1776 General Howe beat Washington on Long Island, killing three hundred men and capturing more than a thousand. Washington retreated to White Plains, then into New Jersey and Pennsylvania, while the enemy camped at Trenton. On Christmas night in 1776 he crossed the Delaware River and surprised the enemy, then drove the British back toward New York. At Saratoga in 1777, about 180 miles, or 290 kilometers, north of New York City, the British lost, and France joined to avenge the Seven Years' War. Near Philadelphia, then the seat of government, his men fought into fall, then starved at Valley Forge, and three thousand deserted. In early 1781 he marched south with French troops and ships to Yorktown, Virginia. On October 19, 1781, the surrounded British surrendered, and Washington had led the colonists to independence.

6After the war, Washington wanted a strong federal government for the young nation. James Madison asked him to the Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia in the hot summer of 1787. Madison urged the title President of the United States, not His Elective Majesty or His Mightiness. Those delegates, the Founding Fathers, made a Constitution, and in February 1789 they unanimously elected convention president Washington. His strength and military record won them over, though he wished only to live and die an honest man on his farm. He read an inaugural address to Congress, a custom presidents still follow, as Barack Obama did in 2013. He gave the first State of the Union in 1790, and today it usually comes in February. He set up the cabinet and served only two terms, a custom kept until 1940 and made law in 1951.

7In April 1789 he traveled from Mount Vernon to New York City and was inaugurated before a joyful crowd. He pledged to follow the Constitution, with a president, a Congress, and a Supreme Court. He listened to others, but he was not afraid to decide, and Thomas Jefferson said his mind was sure. Treasury secretary Alexander Hamilton wanted a national bank and wanted the nation to pay state war debts. Secretary of State Jefferson agreed, if the capital would sit in a southern state, and Washington, D.C., now lies between Maryland and Virginia. Voters reelected Washington in 1792, and his second term was harder, including the Whiskey Rebellion over a whiskey tax. He sent militia to stop that revolt, then kept the nation neutral when France and England went to war. He sent Justice John Jay to Britain, but many hated the pro-British treaty and criticized him in public and in the press.

8In his Farewell Address, Washington warned against alliances with European nations that could pull the country into wars. He also warned that too large an army could threaten republican liberty. He retired to Mount Vernon in early 1797 and spent more time with his family. On December 12, 1799, he had a sore throat and went to bed exhausted. Doctors treated him, but he died on December 14, 1799, at age sixty-seven. As the first president, his courage, confidence, discipline, and take-charge ways set a tone later presidents tried to follow. Henry Lee called him first in war, first in peace, and first in the hearts of his countrymen. People still call him Father of His Country, though he was complex and imperfect like any real person. This dollar bill design first appeared in 1963.

9George Washington was born in 1732 in Westmoreland County, Virginia, and in 1735 his family moved to Mount Vernon. In 1754 he fought in the French and Indian War, part of the Seven Years' War. In 1775 he was named commander in chief of the Continental Army in the American Revolution. In 1787 he led the Constitutional Convention, and in 1789 he was elected the first president. In 1794 he faced the Whiskey Rebellion. In 1797 he began retirement at Mount Vernon, and he died on December 14, 1799.

83. The Games Then and Now

1María Colón of Cuba won the women’s javelin final in 1980. Her throw of 68.4 meters set a world and Olympic record then. The Olympic motto is Citius, Altius, Fortius. These Latin words mean Faster, Higher, Stronger. Gold medal winners are the best athletes in the world. The Games began in ancient Greece and promote peaceful competition. Many cities compete for the honor of hosting the Games. Hosting the Summer or Winter Olympics joins a city to that long tradition.

2The ancient Greeks held athletic contests for centuries to honor their gods. Each city-state had its own government, laws, and army, and the states often clashed. Writings say the Games began in Olympia in 776 BCE, though many think they started earlier. The Greeks held four yearly festivals, and the Olympics honored Zeus, king of the gods. Zeus was the sky god of Mount Olympus, so these Games became the most important. A map of that time shows Olympia, Athens, Sparta, and the seas around Greek lands. Early Games had only footraces, then grew to fourteen contests in a hippodrome. Wrestlers could kick and break bones, and crashes, injuries, and deaths were common.

3Thousands of people came from across Greece to watch the Games. Athletes trained for months or years, and the only official prize was a sacred olive branch. Hometowns often gave champions money, and champions never had to pay taxes again. Visitors bought food and lodging, and Olympia was a place for meetings and reunions. The grounds had a hotel, a pool, a sauna, a market, a bank, and racing areas. A temple held a huge gold-and-ivory statue of Zeus, one of the Seven Wonders. Ceremonies had a parade, a sacrifice of up to one hundred white oxen, and a feast. A strict truce stopped war, and no one could carry a weapon into Olympia.

4Most Olympic athletes competed nude or wore only small shorts. The Greeks thought loose clothes might trip an athlete. A law banned women from the Games on pain of death, but girls could watch. In 470 BCE, a women’s festival honored Hera, the wife of Zeus. The Games went on after Rome conquered Greece in 146 BCE. Around 393 CE, Emperor Theodosius banned pagan festivals, and Olympia was later buried. In the 1700s, archaeologists searched, and by the 1890s they had uncovered most major buildings. Pierre de Coubertin formed the International Olympic Committee in 1894 to revive the Games.

5Coubertin hoped nations would set aside politics and war, as the ancient Greeks had done. Athletes were to compete for love of the sport, and champions received only a symbolic prize. At first, only amateur athletes could compete in the Games. Jim Thorpe, of the Sac and Fox Nation, lost his 1912 pentathlon and decathlon gold medals. He had played professional baseball briefly, and some people believe racism played a role. His medals were never given back, yet many call him one of the greatest athletes. Greece hosted the 1896 Games, with over two hundred athletes from fourteen countries, but no women. Winners got an olive branch, a certificate, and a silver medal.

6The Olympic flag is lowered at the closing of the 2008 Summer Games in Beijing. The 1900 Games in Paris and the 1904 Games in St. Louis were less successful. Hosts built no Olympic villages, so housing and equipment were poor, and bad weather delayed events. The Games were poorly advertised, crowds were small, and world’s fairs drew people away. In 1906, athletes paraded behind their national flags, and opening ceremonies have continued ever since. Coubertin designed the Olympic flag, first flown in 1920. It is white with five interlocking rings for five settled continents working in peace. At least one of those colors appears on every nation’s flag.

7Chamonix, France, hosted the first Winter Games in 1924, with more than 250 athletes from 16 nations. Eleven of them were women and girls, and there were sixteen events, including skating, skiing, and ice hockey. Sonja Henie of Norway fell at age twelve, then won gold in 1928, 1932, and 1936. She later starred in ice shows and films. Women first competed officially in the Summer Games in Amsterdam in 1928. Officials began using the Olympic torch in 1928, and the relay started in 1936. The torch is lit in Olympia with magnified sunlight and carried to the host city. In 2000, Cathy Freeman lit the cauldron and became the first Aboriginal woman to win individual gold.

8Conflicts sometimes disrupt the Games, and three Olympics were canceled because of war. At the 2020 Games, Raven Saunders, a Black woman, crossed her arms in an X on the podium. She said the X marks where people who face different kinds of discrimination meet. Kim Un Guk of North Korea set a weightlifting world record in London in 2012. The 2020 Summer Games were postponed a year, while the 2022 Winter Games went on as planned. Some athletes could not compete after they tested positive for COVID-19. In 1936, Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party used the Berlin Games to spread racist ideas. Eighteen Black Americans, including Jesse Owens, humiliated them, and Nazi actions later helped cause World War II.

9The Paralympic Games showcase athletes with different disabilities. The first Paralympics were in Italy in 1960, with 400 athletes from 23 nations. The 2021 Paralympics had more than 4,400 athletes from 162 nations. Since the 1988 Summer Games, the Paralympics and Olympics have shared cities and venues. Guides in bright yellow vests use a wrist tether so visually impaired runners stay in their lanes. Today’s training is a hard full-time job, and most early gold winners would not qualify now. In 1924, the men’s 50-kilometer ski race took 3 hours and 45 minutes, but in 2022 it took just over 1 hour and 11 minutes. Chloe Kim won halfpipe gold at the 2018 and 2022 Winter Games.

10Olympic athletes must train harder than ever and use the latest equipment. They need the best trainers and sponsors, and many start at an early age. Many countries have special centers, and Deanna Price trains seven days a week. Some athletes cheat with banned drugs, often with help from trainers or doctors. Since the mid-1970s, officials test athletes, and failed champions can lose their medals. Lance Armstrong had to return his medals after using steroids and growth hormones. Some skating and diving judges may have given unfair points or traded points. The Games keep growing, records fall, and they still stand for fair and peaceful sport among nations.

11Ancient means from a long time ago, or very old. Archaeologists study the remains of ancient cultures. Athletes train for sports that need strength, speed, and skill. Competitors take part in contests, and controversies are disagreements. A motto is a guiding phrase, and character means a person’s moral strength. A procession is a formal parade, and a truce is an agreement to keep the peace. To qualify is to show enough skill for a hard event. Symbolic means standing for an idea, and tarnished means disgraced or made less pure.

84. The Great Charter

1In the late twelfth century, people in England suffered under selfish kings. Trouble began under King Richard I, called Richard the Lionheart. In his ten-year reign, England was nearly bankrupted. Richard taxed the people heavily to pay for the Third Crusade. While he was away, his youngest brother John tried and failed to take the throne. Richard was captured in Austria, and his captors demanded a huge ransom. After he was freed, he forgave John and raised more taxes for a war in France. He died in France in 1199 from an arrow wound and named John as the next king.

2England did not want more taxes, but John demanded them. John was a terrible king in almost every way. He taxed the barons heavily, seized their land, and insulted their wives and daughters. He took hostages from noble families and sometimes killed them even after a ransom was paid. A baron was a noble who received land in return for loyalty and military service. In 1214 the barons swore an oath to get fair treatment from the king. In 1203 John captured his nephew Arthur, age fifteen, a rival backed by King Philip II of France. People believed John ordered Arthur murdered, and some said John killed him himself.

3In 1204 King Philip II defeated John's hired army and reclaimed most English lands in France. Many people scorned and hated John for the loss. When the archbishop of Canterbury died in 1205, the pope wanted Stephen Langton. John demanded Bishop John de Gray instead and seized church lands. In 1208 Pope Innocent III closed England's churches with an interdict. Priests could not say mass or perform marriages, baptisms, or funerals, and later the pope expelled John from the church. The pope allied with Philip to invade England, so in 1213 John accepted Langton as archbishop. John made the pope the feudal overlord of England, and Innocent pardoned him at once.

4Archbishop Langton still wanted John removed from power. He advised about two hundred barons who also wanted the king gone. Not all barons opposed John. William Marshal, the first earl of Pembroke, worked for peace between the nobles and the king. Many thought Marshal was England's most formidable knight, and he had served four kings. The barons first met as a group in July 1213 at St. Albans, near London. They rejected the idea of killing John and chose peaceful means. John agreed to follow Henry I's Coronation Charter, a set of laws more than one hundred years old.

5When John broke that promise, the barons met in November 1214 at Bury St. Edmunds. Archbishop Langton used the Bible and the Coronation Charter to justify their challenge. Robert Fitzwalter became the leader of the barons and guided their plans. Langton was archbishop of Canterbury for almost twenty-two years. The barons refused to pay more scutage for John's wars in France. Scutage was a tax paid instead of military service, and John used it to hire fighters. They drew up demands based on the Coronation Charter, including that the king must live under the same laws as everyone else. If John refused, they would take up arms.

6In January 1215 Fitzwalter and a few barons brought John a draft charter, but talks went badly. John promised an answer by Easter and did not give one. The barons prepared formal demands and also prepared for war. The Magna Carta began as the Articles of the Barons, a Latin list of sixty-three demands. It shielded barons from abusive power and heavy taxes and protected the English Church. It said no free person could be punished without a trial, and twenty-five barons could enforce it. In May 1215 the barons seized London, and on June 15 they met John at Runnymede on the River Thames. John set his royal seal on the charter, which made it official, instead of signing with a pen.

7Few people believed John would keep his oath. He asked Pope Innocent for help, and in August 1215 the pope nullified the charter. Led by Fitzwalter, many barons started a civil war and invited Prince Louis of France to take the throne. William Marshal and some others stayed loyal to the crown. Pope Innocent died of a fever in July 1216, and John died of dysentery in October while facing Louis. John's nine-year-old son, Henry III, became king. Marshal, aged seventy, became regent for his fifth king. In September 1217 Marshal defeated the rebel barons and ended the civil war, and in November Henry reissued the charter.

8Henry was too young to understand the danger, so he relied on Marshal. The civil war continued anyway. Marshal advised him to reissue the charter and show he was not like his father. Henry reissued the charter, and the barons who had doubted him trusted Marshal's word. Henry turned eighteen in 1225 and reissued the charter again. He accepted that no one was above the law. The charter was reissued again in 1297 under his son, King Edward I. In April 2015 the four remaining copies were together for the charter's eight-hundredth anniversary. The charter helped form English Common Law, including innocence until proven guilty and trial by peers. Its ideas later appeared in the U.S. Constitution and the Bill of Rights.

9A charter is an official paper that sets the rights and duties of a person or group. Barons were nobles who held a lower rank in medieval Europe. Scutage was a feudal tax paid instead of military service. A regent rules a kingdom when the monarch cannot rule. To nullify a charter is to take away its legal power. An oath is a formal promise.

85. The Muslim Commander Who Won Back Jerusalem

1Nearly nine hundred years ago, a boy named Yusuf lived in the Middle East. That region was rich in culture and history, and it is the birthplace of Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. Yusuf became Salah al-Din, perhaps the most famous Muslim military leader of all time. Followers of the three faiths share Jerusalem, one of the world's oldest cities, with many sacred sites. Passions there run deep, and many empires have wanted Jerusalem. The map shows Tikrit, Aleppo, Damascus, Baghdad, Hattin, Jaffa, Jerusalem, Cairo, and nearby seas and deserts. Today Middle Eastern countries include Turkey, Cyprus, Syria, Lebanon, Iraq, Iran, Israel, Palestine, and Jordan. They also include Egypt, Sudan, Libya, Saudi Arabia, Yemen, Oman, Qatar, Kuwait, and the United Arab Emirates.

2Nearly forty years before his birth, Western European Franks conquered Jerusalem in 1099. Muslims had ruled it for four hundred years. A Christian leader promised safety to the Muslim and Jewish residents, as Muslims had protected Jews and Christians. The Crusaders disobeyed that order and killed thousands. Salah al-Din later wanted to take the city back for Muslims. He was born in 1137 or 1138 in Tikrit, and his father was a wealthy Kurdish chief. Tikrit was in Mesopotamia, now mostly Iraq, plus parts of Syria, Turkey, and Iran. As a baby he left Tikrit for Aleppo, under Sultan Zengi, then moved to Baalbek and Damascus. By age seven he studied at a mosque, and he followed the Five Pillars of Islam.

3When Zengi died in 1146, his son Nur al-Din took part of the kingdom. His father governed Damascus, Uncle Shirkuh led troops, and Salah al-Din joined the army at fourteen. He became the sultan's chief aide and vowed to treat men as equals, as Nur al-Din did. His name means he who honors the faith, and some in the West call him Saladin. The Citadel in Cairo was built on his orders from 1176 to 1184 to guard against the Crusaders. In his late twenties he went to Egypt with Shirkuh so the Franks would not take it. Vizier Shawar changed sides and planned to kill Shirkuh, but a religious leader made Shirkuh vizier. Shirkuh died nine weeks later, and in 1169 Salah al-Din became vizier and commander at age thirty-one.

4Salah al-Din named the Ayyubid dynasty for his father Ayyub and vowed to free Jerusalem from the Franks. A new Muslim era began as he improved Egypt and built schools for scholars from Europe and Asia. He refused a palace of four thousand rooms, lived simply, and gave away most of its riches. Pope Urban II ordered the First Crusade in 1095, and fighters believed their sins would be forgiven. In the 1180s, Franks who had held Jerusalem for eighty years fought over who should rule it. Raynald of Châtillon broke treaties and raided Muslim towns, unlike respectful Raymond of Tripoli. Guy of Lusignan became king, and Salah al-Din vowed to drive out the Franks and kill Raynald. In July 1187 he besieged Tiberias, so Guy marched with twenty thousand men.

5Guy's army ran out of water on the hot plain while Salah al-Din's men attacked. The next morning at Hattin, his army defeated the determined Franks and killed many. Guy, Raynald, and many knights were captured, and many soldiers were spared but enslaved. Raymond escaped but died weeks later, and Salah al-Din spared Guy but executed Raynald. He freed the men at Tiberias, took the castle, and dealt the Franks a devastating defeat. From 1187 to 1192 his battles touched Hattin, Tiberias, Acre, Tyre, Jerusalem, and nearby seas and deserts. On October 2, 1187, after a two-week siege, he took Jerusalem. Unlike 1099, he killed few Christians, left shrines unharmed, and let prisoners buy freedom if they would not attack.

6His brother freed a thousand poor captives, and Salah al-Din freed all the older prisoners. The other Christians were enslaved, but Jerusalem was under Muslim control again. He had delayed Tyre, so Christian refugees strengthened that fortress and refused to surrender. He freed Guy, who besieged Acre, but European reinforcements were on the way. For 638 days, Muslims were inside Acre, Guy's army around them, and Salah al-Din outside. News of Jerusalem's fall led Europe to start the Third Crusade. In spring 1191 Philip Augustus of France arrived, then Richard the Lionheart of England. A month later Richard took Acre and killed three thousand prisoners when funds came too slowly.

7In August 1191 Richard marched about 130 kilometers, or 80 miles, south toward Jaffa. Salah al-Din's archers attacked without stopping, but Richard kept his rested men strong. The Muslim army had fought for years and lost Jaffa and other coastal cities. He fortified Jerusalem, but in January 1192 brutal weather turned the Franks back. John was seizing Richard's lands, so Richard looked at Jerusalem, saw his army was too small, and left. Salah al-Din never met Richard, but his brother negotiated a truce on September 2, 1192. Franks kept the coast from Tyre to Jaffa, but Jerusalem stayed Muslim and open to Christian visitors. The truce lasted three years, ended the Third Crusade, and won Christian respect.

8His son built a mausoleum in Damascus in 1193, and it was restored in 1898. He died there on March 4, 1193, six months after the truce, at fifty-five or fifty-six. Because he gave everything away, there was no money for a proper burial. His family ruled Egypt and nearby lands until another group gained power in 1250. Jerusalem remained under Muslim rule until World War I. A statue of Salah al-Din on horseback stands today in Damascus, South Syria. Muslims revered him for unity and reclaiming Jerusalem for Islam, and many Christians esteemed him too. Near death he told his oldest son that gentleness and kindness had won men's hearts.

9Salah al-Din was born in Tikrit, Mesopotamia, in 1137 or 1138. From 1152 to 1169 he served under Nur al-Din, the ruler of Syria. In 1169 he became ruler of Egypt and commander of Egypt's Syrian troops. Nur al-Din died in 1174, and Salah al-Din began to unite the Muslim states. In 1185 he united the Muslim states, and on July 4, 1187, he won the Battle of Hattin. On October 2, 1187, he recaptured Jerusalem after a two-week battle. The Third Crusade began in 1189, Acre's battle ended on July 12, 1191, and Jaffa's ended on August 4, 1192. A truce with Richard the Lionheart came on September 2, 1192, and Salah al-Din died in Damascus on March 4, 1193.

86. The Pharaoh Who Ruled for Sixty-Six Years

1Queen Nefertari, first wife of Ramses II, appears in a colorful image. Ahead are a famous pharaoh, a royal surprise, growing up, the young warrior and king, battles, the close of the New Kingdom, the title Ramses the Great, and a word list. A colossal statue of him weighs 6.58 metric tons, or 7.25 tons. The British Museum holds it now. It was found first in his temple, the Ramesseum, at Thebes in Egypt. Power came during Egypt's golden age to the pharaoh whose name is written Ramses II and also Ramesses II. About five hundred years, from 1550 to 1080 bc, are called the New Kingdom. The Eighteenth, Nineteenth, and Twentieth Dynasties rose and fell in that age. Inside the Nineteenth Dynasty, he was the king who came third. The reign sat near the middle of the period. About sixty-six years passed, from 1279 until 1213 bc. Length like that was astonishing. Most people then died before forty-five. Fame grew until he was among Egypt's best-known pharaohs, earning the title Ramses the Great.

2Birth was around 1303 bc. The father was Seti I, a military commander. The mother was Mut-Tuy, said MOOT TOO-ee. An older sister may have been named Tia. A younger sister may have been named Henutmire, said he-nuht-MEE-ray. Pharaoh was an unlikely future. The parents were not even royal. King Tutankhamun, pharaoh then, died with no heir. Ay, his vizier, briefly became pharaoh. Horemheb took Ay's place after only a few years. Horemheb had commanded Tutankhamun's army. The grandfather, a general called Paramessu, had served in that army beside Horemheb. As pharaoh, Horemheb named Paramessu heir. Several years later Paramessu took the throne. He renamed himself Ramses. The family became royalty, starting the line called the Nineteenth Dynasty. Grandfather likely became ruler near the boy's tenth birthday. A few years after that, Seti I reached the throne, and the son stood next. A map of the reign, 1279 to 1213 bc, marks the Orontes River and Kadesh. It marks the Mediterranean Sea, Pi-Ramesse, and the delta of the Nile. The Nile itself, Abydos, Karnak, and Thebes are shown. So are the Ramesseum, the Red Sea, the Egyptian Empire, Abu Simbel, the Hittite Empire, and Nubia. Early life is poorly known. Artwork and carvings in buildings he later raised supply what is known. Home was probably in the family's house in the Nile delta. Lessons would have included reading and writing. Mathematics would have been taught. Science would have been taught. Geography, history, and medicine would have been taught as well.

3He would have learned from texts called the Books of Instruction. Those texts taught children how to live well. Later he may have entered the Prince's School, for children of royalty, of nobles, and of officials. He was named successor to Seti I and made crown prince while still young. Much of the schooling was training beside his father at a pharaoh's work. Someday the army would be his to lead in battle. Strength and endurance had to be built, likely from early childhood. Challenges meant to ready him for fighting included catching bulls with rope and mounting horses that were still wild. At Abydos, carved pictures in Seti I's temple show two scenes. One scene gives a gift to Amun, a god. The other is the prince roping a bull. A captain's title in the army came early, perhaps in name only. Titles and authority given young prepared the nation for his later rule. As a teenager he counted as an adult in many ways. Military campaigns with his father taught diplomacy and war, preparation for being pharaoh. He kept his own household. Marriage came too, probably at only fifteen. Nefertari was the first wife and the favorite. A rich tomb built for her shows a deeper care than he gave the rest. Words cut there dedicate the tomb to Nefertari, called the chief queen, the woman for whom sunlight shines. Many wives were common for rulers. He was no exception. Historians think eight or more royal wives came over the decades, plus several minor wives. Nefertari stayed chief wife until she died. At least five children were theirs. Amen-her-khepeshef was the oldest son and the heir. Say the name as ah-muhn, then hair, then KE-pe-shef.

4Thirteen years was the length of Seti I's rule. Ramses was probably co-ruler in the final years. Either way, his role in that rule was important. Military campaigns were his charge. Courage in war became his reputation. One campaign is shown in artwork at the Beit el-Wali temple, said BAYT EL WAH-lee, in southern Egypt, then called Nubia. He charges in a chariot. Two oldest sons follow in smaller chariots: Amen-her-khepeshef and Khaemwaset, said kahm-WAH-set. Historians place the fight during a Nubian rebellion. Nubia lay south of Egypt. Gold was there, and other riches too. Control of it often set Egyptians and Nubians against each other. Kings in Egyptian art are usually drawn larger than everyone else, so viewers see who is in charge. Seti I died when Ramses was about twenty-five. The son became pharaoh, leader of the military, of religion, and of justice. Because a pharaoh led religion as well as politics, the reign opened with a year of festivals and coronation ceremonies. Four new names joined his birth name. Symbols showed their religious weight. The Horus name was Kanakht Merymaat. Horus, shown as a falcon, rests above the palace. Kingship was the domain of that god. The Nebty name was Mekkemetwafkhasut. A cobra stood for Lower Egypt and a vulture for Upper Egypt. With the palace, Nebty stood for the goddesses of both lands. The Golden Horus name was Userrenput-aanehktu. A bee meant Lower Egypt and grass meant Upper Egypt. Horus on gold meant the king's life would not end. The prenomen was Usermaatre-setepenre. It stood for rule over both Upper Egypt and Lower Egypt.

5New names, Egyptians believed, showed the gods' protection and showed that the pharaoh himself was divine. Early on, he restarted architectural jobs his father had ordered. Stoneworkers and artisans had been told by Seti I to raise a huge religious hall at Karnak. Columns numbered 134, each at least 21 meters, or 69 feet, high. Walls received slow, careful raised relief, also called bas-relief. Background is cut away so the pictures stand up. Ramses soon ordered a faster method, sunk relief. Pictures are cut straight into the stone instead of by clearing the background. Temple building moved at double the old rate. No other ancient Egyptian pharaoh raised more temples. Visitors look tiny beside the columns of Karnak's Great Hypostyle Hall. Floor space of the hall is 5,000 square meters. That is 53,820 square feet. The Ramesseum was meant to honor him and to keep his memory alive forever. A temple for Nefertari was cut into a solid mountain of rock. Important building filled his life. The mortuary temple called the Ramesseum, at Thebes, is among the most impressive works. Another is the lovely temple raised at Abu Simbel for Nefertari, whom he loved. A new capital was ordered, replacing Memphis, capital in the Old Kingdom from 2649 to 2150 bc, and replacing Thebes. During New Kingdom Egypt, from 1550 to 1070 bc, Thebes was the capital and the center of religion. The city was named Pi-Ramesse, loosely translated Ramsesopolis. It sat in Egypt's far north and covered 18 square kilometers, or 7 square miles. From there he could watch the Hittites more closely. Those long-standing enemies lived eastward. The region is the one now called Syria.

6Before the Nineteenth Dynasty, Hittite forces east of Egypt had seized some Egyptian territory. Seti I had started to rebuild Egyptian power and planned to retake land. When the new king took the throne, the Hittites tested his mettle. They attacked and took Kadesh back. The city mattered because the main route for trade ran there, following the Orontes River. Early on, Ramses defeated those Hittite forces. Many small provinces came back, including some his father had failed to regain. During the reign's fifth year he led a huge force toward Kadesh, hoping to take it back. Soldiers numbered about 20,000. Chariots numbered about 2,000. That battle became one of the reign's most famous events. The Hittite attack was the earliest recorded military ambush. Their force included 2,500 chariots. Together the sides fielded about 4,500 chariots. No chariot battle on record has been larger. The story was carved on pylons and on temple walls across Egypt and Nubia. The Egyptian telling is therefore among the best-documented events of ancient Egypt. Art shows him larger than every other figure, clearly beating the enemy. His account goes further and suggests he faced the enemy alone. Some Kadesh scenes are unusual. Most battle art shows a pharaoh's enemies collapsing in fear or in death. These pictures surround him with a powerful Hittite army of soldiers, weapons, horses, and chariots. The Hittites look like equal adversaries. Why use so different a style? Because the result was not the victory he wanted believed. He was nearly killed. Neither side could claim a clean win. Egypt's result was closer to a draw. Records from both Egypt and the Hittites, pieced together, make the true story more complex than his official version. Scholars think the army split while nearing the city. His group was the lead division, known as the Army of Amun. Another division trailed by about one day's march. Another, experts think, swung around to strike the city from the far side.

7Spies likely convinced him the Hittites were many miles off. He soon learned they were dangerously near and preparing to attack. Word went to the other divisions. The ambush overran the reinforcements that might have reached him. The Hittites then charged his much smaller force. His own telling says he held the enemy off by himself while the rest of the army fled. Other records say an elite division called the Ne'arin arrived just in time and saved him. Heavy losses on both sides brought a truce. He pulled his forces back to Egypt. A detail from battle art, also using the name Qadesh, shows Hittites surrounding him. Across the following year he ordered writings cut in stone. Bulletins numbered at least seven. Poems numbered eight. Every one of them made him the hero. Some experts say this was history's first known propaganda campaign. Hostilities did not end. About fifteen years later the nations again neared war. Battle so far from home was hard, so talk looked wiser than fighting. During year twenty-one of the reign, he and the Hittite king settled on a treaty of peace. Two copies survive. One uses Egyptian hieroglyphs. The other uses Akkadian, the Hittite language.

8Egypt gave up any right to Kadesh and to the land around it. War ended, and a clear boundary stood between the nations. Clauses of a kind still used in modern peace treaties were included. One provided alliance if foreigners attacked. Another was a mutual promise not to strike each other's territory. Visitors can see a copy hanging inside the building where the United Nations General Assembly meets. A Hittite princess became his wife thirteen years afterward, and the marriage sealed the deal. Rule lasted until 1213 bc, sixty-six or sixty-seven years, and ended in natural death at age ninety-one. Arthritis, dental trouble, and arterial disease marked his last years and may have helped cause death. Amen-her-khepeshef, oldest son and first heir, died before him. So did the eleven sons who stood next. Merneptah, the thirteenth son, became pharaoh and ruled for a decade. Decline of the Nineteenth Dynasty had already begun. Control of Nubia was lost. Magnificent temples were left to desert sand. Only 150 years after the death, the New Kingdom ended. Fame in ancient Egypt was so great that at least nine later pharaohs took his name. Ramses the Great is the modern title, partly from military success. Territories lost under earlier pharaohs were taken back, and Egypt controlled more land than ever. Monuments and temples beyond any other pharaoh's count were his doing. People still admire them and study them. Statues, elaborate pictures, and hieroglyphs hand historians a deep store of facts. Ancient Egyptian life is what those facts describe. From a modern view, those are the real grounds of his greatness. Art, architecture, and historical records were left behind, and they let us understand the people and the culture of his time more clearly. At Abu Simbel, two temples are cut from sandstone. The bigger one's doorway has giant sculptures of him on both sides.

9Dates on a timeline include these. A scale mark sits at 1310 bc. Birth is 1303 bc. Ramses I becomes pharaoh in 1298 bc. Seti I becomes pharaoh in 1291 bc. Marriage to his first two wives is 1289 bc. A Nubian revolt is put down in 1281 bc, with his two oldest sons taken into battle. Ramses II becomes pharaoh in 1279 bc, and work on the Ramesseum starts around then. The fight at Kadesh is 1274 bc. Work at Abu Simbel begins around 1264 bc. The Ramesseum is finished in 1259 bc. Peace with the Hittites is 1258 bc. Nefertari dies in 1252 bc. In 1244 bc Isetnofret, the second wife, dies. He marries a first Hittite princess, and Abu Simbel is finished around then. A second Hittite princess is married in 1231 bc. Death at age ninety-one is 1213 bc. A scale mark sits at 1210 bc. Campaigns are planned strings of actions aimed at chosen goals. Pharaohs are the rulers of ancient Egypt. Propaganda is news, art, or other media that often uses false or stretched information to sway people. Diplomacy means the skill of bargaining. It is also the practice of that bargaining, carried on by people who speak for different countries. Pylons are towers of great height, or other structures that stand upright. Supports are a common use. A dynasty is a run of rulers who share a family. A successor follows another person in a job or in an elected post. Hieroglyphs are pictures and symbols that work as writing. Ancient Egypt is where they are best known. A truce is an agreement to stop fighting. A legacy is something passed from past to present. Vizier names an official of high rank. Ancient Egypt used the title. Some Muslim countries have used it too. Mortuary means related to burial.

87. The Prince from Pella Who Marched Across Asia

1A map of the empire at its peak in 323 bce also marks the route of exploration. Labels include Macedonia, the Caspian Sea, and the Black Sea. Taxila is marked. So are Asia Minor, the Hydaspes River, and Persia. Babylon, the Mediterranean Sea, and Alexandria appear. India, the Persian Gulf, and the Euphrates River appear. Egypt, the Arabian Sea, the Nile River, and the Red Sea appear as well. Sections ahead cover the beginning, years as a prince, the rise to king, conquest, a Persian view, the legacy, and a word list. Alexander III was born a prince. The time was more than twenty-three centuries ago. The city was Pella. Macedonia was the kingdom around it. Nations and kingdoms, near and far, would fall to him in a short life. Violent oppression marked the journey. Legend has rarely produced a leader so famous, or a conqueror so famous. Land and power were not his only drives. He deeply wanted to pass beyond anywhere people had traveled. Aristotle, among the most learned men of the age, was his teacher. New ideas appealed to Alexander. A thirst for knowledge pushed him farther, so he could learn more. The map's date is 323 bce, when the empire was at its largest, and it also traces where he explored. Macedonia and Egypt are on it, with Persia, India, Babylon, and Alexandria. Seas on it include the Black Sea, the Caspian Sea, the Mediterranean Sea, the Arabian Sea, and the Red Sea. Rivers include the Hydaspes, the Euphrates, and the Nile. Aristotle's teaching fed a hunger to learn, and that hunger pushed the marches.

2Birth was in 356 bce. Philip II, the ambitious father, had studied military strategy while captive as a young man in neighboring Greece. Strong armies there were his classroom. Home again, he seized Macedonia's throne from his nephew Amyntas. A superior, well-trained army secured his rule over Macedonia and the Greek states around it. Callisthenes, said kuh-LIS-thuh-neez, was a writer who recorded the life. Much of that writing vanished over time. Later authors kept pieces of the stories. Because so much finally rests on one source, the biases coloring it matter. Across more than two thousand years, a writer on Alexander's payroll cannot be treated as pure fact. Ask how enemies might have told the same events. Conquests and the costs of war were smoothed over. The writer did not always paint Alexander in the best light. Disagreement with Alexander ended in the writer's early death. Today a statue in Pella, Greece, shows Alexander on the horse Bucephalus. Olympias, the mother, was not born a Macedonian. She feared the throne might skip her son for that reason, and that her own place would vanish. She raised him to be king and would accept nothing less. Ambition from both parents passed to him. At twelve he showed a strong will. Philip refused to buy a superb horse that was also nervous. The name was Bucephalus, said byoo-SEF-uh-luhs. Alexander saw that the unbroken animal feared its own shadow. He took charge. Turning the head, by the reins, away from the shadow would calm it. He was sure of that. He leaped onto the back and rode off easily. The horse stayed his constant companion.

3Philip was often gone, taking control of other Greek lands. Experts received the job of educating and training the son for kingship. Greek youths learned riding and hunting first, so they could fight well. Sword, javelin, and bow joined those skills for success in brutal battle. Tests of manhood demanded two killings: a wild boar, and a man during battle. Alexander managed both. History, politics, and ethics were studied too. At thirteen, Aristotle was brought to Macedonia. The well-known Greek philosopher became the teacher. Intelligence and knowledge earned Aristotle respect. Literature, science, medicine, and philosophy caught Alexander's interest through him. A lifelong love of culture and of art began there. A statue of Aristotle stands at Stagira, Greece, his birthplace. In 340 bce Philip left for battle and made Alexander regent. At sixteen, during that absence, Alexander stopped a small revolution. Still in his teens, he commanded a section of troops in some of Philip's battles. Military skill was honed for kingship. Change came in 337 bce. Philip married a woman born in Macedonia, threatening Alexander's claim. Philip also began thinking about a larger empire. Persia was the strongest empire in Asia, and Greece counted it an enemy. Lands Greeks claimed had been seized by Darius I and by his son Xerxes, said ZURK-seez. That seizure sat more than a century in the past. Philip wanted some of those lands back. Growth of empire and of wealth, through an Asian conquest, was also his plan. Newly won Greek allies would help. Those allies formed the League of Corinth, which joined city-state armies to free Greek cities from Persian control. In 336 bce the feared birth happened. Philip's wife had a daughter. King Philip was assassinated before that year ended. The new wife and the baby were killed on Olympias's orders.

4Kingship arrived at age twenty. First he called for support from his father's army. Trust had been earned while he served under Philip. Persia, now ruled by Darius III, required a strong army. Philip's plan to rule Persia would be carried through. A map of Macedonia and the city-states marks the Black Sea, Macedonia, and Pella. The map treats Asia Minor as a piece of Persia's empire. The Aegean Sea, Delphi, Thebes, Corinth, and Athens appear. Some of the strongest capitals of Greek city-states are on that map. The father's army would not be enough. Membership in the League of Corinth brought support from most other Greek city-states. Leaders in Thebes and in other states had disliked Philip's growing power. More and more refused Alexander's ambitious plans. Revolution might end Macedonian control of Greece and block the move into Asia. He met opposition directly, determined not to lose Greece. Speech could persuade. Intimidation and force were also acceptable tools of control. Thebes and other League city-states began to oppose him. Territories around Macedonia did too. His army crushed the rebellion. Thebes was the warning he left for everyone else. Six thousand citizens were killed. Thirty thousand more were sold into slavery. The severity left no doubt. Merciless and ferocious methods would be used until every Greek city-state submitted. One year after becoming king, he was ready. New lands, new cultures, and the Persian Empire were the plan. At twenty he needed the army that had trusted him under Philip, because Darius III now ruled Persia. Greek city-states on the map include Athens, Thebes, Corinth, and Delphi, with Pella in Macedonia. Thebes lost six thousand people to death and thirty thousand to sale as slaves when it resisted. A year after the crown was his, the march toward Persia could begin.

5Spring of 334 bce opened the march into Asia. Botanists, zoologists, and surveyors came along to study the lands ahead. Boats carried him along the Hellespont. That tight channel joins two seas, the Aegean and the one called Marmara. Landing in Asia Minor, now Turkey, he threw a spear into the ground. The claim was staked with dramatic flair, a tribute to warriors and heroes of earlier times. Soon the armies met at the Granicus River. Foot soldiers and riders filled both sides. A route map through Asia Minor shows the Black Sea and Macedonia. It shows the Sea of Marmara, Gordium, and the Hellespont. The Granicus River is marked. Asia Minor appears as part of the Persian Empire, with the Aegean Sea, Issus, and the Mediterranean Sea. That region, Turkey today, was the Persian Empire's northernmost part. Darius III stayed out of the fight. Historians say Persia's soldiers were less ready than Macedonia's, and no strong plan guided them. Speed and better weapons overwhelmed it. Victory followed. The fight probably lasted about an hour. An ax nearly killed Alexander. A companion from childhood is said to have saved him. After the cavalry, foot soldiers in a phalanx formation moved in against anyone still standing. Thousands of well-trained Greeks faced Persia. Masterful archers were there, with cavalry and infantry. A tight formation called a phalanx was used. Soldiers marched shoulder to shoulder in helmets and body armor, carrying shields, daggers, and spears.

6Vision and leadership from Alexander were what made the rest matter. Example was his method. He went ahead of the armies. If they lacked water, he lacked it too. If dead horses forced soldiers to walk, he walked. Weapons experts and engineers were employed. Strategies were communicated deftly. Speed and flexibility marked the fighting. Cities along the Aegean Sea were reclaimed. Fall of 333 bce brought Darius III and his army against Alexander at the Battle of Issus. Persia had the larger numbers. Infantry went in with cavalry on the flanks. The bloody fight still went to Alexander. Darius fled to Babylon and abandoned his army. The win was decisive. Rule of the Persian Empire was a step closer. An ancient mosaic shows the two men fighting in that battle. Next came a move south, to beat the Persian fleet by taking cities on the Mediterranean shore in Syria and in Phoenicia, Lebanon today. Refusal to surrender meant bloodshed. Tyre resisted seven months. Many of its citizens were killed before defeat. The coast brought them to Egypt during autumn of 332 bce. Persia's leader in that land gave up quickly. Greece and Macedonia respected Egypt's history as a civilization. Egyptian governors were appointed. Egyptian religion was encouraged. Weary of Persian rule and of many wars, Egypt welcomed him. Alexandria was founded where the Nile meets the Mediterranean. It was the first of twenty cities to carry his name. With the city underway, further Persian lands were the next goal. Departure from Egypt came in summer 331 bce. Babylon, in Mesopotamia, now Iraq, came next. Then he crossed the Euphrates, a river that runs toward the Persian Gulf. Darius, the old enemy, was near.

7After Issus, Darius rebuilt and prepared another meeting. October 331 bce brought the Battle of Gaugamela. Persia again had more soldiers. Even so, the Macedonian king, the officers with him, and the soldiers still crushed the Persian side. One thousand Macedonians died. Persian dead were far more numerous, about fifty thousand. Darius fled again. After Gaugamela, rule over Persia's empire sat nearer to his grasp. He hurried on through Asia. Before he could kill Darius, a local ruler named Bessus did it and made himself king. Focus shifted to Bessus. Capture came, then death, as punishment for murdering Darius. More land and more people fell under Alexander. The year 324 bce brought two marriages. One wife was a princess of the local land. The other was Stateira, whose father was Darius III. Many officers married Persian women. Persian ways entered his life. He dressed in Persian clothing. He expected low bows, the Persian form of honor. Not every Macedonian agreed. Men who had followed him across a decade were weary. Home was what they wanted. He wanted the empire pushed on, toward the east. During 327 bce he talked them into a region they named India. Afghanistan and Pakistan occupy that region today. Where local tribes resisted, the invasion left thousands dead. An arrow punctured his lung in one fight. The injury was severe, but he recovered. Soldiers burned the palace of Darius at Persepolis, in present-day Iran. Until Alexander destroyed it, the Persian Empire was among the widest super powers of the ancient world. Cities were razed on the eastward quest. Symbols of Zoroastrianism, the ancient religion of Iran, were destroyed. Deep respect for Persian culture later made him regret the destruction he had wreaked. Soldiers wrecked the tomb of Cyrus the Great, a famous Persian leader. Alexander afterward paid to repair it.

8Spring of 326 bce brought him to Taxila. Taxiles, the ruler, did not resist. Troops were given, and elephants, an important battle resource of the region. In return, Alexander was asked to fight Porus, an enemy who ruled nearby Indian lands. June found the army at the Hydaspes River, said hy-DAS-peez. Whether Alexander used elephants is unclear. Elephants of Porus did damage the Greeks, then panicked from the fight's intensity and retreated. Porus surrendered. It was the last big battle. Efforts to push farther east failed. Weary troops mutinied and persuaded him to turn toward home. Fever struck after he reached Babylon. Death came in June 323 bce. The body was taken to Alexandria, in Egypt, and placed in a golden casket. Honors followed there and in Greece. The reign lasted twelve years and eight months. Age at death was thirty-three. Brutality and widespread destruction were his. Armies under him killed a number estimated near 750,000. History has mostly smoothed over the horrific tactics and treated him as an excellent leader and commander. A shared vision unified followers. Battle was led with superb understanding. Greek cities under Persian rule were taken back. The empire then reached Egypt and a large share of central Asia, regions Europeans had never explored, let alone conquered. Generals of later ages copied him. Those generals killed Indigenous people and stole from their land. People he met were introduced to Greek culture. That prepared the way for later rulers who forced their own cultures and religions onto the conquered. Fifteen years of conquest brought no lost battle. Ambition without restraint, a turn toward violence, and genius in war combined. The result was a kind of conqueror new to the world.

9A conquest timeline runs from a mark at 360 bce to a mark at 320 bce. Birth in Macedonia is 356 bce. Bucephalus becomes his horse in 344 bce. Aristotle becomes the teacher in 343 bce. A revolt on the eastern border of Macedonia is stopped in 340 bce. Philip is killed in 336 bce, and Alexander becomes Macedonia's king. The advance into Persia and the win at the Battle of Granicus fall in 334 bce. Darius and the Persian army lose the Battle of Issus in 333 bce. Tyre is captured in 332 bce, then Egypt is invaded and welcomes him. Darius and the Persians lose the Battle of Gaugamela in 331 bce. Darius is killed in 330 bce. Conquest of central Asia continues in 327 bce, with a push into India. Porus loses the Battle of Hydaspes in 326 bce. Death in Babylon is 323 bce. Someone ambitious wants badly to succeed, or to reach a hard goal. Ships or other vehicles under one commander or owner form a fleet. Assassinated means slain by an attack that was planned, and politics is often the motive. Soldiers trained and equipped to fight on foot are infantry. People who study plants are botanists. A person seeking knowledge and truth about life, or studying philosophy, is a philosopher. Soldiers who fight from horseback, or troops who fight from armored vehicles, are cavalry. A regent reigns when the monarch cannot. A city-state is a city, or a built-up district, behaving as a country of its own. Surveyors measure land and name the physical features they find. Moral principles that guide behavior are ethics. Positioned at one side or at both sides is what flanked means.

88. The Researcher Who Won Two Science Prizes

1Ahead lie her early years, a long wait, arrival in Paris, two kinds of rays, public honors, darker days, work at the front, later years, gifts she left, and a word list. She is introduced as a trailblazer. Scientific instruments crowded the laboratory of Marie Curie. Some tools there were inventions of her husband, Pierre. Others came from Jacques, Pierre's brother. Few women worked as scientists then. Even so, research by one woman, and the discoveries that followed, altered the world. She departed her homeland for science and for math. A leading university was the place. Obstacle after obstacle seemed to stand in her path. She kept going. No woman before her had received a Nobel Prize. No other person has ever taken Nobel Prizes in two separate fields of science. That scientist was Marie Curie. The picture of that laboratory shows instruments packed into the room. Pierre built some of them. Jacques, the brother of Pierre, built others. Science was rarely a woman's work then. She still left home for math and for science at a major university. Barriers kept appearing. She did not quit. A Nobel Prize reached her ahead of any other woman. The prizes sit in two sciences, not in a single field. Nobody else has been honored that way.

2A photograph seats Marie Curie in the center, with her brother and her sisters. Left to right, the others are Zosia, Hela, Joseph, and Bronya. Birth came on November 7, 1867. The baby was Maria Sklodowska, later called Marie Curie. Warsaw, Poland, was the city. Childhood used the name Manya. Five children shared the family, and Manya was the youngest. Their mother had led a school as headmistress. She left that post when Manya arrived. Math and physics were the father's subjects at a high school for boys. Poland was not a country of its own in the year of her birth. Wars had ended in a division of the land in 1815. Russia held part. Prussia held part. Austria held part. Rule over the family's region belonged to the Russian Empire. Wiping out a Polish national identity was the empire's aim. Fear shaped Manya's childhood. Loyalty to Poland could put lives in danger. Speaking the Polish language could do the same. A family picture from the 1880s shows her beside her father, with Bronya and Hela. Teaching work ended for the father in 1873. Support for Polish independence was the cause. Money grew scarce. Boarders had to be taken in. Typhus, a deadly infection caused by bacteria, killed Zosia, the oldest sister, in 1876. Two years after that, the mother died. Manya was ten. What the father offered was care for the mind and care for the feelings. Classic literature was read aloud. Physics lessons used equipment from his old teaching post. Curiosity and brightness marked the child. Schoolwork was outstanding. Physics came easily, and math did too. Graduation from high school arrived in 1883, at age fifteen, with the top honors.

3Further schooling was the wish of Manya and of her sister Bronya. The University of Warsaw would not admit women. Leaving Poland was required, and money was short. Their answer was Warsaw's floating university. Teachers and thinkers from Poland offered it free, though the classes were illegal. Attics held some lessons. Basements held others. Europe's finest universities were far stronger. The classes still kept Manya up to date on new science. Both sisters aimed at the Sorbonne in Paris. Tuition money was missing. A bargain was struck. Earnings from Manya would pay for Bronya. After the degree, Bronya would repay the help. Five years of work as a tutor and as a governess followed. Spare hours went to math, to chemistry, to physics, to sociology, and to literature. That labor showed her the right path. Math and physics were it. Once Bronya's schooling was paid, Manya's turn arrived. Then and now, the Sorbonne ranks among the world's finest universities. Paris became her home in 1891. She was twenty-four. Enrollment at the Sorbonne came with a new name, Marie, the French form of Maria. Two years of hard study put her first in the class. The degree was a master's in physics. One year later, a second master's arrived, this time in math. Before the math degree was done, a commission asked her to study steel. The question was how different kinds of steel behave around magnets. Large equipment meant she needed a laboratory. Spring of 1894 brought an introduction. A colleague presented Pierre Curie, a professor of physics whose magnetism research had broken new ground. He directed the laboratory at a Paris school called the Municipal School. Industrial physics and chemistry were its subjects. Space in that lab was arranged for her. A photograph shows the newly married couple, Marie Sklodowska Curie beside Pierre Curie.

4The wedding itself was simple. Honeymoon travel was a bicycle trip. At the start they were only two scientists, each admiring the other's mind. Love grew from that respect. July 1895 was the marriage month. Research filled her days, yet she also earned a certificate for teaching. Young women were the students she hoped to teach in science. Once that research ended, a doctorate at the Sorbonne became the next aim. A daughter, Irene, was born to Marie and Pierre in 1897. Mothers of that era were expected to remain home with children. Marie stayed with her science. Pierre's father moved into the home and cared for Irene, so the couple could keep working. A topic was still needed for the doctoral study. Physics had just produced two major discoveries. Late in 1895, X-rays were found by Wilhelm Roentgen, a physicist from Germany. Early the next year, rays from the element uranium were found by Henri Becquerel, a physicist from France. Those rays were weaker than X-rays. Fascination with X-rays pulled many scientists into deep study. Marie chose the uranium rays instead. She wanted to know what those rays did to air. An electrometer was her tool. Air blasted by uranium rays carried electric currents almost too faint to notice, and she measured them. Becquerel's observations held up. Every form of uranium gave off electricity. A larger amount of uranium meant stronger rays. She formed a hypothesis and later proved it. The rays belonged to the structure of uranium itself. They were not produced by its physical condition. They were not produced by its chemical condition either. A new question followed. Was uranium alone in making air carry electricity more easily? Every element known at the time was tested.

5Thorium, she found, sent out rays as well. A new word, radioactivity, was hers. It names rays leaving the nucleus, the center of an atom. Tests continued on many materials. Pitchblende, a mineral that holds uranium, was one of them. The rays from it were stronger than the uranium inside could explain. A second radioactive element, still unknown, had to be in the pitchblende. That was her conclusion. Until then, Pierre Curie had studied crystals on his own. The year 1898 brought a change. As her work advanced, he paused his own project and joined the radioactivity study. Hunting a new element gripped them both. Long research produced two elements nobody had known. Polonium took its name from her homeland. Latin supplied radium's name, from that language's word meaning ray. Understanding in science shifted in a deep way because of what she learned about uranium rays. Atomic physics rests on that shift. Scientists then believed an atom could not be split into smaller pieces. Electrons were found by someone else around the same time. The person who showed that atoms hold a huge store of energy was Marie. Her research led toward machines such as the linear accelerator. A radioactive energy beam from that device is used to kill cancer cells. People in industry were fascinated. Radium produced light and also heat. New inventions seemed possible. Scientific breakthroughs seemed possible too. Pierre showed that living flesh could be harmed by radium's radioactivity. Treatment of cancer, and of other illnesses, became imaginable. Companies offered laboratory space. Raw materials and staff were offered too. Radioactive material was pulled from ore and used in medicine and in other work. Experiments on atoms confirmed her suspicion. Powerful energy sat inside atoms. Illness was common for Marie and Pierre during the research. Hard work might have been the cause. Radiation might have been the cause. Blame on radiation was an idea Marie rejected. Today it is known that radiation can sicken people and can kill.

6Years of close shared labor bound Marie and Pierre. June 1903 brought her Doctor of Science degree. Inside France, no woman had received a doctorate before her. Across Europe, no woman had received a doctorate in science before her. She had led much of the new physics work done with Pierre. A Nobel Prize, among the most honored awards on earth, nearly passed her by because she was a woman. The 1903 prize in physics was first aimed at Pierre Curie and at Henri Becquerel. A mathematician who sat on the nominating committee, and who championed women in science, warned Pierre. Leaving Marie off, Pierre answered, would be a grave injustice. Her name was added.
