December 1903 gave the prize jointly to her, to Pierre, and to Becquerel. Pioneering radiation work was the reason. No woman had won a Nobel Prize before. Fame around the world arrived at once. Pierre was promoted to professor at the Sorbonne. Pay was granted to Marie, and leadership of the laboratory as well. Attention and new duties gave her energy. Research and teaching continued. Explaining the discoveries to the public pleased her. A second daughter, Eve, arrived in 1904. Around then, the Sorbonne provided a fresh laboratory.

7That 1904 laboratory finally gave the Curies more room. Success was high when disaster came. Pierre crossed a street in 1906. A wagon pulled by a horse ran him down. Death was instant. Word of it traveled the world. Shock left Marie numb. In time she found the will to continue. His teaching post was offered to her. The post's title was Professor of General Physics. The school was the Sorbonne. No woman had been a professor there before. A modern laboratory, she hoped, would honor his memory. Publication of her textbook, A Treatise on Radioactivity, came in 1910. She set an international standard for how much radiation radium gives off. Scientists worldwide named the unit the Curie, recognizing what she had done. A life timeline runs this way. Birth in Warsaw, Poland, falls on November 7, 1867. High school graduation is 1883. The move to Paris is 1891. A physics master's is 1893. A math master's is 1894. Marriage to Pierre Curie is 1895. Study of Becquerel rays, and the birth of daughter Irene, fall in 1897. Discovery of polonium and radium is 1898. A physics doctorate and the Nobel Prize in Physics fall in 1903. Eve's birth is 1904. Pierre's death, and her rise as the Sorbonne's first female professor, fall in 1906. A Nobel Prize in Chemistry arrives in 1911. Portable X-ray machines enter her World War I work in 1914. The war ends in 1918, and the Radium Institute opens. Death comes on July 4, 1934. Late in 1910 she sought an empty physicist seat at the French Academy of Sciences. Edouard Branly was the only serious rival. His work had advanced wireless telegraphy. Supporters of Branly spread rumors about Marie that were false, hoping to shrink her chances. Defenders spoke for her. Branly still won the seat. A second Nobel Prize reached her in 1911, this time for chemistry. Radioactivity research was honored, along with finding radium and polonium. No scientist before her had two Nobel Prizes. No one else, even now, has won in two different sciences.

8On October 31, 1914, French soldiers cluster at a truck that carries X-ray gear. The equipment is hers, and it can move. During World War I those machines surely saved many wounded men. War began in the last part of July 1914. Days later, Germany entered France. Most of her staff left to fight. Supplies for research ran short. She searched for a way her science could serve the war. Portable X-ray machines, usable in the field, became her cause, so wounded soldiers could be treated. She poured herself into the project. Wealthy owners were persuaded to give cars. Twenty stations that could travel were set up. Two hundred fixed installations were set up as well. Coordinating help was not enough for her. She learned the X-ray equipment. She taught herself driving, so she could run the portable machines in person. A 1921 ship took her to New York. Daughters Irene and Eve toured the United States with her. She stands at the center of that group. After the war she worked without rest, and with success, to make the Sorbonne's Radium Institute a world-class place for radioactivity research. Chemistry's Nobel Prize reached Irene and her husband during 1935. Marie did not live to celebrate it. Extreme danger from radioactive substances is clear now. It was not clear in her lifetime. Death came on July 4, 1934, at age sixty-six. The illness was a kind of anemia often linked to long exposure to radiation. Burial placed her beside Pierre. Paris holds the Panthéon, resting place of France's most brilliant citizens, and the remains were moved there in 1995. For her own achievements she was the first woman buried there, and the only one.

9Atoms were understood differently after her work. Medicine gained new frontiers. Radiocarbon dating, a method for judging the age of old organic material, grew from that work as well. She showed that careful science, done on purpose, can produce extraordinary breakthroughs. The science mattered. The legacy reached further. Discrimination kept pressing on her. Certainty about her purpose stayed clear, and determination never wavered. The world received a model that inspires. She said life is hard for every person. She asked why that should stop anyone. What she demanded was perseverance, and confidence in oneself above everything. People, she said, should trust that a gift points them toward a task, and that the task can be reached. Staying determined and committed, even through challenge or delay, is perseverance. Too few red blood cells is the blood condition called anemia. Discrimination means treating a person or a group unfairly. Gender can be the basis. So can race, age, religion, or some other difference. Matter, motion, and energy are the subjects of physics. Prestigious describes something people honor, respect, and place in high standing. Detecting differences in electric currents is the job of an electrometer. Making enormous changes is what revolutionized means. A substance that cannot be split into simpler substances, and that contains only one kind of atom, is an element. Paris, France, is home to the university called the Sorbonne. Invisible energy that can pass through many solid substances is what X-rays are. Forming a hypothesis, an informed guess, is what hypothesized means. Each year, six Nobel Prizes are given. The fields are chemistry, economics, literature, medicine, and physics, with one prize also for advancing world peace.

89. The Roman Who Seized Power and Remade the Calendar

1Ahead are the shaping of a Roman empire, the world of his time, early life, military strategy, political strategy, the return to Rome, a legacy, and a word list. Gaius Julius Caesar was a military commander, a politician, and an acclaimed orator, and he was a complex man. Love came from the people and from his soldiers. Dealings with enemy combatants and with political foes were ruthless. Negotiation was a skill, and politics was cunning. Many in the Roman Senate still judged him lawless, hungry for power, and dangerous to Rome. Charm was part of him. Humor appeared at times. Above all he was an achiever. Energy and drive had no limit. A lifetime held many accomplishments. The world map changed under his leadership. Language changed. Government changed. Even the calendar changed. Soldiers and ordinary people loved him, yet enemies and political rivals met a ruthless man. The Senate's fear was that he was lawless, mad for power, and a danger to Rome. Charm and jokes sat beside that drive. Energy seemed to have no edge. Maps, languages, governments, and even the calendar shifted because of what he did.

2At the start, Rome was a city-state. That means a city joined with the countryside that supplied its food, acting as one political body. Neighboring city-states on the Italian Peninsula mostly shared language, culture, and religion with Rome. Fighting happened. Alliances happened too. Rome, in time, became the dominant city-state. Legend says kings once ruled it. Six of those kings were kind. The seventh spread terror. In 509 bce, legend says, the people rose and expelled that seventh king, Superbus. Citizens of the new Roman Republic deeply distrusted rule by one monarch alone. A legislative body, the Senate, was the reliance. Men in it were chosen by two consuls, magistrates elected every year. Consuls, not a king, oversaw government. If war created an emergency, a dictator could outrank the consuls. The post could not last. Two classes filled the Republic. Wealthy aristocrats were patricians. Plebeians included landowners of smaller means. Everyone outside the aristocracy was counted with them. Tension between the classes never left. A map of the Republic from 200 to 100 bce shows the Atlantic Ocean and Gaul, meaning France. Macedonia and the Black Sea are marked. Rome, Spain, and Asia, meaning Turkey, are marked. Greece, the Mediterranean Sea, and Africa are marked. One shade is the Republic in 200 bce. Another is the Republic in 100 bce. Birth came during rapid expansion, and that growth would stir turmoil among Romans. The system let the Republic flourish. By 250 bce most of the Italian Peninsula was under Rome. Spain was taken to the west. Gaul, today's France, was taken to the north. Macedonia and Asia, today's Turkey, were taken to the east. Northern Africa was taken to the south. Conquered regions became provinces under governors. Governors were eager for the post because it paid well. Huge sums could be made by shipping grain to Rome, and by shipping enslaved people there too. Corruption in those governments was rampant.

3Ordinary citizens back in Rome gained nothing from the provinces. The local economy was poor. The split between upper and lower classes grew so unbearable that the Social War followed, from 91 to 89 bce. At his birth, two men competed for power. Lucius Cornelius Sulla had the patricians. The plebeian side was the one Gaius Marius represented. Birth fell on July 12 or 13, in 100 bce. The family was patrician, yet not especially rich or influential, and it sympathized with plebeian causes. Women in his world held little power. Formal entry into politics or government was closed to them. Marriage was a key route to power and influence for them and for their families. The family was not prominent until an aunt married Marius, the leader opposed to Sulla. That marriage lifted the family's political and social standing. Little is known of the early years. Parents gave him a strong education. At sixteen the father died suddenly, and the son was pushed to the head of the family. He married Cornelia, daughter of an ally of Marius and tied to Rome's most influential families. Soon Sulla rose to power and ordered the young husband to divorce her. By refusing, he stood openly beside Marius. The plebeian cause became his own. Danger was great. Property could be stripped away, and life itself was at risk. The army was his escape from Rome. Patrician rank made him an officer. Planning battles and fighting them pleased him. Legionnaires, the soldiers, liked him. Sulla's death in 78 bce brought a return to Rome and a political career. Law work came first. Oratory, meaning public speaking, was the next study. Pirates kidnapped him while he sailed to Greece to begin it.

4His own accounts say he befriended the captors. As a joke he insisted the ransom be set higher, and they raised it. After paying, he joked that payback would come. A small naval force was later raised. The pirates were captured and crucified. Political triumphs then strung together in Rome. He moved skillfully through the city's many intrigues. Cornelia's death in 69 bce led to a political marriage with Pompeia, daughter of the powerful ally Pompey. With Pompey mentoring him, important offices followed. Divorce from Pompeia came later. In 61 bce he was made governor of Farther Spain, today's western Spain and Portugal. Age and a balding head led him to wear laurel leaves as a crown. After that governorship he returned and, in 59 bce, won election as consul, a prestigious office. Patrician senators opposed him vehemently. He still got himself named governor of Cisalpine Gaul, today's northern Italy, and of Transalpine Gaul, today's France. Recruitment and expansion had ample ground there. Lands north of Rome counted as frontier. Those lands are now the north of France, plus Germany and Belgium. Earlier ambitious governors had crossed it with little success. People in Rome knew little of the northern tribes. Soldiers feared them and respected them. Advantages still belonged to Caesar's men, though the northerners were bigger, stronger, and tougher. Opponents usually had far greater numbers. Roman legions were much better organized. Their chain of command let them maneuver quickly and well. Equipment was more advanced. Most of all, they had Caesar.

5Keen military instincts and brilliant tactics were his. Infectious energy motivated people. Battle found him physically tough and utterly without fear. He led on foot and required officers to do the same. Siege engines, machines for attacking fortified forces, were built on his orders and saved countless Roman lives. Soldiers gave respect and loyalty. Others gave criticism. Ruthlessness in battle was notorious. Women could be killed or starved. Children could be too. So could other people who were not fighting. None of that troubled him. Harsh tactics brought great victories, yet even his own age found them extreme. One device that worked was the battering ram. Soldiers stood under a shed for protection. Chains held a heavy ram, and they swung it until fortified gates broke. In Gaul the soldiers started nervous, then defeated adversaries again and again. Setbacks came at times. Many scholars still rank him among history's greatest generals. The Rhine River was bridged. Armies entered Germany. The English Channel was crossed into Britain. In 52 bce a last united stand by the Gallic tribes was faced and beaten. Gaul was finally one. Exploits and looting there built a large personal fortune and great glory. Rome's future, and the future of Gaul and of what became modern Europe, felt the impact. Readers who want more on the campaigns can read the man himself. He wrote about what he lived. What he wrote about fighting in Gaul still survives, which is remarkable. Writings on his other conflicts survive too. Historians agree he likely cast his own actions in a positive light. Readers who look past that find gripping accounts of famous events. Students of Latin are often required to read the writings. Lionel Royer painted the scene in 1899. Vercingetorix yields. The moment follows the fighting at Alesia.

6Political agents and allies worked for him in Rome while he stayed in Gaul. General and politician both, he had to stay sharp amid Rome's political perils. The alliance with Pompey was cemented in 59 bce, the consul year, when Pompey married Julia, Caesar's daughter. Caesar then joined Pompey to Crassus, one of Rome's wealthiest men. The pair had been political opponents. Uniting them was a brilliant stroke. Together, Pompey, Caesar, and Crassus, called the First Triumvirate, held massive political sway. One coin, struck in 44 bce, carries Julius Caesar's face. The back of the coin carries Venus. The family traced its origins to that goddess. As his star rose, the other two grew resentful. Julia's death in 54 bce cut the marriage tie between Pompey and Caesar. Crassus died in battle the next year. Bitter rivalry replaced the old alliance. Triumphs in Gaul, as news of them reached Rome, pushed Pompey closer to the patrician faction, which saw Caesar as a threat. In 50 bce he wanted to come home. Senators insisted the legions leave his command. Pompey was not told to relinquish his armies. Patrician Senate leaders, Caesar knew, feared him. Without the army, he suspected, return would mean arrest and possibly death. While he fought in Gaul, friends and agents kept working for him back in Rome. The marriage of Pompey to Julia, his daughter, sealed their tie in 59 bce, the year of the consulship. Crassus, very rich and once Pompey's opponent, was pulled into the same pact. People call the three the First Triumvirate. A coin from 44 bce shows him, and Venus is on the other side, because the family claimed that goddess as an ancestor. Julia's death in 54 bce broke the family tie. Crassus died in battle the next year. By 50 bce the Senate wanted his legions given up, but not Pompey's. He feared arrest, or death, if he came home alone.

7So in 49 bce he brought the army to the Rubicon River, the border between Cisalpine Gaul and Italy. He knew the crossing would count as war. His aim was to seize Rome's corrupt government and reform it. Civil war with Pompey's men was ignited. Seasoned troops quickly beat Pompey's. Pompey fled into Egypt. Assassins there killed him. Ptolemy, who ruled Egypt, had given the order. Caesar followed. There he met Cleopatra, Ptolemy's sister, and a relationship began. She and Ptolemy were rivals for Egypt's rule. She saw a strong ally. A son was born to them, and with his help she took Egypt's throne back. Return to Rome came in 46 bce. The title he took for himself was dictator, over the Senate. Concentrated power enraged and frightened opponents. Romans had sworn never again to accept one monarch. He seemed to be aiming at exactly that. A picture shows the legion led across the Rubicon into Italy. He led the state only briefly, yet many reforms appeared. Taxation was updated. Great public works began. The Senate was expanded, and for the first time it included people from cities other than Rome. Many were his allies. He was surprisingly lenient and also gave important posts to some of Pompey's supporters. Reform of the republic had been his intent. A group of senators still conspired. The date was March 15, 44 bce, called the Ides of March. Attackers struck him and left him dead. A map of the Republic in 45 bce shows Cisalpine Gaul and the Atlantic Ocean. Transalpine Gaul, meaning France, is marked, with Macedonia and the Black Sea. Rome, Spain, and Asia, meaning Turkey, are marked, with Greece, the Mediterranean Sea, and Africa. The map is the Republic at the time of his death.

8In 1865 a painter from Germany, Karl Theodor von Piloty, made a picture of the killing. Murder made Caesar a martyr at once. Romans declared him divine in 42 bce. The killing also opened chaos, and a war inside Rome followed. Conflict ran for years. Then a great-nephew, Octavian, rose. He became Augustus Caesar and Rome's earliest emperor. The judicious reign of Augustus let the empire steady itself. Brutal and cunning as Caesar was, military victories widened Roman influence and laid foundations for the Roman Empire. Greek and Roman knowledge spread into new territories, including Roman ideas of governance, of military organization, and of law. Gaul, which he had conquered, was among those lands. Reforming the Roman calendar ranks among his greatest achievements. The old one was lunar, based on the moon's monthly cycles, and it counted 355 days. A year in most calendars used now has 365 days. Leaders before him picked where those extra ten days would sit. That power let them shift elections and holidays to suit themselves. Astronomers helped him build a new calendar based on Earth's movement around the Sun, a solar calendar. Extra days were placed in specific months. The leap year was introduced. July is named for him. Inside the empire, newly conquered peoples took on parts of Roman culture. Greek stayed dominant in the eastern Mediterranean. Elsewhere, Latin became the main language of commerce and of society. His leadership therefore shaped the future of lands that would be joined, in politics and in society, under the Roman Empire.

9Life dates include these. Birth is 100 bce. The father dies, and marriage to Cornelia comes, in 84 bce. During 83 and 82 bce, Sulla takes charge in Rome. Sulla dies, and Caesar returns to Rome, in 78 bce. Kidnapping by pirates is 75 bce. Election as Pontifex is 73 bce. Cornelia's death is 69 bce. Marriage to Pompeia, daughter of ally Pompey, is 67 bce. Election as Pontifex Maximus is 63 bce. Divorce from Pompeia is 62 bce. Appointment as governor of Farther Spain is 61 bce. From 60 to 59 bce he returns to Rome, is elected consul, marries Calpurnia, and forms the First Triumvirate. In 58 bce he becomes governor of Cisalpine Gaul and of Transalpine Gaul, and he defeats Germanic tribes. The year 55 bce brings a defeat of Germanic tribes who had entered Gaul. Legions cross the Rhine. Britain is invaded. Julia, the daughter married to Pompey, dies in 54 bce. Crassus is defeated and killed in 53 bce. In 52 bce Vercingetorix unites rebel tribes in Gaul, and the uprising is suppressed. The Rubicon is crossed, and civil war begins, in 49 bce. The Ides of March assassination is 44 bce. Members of a society's highest class, usually wealthy and powerful, are the aristocracy. Martyr names someone whose beliefs, or whose deeds, bring suffering or death. An orator speaks in public. Eloquence is what marks the best of them. Generous or kind is what benevolent means. When a city or a built-up district behaves as its own country, it is a city-state. Pitiless, cruel, and wholly without morals is what ruthless means. Secret plans, or the making of them, are intrigues. Someone skilled at careful planning toward a goal is a tactician. Good sense or wise judgment is what judicious means. Strongly and with great emotion is what vehemently means. Very forgiving or tolerant is what lenient means. Producing a lot of money, or profitable, is what lucrative means.

90. The Super School Bus System

1School buses can cut carbon emissions when they replace private cars on the road. The average bus carries fifty-four students and can replace about thirty-six private vehicles. This change, plus newer greener technology, can help keep the air cleaner. Buses use more gas than cars to travel the same distance because buses are bigger. When you count the passengers, buses use fuel better and pollute far less. The chart measures gallons used on a ten-mile, or 16 kilometer, trip. Thirty-six family vehicles use 14.4 gallons, or 54.5 liters. A diesel bus uses 1.4 gallons, or 5.3 liters. A hybrid bus uses 0.8 gallons, or 3 liters. In 1943, children at an army base rode a horse-drawn bus so the country could save gasoline and tires in World War II.

2Sarah walks out on a freezing day to a bus stop one block from home. Shower water freezes in her hair, but the bus arrives on time. She greets the driver and reviews her science test on the way to school. This daily ride is so common that few people ask how the system works. At the start of the 2016 school year, Houston added forty-four buses with three-point belts for every rider to a fleet of 1,100. Some people debate bus belts, since buses have stricter safety rules and drivers cannot watch more than fifty students. In 2016, a New York district introduced a fully electric bus with zero emissions that travels about 120 miles before a recharge. Propane costs less than diesel and cuts emissions, while hybrids use diesel plus electric power and in 2007 drivers reported almost twice the mileage.

3Coordinators, drivers, and mechanics work together, and school buses are the safest ride for students. The National Safety Council says they are forty times safer than private cars. Drivers train hard, buses are checked often, and exits, strong roofs, and close seats that absorb impact protect students. Most states do not require belts, but Texas, New York, and California do. Flashing stop signs and cameras inside and outside help, and more safety tools will come with new technology. Each district, not one central authority, directs its own buses and a small army of workers. Highways and unpaved lanes link remote rural areas with towns and cities. Local property taxes, which also pay for police, fire departments, libraries, and schools, fund the buses, and some states help because everybody is entitled to an education.

4Moving students to school and home is an enormous job. U.S. public school buses use more vehicles and carry more people than any other mass transit. In 2013, about 480,000 buses carried a little more than half of public school students each day. The school bus fleet has more than twice as many vehicles as all other U.S. mass transit combined. In Hong Kong, 90 percent of travel is mass transit, and seven million people ride daily. In 2013, twenty-six million U.S. students rode school buses each day. The system is huge because the country is large, the population is large, and many places lack other student transit. Rural areas often have no public transit, and the Kingman, Arizona, system covers more land than Delaware.

5In 1973, white children rode a bus from a North Carolina suburb to Charlotte's inner city. In 1979, black children and their moms rode a bus across Cleveland, Ohio, under a desegregation plan. Coordinators now plan routes for districts that have consolidated schools. Consolidation joins several smaller schools in one larger building. Students can share resources, so education costs can fall. Some students must travel much farther, so routes grow larger and more complex. In rural Texas in the mid-1990s, one of the longest routes carried some students about 100 miles each way. Those students spent more time on the bus than they did in school!

6In the later twentieth century, districts used buses for a new goal called school integration. Integration means bringing African American and white students together in schools. Before 1954, many schools were segregated, so black and white students went to separate schools. Those schools were not equal, and white students usually got better chances and more resources. In 1954, the U.S. Supreme Court case Brown v. Board of Education said segregation discriminated against African American students. Integration began, but it met fierce resistance in the South. In Northern and Western states, segregation was de facto because students already lived in separate neighborhoods. In the 1970s and 1980s, schools bused black students to white schools and white students to black schools.

7This practice was called desegregation busing, and it was controversial. By the 1990s, most districts had stopped it. Delaware is the second smallest state, at 1,954 square miles. The Kingman Unified School District covers more than 3,000 square miles. If that district is 3,000 square miles, it is 1,046 square miles larger than Delaware. Coordinators study many factors so wide routes work well. They limit daily commute time, and each district sets a safe walk range to the stop. Many districts bus students who live more than 2 miles away, or who must cross a highway, and they plan routes before school starts.

8American public schools moved students long before the modern school bus. In the 1800s, rural students used one-room schoolhouses and walked or rode wagons and sleds. Horse-drawn wagons stopped at set points, and around 1910 a stagecoach bus waited at a Colorado high school. Later, motor vehicles replaced wagons, but districts still planned routes and carried students to school and home. A bus from 1925 looked unlike modern buses, and 1920s buses resembled an extra-long Model T before buses grew larger. Yellow was chosen because it is easy to see, so drivers can stop in time for students to board. Federal law requires the color National School Bus Glossy Yellow. The words School Bus must be at least 8 inches high so buses are easy to recognize.

91. The War That Made a Country

1A timeline of the quarrel runs through several famous events. The French and Indian War was one part of Europe's Seven Years' War. Parliament later passed the Sugar Act. The Quartering Act and the Stamp Act followed. So did the Townshend Acts. Violence in Boston became known as the Boston Massacre. Colonists dumped tea in what people call the Boston Tea Party. The Coercive Acts, renamed the Intolerable Acts, came next. The First Continental Congress met. On April 19, 1775, war began at Lexington and at Concord. The United States did not start as its own country. It started as thirteen colonies. Great Britain ruled them. So did the English king, George III. Britain placed taxes on the colonists. It also enforced new laws that people disliked. Colonists objected. They said a tax was unacceptable when they had no representative speaking for them in Parliament. Parliament seemed unwilling to honor the Bill of Rights of 1689. That bill covered every citizen of the British realm. Colonists were included. As time passed, bad feeling grew. Violence grew with it. King George III tried to tighten his grip. He used harder taxes. He used threats of military force. A chain of events pushed the two sides into open fighting. The Boston Tea Party was part of that chain. The clash came on April 19, 1775. British soldiers met colonists in two Massachusetts towns. One town was Lexington. The other was Concord. Shots were fired. A separate note explains a famous cry. King George would not cancel the taxes. A fight for independence began to look unavoidable for the colonies. Patrick Henry went home to Virginia after the First Continental Congress. In a speech there he said he would take liberty even if the other choice was death. During the war, Patriots shouted a short form of that idea. Their battle cry was Liberty or Death.

2The first shots came on Lexington's village green. Which side fired the opening shot is still unknown. Ralph Waldo Emerson later wrote a poem called Concord Hymn. Because of that poem, people remember the opening shot as one the whole world heard. War had started. Britain stood on one side. The thirteen colonies stood on the other. The ground they fought on already had owners. For thousands of years, Native peoples had made that region their home. By 1775, the coming of Europeans had killed millions of Native people. The next century would bring millions more deaths. Land from one coast to the other would be taken from them. A new meeting gathered on May 10, 1775. It was the Second Continental Congress. The place was Independence Hall. The city was Philadelphia, in Pennsylvania. Fifty-six delegates were there. With one shared vote they picked a commander. George Washington got the job. He was a Virginia delegate. He had once been an officer in the British army. Until then, people knew those troops by another name. They were the New England militia. Congress chose a new name, the Continental Army. The new name was meant to build unity among the colonies. Volunteers from all thirteen colonies would fill the ranks. Easy is not a word for Washington's task. His soldiers were a mixed, poorly prepared group. Farmers were among them. Carpenters were among them. Blacksmiths were among them. Weapons were few. Training was thin or missing. His orders said to capture every armed enemy. Destroying those enemies was the other allowed choice. Across the field stood Britain. That army was powerful. It was trained. It was well supplied. Washington expected to fail. He said so to Patrick Henry, a Virginia lawyer. From the moment he took command, Washington believed, his fall would begin. He also believed his good name would be ruined. He still trusted American independence as a cause. Command was the duty he accepted. He insisted on serving without pay. Independence was not every colonist's wish. His new troops were near Boston. Washington went to meet them around Concord and Lexington. Congress kept trying to repair the break with Parliament. A petition left the delegates' hands. King George III was the person they addressed. They asked again for colonists' rights. They asked him to call the colonists loyal English subjects. The king would not even receive the petition. His answer was a hard judgment. He said the colonists had moved into open rebellion. He said that rebellion was openly declared.

3In short, wanting independence made a colonist a traitor to the crown. Native peoples felt the war deeply. Separation was King George III's aim. He wanted Native peoples on one side and colonists on the other. He hoped the gap would stop violence between the two groups. Some lands had been set aside by Great Britain for Native peoples. Colonists disliked that decision. When the fighting came, Native peoples did not all choose one side. Some joined the Patriots. Others joined the British. At times a nation split. At times an alliance split. Britain's loss handed the United States a huge stretch of land. Native peoples had lived on that land for centuries. They lost more than ground. Cultures were lost. Countless lives were lost. Native resistance to Britain came before the American fight. A picture shows the Ottawa leader Pontiac visiting the British. The year is 1763. Soon afterward he tried to drive the British out. Support came from the Great Lakes region. Almost all the tribes there backed him. The struggle called Pontiac's War carries his name. It lasted from 1763 to 1766. While Congress sat in Philadelphia, colonial soldiers won a fort. The place was Fort Ticonderoga, in New York. Ethan Allen was a rough, tough farmer from New Hampshire. He and other local farmers had formed the Green Mountain Boys. A British fort stood on Lake Champlain. Congress asked Allen's group to capture it. Another soldier received orders too. His name was Benedict Arnold. Connecticut had given him an official commission to seize the fort. Both men wanted to lead. They argued for the whole journey. On May 10, 1775, they still took the fort together. The next day a second fort fell. It stood at Crown Point. Allen and Arnold captured it. Colonial spirits rose. The northern border was now safer from British attack. The wins also announced a plain fact. War had truly started. Colonists had to choose. Loyalists wanted to stay part of Britain. Patriots wanted independence from Britain. No middle choice remained.

4Lexington's opening battle had sent British soldiers back toward Boston. Major John Pitcairn led that retreat. Colonial soldiers camped outside the city and kept gathering. In time about 16,000 Patriot troops ringed Boston. The British supply line into the city was cut. General Thomas Gage saw a danger. Patriot troops might fortify hills across the Charles River. One hill was Bunker Hill. The other was Breed's Hill. Both stand in Charlestown. A map shows the British path. After losing at Lexington and at Concord, they fell back to Charlestown. They then crossed the river into Boston. Labels on that map include Lexington, Concord, Boston, and the Atlantic Ocean. The date was June 16 in the year 1775. Orders that night came from General Artemis Ward. He told Patriot soldiers to dig trenches. The hill he named was Bunker Hill. The soldiers misunderstood. They went instead to Breed's Hill. That hill sat closer to the British. Morning showed the slope covered with soldiers. Trenches covered it too. General William Howe brought the British response. Ships carried them over the Charles River. Cannons fired as they came. Patriots stood at a disadvantage. Their training was weak. They faced professional soldiers. Gunpowder was very scarce. Officers told them to save every shot. Fire, they said, only when the enemy was near enough that the whites of their eyes showed. The plan worked. British soldiers rushed uphill. Americans held their shots until the last moment that was still safe. Many attackers died. More British troops landed and charged again. Americans again waited, then fired. A third wave finally broke the defense. Gunpowder was gone. The Americans had to retreat. Britain took Breed's Hill. Britain also took Bunker Hill.

5A map of the fight marks the Mystic River and the Charles River. It marks Breed's Hill, Bunker Hill, Charlestown, Boston, and Copp's Hill. Patriot soldiers held one set of positions. British soldiers held another. Control of the two hills went to Britain. The price was high. British losses passed a thousand. The count includes both the wounded and the dead. Patriot losses were 441 men. Even in defeat, Patriot spirits rose. They had shown they could stand in a fight against a larger body of professional soldiers. Most of the action happened on Breed's Hill. People still name the fight for Bunker Hill. July 1775 is when General George Washington reached the army. His troops kept the British shut inside Boston. The shut-in lasted nearly a year. Canada was the next worry, so he sent men to invade it. He did not want Britain landing there and then marching south into New York. General Richard Montgomery led Patriots who took Montreal. The month was November 1775. Quebec was Arnold's target. He led the assault there. Severe December weather made that attack fail. Through the winter, Patriots turned captured British cannons on the soldiers inside Boston. The British left the city on a March day in 1776. The day of the month was the 17th. Thousands of Loyalists left with them. Washington's troops marched in as winners. A picture shows cannons the Continental Army used against the British.

6A saying still heard today is an invitation to sign a paper in a bold way, using the words John Hancock. The saying reaches back to 1776. That year Hancock signed the Declaration of Independence in a large, fearless hand. Fifty-three other people still needed to sign. His large name encouraged them. Thomas Paine, a Patriot, wrote a pamphlet called Common Sense. In it he said independence was the only right choice for the colonists. He challenged British authority. Most readers could follow him because the language stayed plain. About 150,000 copies sold within a few months. Many Loyalists shifted toward independence because of it. In June 1776 Congress picked a committee. The committee would write a statement. The subject was the colonists' right to govern themselves. Thomas Jefferson was the youngest member of Congress. He became the actual writer. People knew his skill with words. July 4, 1776, was the day Congress said yes. The document was the Declaration of Independence. Each of the thirteen colonies then passed it. With that yes, a new country existed. People called the new country the United States of America. Colony, the old name, no longer fit. The colonies were now called states. Hard days came next. Patriots lost fight after fight. A month after the Declaration was signed, General William Howe moved a huge force by ship. British soldiers entered New York Harbor. Their number was 30,000. The Battle of Long Island ran for three days. Outnumbered Patriots finally retreated. They went south across New Jersey. Philadelphia was the direction of that retreat. Britain occupied New York City. In another fight, Patriots surrendered Fort Washington. Patriot losses in that stretch passed 2,000. Some were dead. Others were prisoners. Three days was the length of that stretch. Nathan Hale is honored by a statue. He was a teacher, 21 years old. New York City held British troops. Hale volunteered to spy on them. He was caught. He was hanged. His final words said he was sorry to have only a single life to offer his country.

7Benedict Arnold had been a brave general. He believed Congress had treated him badly. He believed the Continental Army had too. In 1779 Washington gave him a fort. The fort was West Point, on the lower Hudson River. Arnold planned to sell that fort to the British. The plan came to light. The exposed plot made him a traitor. He then entered Britain's army. Earlier, in October 1776, his gunboats lost a fight. The place was Lake Champlain, in Canada. The Patriots still fought so hard that Britain grew worried. Beating the rebels might be harder than expected. The date of a bolder strike was December 24 in 1776. Boats carried George Washington and his men over the Delaware River. The target was Trenton, in New Jersey. Hessian mercenaries were the enemy there. Those hired soldiers came from Germany. They were allied with the British. The crossing took one night. Patriots got 2,400 men to the far bank. The river was icy. Sleet fell. Snow fell. The battle that followed lasted less than an hour. The Patriots won. It was the war's first major victory. A few days later Washington beat the British again. That fight was at Princeton, also in New Jersey. The two wins lifted Patriot spirits. A picture shows Washington accepting a surrender. The place is Trenton, and the year is 1776. Britain struck back in June 1777. General John Burgoyne led a large army south out of Canada. His plan aimed at the Hudson River around Albany, New York. Taking that area would cut New England and New York off from every other colony. During the march he took Fort Ticonderoga back. Patriot soldiers stopped his push at the Battle of Saratoga. The month was October. Burgoyne surrendered about 6,000 men. A map of his march south from Canada shows Lake Champlain twice. It shows Fort Ticonderoga. It names Riedesel, St. Clair, and Phillips. It marks British troops and British military leaders.

8People look back on Saratoga as a major turn in the war. France and other countries in Europe could now see that the Patriots might win. In 1778 France entered the fight. Great Britain was its old enemy. France sent supplies to the Continental Army. Spain soon declared war on Britain. The Netherlands did too. Shortage still haunted the Continental Army. Food was often missing. Clothing was often missing. Shelter was often missing. At Valley Forge, in Pennsylvania, Washington's troops lived through a freezing, hungry winter. Supplies arrived only after that suffering. June 1778 brought the next big fight. The terrible winter was behind them. Washington attacked the British army at the Battle of Monmouth. General Henry Clinton now commanded the British. Neither side won. No later battle in the northern colonies matched it in size. It did show something important. Patriots could meet Britain's soldiers on equal footing. Valley Forge has a National Memorial Arch. Washington's words are cut into it. He said the soldiers were naked and starving, yet their patience and loyalty were beyond enough praise. Women could not serve in the army. They still served the war in other ways. One way was making homespun cloth at home. The Stamp Act had passed in 1765. After that, many women boycotted British goods. They made replacements themselves. That home labor was an act of protest and of rebellion. The Daughters of Liberty even spun thread in public demonstrations. Women made bullets. They sewed blankets. They sewed uniforms. They raised money. At the camps they cooked. They cleaned. They nursed the injured and the sick. They searched for food. Carrying water out to soldiers under fire put some women's lives in danger. Mary Ludwick Hays stepped in for her husband, William Hays, after he was wounded. History remembers her as Molly Pitcher. At the Battle of Monmouth she carried water for the soldiers. She also carried water for the cannon. That work earned her the nickname Molly Pitcher.

9British forces took Savannah, in Georgia, in December 1778. They next attacked Charleston, in South Carolina, and captured it in May 1780. Another win came at Camden, also in South Carolina, in August 1780. Those three battles had the war's highest casualty rates. Loyalty to Britain was common among colonists who lived in the South. Britain was winning the South. Patriots refused to quit. The turn began in October. Patriots won at King's Mountain, in South Carolina. The fight lasted a quick sixty-five minutes. Few battles in the war left British soldiers out entirely. This one did. Patriots fought Loyalists. More Patriot wins followed in 1781. January brought a win at Cowpens. April brought a win at Hobkirk's Hill. Those victories pushed General Charles Cornwallis north. Virginia was where he was forced to go. He had helped Britain win at Long Island in 1776. The year 1780 put him at the head of Britain's southern troops. The French alliance began to repay the Patriots. French soldiers helped hold the British back. They also fought beside colonists in the force Washington led into Virginia. The war's fighters included thousands of Black people. They did not all choose the same army. Most were enslaved. Most joined the side that seemed more likely to offer freedom. Great Britain's side included Black fighters. The number was more than 20,000. The Patriot side drew Black fighters too. Estimates run from 5,000 up to 8,000. Freedom was still decades away for many enslaved Black people. James Armistead stands as one American hero of that fight. Before the war he was enslaved in Virginia. His role was to serve as a double agent. He was good at it. The story he acted out was simple. He seemed to be a runaway loyal to Britain. Before long, Britain trusted him with a spy job aimed at the Patriots. The secret ran the other way too. Patriots were using him to watch the British. General Lafayette received battle plans from him. Those plans belonged to the British. Those details were ones the Patriots needed at Yorktown. Winning the wider war depended on Yorktown. After the fighting, a law called the Act of 1783 came into force. It freed enslaved soldiers of the Revolution. Armistead's work as a spy kept him out of that freedom. He went back to life as a slave. Freedom arrived years afterward. The help came from the French officer who had commanded him. Armistead added Lafayette to his own name. The added name showed thanks. It also showed the bond they shared. A painting from 1824 shows James Armistead Lafayette.

10A picture shows Cornwallis giving up to Washington at Yorktown. The war's most important battle was about to start. Twenty-four French ships met nineteen British ships. Cornwallis and his troops needed rescue. Britain had sent those ships for that job. Yorktown sits on the Virginia coast. The French fleet drove the rescue away. It also brought more soldiers for the land fight. French troops and Patriot troops moved in. They laid a siege around the British army. Three weeks passed. The British surrendered on October 19, 1781. That surrender ended the Revolutionary War. Victory belonged to the Patriots. The Peace of Paris arrived in 1783. Only then was independence from Great Britain official. The treaty gave the United States all the North American land west to the Mississippi River. Neither government truly owned that ground. The rightful holders were Native peoples. Colonies that had leaned on another country now had to join together. They had to build a nation from the start. Several people shaped the war. George Washington commanded the Continental Army. He later became the country's first president. Thomas Gage commanded British troops in the colonies. After Lexington and Concord, his army was trapped in Boston. John Burgoyne commanded the British northern army. He captured Fort Ticonderoga. He was later beaten at Saratoga. King George III was twenty-two when he became king of Great Britain. Keeping the colonies was his fixed goal. Cost did not change his mind. The Declaration of Independence came from Thomas Jefferson's pen. Thomas Paine wrote the booklet Common Sense. It moved many colonists to choose independence. From 1775 until 1778, William Howe was Britain's top commander on the North American mainland. The year 1778 brought a change of command. Henry Clinton took Howe's place. Pictures show George Washington and King George III.

11A few words unlock this history. Abandoned means left behind. A Loyalist lived in the thirteen colonies and stayed with Great Britain while the American Revolution was fought. Amends are acts meant to make up for a harm or a loss. Mercenaries are soldiers who will fight for any army that pays them. A casualty is a person hurt, killed, or missing in a war, an accident, or a disaster. Momentum is staying power. It is what keeps a movement going, or keeps it growing, as time passes. A commission is an official order, usually military, that requires someone to do a duty. Morale is the confidence or enthusiasm a person or a group feels while working toward a goal. A conflict is a clash of ideas, principles, or opinions. The word also means a fight, a battle, or a war. A Patriot backed independence. The people in question lived in the thirteen colonies, and the time was the American Revolution. Delegates are people chosen or elected to represent others and act for them. A petition is a formal written request. A large number of citizens often sign it. Independence is freedom from another power's control, influence, support, or help. Retaliated means struck back after being attacked. Nations use a treaty when they want a formal deal. Groups can use one too. The deal may promise peace or friendship. Self-governing means having the right to make and enforce laws without outside control. Unity is the quality of being joined in one group, one purpose, or one identity. In a siege, attackers ring an enemy and stay there. The stay is long. Attacks may continue. Food and other supplies are cut off. A map of important sites names Quebec, Ticonderoga, Boston, Concord, and Long Island. It also names Valley Forge, Yorktown, King's Mountain, Camden, Charleston, and Savannah. The Atlantic Ocean borders that map.

92. Tombs of Egypt's Golden Age

1A map of Egypt marks the Mediterranean Sea, Cairo, Memphis, and the Nile. Luxor, once called Thebes, appears beside the Red Sea. This book opens with a famous treasure. It then explains what this royal burial ground is. It explains how kings prepared for the afterlife, and what a tomb held. It follows how a royal tomb was cut and how its art was made. It looks at the valley now, and at treasure still to be found. Word meanings come last. November 1922 brought a staircase into the light. Howard Carter, a British archaeologist, uncovered the steps down to King Tutankhamen. Say that name toot-an-KAH-muhn. Explorers had thought Egypt's Valley of the Kings had no finds left. This tomb proved them wrong. Its royal seal was still whole. No earlier royal tomb in the valley had been found that way. Tutankhamen was among the least important pharaohs buried there. Four chambers made his tomb one of the smallest. Even so, the packed objects numbered more than five thousand. Many of those objects were solid gold. His golden funeral mask is inlaid with colored glass and with semiprecious stones. It ranks among Egypt's most famous treasures. Workers had laid the mask over the mummy, covering both the head and the shoulders.

2Few burial grounds on Earth match the Valley of the Kings for magnificence. Almost every pharaoh of Egypt's golden age lies here. That age is the New Kingdom. Three dynasties ruled it: the Eighteenth, the Nineteenth, and the Twentieth. The dates run from 1550 until 1080 bc. The length of that age is about five hundred years. Sixty-three tombs are known. A map marks KV 62 as Tutankhamen, KV 9 as Ramses IV, KV 57 as Horemheb, and KV 17 as Seti I. Some tombs are missing from the map. A few lie farther west. The key shows a discovered tomb and the label KV for Kings' Valley. During this age, Thebes was Egypt's capital and its religious center. Today that city is Luxor. Temples there honored the empire's pharaohs. Ancient Egyptians believed those rulers joined the gods after death. A mummified king needed a place where his body could rest undisturbed. His spirit still had to journey toward the afterlife. Al Qurn, pronounced el GOORN, is a mountain shaped like a pyramid above the valley. The pyramid stood for Ra, pronounced RAH, the Sun god. Across the Nile, a vast desert wadi offered a practical site. Say wadi as WAH-dee. It is a valley with steep sides. Soft limestone was plentiful, and tombs could be chiseled from it. Steep cliffs and a single way in made guarding easier. Thebes lay several hours' walk away, which helped keep robbers off.

3Ancient Egyptians ranked a pharaoh's tomb nearly as high as the palace he had lived in. The tomb guarded the body. People believed that body could live again after burial. Mummification took seventy days so the body would not start decomposing. Priests took out the internal organs, mummified them, and set them in a stone box. That box is a canopic chest. Nested coffins then held the body. A stone sarcophagus held the coffins. Granite or quartzite was carved for it. Weight could reach 9 metric tons, or 10 tons. The spirit needed protection too, while it moved through the underworld. Amulets went into the mummy's wrappings. Statues of protective gods went into the sarcophagus. One picture shows Howard Carter lifting a cover from Tutankhamen's third coffin, the innermost one. At many tomb entrances, Ra's names and prayers appear with pictures and hieroglyphs. Spells and prayers called funerary compositions covered walls and ceilings. Sometimes they covered the sarcophagus. Hieroglyphs and images ran down those surfaces in tall columns. Some spells were meant to bring the body back to life. A second group of spells sat within the sarcophagus. Their aim was to frighten demons. Those demons might try to sabotage the soul's journey. The writings had a third job. They guided the soul through trials on the way to the afterlife. Egyptians believed the pharaoh's soul had to travel west. It went through the underworld beside Ra. Obstacles and dangers waited along that road.

4A king was expected to want things in the afterlife, so royal tombs stored a wide supply. Wooden models filled storerooms, including boats and chariots. Cosmetics, clothing, and board games counted as personal goods. Furniture and lamps counted as everyday goods. Gems of high value were stored as treasure. Jewelry made of gold was stored too. So was artwork. Fruit sat in baskets. Preserved meat sat in boxes. Juice and other drinks sat in pots. Servants would be needed too. Servant figures filled that role, and they numbered in the hundreds. Each figure is a shabti, said SHAB-teez. The word means answerer. A spell on each figure was meant to animate it when the master called. Tutankhamen went into the tomb with 413 of these figures. Whether wood or stone, the small statues teach a great deal about beliefs and customs. Murals cover the burial chamber of Ramses VI, a king of the Twentieth Dynasty. Tombs in the valley share many features. Elaborate paintings and hieroglyphs decorate most of them. Halls and rooms often follow the same series. An entryway opens into a hall. Egyptians gave it this name: the passage of Ra. Images there often show the Sun god's many forms and names. Farther in, the hall of hindering often has a deep well cut into the floor. Experts think the pit may have slowed robbers. It may also have guarded against floods. Every plan ends in the burial chamber. Egyptians sometimes called that room the House of Gold. Storerooms opening off most of these chambers held furniture and supplies.

5Shared features did not make the tombs copies of one another. No pair in the valley is identical. Taste of the ruler decided the build and the decoration. Cutting started while the king still lived. Death left the builders only seventy days. By then mummification would be done, and the burial could not wait. An unfinished tomb might be rushed. Paintings or rooms could be left half done. Death came for Ramses IV while his tomb was still unfinished. Workers recut a chamber that already existed and used it for the burial. Other kings were buried in a tomb that was not the one begun for them. In the tomb of Ramses IX, experts think only two corridors had plaster before he died. The workmanship looks hurried. Layouts changed from early tombs to later ones. Early plans turned left once, or more than once. Later plans ran without turns. Experts think a straight line kept crews from cutting into older tombs by accident. A shared set of rooms can be labeled this way. A is the entrance. B is the passage of Ra. C is the hall of hindering, and it holds the deep well. D is the chariot hall, with sets of pillars. Chariots, though, have never turned up in that hall. E is the burial chamber.

6Time changed how the tombs looked and how they were laid out. Early New Kingdom work, in the Eighteenth Dynasty, is more than three thousand years old. Those tombs tended to be smaller than later ones. Their floor plans usually bent left in one or two turns of ninety degrees. Even now, workers raise walls above tombs. Falling debris would otherwise clutter the entrances. Placement shifted as well. Early in the New Kingdom, royal tombs sat at the bottoms of cliffs. Rain then washed water and debris down over an entrance. Later rulers more often put entrances on lower slopes. One reason may be that later tombs were meant to be opened again after burial. Another may be crowding in the valley. A tomb in a straight line was also less likely to strike another tomb. Experts think cutting began very early in a reign, close to the day power passed to a king. The first critical choice was the spot. The vizier, pronounced vi-ZEER, made it with senior workmen. He was the highest official of the court. A bad spot could force a new plan or a move. More than once, crews had already begun cutting when the first choice was abandoned. A workers' village explains much of this. Most digging at Deir el-Medina took place from 1922 to 1951. About four hundred tomb workers lived there with their families. The village sits about 1 kilometer, or 0.6 miles, south of the valley. Writings left in that village are a main source for knowledge of this royal burial ground.

7Limestone bedrock had to be cut for every tomb. Copper or bronze chisels started the rough passages. Wooden mallets drove them. Hand axes with stone blades helped. At the beginning, the passage was so tight that only one or two men could cut at once. A basket brigade of other workers carried debris out. A line painted by the foreman ran along the ceiling. That line was the reference for measuring, while walls, ceiling, and floor were refined. Simple tools still produced turns of ninety degrees. They also produced vertical walls that stayed parallel. The accuracy was remarkable. Decoration began once the cutting had gone far enough. Plasterers spread white gypsum plaster over the surfaces. Scribes drew vertical lines and horizontal lines. Those lines boxed in scenes and texts. Hieroglyphs and figures were sketched next. A supervisor came behind the scribes and corrected the work. Artists then painted blocks of color and filled in details. Sometimes they carved a relief. Parts of a scene were cut away so other parts stood out. Cutting away the background left raised figures, and that result is a raised relief. Details were carved into the figures before any paint. Horemheb's unfinished tomb still shows the first sketches and the corrections. Red ink marks the scribe's outlines. Black ink marks the supervisor's corrections. Because Horemheb died before the tomb was fully done, the steps remain visible. Scribes first outlined text and scenes in red. A supervisor checked those outlines and corrected them in black. He might fix a figure's proportions. He might note a missing image. Artists then traced the corrected images in black ink. Finishing work could include cutting the background away so figures stood up from the wall. Paint came last.

8Treasure hunters crowded the valley in the early 1800s. Like the robbers of ancient times, they took whatever could be sold to rich collectors. The year 1857 changed that pattern. Egypt's government set up the Antiquities Service. Its job was to protect ancient monuments and artifacts. Explorers today use methods meant to protect tombs and to preserve what is inside them. The year 1979 put the valley on an early World Heritage list. A special department inside the United Nations made that choice. Yearly visits pass one million. Tissue taken from mummies found here lets scientists study diet. It lets them study disease. It can even suggest how someone died. On a typical day, four to five thousand tourists come. Eighteen tombs open to the public, but not all at once. They rotate. One ticket lets a visitor choose three tombs from those open that day. One tomb is the exception. Tutankhamen's tomb needs an extra ticket. Objects first found in his tomb are kept at the Cairo Museum of Antiquities. A careless touch can discolor ancient paint. It can damage carvings. Rotation gives each tomb regular time away from crowds. Planned closures also leave time for restoration and for maintenance. Experts hope those breaks will offset the harm of staying open to the public.

9Decades after Carter's famous find, the valley gave up few fresh secrets. The year 1989 changed that. Egyptologist Kent Weeks studied a tomb called KV 5 more closely. Earlier labels had dismissed it as dull. Flood debris was cleared away. A corridor nobody had known about led to at least 150 chambers. The valley ranks among the richest archaeological sites anywhere. If the experts are right, more history is still buried. Scientists are excavating a tomb made for sons of the king Ramses II. That tomb is KV 5, and it is the largest in the valley. They are studying it as they dig. Difficult words in this book can be read as follows. To animate something is to bring it to life, or to make it lively. Hieroglyphs are picture-symbols used as writing, above all in ancient Egypt. To culminate is to arrive at the high point or the end. A mummified body has been embalmed and wrapped in burial cloth. Debris is the scattered leftover after the rest of something is gone or destroyed. Parallel lines or paths run the same way and stay an equal distance apart. Decomposing means rotting or breaking into smaller parts. Pharaohs is the title ancient Egypt gave its kings. Stone that has been quarried has been dug out for building, such as slate or marble. Dynasties are lines of rulers who share a family. A sarcophagus is a stone coffin from ancient times, often carved and richly decorated. Gypsum is a soft white mineral that plaster is made from.

93. Trains Built for Great Speed

1An ICE train, the Inter City Express, takes a bend in Germany. Racing Across Open Country. Where These Fast Trains Began. What Makes Them Go. Three Ways to Be Fast. The Shinkansen. The TGV. Maglev. Worries About Safety. Why These Trains Help. What Success Requires. The Years Ahead. A TGV rolls past sunflowers in a French field. Racing Across Open Country. Friday morning in Paris. A very fast train is leaving for Avignon, pronounced ah-veen-YONE, far to the south in France. The train is sleek and modern. You sit in comfort while it carries you into open country. Speed on the tracks can reach 186 miles per hour, which is 299 kph. A car would need seven hours for this trip. The train needs 2 hours plus 36 minutes. Science fiction seems to describe it. Scenes like this are ordinary, though, in countries around the world, because these trains exist. Millions of riders, spread through more than a dozen countries, already use them. Further countries are planning systems of this kind, or building them, so transport in this century, the twenty-first, can keep up.

2Where These Fast Trains Began. Speed on rails is old news. Some trains of the 1930s already reached about 100 mph, or 161 kph. Airplanes were not yet a common way to travel, so a long trip usually meant a train. Diesel fuel ran the engines on most of those early fast trains. An electrical generator took power from the diesel engine. Electricity from that generator turned the axles at the front of the train. Japan showed the world the first modern design when it hosted the Olympic Games in 1964. The train was the Shinkansen. People also call it the bullet train. Its first run linked Tokyo with Osaka. Average speed sat near 135 mph, or 217 kph. A chief breakthrough was the power source. Electricity did all the work. Fossil fuels did none of it. An early bullet train from Japan rushes past the city of Kyoto. London is where a Eurostar train sits waiting in a station. The 1970s saw Italy and Germany send out fast trains of their own. France built a large network for its fast trains in the 1980s. Spain opened service in the 1990s, on a system that is now the longest of its kind in Europe. A tunnel under the English Channel, sometimes called the Chunnel, was finished in 1994. A fast train can now go from London to Paris in two hours and fifteen minutes. Across Western Europe these trains race at 150 mph or more, which is 241 kph or more.

3Today, no fast-rail system on Earth runs longer than the one in China. Work began in 2004. The network grew with great speed. More than 3,728 miles of line, or 6,000 km, went in before six years had passed. Use of these trains spread widely across China. No country has more people. The count is above 1.3 billion, about 20 percent of everyone on Earth. Large cities are many, and the capital, Beijing, is one of them. Cars are still missing from many households. A fast train gives those people a needed way to move quickly from city to city. What Makes Them Go. Designs differ, yet some traits are shared. The shape is streamlined, like the nose of a jet airplane. Air slips smoothly over that shape. Drag, which means air resistance, stays small. Less energy is then needed to reach a high speed and to hold it. A Japanese train is shown above a Russian one. The look is not the same. Many features still match.

4A drawing labels the pantograph. Electricity from wires overhead runs most of these trains. A device called a pantograph joins the train to those wires. The link can break, as it does inside a tunnel. Battery power then carries the train until the pantograph joins the wires again. Some places skip the overhead wires. Current then travels in the tracks under the train. The tracks themselves are a vital part of the system. Welding joins them, so the whole length is smooth and the joints are gone. Builders keep the line as straight as they can. Curves would force a slowdown. A tunnel or a viaduct lets the line pass under an obstacle or over it, instead of bending around. A curve, when one is required, stays as gentle as possible, so speed can hold. A bend that is too tight means a slower train, or a train that might leave the rails. Computers at a central control keep the traffic safe. At top speed the engineer cannot read a sign the train flashes past. Every signal, including when to stop and when to switch tracks, must reach the engineer by electronics. Some of these trains lean as they take a corner.

5Not Fully in the Fast Class. In 2011 the nearest thing the United States had was Amtrak's Acela Express. One end was Washington, D.C. The other end was Boston, Massachusetts. New York City lay on the way. Top speed is 150 mph, or 241 kph. For most of the route the pace is only about half of that. Slower ordinary trains share the same tracks, and that sharing caps the speed. Three Ways to Be Fast. Popularity grew, and newer technology pushed the pace higher still. Many trains now in service average from about 150 mph, or 241 kph, up past 200 mph, or 322 kph. A few can exceed 300 mph, or 483 kph. Speeds that high are not the usual choice when passengers are aboard. Fast is true of all of them. The way they work is not the same. Three chief kinds stand out: the Shinkansen, the TGV, and the maglev. The Shinkansen. What sets a Japanese Shinkansen apart is the job of each car. Every car acts as a small electric locomotive. Forward push comes from each one. Extra cars may join the set, or cars may leave it, and performance stays the same. A motor in every car also means a very quick gain of speed and a very quick loss of it. Stops can come more often, and the schedule can still be kept. A Shinkansen passes Mount Fuji in Japan.

6Success for the TGV in France has been strong. TGV is short for train a grande vitesse. Those French words name what English calls a high-speed train. France was where these trains were used first. Gas turbines, similar to jet engines, supplied the power at the start. Electricity came later, as it had for the Shinkansen. Axles are handled differently. Each TGV car shares axles with the car ahead and the car behind. Neighboring cars rest on one base of two axles. That base is a bogie. Power is different too. Only two power cars drive a TGV set. One pulls from the front. One pushes from the rear. That push-and-pull plan costs less than the Shinkansen plan, in which every car makes its own power. The cheaper plan has a limit. Railcars cannot be added or removed with ease. Maglev. The Shinkansen and the TGV are mostly better versions of older train ideas. Maglev rests on a technology that is wholly new. The name is short for magnetic levitation. Magnets supply the power, and the train flies along the track without touching the ground. An electromagnet is a device of steel or of iron. It turns into a magnet only while electric current runs through a coil nearby. A maglev travels a test track in Germany.

7Special tracks called guideways carry a maglev. Coils sit in those guideways, and electric current runs through the coils. A household magnet can pull an object or push it away. The maglev and its guideway push and pull on each other with forces of that same kind. The train levitates. It floats above the guideway and never touches it. Friction is gone. Vibration is gone. Nothing of that sort cuts the speed or makes a noise. Quiet and pace are therefore usually better than on other fast trains. Forward motion also comes from magnetic force. An ocean wave shoving a surfer is the picture. Guideways for maglev stand in China. Building a maglev system costs more than building other fast trains. Japan runs maglev trains that riders board on ordinary scheduled trips. China does too. South Korea does too. Other countries are testing systems, or planning to build them, for later years. How a maglev stays on its path: matching magnets shove one another and hold the train in the center of the guideway. A pair of unlike magnets raises the train clear.

8Worries About Safety. High speed makes safety a major worry. Several protections are built into the design. A crash with a car is less likely because these lines usually do not cross a road on the same level. The train goes over the road or under it. Fences line many of the railways so animals stay out. Sensors warn the operators if something may be blocking the rails. On March 11, 2011, a powerful quake struck Sendai in Japan. Warning came early. Power was cut. Twenty-seven Shinkansen trains were in the struck area, and they lost that power. Emergency brakes came on by themselves. The trains stopped safely. Passengers were not injured. Protections do not erase every accident. Lightning struck nearby during China's summer in the year 2011. A fast train lost its power. A second train hit it from behind. Many lives were lost. The crash was a tragic reminder. Travel on the ground at high speed always carries some risk. Why These Trains Help. Set beside other ways of moving crowds, these trains offer many gains. A short hop can be quicker and easier by bus. A very long hop is a better job for an airplane. Trips from one hundred miles to five hundred miles suit the fast train perfectly. On those distances a bus is much slower. An airplane is no faster once you count the hours spent at the airport before the flight and after it. Comfort can be greater. Booths or tables are often there to sit at. Electrical outlets are plentiful, ready for gadgets. Around takeoff and landing, an airline passenger may not use a cell phone or another personal electronic device. A train passenger may use them at any moment. Reporters test the seats of a new fast train in China.

9Power for these trains can be drawn from many sources. Carry a normal load of passengers and the fast train uses fuel far more efficiently than a car, a bus, or an airplane. Electricity runs them, not fossil fuels, so they do not themselves let out the greenhouse gases that feed climate change. Coal still makes much of the world's electric power. That share is expected to fall as the world turns to sources that can last, such as the sun and the wind. The trains should therefore grow even kinder to the environment as years pass. A further major gain is relief for other transport systems. A road can hold only so many travelers at one moment. An airport has the same kind of limit. Capacity is the name for how many travelers a system can handle in an hour. Fill a highway or a freeway to that limit and huge jams follow. Movement can drop to a crawl. It can stop for hours at a stretch. Airports can overload in a similar way. Adding roads or airports to raise capacity is not a choice in many places. A railroad takes less land than a highway. A fast line can often be laid into those tight places, and the strain on the other ways of travel can ease. Jams on freeways can shrink because of these trains.

10Flying Across Spain. Spain's fast-train system is named Alta Velocidad Espanola. In Spanish the words mean Spanish high speed. The initials, AVE, are a Spanish word for bird. What Success Requires. Gains do not make fast rail the right answer for every region's transport needs. Building the systems can be very costly. Each mile of new track can cost many millions of dollars. Some countries treat that building cost as an investment in years ahead. Other countries ask whether an investment so large is worth making. A wonderful train still fails if too few people ride it. Economic sense, and environmental sense, both ask that each train carry as many passengers as it can. Building therefore fits only where crowds make the trip again and again. High population density means many people packed into a limited space. Europe has had success with these trains. Japan has had it. China has had it. One reason is that all three contain many areas where population density is high. In Germany, riders wait to board a fast train.

11An artist's drawing shows how fast rail could change travel in California. The Years Ahead. Growth is rushing forward. Fresh lines appear in countries that did not have them, and on continents that did not have them. Europe means to join its many separate systems into one gigantic network across the continent by 2025. Morocco is building the first system of this kind in Africa. In the United States, California is where the first true network is being developed. Finish it as planned and Los Angeles can be linked with San Francisco. The ride would take less than 2 hours plus 20 minutes. Speed can reach 220 mph, or 354 kph. World population is rising. Worry about energy sources is rising. Worry about the environment is rising. Fast trains will matter greatly as the world tries to meet its need to move people. An axle is a bar. Wheels turn around it. Greenhouse gases sit in the atmosphere of Earth. They trap heat. Global warming grows because of them. Economic describes what has to do with buying and selling goods and services. A network is a set of things, or of computers, joined to one another. An engineer is the person charged with running a train safely. An obstacle is something in the way, blocking progress or movement. Fossil fuels are energy sources dug from the ground. Coal is one. Oil is one. Natural gas is one. A sensor notices a signal. It also notices when conditions shift. Then it reacts. Fuel efficient describes fuel used well. Miles traveled for each gallon are the measure. Sustainable describes a use that does not use a resource up completely or damage it for good. A generator is a machine. Motion goes in. Electricity comes out. A viaduct is a low bridge over dry land or over a long valley.

94. Trains That Carried Children to Safety

1Soldiers from Germany entered the Czech capital on military motorcycles. People stood silent and watched. Vera Gissing still remembers that invasion. March 15, 1939, was the day. She was young, and she was Jewish. Tanks woke her. Soldiers from the German army were marching. The streets were those of Prague, capital of Czechoslovakia. Rooms in the family house were taken over. German was the only language the soldiers would allow. Her father would not obey. A soldier spat. She saw the spit hit his face. The day was bad. Worse days were coming.

2Girls from the Eberstark family left the station in Prague on a day like that. Their parents were never seen by them again. Gissing's own departure is just as clear in her memory. Dozens of other Prague children shared the train her parents chose for her. Her eleventh birthday had not yet arrived. Best clothes were what she wore. A tag with a number hung from her neck. Steam from the engines rose at the main railroad station. It wrapped around parents and children waiting to say goodbye. Children were held close. Love was whispered. Hope was whispered. Speaking in 2002, she said the anguished look on her parents' faces that morning would stay with her forever. The memory was already sixty-three years old. Children climbed aboard one after another. England was where the train was bound. Gissing kept trying to hold her parents' faces in sight as the cars pulled out. She did not yet know those faces were gone from her life. She also could not foresee the fate waiting for them, or for most of the other parents standing there. They would be sent off to die. A man from Great Britain was unknown to her then. He chose to save her. For nearly fifty years he told nobody what he had done.

3London in 1938 was home to a banker named Nicholas Winton. He was twenty-nine. A ski trip in the Alps was the Christmas plan he shared with Martin Blake, a close friend. The Alps never happened. Blake, just before the departure, asked Winton to join him in Prague instead. Humanitarian work was already Blake's task there. Jewish families by the thousands had been forced out of the Sudetenland. That region lies in the north of Czechoslovakia. Food was needed. Other help was needed. Jewish organizations and Christian organizations worked side by side. Among the Jewish groups were Youth Aliyah and the Children's Aid Society. The Kindertransport was another. Winton once explained the trip. Europe's crisis had been their topic again and again, close to daily. He had not imagined that he himself would start working. The job turned personal because of his background. The family line was German and Jewish. Christianity was the faith his parents took up when they moved to England as immigrants. Stay in Germany, and the desperate case might have been theirs. Adolf Hitler, Germany's leader, was behind a sinister plot, and the Sudetenland takeover was one piece of it. Anger still burned from his years as a soldier. Germany's defeat in World War I, in 1918, was the wound. He laid part of the blame for that loss on Jewish people. He laid part of the blame for the depression that followed on them too. Black people were blamed. Disabled people were blamed. LGBTQ+ people were blamed. Roma people were blamed. In his view Jewish people formed an inferior race. Murder, he believed, was required if society was to be rid of them entirely. He helped start the German Worker's Party once the war had ended. The Nazi Party grew out of it. Restoring Germany's power in the world was the goal. Crowds responded when he spoke. He could stir them. He could push them toward action. Popularity followed, and then the title of chancellor. Control of the government was seized. Every rival political party was banned. The military began to grow. A secret plan aimed at land Germany had been compelled to surrender. The Treaty of Versailles, signed when World War I ended, was the document that had taken that land.

4Some residents of the Sudetenland raised a salute when German troops came in. Fear drove others out. Motion on the plan began in 1936. France had been given certain land, and by 1940 Hitler had taken that land back. Austria fell to him earlier, by two years. He had been born there. Objection came from leaders in other European countries. Intervention did not. Stopping him was left undone. The Sudetenland was the next target after Austria.
