Germany and Czechoslovakia share a border there, and German was the language of many local people. France, Great Britain, and Italy sent leaders to meet him in 1938. The Czechs counted those three as allies. War was the outcome they refused. His demands were signed into the Munich Agreement. German rule received the Sudetenland. Citizens across Europe already doubted him. Further conquests, they believed, were his real intention. Fear ran especially deep among Jewish people. Law after law in Hitler's Germany had been aimed at them. A lawyer's work was closed. A doctor's work was closed. A journalist's work was closed. Public hospitals could not be used. After age 14, public schools could not be attended. A marriage was banned if the other person was not Jewish. One belief fed every rule. Greatness, Hitler thought, would return only after Germany was cleansed of races he judged inferior. Wartime photographs often show Jewish men, women, and children wearing a star with six points. Two triangles fitted together are a common way to draw it. Another name is the Star of David. For thousands of years it has stood as a symbol of Judaism. Nazi orders during the war put that star on every Jewish person. Identification by non-Jewish people became easy. Shame was the point of the badge. Discrimination was the result the badge was meant to stir. The order covered every Jewish person older than six, in each country under German control.

5Steps grew harsher. Jewish people born in Poland, and Jewish people born in Russia, were to be collected by the army and taken out of Germany. Only what a person could carry was allowed. Homes were left behind. Trucks took some of them. Wagons took others. The border was where they were dumped. Being forced out was still not the worst. Nazi concentration camps soon held 30,000 Jewish people from Germany, seized and hauled there by the army. Think of a camp as a prison. Life there meant work under torturous strain that broke bodies. Execution was what Hitler ordered next. Terror pushed Jewish people all across Europe to flee Nazi persecution. Prague's Jewish citizens, who were citizens of Czechoslovakia, were already packed into filthy camps. Those camps were meant only as brief shelters. A visit from Winton showed him how bad the conditions were. New homes were the aim of some aid groups. He saw that elderly people and sick people got the attention. Czechoslovakia's Jewish children seemed to have no plan at all. Saving them became his decision. His words appear in a film made in 2002 about his life. Bad is how he described the situation. Refugees and helpers alike felt time was running out. Germans would reach the rest of Czechoslovakia soon. Escape looked impossible. No destination was obvious. They were stuck. A hotel on Wenceslas Square became his base in Prague. The dining room held his table, and he sat there day after day. Parents arrived hoping to place children where Hitler could not reach them. Families outside Czechoslovakia were the shelter he wanted to find. Trains were already moving thousands of Jewish children out of Germany and out of Austria toward safety in Great Britain. That program's name was the Kindertransport. A similar effort, he believed, could rescue thousands of children from the Czech lands. News traveled quickly. Families learned that an Englishman was working from Wenceslas Square. Hundreds of desperate families crowded the hotel. Two assistants were hired so the families could be helped. England was his next stop. Homes had to be found. Money for the rescue had to be raised.

6Refugee families from the Sudetenland were housed in a Czechoslovak school. Youngsters and adults lay crowded together. Straw mattresses on the floor were the beds, and people slept side by side. Letters went out from London to governments in many countries. Winton asked each one to accept the children. Refusal was common. A child without parents was against the law in those places. Help came from only two: Sweden, and Great Britain. Strict rules still governed entry to England. Every child needed a family waiting. A fee was also required. It was meant to pay, later, for sending the children back to Czechoslovakia when safety returned. Each child cost fifty pounds. People treated that price as a small fortune. The same sum was worth over 3,400 dollars in U.S. money. Donors were asked for whatever they could give. The gap was filled by Winton himself. Ads in papers all over Great Britain sought families. Religious organizations were asked as well. Photographs of the children were sent or posted nationwide. He hoped a human face would move strangers to act. Paperwork was the other battle. Contacts in the German government and in the British government were pressed for permits. Children had to cross Europe. They had to be allowed into England. Delay sometimes led Winton, with a few helpers, to create permits that were not genuine. His comment was that the group had only made a slow system move faster.

7The first success came by air, not by rail. March 14, 1939, sent the earliest group, fifteen children, from Prague toward Great Britain. Six further months brought seven trains out of Wilson Railway Station. Children rode out of Prague, crossed the whole of Germany, and reached Holland's coast. A ferry carried them over the English Channel. Another train finished the trip in London. New families took the children in their arms at a London station. Winton watched, smiling. He is photographed in 1939 with one small child he had brought out of Czechoslovakia. Safety was reached by 669 children in all. Keepsakes from home traveled with some of them. Letters of thanks, written by parents to the new British families, traveled too. Family houses took most of the children. A boarding school for Czech pupils in Wales took others. Plans existed for train number eight. The date was to be September 3, 1939. Another 250 children would have been aboard. Poland was invaded by Hitler's army that same day. Borders under German control all slammed shut. Nobody ever saw that train or those children again. Nearly six years of horrible fighting followed. Countries around the globe were pulled in. People came to call that war World War II.

8Male prisoners stand on one side of a barbed-wire fence in a picture. Female prisoners stand on the other. The place is a German concentration camp, and a guard keeps watch. Hitler's decision in 1941 was that every Jewish person must be killed. The decision belonged to his war plans. Concentration camps swallowed millions. Work continued until people grew too weak to live. Dying that way still seemed too slow to the regime, which was brutal. Murder replaced waiting. The name Holocaust is given to this attempt to wipe out the Jewish population. Shoah is a Hebrew word some Jewish people use instead. A whirlwind of destruction is what it means. Murder during the war took six million Jewish people. Children were more than a million of that number. People who were not Jewish were murdered in the millions as well. Human history holds few crimes judged more atrocious. Rescue work ended when the war closed in. Other help was what Winton looked for next. Relief work with the Red Cross occupied him. The Royal Air Force came later, and he learned to fly as a pilot. Peace returned him to banking. Marriage and a family followed. Silence about the children lasted until 1988. Grete, his wife, found the secret without meaning to. An attic hid a leather briefcase gone dusty. A worn scrapbook inside held the children's pictures. Each photo sat beside a name, plus notes about that child's family back in Czechoslovakia. The British family that had offered to guard the child in wartime was recorded too. Papers and letters spelled the work out in detail. She pressed him to speak. An article appeared in a newspaper. A British television program, That's Life, told his story in that same year. The audience held a surprise. Rescued children, more than two dozen of them, had come to thank him.

9The reunion was emotional, and the author Vera Gissing was there. A biography of Winton is one book she has written since. Another book tells her own war childhood. In her words, he got most of the Jewish children of her Czech generation out. Meeting a parent again was rare. Concentration camps were where those parents perished. Stay behind, and the children would have been killed next to them. She says they had been spirited away, and that was the difference. One generation is not the end of the story. Descendants of the 669 children now number as many as 5,000. A London station picture shows some of Winton's Children coming to meet the man who rescued them. They were marking seventy years since the evacuation. Old age has replaced the childhood flight. The name Winton's Children is one many of them still use. Research science, religious leadership, and film are fields where some of them later did remarkable work. Honors have come from the government of Great Britain and from the government of the Czech Republic. Queen Elizabeth II made him a knight in 2002. Bravery, service, or success is what that award marks. The Czech Republic's highest honor reached him in 2014. The award is titled Order of the White Lion. A far-off planet carries his name, given by two astronomers from the Czech lands. Kneeling comes first at a knighthood ceremony. Each shoulder is tapped with a sword. A medal follows, and a title. A man who is a British citizen becomes sir. A woman who is a British citizen becomes dame. Great Britain's monarch performs the ceremony, or some other member of the Royal Family. Soldiers once stood almost alone in that title. Artists can be knighted now. Athletes can. Politicians, humanitarians, inventors, and scientists can. Others can too.

10Seventy years after his last train, the year 2009 brought a railroad trip along the same path his children had ridden. The journey copied the final portion of the old ride linking Prague with London, and in that way it honored the past. People he had saved rode again. Liverpool Street station in London is where he waited, arms wide, to greet them. His 100th birthday celebration had happened only a few months before. Gissing grew up thinking of a savior and not knowing the man's name. Winton, for a long stretch of years, believed he had done nothing worth special praise. Meeting her, and meeting others he had saved, was what finally let him see the scale of what he had made possible. She helped write a book whose title names Nicholas Winton and also names the Rescued Generation. The year of that book was 2002. She writes of parental courage as war clouds gathered. Strangers in another country had to receive their only children. Families in Britain had to agree to take them. Strip Winton out of the story, she says, and every hope and every offer of help would have failed. She can sit in a garden now because of him. Grandchildren play. Laughter reaches her. Her daughter's voice calls the family inside for tea. The scene is ordinary. She says she can never treat it as something she was owed.

11Laughter in one picture belongs to Winton and to a grandson. The boy's grandmother was a girl saved seventy years before. After the secret surfaced, Winton talked often about why he had acted for the Czech children. Heroic is a word he refused. Special is a word he refused. Silence, he said, fit a deed he did not see as grand. He had noticed events unfolding, and he had given whatever help he could. A ring was the thanks some saved people offered. Its inscription comes from the Talmud, a book of Jewish law. Save a single life, the line teaches, and the world is saved with it. Death came for Sir Nicholas Winton on July 1, 2015. He was 106. The day matched an anniversary, the 76th, of one departure from Prague. That journey had taken the biggest group of children, a count of 241. Words in this book can be read as follows. Anguished describes a person full of pain or of grief. Jewish can refer to a people's culture, to a religion, or to a group identity. Atrocious describes what is cruel, evil, or extremely bad. A keepsake is kept, or given, so a person, a place, or an event will not be forgotten. People held in a concentration camp are kept there against their will. Conditions are usually harsh. The reason is membership in an ethnic group, a minority, or a political group. If a law or a rule forbids something, that thing has been prohibited. Refugees run from famine, from war, from persecution, or from a natural disaster. Often they have nowhere definite to land. Hebrew points to the ancestors of today's Jewish people, those who lived around Jerusalem. A regime is government in a form that is rigid and that controls tightly. Systematic killing by the Nazis in World War II, above all of Jewish people, is the Holocaust. To be spirited away is to be carried off in secret. Humanitarian work is help for people, above all help that lessens pain and suffering.

95. True Bandits of the Frontier West

1The parts of this book come in this order. A deadly day in Coffeyville comes first. Then comes the James-Younger Gang. Then comes the Kid. Then comes the Buck Gang. Then comes the Wild Bunch, led by Butch Cassidy. Then comes why these stories became legend. A word list comes last. A group called the Dalton Gang had three brothers at its head. Bob Dalton was one. Emmett Dalton was another. Gratton Dalton was the third. A Deadly Day in Coffeyville The same three brothers were the outlaws people followed under the Dalton name. The frontier inside the Oklahoma Territory was the ground they crossed. That land is the state of Oklahoma today. Banks were robbed. Trains were held up. The crimes came in the early 1890s. They wanted a bolder act of banditry. They were sure it would bring fame. They were sure it would bring fortune too. The plan was to rob two banks at one time. The town was Coffeyville, Kansas, the place they came from.

2The date was October 5, 1892. Coffeyville is where the brothers rode in. Two accomplices rode with them. Fake mustaches and goatees were part of the disguise. The plan came apart fast. Street construction forced them to tie the getaway horses a block from the banks. Old neighbors were not fooled by the fake hair. Word spread through town that the gang had arrived and meant trouble. When the robbers stepped out carrying the loot, townspeople were already armed. The guns had been borrowed from a hardware store nearby. Until 1890 the Dalton brothers had worked as lawmen. They turned to crime after they were not paid for a job. The shooting lasted twelve minutes. Four people from town were dead. Four of the five outlaws were dead too. Emmett Dalton was the only one of the gang still alive, and he was badly hurt. A court tried him and gave him life in prison. Fourteen years later he was paroled, because his behavior had been good. The Dalton Gang’s end shows how outlaw life often went. It was harsh. It was violent. It was short. Books, movies, and television later made those Wild West deeds look grander than they were. The criminals are shown as gunfighters who fear nothing. They are shown as joking figures like Robin Hood. They are shown as cruel villains. The real record was much duller and meaner. A jail in that West was not a place anyone would call grand.

3Frank James is on the left in one photo. Jesse, the younger brother, is on the right. James and the Youngers The Old West had many dangerous bands. The gang built around the James brothers and the Younger brothers was among the worst. A Missouri farm was where Jesse grew up. Frank, who was older, grew up on that farm too. Enslavement was splitting the region. It was splitting the nation as well. Slavery was legal in Missouri. South of it lay states that also allowed slavery. North of it lay states that did not. People were enslaved by the James family. The family took the South’s side in the Civil War. Both brothers were with guerrilla fighters by 1864, and killing was part of that riding. Frank’s age was twenty-one. Jesse’s age was sixteen. Another photo shows the Younger family. From the left the brothers are Bob, then Jim, then Cole. Henrietta, their sister, stands with them. Fighting ended in 1865. Missouri’s people began putting lives back together. Farm work was not what the James brothers went home to do. Their skills were narrow and specific. A different trade fit those skills. Liberty, Missouri, saw about a dozen riders come in. The date was February 13, 1866. Clay County’s savings bank was the target. The take was 62,000 dollars. That was an enormous amount then. For ten years after that, one robbery followed another. At some of those times the Younger brothers were with them. Cole was one. Jim was one. Bob was one. Still other outlaws came and went. The raids hit dozens of banks. Small towns in Missouri supplied most of the targets. A Kansas City fair lost its ticket office to them in 1872.

4They planned like a drilled military unit. They hit targets with precision. Bank tellers and townspeople were sometimes left dead or wounded when the riders left. The gang shifted from one hideout to another. Friends helped them stay ahead of lawmen. Help also came from people who had sided with the South while that war was fought. Newspapers received letters written by Jesse James. The letters denied what the gang had done, or tried to excuse it. Editors who sympathized with him helped shape what the public believed. He wanted people to see his men as “bold robbers.” He also wanted them seen as Robin Hoods of their own time. Little evidence shows the gang ever gave to anyone except its own members. In 1873 the targets changed. Trains were robbed. Stagecoaches were robbed. Tens of thousands of dollars came out of safes and lockboxes. Money also came from the pockets of passengers. Authorities answered with manhunts that kept growing. Rewards as high as 25,000 dollars were offered for the James brothers. Nothing came of those rewards. In 1876 about ten outlaws traveled to Minnesota. Their target was the First National Bank in the town of Northfield. Local people saw what was happening and armed themselves quickly. Within minutes they poured heavy fire onto outlaws who were stunned. The gang shot a path out of town. Two members of the gang were dead. Two people from town were dead. A huge manhunt followed. Two weeks later the three Younger brothers were caught. They were wounded. A court convicted them and sent them to prison. Frank and Jesse got away and rode back to Missouri. They still did not quit. A new gang was formed. Now and then they robbed a bank, a train, or a stagecoach. On April 3, 1882, a member of Jesse’s own gang killed him.

5Frank James soon surrendered himself. He thought his brother’s ending would be his own. Dozens of heists were the gang’s total. The dead numbered at least seventeen. More deaths are likely. Frank faced a jury in Missouri. The year was 1885. The jury refused to call him guilty. Books Sold for a Dime Paperbacks known as dime novels were inexpensive, and crowds bought them. Sales ran through the nineteenth century. They ran into the early twentieth century as well. Ten cents was a typical price. Some copies cost even less. Made-up stories of frontier bandits and of lawmen were some of the best sellers. Writers produced the tales quickly. Real criminals were often dropped into the plots. To give readers a thrill, events were stretched past the truth. Some plots were invented outright. Indigenous nations were drawn falsely in many of these books. Those peoples already lived in the West when the outlaws arrived. The pages called them violent. The pages called them hostile. The pages called them savage. Jesse James and the riders with him were handled another way. Writers made them antiheroes who excited an audience. An antihero stands at the center of a story. Readers like that character. The character still does not behave as a hero would. The Kid For notoriety, the Jameses and the Youngers may top every other gang of the period. Among single outlaws, one nickname is recognized faster than the rest. That nickname is Billy the Kid. Birth papers name him Henry McCarty. The year was 1859. The city was New York. The New Mexico Territory is where his early teenage years were spent. A laundry in 1875 lost clothes to him, and a jail held him for the theft. He left by climbing out through the chimney. The Arizona Territory was the place he ran to. Reports say that 1877 brought the first time he shot a man. Jail followed once more. So did another escape. New Mexico was where he returned. By then he used the name William H. Bonney. People said “the Kid” because his looks and his manner were boyish. The Lincoln County War is the fight that turned his life fully toward crime. The New Mexico Territory was the setting. Ranchers there fought over land. They fought over money. They fought over power. John Henry Tunstall, young and British, hired him as a hand on a ranch. The two grew close. Tunstall’s enemies had real power. February 1878 is when those enemies’ gang killed Tunstall. Sheriff William J. Brady led the gang. The sheriff’s pay came from a man who competed with Tunstall.

6Soon after that killing, the Kid joined a group called the Regulators. April brought an ambush. Sheriff Brady died in it. A deputy died with him. The Kid was a leading suspect. A warrant called for his arrest. In 1880 a reward of 5,000 dollars was added to make capture more tempting. Sheriff Pat Garrett took over the hunt. December of 1880 is when the Kid fell into Garrett’s hands. April of the next year brought the trial. The court found him guilty of murdering Sheriff Brady. The sentence was hanging. Lincoln was the town where he was locked up. On the way back from the outhouse he slipped out of his handcuffs. The guard’s revolver ended up in the Kid’s hand. That guard did not survive. Another deputy heard the shot and ran toward it. The Kid shot that deputy too. He was free again. Three months later Garrett found the fugitive. Garrett fired twice. The Kid died. Newspapers across the country carried the story. A year after that, Garrett published a book. A ghostwriter helped him. The title started with the words An Authentic Life. The rest of the title named Billy the Kid. Much of the book’s accuracy has been doubted. Even so, the account fixed the Kid’s legend in place. More than fifty movies have been made about him. Not an Ordinary Boy People called Henry McCarty a kid. Twenty-two men still died because of what he did. His life was short and brutal. Pat Garrett, sheriff in Lincoln County, wrote a biography of Billy. He wrote it only eight months after the shooting. The place was Fort Sumner, in New Mexico. Garrett’s shots came in 1881. Billy’s age was twenty-one and no more. Historians did not treat Garrett’s book as accurate. Later editions filled gaps. They also corrected details of Billy’s childhood. Readers still loved the book.

7The Buck Gang had five members. A photo from the day before the hanging lines them up. Maoma July is at the left. Sam Sampson stands next. Rufus Buck stands next. Lucky Davis stands next. Lewis Davis stands at the right. Five Riders Called the Buck Gang Rufus Buck was one of the five. Lucky Davis was another. Sam Sampson was another. Maoma July was another. Lewis Davis was the last. The land they moved through is Oklahoma now. Each man was Black, or he was Indigenous and Creek. White settlers were coming into the territory. Rufus Buck was furious about that. The other four shared his anger. Their crimes were packed into thirteen days during 1895. General stores were robbed. Horses were stolen. They shot a boy whose father served as an official at a boarding school. A deputy marshal was killed. Flatrock Creek was the site of the gun battle that captured every member. Okmulgee lies seven miles south of that creek. Arkansas was the next stop. The city was Fort Smith. A federal courtroom tried them there. Isaac C. Parker was the judge who heard it. He became known for death sentences. The count of people he sent to die was over 150. Those sentences could not be appealed. A conviction came down on each gang member. They asked the country’s highest court, the U.S. Supreme Court, to undo the verdict. That court agreed with Parker. July 1, 1896, was the day all five were hanged. Fort Smith was the place. Officers of the Law Outlaw tales come paired with tales of Old West officers. Sheriffs appear in them. Marshals appear in them. Deputies appear in them. A badge shaped like a star is pinned on the chest in the usual picture. A six-shooter sits on the hip. Some officers were appointed. Some were elected. Keeping the peace was the assignment. The work asked a lot, and danger was sometimes part of it. A number of these officers were little different from criminals. Bass Reeves shows the other kind of person the work could attract. Enslavement was in his past. The year 1875 is when he became a deputy marshal for the United States. No Black man had held that post before him. About three thousand suspects were brought to justice through his work. His mind and his courage were what he relied on.

8Cassidy’s Wild Bunch Western towns, and western states, wanted to drop a lawless name as the nineteenth century closed. Outlaw stories still entertained people. Leaders in politics and in business did not want their banks robbed. They did not want their trains stopped and looted. They did not want their cattle rustled. They did not want their citizens put in fear. Law kept extending its reach toward the gangs. A telegraph, or a newspaper, could report a crime faster than the riders could find a hiding place. Fame for outlaw behavior still came to the Wild Bunch while the frontier era ended. The leader was Butch Cassidy. The Rocky Mountains were the region. The years ran from 1889 through 1901. Robert Leroy Parker was the name given at birth to the man called Butch Cassidy. Utah was the birthplace. The year was 1866. Ranch work is what he left home to find, while he was still in his early teens. The surname Cassidy may have come from a friend who stole cattle. Butch is said to recall a stint spent working where meat was cut. The first bank he robbed, with accomplices beside him, was in 1889. Telluride, Colorado, was the town. The theft was more than 20,000 dollars. A lonely stretch of Wyoming is where they hid after the escape. He repeated a pattern several times. Take the money, ride far, and stay quiet. Horse theft brought an arrest five years later. The prison term was two years. Release is when he pulled the Wild Bunch together. One rider was Elzy Lay. Another was Ben Kilpatrick. Another was Will Carver. Another was Harvey Logan, known as Kid Curry. More riders joined them. Harry Longabaugh came in during 1897. People came to call Longabaugh the Sundance Kid. Trains and banks were the holdup targets. The stolen sums reached the tens of thousands of dollars. Humor, of a defiant kind, was part of Cassidy’s style. A Nevada bank the gang had already robbed once received a photo of the riders in the mail. Cassidy’s note thanked that manager for letting them make a “withdrawal.” Another photo lines the Wild Bunch up. The left-hand man is Harry Longabaugh, also called the Sundance Kid. Next is William Carver, who went by News. Next is Ben Kilpatrick, called the Tall Texan. Next is Harvey Logan, or Kid Curry. The man on the right is Robert LeRoy Parker, the one known as Butch Cassidy.

9The gang developed a reputation for keeping clear of violence. The name may not have matched the truth. A boast is credited to Cassidy. He claimed no man had ever died by his own hand. The desperadoes who rode with him could not say that. National newspapers gave the Wild Bunch a following, as they did for other gangs that lasted. Officers were drawing closer. Wyoming, in 1899, was where the gang robbed a train. What followed was a fierce hunt by a very large posse. Hunters from the Pinkerton agency, the National Detective Agency, were on the trail as well. Cassidy slipped away once more. Capture or death found several of the others. Argentina was the next move, a year later. Cassidy went. Longabaugh went. Etta Place, a friend to the gang, went too. They bought a ranch and lived there. After that, the record turns unclear. One photo places William A. Pinkerton in the middle. Pat Connell, a special agent for the railroad, is on the left. Sam Finley is on the right. Argentina’s turn came in 1905, when two outlaws from America robbed a bank there. Witnesses described men who matched Cassidy and the Sundance Kid. Bolivia, in 1908, lost a payroll in a robbery. The same pair was blamed. Both of those outlaws died in the shooting that followed. For a long time, historians treated that battle as Cassidy’s last stand, and as the Sundance Kid’s too. Rumors in the years after said the pair had slipped back into this country. The rumors said the outlaw life was over for them. A ranch in Utah was the new start credited to Longabaugh. People close to Cassidy, friends and family, said he came to see them long after the reported deaths. Proof of those visits has never appeared.

10Women Outlaws, Called Bandit Queens Arizona, in 1899, is where Pearl Hart stopped a stagecoach. An accomplice was with her. The take was over 400 dollars. A week was enough time for the law to catch both of them. Papers across the country carried the story. The reason was simple. Hart was a woman. Time with Cassidy’s Wild Bunch included Etta Place. It also included Laura Bullion. The “Bandit Queen” name belonged to Belle Starr. Myra Maybelle Shirley was the name she was born with. Missouri was where she grew up. The James brothers were people she knew. The Younger brothers were people she knew. Sam Starr became her husband. Horse theft brought an arrest for the couple in 1883. A conviction followed. The year 1889 is when she was killed. She was riding toward home. The attack was an ambush. No one ever solved it. Stories That Turned into Legend Only a brief span of American history is what people mean by the Old West. Wagons with covers crossed that span. Drives of cattle crossed it. So did gunfights, and so did frontier towns with little law. A few decades held the whole rise and the whole fade. The year 1900 found it almost finished. What remains is a mythical picture. Heroes fill the tales. Villains fill them. Hardship and courage fill them too. Outlaws stand in the middle of that myth. One version makes them charming desperadoes. That version adds hearts of gold, already worn down. Another version makes them killers with no pity. Survival meant taking what belonged to others. It meant staying about a day of riding ahead of any officer. Excitement is easy to imagine. Fear was the feeling that did not leave. People still ask why these criminals hold attention. One answer is the dream of danger that never stops, and of moments that decide who lives. Another answer is the pleasure of picturing every rule tossed aside. The pull, whatever it was, grabbed many American imaginations in that era. It grabs them now.

11A map marks where these outlaws struck. All of the places lie west of the Mississippi. The Dalton Gang On June 1, 1892, marked A, they robbed a train at Red Rock, in Indigenous Peoples’ Territory. On October 5, 1892, marked B, they attempted a bank robbery in Coffeyville, Kansas. The James-Younger Gang On February 13, 1866, marked C, they robbed a bank in Liberty, Missouri. On September 26, 1872, marked D, they robbed a ticket office at the Kansas City Exposition, in Kansas City, Missouri. On July 21, 1873, marked E, they robbed a train in Adair, Iowa. On September 7, 1876, marked F, they attempted a bank robbery in Northfield, Minnesota. Billy the Kid On August 18, 1877, marked G, he killed a man at Fort Grant, in Arizona. On January 10, 1880, marked H, he killed a gunman at Fort Sumner, in New Mexico. On April 28, 1881, marked I, he killed two lawmen in the New Mexico town of Lincoln. Cassidy’s Gang, Called the Wild Bunch On June 24, 1889, marked J, they robbed a bank in Telluride, Colorado. In 1894, marked K, there was a horse theft in Dubois, Wyoming. On June 2, 1899, marked L, they robbed a train in Wilcox, Wyoming. On September 19, 1900, marked M, they robbed a bank in Winnemucca, Nevada. The Buck Gang On July 30, 1895, marked N, they killed John Garrett, a deputy marshal of the United States, in Okmulgee, Oklahoma. Words to Know stint (n.): a stretch of time spent at a job or an activity. glamorized (v.): made something look more appealing or more exciting than it truly was. guerrilla (n.): a fighter in a small, independent band that usually attacks by surprise. accomplices (n.): people who help someone do a wrong or illegal act. heists (n.): thefts from a person or a place; robberies. ambushed (v.): attacked by surprise from a hiding place. desperadoes (n.): people who take daring, risky actions that are often crimes. notorious (adj.): famous mainly because the thing they are known for is bad. posse (n.): a group a sheriff gathers to help catch criminals or to enforce the law. polarized (v.): split apart by clashing opinions, beliefs, or ideas. exploits (n.): acts that are remarkable or heroic. flaunted (v.): showed something openly so other people would notice.

96. Tusks, Trade, and Living Elephants

1A hippo in one photo is not a living animal. It is a carving made from ivory. The parts of this book come in this order. Treasures that are hard to trust come first. Then comes a definition of ivory. Then comes what elephants are like. Then comes the buying and selling of ivory. Then comes the work of saving elephants. Then comes how little time is left. A word list comes last. Treasures That Are Hard to Trust Your tour of several countries in Asia is nearly done. A perfect souvenir for home is still missing. Tents stand in busy lines, with carts and tables among them. You walk along those lines. The place is an outdoor market. The noise pushes you toward the far end. One table there draws your attention. Sculptures cover the table. Most of them show animals. Two small white pieces are labeled “ivory.” The price is high. They are beautiful. They are small enough to carry on a long flight home. The seller talks about the artist who carved them. He stresses the skill in the work. He says the pieces will last forever. Key facts are left out. He never says what ivory is. He never says how it was obtained. He never mentions the illegal trade in wildlife. That trade is what makes such sculptures available. He never mentions the brutal killing of elephants.

2What Ivory Is Ivory is a hard substance, cream in color. It forms the tusks of elephants. Less often, the same word is used for tusks of other animals. Walruses have such tusks. Hippos have them. Narwhals, a kind of whale, have them. Wild boars have them. A tusk is a very long tooth. It sticks out of the mouth even when the mouth is shut. In most mammals that have tusks, the tusk is an upper canine tooth. In elephants, the tusks are the front teeth, called incisors. The material is dentine, a hard bony tissue. Enamel, which is harder, covers the tips of an elephant’s tusks. Time wears that enamel away. Tusks keep growing for the elephant’s whole life. A photo shows an African elephant skull with the tusks still in place. Living elephants belong to an African kind or an Asian kind. Of the two, the African kind is larger. They divide further into forest elephants and savanna elephants. Both males and females grow tusks in each of those species. Savanna elephants are the bigger species. Their tusks can pass 2.1 meters in length. That is about 7 feet. Among Asian elephants, some males grow tusks that stand out. Other males, and most females, grow tusks that are thin and short. Those short tusks often break off. A tusk is a structural adaptation. It gives an elephant a better chance to survive. Food can be gathered with tusks and carried with them. Roots and minerals can be dug up. Tusks are used for display. They are used as weapons. In the dry season, some elephants dig water holes with them. The trunk gains protection from the tusks. The base of each tusk sits deep in the upper jaw. Killing the elephant is the only way to take those tusks. One photo shows digging. Another shows lifting. Both jobs use the tusks.

3About Elephants No land animal on Earth is larger. Height at the shoulder can reach 3 meters. That is about 10 feet. Weight for a male of the African kind can reach 6 metric tons. That is about 13,200 pounds. The body lumbers. The ears are huge. The trunk is huge. Even so, these animals are extremely intelligent. Brain size compared with body size matches our own. The complexity matches too. They rank among the most intelligent animals on Earth. Old Relatives Mastodons and mammoths once shared a mammal family with elephants. No other member of that family is still alive. Both of those are extinct. The closest living relatives are hyraxes. A hyrax is small, furred, and a plant-eater. It looks a little like a prairie dog. Manatees are also close relatives. Dugongs are too. Those two look as if dolphins would be nearer kin. Even so, elephants, hyraxes, manatees, and dugongs share one ancestor from long ago. A hyrax can weigh up to 5 kilograms. That is about 11 pounds. A dugong can weigh up to 300 kilograms. That is about 661 pounds. Top weight for an elephant is 11,000 kilograms. That is about 24,251 pounds. In South Africa, a matriarch leads her family toward a water hole. Elephants solve problems with skill. They use tools. They often invent new methods by working as a group. Some live into their seventies, as long as some humans. Social bonds are strong. Female family groups last for life and span several generations. An older female, the matriarch, guides them. She keeps the family together. She keeps them safe. She leads them to food and to water. In a drought, a matriarch has been known to find a water hole not visited for decades. Emotions are complex. Elephants have been seen laughing and playing. They show deep compassion. When one is in distress, others stand beside her. Trunks soothe her. Soft sounds comfort her. Humans do something similar for a troubled friend. We use a hand, not a trunk. Grief appears when a family member dies.

4Two young African elephants mourn an adult female who has died. Intelligence is not the only reason elephants matter in the animal kingdom. Scientists call them a keystone species. Many other species depend on a keystone species. Balance in the ecosystem depends on elephants. Water holes they dig also serve other animals. Trees and bushes they clear open habitat for grassland species. Trails they make can slow a spreading fire. The same trails help water drain. Some seeds will not start to grow until they have passed through an elephant’s gut. Dung can enrich worn-out soil enough for people to raise crops. In short, the ecosystems they live in need them. Around 1925, a hunter in Sudan poses with trophies from elephants. The Ivory Trade People have prized ivory for thousands of years. It has been carved into art. It has been made into jewelry and into many other objects. Tusks have been one reason Asian elephants were killed. They have also been killed for meat and for skin. African elephants still suffer more from the trade. Two facts explain that gap. One fact is tusk size. African tusks are bigger. Females grow tusks as well as males, which makes more ivory available. Across two centuries, the drop in numbers is hard to face. An estimate for the year 1800 put Africa’s elephants at twenty-six million. In the early 1900s, wealthy people from the West liked to kill African elephants on safari. Demand was also high for ivory goods. Piano keys were one item. Pool balls were another. Combs and brush handles were others. National Geographic is one source for what came next.

5By 1913, yearly ivory use in the United States was about 181 metric tons. That is about 200 tons. African elephants were down to about ten million. Demand jumped sharply again in the 1970s and the 1980s. Poachers were taking African elephants at an estimated pace of one hundred thousand a year. Poached means killed against the law. The animals were in serious trouble. Something had to stop the decline, and it had to happen fast. A Word on Poaching Poaching usually means taking a wild animal against a law written to protect wildlife. The act may be a hunt. It may be a capture. It may be a killing. Illegal traps and illegal shooting are included. The land may be public. It may be private. Profit is the most common motive. Sport is another. Rangers and game wardens are the people who enforce the laws against it. In Kenya, rangers and vets try to free an elephant’s feet from a poacher’s snare. A 2016 photo shows a parks official in Zimbabwe looking over ivory the country has stored. In 1989 an international agreement called CITES banned the ivory trade. Say the name SY-teez. The agreement governs trade in plants and animals that are endangered. The ban made the public far more aware of the crisis. Prices fell steeply as buyers pulled away. Elephant numbers began to recover. The worldwide ban could have led to a long recovery for African elephants. Ten years of rising numbers changed the politics. Four African countries asked CITES for permission to sell ivory they had stored. Namibia made the request. Botswana made it. Zimbabwe made it. South Africa made it. They said elephant numbers at home were stable, or were going up. They also said the sales would be limited.

6Only tusks from natural deaths would be sold, they said. Tusks from earlier culling would be included. Culling means killing elephants to hold their numbers down where space is limited. CITES allowed a sale in 1999. Buyers had to be countries with strict rules against illegal trade. No buyer except Japan met the test. A second sale came in 2008. This time both Japan and China bought ivory. That second sale raised demand, which was not the plan. It also suggested that legal trade might return someday. Illegal killing for tusks then shot upward. Many countries began storing ivory. They hoped for huge profits later. Some countries have burned the ivory they stored. Burning means that ivory can never be traded outside the law. A figure of 26 million sits beside this story. The crisis has kept growing. It has reached a tipping point. Each year, poachers now kill more African elephants than are born. If that pattern is not reversed quickly, elephants face doom. Doom would not wait for a far-off age that nobody can picture. It can arrive within the lives of people alive now. WildlifeDirect put the 2018 count of living African elephants under 400,000. The yearly kill was about 35,000. Buyers in Asia were the reason for that ivory. Should the pace stay the same, extinction is guaranteed by 2030. A chart of African elephant numbers uses rough estimates for most years. The counts for 1979 and for 2016 are the exceptions. The Great Elephant Census is the source. Marks on the chart include 1.3 million. They include 600,000. They include 352,000. Years on the chart include 1800. They include 1913. They include 1979, 1989, and 2016. One label on the chart reads 10 million.

7In Kenya, a caretaker walks beside an orphaned elephant calf. Extinction is not the only tragedy tied to this trade. Elephants that survive a killing, and that lose family, carry trauma. Some become aggressive. Some become antisocial. Young males seem especially hurt when mothers are gone. Older males being gone hurts them too. Orphaned adolescents have gone on killing sprees. Other young elephants have been targets. Other species, including rhinoceroses, have been targets. Humans have been targets. Young females who saw killings sometimes grow up without mothering skills. They may reject their babies. Scientists are not surprised. Elephants are highly intelligent, and their social bonds are strong. Another worry is the danger facing rangers who protect them. Long ago, “poacher” usually meant a poor villager. The animals taken were few, and the meat was meant for the family. Rangers often made the arrest without violence. Today’s poachers are nothing like that. They use the newest weapons. The attacks are planned with care. April 2016 brought one such attack. Heavily armed poachers came after elephants in Garamba National Park. The park is in the Congo, in its Democratic Republic. Three rangers were killed. The park’s manager was hurt badly. Similar attacks have happened in other parts of Africa. From 2009 through 2017, wildlife poachers killed more than 450 rangers. A report dated July 2018 came from an international group of rangers. It said 107 rangers had been killed in the year before. Poaching has another result. More elephants are born with no tusks. Mozambique fought a civil war from 1977 to 1992. In Gorongosa National Park, about 2,500 elephants had lived there. Roughly 92 percent were slaughtered. Ivory paid for weapons. Meat fed the fighters. Of the 200 or so that survived, most had no tusks. Under ordinary conditions, only about 4 percent of female African elephants are born without tusks.

8Since that war, more than 50 percent of females born there have no tusks. The same rise shows up elsewhere in Africa, wherever poaching is frequent. Genetics helps explain the shift. Where ivory poaching is common, a tuskless elephant is more likely to live. It is therefore more likely to pass tusklessness to its young. A change like that would normally need a great many generations. Heavy poaching speeds it up. Tuskless elephants get an enormous advantage in staying alive. The situation also raises a question. How does an elephant get by with no tusks? Scientists who study elephants are only starting to look into that. Grasses make up more of the diet when tusks are missing. They eat fewer woody plants than elephants that have tusks. Nobody yet knows what that diet change will do to their health. Nobody yet knows what it will do to survival over a long time. Other Dangers Poaching is a formidable threat. Elephants face other risks too. Habitat loss is one. Long ago, elephants traveled great distances for food and water. They followed migration paths that were already ancient. Humans have pushed farther into that territory. Homes, farms, and roads have been built. Railroads and pipelines have been built. A great deal of the old range is gone. What remains is broken into pieces more and more often. Lost and broken habitat blocks the way to resources. It also separates elephant groups. Mate choice can shrink. Genetic diversity can shrink. That diversity matters for survival. Conflict with humans is another risk. More people nearby means more clashes. Outside protected areas, elephants and people compete. Food is one prize. Water is another. Space is another. Food is what draws elephants into some villages. Crops are damaged. Property is damaged. People trying to chase the animals off often leave them dead or hurt. People are sometimes killed or hurt by the elephants as well. In Kenya, people watch an elephant from the far side of a fence. The fence is there to protect crops. Culling is a third risk. Clashes can grow so severe that wildlife managers kill many elephants at once. The aim is to hold the numbers down. Like poaching, culling often leaves trauma in the elephants that survive.

9Saving Elephants Keeping elephants from extinction takes action across the world. Governments have a part. Organizations have a part. Individuals have a part. A key piece is the law. National rules and international rules need to ban ivory sold as a business. Right now, CITES forbids all commercial international trade in ivory. The ban covers African elephants. It covers Asian elephants. Several countries with large ivory markets already forbid commercial trade, or they will ban it soon. The United States is one. The United Kingdom is one. China is one. Singapore is one. A major step came in December 2017. China had been the world’s largest ivory market. It banned every domestic sale. Carving factories closed. Shops closed. Ivory is still bought and sold in some other Asian countries. Pressure is on them to follow China’s lead. A ban must also be enforced, or it fails. China’s shops stopped offering carvings like the ones in a photo. The 2017 ban is the reason. Desire for ivory is a second piece that must be solved. High demand keeps illegal trade alive even when laws exist. If demand falls sharply, trafficking stops paying. The killing of elephants stops paying with it. Conservation groups work without pause to teach the public about the danger elephants face. The teaching is especially active in Asia, where demand is still high. While they work to lower that demand, several groups report a gap in knowledge. Many people do not know that an elephant must die before its tusks can be taken. Public campaigns are correcting that false idea. In April 2019, people marched in Kenya. They marched against poaching and against the illegal wildlife trade.

10People Who Fight for Elephants Many people give this rescue effort their full attention. Bryan Christy, an investigative journalist, is one. He had a realistic fake tusk built. A GPS tracker was hidden inside it. He placed the tusk in an African region known for ivory poaching. Then he followed the path it traveled. What he found was this. African terrorists were carrying out the poaching. A terrorist group uses violence, or the threat of it, to chase its goals. Support was coming from senior officials. Some of them served in government. Some served in the military. National Geographic printed Bryan Christy's ivory findings in its edition for 2015. Dr. Sam Wasser is a conservation biologist. Seattle is his base, on the faculty at the University of Washington. He studies elephant DNA in order to fight poaching. For more than twenty years he has used DNA from elephant dung. What he builds is a genetic map of elephant populations. Poached ivory can be traced to a place on that map. Law enforcement can then focus on those places. A large share of illegal ivory leaves Africa for Asia by way of Hong Kong. In 2013, three schoolgirls in Hong Kong formed a group. Nellie Shute was one. Christina Seigrist was another. Lucy Skrine was the third. They taught people that ivory and elephant deaths are connected. A petition gathered more than eighteen thousand signatures. It asked the government in Hong Kong to get rid of a huge ivory store. Smugglers had been the source of that store. The destruction finished in 2016. It was one of the largest ivory-destruction projects known. Local communities are another part of the rescue. People who have clashed with elephants often feel negatively about them. Those people need support, so that killing is not the only choice left. Conservation groups teach local residents about elephant habits. They teach about habitats. They teach about extinction risk from poaching and from lost habitat. They explain ways to live alongside elephants. Farmers learn from one group to set red pepper plants along the edge of a crop. The plant irritates an elephant's eyes and nose. The elephant leaves. The groups also ask people to value elephants as a treasure belonging to the country itself. The animals can be a source of pride. They can draw tourists. They can bring income. Young people are urged to take part in keeping elephants alive. One photo shows a visit to an elephant orphanage in Kenya. The visitors are schoolchildren.

11Three elephants in Botswana walk toward a water hole. The time is sunset. Little Time Remains Picture that outdoor market in Asia once more. Beautiful ivory sculptures are still on the table. Buyers who never learn the source of ivory will not stop. Elephant numbers will keep falling. The sharp drop in elephant populations is a complex subject. It is also a controversial one. People disagree about a total ban on ivory trade versus rules that would manage the trade. Some say only a total ban can save elephants. Others say a total ban will push the illegal trade higher. Prices would rise. Poachers would have more reason to keep killing. Will time run out while people argue over the answer? The clock does not stop. For now, two facts are sure. About one hundred elephants die in this killing every day. A world that had no elephants would be a poorer place to live. Words to Know brutal (adj.): cruel, and willing to use violence without pity. essential (adj.): something that cannot be left out. habitat (n.): the outdoor home a plant or an animal is suited to. trafficking (n.): trade that the law does not allow. genetics (n.): the study of traits moving from parents into their young. consumption (n.): the taking and using of goods or resources, at times until little remains. endangered (adj.): facing a real chance of being wiped out entirely. adaptation (n.): a body feature, or a feature of a species, that improves survival in a given setting. slaughter (n.): killing people or animals in large numbers, done with cruelty. trauma (n.): deep emotional pain, most often after a frightening event. conservation (n.): care that keeps wild places safe, along with the plants and creatures in them. extinction (n.): the point at which every member of an animal group or a plant group is gone.

97. When Colors Do Not Look the Same

1A picture sets two crayon boxes side by side. Picking a red crayon is much simpler for someone who sees every color. It is harder for someone whose red and green look alike. Picture a crayon box that shows only grays, blues, and yellows. Picture a traffic signal whose red lamp and green lamp look nearly the same. That is one way the world can look to a person with color blindness. Their view is not the view of people who see the full range of color. Color blindness is the most common genetic condition on Earth. In the United States alone, it affects more than ten million people. The name is misleading. This condition does not make a person blind. Doctors now prefer another name. They say color vision deficiency, often shortened to CVD. Most people who have CVD still see some colors. What they lack is the full ability to see certain colors. Sometimes that ability is only weaker, not gone.

2CVD is easier to grasp once color is understood as light. Different colors are different wavelengths. A prism can split white light into a rainbow. What the prism really does is sort those wavelengths. Longer wavelengths sit at the red end of that spread. Shorter wavelengths sit at the purple end. An object looks a certain color because of what it does with light. It absorbs some wavelengths. It reflects others. A ripe strawberry looks red for a clear reason. It reflects the long wavelengths that we call red. Reflect short wavelengths instead, and that same berry would look blue. Flower petals can look red for the same reason. They send back long red wavelengths. Leaves look green because they send back medium wavelengths, the ones we call green. A diagram of the eye shows the path of sight. The cornea collects light from outside and starts to focus it. Rods and cones line the retina along the rear wall. Those cells note the view. Opening and closing the pupil is the work of the iris. More light enters, or less light enters. The optic nerve carries messages to the brain about the view. The pupil is a hole at the center of the eye. Light passes through that hole. The lens changes shape and finishes the focus. People see color because special cells answer differently to different wavelengths. Light comes into an eye. The lens sets that light on the retina. The retina is a thin sheet of tissue inside the eyeball, behind the lens. Light there wakes cells that sense it. Some are rod cells. Some are cone cells. Awake cells send electrical signals. The path is the optic nerve. The brain turns those signals into images.

3No cells in the retina are more sensitive than rod cells. They let you see when light is extremely dim. They cannot separate one color from another. Color vision is the job of cone cells. Each cone holds one of three light-absorbing molecules. Those molecules are called photopigments. One kind detects blue light. One kind detects green light. One kind detects red light. Mix those three main colors, and thousands of colors become visible. CVD follows when one or more photopigments fail to work properly. A side note compares human sight with other animals. A picture contrasts human vision with honeybee vision. Most animals see fewer colors than people do. Dogs, for instance, see only shades of blue and of yellow. A bull cannot see the color red. Some animals see more colors than humans. Birds are among them. Bees are among them. Butterflies are among them. Their extra range includes ultraviolet light and infrared light. Those wavelengths are invisible to people. Animals use color information for several jobs. They signal one another. They hunt prey for food. They defend themselves from predators. The most common form of CVD is the red-green kind. Telling red from green becomes difficult. The condition is hereditary. It shows up most often in Caucasian people whose ancestors lived in northern Europe. Men have it more often than women. Among men, the rate is one out of twelve. Among women, the rate is one in two hundred. The usual cause is a fault in the green photopigment. Without that green pigment, green objects look reddish. Yellow objects look reddish too. A fault in the red photopigment can cause red-green CVD as well. Then red objects look green or black. Orange objects do too. Yellow objects do too. People with this condition still see clearly. Red cones and green cones overlap in the wavelengths they detect. Incoming light can still be detected even if one cone type is missing. Detection can continue even if that cone type is malfunctioning. A comparison picture sets ordinary color sight next to red-green CVD sight. Red, yellow, and green are marked in each view.

4Another comparison picture lines up three views. One is full-color vision. One is red-green CVD. The third view is the blue-yellow form of CVD. That form shows up when the blue photopigment fails or is missing. It is fairly rare. Worldwide, it appears in about one person out of every ten thousand. Unlike the red-green form, it is equally common in men and in women. Blue cone cells are completely absent in some people with this form. They see blue as green. They see yellow as violet, or they see it as gray. More often, the blue cones work only in part. The result is trouble separating yellow from pink. Red is hard to separate from pink too. The harshest form is complete CVD. Defects in this form hit at least two cone types out of the three. One kind of cone might seem like enough for color. It is not. The brain must compare signals from at least two different cone types before it can name a color. A person who has only blue cones can still detect blue wavelengths. That person cannot tell colors apart. Some traffic lights add shapes to their colors. Drivers with CVD can read the shape even when the color is unclear. People missing two or more cone types are often very sensitive to light. Clear sight can be hard, especially in bright light. They must lean on rod cells for most of their vision, or for all of it. Rod cells work only when the light is dim. Worldwide, about one person in thirty thousand lacks all three cone types. With no working cones, the world appears in black, in white, and in gray.

5CVD can bring real challenges. Color-coded information is one example. Maps may be hard to read. Graphs may be hard. Charts may be hard. Children can struggle with schoolwork. The struggle is worse if nobody has found the CVD yet. Chalk that is yellow, written on a chalkboard that is green, is hard to read for someone with red-green CVD. Every type of CVD can make color choice hard. Art projects suffer. Science projects suffer. Safety can suffer too. Fire hydrants are often painted red or yellow so they stand out. Car warning lights often use those colors. Emergency equipment often uses them. Someone who sees every color notices those bright marks. Someone with CVD may miss them completely. Sunburns can be hard to spot. Rashes can be hard to spot. Meat that is undercooked can be hard to spot. A job choice can be affected. Some jobs demand full-color vision. A geologist is one example. A commercial airline pilot is another. Other jobs grow much harder without full color. Interior design is one. Photography is one. Food inspection is one. Even so, people with CVD can usually find a way through those problems. Almost any job can still be done well. Testing has a standard tool for red-green conditions. It is called the Ishihara Test. The test uses pictures made of dots. The dots differ in size. They differ in color. Someone who sees every color can find a number inside the picture, or a shape. A person with red-green CVD may not be able to name that hidden mark. The mark may be difficult. It may be impossible. Similar tests look for yellow-blue CVD. A picture of the test asks a simple question. Can you find the hidden numbers or shapes inside the circles?

6A picture shows special sunglasses. With them on, a person who has red-green CVD finds the world much richer in color. No cure for CVD is known today. New tools have still appeared, thanks to modern technology. Phone apps can do useful jobs. One job is naming a color. Another job is suggesting a complementary color, a color that balances or completes the first. Matching clothes becomes easier. Ripe fruit at a store becomes easier to judge. Some apps can name a color only after the user takes a photo. Other apps read the colors in the camera's viewfinder. No photo is required first. The naming happens while they look. Researchers have also built lenses with a high-tech tint. Those lenses filter out particular wavelengths of light. Sunglasses made with the lenses help a person with red-green CVD tell the two colors apart. A true treatment does not exist yet. That may change. Scientists recently tested a workaround on squirrel monkeys that had red-green CVD. The monkeys had no red photopigment. Red and green looked the same to them. The tool the researchers used is called gene therapy. It changes traits. They built a special virus. The virus carried the gene for the red photopigment. Green cone cells in the monkeys received that gene. About twenty weeks later, the treated monkeys could tell red dots from green dots. A picture shows a squirrel monkey taking a color test. The news mattered because these monkeys had lived with CVD from birth. Many doctors had predicted full color would be impossible for them. Many scientists had agreed. The needed brain connections, they thought, would never have formed. Those connections usually grow while an animal is young. The connections are what let the brain read color information. Adult squirrel monkeys now show that a workaround exists. People who want full-color vision have a reason to hope.

7CVD is fairly common. Anyone can inherit it. Maybe you have it. Maybe someone in your family has it. Maybe you know a person who does. Finding CVD early helps. People can understand what they are seeing. They can adjust. Certain activities become harder. Most people with CVD still get along just fine. The world may look a little different to them. That difference does not stop a rich life. It does not stop a fulfilling life. A few words help with this topic. Ancestry means family members and relations from earlier times. Molecules are the smallest parts of a substance that can exist on their own. One or more atoms make a molecule. Complementary describes something that completes, balances, or improves something else. Photopigments are natural compounds. They change chemically when they take in light. Cone cells sit in the retina. They sense color, and they work best in bright light. A prism is clear. It bends light until a rainbow of colors appears. Defects are weaknesses, imperfections, or failures. Images land on the retina, a tissue deep inside the eye, and that tissue sends them on to the brain. A genetic condition is a physical condition passed down in a family. The cause is a fault in a gene, or in several genes. Rod cells sit in the retina. They sense light. Dim light is where they work best. Hereditary means a trait traveled from parents down to their children by way of genes. Wavelengths are the distances between one high point of a wave and the next, or between one low point and the next.

98. When Comic Fans Gather

1Batman shares a quiet moment with Robin and with the Joker at the New York Comic Con of 2014. Imagine an auditorium packed with thousands of other fans. You wait for the stars to arrive onstage. Your Chewbacca costume feels pretty warm. Two rows down, another fan wears an armored helmet. You guess that helmet is even warmer. Which character is he supposed to be? You turn your head for a clearer view. All at once, people are on their feet and cheering. You leap up. The wait is over. Robert Downey Jr. walks out. Several movies have cast him as Iron Man. A grin is on his face. Roses fly toward people seated in front. With that, the Avengers panel begins. Color, crowds, and pop culture fans are what a comic con is made of. A collector of comic books will find a place here. So will someone who watches cartoons. So will someone who goes to the movies or plays video games. Fans shorten the name of these conventions to cons. The gatherings occur worldwide. Huge venues host some of them. Attendees can number in the thousands, and the schedule can cover multiple days. Other cons are tiny. An afternoon may be all they last, or a single day. Programming reaches every sort of fan. Children are welcome. Adults are welcome. Serious gamers fit in. Obsessive readers fit in. So does everyone between those poles. Attendance at some larger cons passes 130,000 people in a year.

2Comic cons began halfway through the twentieth century. The purpose was a meeting place. Fans could trade comics there. They could talk about the books. Comic books first began in Europe and Japan. They did not take hold in American popular taste until the 1930s. The release of Superman was the moment. Superheroes dominated the books in that period. Devoted fans gathered around them. Organized meetings arrived in the 1960s and the 1970s. Growth of the conventions was quick once that started. One early organizer was Shel Dorf. His own work was drawing comics. Detroit in the 1960s was where he held small fan meetings. He later founded a convention that people now call CCI, or Comic-Con International. The city was San Diego. The year was 1970. Year one drew about 100 fans. Today it is the biggest comic con in the nation. After that success, hundreds of further cons sprang up. Antarctica is the only continent that has no con. Seats disappear quickly. To be certain of a ticket, a few fans sleep outside for several days.

3A 2015 book fair shows college students browsing comic books. Explosive growth needs an explanation. The first part is a new wave of popularity for the books themselves. Readership was wide in the Golden Age. Those years were the 1930s and the 1940s. After the midpoint of the twentieth century, readership fell. Some readers of that later time called comics poor literature. Others called them something only for kids. Fresh ground opened in the late 1980s and the early 1990s. Neil Gaiman wrote the series The Sandman. Watchmen joined Alan Moore with Dave Gibbons. John Higgins joined that same team. Both works drew readers who stayed loyal. Critics praised them. Popular interest has climbed since then. So has interest from critics. New topics and new styles are still being explored by writers and artists. Today's comic books cover more ground than they ever have. Superhero tales of the traditional kind share space with war stories. Family drama is in the mix. Everything between those poles is there too. Graphic novels branched off from comic books. At the moment, young adult fiction counts some of them among its favorite titles. Nonfiction's newest edge includes graphic memoirs. Maus, by Art Spiegelman, is both a graphic memoir and a novel. Interviews with his father, who survived the Holocaust, are the basis. The Pulitzer Prize went to Maus. Few literary awards in the country stand higher. As the topics widened, the audiences widened. A fan of any gender can find a story to relate to. The same is true for any color, any age, and any nationality. Convention crowds have climbed in a dramatic way. The International Berlin Comic Festival is where Spiegelman speaks about Maus.

4San Diego Comic Con in 2017 puts Black Panther actors on a panel. Michael B. Jordan is one of them. Danai Gurira is the other. Hollywood supplies the second reason for the boom. Movies of recent years, built on comic characters, have succeeded on a huge scale. Interest in the comics rose with them. So did the number of people at cons. Favorites with audiences include a 2008 film, Iron Man. They include Spider-Man movies made in the 2000s. They include another 2008 film, The Dark Knight. They include a 2017 film, Wonder Woman. They include a 2018 film, Black Panther. New fans arrived because of those hits. Programming at cons now gives movies a large role. Panels regularly feature famous actors from those films. Writers come too. Directors come too. The crowds they draw are huge. Tripoli hosted the 2017 Libya Comic Convention, and artists there drew illustrations in manga style. The story does not stop at movies. Video games now belong at cons around the world. Television shows belong there. Novels of science fiction and of fantasy belong there. Some fans found the shared audience too broad. They split off and built conventions for one genre. Attendance is strong where the focus is anime and manga. Japan is the source of those animated films and those comic books. Separate cons exist for people who love classic comics and collect them. Separate cons exist for sci-fi fans and for fantasy fans. Steampunk has cons. Horror has cons. Humor has cons. Many other themes do too.

5The United States holds comic cons in cities from coast to coast. Leave the giant events of San Diego and New York, and the crowds shrink. Enthusiasm among fans stays huge. A town near you may have a con on the way. A local newspaper can say so. An online listing can say so. What you find may surprise you. At many smaller cons, local artists and local fans mix with cartoonists whose names are widely known. Movie stars mix with them too. The star of a show you love might be present at any con in the country. The writer of books you love might be present. Meeting local artists is likely. Making new friends is likely. London's 2016 MCM Comic Con shows Captain America in a fight with Loki. CCI: San Diego shows costumed viewers at an early showing of Star Wars Legends. Celebration of creative works and of fandom is only part of the point. Fans also get space to display creativity of their own. An independent film festival joined CCI: San Diego in 2005. Filmmakers who were still aspiring could send in work and compete for prizes. Showings continued across all four days. Categories open to submissions now include action and adventure. They include animation. They include horror and suspense. They include films drawn from comics. Experts who work in the industry sit on the judging panels. Filmmakers gain a valuable chance to receive feedback.

6Dressing up is an old comic con custom called cosplay. The costumes portray characters out of comic books. They also portray characters out of anime, manga, animated films, and further fantasy genres. Japan coined the word. It blends two English words, costume and play. Worldwide, fans treat the hobby as serious business. Costume sellers can supply an outfit. A builder can make one to order. A fan can sew one by hand. Realistic props are common. A character's weapons and other accessories are examples. While the outfit is on, some fans behave as that character would. Detail can be slight, or it can be astonishing. Eye color can be changed with contact lenses. Temporary tattoos can be designed for a closer likeness. Working out the build of a costume is, for many fans, a large share of the pleasure. Worldwide cons give cosplay a central place. Exhibit halls hold vendors who sell outfits. Costumed fans in the audience can number in the hundreds. Contests are common. Photos, skits, and interviews let cosplayers present their characters. Meeting the makers in person is another draw. A favorite star may describe what it was like to make a comic, a film, or a show. A direct question from the crowd is sometimes allowed. A photo with the celebrity may be possible. An autograph may go onto a comic or a poster. Fans treasure those personal moments as memories. Celebrities, for their part, often report good memories of their own. The fans, they say, tend to be warm. They tend to be friendly. They tend to be devoted. Stan Lee was a legend in three roles. He wrote. He edited. He published. Comic cons saw him often. Many of the best-known superheroes at Marvel Comics exist partly because of him. One is the Incredible Hulk. Another is Spider-Man. His death came in 2018.

7Creative energy at a con gathers in the exhibit hall. Mingling and talk happen there. On display is material tied to comics. Movies are represented. So are TV, games, and further pop culture. Buying comics is possible. Trading them is possible. Action figures, toys, and similar merchandise are for sale too. A seasoned collector may locate an edition that is rare or one of a kind. A new collector may begin a collection with a head start. Artists and writers often meet fans in a signing hall. Publishers sometimes meet hopeful artists and writers in a portfolio review area. The aim for those hopefuls is a contract for a book. Simply standing in the hall still offers plenty. Trailers and full movies play on a steady schedule. Seeing a celebrity remains possible at any moment. Merchandise in bright colors never seems to run out. A New York Comic Con display is packed with dolls offered for sale. Hayao Miyazaki, at the center of a panel, speaks during the 2009 San Diego comic con. Animation in Japan loves his work. His other roles include director, producer, screenwriter, and author. He draws manga. Studio Ghibli lists him as a co-founder. Controversy has traveled with the growth. Certain fans of comic books say the largest cons grew far past a good size. They say attention drifted too far from the books themselves. Movie fans, TV fans, and game fans, in this view, can bury the spark that started cons. A fairer label for many events would be pop culture convention, rather than a convention only about comic books. Devoted fans also argue with one another. The dispute may be who holds the most knowledge of a series, a film, or an invented world. Silly as that sounds, it shows something real. The audience feels a deep emotional tie to these works.

8Readers of comics, and the people who attend cons, are not the crowd they once were. Men made up most of that crowd in earlier years. Women are about forty percent of recent attendees at CCI: San Diego. Under age thirty, attendance splits by gender at about half and half. Younger fans are finding cons as a generation. Recent cons count more than half their people as younger than twenty-nine. Bigger crowds come with that wider mix. Most fans are glad of it. Portland, Oregon, hosted a Wizard World Comic Con where a girl looks through comics. Larger issues from the wider world can be discussed at a con. Serious subjects appear in some authors' work. Equality of race is one subject. Equality of gender is one. Politics is one. War is one. Not every reader wants those stories. Banned book campaigns have targeted some of them. A community, in such a campaign, asks a school or a library to remove a title from its shelves. Adult language, or adult themes, has brought challenges to Spider-Man comics. The same has happened to Batman comics. Recent panels have taken up censorship. The speakers include readers, teachers, and librarians. Fiction describes some comics. Nonfiction describes others. Teaching is the goal of some. Fun alone is the goal of others. Big social problems and adult themes fill some pages. A flight into fantasy worlds fills others. A shelf question follows from that mix. Do libraries and schools keep every comic in one place, or do they separate them? A social question follows too. What part should comics play in the wider society? Panels return to these questions often. Some school districts have banned the Sandman series by Neil Gaiman.

9Boundaries around comics keep moving outward. The shift can be hard. Even so, cons are living through an exciting period. Today's comics, together with other pop culture media, come in vast variety. Audiences for the books and for the conventions have grown bigger. They have grown more varied. Somewhere in a comic, a fan can find a face like their own, whatever their age, gender, or nationality. Superman is one way a hero can look. A young girl from Botswana is another way. A reporter working on the ground in Bosnia is another way. Events inside a comic have no ceiling. The hero's identity has no ceiling either. That openness, in the end, is the pull toward comic cons. Stories, and the cons those stories feed, make worlds in which an everyday person turns into a hero. Virtually any person can wear that role. Possibility swallows people up. They put on the clothes of a character they love. They swap books. They swap trivia questions with fans beside them. They greet an artist with a handshake. The experience is one that many people repeat. A young girl at CCI: San Diego models a stormtrooper outfit from Star Wars, colored pink. Words in this book have special uses. Merchandise is the goods people buy and the goods people sell. Censorship is the cutting or blocking of a publication, a play, or a film, in whole or in part, because someone judges the content offensive or threatening. A panel is people asked to speak with knowledge on a subject while an audience listens. A controversy is an argument over some issue. Pop culture is the set of popular ideas that mass media carries, ideas that belong to ordinary modern life. A convention is a big meeting, able to run for several days, where people talk about work or about an interest held in common. Readership is who reads a work, or who reads a kind of writing. Diversity is many different things present at once. A screening is a planned showing of a movie or a television program. Fandom is every follower devoted to one interest. Sports, entertainment, and celebrities are examples. A venue is a site that holds an organized event. A memoir is a written account of experiences a person has had.

99. When Weather Turns Dangerous

1When the Natural World Turns Harsh Many climates stay on one pattern. Daily life stays smoother when that pattern holds. Interest comes from weather that arrives with the seasons. A gentle rain can fall in spring once the air is warm enough. The first snow can fall in winter once the air is cold enough. People often grow bored if one pattern lasts too long. They then wait with impatience for a large shift. Ordinary days gain drama from the weather. Drama is not always the end of the story. Weather can turn dangerous. It can also turn destructive.
