Thunderstorms, tornadoes, and hurricanes rage with awesome force. That same force is frightening. These three events of nature can cause havoc on Earth. A calm afternoon faces a coming thunderstorm.

2A diagram shows one path that builds a thunderstorm: clouds, a cold front, and warm, moist air. Thunderstorms No other violent weather event happens as often as the thunderstorm. Several inches of rain can fall on one area in little time during a major storm. Stiff winds rise as well. Flash floods, hail, and lightning are hazards these storms create. Lightning ranks as the worst hazard. Every thunderstorm brings it. Formation starts when a huge body of warm, damp air climbs far into the atmosphere and then loses heat. Heat taken up from the ground is one reason that warm air climbs. Summer days often work this way. The Sun pours plentiful heat into the ground. Later the ground gives that heat off. Air above the ground grows warmer. A meeting with a cold front can also shove warm, moist air upward. Cold air packs more densely than warm air. Warm air therefore slides above the leading edge of the cold front. Higher up, the warmer air spreads out. Cooling follows that spreading. Once the chill is great enough, water vapor condenses. The vapor changes from a gas into a liquid. Puffy clouds appear. Their name is cumulus clouds. Some of those clouds grow into cumulonimbus clouds. A cumulonimbus cloud is huge. A wide area spreads across its top. Thunderstorms come from these clouds. A great load of condensed water can gather inside a cumulonimbus cloud. The load grows too heavy to remain aloft. Rain then falls. Intense rain from a major storm arrives in a brief span. Flash flooding can follow. Farms and homes can be wiped out. People who are not ready for the massive downpour can die. Strong air also rushes downward from the cloud. At the ground, those downdrafts may become stiff winds.

3Thunderstorms come in two main kinds. One kind is ordinary. The other kind is severe. Ordinary storms are the usual ones of summer. A typical storm lasts from 30 to 60 minutes. The heat eases, and people welcome that relief. Severe storms are also called supercell thunderstorms. They are huge, and they rotate. Several hours can pass before they end. Extremely heavy rain falls. High winds blow. Anxiety among people rises with those winds. Hail can form in a severe storm. The hailstones may be large. Some reach the size of baseballs. Some grow even larger. Severe storms make up about 10 percent of all thunderstorms. Tall towers in Panama City, Panama, take lightning strikes. Buildings there are struck as well. Lightning is the greatest danger in every thunderstorm. Picture a huge spark flashing across the sky. Lightning is that spark. Wildfires can start from it. People can be killed by it. Electric charges build up inside storm clouds. That buildup causes lightning. A bolt is a flow of those charges as they seek opposite charges. The opposite charges may sit in the clouds. They may also sit on the ground. Bolts that leap from cloud to ground put people in danger. Each bolt travels inside a narrow channel of air. Flash heating drives that air to about 54,000 degrees Fahrenheit, or 30,000 degrees C. The Sun's surface is about five times cooler than this. Explosive heat makes the air in the channel expand with violent force. A shockwave follows that expansion. We hear the shockwave as thunder. Thunderstorms take their name from that sound. One fire began when lightning struck. Twenty homes were destroyed.

4Tornadoes Some supercell thunderstorms spawn tornadoes. No other weather event on Earth is more violent. Picture a cloud that spins and drops in a funnel shape. It is large. That cloud is a tornado. It reaches down from the base of a big storm cloud. A narrow, snakelike form is common. Other tornadoes look like wide columns. A column may stretch as far as a mile across, or 1.6 km. Forward speed along the ground averages 30 miles per hour, or 48 km per hour. Some tornadoes move more than twice that fast. A strong updraft forms inside the funnel. Almost anything not fastened firmly to the ground can be sucked up. Vehicles can be lifted. Mobile homes can be lifted too. Once a tornado touches the ground, it usually looks dark. Dirt and debris drawn upward cause that dark look. Tornado Alley takes in these states from north to south: Minnesota, then South Dakota, then Iowa, then Nebraska, then Colorado, then Kansas, then Oklahoma, and then Texas. Almost any place in the world can be struck. The United States sees about 75 percent of all tornadoes. About 750 of them happen there every year. On average, 100 people die from them each year. Most tornadoes in the U.S. form in a broad region of the central United States. People call that region Tornado Alley. The Great Plains suit tornado growth very well. The land is flat. Canada sends cold, dry air. The Gulf of Mexico sends air that is moist and warm. Those air masses can meet. Supercell thunderstorms often follow when large masses of those two air types converge. Storms of that kind are ideal makers of tornadoes.

5Winds inside a major tornado can spin faster than 300 miles per hour, or 480 km per hour. A truly powerful tornado can rip a wood-frame house from its foundations. The house can be lifted far into the air. Destruction along the path may run as far as 50 miles, or 80 km. On May 3, 1999, one of the strongest tornadoes ever recorded tore through the suburbs of Oklahoma City. Twisters struck Tornado Alley across four days. This tornado was part of that onslaught. Doppler radar measured the winds at 318 miles per hour, or 512 km per hour. Thirty-six people were killed. Homes and other buildings were destroyed. The count passed 10,000. After that tornado, residents of Oklahoma City search the debris for belongings. Nothing matches a major tornado for sheer violence inside a limited area. People along seacoasts know a wider threat. A hurricane can wreck land across a much broader swath. Hurricanes A hurricane is a huge storm that rotates. It grows over warm ocean water in summer or in fall. Most of them form over the Atlantic Ocean. Many also form over the Gulf of Mexico. The Caribbean Sea is another common birthplace. Some also form in the northeastern Pacific Ocean. Storms of the same kind form in the Western Pacific and in the Indian Ocean. People there call them typhoons or severe tropical cyclones. On Reunion, an island in the Indian Ocean, people brace for a severe tropical cyclone.

6A satellite view shows Hurricane Katrina just before landfall in the southern United States. Low air pressure is where a hurricane begins. Winds circle around that low-pressure area. Warm, moist air is drawn up from the sea underneath. The area grows into a tropical storm. Moisture turns into clouds. A great amount of energy is released. If growth continues, that energy keeps the storm going. Wind speed may reach 74 miles per hour, or 119 km per hour. The storm is then a hurricane. Seen from space, the storm resembles a huge pinwheel. Rapidly circling storm clouds pile up in a towering mass around the outer parts. The center is calm. People call that calm center the eye. Wind and rain are absent there. Width can reach 600 miles, or 965 km. At landfall, coastal places are drenched by hammering rain. Heavy winds buffet those same places. A major hurricane can push winds past 150 miles per hour, or 240 km per hour. Roofs can be torn from many houses. Gusts in a major hurricane can equal the wind speed of the strongest tornado. Low-lying communities face a still greater danger. A wall of water, the storm surge, is driven toward land by the winds. In a major hurricane that wall can stand 20 feet high, or 6 m. Flooding can spread far inland. Lives can be lost there. Hurricane Katrina, in August 2005, ranks among the worst recent hurricanes to strike the United States. Severe destruction hit the Gulf Coast. Thousands of people were killed. The states hit were Louisiana and Mississippi. Alabama was hit too. So were Georgia and Florida. Two weeks later, Venice, Louisiana, was still flooded. Every part of town had water at a depth of two feet or more.

7Closing Thoughts Some parts of devastating weather can be guarded against. A full escape is not possible. Places in the United States that miss tornadoes and hurricanes may still face broiling summers. Harsh winters are another possibility. Along the West Coast, moderate weather is often balanced by earthquakes and brush fires. A person choosing a home should weigh the area's usual climate first. Extremes and the worst calamities matter less than that general pattern. The usual weather is what brings both steadiness and drama. Air pressure is the push of air within the atmosphere. A cold front is the leading side where cold air, moving as one mass, meets warmer air. Cumulonimbus clouds tower upward, with flat bases down low and tops that spread out. Thunderstorms often show these clouds. Doppler radar tracks objects by measuring how fast they move. Storms and precipitation are common targets for this tool. A supercell thunderstorm is built from thunderclouds that rotate and reach high into the sky. Tornadoes, hail, and lightning often come from it. Readers can look up Oklahoma City, the storm surge, Tornado Alley, typhoons, clouds, the eye of a hurricane, the Great Plains, hail, Hurricane Katrina, and lightning.

100. Wild and Wacky World of Wigs

1People have cared deeply about hair through all of recorded history. Wigs have mattered from ancient Egypt to modern times. People wore them to look good or to show their place in society. Wigs made from human hair are the most durable. They are also easier to cut and style than synthetic wigs.

2A full wig, also called a periwig or peruke, covers the head down to the neck. A toupee covers only part of the head, and double-sided tape can hold it on. Extensions are hair or fiber added with pins, clips, or glue. Wigs may be wool, goat hair, horsehair, straw, grasses, or plastic such as nylon, in every color. Human-hair wigs looked most natural, but they cost more and could need six to ten heads of hair. Today many people prefer nylon wigs because they cost less and are easier to care for. Until the 1700s, hair was looped on a fitted mesh cap and fixed with beeswax, resin, or glue. A ventilating needle knots that hair, and a later ribbon let one wig fit many heads.

3The oldest known wigs date to 1400 BC in Egypt. Tomb art and sculpture show their thick curls and braids. People wore wigs to look like the gods and to cover bald spots. A full head of hair meant a person was strong and healthy. Some wigs reached the waist, and beeswax held the shape like hairspray. Kings used human hair with ivory and silver, the rich used wool or goat hair, and the poor used straw. In the film Cleopatra, each hairstyle for Elizabeth Taylor needed three wigs. In Asia, wigs were rare in daily life but important in Japanese and Chinese theater.

4Hairstyles of goddesses such as Aphrodite may have shaped the fancy wigs of Greek women. Wealthy people in Greece and Rome wore false hair. Noblewomen wore many braids and curls pinned high on their heads. Hairpins held the larger curls in place. More braids and ornaments showed higher social status. They liked blond and red human hair. Some used extensions to add volume. Some Roman elites kept blond and red-haired Germanic slaves so hair for wigs was ready. Rich men and women hid bald spots with wigs.

5After the Roman Empire, wig use fell out of fashion for several centuries. King Louis XIII of France brought wigs back in the early seventeenth century when he started to go bald. He was only twenty-three and feared the court would not respect him. His wigs had a middle part and soft waves to the shoulders, and noblemen copied him. Mostly men wore full wigs, while many women used extensions in their coiffures. Fancy styles were built over a frame, set with pig fat, and powdered with scented starch. Some stood three feet tall, held model ships, and stayed unwashed for up to three months. A 1778 cartoon shows these wild French wigs.

6The pig fat went bad and drew cockroaches, mice, and rats that nested in the hair. Women used a long claw stick to scratch without disturbing the style. In Western Europe, wigs marked doctors, barristers, judges, clergy, and nobles. Many of these wigs were stiff horsehair, which cost less than human hair. British judges and barristers still wear wigs in court. Toupees of the 1700s were curled and powdered, but cooler and lighter than heavy full wigs. In 1795 a British tax on wigs and powder lasted a few years, raised money, and helped end the trend. By the 1850s old wigs were sold as mops and rags, and bigwig meant an important person in a huge wig, like Edward Willes.

7In the twentieth century, people began to make wigs from nylon threads. Nylon looked like human hair, cost less, and came in any color of the rainbow. People wear wigs to look stylish or to change their appearance. People who are bald may wear wigs to feel better about themselves. Clowns and actors may wear wigs as part of their costumes. Styles change, but wigs have played an important role in human history. No one knows what the next great hairstyle will be. Illness or treatment can cause hair loss, doctors may prescribe wigs, and groups such as Locks of Love use donated hair to make wigs for children.

101. Wild Partners That Share the Work

1In the opening picture, yellow tangs swim as a group and pick algae off a turtle. The turtle is green. This book then explains partnerships in the wild. It looks at food traded for safety, at cleaning, at shared homes, and at hunts made easier by a partner. It looks at animals that hitch a ride, at pollination, and at seeds carried to new ground. A closing thought follows. Word meanings come last. Another picture shows a crocodile holding its jaws open for a small bird, the Egyptian plover. Leftover food is picked from the teeth. Wild life is hard. Food can be scarce. A good home can be scarce. Pests are everywhere. Something is nearly always ready to eat you. Those pressures push many species into unusual partnerships. Each partner does its own task, and both gain. One animal may stand guard against predators. The other may offer a cleaning, or a steady supply of food. Science calls these pairings symbiotic relationships. Symbiosis comes from ancient Greek. One root means with. The other means living. The year 1877 is when scientists first used the word for wild species. They were writing about lichens. A lichen is a complex organism, often full of color. A fungus and a kind of algae usually make it up. Those two live and work tightly together.

2Researchers have kept finding these partnerships ever since. Deep oceans hold them. Dry deserts hold them. Mountains and forests hold them too. Some pairs surprise everyone. A shrimp that works hard may team with a fish that sees sharply. A colorful clownfish may team with a venomous sea anemone, pronounced uh-NEM-uh-nee. A rodent that lives on the ground may team with a tree that towers overhead. Fascination is only part of the story. For the species involved, the partnership can decide life or death. Bees would struggle to live without flower nectar. Those same flowers would struggle to reproduce if bees did not carry their pollen. A home version is easy to picture. A pet dog offers love. It offers companionship and protection. The dog receives meals, notice, and shelter where it can live without harm. Each side gains. Starlings in one picture stay close to a red deer so they can pick insects off its body. The bargain is not always equal. Partnerships that last for thousands of years, or for millions, last for a clear reason. Each species gains enough to make the deal worth keeping. Some scientists think interdependence between different species helps explain Earth's variety of plants and wildlife. Variety inside a species may grow this way too, not only variety across species. An animal may spread into a place that is less than ideal. There it may collaborate with species already native, and survival gets easier. Given time, a subspecies can appear. Kinship with the parent species remains close. Traits, features, or behavior have become different. Examples of the many kinds of partnership come next. The partners themselves are called symbionts.

3Knowing someone is watching your back can matter. Bright clownfish of the Indian Ocean need every kind of help if hunters are not to catch them. One method is a refuge inside the tentacles of a sea anemone that carries venom. An anemone looks like a plant. It is a marine animal. It fastens itself to rock or to some other surface and waits. Prey has to come to it. A small fish or a shrimp that brushes the soft tentacles meets a toxin. Paralysis follows. The anemone pulls the helpless prey into its mouth. Clownfish are a special case. They build immunity on purpose. A tentacle is touched once, or twice. The fish waits. It touches again. Small doses, repeated, slowly lay down a mucus coating on the skin. That coating is protective. A picture shows a striped clownfish, cautious, hiding among those tentacles. Harmful contact is blocked by the mucus, so the fish can swim there and stay unhurt. Lunch for a predator becomes a dive into cover. While the clownfish moves among the tentacles, it also works as a lure. The hunter is drawn into stinging arms. The anemone kills that fish. Both partners then have a meal.

4On African ground, ostriches and zebras often eat side by side. Eyes and ears are shared. Ostriches see well. Zebras hear extremely well. A lion on the stalk, or some other hunter, is easier to notice together than alone. The pair can flee before the attack lands. Impalas and baboons in Africa keep a similar watch. Hearing in an impala is superb. Vision is excellent. Smell is acute. Danger spotted first by the impalas shows in alert posture and in the shake of horns. Baboons take the warning. Loud screams raise the alarm. Teeth that look intimidating help drive the predator off. A map of this region marks Europe, Africa, the Indian Ocean, and the Atlantic Ocean. One picture shows the mixed herds feeding, each ready to warn the other. Cleaning is another kind of help, aimed at places a body cannot reach. On many reefs a small silvery fish, the cleaner wrasse, does that job. It works almost like a dental hygienist of the deep, serving bigger fish such as butterflyfish or angelfish. A cleaning station is the wrasse's post. Large fish wait their turn with patience. Eating the helper would seem easy. It does not happen, because the wrasse dances in a way that soothes and seems to hypnotize. The big fish relaxes and, at last, opens its mouth. The wrasse shoots into the mouth and back out. It does the same at the gills. Fungus is cleared. Parasites are cleared. Dead skin and other debris are cleared. One picture shows a giant moray eel. A bluestreak cleaner wrasse is cleaning the teeth and the mouth. The wrasse leaves with a snack. The larger fish is left clean and healthy.

5A similar cleaning happens on the Galapagos Islands. Some of Darwin's ground finches do the work, and tortoises receive it. When a tortoise is ready, it takes a particular posture. Neck and legs stretch out. Neighboring finches swoop in and peck parasites the tortoise cannot reach. The tortoise stays absolutely still. It looks as if it has entered a trance while the birds work. Fuller stomachs are the birds' pay. A pest-free body is the tortoise's pay. A map places the islands off the Americas, between the Atlantic and the Pacific. One picture shows the finches clinging to neck and legs, picking ticks. Sharing a house is harder when the roommate is nothing like you. Cliffs high on the New Zealand shore hold one of the oddest pairs. The tuatara, pronounced too-uh-TARR-uh, is a slow reptile that looks like a lizard. Building a nest is usually more effort than it wants. The sooty shearwater is a fast-flying bird. They use one residence, but not at the same hour. Night is the tuatara's active time, so the day is spent in the burrow. While it is home it eats burrow bugs. It also eats the parasites the bird hates. That is its housekeeping. A map of this region marks Asia, Australia, the Pacific, the Indian Ocean, and New Zealand. The bird hunts while the reptile tidies. Night brings the shearwater back, and by then the roommate is out. Dirt is loosened. Droppings draw insects the tuatara likes to eat. The odd couple rarely meets. Home is shared anyway, and so is a partnership both of them welcome.

6North America's tiniest owls are the burrowing owls. They nest under the ground in holes another animal has left. A picture shows that life. They also warn neighbors when a predator comes near. Digging is beyond them. Hiding in a hole is not. Their petite size fits abandoned tunnels once used by prairie dogs or by gopher tortoises. A tiny owl may claim an empty burrow while the former resident has only moved next door. Each animal sounds a warning if danger approaches, and each is safer for it. Forest mice share a home with burrow beetles, and both gain. Fleas in the mouse's fur are a snack for the beetle while the mouse sleeps. An absent mouse gives the beetle time to hunt other bugs through the shared burrow. The beetle eats well. The mouse keeps a home free of pests. The ocean has house-sharers too. Every animal species is playing a survival game. Survival is harder if danger cannot be seen. That is the problem for snapping shrimp on the ocean floor. They are nearly blind, and they dig burrows in the seabed. Moving sand to build the home leaves them open to hungry predators. A partner solves it. The goby fish stays alert. Sharp sight lets it notice trouble quickly. As the shrimp shifts sand, the fish hovers near the antennae and keeps watch. A flick of the tail touches those antennae when danger is close. The shrimp gets the signal to take cover. At night the fish may sleep in the burrow. It may also hide there. The shrimp shares that shelter. For these two sea dwellers, the partnership fits perfectly. One picture shows them building a home together.

7High in America's Rocky Mountains, three lives lock together. A huge grizzly bear, a small red squirrel, and the white bark pine all need one another, and they need the tree's nuts, if their diets are to stay healthy. Pine nuts are a high-calorie food for the bears and for the squirrels. Squirrels eat some nuts at once. They bury others to dig up later. Smell, which is strong in the bears, leads them to those caches. Nuts are eaten. Droppings left after digestion carry some of the seeds away. New trees sprout and grow. Later generations of bears and of red squirrels then find still more nuts. A ride on a hunter is a different bargain. Most small fish stay far from sharks. The remora, a slender fish, does the opposite. It tries to get as close as it can. On top of its head sits a flat disc with ribs. The disc works as a suction cup and locks the remora to a shark's underside. One picture marks that fish with an arrow, stuck to the belly so it can travel and share meals. Swimming alone is possible, and remoras often do it. Sometimes a shark is simply an easier, more efficient ride. Another large animal can serve the same way. Once attached, the remora follows every hunt and every meal. Scraps that escape the jaws become its food. A service goes back the other way. Parasites that have hitched on the host are eaten. The host stays clearer of passengers that do less good.

8The suction disc was not always a disc. It is a dorsal fin that changed. Thousands of years of evolution produced it. Strange headgear is not only a remora trait. Some hermit crabs in the Mediterranean Sea seem to wear an odd hat. The hat is a sea anemone along for the ride. Long tentacles on that anemone carry venom. A hard shell protects the crab from them. Predators meet the anemone instead of an easy crab. The crab's messy eating is the anemone's gain. Scraps hang in the water, and the anemone eats them. Hitchhikers are not only marine. In Africa a small bird, the oxpecker, often rides a hippopotamus rather than spend effort hunting insects alone. Bugs are plucked from the skin and eaten. The bird gets a meal and easy travel. The hippo is picked clean of pests. One picture shows a group of these birds on a hippo's back, doing exactly that work. Bats do more than feed spooky stories. Across much of the world, many plants survive only because a bat visits them. Sweet food is what the plants give back to their furry, winged visitors. Pollinators are the group bats belong to. Pollen is moved from stamens, the male parts of flowers, to pistils, the female parts, while the animal eats. The transfer is inadvertent. It fertilizes the blossoms, so the plant can reproduce and spread. Night is when bats often work. Heads sink deep into a flower's center. Sugary nectar is drunk. Pollen rich in protein is eaten. Sticky pollen often dusts the head after a blossom. It dusts the body too. The next flower receives that pollen. Flowers keep exchanging it. Bats keep a steady supply of nectar and of pollen they find delicious. One picture shows a long-nosed bat at an agave plant loaded with pollen. Where these bats live, agaves depend on them more than on other pollinators. Cacti depend on them too.

9Honeybees, like bats, pollinate actively, and plant reproduction depends on them. Nectar draws a bee into a flower. Flecks of pollen often cover it when it leaves, and the next stop receives that pollen. Hummingbirds work in much the same way. Feathers and bills pick up pollen as the birds dart among blossoms. Some pollinators are offered more than food. A female yucca moth is picky about where eggs go. She prefers to spread her hundreds of eggs across several yucca flowers. The eggs gain a safe home. The flowers gain too, because pollen rides with her from bloom to bloom. One picture shows a honeybee at a dandelion, gathering nectar and leaving pollen on the next bloom it finds. Seeds need their own partners. High in a Brazil nut tree, one picture shows the pods hanging in clusters. A tree or any other plant that cannot move its seeds will grow in only one place. Crowding follows. Light and water become a contest. Survival odds are better if seeds travel far and new plants grow up to make seeds of their own. Animal partners do that dispersing for many plants. In the Amazon rainforest, one remarkable pair is the Brazil nut tree and the agouti, a rodent about the size of a cat. The tree can stand 200 feet tall or more, which is 61 meters. Seedpods are about the size of a grapefruit. They are hard and tough. They may drop 100 feet or more, about 30.5 meters. Striking the soil still may not break them.

10Jaws of the small agouti are strong enough to crack those tough pods. One picture shows that bite. New Brazil nut trees can sprout from droppings the agouti leaves behind. The drop fails. The agouti succeeds. Thick shell yields to its teeth and to the power of its jaws. Some seeds are eaten. Others are buried well away from the parent tree, scattered through the forest. Those buried seeds sprout in time. The long process starts again. Desert mistletoe uses a different carrier, a bird called a phainopepla, pronounced fay-no-PEHP-luh. Seeds sit inside the berries. The bird snacks on them, using its beak to pull skin off the fruit. Undigested seeds leave wherever the droppings fall, and that is how the plant propagates. Without these natural partnerships the world would be very different. Many species would face predators and pests with less defense. Smaller bits of habitat would be more likely to hold them apart from others. Blooming and spreading would be less likely. Food choices would be fewer. Partners would suffer. So would other inhabitants of Earth's ecosystems. Scientists are still learning how these extraordinary relationships work. New ones are still being found. Shallow sunlit water has symbiotic partners. Deep dark caverns have them too. They help each other survive, and they help each other thrive. One closing picture returns to New Zealand. On cliffs above the shore, sooty shearwaters and tuataras keep their unusual shared home.

11Grazing impalas stir insects up, and baboons get an easy meal from that stir. The payback is a warning call if danger comes close. A picture shows that trade. Every symbiotic relationship differs a little. The benefit to each species differs a little too. All of them help hold balance inside their ecosystems. Taken together, their effect on the wider world is a good one. Diversity is promoted. So is sustainability for living things. A better chance then belongs to fish. It belongs to birds, to humans, and to many other organisms. They can survive. They can reproduce. They can live lives that are longer and healthier. Hard words can be read this way. Assume, in this book, means to take on a certain pose or a certain role. To fertilize is to join male and female reproductive cells so a new animal or a new plant can form. A hygienist works as a professional for health and cleanliness. A nurse is one example. A dental assistant is another. Interdependent means depending on one another, as organisms in an ecosystem do. Intimidating means frightening or overwhelming. Mucus is a thick, slimy liquid made in a body. It protects tissues and keeps them wet. Nocturnal describes something active at night rather than in the day. A parasite is a plant or an animal that grows on another and feeds off it. To propagate is to reproduce, creating again and again. A refuge is somewhere safe, somewhere comfortable, or somewhere protected. Symbiotic describes a relationship that benefits different kinds of organisms. Venomous means able to push venom, a poisonous fluid, into another body by striking, biting, or stinging.
